Line 128: avc->last_ps_idx = (s32) gf_bs_read_ue(bs) stores an attacker-controlled Exp-Golomb value; the '< 0' check catches only the sign-flipped half (values >= 2^31), so any value 0..2^31-1 passes with no upper bound. All indexing uses of last_ps_idx occur in callers not shown, so an out-of-bounds impact is not instantiated in this code; it is a latent bounds gap (CWE-129 class) that callers must validate.

If the unshown avc_parse_slice in the real binary in fact guarantees n_state.sps != NULL on every non-negative return, the primary crash is unreachable in that binary; that guarantee is not quotable from the given code and per the analysis rules may not serve as a guard.

verdict.summary: RestoreTensor indexes input(2) (shape_and_slices) with restore_index after validating only input(1)'s element count, and its sole count check `size > restore_index` also admits negative restore_index. An attacker controlling the op's input tensors (shape and content) supplies a short or empty input(2), making `context->input(2).flat<tstring>()(restore_index)` a heap out-of-bounds read; `tensor_name_t.flat<tstring>()(restore_index)` is likewise out-of-bounds for negative restore_index. Impact: crash/DoS and potential heap disclosure via the OOB-read tstring flowing into ParseShapeAndSlice and DebugString error output.

evidence.reason: Primary sink: input(2) is indexed by restore_index with no element-count validation anywhere in the function (the only size check, line 18, constrains input(1)'s NumElements, a different variable). Trigger: restore_slice=true, restore_index=0, input(1) with 1 element, input(2) as a 0-element tensor — attacker-fed op inputs — yields an out-of-bounds heap read of a tstring at index 0 of a zero-length buffer; the OOB bytes then reach .empty()/ParseShapeAndSlice/DebugString.

Missing-check site: this is the only count check in the code; `size` is bound to input(1)'s NumElements (line 17), so no check exists for input(2), and this check under-admits at the minimum bound — with restore_index = -1 and size = 0 the comparison 0 > -1 passes, so the negative index reaches the input(1) indexing on line 23 out-of-bounds.

Secondary sink of the same root class: guarded only by `size > restore_index`, which is correct at the upper bound (restore_index == size is rejected) but never rejects restore_index < 0; restore_index is an int parameter with no quoted non-negativity contract, so restore_index = -1 is within its declared width domain and produces an out-of-bounds read before the tensor buffer.

assumptions: Internal callees not shown (TensorSliceReader::HasTensor/CopySliceData/status, ParseShapeAndSlice, allocate_output, expected_output_dtype, slice_reader_cache) cannot be quoted; their return values that this code consumes are sentinel-checked here (OP_REQUIRES/OP_REQUIRES_OK at lines 39, 44-47, 63-65, and the READER_COPY macro), so no unchecked internal sentinel use was found.

restore_slice and restore_index are parameters of a caller not shown; per the width-domain rule their full declared domains (true; any int) were treated as instantiable, which is what makes the line-60 and line-23 triggers reachable without relying on caller behavior.

file_pattern content is attacker-controlled and is used to open checkpoint files; this is the documented purpose of the restore op, so it is recorded as by-design for this snippet rather than a path-traversal defect.
limitations: The line-23 negative-index read additionally requires the unseen caller to pass a negative restore_index (no caller is shown; upstream TensorFlow passes 0 or a non-negative loop index). It is reported because no quoted contract in this code documents restore_index >= 0, but the line-60 finding stands independently of it with restore_index = 0.

Info disclosure beyond the crash requires the out-of-bounds bytes to parse as a valid shape so that parsed_shape.DebugString() reaches the error output; a failed parse degrades the impact to denial of service, which is already a security impact for the process executing untrusted graphs.
Cosmetic: the dtype-mismatch error message uses expected_output_dtype(0) instead of expected_output_dtype(restore_index), producing a wrong type name in the error text only; no security effect.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability confirmed. The local-entry loop is bounded by the quoted check ptr->size / (ptr->long_offsets ? 16 : 12) < ptr->entry_count, whose divisor exactly matches per-entry consumption (8+8 or 8+4 bytes) and whose operator direction is correct at both boundary values; every bitstream field read in both loops is preceded by an ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE(ptr, N) whose byte count exactly matches the following read and which returns GF_ISOM_INVALID_FILE when the declared box size is exhausted; all allocations are NULL-checked. The absence of an aggregate size check for global_entry_count is neutralized by these per-field guards, and the allocation-heavy unbounded-iteration scenario requires the unshown box parser to accept a declared size exceeding the file.

assumptions: ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE(ptr, N) is a project macro whose body is not shown; per GPAC's documented idiom it returns GF_ISOM_INVALID_FILE when ptr->size < N and otherwise subtracts N. Every field read in this code depends on this semantics.
gf_bs_read_int/u16/u32/u64 are GPAC bitstream readers treated as bounds-safe (return 0 or partial data past end of stream, never out-of-bounds).
ptr->size is set by the box parser (not shown); whether it is validated against actual available file bytes is not quotable from this code.
ptr->local_access_entries / ptr->global_access_entries lists are assumed created in the box constructor (not shown); gf_list_insert return values at lines 20 and 39 are ignored.
limitations: The global-entry loop lacks an aggregate size check analogous to the one guarding entry_count (asymmetric validation). Its safety rests on per-field ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE guards bounding iterations by the declared box size; with an honest declared size the worst case is an early GF_ISOM_INVALID_FILE return plus transient allocations proportional to input size.

Speculative resource-consumption scenario (CWE-400): if the unshown parser accepted a declared box size far exceeding the actual file, global_entry_count up to 2^32-1 could drive up to ~4 billion iterations of small allocations (each NULL-checked, ending in GF_OUT_OF_MEM) and CPU work from a tiny file. The precondition (framework accepting oversized declared boxes) could not be instantiated or quoted from the given code, so this is not scored as a vulnerability in this code.

Unchecked gf_list_insert return values could leak one GF_AfraEntry/GF_GlobalAfraEntry on an OOM path; no use-after-free or double-free is possible (an entry is either in the list or orphaned, never both).

verdict.summary: BD_DecMFFieldVec reads the vector item count nbFields directly from the attacker-controlled BIFS bitstream with up to 31 bits (domain [0, 2^31-1]) and performs no sanity check before using it as the allocation item count in gf_sg_vrml_mf_alloc, as the QP14 length in gf_bifs_dec_qp14_set_length, and as the decode loop bound. A count such as 0x20000000 for an 8-byte SF element type wraps the allocation size computation to a zero/tiny buffer while the loop still decodes nbFields items, producing a massive heap out-of-bounds write; smaller over-limit counts yield attacker-scaled allocation and iteration from a few bytes of stream. The single missing guard is a bounds check on nbFields immediately after it is read.

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: nbFields is read from the attacker-supplied bitstream with an attacker-chosen width of up to 31 bits, giving it the full domain [0, 2^31-1]; no statement in the function validates, clamps, or masks it before its uses.

Sink: the unvalidated attacker-controlled count is passed as the allocation item count; for wide SF element types (e.g. 8-byte SFVec2F) a count of 0x20000000 wraps the 32-bit size computation to a zero-sized allocation that succeeds, and the following loop (line 32) then decodes and writes nbFields items through it, causing a heap out-of-bounds write. The checked error return on the next line only catches allocator error codes, not the wrapped size.

The decode loop is bounded solely by the unvalidated attacker-controlled nbFields (same for the MFNODE loop at line 43, which has no matching allocation at all), enabling both the out-of-bounds item writes into the undersized buffer and attacker-scalable allocation/iteration from a few bytes of input.

assumptions: gf_bs_read_int(bs, n) returns an n-bit field from the stream (standard semantics); no local check exists on the value.
gf_sg_vrml_mf_alloc sizes the buffer as item-count times element width; the exact wrap point depends on the element width of field->fieldType, but any width >= 2 bytes wraps for counts near 2^31.

Internal callees gf_bifs_dec_qp14_set_length, gf_bifs_dec_node, gf_sg_vrml_mf_get_item, gf_bifs_dec_sf_field are not shown; their error sentinels are checked locally, but no callee contract quoted in this code bounds nbFields.
limitations: The qp14 path (line 25) passes the same unvalidated count to a callee whose behavior is not shown, so its specific impact is not characterized; it shares the same missing guard.
The MFNODE loop's per-iteration work is bounded by stream content because a NULL node exits with an error, so the strongest instantiation is the non-MFNODE vector path.
Exact heap-overflow magnitude depends on the element width of the decoded field type; the amplification/oversized-allocation consequence holds for any over-limit count.

verdict.summary: This is the post-2017 hardened ImageMagick EXIF parser. Every memory sink (directory pointer, 12-byte IFD entry reads, format index, value pointer p in both inline and offset paths, multiple-value/fraction reads spanning number_bytes, EXIFMultipleValues buffer writes, and directory-stack pushes) is covered by a quoted bounds check verified in execution order, and the buffer-write length is clamped after every add. The single residual anomaly is that the overflow guard 'if (number_bytes < components) break;' is incomplete on ILP32 builds: for components in [0x24924925, 0x2FFFFFFF] with 8-byte formats the wrapped product still passes, enabling an out-of-bounds read of up to ~4GB given a >=614MB crafted EXIF profile. On the platform as written (64-bit ssize_t/size_t, components <= 2^31-1, product <= 2^34) the multiplication cannot wrap, the guard is never under-admitted, and no trigger is instantiable, so the code is not vulnerable as analyzed.

assumptions: FormatLocaleString has vsnprintf semantics: it writes at most length-1 characters plus a NUL and returns the would-be length; the macro clamp 'if (length >= (MaxTextExtent-1)) length=MaxTextExtent-1;' absorbs the overshoot return, so buffer writes stay in bounds.

AcquireString(property) allocates strlen(property)+MagickPathExtent bytes (standard ImageMagick behavior), which makes 'FormatLocaleString(key,MaxTextExtent,...)' safe despite key being sized from the short property string.

ReadPropertySignedLong/ReadPropertyUnsignedShort/ReadPropertyUnsignedShort read 2 or 4 bytes within the ranges implied by their widths; ReadPropertyByte advances exif and decrements length per byte and never advances past length==0, so the post-scan exif/length pair consistently delimits the remaining buffer.
NewSplayTree with NULL comparators performs pointer comparison of keys, which the q-dedup ('if (GetValueFromSplayTree(exif_resources,q) == q) break;') depends on for loop prevention.
SetImageProperty internally copies and validates the key/value strings; no injection sink exists at that call site in this code.
limitations: 32-bit-only integer wrap (speculative per width-domain analysis): 'number_bytes=(size_t) components*tag_bytes[format];' followed by 'if (number_bytes < components) break;' fails to detect the wrap on ILP32 builds for components in [0x24924925, 0x2FFFFFFF] with tag_bytes 8 (DOUBLE/SRATIONAL/URATIONAL) or [0x55555556, 0x5FFFFFFF] with tag_bytes 4. The wrapped number_bytes then bounds the dir_offset check while EXIFMultipleValues/EXIFMultipleFractions read components*size (~4.9GB) bytes, causing a massive out-of-bounds read (CWE-190 leading to CWE-125) with the read data formatted into stored image properties. Trigger additionally requires an EXIF profile of at least ~614MB and a 32-bit compilation; on 64-bit targets where ssize_t/size_t are 64-bit the product cannot wrap and the code is safe. Precondition not instantiable on the platform as written.

The duplicate-tag check 'for (i=0; i < level; i++) if (directory_stack[i].directory == (exif+tag_offset1)) break;' compares stored directory pointers against exif+tag_offset1 rather than against the actually pushed exif+offset, so it almost never fires. This weakens cycle prevention but has no memory-safety impact: stack depth is capped by 'level < (MaxDirectoryStack-2)' guards (max index 14 of 16) and entry reprocessing is prevented by the splay-tree q dedup.

EXIF_FMT_SINGLE and EXIF_FMT_DOUBLE values are read with ReadPropertySignedLong and formatted as integers, misrepresenting float payloads in output properties; functional misrepresentation only, no memory-safety impact.
SetImageProperty is called with a const cast away from the Image pointer, as the ImageMagick API requires; no defect local to this code.

Requesting a tag whose entry also matches TAG_EXIF_OFFSET/TAG_GPS_OFFSET/TAG_INTEROP_OFFSET ends processing of the current directory early ('break;' at the end of that block), skipping subsequent entries; functional behavior only.

verdict.summary: gen_assignment is an internal compiler helper operating on parser-built AST nodes and codegen register bookkeeping. All branchable values it consumes are explicitly boundary-tested (rhs NULL, missing args, idx sentinel, argument count wrap into the 15-limit array protocol), and unknown node types are rejected by codegen_error default arms. The unchecked tree->cdr chain dereferences rely on the parser's grammar-shaped nodes; no source-level input can produce a malformed node reaching this code, so no trigger is instantiated.

assumptions: The parser and calling codegen (not shown) produce grammar-conformant AST nodes: each NODE_* type carries the fields this code dereferences (tree->car type tag, tree->cdr symbol, CALL nodes with cdr->car method and cdr->cdr argument list).

Internal generator helpers (gen_values, gen_hash, gen_move, gen_setupvar, gen_vmassignment, gen_setxv, genjmp2_0, pop_n, pop, push, cursp, new_sym, attrsym, genop_1/2/3, codegen_error) behave per their mruby codegen semantics; gen_values returns the pushed argument count, at most its limit, or a negative sentinel for variable-length argument lists.
lv_idx returns a positive in-scope local register index or a non-positive sentinel when the local is not in scope, which the else arm routes to upvar handling.
gen_assignment is invoked only from the compiler's own codegen pass with parser-built nodes; it is not an exported or callback entry point.
limitations: The dereferences tree->cdr, tree->cdr->car, tree->cdr->cdr->car and tree->cdr->car->cdr have no NULL checks; if the not-shown parser ever emitted a node whose shape contradicted its type tag, this would be a NULL dereference crash inside the compiler process. No source text can instantiate this since the parser grammar fixes node shapes and rejects invalid input before this function runs.
push() has no visible capacity bound; pathologically nested or wide constructs could exhaust codegen registers. Any such defect would reside in push()/genop helpers not shown in this code.

The 'if (n == 14)' keyword-argument conversion branch appears unreachable because gen_values is called with limit 13 whenever keyword arguments are present; this is dead defensive code with no security effect.

Correctness of the stack balancing in the NODE_CALL keyword/splat packing paths was verified by simulation against the expected mruby opcode register conventions (OP_ARRAY, OP_ARYPUSH, OP_SEND with n=15); the opcode semantics themselves are not shown and are treated as characterizable compiler internals.

verdict.summary: The chunk-offset bounds checks in DecodeChunk perform the addition offsets[i] + header_bytes in unsigned 64-bit before comparing against the buffer size. A crafted offset-table entry near 2^64 (e.g. 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFEC) wraps the sum to a small value, bypassing the check; data_ptr then becomes head - 20 (tiled) or head - 7 (scanline), and the subsequent memcpy calls read up to 20 bytes before the heap buffer. The leaked bytes also flow into exr_image tile offset fields, giving a disclosure path, and can fault if the buffer starts a page. Root cause: unsigned integer overflow (CWE-190) inside the guard; impact: out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) at the memcpy sinks.

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted values: offsets is the file-parsed chunk offset table (producer not shown in this code), a vector of 64-bit unsigned integers whose full domain is attacker-instantiable per the width-domain rule.

Defective guard (tiled path): the sum offsets[tile_idx] + 20 is computed in unsigned 64-bit and wraps to [0,19] when offsets[tile_idx] is in [2^64-20, 2^64-1], so the check passes for offsets far beyond the buffer; this is the only check on offsets in the tiled branch.

Out-of-bounds read sink: with offsets[tile_idx] = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFEC and size >= 1, line 94 passes (sum wraps to 0), line 103 computes data_ptr = head - 20, and this memcpy reads 16 bytes before the heap buffer; the leaked bytes are later stored into exr_image->tiles[tile_idx].offset_x/offset_y at lines 149-152.
Defective guard (scanline path): offsets[y_idx] + 8 wraps to [0,7] for offsets[y_idx] in [2^64-8, 2^64-1], bypassing the check; mirrored instance of the same single defect as line 94.

Out-of-bounds read sink: with offsets[y_idx] = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF9 and size >= 8, the wrapped guard at 184 passes, line 192 computes data_ptr = head - 7, and this memcpy reads 4 bytes before the buffer (line 197 reads 4 more, 3 of them out of bounds).

assumptions: Pointer arithmetic head + offsets[i] with offsets[i] near 2^64 wraps to head - k on two's-complement targets (nominally UB in C++, but the universal behavior of real 64-bit platforms); without wrap the pointer itself would be the fault, still an attacker-induced crash.

offsets entries originate from the EXR chunk offset table parsed elsewhere in the library (producer not shown); per the width-domain rule every uint64 value is treated as instantiable, and no statement in this code narrows it.
limitations: Unchecked calloc result at lines 82-83 is dereferenced at line 87 (exr_image->tiles[tile_idx]); an attacker can force a huge num_tiles (offsets.size()) allocation, so a NULL-deref denial of service is plausible, but the actual allocation failure depends on allocator/overcommit behavior (CWE-476, DoS-grade).

Return values of the not-shown internal callees tinyexr::AllocateImage (lines 87, 174) are consumed without NULL sentinel checks; sizing and failure behavior of that callee are unquotable from this code.

tile_coordinates[0]/[1], read from the file (or OOB memory on the wrapped path), are passed unvalidated into tinyexr::DecodeTiledPixelData (line 135); any misuse of these tile indices inside the not-shown callee cannot be evaluated here.
static_cast<int>(num_tiles) at line 154 truncates a size_t; any impact depends on a consumer not shown.
The non-atomic invalid_data flag under the OpenMP parallel loop is a benign data race with no security effect.

The non-wrap side of both offset guards is correct: offsets = size - 8 (scanline) or size - 20 (tiled) passes with data_size = 0 and every subsequent data_len is rejected, so the boundary defect exists only on the wrap side.

verdict.summary: The bounds checks on attacker-controlled 64-bit chunk offsets, `offsets[tile_idx] + sizeof(int) * 5 > size` (tiled path) and `offsets[y_idx] + sizeof(int) * 2 > size` (scanline path), perform the addition in unsigned 64-bit arithmetic before comparing. An offset near 2^64 (e.g. 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFEC) wraps the sum past 2^64 to a small value, the check passes, and `head + offsets[i]` yields a pointer before the start of the data buffer. The subsequent memcpy calls then read out of bounds (heap underflow read of up to 24 bytes), with the first 8 bytes additionally stored into exr_image tile/image metadata (offset_x/offset_y), giving a crash or information disclosure from a crafted EXR file.

evidence.reason: Defective guard: the addition `offsets[tile_idx] + sizeof(int) * 5` is evaluated in unsigned 64-bit and wraps for offsets in [2^64-20, 2^64-1], so the comparison tests the wrapped sum, not the offset. Trigger: offsets[tile_idx] = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFEC makes the sum 0, `0 > size` is false, and the unbounded offset flows to line 103 (`head + offsets[tile_idx]`) and the line 106 memcpy. Root cause: integer overflow (CWE-190) in the bounds check on attacker-supplied chunk offsets.

Out-of-bounds read sink: with the wrapped offset 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFEC, data_ptr (line 103) = head - 20, so this memcpy reads 16 bytes before the start of the chunk data buffer. The read values reach exr_image->tiles[tile_idx].offset_x/offset_y (lines 149-150), disclosing heap memory to the caller; subsequent memcpy at line 121 reads head-4 as data_len. CWE-125 realized via the CWE-190 guard defect.

Same defective guard in the scanline path: `offsets[y_idx] + sizeof(int) * 2` wraps mod 2^64. Trigger: offsets[y_idx] = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF8 makes the sum 0, the check passes, and line 192 computes data_ptr = head - 8, reaching the memcpy sinks at lines 195 and 197 unguarded.

Out-of-bounds read sink: with offsets[y_idx] = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF8, data_ptr (line 192) = head - 8, so this memcpy and the following one at line 197 (data_ptr + 4 = head - 4) read 8 bytes before the buffer, decoding attacker-influenced out-of-bounds heap memory as line_no/data_len. No statement anywhere on the path bounds offsets[y_idx] before this use.

assumptions: `offsets` elements are raw chunk offsets parsed from the EXR file's offset table by a caller not shown in this code; per the width-domain rule their input surface is the full uint64 domain, and no quoted statement in this code narrows them.

Internals of tinyexr::AllocateImage, DecodeTiledPixelData, DecodePixelData, and ComputeChannelLayout are not shown; their behavior (allocation sizing, NULL tolerance, per-row bounds of line_no/num_lines) is treated as unknown and never used to demote or promote a candidate.

64-bit platform assumed (size_t and tinyexr_uint64 both 64-bit), consistent with the code's own `sizeof(void*) == 8` branch; on a 32-bit build the additions are evaluated in 64-bit and the specific wrap above does not occur.
limitations: Unchecked allocation sentinels: `calloc` (line 82-83) and `AllocateImage` (lines 87, 174) results are never tested; a NULL tiles pointer makes line 87 write through NULL-derived memory. Recorded, not primary: triggering needs an attacker-scale allocation failure while the offsets vector itself already consumes comparable memory (weak amplification, crash-only), and the images NULL dereference lands inside not-shown callees.

Signed-overflow UB at `data_window[2] - data_window[0] + 1`, `data_window[3] + 1`, and `line_no + num_scanline_blocks` was boundary-tested (INT_MAX, INT_MIN, wrap points); every reachable wrap results in num_lines <= 0 or line_no < 0 and is rejected by the quoted checks, and line_no + num_lines provably stays <= data_height, so no out-of-bounds path was instantiated there.

`total_data_len` (size_t product of width*height*channels) can itself wrap for extreme num_channels, but the per-channel loop that would misuse it resides in not-shown AllocateImage; impact chain not instantiated here.
Truncating casts `static_cast<int>(num_blocks)` and `static_cast<int>(num_tiles)` require more than 2^31 offset-table entries (a multi-gigabyte input) and were not instantiated.
The `pixel_types[c] = requested_pixel_types[c]` loop trusts that both arrays were allocated with num_channels entries by the not-shown header parser; an unquotable contract, kept out of the verdict.

verdict.summary: The allocation size bd->startspaces + bd->endspaces + bd->textlen + 1 is computed in 32-bit int arithmetic from three struct fields that this code never validates for range, sign, or overflow. Values within the declared int width (e.g., startspaces = endspaces = 0x7FFFFFFF, textlen = 2) wrap the sum to 1, so alloc returns a 1-byte buffer that passes the == NULL sentinel check; the subsequent vim_memset/mch_memmove calls then copy the full unwrapped (size_t)-cast lengths into the undersized heap buffer, a heap out-of-bounds write (memory corruption). The only quoted guard, the NULL test, covers the allocator's failure sentinel but not the wrapped size.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the allocation size is an unchecked 32-bit int sum of bd->startspaces, bd->endspaces, and bd->textlen, none of which is range- or sign-validated anywhere in this code; with in-width values (0x7FFFFFFF + 0x7FFFFFFF + 2 + 1) the sum wraps to 1, so alloc returns a 1-byte buffer that passes the == NULL check, while the copies below use the raw unwrapped lengths.

First out-of-bounds write of the instantiated trigger: (size_t)bd->startspaces = 0x7FFFFFFF bytes are memset into the 1-byte allocation produced by the wrapped size at line 7; the same holds symmetrically for bd->textlen and bd->endspaces at lines 13 and 15 (a negative field would likewise become a huge size_t).

Second overflow site of the same trigger: the copy length is the raw bd->textlen widened to size_t, not the wrapped allocation size, so the memmove writes textlen bytes into the undersized heap buffer; no guard on any path rechecks the size against the allocation.

assumptions: y_current is non-NULL and y_current->y_array is allocated and dimensioned for y_idx by the unshown caller (op_yank) — no statement in this code asserts it; recorded as an unquoted contract.

bd->textstart points to readable memory spanning at least bd->textlen bytes (producer not shown); the read at line 21 stays within textstart[0..textlen-1] given s starts at textlen and the s > 0 loop condition.
mb_head_off is the standard Vim helper returning a non-negative head-byte offset; its only effect here is that pnew steps back 1 while s steps back 1+head_off, which keeps pnew >= buffer+startspaces.
limitations: y_idx (line 10) indexes y_current->y_array with no local bounds check; classified as a caller-contract value because its producer is the same-trust-domain caller loop and no trust-boundary party can set its content — the contract itself is not quotable here, so this remains an unverified assumption rather than a dismissed vulnerability.

The exclude_trailing_space back-walk (lines 19-25) under-decrements pnew for multibyte whitespace (pnew -= 1 while s -= 1+mb_head_off), which can leave residue bytes of a multibyte space in the yanked text; this is a functional correctness issue, not memory unsafety, since pnew provably never goes below buffer+startspaces.

The exact reachability of ~2^30-scale bd field values depends on the unshown block-prepare producer's geometry; per the width-domain rule the full int domain was treated as instantiable, and no statement of this code bounds the fields below that scale.

verdict.summary: CopySliceData reads a record from a checkpoint sstable, parses it, and passes the parsed proto's data buffer to CopyDataFromTensorSliceToTensorSlice without verifying that the data contains the number of elements demanded by the slice extents and shape. A malicious checkpoint can supply a well-formed record whose data field is short (or empty) while the metadata declares large slice extents, causing an out-of-bounds read of attacker-chosen length during the copy; the read bytes are written into the output tensor, giving heap disclosure or a crash.

evidence.reason: Root cause: this copy call consumes the attacker-controlled data span extracted from the parsed checkpoint record (sts.data().data()) together with attacker-influenced slice extents (slice_s) and shape (tss->shape()), with no validation on any path that the source span has the number of elements the copy will read. Trigger: a crafted checkpoint whose metadata declares a large slice (e.g. 1,000,000 elements) and whose sstable record under the computed key contains a well-formed SavedTensorSlices proto with only 1 (or 0) data values; Get and ParseProtoUnlimited both succeed, then the copy reads 1,000,000 elements from the short buffer, an out-of-bounds read whose contents land in the output tensor.

Origin of the tainted data: the raw record content of the attacker-supplied checkpoint file is loaded into `value` here; after a successful parse it flows to the unvalidated source operand of the copy at lines 40-42.

assumptions: The upper bound of `idx` at sss_[idx] (line 28) is presumed maintained by unshown loading code that populates fname_to_index_ consistently with sss_; CHECK_GE(idx, 0) at line 25 guards only the lower bound and the -1 FindWithDefault sentinel.

checkpoint::TensorProtoData<T> and CopyDataFromTensorSliceToTensorSlice are project-internal callees not shown; per the call-site rule the defect stands even though the faulting access lands inside the copy callee.
The destination buffer `data` is sized by an unshown caller; the instantiated defect is the out-of-bounds read on the source side, which is fully attacker-controlled.
limitations: idx >= sss_.size() (upper-bound OOB on sss_[idx]) cannot be instantiated without an unshown producer inserting a bad mapping; speculative, not counted.
If FindTensorSlice's `details` under-cover the requested `slice`, parts of `data` would remain uninitialized (CWE-908); the coverage guarantee is in unshown code, speculative.
`sts.data()` unset yields an empty source span, which is an instance of the same primary defect, not a separate finding.

verdict.summary: gen_hash miscounts its accumulated pair count 'len' and consumes it to size stack-pop operations (pop_n(len*2+1)/pop_n(len*2)) and OP_HASH/OP_HASHADD pair-count operands. First, the guard arming the flush path, 'if (val && cursp() >= slimit)', is skipped entirely when val is zero, so len grows per tree node without any stack-space bound; then the caller is expected to flush using len, producing pop_n(len*2+1) with len possibly exceeding the 10-bit stack limit (slimit up to INT16_MAX=32767, stack depth only 1024), causing the stack pointer to wrap into negative/attacker-influenced values and corrupting codegen state. Second, slimit is fixed once at entry but the hash switches to GEN_VAL_STACK_MAX after update becomes TRUE, so the interval-bound check uses a stale limit until the next iteration, allowing cursp() to exceed GEN_VAL_STACK_MAX before flushing. No statement in the code bounds len against the actual stack domain or recomputes slimit on the update transition.

evidence.reason: Unbounded accumulation of len: each else-branch tree iteration executes len++ with no check of len, cursp(), or remaining stack space on this arm; the flush guard 'if (val && cursp() >= slimit)' is skipped when val is zero, so len grows without any bound until the caller's final 'pop_n(len*2+1)' consumes it.

Stale/wrong bound: slimit is computed once at entry (either GEN_VAL_STACK_MAX or INT16_MAX) but the hash switches to a GEN_VAL_STACK_MAX layout after update becomes TRUE, so the 'cursp() >= slimit' check can use a limit up to 32767 against a stack whose depth domain is only 1024, allowing cursp() to exceed the real limit before flushing.

assumptions: pop_n(n) subtracts n from the stack pointer and genop_2(s, OP_HASH, cursp(), len) emits len as a pair count in a 16-bit immediate; these are standard mruby codegen helpers whose semantics are universally known per discipline 3.

GEN_VAL_STACK_MAX and GEN_LIT_ARY_MAX are compile-time constants; slimit is therefore attacker-influenced only through cursp(), which is driven by the tree structure built from the parsed source, i.e. attacker data per discipline 4.

val is the caller's requested stack slot or a negative sentinel; the code quotes 'return -1' for the variable-length path and the guard 'if (val && ...)' only treats val as a boolean, so val's negative sentinel and any positive value above 10 bits are both in its declared domain.
limitations: The val == -1 no-ops discussed in STEP 3 candidate 3 were folded into the primary miscount: the same quoted guard 'if (val && cursp() >= slimit)' skipping on the val==0 arm produces both the overflow trigger and the variable-length return.

Confirmed candidates whose impact overlaps the primary (stale slimit, unbounded len) were not double-counted; a single fix (bound len against the actual stack domain and recompute slimit when update flips TRUE) addresses both.

The upstream caller that ultimately consumes the returned len is not shown; however, the defect is already instantiated inside gen_hash itself via pop_n(len*2+1), so the analysis does not depend on any unshown code.

verdict.summary: BM_ParseGlobalQuantizer unregisters the current scenegraph global_qp (freeing it when its refcount reaches 0) without checking whether the freshly parsed node IS that same node, which BIFS USE references make possible; the function then reads and writes through the freed pointer (gf_node_get_tag, ActiveQP->isLocal, node->sgprivate->num_instances), yielding a use-after-free with attacker-influenced memory corruption in the media-parsing process.

evidence.reason: Missing-check site: the node parsed at line 6 can alias codec->scenegraph->global_qp (BIFS USE of a previously DEF'd QP node, state established by this function's own line 24 and refcount set at line 27). gf_node_unregister decrements num_instances and frees the node at zero, so when the existing global_qp's only remaining reference is the scenegraph's, this call frees the very node the function continues to use: no statement in the code compares node with codec->scenegraph->global_qp before this unregister. The required guard is a single comparison (skip or special-case when global_qp == node); the mention sweep shows it appears nowhere.

Taint origin: the node is produced by parsing the attacker-controlled bitstream bs; under the width-domain rule its pointer domain includes any node in the scene, including the current global_qp, and nothing in this code narrows it to a fresh allocation.

Post-free sinks: when node was freed at line 11 (self-referential USE case), gf_node_get_tag(node) at line 16 is a use-after-free read and these statements are use-after-free writes (isLocal = 0 and node->sgprivate->num_instances = 2 write through the dangling node), and line 31 stores the dangling pointer into a command for later application; with heap grooming via prior bitstream commands this is attacker-influenced memory corruption, not a mere crash.

assumptions: gf_node_unregister(node, parent) decrements node->sgprivate->num_instances and frees the node when it reaches 0; this is the GPAC refcount semantics the code itself relies on (it unregisters wrong-tag nodes at line 17 and hardcodes num_instances at line 27).
gf_bifs_dec_node can return an existing scene node when the bitstream encodes a USE of a previously DEF'd node; the aliasing state is otherwise established by this code's own line 24.

The decoded command list is later applied and its entries deleted, releasing the command's node reference (gf_sg_command_del unregisters inf->new_node), leaving the global_qp node with a refcount of 1 held only by the scenegraph between commands.
node->sgprivate is allocated by the node constructor inside gf_bifs_dec_node and is non-NULL for any non-NULL returned node.
limitations: Unchecked allocation results: com = gf_sg_command_new(...) at line 29 and inf = gf_sg_command_field_new(com) at line 30 are not NULL-checked, so inf->new_node = node at line 31 would dereference NULL on allocation failure; this trigger requires an environment allocation failure the attacker cannot reliably induce, so it is recorded as a robustness issue, not a vulnerability.
node->sgprivate is dereferenced at line 27 without a local NULL check; NULL here would require the unshown node constructor to fail, an unquotable contract, so this candidate is speculative.

The direct refcount assignment num_instances = 2 also mis-accounts references in non-freeing alias cases (references held by other parents or commands are silently dropped), which can produce premature frees later in the command-application pipeline not shown here; recorded as a secondary consequence of the same root cause.

verdict.summary: mrb_vm_exec executes instruction-stream operands (register indices a/b, pool/syms/rep indices, jump offsets) without any bounds validation against irep->nregs/slen/plen/ilen. An attacker who supplies the bytecode (the irep this exported executor consumes) can set an 8/16-bit register operand up to 255/65535 against a small nregs, making e.g. `regs[a] = regs[b];` an out-of-bounds 16-byte heap read and write on the VM stack; syms[b]/pool[b] reads and unchecked jump targets add OOB read and wild instruction fetch. No statement in the code bounds these values; the only bounds-shaped statements (mrb_stack_extend sized from nregs, the NDEBUG-compiled-out mrb_assert on the break-restore path, the UPVAR MRB_ENV_LEN checks) never constrain the operands reaching the sinks.

evidence.reason: Primary sink: register operands a and b are fetched from the bytecode and used to index the frame stack (regs = mrb->c->ci->stack, sized from irep->nregs) with no check of a or b against irep->nregs anywhere in the function. An attacker-supplied irep with OP_MOVE operands a=b=255 and nregs=4 makes this statement a 16-byte out-of-bounds read and write on the heap VM stack (memory corruption).

evidence.snippet: mrb_vm_exec(mrb_state *mrb, const struct RProc *proc, const mrb_code *pc)
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted data: proc->body.irep (line 4) and its pool/syms/iseq arrays carry the parsed bytecode from a not-shown producer with no documented or enforced precondition in this code; per the width-domain rule its operands (a: uint32_t, b/c: uint16_t, fetched 8/16-bit) are attacker-instantiable and flow unchecked into the register, pool, symbol, rep, and jump sinks.

assumptions: FETCH/CASE/NEXT/INIT_DISPATCH macros, ARGUMENT_NORMALIZE, uvenv, catch_handler_find, prepare_missing, cipush/cipop and mrb_stack_extend are not shown; standard semantics were assumed (mrb_stack_extend allocates at least the requested slots) and the verdict does not rest on their internals.

Operand widths (8-bit, widened to 16-bit by OP_EXT1/2/3) are inferred from the not-shown fetch macros; even the narrowest 8-bit domain (0-255) exceeds any small irep->nregs, so the trigger does not depend on the wider encodings.
mrb_assert is compiled out under NDEBUG, so it was not treated as a guard in release builds.
limitations: mruby's documented project stance is that irep bytecode must come from the trusted mruby compiler and mrb_load_irep performs no validation; under a strictly trusted-bytecode deployment the trigger is not instantiable by an external party. That contract is not quoted or enforced anywhere in the given code, so it cannot serve as a guard here, but it is the standard caveat for this interpreter.

OP_ARGARY/OP_BLKPUSH contain an off-by-one: the guard `MRB_ENV_LEN(e) <= m1+r+m2+1` omits kd, so with kd=1 and MRB_ENV_LEN(e) == m1+r+m2+2 the read stack[m1+r+m2+1] is one past the env; triggerable only with compiler/operand inconsistency and subsumed by the primary defect under the attacker-irep model.

`blk` in the OP_SEND/OP_SUPER paths is expected to be set by the not-shown ARGUMENT_NORMALIZE macro; if it were not, an uninitialized value would reach mrb_proc_p — could not be verified from the given code and is recorded as an assumption, not a finding.

verdict.summary: The Gather kernel validates only the sign of the attacker-supplied positions/indices (rejecting negatives) but never checks their upper bound against the input tensor's dimension along the gather axis, then passes the raw indices into the gather operation, which uses them as element indices into the input buffer; any positive index >= dims[axis] (e.g. 2000000000 for a 10-element axis) passes the only guard and induces an out-of-bounds read at an attacker-chosen scaled offset, whose contents are written to the readable output tensor (disclosure) or crash the process.

evidence.snippet:
optimized_ops::Gather(op_params, GetTensorShape(input),
                        GetTensorData<InputT>(input), GetTensorShape(positions),
                        GetTensorData<PositionsT>(positions),
                        GetTensorShape(output), GetTensorData<InputT>(output));
evidence.reason: Root cause: this call site passes the attacker-controlled positions tensor (gather indices) into an indexing operation with no upper-bound validation on any path in this code; the only guards (lines 8 and 13) enforce non-negativity alone. Trigger: a positions value of 2000000000 (within the int32 PositionsT width domain) with a 10-element axis passes the `< 0` check and TF_LITE_ENSURE, then is used as an element index into the input buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read whose contents land in the readable output tensor.

Origin of the tainted indices: the positions tensor data (attacker-controlled across the model/inference trust boundary) enters here; its full declared-width domain is instantiable, and the subsequent loop only constrains its lower bound (indexes[i] < 0), leaving positive out-of-range indices free to reach the gather sink.

assumptions: PositionsT is a signed integer type (e.g. int32/int64), implied by the `indexes[i] < 0` test; positive values up to the type maximum pass that test.

optimized_ops::Gather uses the positions values as element indices along the gather axis into the input tensor, which is the defining (characterizable) semantics of the gather operation; no other behavior of this unshown internal callee is relied upon.
This function is the TFLite Gather Eval kernel; model data and runtime inference tensors cross a trust boundary, so positions contents and params are attacker-data per the width-domain rule.
limitations: Secondary candidate: `op_params.axis = params.axis;` (line 16) passes the model-supplied axis and batch_dims unvalidated into the same call; if axis is outside the input rank the callee's dimension access is also out of domain. Its harm plays out entirely inside the unshown callee reading dims[axis], and axis is often validated in a Prepare phase not given, so it does not drive the verdict or the CWE.

`num_indices = positions->bytes / sizeof(PositionsT)` floors when bytes is not a multiple of the element size; this under-counts the validation loop but is benign relative to the primary defect (the upper bound is missing for every index regardless).
No OOB write was simulated: gather writes to output are bounded by the output shape, so the impact is out-of-bounds read (disclosure/crash), not corruption.

verdict.summary: handle_PORT parses the client-supplied PORT argument with sscanf("%d,...") into unchecked signed ints and formats them with an unbounded sprintf into a 16-byte stack buffer (char addr[INET_ADDRSTRLEN]). Any component outside [0,255] (e.g. 2147483647, or negative values) overflows addr with attacker-influenced bytes; the only validation, inet_aton(), runs after the write and cannot protect it. The sscanf return is also never checked, so partial arguments leave a..f uninitialized.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds stack write: addr is char[INET_ADDRSTRLEN] (16 bytes) but a,b,c,d are unvalidated signed ints from the client's PORT command; e.g. 'PORT 2147483647,2147483647,2147483647,2147483647,1,1' makes sprintf write 44 bytes into the 16-byte buffer. No range check, clamp, mask, snprintf bound, or sscanf return check exists anywhere before this sink; the inet_aton check at line 18 executes only after the overflow.

Origin of the tainted values: %d accepts any signed int (full int width, including negatives) from the attacker-controlled string, and the conversion count is discarded, so partial arguments leave the remaining variables uninitialized before line 15 consumes them.

assumptions: str is a NUL-terminated C string supplied by the FTP command dispatcher; its content is fully client-controlled (network trust boundary).
ctrl fields (sd, data_sd, data_address, data_port) are set/allocated elsewhere; data_address is assumed at least sizeof(addr)+1 since strlcpy sizes it safely regardless.
send_msg, ERR, DBG, uev_io_stop, close behave per their standard/documented semantics.
limitations: ctrl->data_port = e * 256 + f (line 25) is unvalidated and can wrap or be out of range (also enables classic FTP-bounce/SSRF to an attacker-chosen host:port), but the connect() consuming data_address/data_port is not in this code, so that impact is not instantiated here.
Uninitialized a..f from a partial sscanf (e.g. 'PORT 1,2,3') cause undefined behavior at the same sprintf sink; folded into the primary finding rather than counted as an independent defect.
Robustness only: none observed beyond the primary memory-corruption finding.

parse_errors: no valid JSON verdict found in output

verdict.summary: This op-kernel handler consumes attacker-controlled tensor data (indices, values, shape, reduction axes), but the only memory-write sink, out_flat(idx) = reduced_val(), is directly preceded by a quoted bounds guard (OP_REQUIRES(ctx, idx >= 0 && idx < out_flat.size(), ...)) that edge-tests correctly at both bounds (negative/wrapped indices rejected by idx >= 0; one-past-the-limit rejected by idx < out_flat.size()), and the coordinate/stride size mismatch is preempted by a quoted OP_REQUIRES on g.group().size() == output_strides.size() before the flat index is computed. All remaining candidates depend on the behavior of internal callees not shown in this code (ValidateInputs, SparseTensorReduceHelper, TensorShape, SparseTensor::Create, Reorder), whose contracts are unquotable here and therefore cannot instantiate a trigger under the analysis rules.

assumptions: ValidateInputs (line 7) is a project-internal callee not shown; it is assumed to validate shape_t and reduction_axes_t (dtype, non-negativity, axis range), but no enforcement is quotable in the given code.

SparseTensorReduceHelper (line 18) is not shown; reduction.group_by_dims, reorder_dims, and reduced_shape are assumed internally consistent (dims within the tensor rank; reduced_shape product matching the strides mapping), an unquotable contract.
SparseTensor::Create and sp.Reorder/sp.group are not shown; index-content validation and group machinery bounds are assumed performed there.
Op::template Run<T> is not shown; it is assumed to accumulate only within the scalar temp reduced_val and the group's values view.
TensorShape(shape_vec) behavior on negative or zero entries is not shown; a CHECK-fail DoS on invalid shape values is possible in that callee but is not instantiated by any statement of this code.
limitations: shape_vec(reduction.group_by_dims[d + 1]) would read out of bounds if SparseTensorReduceHelper emitted a dimension index outside shape_vec's range; this requires an unshown callee to produce an out-of-domain value, so it is speculative, not a vulnerability in this code.

Signed int64 overflow in output_strides[d] = output_strides[d+1] * shape_vec(...) and in idx += coords[i] * strides[i] is undefined behavior for extreme attacker shapes, but the consumed result idx is bounds-checked against [0, out_flat.size()) before the only write, so no out-of-domain memory access is reachable.

A CHECK-fail (process abort) inside TensorShape(shape_vec) on negative shape entries would be a denial of service triggered by the graph submitter; the abort occurs inside a callee not shown and its trigger is not instantiated by a quoted statement of this code.

output_strides.size() - 2 underflows in size_t arithmetic when group_by_dims.size() == 1; the narrowed int value (-2) causes the loop to be skipped, so no out-of-range access occurs, but the narrowing conversion is implementation-defined in principle.

verdict.summary: Prepare consumes model-controlled tensor shapes and SVDF options without adequate validation. It reads input/weights_feature/weights_time dimension values via dims->data[i] without ever checking those tensors have that many dimensions (only state is rank-checked at line 47), causing a heap out-of-bounds read with a 0- or 1-dimensional tensor from a malicious .tflite model (CWE-125). Separately, rank is only checked with 'rank != 0' instead of 'rank >= 1', so a negative rank (e.g. -1) passes all checks, makes num_units negative, and the negative dimension is written into the size array and passed to context->ResizeTensor (CWE-20), yielding a crash/DoS of the process loading the model and unvalidated negative values entering allocation sizing.

evidence.snippet:
const int batch_size = input->dims->data[0];
  const int num_filters = weights_feature->dims->data[0];
evidence.reason: Dimension values are read from model-controlled tensors without any check that the tensors have any dimensions; for a 0-dimensional (scalar) input or weights_feature, dims->data[0] reads past the end of the heap-allocated TfLiteIntArray (out-of-bounds read). The only dimensionality check in the code, 'TF_LITE_ENSURE_EQ(context, NumDimensions(state), 2);' at line 47, applies to state only and runs after these reads. Trigger: malicious model declaring a rank-0 input tensor.

data[1] is read from weights_time, input, and weights_feature with no check that dims->size >= 2 anywhere in the code; a malicious model declaring any of these tensors as 1-dimensional makes each read a heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125), the primary defect.

The only validation of the model-controlled SVDF rank uses '!=' instead of '>= 1', under-admitting every negative value. With rank = -1 and num_filters = 8, line 28 passes (8 % -1 == 0) and line 29 computes num_units = -8; no positivity check exists for rank, num_units, batch_size, or num_filters on any path. This is the missing lower-bound guard (CWE-20).

Sink of the negative-rank taint: the attacker-derived negative num_units (and an unvalidated possibly-negative batch_size) is placed into the resize size array and passed to context->ResizeTensor at lines 56-57, handing unvalidated negative dimensions to the interpreter's allocation path, causing a CHECK-fail/DoS in the process loading the untrusted model.

assumptions: node->builtin_data and node->user_data (lines 2-4) are assumed non-NULL as provided by the framework's op registration/init path; this code performs no local check, so a NULL would crash at params->rank (unquoted contract).
GetInputSafe/GetOutputSafe/GetTemporarySafe are relied on per documented TFLite semantics: they validate tensor existence/index, not dimensionality or shape values.
Returns of TfLiteIntArrayCreate/TfLiteIntArrayCopy are consumed without sentinel checks; failure requires allocation failure the attacker cannot induce.
limitations: Signed integer overflow in 'memory_size * num_filters' (line 50) can wrap and weaken the state-size consistency check (CWE-190), but exploitation of the resulting inconsistent state happens in Eval, which is not shown; impact chain not instantiated here.

The int8 branch dereferences input_params->scale->data[0] and sibling quantization pointers (bottom of function) without NULL checks; a model declaring int8 tensors without quantization metadata would produce a NULL dereference, but this depends on the unshown model-to-tensor conversion behavior and is recorded as a secondary risk, not a primary finding.

The exact failure mode of context->ResizeTensor with negative dimensions (CHECK-fail DoS vs. further size miscomputation) is the only characterizable-callee dependency in the impact chain for the CWE-20 finding; either way an attacker-controlled invalid size value crosses unvalidated into allocation logic.

verdict.summary: The oversized-output guard in IsConstantFoldable computes out_shape.num_elements() * DataTypeSize(n->output_type(i)) in 64-bit arithmetic with no overflow check; an attacker-supplied fully-defined shape (e.g. [2^61] with DT_DOUBLE) makes the product wrap to 0, so the comparison against max_constant_size_in_bytes fails open and a node producing an astronomically large tensor is declared constant-foldable, defeating the pass's only bound on attacker-amplified resource consumption when folding untrusted graphs.

evidence.reason: Integer overflow at the size-limit sink. num_elements() (int64_t) multiplied by DataTypeSize (size_t) wraps modulo 2^64: a fully-defined attacker-derived output shape of [2^61] elements with dtype DT_DOUBLE (size 8) yields 2^61 * 8 = 2^64 ≡ 0, so '0 > max_constant_size_in_bytes' is false and the oversized-output skip (return false) is never taken; the node falls through to 'return true' and is constant-folded despite exceeding the byte limit. This comparison is the sole guard (comment: 'We can skip the node if an output is known to be oversized'), no overflow check, clamp, division reformulation, or re-check exists on any path, enabling a tiny untrusted GraphDef to induce unbounded tensor materialization in the optimizing process.

assumptions: MaybeReplaceShapeOp (line 13) returns false for the attacker-chosen non-shape node; it is an unshown internal predicate whose false (miss) result is its in-domain failure sentinel, and its return is sentinel-checked here.

shape_map is populated by the surrounding optimization pass from shape inference over the attacker-supplied graph, so the dimension values it stores are attacker-derived content under the width-domain rule.
The constant-folding driver materializes output tensors for nodes this function accepts; that consumer is not shown but is the sole reason the max_constant_size_in_bytes bound exists.
limitations: n->output_type(i) at line 29 is indexed with i bounded only by shape_it->second.size() (line 26), not by the node's output count; an out-of-bounds read would require the unshown shape_map producer to store more shapes than the node has outputs, an arity contract of the internal pass rather than attacker-instantiable content, so it is not promoted to a primary finding.
If shape_map == nullptr (line 22), the oversized-output check is skipped entirely; this is a caller-configuration condition not instantiable by the attacker in this code.

num_elements() itself can wrap inside PartialTensorShape for products of dimensions exceeding int64 range (e.g. dims [2^62, 4]); this is the same defect class feeding the same sink and is covered by the primary finding.
n->DebugString() at the VLOG statement writes attacker-influenced node text into logs; treated as low-value log-content noise, not a primary vulnerability.

verdict.summary: finderrfunc is a static internal LuaJIT stack-walking routine. All pointer dereferences are guarded in execution order: the outer loop condition 'while (frame > bot && cf)' bounds the frame pointer above the stack base (making even the (frame-1) read in FRAME_CONT in-bounds) and checks cf for NULL before each iteration, and the inner loop checks 'if (cf == NULL) return 0;' after unwinding cf. All arithmetic inputs (ftsz, cframe_nres, errfunc indices) are VM-maintained frame metadata produced by the interpreter's own frame-push/call machinery, not by any value crossing a trust boundary into this function's parameters; no guest-controlled raw offset, size, or index reaches a sink here. No attacker-data input, no unguarded sink, no instantiated trigger.

assumptions: The frame chain (L->stack, L->base, L->cframe, ftsz, cframe_nres, cframe_errfunc) is maintained consistently by the interpreter's frame-push/call code elsewhere in the same VM; this function reads but never writes that metadata, and no statement in this snippet derives a pointer or size from raw guest-controlled data.
Macros such as frame_prevl/frame_prevd/restorestack/savestack are standard LuaJIT inline accessors with their usual semantics (stack-relative arithmetic).
limitations: Candidate (frame-1)->u32.lo in FRAME_CONT: dismissed only because the guard 'while (frame > bot && cf)' provably keeps frame-1 >= bot at the minimum passing boundary (frame == bot+1); this is a quoted, in-order guard, not an assumption.

A corrupted frame chain or inconsistent cframe_nres/ftsz (e.g., from a separate memory-corruption bug elsewhere in the VM) could make this walker read out of bounds; producing such corruption requires a defect outside the given code and is therefore speculative here.
lua_assert(0) in the default arm is compiled out in release builds; the following 'return 0' keeps the path fail-closed, so this has no security effect.

verdict.summary: ParseEquation never validates that the parsed equation produced at least one input operand. num_inputs = input_str.size() (line 16) can be 0, leaving input_label_counts resized to 0 (line 27); the label_types loop then evaluates `num_inputs == 1` (false for 0) and indexes (*input_label_counts)[0] and [1] (lines 53-54) on the empty vector, an out-of-bounds read (null-deref crash for a fresh empty vector; stale/uninitialized read if the out-param retained a prior buffer) triggered by attacker-controlled equation content.

evidence.reason: Sink: operator[] indexes element 0 (and 1) of input_label_counts, which was resized to num_inputs (line 27). The only conditional on num_inputs is the equality `num_inputs == 1`, which is false when num_inputs == 0, so execution falls through to an out-of-bounds read of an empty vector. No emptiness or minimum-count check on the parse result exists anywhere on any path.

Taint origin: num_inputs is taken directly from the unvalidated output of ParseEinsumEquation (line 11) with no check that at least one input operand was parsed; 0 is within the full domain of the callee-produced size, and this unchecked value drives the resize(0) that makes the line 53-54 indexing out of bounds.

assumptions: MapToLabels (not shown) is assumed to assign consecutive non-negative labels < num_labels and to push kEllipsisLabel (an out-of-range constant) for ellipsis; the branches `if (label != kEllipsisLabel)` at lines 33/42 are the only guards those index sinks rely on. Per discipline 3 this unshown-callee behavior can neither create nor excuse a trigger.
GetDimensionType (not shown) is assumed to return a valid DimensionType; its result is stored into a vector sized num_labels, so no memory-safety consequence in this code.
kEllipsisLabel is an unshown constant; every indexing path with that value is excluded by the quoted `!=` branches.
limitations: The num_inputs == 0 trigger requires the unshown ParseEinsumEquation to return an empty input operand vector; if the actual parser in the full project always emits at least one (possibly empty) operand string, the trigger is unreachable there. Judged solely on the given code per the width-domain rule, no quoted statement forbids it.
Impact is an out-of-bounds read / crash (denial of service) rather than memory corruption; no out-of-bounds write is reachable in the shown code.
If the equation produced more than two inputs, indices [0] and [1] at lines 53-54 remain in range, so no additional defect arises.

verdict.summary: BM_ParseGlobalQuantizer releases the parsed node twice with gf_node_unregister (lines 32-33) where its own comment requires registering it twice for the two owners (scenegraph global_qp and the command field). For an attacker-instantiated USE node with num_instances == 1, the first unregister frees the node, the second unregister operates on freed memory (UAF write/double free), and the subsequently stored pointers (codec->ActiveQP, scenegraph->global_qp, inf->new_node) dangle and are dereferenced later, giving heap memory corruption from a crafted BIFS bitstream.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the comment requires acquiring two references (one for the command, one for the scenegraph global_qp that both store the node pointer), but the code calls gf_node_unregister twice instead. The code itself establishes at lines 20-21 that decrementing num_instances to 0 via gf_node_unregister frees the node. Trigger: attacker sends a BIFS GlobalQuantizer command whose node is a USE of an in-scene QuantizationParameter with num_instances == 1; the first unregister frees the node and the second unregister decrements and dispatches destruction on freed memory (use-after-free write), while the two owners still hold the pointer.

Use after release: after the double gf_node_unregister freed the node (when its reference count was 1 or 2), the command field stores the dangling pointer, which is dereferenced when the command list is applied; codec->ActiveQP and codec->scenegraph->global_qp (set at lines 27-29) dangle identically and are consumed by subsequent BIFS decoding, completing the memory-corruption impact chain.

Origin of the tainted value: the node is decoded from the attacker-controlled bitstream and can be either a freshly created node (num_instances == 0) or a USE of an existing scene node (num_instances >= 1, as the code's own comment at line 18 states), letting the attacker pick the state that triggers the premature free at lines 32-33.

assumptions: gf_node_unregister decrements num_instances and destroys the node when the count reaches 0; this is derived from the given code itself, where lines 20-21 set num_instances to 1 before unregistering specifically so that a node with count 0 gets destroyed on the error path.

num_instances is treated as an unsigned counter; in the fresh-node path (count 0) the two unregisters wrap it to 0xFFFFFFFE, corrupting the reference count (leak), while the USE-node path (count 1 or 2) frees the node in-function, which is the instantiated trigger.
limitations: Return values of gf_sg_command_new and gf_sg_command_field_new (lines 35-36) are not checked for NULL, but failure requires allocation failure that the attacker cannot directly induce; robustness issue only.

The non-QP USE-node branch (lines 19-22, line 23) returns without unregistering a node gf_bifs_dec_node may have referenced, which at worst leaks one reference; this matches the branch's own documented intent and is not a memory-safety defect.

verdict.summary: The Gather kernel wrapper passes attacker-controlled positions indices (runtime tensor data whose values index into the input tensor) to optimized_ops::Gather without any local bounds validation against the input tensor's dimensions, and unconditionally returns kTfLiteOk, discarding any error status from the callee. An attacker supplying an out-of-range index in the positions tensor triggers either an out-of-bounds memory access inside the gather operation or, if the callee detects the error, a fail-open where the wrapper converts the failure into a success return and the runtime consumes uninitialized or incorrect output data.

evidence.reason: The call to optimized_ops::Gather passes raw attacker-derived index data from the positions tensor into an indexing operation with no bounds validation anywhere in this function, and the return value of the callee is discarded, followed by an unconditional `return kTfLiteOk` that reports success regardless of the operation's actual outcome. The trigger is an out-of-range positions value (e.g., 999999 when the input dimension along the gather axis is 10), which is within the declared width domain of PositionsT and reaches the sink unguarded.

Origin of the tainted data: the positions tensor's raw data pointer, containing attacker-controlled index values whose full domain is the declared width of PositionsT, is extracted here and passed directly into the gather operation without any validation against the input tensor's shape.

assumptions: The internal behavior of optimized_ops::Gather is not shown; per discipline 3 its validation behavior cannot serve as a guard for this code, and per the width-domain rule the positions values' input surface is the full domain of PositionsT.
params.axis and params.batch_dims are treated as model-file-derived attacker-data; no quoted statement in this code constrains them to the input tensor's rank or any valid range.
The callee may return void or TfLiteStatus; in either case, this wrapper's unconditional kTfLiteOk return cannot propagate any error condition to the caller.
limitations: Whether the out-of-bounds access occurs inside the callee (no callee-side bounds checking) or the error is merely swallowed (callee-side checking with discarded return value) depends on the not-shown implementation of optimized_ops::Gather; both paths constitute a vulnerability at this call site per discipline 3.

The exact memory corruption impact (how far out of bounds the read reaches) depends on the callee's index arithmetic, which is not shown; the defect is the missing validation at this function's entry point.

verdict.summary: Byte-order-confused bounds check on hdr->rtcp_common.length (read as native integer without pj_ntohs) is ineffective on little-endian machines, allowing network-length=1 packets to pass. This causes an integer underflow in rpsi_len = (pj_ntohs(...)-2)*4, producing a huge unsigned value that wraps through all subsequent bounds checks (rpsi_len+12, rpsi_len*8), resulting in pj_strset being called with a massive string length (~536 million bytes on 32-bit truncation) pointing past the actual RTCP buffer. Any subsequent use of the output rpsi->rpsi string by the caller is a massive out-of-bounds read, potentially disclosing memory contents or crashing the process.

evidence.reason: Root cause: this check reads the network-byte-order 16-bit length field as a native integer WITHOUT pj_ntohs conversion. On little-endian machines, a network value of N=1 (bytes 00 01) reads as native 0x0100=256, so 256<3 is false and the check passes. The check is ineffective, allowing small N values to reach the underflow on line 24.

Defective statement: when the network-order length N=1 (which passes the defective check on line 18), pj_ntohs correctly yields 1, and (1-2)*4 = -4, which wraps to 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFC when assigned to unsigned pj_size_t rpsi_len. This huge value then wraps through the check on line 25 (rpsi_len+12 wraps to 8, so length<8 trivially passes) and the check on line 37 (rpsi_len*8 wraps to huge value, not less than 16+padlen), reaching the sink at line 45 where pj_strset sets a massive string length.

assumptions: pjmedia_rtcp_fb_rpsi.rpsi_bit_len is assumed to be at least pj_uint32_t width; with 16-bit truncation the resulting string length is ~8KB, still far exceeding a small RTCP buffer
The code runs on a little-endian machine (x86, ARM LE) where the byte-order confusion manifests; on big-endian the line 18 check works correctly
pj_strset only sets ptr and slen fields without memory access; the actual OOB read occurs when the caller subsequently uses the rpsi->rpsi string
limitations: The direct OOB read impact requires the caller of pjmedia_rtcp_fb_parse_rpsi to subsequently use the returned rpsi->rpsi string (e.g., pj_strlen, pj_strcpy, comparison), which is not shown in this code; however, the defective validation and the setting of the massive length are fully instantiated within this function
The 1-byte OOB read at offset 12 (padlen = *p++) when length exactly equals 12 is a secondary consequence of the same underflow and is not separately reported

verdict.summary: LSTMBlockCell Compute performs shape validation on every input tensor except the peephole weights wci, wcf, and wco. When use_peephole_ is true, the functor call passes these tensors as vec<T>() views with no check that each holds cell_size elements, so an attacker-supplied undersized (e.g., empty) wci/wcf/wco tensor causes an out-of-bounds heap read of up to cell_size elements inside the LSTM fprop functor, with the leaked values influencing attacker-retrievable gate outputs (i/f/o).

evidence.snippet:
h_prev_tensor->matrix<T>(), w_tensor->matrix<T>(), wci_tensor->vec<T>(),
        wcf_tensor->vec<T>(), wco_tensor->vec<T>(), b_tensor->vec<T>(),
evidence.reason: Sink: the functor call consumes wci/wcf/wco tensors whose shapes were never validated anywhere in this function, although every other tensor is checked with OP_REQUIRES. With use_peephole_ true and wci of size 0 while cell_size is 8 (all quoted shape checks still pass), the functor reads wci[i] for i in [0,8) past an empty buffer — an out-of-bounds heap read (CWE-125) whose values flow into attacker-retrievable outputs.

Origin of the tainted value: the attacker-supplied wci tensor enters here (likewise wcf at line 18, wco at line 21), and the only check performed is on fetch success — no OP_REQUIRES on its shape follows anywhere, unlike for cs_prev, h_prev, w, and b.

assumptions: The functor functor::LSTMBlockCellFprop is characterized per discipline 3 as a well-known TensorFlow kernel that indexes wci/wcf/wco per cell index [0, cell_size) when use_peephole_ is true; the OOB read lands inside the callee but the unvalidated call site in this code is the defect.
Tensor::vec<T>() performs only DCHECK-rank validation in release builds and sizes the view from NumElements(), so it does not enforce a minimum length of cell_size.
use_peephole_, forget_bias_, cell_clip_ are attacker-set op attributes (session user), typical of TF op kernels.
limitations: The check at line 35 (cs_prev_tensor->dim_size(1) == cell_size) is tautological because cell_size is defined from that same dim at line 28; it is redundant but not a security defect since cs_prev is the source of the value.

Potential int64 overflow in input_size + cell_size and cell_size * 4 (lines 49, 53, 58) is speculative: such dimensions could not be materialized in the already-allocated x and cs_prev input tensors, so the trigger values are not instantiable.
If use_peephole_ is false, the functor does not read the peephole weights, so the trigger requires the attacker to set that attribute — an attacker-controlled op attribute, hence within scope.
Passing a multi-dimensional wci (rank confusion) may additionally cause a CHECK failure crash in vec<T>() in debug builds; subsumed by the primary missing-validation defect.

verdict.summary: Array.prototype.splice snapshots the array length before converting the start and deleteCount arguments, but those conversions (njs_value_to_integer, ECMA-262 ToPrimitive) can invoke an attacker-supplied valueOf that shrinks the live fast array. delete and delta are then clamped against the stale snapshot (delete = min(max(delete,0), length - start); length+delta > NJS_MAX_LENGTH checks only the stale upper bound), so at 'array->length += delta' the live length (0) plus a negative delta wraps the unsigned length field to ~2^32-3 while the data allocation holds 3 elements. Any subsequent element access by the script (index < huge length passes the fast-array bounds check) becomes an out-of-bounds read and an out-of-bounds write of a 16-byte njs_value_t, i.e. attacker-driven heap memory corruption.

evidence.reason: Sink: delta is computed (line 45) from delete clamped against the stale length snapshot taken at line 16, while array->length here is the live length that attacker JS (valueOf invoked by the argument conversions at lines 21/37) may have shrunk. With live array->length = 0 and delta = -3 (a = [1,2,3]; a.splice({valueOf(){a.length = 0; return 0;}})), 0 + (-3) wraps the unsigned length field to ~4294967293 (or 2^64-3) against a 3-element allocation. No statement on any path revalidates delta against the live length: line 47 checks only the stale 'length + delta' upper bound, and line 94 re-tests only the fast-array flag. The corrupted length field turns the script's next a[i] read/write into an out-of-bounds heap access.

Origin of the tainted state: this conversion implements ECMA-262 ToPrimitive/ToInteger and executes an attacker-supplied valueOf on the start argument, after 'length' was already read at line 16. The valueOf can shrink or otherwise mutate the array (a.length = 0), after which every length-derived bound in the function (lines 26, 32, 42, 45, 47) is stale. The equivalent window exists at line 37 for the deleteCount argument. The missing re-read of this's length after these calls is the precondition whose absence makes the line 115 wrap reachable.

assumptions: njs_value_to_integer implements ECMA-262 ToInteger via ToPrimitive and therefore invokes attacker-supplied valueOf/toString on object arguments; this is standard, universally known ES conversion semantics.

Setting a smaller length on an njs fast array (a.length = 0) retains the fast_array flag and the existing data allocation (truncate-in-place), so the second njs_is_fast_array(this) check at line 94 still passes after the mutation.
The internal njs_array_copy_within treats a negative count (array->length - (start + delete) = -3 here) as zero iterations and returns NJS_OK; its body is not shown.

njs_object_length initializes *length on a NJS_DECLINED result (only NJS_ERROR is checked at line 17); if it does not, 'length' at line 16 would be uninitialized stack data consumed by the later arithmetic.
njs_array_t.length is an unsigned field (uint32_t or uint64_t depending on njs version); 'array->length += delta' with a negative int64 delta therefore wraps rather than saturates.
limitations: The out-of-bounds access itself materializes in later njs VM element-access code (not shown) when the script reads or writes a[i] on the corrupted array; it is directly instantiable by the same attacker script through universal fast-array semantics, but the faulting instruction is outside the given snippet.

The collection loop at line 62 reads post-truncation elements that njs marks invalid and returns them in the deleted array; exposing invalid njs_value_t values to script is a robustness/type-confusion concern but was not proven to be an out-of-allocation access, so it is not counted as a primary finding.
The slow-path branches (property-based copy_within, delete loop, njs_object_length_set) remain within njs's property machinery under the same reentrancy trigger and were not found memory-unsafe.
The 32-bit-only overflow scenario inside njs_array_alloc sizing with ToLength-maximal delete counts is guarded here by the NULL check at line 55 and was not pursued.

verdict.summary: The SVDF Prepare kernel reads tensor dimension values from the attacker-controlled model (tensor dims arrays, SVDF rank) without validating tensor dimensionality or sign. weights_time->dims->data[1] (and input->dims->data[1], weights_feature->dims->data[1]) are read with no NumDimensions check, so a model declaring 1-D tensors causes heap out-of-bounds reads (CWE-125); an OOB-read batch_size further flows into tensor sizing. Additionally, TF_LITE_ENSURE(context, rank != 0) admits negative rank (or negative num_filters satisfies num_filters % rank == 0), producing negative num_units that is written into the output size array and passed to context->ResizeTensor, feeding attacker-derived negative sizes into the tensor memory-sizing operation with no positivity check anywhere (CWE-20).

evidence.reason: Heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125): dims is a TfLiteIntArray whose size is model-controlled; a crafted model declaring weights_time as 1-D makes data[1] read one element past the allocation. Mention sweep over all weights_time mentions (lines 15-17, 30, 33, 133-135, 194-197) shows no dimension-count check; the only NumDimensions check (line 47) covers state and runs after this line.

Same unguarded OOB read class: input and weights_feature dimensionality are never checked (no NumDimensions(input/weights_feature) anywhere), so a model with 1-D input or weights_feature reads past the dims heap allocation; the OOB-read value from input->dims->data[0] (line 25, scalar input) additionally flows into ResizeTensor sizing at lines 54 and 75.

Origin of the missing sign guard: the check rejects only rank == 0; edge-testing both bounds shows rank = -1 is admitted, so num_units = num_filters / rank becomes negative (num_filters = 2, rank = -1 gives num_units = -2); negative num_filters (e.g. -4 with rank 2) passes num_filters % rank == 0 the same way. No statement in the code checks rank > 0 or num_filters >= 0.

Sink of the negative-size defect: with the instantiated trigger (rank = -1, num_filters = 2), num_units = -2 is written into the output size array and passed to context->ResizeTensor, feeding an attacker-derived negative dimension into the tensor memory-sizing operation with no positivity check on any path (mention sweep for num_units: lines 29, 37, 55, 172; for num_filters: lines 26, 28, 33, 49-50, 76, 161-164, 172 — all equality/definition, none a bound).

assumptions: The .tflite model file crosses a trust boundary: tensor dims (TfLiteIntArray: int size followed by the data array), SVDF params->rank, and quantization details are flatbuffer-sourced attacker data; this Prepare function is the validation intake point.
GetInputSafe/GetOutputSafe/GetTemporarySafe return non-NULL tensors on success per their documented contract (existence validation), which the code checks via TF_LITE_ENSURE_OK.

ResizeTensor is the interpreter's tensor memory-sizing operation; the negative dimension passed at the call site is the defect even though the resulting misallocation occurs inside the not-shown callee.
limitations: TfLiteIntArrayCreate/TfLiteIntArrayCopy results (lines 53, 74, 104, 118, 134, 149, 163, 171) are used without NULL checks; trigger requires malloc failure on small fixed-size allocations, not attacker-instantiable — robustness only.

params/op_data (lines 2-4) are dereferenced without NULL checks; NULL user_data/builtin_data requires the framework Init/parse contract to be violated, not model content — contract question, not a vulnerability here.

Full-integer path reads input_params->scale->data[0] etc. after only checking quantization.type != kTfLiteNoQuantization; a model declaring an empty scale array would be another CWE-125 instance, but the loader's handling of empty scale lists is not shown — same class as the primary finding, not separately evidenced.

memory_size * num_filters (lines 49-50) can overflow signed int before the ENSURE_EQ comparison, but memory_size is not used after that check, limiting impact to a potentially bypassed shape comparison.

The precise downstream effect of negative dimensions (misallocation vs. graceful rejection) happens inside the interpreter's ResizeTensor/allocation code, which is not shown; the defect is recorded at the call site passing the out-of-domain size per the size-passing rule.

verdict.summary: The sparse reduce kernel writes the reduced value at out_flat(idx) (line 64) where idx is computed from attacker-controlled sparse-tensor coordinates and shape-derived strides, with no bounds check anywhere in this code tying idx to the allocated output size. Out-of-range index coordinates (indices tensor content, full int64 domain) or int64 overflow in the stride/index arithmetic (lines 41, 53) yield an out-of-bounds heap write with attacker-influenced value, corrupting the host TensorFlow process.

evidence.snippet:
const int64_t idx = CoordinatesToFlatIndex(g.group(), output_strides);
      out_flat(idx) = reduced_val();
