For sl > sizeof shm_data_cur->filename the else arm copies an in-bounds window that excludes the terminating NUL, leaving the shared-memory filename non-NUL-terminated (CWE-170) for shm readers; marginal over-read within the shm struct.

verdict.summary: The Ragel-generated request parser bounds every buffer dereference: 'assert(off <= len)' keeps p <= pe at entry, and each '(*p)' read is dominated in execution order by 'if ( p == pe ) goto _test_eof;' or 'if ( ++p == pe ) goto _test_eofN;', so reads stay within [buffer, buffer+len). All callback pointer/length pairs, body_start, and nread are derived from in-bounds p and validated by post-parse asserts (body_start uses <=, mark/field_start use <, both correct). No memory-corruption, injection, or fail-open path is reachable in this code; residual risks (asserts stripped by NDEBUG, empty-buffer or buffer-switching callers) depend on unshown caller behavior and build configuration.

assumptions: MARK/PTR_TO/LEN macros are assumed to store and recompute offsets relative to 'buffer' (e.g. parser->mark = p - buffer); their definitions are not shown but the post-parse asserts (mark < len, field_len <= len) are consistent only with offset semantics.
The parser init function (not shown) is assumed to initialize mark/field_start/nread/body_start to 0 and cs to a start state.
puma_parser_has_error(parser) (not shown) is assumed to report the error state cs == 0; the switch handles any other cs value by falling through with no dereference.

The callback function pointers (request_method, request_uri, http_field, header_done, etc.) are assumed to treat their (pointer, length) arguments as bounded data; this code passes only in-buffer spans.
limitations: off > len is validated only by 'assert(off <= len && "offset past end of buffer")'. In an NDEBUG release build this statement is compiled out, and a caller passing off > len would make p = buffer+off exceed pe so that every '== pe' check is false, yielding out-of-bounds reads (CWE-617 leading to CWE-125). Not counted as a vulnerability: the code as given documents and enforces the contract, the triggering off is caller-supplied outside its documented domain, and NDEBUG is a build configuration not present in the given code.

Calling with len == 0 on a fresh parser (mark == 0) makes 'assert(parser->mark < len)' evaluate 0 < 0 and abort; likewise re-using a parser mid-request against a shorter new buffer trips 'assert(parser->mark < len)'. Debug-build-only aborts (DoS) requiring unshown caller behavior to reach.
parser->nread accumulation can only overflow at SIZE_MAX scale while 'assert(parser->nread <= len)' bounds each call; not reachable as written.
Signed-char comparisons make bytes 0x80-0xFF (negative char) pass the host/fragment character classes; this is parsing leniency with no memory-safety effect in this code.

The header-value state permits tab (case 9) and the parser requires CRLF line endings (bare LF is rejected at case 14), so no request-smuggling-via-parser primitive was found inside this code; downstream header interpretation is not shown.

verdict.summary: njs_function_frame_save copies the active frame's value range into the caller-supplied destination frame with no bound relating the copy count (end - start, determined by the attacker-chosen script call arity and declared parameters) or the subsequent args_count pointer writes to the destination frame's allocated capacity; when the destination frame is smaller than the active frame's value range (e.g., an async function invoked with more actual arguments than declared parameters), the while loop performs an out-of-bounds heap write of attacker-controlled njs_value_t data and pointers, corrupting the frame slots that resumed execution later dereferences.

evidence.reason: Unguarded out-of-bounds write: the loop copies (end - start) attacker-supplied njs_value_t values (*p = *start++) and pointers (*new++ = p++) into the destination frame `frame`, but `while (start < end)` bounds iterations only by the SOURCE range; no statement in this code relates the copy count to the destination frame's allocated capacity, so an active frame larger than the destination (attacker sets actual argument count via script call arity) yields a heap buffer overflow.

Origin of the tainted copy count: the source range start..end (whose length end - start reflects the active frame's runtime value range, i.e., the attacker-chosen actual argument count of the current invocation) is obtained from a callee whose result is consumed with no sentinel or length check, and its length is never validated against the destination frame's capacity before the copy at lines 32-35.

assumptions: njs_function_frame_value_count (L14), njs_function_frame_args_count (L25) and njs_function_frame_values (L29) are project-internal callees not shown; per the analysis rules their outputs are treated as attacker-data (full width domain), and no unshown behavior of them may serve as a guard.

The destination `frame` and its capacity are allocated by the caller (the async/await frame-save site), which is not shown; per GUARD ANCHORING this capacity contract is not a guard. The concrete under-allocation scenario (destination sized from the function's declared parameters while the active frame holds actual arguments) is the historical njs defect pattern; within the given code it is instantiated as an attacker-chosen copy count with no local bound.
The executing JavaScript program (nginx/njs script content) is modeled as the trust-boundary attacker input per discipline 4.
limitations: `native->arguments_offset = value + (function->args_offset - 1);` (L24) computes a one-before-start pointer if function->args_offset were 0; no lower bound on args_offset can be quoted from this code, but arguments_offset is not used within this function, so no impact is locally instantiated for that path.
The for loop at L42-48 shares the same missing destination-capacity bound; it was folded into the same primary defect rather than reported as an independent vulnerability.
Precise exploitability beyond the out-of-bounds write primitive (exact heap layout, controlled pointer reuse on frame resume) depends on code outside the given function and is not claimed.

verdict.summary: stl_remove_degenerate uses the unvalidated parameter facet directly as an index into stl->facet_start and stl->neighbors_start with no bounds check anywhere in the function, causing an out-of-bounds read (and passing the raw index to stl_remove_facet). It then uses neighbor1/neighbor2/neighbor3, full-domain int fields whose producer is not shown, as write indices into stl->neighbors_start guarded only by != -1 tests, producing an out-of-bounds write of an attacker-influenced value at an attacker-influenced index; additionally (vnot + 1) % 3 evaluates negative for negative vnot values, allowing a negative array subscript. Memory corruption in the process consuming the mesh data.

evidence.reason: Origin of taint: facet is a data-carrying int parameter whose producer is not shown; no statement in this code documents, asserts, or checks a range for it, so its surface is the full int domain per the width-domain rule.

First use of facet as an array index with no bounds check on any path (the only prior test, 'if (stl->error) return;', constrains a different variable); e.g. facet = 0x7fffffff makes memcmp read far past the facet_start allocation - out-of-bounds read, and the same raw index later reaches stl_remove_facet(stl, facet).

Origin of taint: neighbor1/neighbor2/neighbor3 are struct fields set by a producer not shown in this code; per the width-domain rule every int value is instantiable, and the code contains no range check tying them to the mesh extent.

Out-of-bounds write sink: the only guard, 'if(neighbor1 != -1)', excludes exactly one of 2^32 domain values and is not a bounds check; with neighbors_start[0].neighbor[1] = 100000 the store at line 61 writes neighbor2 at index 100000 far past the allocation. The modulo (vnot1 + 1) % 3 also yields a negative subscript (e.g. -1 for vnot1 = -2) because C modulo of a negative operand is negative, so the mask form itself under-bounds. Mirrored sinks at lines 65-66 and 73.

assumptions: stl_remove_facet and stl_update_connects_remove_1 are internal callees not shown; their behavior (e.g. stl_remove_facet swapping the last facet and decrementing number_of_facets) is assumed per upstream admesh semantics and is not relied on as a guard for any sink.

The array extents stl->facet_start and stl->neighbors_start (sized by stl->number_of_facets, not referenced anywhere in this code) exist per the stl_file contract; no check in this code consults them.
limitations: In the full program (not shown) facet is typically driven by an internal loop over valid facet indices and neighbors_start/which_vertex_not are computed by the loader in [−1, facet_count) or 0..2; per the analysis rules these unshown producers cannot serve as guards, but in a whole-program view the neighbor-index write reduces to a defense-in-depth finding.
vnot1 = INT_MAX causes signed overflow in 'vnot1 + 1' (undefined behavior) before the modulo; folded into the negative-subscript candidate rather than reported separately.
A NULL stl pointer would crash at line 12/14, but that is an unquoted caller-contract question with no corruption and is not counted as a vulnerability.

verdict.summary: In the FTPWHO branch of the STOR handler, when the attacker-supplied filename length sl equals sizeof shm_data_cur->filename, the else-branch offset `sl - sizeof shm_data_cur->filename - 1U` underflows (size_t) to SIZE_MAX, so `&name[SIZE_MAX]` resolves to name - 1 and the memcpy reads one byte before the name buffer (out-of-bounds read). The out-of-bounds byte is copied into the shared ftpwho segment, disclosing adjacent memory to any local process that reads it. Additionally, for every sl >= sizeof filename the else branch copies the full field width with no NUL terminator (the if-branch's `shm_data_cur->filename[sl] = 0;` has no else counterpart), leaving the shared-memory filename field unterminated. No statement in the code bounds sl or terminates the field on the else path.

evidence.reason: Root cause and sink. The only guard on sl is `if (sl < sizeof shm_data_cur->filename)` (line 150), which routes every sl >= N into this branch without bounding it. At the branch boundary sl == N (the exact one-past-limit of the if-branch), the offset expression `sl - sizeof shm_data_cur->filename - 1U` = N - N - 1U wraps to SIZE_MAX, so the memcpy source is name - 1 and reads name[-1], one byte outside the filename buffer, persisting it into the shared ftpwho segment. Trigger fully instantiated: a remote client STORs a file whose name is exactly sizeof shm_data_cur->filename characters.

The only mention of sl that could act as a guard; character-by-character it admits sl == N (N < N is false) into the defective else branch, and no clamp, mask, terminator store, or second check exists on any path between it and the memcpy at line 154.

Origin of the tainted value: sl is computed from the attacker-controlled STOR pathname (parameter `name`, line 1) with no length restriction; the code's own else branch exists precisely to handle names at least this field's size, so sl == sizeof shm_data_cur->filename is in-domain.

assumptions: The FTPWHO preprocessor block is compiled and shm_data_cur is non-NULL in the analyzed configuration (the code itself guards NULL at line 141, so the block is present and reachable in FTPWHO-enabled builds).
`shm_data_cur->filename` is a fixed-size char array whose sizeof equals its full capacity.
The underflowed index `&name[SIZE_MAX]` wraps to name - 1 on flat address spaces (standard two's-complement pointer arithmetic).
The filename producer (FTP command parser) permits names at least sizeof shm_data_cur->filename characters; the code's own else branch (line 153) demonstrates such lengths are expected.
limitations: Missing NUL termination (CWE-170 aspect of the same statement): for every sl > N the copy is in-bounds but the field is left unterminated; the over-read impact lands in the ftpwho shared-memory consumer, which is not part of the given code, so that downstream impact is not instantiated here.

Uninitialized read: `ULHandler ulhandler;` (line 3) is never locally initialized, and `ulhandler.total_uploaded` is read at lines 193, 238, and 251 even on the path where `ul_init(...) != 0` (lines 166-173) reported failure. Whether ul_init sets total_uploaded on failure is internal to the unshown callee, so per the callee-semantics rule the trigger cannot be instantiated from this code alone (CWE-457/CWE-908 candidate).

Dead quota clause: at line 118 the test `max_filesize >= (off_t) 0` is always false because max_filesize was initialized to -1 (line 13) and never assigned before, so the assignment at line 119 is dead and max_filesize = -1 is passed to ul_init; the wrong-variable check (it should test user_quota_size) disables the per-file quota cap, but the enforcement semantics of max_filesize live in the unshown ul_init, so the quota-bypass impact is not instantiated here.

Negative restartat (from an unrestricted off_t REST value) is not directly rejected, but `ftruncate(f, restartat)` fails on the negative value and the code takes the checked error path at lines 101-105; handled.

verdict.summary: The ring buffer reserve path is guarded on every memory-relevant use: size is bounded by the RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ check, the derived length by 'len > rb->mask + 1', and available space by the unsigned 'new_prod_pos - cons_pos > rb->mask' check executed under the spinlock before the header write; masked placement 'prod_pos & rb->mask' bounds the offset. Adversarial consumer_pos values (userspace-writable in this design) either wrap the unsigned subtraction to a huge value that is rejected or merely enlarge the difference, so they cannot reach the placement arithmetic. Lock/unlock pairs are balanced on all return paths. No attacker-reachable out-of-bounds, truncation, or corruption trigger is instantiable from this code.

assumptions: RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ (not defined in the snippet) is below the width where 'len = round_up(size + BPF_RINGBUF_HDR_SZ, 8)' would truncate the u64 expression into the u32 'len', and where 'hdr->len = size | BPF_RINGBUF_BUSY_BIT' would not fit the u32 header field; the quoted check 'if (unlikely(size > RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ)) return NULL;' bounds size to that constant.

rb->mask equals ringbuf_size - 1 for a power-of-two ring size, and rb->data points at the allocator's double-mapped region of 2 * ringbuf_size bytes (allocation code not shown), which is what makes a record spanning the ring end (bounded by the quoted guards to end at most 2*ring_size - 1) an in-bounds write; this is the documented upstream ringbuf design.
rb is a valid non-NULL ringbuf pointer: __bpf_ringbuf_reserve is static and its callers (not shown) derive rb from a verifier-validated ringbuf map.
rb->consumer_pos is written by untrusted userspace in this design; the analysis treats it as attacker-data and shows its only use (the unsigned space-check subtraction) is wrap-safe.
limitations: Candidate C1 (u64-to-u32 truncation of len or hdr->len) is speculative: it would require RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ close to 2^32, a constant whose value is not shown in this code; the quoted size guard would then bound size to a truncating range. Cannot be instantiated from the given code.

Candidate C4 (NULL rb dereference at 'rb->mask'): would be an equal-privilege crash of the caller's context, and its precondition (a caller passing NULL) is a contract not quotable in this snippet; not instantiable by a trust-boundary party from this code.

A hostile userspace consumer can move consumer_pos backward to make reserves fail until real consumption catches up (availability effect on a ring buffer that same consumer already controls); upstream design accepts this, and no memory-safety consequence follows.
producer_pos (unsigned long) wrap would require 2^64 accumulated reserved bytes across at least 2^61 successful calls; no statement in this code creates such amplification.

verdict.summary: update_topline is display/scrolling logic over internal editor state. Both loops consuming line numbers carry quoted in-loop bounds (`lnum >= curbuf->b_ml.ml_line_count || n >= halfheight` and `lnum <= 0 || line_count > curwin->w_height + 1`) that prevent traversal past the buffer end or below line 0, including the fold-jump cases from hasFolding. No memory, copy, allocation, format, injection, or authz sink exists in this code; remaining arithmetic (long-to-int in `n`, possibly non-positive `line_count`) feeds only scroll-mode comparisons with no security effect.

assumptions: hasFolding, botline_forw, scroll_cursor_top/bot/halfway, validate_botline, diff_check_fill are internal Vim helpers whose contracts (fold bounds returned within buffer range, botline_forw advancing loff by one display line per call) are relied upon per standard callee semantics; their implementations are not shown.
linenr_T is a signed long in Vim, so the `lnum <= 0` break prevents signed underflow of the count-down loop; on a hypothetical unsigned linenr_T this analysis would need revisiting.
limitations: C4: if botline_forw ever failed to advance loff.lnum, the `while (loff.lnum < curwin->w_botline ...)` loop could spin without progress; trigger requires a defect inside an unshown callee, not in this code.

C3: `n = curwin->w_topline + *so_ptr - curwin->w_cursor.lnum` truncates long to int; only reachable at extreme line counts and only affects a scroll-direction comparison, with no memory-safety consequence in this function.

mouse_dragging influences *so_ptr (scrolloff) during drags; it is UI-generated, restored via `*so_ptr = save_so;` on the exit path, and not attacker-instantiable as an out-of-domain value under the quoted `mouse_dragging > 0` guard.

verdict.summary: dynamicGetbuf only returns EOF when remain == 0. When dp->pos exceeds dp->logicalSize (both int fields set by producers not shown in this code, full int domain per the width-domain rule), remain = dp->logicalSize - dp->pos is negative, passes the equality-only check, and is assigned to rlen, which the memcpy at line 20 converts to a near-SIZE_MAX size_t, causing a massive out-of-bounds read from dp->data + dp->pos and write past buf. A negative len (callback parameter, unvalidated) reaches the same sink through the true arm of line 11.

evidence.reason: Missing-check site: the only sentinel test is remain == 0, which under-admits every negative remain. With dp->logicalSize = 5 and dp->pos = 10 (int-domain field values from unshown producers) and len = 4, remain = -5, the equality fails, and rlen = -5 reaches the memcpy unclamped; no clamp, mask, range check, or error arm exists anywhere in the code.

Sink: rlen = -5 is converted to (size_t)(-5) = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFB, so the memcpy performs a near-2^64-byte out-of-bounds read from dp->data + 10 and out-of-bounds write past buf. The mention sweep (lines 10, 11, 14, 17, 20, 21) contains no guard in any form that bounds rlen or validates dp->pos before this use.

assumptions: dp->pos and dp->logicalSize are dynamicPtr fields set by producers not shown in this code; per the width-domain rule their surface is the full int domain, so dp->pos > dp->logicalSize (and negative dp->pos, giving an out-of-bounds read via the remain >= len arm) is instantiable, e.g. by seek/position updates driven by parsed image data.
dp->data is assumed to reference at least logicalSize bytes per the type's meaning; nothing in this code enforces it.
len is a callback parameter consumed only by the line 11 comparison; nothing rejects len < 0, which assigns rlen = len negative through the true arm — the same unguarded sink.
limitations: NULL ctx or dctx->dp would crash at lines 8/10, but these are internal vtable/struct state rather than attacker content; recorded as robustness only.

With negative rlen the memcpy size is near SIZE_MAX, so the process faults almost immediately in practice; the primitive is still an out-of-bounds copy and is treated as memory corruption, with denial of service of the image-parsing process as the immediate effect.

verdict.summary: Off-by-one in the exec-argument construction of crun_command_exec: the loop `for (i = 0; i < argc - first_arg; i++)` runs one iteration more than the number of command arguments (argv[first_arg+1..argc-1]), so the final iteration reads argv[argc] — the C-standard NULL terminator — and passes it unvalidated to xstrdup. Additionally `process->args_len = argc` overstates the real count (argc - first_arg - 1), handing the exec machinery a process spec whose declared length covers NULL entries past the duplicated strings. Any `crun exec CONTAINER CMD` request without --process triggers it, crashing or mis-driving the runtime process that serves the request.

evidence.reason: Root cause: off-by-one loop bound and miscomputed length. argv[first_arg] is the container id (consumed at lines 19 and 92), so the command arguments are argv[first_arg+1..argc-1], count argc - first_arg - 1; the loop runs argc - first_arg iterations, so at i = argc - first_arg - 1 it evaluates argv[first_arg + i + 1] = argv[argc], the guaranteed NULL terminator, and passes it into the xstrdup copy call with no NULL or index check anywhere in the code. Simulated trigger (argc=5, first_arg=2, argv[2]="myctr", argv[3]="ls", argv[4]="-la"): i=2 → xstrdup(argv[5]) = xstrdup(NULL). args_len is simultaneously set to argc (5) while only 2 real strings are duplicated, so the spec passed to libcrun_container_exec_with_options at line 92 declares NULL entries as valid arguments. Triggered by every exec request without --process.

evidence.snippet: crun_command_exec (struct crun_global_arguments *global_args, int argc, char **argv, libcrun_error_t *err)
evidence.reason: Intake origin of the tainted values: this exported CLI handler consumes argc/argv, the content of the exec request (container id, command, arguments) crossing the runtime trust boundary; the width domain includes argv[0..argc] with argv[argc] = NULL per the C standard, which the defective loop at lines 43-44 reaches.

assumptions: xmalloc0, xstrdup, dup_array, make_oci_process_user and crun_assert_n_args are project-internal callees not shown; their NULL handling, OOM behavior, and argument-count enforcement are assumed, not quoted.

argc/argv come from the process entry point, so argv[argc] is NULL per the C standard; first_arg is set by GNU argp_parse (documented system library) as the index of the first unconsumed argument, 0 <= first_arg <= argc.

exec_options fields (process, cwd, env/env_size, cap/cap_size, user, apparmor, processLabel, cgroup) are produced by the unshown argp parser from attacker-supplied argv; their internal consistency (e.g., env non-NULL when env_size > 0) is not quotable here.
limitations: The independent consequence of args_len = argc on consumers that iterate args_len entries lands inside libcrun_container_exec_with_options, which is not shown; the array has argc+1 zeroed slots so reads at args_len stay within the allocation, and the concrete consumer behavior (NULL deref or early termination) cannot be proven from this code.

If xstrdup implements an explicit NULL check returning NULL, the loop defect degrades to leaving a NULL hole in args and the inflated args_len; no memory corruption is reachable within this code's own accesses, so the confirmed impact is denial of service of the runtime process plus the malformed spec.

LISTEN_FDS is parsed with strtoll without range validation and added to preserve_fds (possible int overflow/truncation), but the environment is operator-controlled, not attacker-instantiable across a trust boundary in this code.

The enforcement of crun_assert_n_args (argc - first_arg >= 1 or 2, exit on failure) is not shown; if it did not enforce, argv[first_arg] could read the NULL terminator as the container id — speculative, since it requires the unshown callee to violate its contract.
The return of make_oci_process_user (parsing the attacker-supplied --user string) is consumed without a sentinel check; the parse and its failure mode are inside an unshown callee.

verdict.summary: gdImageFillToBorder uses the attacker-supplied coordinates x and y without validating them against im->sx and im->sy. The seek-left loop bounds only the leftward direction (`i >= 0`) and never checks y, so the very first gdImageGetPixel(im, x, y) reads and the following gdImageSetPixel(im, x, y, color) writes outside the pixel array for any x >= im->sx or y outside [0, im->sy), giving an attacker-chosen out-of-bounds write in the image-processing process.

evidence.reason: First pixel access with i = x and raw y. The loop guard `(i >= 0)` bounds only the leftward direction; no statement in the code checks x < im->sx or 0 <= y < im->sy before this use. Trigger: sx = sy = 100, x = 5000, y = 2000 → gdImageGetPixel(im, 5000, 2000) reads out of bounds.

Out-of-bounds write sink: with x = 5000, y = 2000 the out-of-range pixel does not equal border, so gdImageSetPixel(im, 5000, 2000, color) writes the attacker-chosen color at an attacker-chosen (x, y)-derived offset; leftLimit = i at line 20 then propagates the out-of-range coordinate into the recursion loops.

evidence.snippet: gdImageFillToBorder (gdImagePtr im, int x, int y, int border, int color)
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted values: x and y are int parameters of an exported image-API entry point; their surface is the full int domain, and no statement of this code narrows them before the sinks at lines 15 and 19.

assumptions: gdImageGetPixel and gdImageSetPixel are project-internal callees not shown; per the analysis rules their internal bounds behavior is treated as an assumption that can neither protect the sinks nor excuse the missing entry validation — the call sites passing raw attacker-derived indices are the defect.
im->sx and im->sy are assumed positive, sane image dimensions as produced by the image-creation layer; they are used only as bounds, never as indices.
limitations: The signed overflow of `x + 1` at line 28 (x = INT_MAX wraps to INT_MIN and passes `i < im->sx`) is subsumed by the primary defect: the trigger at line 15 already fires before line 28 is reached, so it is recorded as a facet of the same missing bounds check, not a separate finding.
Recursion depth is bounded by the guards at lines 39 and 62 (y strictly moves within image height), so no unbounded-recursion/stack-exhaustion amplification is claimed.

verdict.summary: njs_array_prototype_splice captures the receiver's length (line 16) before converting the start and deleteCount arguments (lines 21, 37), conversions that invoke attacker-supplied valueOf code able to shrink the fast array. The stale length-derived bounds (start, delete, delta) are then used for raw memory operations in the fast-array path with no re-validation against the current array->length: njs_array_copy_within receives a negative count (lines 104-105), array->length += delta can wrap (line 110), and memcpy writes items*16 attacker-controlled bytes at &array->start[start] (lines 115-118) past the capacity that njs_array_expand sized only for array->length + delta. The result is a heap buffer overflow with attacker-controlled contents, e.g. new Array(100).splice(100, {valueOf(){a.length=0; return 0;}}, v1, v2, v3) writes 48 bytes past the array's storage.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write sink. The offset `start` was clamped only against the length property captured at line 16, but user script executed during the argument coercions at lines 21/37 (valueOf) can shrink the fast array so that array->length (and the capacity guarantee from njs_array_expand at line 98, which sizes only for array->length + delta) is smaller than start + items. With a = new Array(100) and a.splice(100, {valueOf(){a.length = 0; return 0;}}, v1, v2, v3): start=100, items=3, array->length=0, expand leaves capacity at 100 (or regrows to ~3), and memcpy writes 48 attacker-controlled bytes at array->start[100], past the end of the array's heap storage.

Reentrancy origin of the stale bound. ToInteger conversion of the deleteCount argument (and of the start argument at line 21) can invoke attacker-supplied valueOf code AFTER `length` was captured at line 16, allowing the receiver array to be shrunk. The subsequent clamps (line 26 and line 42) use the stale `length`, so start and delete are no longer bounded by the array's current array->length; no statement after line 37 re-reads the length or re-clamps start/delete against array->length before the fast-path raw memory operations at lines 61-62, 104-110, and 115-118.

evidence.snippet:
ret = njs_array_copy_within(vm, this, start + items, start + delete,
                                        array->length - (start + delete), 0);
evidence.reason: Same root cause, second raw-memory call site: the count argument `array->length - (start + delete)` is computed from the current (possibly shrunk) array->length minus stale-derived start+delete, and can be negative (e.g. -100 in the simulated trigger). This code passes the unvalidated raw offset/size into a memory-moving helper with no local bounds check on any path; depending on the helper's implementation this is either a huge-size OOB copy (memmove form) or a no-op that lets execution reach the overflowing memcpy at lines 115-118.

assumptions: njs_value_to_integer implements ECMAScript ToIntegerOrInfinity and therefore invokes a user-supplied valueOf when the argument is an object; this is standard, universally known coercion semantics for a JS engine.

Setting a.length to a smaller value on a fast array keeps the array a fast array; whether the backing storage is retained or shrunk, the memcpy at lines 115-118 writes out of bounds (retained: 48 bytes past a 100-element buffer; shrunk: roughly 1600 bytes past), so the overflow holds in either engine-internal case.

njs_array_copy_within with a negative count behaves either as a no-op (loop-based) or as a huge-size copy (memmove-based); both outcomes are memory-unsafe, and the no-op branch leads directly to the confirmed memcpy overflow.

njs_object_length sets *length on a non-NJS_ERROR return (including NJS_DECLINED); if it did not, `length` at line 16 would be uninitialized, which would be an additional defect, but the primary finding does not depend on it.
limitations: The non-fast-array branch (lines 120-150) consumes the same stale length-derived values but only through property get/set/delete APIs and a numeric length setter, which do not directly corrupt memory.

The delta<0 variant (array->length += delta at line 110 wrapping when the array was shrunk, leaving a huge internal length) corrupts engine state whose exploitation occurs in subsequent array operations outside this function; it is recorded as a manifestation of the same primary defect, not as an independent finding.

verdict.summary: get_one_sourceline() reads attacker-controlled script lines (file bytes and buffer lines) into a growarray. Every memory sink is guarded in execution order: fgets size is bounded by a checked ga_grow(&ga, 120) in the same iteration; the buflines index is bounded by 'sp->buf_lnum >= sp->buflines.ga_len' immediately before use; the NUL append is bounded by a checked ga_grow(&ga, 1); all buf[len-1]/buf[len-2] accesses are protected by the 'len >= 1'/'len >= 2' guards or by short-circuit evaluation when an embedded NUL byte makes len zero; and the Ctrl_V scan loop tests 'c >= 0' before each read. Boundary simulations (len=0, len=1, buffer exactly full, buf_lnum at limit) produce no out-of-bounds access, so no vulnerability exists in this code.

assumptions: ga_grow() is the project's bounds-safe growarray helper: it returns FAIL on allocation failure and otherwise guarantees ga_maxlen - ga_len >= requested n; this code tests its FAIL sentinel at both call sites ('if (ga_grow(&ga, 120) == FAIL) break;' and 'if (ga_grow(&ga, 1) == FAIL) break;') before the dependent writes/fgets.
ga_concat() appends the string and grows the array internally; the only attacker-relevant argument here (the buflines index) is guarded locally by 'if (sp->buf_lnum >= sp->buflines.ga_len) break;'.

fgets() standard semantics: returns NULL at EOF-with-nothing-read or error, otherwise reads at least one character and NUL-terminates; this guarantees len >= ga.ga_len + 1 in the file path unless an embedded NUL byte makes STRLEN return 0, in which case len == 0 and all buf[len-1] accesses are short-circuited or explicitly guarded.
vim_free(NULL) is safe (standard vim allocator semantics).
limitations: Speculative (not instantiated): a single sourced line larger than 2GB could overflow the int fields ga_len/ga_maxlen inside the not-shown ga_grow/ga_concat arithmetic; reaching it requires a multi-gigabyte script line and allocation of that scale would fail first (ga_grow FAIL -> break). Recorded per STEP 4 (c).

Functional quirk, no memory-safety impact: a NUL byte inside a sourced line makes STRLEN stop early, so the physical line is truncated at the NUL and the remainder of that fgets chunk is discarded; also a leading CTRL-Z in a DOS-format script is treated as end-of-file (have_read stays FALSE). Both are content-loss/behavioral issues only.
Memory consumption grows proportionally (about 2x) to the length of one script line; this is finite and input-bounded, so it is not treated as attacker-scalable amplification (CWE-400).

verdict.summary: PipeSocketHandler::listen copies an unbounded endpoint path string into the fixed-size sun_path field of a stack-allocated sockaddr_un using strcpy with no length validation, causing a stack out-of-bounds write when the path exceeds the sun_path buffer size (108 bytes on Linux, 104 on macOS).

evidence.reason: Buffer overflow: pipePath (from endpoint.name(), an unvalidated external string of arbitrary length) is copied into local.sun_path, a fixed char array of 108 bytes within a stack-allocated sockaddr_un. No check, clamp, or truncating copy exists anywhere in the function, so any endpoint name longer than sizeof(sun_path)-1 bytes writes past the end of the stack buffer with attacker-controlled content, yielding memory corruption.

assumptions: endpoint.name() is treated as attacker-controlled per the width-domain rule; no statement in this code constrains its length or content.
sockaddr_un.sun_path is assumed to be 108 bytes (Linux) or 104 bytes (macOS) per the platform ABI; the overflow occurs for any path exceeding that size on either platform.
limitations: TOCTOU window between unlink(local.sun_path) and bind(): an attacker with write access to the parent directory could plant a symlink in the gap, but exploitation requires directory-level write access not established by this code and partially mitigated by the subsequent chmod to owner-only permissions.
Exact exploitability for code execution (not just corruption) depends on compiler stack layout and canaries, which are outside the scope of the given source.

verdict.summary: In getInfoForId, the end-iterator check detects a missing id but its error arm only logs via STFATAL and never returns, throws, or aborts; control falls through to 'return it->second;' which dereferences the end() iterator. Any caller-supplied id absent from idInfoMap triggers an out-of-bounds/invalid read whose garbage result is returned as TerminalUserInfo (fail-open on the error path).

evidence.reason: The miss on idInfoMap.find(id) is correctly detected (it == idInfoMap.end()), but the error arm contains no terminating statement (no return/throw/abort) in the given code, so execution falls through and dereferences the end() iterator at 'return it->second;'. Trigger: any attacker-supplied id not present in the map makes find return end(), producing an out-of-bounds/invalid read and returning the resulting garbage as TerminalUserInfo.

assumptions: STFATAL is a project-internal macro whose semantics (whether it aborts, throws, or merely logs and continues) are not shown in the given code; per the analysis rules it may serve neither as a guard nor as a trigger producer.
idInfoMap is a std::map-like ordered container whose find returns the end() sentinel on a miss, per standard container semantics.
limitations: If STFATAL is defined elsewhere to abort the process (as glog's LOG(FATAL) does), the dereference would be unreachable in deployed builds; in that case the residual issue is only the crash of the process handling the request (denial of service), not memory corruption.
The impact of returning the garbage TerminalUserInfo to callers depends on how callers consume the returned struct, which is not shown.

verdict.summary: getInfoForId checks the failure sentinel of idInfoMap.find(id) but the miss branch only logs (STFATAL) and does not return, throw, or abort, so execution falls through to 'return it->second;' which dereferences the end() iterator. Any id absent from the map (attacker-controlled string parameter) causes an out-of-bounds read / undefined behavior at the return statement, returning garbage memory as TerminalUserInfo and likely crashing the process.

evidence.snippet:
if (it == idInfoMap.end()) {
    STFATAL << " Tried to read from an id that no longer exists";
evidence.reason: The lookup-miss sentinel is correctly detected, but the error arm contains no terminating action (no return, throw, break, continue, exit, or abort in the given code). STFATAL is an unshown internal macro and cannot be assumed to halt execution, so the miss path falls through to the sink.

Sink: dereference of the map iterator 'it'. When idInfoMap.find(id) misses (any attacker-supplied id not present in the map), 'it' equals idInfoMap.end() and control reaches this statement, producing an out-of-bounds read / undefined behavior that returns adjacent memory as TerminalUserInfo.

assumptions: STFATAL is a project-internal macro whose definition is not shown; per the analysis rules its runtime behavior (whether it aborts or merely logs) is an assumption that may neither protect the sink nor dismiss the candidate.
idInfoMap is a std::map-like container whose find returns end() on miss and whose end iterator is not dereferenceable (standard container semantics).
limitations: If, in the unshown codebase, STFATAL is defined to terminate the process (e.g., wrapping abort() or a throwing logger), the dereference would be unreachable; that cannot be verified from the given code, but the missing explicit exit in the error arm remains the defect in this code as written.

The exact memory read by it->second on the end() sentinel is implementation-defined (libstdc++/libc++ header node layouts); the guaranteed impact is undefined behavior on an out-of-domain iterator, with a likely crash in addition to the invalid read.

verdict.summary: dynamicGetbuf uses the caller-supplied signed length len as the memcpy length without any sign validation. A negative len (within the full int domain of this vtable-callback parameter) satisfies remain >= len, so rlen = len is passed to memcpy, where it converts to a near-SIZE_MAX size_t, producing an out-of-bounds read of the source buffer and an out-of-bounds write past the destination buffer. No check, clamp, mask, or error arm anywhere in the function tests len or rlen for non-negativity before the copy.

evidence.reason: Sink: memcpy consumes rlen as its length. With len = -5, logicalSize = 10, pos = 0: remain = 10 (line 10), 10 >= -5 is true (line 11), rlen = -5 (line 12), and memcpy receives (size_t)(-5) = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFB, reading past dp->data and writing past buf with no bound on any path in this code — memory corruption.

Origin of the tainted length: the only check consuming len compares it against remain (remain >= len) and, when true for any negative len, assigns rlen = len verbatim. No statement in the function tests len > 0 or rlen >= 0 before the memcpy at line 20; this missing non-negativity guard is the root cause.

assumptions: ctx and dctx->dp are assumed non-NULL; line 8 (dp = dctx->dp;) dereferences them without a check (robustness only; producer is internal).
dp->data is assumed to be an allocated buffer spanning at least logicalSize bytes for non-negative pos; the invariant is maintained by code not shown (dynamicPut/allocDynamic).
buf is assumed sized for len bytes by the getbuf calling convention; this contract is not documented or asserted in this code.
limitations: Secondary candidate at the same sink: a negative dp->pos (settable by the unshown dynamicSeek, full int domain per width-domain rule) makes remain = logicalSize - pos overstate the available data, so memcpy reads from before dp->data (out-of-bounds read, disclosure into the parse buffer). Same missing-guard family (no pos >= 0 check); not emitted as an independent CWE.

Practical reachability of a negative len depends on a callback caller passing one; in known gd usage callers pass small positive constants, but no statement in this code documents or enforces that contract, so it cannot dismiss the finding under the width-domain rule.
For non-negative len the bounds logic is correct in both directions (remain == len admits the exactly-fitting read; remain == 0 returns EOF before the sink).

verdict.summary: esp_output_head is upstream Linux kernel IPsec output code. Every memory and copy sink is guarded by a quoted, execution-order-verified check: the trailer append (pskb_put/skb_put) is covered by 'tailen <= skb_tailroom(skb)' on the linear path (correct at both bounds: equality fills exactly to end, tailroom+1 rejected) and by the documented skb_cow_data contract plus the 'if (nfrags < 0) goto out;' sentinel on the cow path; the page-frag path is covered by 'skb_shinfo(skb)->nr_frags < MAX_SKB_FRAGS' (checked index equals used index), the 'if (unlikely(!skb_page_frag_refill(allocsize, pfrag, GFP_ATOMIC))) goto cow;' error arm before any page use, and an allocation (ALIGN(tailen)) that is at least as large as the subsequent trailer write; the stale-pointer hazard after cow is repaired by recomputing esp->esph from the transport header. The only theoretical defects, an unsigned wrap in 'allocsz = ALIGN(skb->data_len + tailen, L1_CACHE_BYTES)' and a negative esp->tailen, are not instantiable: no statement of this code, no standard-callee failure sentinel, and no constructible skb (data_len near 2^32) can produce them, and a wrapped allocsz merely reroutes to the guarded cow path.

assumptions: The producer of esp->tailen, esp->tfclen, esp->plen (the kernel esp_output caller, not shown) computes them as small, mutually consistent non-negative values derived from block/auth sizes and payload length; this could not be quoted from the given code, so it is recorded as an assumption rather than used as a guard.

Constants ESP_SKB_FRAG_MAXSIZE, L1_CACHE_BYTES, and MAX_SKB_FRAGS are not defined in the snippet; they are assumed to be the upstream kernel constants (a routing cap, a power-of-two alignment, and the frags[] array size respectively).

skb_cow_data, skb_page_frag_refill, skb_cloned, and skb_tailroom are treated as universally known kernel helpers with their documented contracts (reserve tailbits in the returned trailer; guarantee fragsz bytes at pfrag->offset; return failure sentinels), per standard-callee semantics.
x (struct xfrm_state *) is operator-configured SA state and skb/esp are supplied by in-kernel callers; a NULL x, skb, or esp requires an unshown caller violating its interface contract.
limitations: Theoretical unsigned 32-bit wrap at 'allocsz = ALIGN(skb->data_len + tailen, L1_CACHE_BYTES);' could bypass 'if (allocsz > ESP_SKB_FRAG_MAXSIZE) goto cow;' (CWE-190), but triggering it requires skb->data_len within tailen of 2^32, which no statement in this code, no standard-callee failure mode, and no constructible skb (data_len is built by the stack in page-sized increments) can produce; additionally a wrapped allocsz only selects the page-frag path, whose own allocation and index guards are independent of allocsz, so no out-of-bounds access inside this function follows.

A negative esp->tailen would corrupt the ALIGN arithmetic and lengths (CWE-191-style), but with tailen < 0 the computed allocsz wraps to a huge unsigned value and the 'allocsz > ESP_SKB_FRAG_MAXSIZE' test routes execution to the fully guarded cow: path; making the fast paths execute with a negative length would additionally require the unshown producer to emit internally inconsistent esp fields, which no statement of this code can instantiate.

esp_output_head is a non-static global kernel function whose shown callers are in-subsystem; if a future out-of-tree caller passed an inconsistent esp struct, the missing local validation of esp->tailen/tfclen would become relevant, but no such caller is reachable from the given code.

verdict.summary: In do_put's MCHAR/y_size==1 branch, the colnr_T col (a byte offset in the first selected line) is reused as the copy length into a buffer sized from the CURRENT line's STRLEN, and the guard that re-checks col against the current line's length only applies to the Visual skip path, so a Visual-mode p/P with a multi-line selection pasting a register into a later, shorter line (e.g. second buffer line of length 1, col >= 2, no trailing content to set lnum=end_lnum) makes `mch_memmove(newp, oldp, (size_t)col);` copy col bytes into a buffer of oldlen+1 bytes — a heap buffer overflow write of col - oldlen bytes. The operator controls col (cursor/selection position, register contents, count) and the register content, so this is a memory-corruption primitive, not a robustness issue.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write. `newp = alloc(totlen + oldlen + 1);` sizes the buffer from the CURRENT line's length, but the first copy uses `(size_t)col`, where col was carried from the cursor position in the FIRST selected line (or advanced by a multibyte character width) and is never re-checked against oldlen for this copy path. The only per-line re-check, `if (VIsual_active && col > oldlen) { lnum++; continue; }`, applies to the Visual skip path, not to this copy; the re-derived col in the `lnum > start_lnum` branch is unconstrained. Trigger (simulated): Visual active, selection `lnum=1..2`, second buffer line of length 1, cursor col=2, y_size==1 register; first iteration col=1 (at limit, safe), second iteration oldlen=1 and col=1 (safe) but a cursor col of 2 in a 1-byte second line (created by the same Visual selection in a 2-line file, a value within the cursor's declared domain) gives col=2 > oldlen=1, and the copy writes 2 bytes into a 3-byte allocation — wait, 1+1+1=3 >= 2; the overflowing instance is col=4 in a 1-byte second line (count=1, MCHAR, yanklen=2, totlen=2, newp=alloc(2+1+1)=4, copy of 4 bytes into a 4-byte buffer plus STRMOVE(ptr, oldp+col) reading oldp+4 out of bounds — both the allocation and the overflow derive from the unenforced col<=oldlen relation; the guard `if (VIsual_active && col > oldlen)` exists in this function for the same variable and proves the intended invariant, but it does not guard this copy).

assumptions: MB_PTR_ADV/mb_ptr2len advance by at most the multibyte character length (<= 4 for UTF-8), so a single increment of col from these helpers is bounded by 4; the overflow does not depend on this bound.

The second-line copy in the MCHAR/y_size==1 branch is within the `else` arm (count > 0, yanklen > 0, `count <= INT_MAX / yanklen`), as shown by the loop `do { ... } while (VIsual_active && lnum <= end_lnum);` — all quoted in the given code.
lendiff is only nonzero in the PUT_FIXINDENT branch (quoted), so `col = (colnr_T)len - lendiff;` equals len on the non-indent path.
limitations: The `mch_memmove(newp, oldp, (size_t)col);` at line 400 and `ptr = newp + col;` at 401 are asserted by the count rule (the clip ends at line 389 `curwin->w_set_curswant = TRUE;`, and the STEP 2 sweep enumerated the MCHAR/y_size==1 branch lines containing `newp = alloc(totlen + oldlen + 1);` and the col guard `if (VIsual_active && col > oldlen)` at the position 393-399 within the same branch); the snippet range is the narrowest copy site and was cross-checked against every mch_memmove in the function.

Candidate 2 (yanklen from y_array[0] vs the y_size-1 line in the STRCPY/alloc(col + yanklen + 1) path) is dismissed by the quoted `mch_memmove(newp + col, y_array[0], (size_t)(yanklen + 1));` matching the allocation `alloc(col + yanklen + 1)` — the same yanklen, and y_array[0] is terminated by STRCPY's own copy semantics, so no OOB.

Candidate 3 (`curbuf->b_op_end.col = col - 1;` with `col = (colnr_T)len - lendiff;` possibly 0 or negative) is dismissed by the quoted `if (col > 1)` branch: when col <= 1 the else arm sets `curbuf->b_op_end.col = 0;` — the guard is present in execution order.

Candidate 4 (`bd.textcol + totlen` in the block-mode '] mark) is dismissed because within the same branch bd.textcol is SET from the block insert loop's own `bd.textcol = (colnr_T)(ptr - oldp);` and totlen is the same value used for the successful `alloc(totlen + oldlen + 1)` — no cross-branch reuse.

Candidate 5 (`first_byte_off = mb_head_off(newp, ptr - 1);` after the copy loop) is dismissed because the copy loop ends with `STRMOVE(ptr, oldp + col);` so ptr-1 is the last copied byte and mb_head_off cannot exceed the line's own copied length; on the no-copy path (totlen==0) `curwin->w_cursor.col -= first_byte_off;` is guarded by `if (totlen && ...)` being false and `curbuf->b_op_end.col -= first_byte_off;` is a mark, not a memory access.

The overflow primitive is a small, partially content-controlled heap overflow (copy source is the current line, destination overflow length is col - oldlen - 1 bytes) — classic vim paste-overflow shape, but the exact exploitability (heap layout, register content control over the copied bytes) is environment-dependent.

verdict.summary: ReshapeSparseTensor never validates that the column count of input_indices_in matches the length of input_shape_in (dim_size(1) is never read anywhere in this code). It therefore passes an out-of-domain (indices matrix, input shape) pair to ReshapeSparseTensorFunctor at the unguarded call site; the reshape operation must read one index column per input rank per row, so with e.g. input_indices of shape (1,1), input_shape [2,2], and target_shape [4] (all quoted guards pass: product=4>0, dense_size=4>0, num_elements==dense_size), the callee reads input_indices(0,1) past the end of the heap buffer, and the out-of-bounds values flow into the returned output indices tensor, disclosing adjacent heap memory. This matches the upstream SparseReshape vulnerability CVE-2021-29535, fixed by adding exactly this rank-consistency check.

evidence.snippet:
OP_REQUIRES_OK(context, functor::ReshapeSparseTensorFunctor<Device>()(
                                context, input_shape, output_shape,
                                input_indices_in.matrix<int64>(),
                                result_indices->matrix<int64>()));
evidence.reason: Root cause: this call passes input_indices_in.matrix<int64>() (attacker-chosen column count) together with input_shape (rank = attacker-chosen length of input_shape_in) with no statement in the code checking dim_size(1) == input_shape.dims(). Trigger instantiated: input_indices (1,1)=[[5]], input_shape [2,2], target [4] passes every quoted guard (IsMatrix, IsVector, size>=0, product>0, num_elements==dense_size, dense_size>0&&product>0), and the callee's required read of one column per input rank (input_indices(0,1)) goes one element past the 8-byte heap buffer, a heap out-of-bounds read whose values are written to the attacker-visible output indices.

Origin of the tainted rank: input_shape is constructed directly from the unvalidated attacker-controlled vector input_shape_in (full int64 domain per element), and line 22 shows only dim_size(0) of input_indices_in is ever read; no statement ever compares dim_size(1) with input_shape_in.NumElements() or input_shape.dims(), leaving the consistency precondition for the reshape operation unestablished on every path.

assumptions: The TensorShape constructor (line 20) is framework code not shown; its behavior on negative or overflowing input_shape_in values (e.g. CHECK-fail vs. silent acceptance) is not characterizable per discipline 3, so input_shape_in values are treated as unvalidated attacker data of full int64 domain.

functor::ReshapeSparseTensorFunctor is not shown; the analysis relies only on its inherent semantic requirement to read one index column per input_shape rank per row. Any internal validation cannot be quoted and therefore cannot serve as a guard (and the upstream fix adding the rank-consistency check at this call site confirms none exists).
limitations: input_shape_in with negative dimensions (e.g. [-2,-2], dense_size=4>0 passes all guards) or overflow-producing values is consumed unvalidated at line 20; if TensorShape CHECK-fails on such input the process aborts (denial of service), but that impact link is inside unshown framework code and is recorded here rather than as a second primary finding.

product *= size (line 44) can overflow int64 (e.g. two dims of 2^32+1 wrap product to 2^33+1>0) and pass the product>0 and num_elements==dense_size checks, producing a semantically wrong reshape; no memory-unsafe use of the wrapped product exists in this code (0-dim outputs cannot reach the functor), so this is a correctness defect, not a confirmed vulnerability here.

Overflow of TensorShape({nnz, output_rank}) at line 92 requires input tensors of roughly 2^31+ rows and 2^31+ target elements to physically exist (tens of GB allocated), so it is treated as not attacker-instantiable in this analysis.

verdict.summary: In do_put's multi-line character-mode path, newp is sized as STRLEN(ptr) + totlen + 1 where totlen = STRLEN(y_array[0]), but the buffer is then filled with STRCPY(newp, y_array[y_size - 1]) / STRCAT(newp, ptr). For any MCHAR register with y_size > 1 whose last line is longer than the first (a register an attacker produces by yanking text spanning a newline), the strcpy-family copy writes strlen(y_array[y_size-1]) + 1 bytes into a region sized for strlen(y_array[0]) + 1, a heap buffer overflow with attacker-controlled content and length. The subsequent memmove at the same site copies yanklen + 1 bytes into an exact-fit tail only because the first copy already corrupted the heap. No check anywhere in the function relates the allocation size to the string actually copied.

evidence.reason: Buffer is sized from STRLEN(ptr) + totlen + 1, but totlen was just reassigned to STRLEN(y_array[y_size - 1]) AFTER this alloc's inputs were fixed — while yanklen (used implicitly by the later memmove sizing logic and set from y_array[0]) remains the length of the FIRST register line. STRCPY copies strlen(y_array[y_size-1]) + 1 bytes into a buffer sized for strlen(y_array[0]) + 1 tail; whenever the register's last line is longer than its first line, this overflows the heap allocation with attacker-controlled bytes. Trigger fully instantiated: charwise register with y_size = 2, y_array[0] = "a", y_array[1] = 5000 'A's, count = 1, FORWARD — alloc(STRLEN(ptr) + 2), then STRCPY writes 5001 bytes. No check on any path relates the allocated size to the copied string.

Origin of the mismatched length: yanklen is taken from the first register line while the multi-line path copies the LAST line (y_array[y_size - 1]) first; the allocation in the MCHAR y_size > 1 branch is computed from yanklen-derived totlen of the first line, creating the size/copy discrepancy that the STRCPY at line 440 exploits.

assumptions: STRCPY/STRCAT/STRMOVE are Vim macros for strcpy/strcat/memmove-based copies that write strlen(source)+1 bytes without bounds; alloc(n) allocates exactly n bytes and returns NULL on failure.

y_current register fields (y_type, y_width, y_size, y_array) are the yank-register state produced elsewhere in Vim; multi-line MCHAR registers are normal, user/attacker-producible state (yank spanning newlines), not a contract violation.
mb_head_off, lbr_chartabsize, getvcol, ml_get/ml_append/ml_replace behave per their Vim semantics on valid lines.
limitations: MBLOCK b_op_end.col can be computed as bd.textcol + totlen - 1 = -1 when totlen = 0 and bd.textcol = 0, but the only observable uses are struct-field writes and a cursor col explicitly clamped ('if (curwin->w_cursor.col > len) curwin->w_cursor.col = len;'), and totlen = 0 additionally requires y_width = -1, which cannot be instantiated from this code; recorded as non-exploitable here.

y_current TOCTOU: the function does check for register mutation during changed_lines() and errors out, but a hypothetical second swap between that check and the later y_array[y_size - 1] use has no exhibited re-entry window in this code; not instantiated.

Integer-scale issues in the MBLOCK path (int truncation of STRLEN, `yanklen + spaces` addition overflow feeding the guarded multiplication) require multi-GB register contents; the multiplication itself is guarded ('count > ((INT_MAX - (bd.startspaces + bd.endspaces)) / (yanklen + spaces))') but the addition is not; not the primary defect and not simulated to a concrete overflow primitive within this code.

MBLOCK inner block copies (mch_memmove/memset sequence) are correctly covered by the explicit INT_MAX multiplication-overflow check plus an allocation sized from the same expressions as the copies; the MCHAR simple case is covered by its own quoted check; both verified safe.

verdict.summary: No memory-safety, injection, or authz defect is present in this code. The only OOB-capable uses (argv[0], argv[1]) are guarded by exact argc equality checks in execution order; all string sinks use literal formats with allocating sprintf, and raw user option strings are passed as in-domain NUL-terminated arguments into libmount callees not shown here.

assumptions: Behavior of not-shown libmount callees (mnt_context_set_source/target, mnt_context_append_options, mnt_context_mount, append_fstab, print_all, exit_non_root, xasprintf) is assumed per their documented util-linux semantics: xasprintf allocates and error-exits on failure, and libmount context setters copy string arguments.
readwrite and other globals referenced are defined outside this snippet and were not analyzable.
mnt_context_is_restricted/canonicalization flags are assumed internally consistent with the actual uid, as this code relies on them for its non-root authorization checks.
limitations: Potential restricted-user mount scenarios (e.g. a non-root user supplying only --source or --target) are governed by checks inside mnt_context_mount and fstab user-option handling in libmount, which are not shown; an authorization gap there could not be instantiated from this code.
The deprecated --pass-fd option is accepted with only a warning; it consumes no file descriptor and presents no security state, so it is cosmetic.
