verdict.summary: strncpy copies up to sizeof(local.sun_path) bytes into sockaddr_un::sun_path without reserving a NUL terminator and without any length check on the attacker-controlled endpoint name; a path of length >= sizeof(sun_path) leaves sun_path unterminated, so the subsequent string uses (unlink, bind, chmod) read past the end of the stack struct and pass an out-of-bounds-derived path to filesystem syscalls.

evidence.reason: Root cause: strncpy with n == sizeof(local.sun_path) (108 bytes) never NUL-terminates when the attacker-controlled pipePath (copied from endpoint.name() at line 4, unbounded std::string, no length check anywhere) has length >= 108. Instantiated trigger: pipePath of exactly 108 bytes makes strncpy fill all 108 bytes of sun_path with no terminator; unlink(local.sun_path) then scans for NUL past the end of the stack struct local, an out-of-bounds stack read, and passes the garbage-suffixed path to the unlink syscall (same defect feeds bind at line 17 and chmod at line 20). No clamp, length check, sizeof-1 bound, or explicit terminator exists on any path (mention sweep: lines 4, 5, 14, 15, 16, 17, 20, 23, 24).

assumptions: endpoint.name() is produced by code not shown; per the width-domain rule its std::string content and length are treated as fully attacker-controlled with no narrowing.
FATAL_FAIL is a macro that throws/exits on negative returns (inferred from name and usage; internal to the project, not shown).
initServerSocket is an internal callee not shown; its behavior is not relied upon for any guard.
limitations: TOCTOU between unlink(local.sun_path) and ::bind (line 16 vs 17): a local filesystem attacker could race a symlink into place, but nothing in this code makes the containing directory attacker-writable; trigger precondition not instantiated, so speculative.

Window between ::bind and ::chmod (lines 17-20) where the socket file has umask-derived permissions rather than 0700; short race, exploitability depends on local directory permissions not established here.
Return value of ::listen(fd, 5) at line 18 is unchecked — robustness issue only, no security impact demonstrated.
bind passes sizeof(sockaddr_un) including possibly uninitialized tail bytes of local to the kernel; no path back to disclosure exists, so no info-leak finding.

verdict.summary: In create_cache_bins, the dependency-walk loop indexes the deps array (sized cache->hdr->imagesCount) with dep_index = depArray[k] & 0x7fff (up to 32767) with no check against imagesCount, and reads depArray[k] with an attacker-controlled start index and no bound against depListCount, allowing heap out-of-bounds write and read via a crafted dyld shared cache file (when the R_DYLDCACHE_FILTER feature is enabled).

evidence.reason: Root cause: depArray entries are attacker-controlled file data; the mask '& 0x7fff' bounds dep_index only to 32767, never to the imagesCount-sized deps allocation (line 19), and the loop has no bound on k against depListCount (termination relies solely on the attacker-supplied 0xffff sentinel). A crafted cache with, e.g., imagesCount=4, depListCount=8, extras[0].dependentsStartArrayIndex=0 and depArray[0]=0xfffe executes deps[32766]++ on a 16-byte heap allocation: heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787); the loop condition depArray[k] with attacker-chosen k and no 0xffff present walks past the depListCount-sized allocation: out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). img[dep_index] at line 83 is an additional OOB read of the same index.

Origin of the bound the sink violates: deps is allocated with the first header's imagesCount (attacker-controlled ut32 from the file, e.g. 4), while line 80 permits dep_index up to 0x7fff, so deps[dep_index]++ at line 81 writes far out of bounds; additionally j loops to hdr->imagesCount of each subheader (lines 58/102), so a subheader with a larger imagesCount also makes deps[j] (lines 59/65/75/103) out of bounds against this allocation.

assumptions: read_cache_images, read_cache_imgextra, get_lib_name, va2pa, carve_deps_at_address are internal callees not shown; the fields they fill (extras[].dependentsStartArrayIndex, img[], depArray contents) are treated as attacker-controlled file data per the width-domain rule, since this function is the intake point parsing the cache file.
The vulnerable code path requires the operator to enable the documented R_DYLDCACHE_FILTER feature; the attacker supplies the crafted cache file contents, so this does not block the trigger.
limitations: r_buf_read_at at line 112 (magicbytes) has its return value unchecked, so a failed read feeds uninitialized stack bytes into the magic switch (CWE-908); impact is limited to selecting a parse branch, recorded as minor.

The 'depListCount * 2' comparison at line 46 could wrap for depListCount >= 0x80000000, but both sides use the same wrapped expression and triggering would require a multi-gigabyte fread/allocation; speculative, not a primary finding.

verdict.summary: The loop bound `i < abbrev->count - 1` in parse_die subtracts 1 from the unsigned, attacker-influenced abbrev->count without any zero check; when a crafted DWARF file yields a decl with count == 0, the bound wraps to the unsigned maximum, and the loop performs out-of-bounds heap writes via memset(&die->attr_values[i], ...) starting at i = 0. Attacker-triggered heap buffer overflow (memory corruption) in the parser of untrusted binaries.

evidence.snippet:
for (i = 0; i < abbrev->count - 1; i++) {
		memset(&die->attr_values[i], 0, sizeof(die->attr_values[i]));
evidence.reason: Root cause: unsigned underflow in the loop bound `abbrev->count - 1`. abbrev->count is a struct field set by the (not shown) abbrev parser from the attacker-supplied file, so its domain is the full unsigned width including 0, and the mention sweep shows abbrev->count appears nowhere else in this function — no zero/range check, clamp, or wrap-safe form guards it. Instantiated trigger: count == 0 makes the bound SIZE_MAX-scale; the condition `0 < (0 - 1)` is true and the first iteration executes memset at &die->attr_values[0], already out of bounds of the zero-entry attr_values allocation, then continues writing attacker-influenced RzBinDwarfAttrValue data across the heap at increasing i — an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) reachable from a crafted input file.

assumptions: abbrev->count is an unsigned integer type (ut64/size_t per this codebase's conventions); on a signed type the count == 0 case would evaluate the bound as -1 and skip the loop, defusing the primary trigger.

die->attr_values is sized by the caller from abbrev->count (allocation not shown); if it were a large fixed-size array the overflow would merely start at a larger i, still out of bounds for the wrapped bound.
parse_attr_value is a project-internal callee whose semantics are not shown; its behavior is treated as an assumption that can neither cause nor prevent any trigger here.
limitations: buf_end - buf (line 9) can go negative/huge if the unchecked return of parse_attr_value ever advances buf past buf_end; this depends entirely on the unshown callee and is not instantiable from the given code.

The return value of parse_attr_value (line 9) is consumed without a NULL/range sentinel test before being reused as buf and in buf_end - buf; a defect only if the unshown callee can return such a sentinel, which cannot be assumed.
When count >= 1, the bound `count - 1` under-runs by one, skipping the last abbrev attribute definition — a functional under-parse with no demonstrated memory-safety effect in this code.
comp_dir points into attribute->string.content whose backing storage (debug_str or the parsed buffer) is managed outside this snippet; no lifetime defect is provable from the given code.

verdict.summary: In create_cache_bins, when the dyld cache contains an accel table, the file-derived index extras[j].dependentsStartArrayIndex initializes k with no bound against depListCount, and dep_index = depArray[k] & 0x7fff (up to 32767) indexes deps, an array sized from the unrelated field cache->hdr->imagesCount. A crafted dyld cache therefore causes both an unbounded out-of-bounds read of depArray (scan until an accidental 0xffff) and a fully attacker-positioned out-of-bounds heap write at deps[dep_index]++, i.e. heap memory corruption in the process parsing the file.

evidence.reason: k is initialized from the file-derived extras[j].dependentsStartArrayIndex with no bound against depListCount (the depArray allocation size), and the loop condition only tests content (depArray[k] != 0xffff), giving an unbounded out-of-bounds read. The mask & 0x7fff bounds dep_index only to 32767, but deps is allocated with cache->hdr->imagesCount entries; a cache with imagesCount=2 and depArray[1]=0x7fff makes deps[32767]++ write ~131 KB past an 8-byte heap allocation — attacker-positioned out-of-bounds write (CWE-787).

deps is sized from hdr[0]'s imagesCount only, yet it is later indexed by hdr->imagesCount of every sub-header (lines 58-59, 65, 75, 103) and by the masked dep_index (line 81), none of which is bounded to this size anywhere in the code; a sub-cache header with a larger imagesCount, or any dep_index up to 32767, writes past this allocation.

assumptions: read_cache_imgextra, read_cache_images, get_lib_name, va2pa, and the cache-header/accel field widths are internal callees/structures not shown in this code; their outputs are treated as attacker data at full declared width per the width-domain rule, and only their NULL/UT64_MAX sentinel checks present in this code are relied upon.

r_buf_fread_at / r_buf_read_at are treated as bounds-safe buffer readers per standard r2 semantics; the parsing code is reached when the operator enables the R_DYLDCACHE_FILTER feature, which selects the code path but does not constrain any of the attacker-derived index values.
limitations: The vulnerable filter path requires the operator to set the R_DYLDCACHE_FILTER environment variable; the corrupted values themselves are entirely file-derived, so this is a usage precondition, not an absent trigger input.
The eprintf output of file-derived lib names (lines 72, 88) is at most log-forging-grade (CWE-117) in a CLI tool and was not promoted to a finding.
strdup(scan + 1) and the file[256] handling (lines 125-144) were verified safe: the read length is checked against sizeof(file) and file[255] is forced to NUL before string use.

verdict.summary: display_dollar() clamps its colnr_T parameter only against negative values (`col_arg < 0 ? 0 : col_arg`) and never bounds it against the length of the current line before forming the pointer `p + col` passed to mb_head_off(), so any caller-supplied col greater than the line length yields an out-of-bounds read when mb_head_off dereferences that pointer.

evidence.reason: Sink: the pointer `p + col` is formed from the unvalidated parameter and passed into an indexing/scanning operation; col is never compared to the line length, so p + col can point far past the line buffer and mb_head_off dereferences it (out-of-bounds read). Trigger: col_arg = 1000000 (within the int domain of colnr_T) on a line of a few bytes under a multibyte encoding (has_mbyte true).
Origin: the only guard on the attacker-data parameter clamps the negative bound; the upper bound remains INT_MAX, so col reaches the sink unbounded above with respect to the line length.

assumptions: colnr_T is a signed 32-bit int, as in Vim's standard type definitions; hence the post-clamp domain of col is [0, INT_MAX].
mb_head_off(base, p) dereferences the byte at p to test for a multibyte continuation byte, per Vim's documented mbyte API semantics.
ml_get_curline() returns a valid pointer to the current line text for the current cursor position (Vim memline invariant); its unchecked return is noted but is not the primary defect.
has_mbyte is true under any multibyte encoding such as utf-8, which is standard editor configuration, not an attacker precondition.
limitations: The unchecked return of ml_get_curline() (line 17) would only be a defect if that internal callee can return a failure sentinel; for a valid cursor line Vim's memline layer guarantees a non-NULL line, so it is not counted as a primary candidate.

curs_columns(FALSE) at line 20 consumes w_cursor.col which may exceed the line length; that internal callee is documented to handle arbitrary cursor columns when recomputing screen position, so no in-code defect is attributed to that call.
The out-of-bounds read is a read primitive (potential crash or info-influence); no out-of-bounds write path was found in this function.

verdict.summary: copy_page_to_iter_pipe partially initializes a reused pipe_buffer slot (ops, page, offset, len) but never clears buf->flags, publishing the buffer via pipe->head = i_head + 1 with stale PIPE_BUF_FLAG_CAN_MERGE left by a previous anonymous-pipe occupant of the slot. A subsequent write to the pipe then merges attacker data into the page cache of a read-only spliced file (dirty pipe, CVE-2022-0847), enabling arbitrary file-content overwrite and privilege escalation.

evidence.reason: Root cause: this block initializes every field of the newly published pipe_buffer except buf->flags; the mention sweep over all buf field references (lines 21, 23, 25, 35-39) shows no assignment, clear, or mask of flags anywhere in the code, so a stale PIPE_BUF_FLAG_CAN_MERGE from a prior occupant of the ring slot survives and the buffer is published at line 41, giving the merge-into-page-cache permission (dirty pipe, CVE-2022-0847).

Origin of the tainted state: the ring slot selected here is reused memory whose fields (notably buf->flags) retain values from earlier anonymous-pipe buffers set with PIPE_BUF_FLAG_CAN_MERGE; this code selects the slot and, per the sink evidence, republishes it without clearing those stale flags.

assumptions: sanity(i), pipe_full, get_page, and page_cache_pipe_buf_ops are internal callees not shown; their semantics (iterator consistency check, ring-full test, refcount increment, page-cache buffer ops) are assumed per standard kernel behavior and are not guards for buf->flags.
pipe->ring_size is assumed to be a power of two so that i_head & p_mask bounds the slot index; this is an unquoted kernel allocation invariant but is not related to the primary defect.
limitations: The final merge that turns the stale flag into a page-cache write happens in the pipe write path (not shown), but this is the fully characterized dirty-pipe consumption of PIPE_BUF_FLAG_CAN_MERGE; per the analysis rules the uninitialized/stale attacker-influenced value reaching merge-permission control flow is the defect at this code's publication site, so it is not demoted.
The merge fast path at lines 23-27 is correctly guarded by offset == off && buf->page == page; no secondary candidate survived.

verdict.summary: stl_remove_degenerate writes through attacker-influenced neighbor indices read from stl->neighbors_start fields whose producer is not shown: neighbor1/2/3 are used to index neighbors_start after only a '!= -1' sentinel test (no range bound), and (vnot* + 1) % 3 yields a negative index for vnot values <= -2, producing heap out-of-bounds writes at lines 63-64, 67-68, and 75.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write: neighbor1 (attacker-file-derived int field, full int domain per width-domain rule) indexes neighbors_start with only a '!= -1' sentinel check and no range validation; e.g. neighbor1 = 999999999 reaches this write. Independently, vnot1 <= -2 makes (vnot1 + 1) % 3 negative (C99 truncating modulo), e.g. vnot1 = -2 gives index -1. Trigger simulated from line 12 through line 63 with concrete values; result is heap memory corruption with a partially attacker-influenced value.

Origin of the tainted index: neighbor values are read from struct fields set by the not-shown STL loading/connectivity code; no quoted producer contract narrows them, and no validation occurs between this read and the write on line 63.

assumptions: The stl pointer is assumed non-NULL; NULL would crash at line 12 but the producer/caller contract is not shown.
stl_remove_facet and stl_update_connects_remove_1 are project-internal callees not shown; their handling of the raw indices passed at lines 50, 53, 22, 71, 74 is unknown.
The neighbors_start and which_vertex_not fields are treated as attacker-data under the width-domain rule because their producer (STL file processing) is not part of the given code.
limitations: The facet parameter indexes facet_start and neighbors_start without any bounds check (lines 14-17, 26-37, 45-46, 57-60); this is a contract with the internal caller that cannot be quoted, so it was not counted as a primary finding.
stl_update_connects_remove_1 may be called with -1 (line 50 or 53 when both neighbors are -1); impact depends on an unshown callee and was not counted as primary.

verdict.summary: update_topline() performs no memory, copy, format, or injection operations on attacker-derived data. All loops it owns are bounded by quoted checks executed in order (lnum >= ml_line_count, n >= halfheight, lnum <= 0, line_count > w_height+1, loff.lnum < w_botline), each edge-tested at 0, 1, one-past-limit, and extreme scrolloff values. Signed arithmetic on 'scrolloff' can wrap at LONG_MAX scale, but the wrapped values feed only scroll-strategy comparisons and never reach a size, index, or copy sink. Safety of hasFolding/botline_forw calls rests on editor-state invariants maintained in code not shown, with no raw out-of-domain offset computed here.

assumptions: Internal callees hasFolding(), hasAnyFolding(), botline_forw(), diff_check_fill(), check_top_offset(), validate_botline(), scroll_cursor_top/bot/halfway(), and validate_cursor() behave per their Vim semantics (fold start/end clamped to the buffer, botline_forw advances a display line); their implementations are not shown.

Editor-state fields w_cursor.lnum, w_topline, w_botline, and b_ml.ml_line_count are maintained within [1, ml_line_count] by Vim's cursor/window code outside this function; this code adds no local re-validation but also computes no raw offset from them.
Global p_so / window w_p_so ('scrolloff') are set by the option layer not shown; whether a modeline can instantiate extreme values is not determinable from this code.
limitations: Signed overflow candidate: 'curwin->w_topline + *so_ptr' and 'curwin->w_botline - *so_ptr' can wrap if 'scrolloff' (long, producer unshown) is near LONG_MAX/LONG_MIN (CWE-190). The wrapped values are consumed only by loop conditions (which remain bounded by lnum <= 0, lnum >= ml_line_count, line_count > w_height+1) and by strategy comparisons (n vs halfheight, line_count vs w_height+1); no memory size, index, or copy length uses them, so the impact chain is not instantiated in this code.

'int save_so = *so_ptr;' truncates a long option; restoring after an scrolloff > INT_MAX set by the operator corrupts that option value — functional misconfiguration, no security effect per the impact model.

Potential non-termination of the botline_forw while loop if botline_forw() failed to advance loff.lnum; the callee is not shown and is assumed to advance, and no memory access occurs inside the loop in this code.

Possible re-entrancy through a redraw callback before '*so_ptr = save_so;' restores a temporarily modified 'scrolloff'; no re-entry point (callback registration, lock release, signal path) is exhibited in this code, so the window is speculative.

verdict.summary: The bytecode interpreter consumes register operands (a, b, c), pool/symbol indices, and jump offsets fetched directly from irep bytecode with no validation against irep->nregs/ilen/slen/plen. The VM stack is sized only by irep->nregs (mrb_stack_extend(mrb, (irep->nregs < 4) ? 4 : irep->nregs)), so executing an attacker-supplied precompiled irep with an operand such as a=0xFF against a 4-slot stack performs an out-of-bounds read and write of mrb_value slots on the interpreter's stack (regs[a] = regs[b]), and unchecked pc += (int16_t)a in OP_JMP allows fetching/executing beyond the instruction sequence. The only ilen bound is inside a debug-only mrb_assert. This is memory corruption in the embedding process from untrusted bytecode.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write sink: the register operand `a` (uint32_t filled from raw bytecode, full 8-bit domain 0..255, up to 0xFFFF via OP_EXT paths) indexes regs (mrb->c->ci->stack), which is sized only by mrb_stack_extend(mrb, (irep->nregs < 4) ? 4 : irep->nregs). No check, clamp, mask, or allocation anywhere ties `a` to irep->nregs. Instantiated trigger: attacker-supplied irep with nregs=4 and an OP_MOVE operand a=255 writes 251 mrb_value slots past the 4-slot stack, corrupting the host process. Same unguarded class repeats at regs[a+1..a+3], syms[b], pool[b], irep->reps[b], and the regs[a+idx] loop writes in OP_APOST.

Origin of the tainted data: irep (its iseq operand bytes, nregs, ilen, pool, syms) is consumed from proc->body.irep whose producer (compiler or .mrb loader) is not shown in this code. The only integrity check is a commented-out assert (line 3, /* mrb_assert(MRB_PROC_CFUNC_P(proc)) */), so every field arrives at its full declared width and the interpreter is the last line of defense for these values.

assumptions: The FETCH/READ macros (not shown) deliver raw 8/16-bit operands from irep->iseq without bounds narrowing; nothing in the shown code masks or clamps them after fetch.

Reachability assumes the embedding application can execute an irep originating from untrusted data (e.g., mrb_load_irep on a precompiled file); mrb_vm_exec is the raw-instruction execution helper and was judged as intake per discipline 4.
limitations: If the deployment only ever executes ireps produced by mruby's own trusted compiler in-process, the operands are compiler-generated rather than attacker-supplied; under this rubric that is an unquoted external contract, not a guard in this code.

The debug-only mrb_assert(a >= 0 && a < irep->ilen) in OP_JMPUW provides an ilen bound only in debug builds (compiled out under MRB_NDEBUG) and only after first use; recorded as part of the same missing-validation root cause, not a separate finding.

Quoted guards that were verified and dismissed: OP_GETUPVAR/OP_SETUPVAR 'b < MRB_ENV_LEN(e)', OP_ARGARY/OP_BLKPUSH 'MRB_ENV_LEN(e) <= m1+r+m2+1', and the NULL/type checks in OP_EXCEPT/OP_RESCUE/OP_RAISEIF/OP_SUPER correctly protect their respective sinks.

Untrusted-bytecode scenarios confined to crashing only the script author's own process at equal privilege with no corruption would be robustness issues; here the sinks are out-of-bounds read/write primitives, which are corruption regardless.

verdict.summary: The only pointer use, prog->type, is guarded by the quoted NULL check 'if (prog) {' that precedes it in execution order with no bypass; the int parameter dominify only controls whether a constant newline is printed and reaches no dangerous sink; the internal callee calls receive only in-domain arguments (constant -1, 0, and a NULL-checked pointer).

assumptions: pstmlist, pstm, and nl are project-internal callees not shown; their behavior is an assumption, but this code passes them only in-domain arguments (constants -1 and 0, and a pointer already NULL-checked), so per the thin-wrapper rule no defect is attributable to these call sites.
A non-NULL prog is assumed to point to a valid js_Ast, per the internal contract of the parser that produced it; the producer is not shown.
The global minify may be read or written by code not shown, but within this function it is unconditionally assigned from dominify before this function's own reads.
limitations: If the not-shown callees pstmlist/pstm mishandle the AST, that defect lives in code not given and cannot be judged here; this code passes them no attacker-derived raw offsets, sizes, or indices.

prog->type is a field read on a pointer that is only NULL-checked, not validity-checked; forging a non-NULL invalid pointer would require the producer (not shown) to violate its contract, which is a speculative precondition.

verdict.summary: In the BMP v4/v5 header branch, the attacker-controlled field biSize (108 or 124) is used as ReadOK(fd, buffer, biSize - 4), reading 104 or 120 file bytes into the 64-byte stack buffer declared at the top of input_bmp_reader, producing an out-of-bounds stack write of up to 56 attacker-controlled bytes. No statement anywhere in the function bounds the read length to sizeof(buffer).

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write (CWE-787): the branch guard 'Bitmap_File_Head.biSize == 108 || Bitmap_File_Head.biSize == 124' admits biSize values that make the read length biSize - 4 equal 104 or 120 bytes, but 'buffer' is 'unsigned char buffer[64]' (line 4). ReadOK writes attacker-controlled file content past the end of the 64-byte stack array; the mention sweep over every use of buffer and biSize found no clamp, sizeof check, or cap anywhere on any path.

Origin of the tainted size: biSize is parsed directly from 4 attacker-controlled file bytes with no range validation at parse time; the only downstream constraint is the branch condition at lines 189-190, which admits the overflowing values 108 and 124.

assumptions: ReadOK(fd, dest, n) reads exactly n bytes from fd into dest (the semantics every call site in this function, including the error handling, depends on); its definition is not shown in the given code.
ToL/ToS are little-endian readers of 4/2 bytes; their definitions are not shown.
The declared types of the global structs Bitmap_File_Head and Bitmap_Head are not shown; their fields are treated as 32-bit values per the BMP format and the ToL/ToS parses.
BI_BITFIELDS, BI_RGB, BI_RLE4, BI_RLE8 constants are not shown but are treated as the standard BMP compression enumerators.
limitations: ColormapSize = (bfOffs - biSize - 14) / Maps can go negative (e.g. bfOffs = 0, biSize = 40) and only the upper bound is capped ('if (ColormapSize > 256) ColormapSize = 256;'); the negative value reaches ReadColorMap, whose body is not shown, so an OOB inside that callee could not be instantiated in this code. When biClrUsed == 0 and biBitCnt <= 8, ColormapSize is overwritten with 1 << biBitCnt (max 256), which is safe.

The return of ReadImage is stored in image_storage without a NULL sentinel check before at_bitmap_init, and biWidth is truncated to unsigned short after being validated up to ~0x7fffffff/biBitCnt; both at_bitmap_init and ReadImage are not shown, so impact there is speculative.
fseek(fd, bfOffs, SEEK_SET) ignores its return value; a failed seek only mispositions subsequent reads and is a robustness issue, not a security impact in this code.
The trailing '////' on line 54 is a stray comment marker with no functional effect.

verdict.summary: The command-line editor loop is not vulnerable as given. Every memory access consuming keystroke-derived or cursor-index state is guarded by a correctly-operator'd bounds check in execution order ('if (ccline.cmdpos >= ccline.cmdlen) break;', 'if (ccline.cmdpos == 0) goto cmdline_not_changed;', 'ccline.cmdpos > 0' before the 'cmdbuff[cmdpos - 1]' peek), the Ctrl_U compaction loop's indices are provably within the old length by this code's own arithmetic, mb_char2bytes writes at most 6 bytes into the fixed-size IObuff, and the recursion cap 'depth == 50' is exact because depth changes only by +/-1 with a decrement on every exit path.

assumptions: The invariants 'ccline.cmdpos <= ccline.cmdlen' and 'ccline.cmdbuff is allocated with room for cmdlen+1 and NUL-terminated' are maintained by helpers not shown (init_ccline, put_on_cmdline, alloc/realloc logic); the safety of the Ctrl_U 'ccline.cmdbuff[ccline.cmdlen] = NUL;' write rests on that unquoted contract.

Internal callees (nextwild, cmdline_erase_chars, cmdline_insert_reg, put_on_cmdline, trigger_cmd_autocmd, bracketed_paste) are assumed to honor their Vim-internal contracts; their return sentinels (OK/FAIL/CMDLINE_CHANGED/GOTO_NORMAL_MODE) are checked at each call site in this code.
On 'init_ccline(firstc, indent) != OK' the function returns a possibly NULL ccline.cmdbuff; safe handling is a caller contract not shown.
limitations: If the unshown buffer-management helpers ever allowed ccline.cmdlen to exceed the allocated size, the Ctrl_U terminator write 'ccline.cmdbuff[ccline.cmdlen] = NUL;' would become an out-of-bounds write; no statement in this code can produce that state, so the trigger is not instantiated here.

The 'depth == 50' check uses equality rather than >=; this is safe only because depth is incremented and decremented by exactly 1 on every path (all exits converge on theend, which decrements). A future multi-increment path would silently bypass the cap.

Keystrokes may originate from stuffed typebuf (mappings, :normal) potentially influenced by a malicious script; within this code all such values are compared against constants, clamped by guards, or encoded with bounded writers before any memory use.

verdict.summary: thread_call is Squirrel's thread-delegate 'call' handler. The only attacker-influenced values (argument count from sq_gettop and stack contents) are confined by exact guards: the loop bound i < nparams+1 admits only valid stack slots 2..nparams at both boundary values, and the OT_THREAD type test precedes every _thread(o) dereference, with the wrong-type arm throwing before any use. The sq_call count equals the number of items this code pushes. The remaining candidates (calling a suspended or non-idle thread, pop-after-suspension corruption, gettop+1 overflow) all have impact chains that live inside the not-shown sq_call/SQVM machinery or require unreachably large stacks, so they are speculative in this code.

assumptions: Native closures registered with the VM are invoked with 'this' present at stack index 1; this is runtime machinery not shown in the snippet, so stack_get(v,1) is treated as always valid rather than attacker-triggerable.

sq_move(target, v, i) pushes onto the target thread's dynamically growing stack (SQVM::Push/GrowStack), so the pushes at lines 6-8 cannot overflow a fixed target stack; this behavior is not shown in the snippet.
The target thread's stack is assumed to hold the creation-time closure at its base (pushed by sq_newthread, not shown); sq_call's positional closure lookup GetUp(-(nparams+1)) depends on this layout.
sq_call with retval=SQTrue and SQ_SUCCEEDED implies a return value on top of the target stack, which licenses sq_move(v,_thread(o),-1) and sq_pop(_thread(o),1).
limitations: Thread-state confusion: this code never checks _thread(o)->_state before pushing and calling. A script could call t.call() on a suspended or running thread (e.g., t.call(); t.call() after a suspend), making sq_call's positional closure lookup operate on a non-pristine stack. Any resulting frame misalignment or type-confused dispatch occurs entirely inside the not-shown sq_call/SQVM::Execute, so the impact chain is not instantiable from this snippet; the precondition to exclude it (state check) does not exist here.

If sq_call can return success while leaving the target suspended (not shown), sq_pop(_thread(o),1) at line 11 could pop a slot belonging to the suspended frame; depends on unshown sq_call suspension semantics.
stack_get(v,1) executes before any check; an empty calling stack would read out of bounds, but no attacker-visible path can invoke a native closure without its 'this' slot.
nparams+1 at line 7 could only wrap with a stack depth near SQInteger max, unreachable because stack depth is bounded by real allocation.

verdict.summary: display_dollar() uses the unvalidated parameter col as a raw byte offset into the current line buffer at the mb_head_off() call (p + col) without checking that col lies within the line length; any col beyond the NUL terminator (or negative) produces an out-of-bounds read at the call site.

evidence.reason: col (full int-width colnr_T domain, producer not shown, narrowed nowhere in this code) is added to the line pointer p from ml_get_curline() and passed to mb_head_off, which inspects the byte at that address. With col = strlen(line)+k or a negative value, p + col points outside the NUL-terminated line buffer, so the access reads out of bounds; the mention sweep found no length check, clamp, or mask on col anywhere in the function, and the missing guard at this call site is the defect.

Origin of the tainted value: col enters as a parameter whose producer is not shown in this code; its only mentions are the assignment curwin->w_cursor.col = col (line 10) and the out-of-bounds sink p + col (line 17), with no validation on any path.

assumptions: colnr_T is an int-width signed column type (per Vim's typedef), so col's instantiable surface is the full signed-int domain; no statement of this code narrows it.
ml_get_curline() returns the NUL-terminated current line, whose valid index domain is 0..strlen(line); has_mbyte is true in any multibyte/UTF-8 configuration, which gates execution INTO the sink.

mb_head_off is a project-internal Vim callee not shown; per Vim semantics it inspects the byte at its second argument, but the defect stands even on pointer-arithmetic grounds alone since p + col itself leaves the buffer's domain for col > strlen(line).
limitations: The caller of display_dollar is not shown; per the width-domain rule col is treated as attacker-data. In real Vim, callers derive col from cursor state which can exceed the line length (Replace/virtualedit-style states), matching known editor OOB reports; a proven in-tree caller bound of col <= line length would narrow the trigger, but no such contract is quotable here.

curs_columns(FALSE) at line 19 also consumes the tainted w_cursor.col; any misuse there is inside an unshown callee and shares the same root cause (unvalidated col stored at line 10) as the primary finding at line 17.

The subtraction curwin->w_cursor.col -= mb_head_off(...) is bounded below by 0 only because mb_head_off scans backwards no farther than its base argument p (unshown callee); it is not an independent underflow defect.

verdict.summary: This parser helper passes lexer-produced, typed values only as opaque arguments to internal callees (str_checkname, singlevaraux, codestring, luaK_indexed); no memory access, copy length, allocation size, index, or injection sink in this code consumes attacker data, and no missing guard at any local sink exists.

assumptions: str_checkname never returns a failure sentinel that this code dereferences; this code performs no direct dereference of varname, and the callee is not shown (unquoted internal contract).

singlevaraux resolves the environment variable ls->envn successfully, leaving var->k != VVOID; the lua_assert at line 7 is compiled out in release builds and is not a runtime guard, but no local memory sink depends on this invariant.
codestring and luaK_indexed accept the passed expdesc/parser-state arguments without out-of-domain use; their implementations are not shown.
limitations: Candidate C2 (release-build no-op lua_assert after the env lookup, followed by luaK_indexed consuming var) is speculative: the state var->k == VVOID after the env lookup cannot be produced by any statement in this code, and the parser setup guaranteeing _ENV exists is outside the snippet.
The lexer and parser engine (llex.c / lparser.c internals) that actually process attacker source bytes are not shown; if a defect exists in this unit it would reside there, not in these 11 lines.

verdict.summary: The only trust-boundary data (flow selector fl and family, derived from the packet being looked up) flows exclusively into xfrm_policy_lookup_bytype, whose NULL and ERR_PTR sentinels are both checked before any dereference (`if (pols[1])` / `if (IS_ERR(pols[1])`), with pols[0] guarded at entry by `!pols[0]` and `IS_ERR(pols[0])`. The loop bound `i < *num_pols` can reach index 1 only through the guarded `(*num_pols)++` on the validated-pols[1] path, so no in-code path dereferences a NULL or error pointer. Remaining hazards (entry *num_pols outside {0,1,2}, undersized pols array, possible double-put if an unshown caller also frees on the error return) depend on the in-kernel caller violating an implicit contract — no trust-boundary party can instantiate them.

verdict.summary: All allocation, mapping, hardware-read, and format sinks in this PCIe probe helper are guarded by quoted sentinel or bounds checks in execution order (iwl_trans_alloc/alloc_percpu/pcim_iomap_table NULL checks, hw_rev validation, sizeof-bounded snprintf with literal format), and no value crossing a trust boundary reaches a memory, size, index, or injection sink unguarded. verdict.summary: This PCRE2 JIT helper walks compiler-generated bytecode and computes a private-data length. Every memory-relevant sink (the default-arm use of next_opcode's return, the optimized_cbracket index from GET2, the pointer advances driven by PRIVATE_DATA/GET/cc[1] fields, the recurse_check_bit offsets) has no runtime guard inside this function; their safety rests entirely on the well-formedness of the bytecode window, a precondition this code itself asserts (SLJIT_ASSERT(cc != NULL), SLJIT_ASSERT(cc == ccend), SLJIT_ASSERT(PRIVATE_DATA(cc) != 0)). Those fields are written by earlier passes of the same in-process compiler, not by pattern text, so no trust-boundary party can instantiate an out-of-domain value without a separate bug in the unshown compilation stage. All candidates are therefore speculative, not vulnerabilities in this code.

assumptions: next_opcode(common, cc) advances cc by the opcode's size and returns NULL for an unrecognized opcode (callee not shown).
recurse_check_bit indexes common->recurse_bitset, which recurse_bitset_size covers for every private-data/ovector offset assigned by earlier compile passes (callee and init not shown).
PRIVATE_DATA, GET, GET2, and cc[1] read administrative fields written by earlier passes of the same compile job; the pattern author controls character and mark content but not these field values.
SLJIT_ASSERT compiles to a no-op in non-debug builds; it documents invariants but enforces them only in debug builds.
get_class_iterator_size returns a non-negative size for the class opcode at cc + size (callee not shown).
limitations: C1 (CWE-476-shaped): in a release build, if the not-shown compiler ever emits an opcode next_opcode does not recognize, the default arm leaves cc == NULL (SLJIT_ASSERT(cc != NULL) is a no-op) and the loop condition while (cc < ccend) stays true, so switch(*cc) dereferences NULL. The trigger requires malformed compiler-generated bytecode and could not be instantiated from the given code.

C2: common->optimized_cbracket[offset] with offset = GET2(cc, 1 + LINK_SIZE) has no local bound against the capture-group count; an out-of-range index requires the compile stage to write a group number exceeding the bracket count, which contradicts the asserted layout invariants.

C3: pointer advances driven by stream fields (cc += PRIVATE_DATA(cc + 1) for OP_KET, alternative = cc + GET(cc, 1) for OP_COND, cc += 1 + 2 + cc[1] for the MARK family, size = GET(cc, 1) for XCLASS) are bounded only by while (cc < ccend); a negative or oversized field would walk reads outside the window. Requires malformed bytecode.

If an application compiles patterns supplied by an untrusted party, any future compiler-stage bug surfacing here would be at least a denial of service; runtime checks (NULL test after next_opcode, range check on the GET2 group number) would harden this function as the last line of defense.

verdict.summary: The only attacker-controlled value with sinks inside this code, catalog_size (from the on-disk header), is range-checked by 'if (s->catalog_size > INT_MAX / 4) goto fail' before the allocation, the read, and the byte-swap loop. At the admitted maximum (536870911), the product 2147483644 does not wrap 32-bit arithmetic and fits the read-length parameter; the pread length and the allocation use the identical expression; and the loop bound matches the allocated entry count exactly, so the in-place le32_to_cpus writes stay in bounds. Other attacker-controlled fields (tracks, nb_sectors, catalog entry contents) have no consumer within this code.

assumptions: The declared type of s->catalog_size (BDRVParallelsState) is not shown in the given code; the guard analysis assumes the unsigned 32-bit field used by QEMU's actual driver (le32_to_cpu returns uint32_t). If the field were signed int, header values >= 0x80000000 would convert negative, pass the check, and reach g_malloc as a huge size_t (abort/DoS); this scenario is not instantiable from the given code alone.

bdrv_pread semantics (full-read-or-negative-errno vs. positive short counts) are not shown; the code checks only 'ret < 0'. If a short read were possible, g_malloc'd (non-zeroed) catalog_bitmap would be partially uninitialized, but no use of that data occurs within this code.

Zero-initialization of bs->opaque is not shown; the fail path does g_free on the unassigned s->catalog_bitmap field when the first pread fails. QEMU allocates opaque with g_malloc0 (g_free(NULL) is safe), but this is unquoted in the given code.
limitations: This is the post-2014 fixed version of QEMU's parallels_open. The historical vulnerability (CVE-2014-0142 pattern) existed precisely because the 'INT_MAX / 4' check was absent, letting catalog_size*4 wrap so the 'for (i = 0; i < s->catalog_size; i++) le32_to_cpus(&s->catalog_bitmap[i])' loop wrote out of bounds; the quoted check now bounds all three sinks.

Consumers of other unvalidated attacker fields are not in this snippet: s->tracks (division/indexing in parallels_read, potential divide-by-zero), bs->total_sectors, and the catalog entry values used as cluster offsets without bounds checks. These were additional historical parallels-driver defects, but their impact chains lie entirely in code not given and cannot be judged here.
An attacker can force a bounded ~2GB allocation (catalog_entries = 536870911) from a tiny header; this is capped by the guard, so it is at most modest resource consumption, not amplification.
g_malloc aborts the process on allocation failure (GLib semantics), so OOM under the 2GB cap is environment-dependent, not attacker-controlled memory corruption.

verdict.summary: This is mount(8) main() from util-linux. The only trust boundary is a restricted (non-root) invoker of a privileged binary. Every dangerous option path is guarded by the quoted pre-switch check (mnt_context_is_restricted && !strchr("hlLUVvpris", c) && c != TARGET && c != SOURCE -> exit_non_root), which runs before the switch on every iteration; positional argv uses are guarded by the argc==1 / argc==2 branch conditions; source+target combinations for non-root are rejected in branches B, C, and D before the setters; the only string formatting uses literal formats with allocating xasprintf; and the only allocation (mnt_new_context) is NULL-checked at first use. assumptions: libmount callees (mnt_context_set_source/target, mnt_context_append_options, mnt_context_set_fstype, append_fstab) are not shown; their string-copy and fstab user-option enforcement semantics are taken as the documented libmount contract (discipline 3 internal-callee limitation). No local defect depends on them: no local buffer, length, or index is derived from their returns.
exit_non_root() and option_to_longopt() are internal and not shown; this code itself calls exit_non_root(NULL) in branches B/C/D, so NULL input is an intended input for that callee.
xasprintf is taken to allocate and exit on failure per its util-linux contract; srcbuf lifetime (set then free) assumes mnt_context_set_source copies the string.
limitations: The allowed-option string "hlLUVvpris" does not include 't' (types): a restricted user passing -t/--types is rejected. This is over-rejection only (stricter behavior); the OFF-BY-ONE rule was applied at both bounds and omission from a rejection set cannot under-admit. Functional at most, not a security defect.

For a restricted user, an unknown option (c == '?') reaches exit_non_root(option_to_longopt(c, longopts)) before the default arm; option_to_longopt may return NULL for unmatched c. If the unshown callee dereferenced it unconditionally, that would be a robustness bug inside the callee crashing only the invoker's own process at equal privilege — not provable from this code.

Return codes of the mnt_context_* setters are ignored in several arms (e.g., mnt_context_set_source in cases 'L'/'U', TARGET, SOURCE), but no value consumed in this code derives from those returns, so no unchecked-sentinel use exists locally.

assumptions: The caller supplies pols as an array with at least 2 elements: the code writes pols[1] unconditionally in the CONFIG_XFRM_SUB_POLICY branch (upstream caller declares struct xfrm_policy *pols[XFRM_POLICY_TYPE_MAX]). No statement in the given code documents or enforces this.

xfrm_nr struct fields are bounded at policy-creation time (XFRM_MAX_DEPTH) in code not shown; even at full u8 domain the *num_xfrms sum cannot exceed 510, so no integer overflow occurs in this function regardless.

xfrm_policy_lookup_bytype follows standard lookup semantics (may return NULL or ERR_PTR) and xfrm_pols_put releases the first *num_pols entries; both sentinels are locally tested at the use sites in this code.
limitations: C1 (speculative): the write 'pols[1] = xfrm_policy_lookup_bytype(...)' would be out of bounds if a caller provided a 1-element array; the array size is a caller contract not shown, and no attacker-controlled value reaches it.

C2/C3 (speculative): if a caller passed *num_pols >= 2 with unset pols[1..], the loop would dereference an unvalidated entry and xfrm_pols_put would operate on the ERR_PTR in pols[1]; this state is not producible by any statement of this code.
C4 (speculative): the IS_ERR(pols[0]) path leaves *num_xfrms unmodified; impact requires a caller that ignores the negative return, which is not shown.

C5 (speculative): *num_xfrms can reach the sum of main and sub-policy template counts (up to 2*XFRM_MAX_DEPTH); whether the caller's XFRM_MAX_DEPTH-sized state array rejects the excess is decided in xfrm_tmpl_resolve, not shown here.
No lock or RCU read-side critical section is visible in this snippet; lookup consistency depends on a caller-held RCU lock, which cannot be quoted here.

verdict.summary: No memory-safety or security defect is reachable. The pattern length is bounded against the string length by 'if (size > r_size(op1))' (correct operator: size==len admitted with count=0, size==len+1 rejected, so 'count = r_size(op1) - size' cannot wrap), the empty-pattern dereference is prevented by 'if (size == 0) goto found;' before 'ch = pat[0];', and the do-while visits exactly len-size+1 positions so all *ptr reads and memcmp(ptr, pat, size) windows stay inside the string. Simulated triggers (forward/backward matches, size==len, empty seek both directions, both strings empty) all produce pre/match/post objects whose byte pointers and rsizes provably lie within [op1->value.bytes, op1->value.bytes + r_size(op1)]. The only anomaly found is that a backward search with an empty seek constructs the match and post as zero-length strings at position 0 while the lengths correspond to a match at the end; this is memory-safe and content-indistinguishable, so it is recorded as a limitation, not a vulnerability.

assumptions: The operand stack contains at least 2 elements when the operator is dispatched (interpreter operator arg-count contract, not shown).
The push(2) macro checks operand-stack overflow before allowing writes to the new slots (standard Ghostscript operator macro, not shown).

check_read_type(*op1, t_string) / check_read_type(*op, t_string) reject non-string or non-readable operands with an error return, and a t_string object's value.bytes references r_size valid bytes (interpreter object-model invariant).
make_false/make_true write well-formed boolean objects into the named stack slot (standard macros, not shown).
limitations: Backward search with an empty seek ('size == 0' branching to found before 'if (!forward) ptr += count;') yields match and post as zero-length strings anchored at position 0 while pre covers the whole string; the correct backward result anchors the empty match at the end. All constructed objects remain in-bounds and empty strings are content-indistinguishable, so there is no memory-safety, disclosure, bypass, or amplification impact.
'uint size = r_size(op);' reads the rsize field before the type check; it is a plain struct-field read and is safe on any stack object, so no defect arises.
After a no-match loop exit, 'while (count--)' leaves count wrapped to UINT_MAX, but count is dead on that path ('make_false(op); return 0;'), so the wrap is unobservable.

verdict.summary: In string_scan_range, the 'smol optimization' guard `if (needle < to - 4)` performs unsigned 64-bit subtraction that wraps when `to < 4`, making the condition vacuously true. With a scan range smaller than 4 bytes (e.g. from=0, to=1, admitted by `if (len < 1 || len > ST32_MAX)`), `r_read_le32 (buf + (needle - from))` reads 4 bytes from a calloc buffer of 1-3 bytes, a heap out-of-bounds read of up to 3 bytes triggered by attacker-influenced scan-range values.

evidence.snippet:
if (needle < to - 4) {
			ut32 n1 = r_read_le32 (buf + (needle - from));
evidence.reason: Root cause: `to` is ut64 so `to - 4` wraps to a huge value when to < 4, defeating the guard; the guarded read then touches buf[needle-from .. +3] against a calloc(len,1) buffer with len = to - from in {1,2,3}. Trigger instantiated: from=0, to=1 passes the `len < 1 || len > ST32_MAX` check (len=1), allocation is 1 byte, and r_read_le32 reads 4 bytes, a heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted values: `from` and `to` are ut64 parameters whose producer is not shown in this code; per the width-domain rule their full 64-bit surface is instantiable, including to < 4 (e.g. ranges derived from tiny sections of a parsed untrusted binary), which the code never narrows.

r_utf_block_list returns parallel, sentinel-terminated block_list/freq_list arrays as the j-indexing loop assumes.

r_buf_read_at clamps reads to the underlying file buffer size (the '// may oobread' comment refers to reading past file end, not past the heap buffer); its ignored return value is benign because buf is calloc-zeroed.

r_utf8_encode writing 5-6 byte legacy sequences for runes >= 0x200000 could overflow the 4-byte margin at tmp+i, but no printable rune above 0x10FFFF was shown reachable and the callee is not shown; speculative.
bs->vaddr = str_start - pdelta + vdelta + baddr can wrap ut64 and misreport an address in analysis output; misrepresentation of a display address only, no memory-safety impact.
The freq_list/block_list parallel indexing trusts an unshown callee contract; no defect provable.
Impact of the confirmed OOB read is bounded: at most 3 bytes past a tiny heap chunk, the value only zero-tested (no disclosure), crash potential mainly under sanitized builds.

verdict.summary: thread_call ignores the SQ_ERROR failure sentinel of sq_reservestack(_thread(o), nparams + 3) and then unconditionally pushes the root table and nparams-1 attacker-controlled objects onto the target thread's stack (Push and sq_move loop). If the stack cannot be grown (stack overflow / allocation failure, inducible by a script through argument count and memory pressure), each Push/sq_move writes an SQObjectPtr past the end of the heap-allocated stack array, giving a scalable out-of-bounds heap write reachable from script through thread.call.

evidence.reason: The return value of sq_reservestack (SQ_ERROR when the target thread's stack cannot be grown) is not captured or tested anywhere in the function — the mention sweep of every statement referencing _thread(o), nparams, or stack capacity finds no if-check, error arm, clamp, or alternative reservation between the reserve call and the writes. When reservation fails at the exactly-at-limit boundary (target _top == _stack.size()), _thread(o)->Push(_thread(o)->_roottable) writes an SQObjectPtr one past the stack array and the sq_move loop then writes attacker-chosen script objects at successive out-of-bounds indices: a script-triggerable out-of-bounds heap write. The missing guard is a failure-sentinel test of the sq_reservestack result before the first Push.

assumptions: sq_reservestack, sq_gettop, sq_move, sq_call, Push, stack_get are Squirrel's own API; their stack-write/copy/index semantics are taken as documented standard-library behavior (Push writes the object at the current stack top and increments it; sq_move copies an object onto the target stack; sq_reservestack reserves stack space and returns SQ_OK or SQ_ERROR).
The target thread's stack is a heap-allocated array (sqvector of SQObjectPtr) whose capacity is only extended when ReserveStack succeeds.

Script-supplied values (the thread object, the argument count nparams, and the argument objects) are attacker-data per the width-domain rule; the embedding host is the operator across the trust boundary.
limitations: Re-entrancy/state issue (not counted as a primary finding): thread_call performs no check that the target thread's stack actually holds a callable object at the position sq_call computes as -(nparams+1), and no check of the thread's suspended/running state. Calling thread.call twice, or on a suspended thread, can make sq_call consume an arbitrary live or out-of-frame stack slot as the 'closure'. Whether the closure is consumed by a prior call depends on sq_call's unshown stack semantics, so this state cannot be produced by a quoted statement of this code alone; recorded as a state-consistency hazard rather than a primary defect.

sq_move(v,_thread(o),-1) (line 11) pushes the result onto the caller VM's stack with no reservation visible in this function; Squirrel's native-call machinery (not shown) is assumed to have reserved overhead there.

nparams + 3 cannot overflow in practice: SQInteger is a wide signed type and nparams is bounded by the caller's physically allocated stack; the reservation amount (nparams+3) does cover the nparams pushed items plus the return value with slack.

verdict.summary: SQClass::NewSlot writes val into the fixed-size member array _metamethods using the index returned by the unshown callee ss->GetMetaMethodIdxByName(key). The only local constraint is the sentinel test != -1; there is no bounds check, clamp, or mask anywhere on any path, so any returned index outside [0, MT_LAST), including one-past-the-limit and negative values, produces an out-of-bounds write of an attacker-supplied SQObjectPtr (type tag plus union holding object pointers) into the heap-allocated SQClass, i.e. memory corruption directly at the sink line.

evidence.reason: Root cause: unvalidated array index at the sink. mmidx's only producer is the unshown callee ss->GetMetaMethodIdxByName; the mention sweep over the whole function finds only its declaration (line 13), this sentinel test, and the use. The test excludes exactly the value -1 and admits every other SQInteger, so a returned index of MT_LAST (one-past-limit), a large positive value, or a negative value such as -2 reaches `_metamethods[mmidx] = val;` and writes the script-supplied SQObjectPtr out of bounds into the heap-allocated SQClass object (CWE-787). No bounds check, clamp, mask, modulo, or rejecting default arm exists anywhere in this code.

Origin of the taint: key and val are the member name and value supplied by script code crossing the interpreter trust boundary (a non-static handler consuming parsed script values at the newslot opcode / class-slot API). The attacker chooses the key string passed to GetMetaMethodIdxByName and the SQObjectPtr value written at the sink, instantiating the trigger input per the width-domain rule.

assumptions: SQObjectPtr's default constructor initializes temp to OT_NULL; the code relies on this at line 25 (`sq_type(temp) == OT_NULL`). The constructor is not shown; the reliance itself documents the intended contract.

_make_field_idx, _make_method_idx, _isfield, _member_idx macro semantics and the fixed size of _metamethods (MT_LAST) come from project headers not shown; _member_idx is treated as masking the stored index to the array's index range.
_members->Get writes the stored member descriptor and leaves temp untouched on failure (stays OT_NULL); SQTable::NewSlot updates an existing key in place rather than duplicating it.
Unshown class copy/clone construction copies the members table together with the _defaultvalues and _methods vectors, preserving the index invariants created at lines 33-34 and 44-45.
SQVM::IsEqual is assumed to always assign its output parameter isconstructor; it is an unshown callee.
limitations: In the complete upstream Squirrel source, GetMetaMethodIdxByName derives its result from a fixed internal metamethod-name table and returns an index below MT_LAST or -1, which would bound mmidx. That producer is not part of the given code, so per the width-domain rule the full SQInteger domain minus {-1} was treated as instantiable; real-world exploitability of the out-of-range trigger therefore depends on the unshown callee. Recorded here because it cannot demote the finding under the analysis rules, not because it was verified.
Member indices at or above 2^31 would truncate under the _member_idx mask (lines 9/37); reaching that scale requires on the order of 2^31 class members, which no path in this code can produce.

The _locked check at line 5 permits metamethod and static additions to classes that already have instances; this is by-design static-table behavior with no memory-safety or authorization effect observed in this code.
SQVM::IsEqual's output parameter would be read uninitialized at line 28 if the unshown callee could return without assigning it; no such path is shown.

verdict.summary: This is the post-CVE-2022-0843 (Dirty Pipe) fixed version of copy_page_to_iter_pipe. The decisive guard `buf->flags = 0;` clears stale pipe-buffer flags (including PIPE_BUF_FLAG_CAN_MERGE) before the buffer is published with `pipe->head = i_head + 1;`, and the merge path cannot reach a CAN_MERGE anonymous buffer because it requires page identity with the page-cache page. All other sinks are guarded in execution order: bytes is clamped by `if (unlikely(bytes > i->count)) bytes = i->count;` before every use (including `i->count -= bytes;`), ring indices are bounded by the mask `pipe->ring_size - 1`, and `if (pipe_full(i_head, p_tail, pipe->max_usage)) return 0;` rejects before any fresh-slot write. Remaining width-overflow candidates require an iov_iter count or within-page offset above 2^32 whose producers and harmful consumers are both outside this code, so no trigger with a security impact is instantiated.

assumptions: `sanity()`, `pipe_full()`, `get_page()`, and `page_cache_pipe_buf_ops` are same-project internals not shown in the snippet; `if (!sanity(i)) return 0;` is treated as an error-arm guard on iterator state but its checks cannot be enumerated here.

Pipe ring invariants (ring_size >= 2, bufs array allocated with ring_size entries) are maintained by unshown pipe allocation code; the mask `pipe->ring_size - 1` bounds all ring indices only if those invariants hold.
`struct pipe_buffer` field widths (offset, len, flags as unsigned int) are assumed from the kernel ABI for truncation analysis.
The sole caller path (copy_page_to_iter / splice) bounds `offset` to a within-page value and `bytes` to a page-segment length; this producer is not shown, so those bounds are not relied on as guards.
limitations: Historical Dirty Pipe primitive (CVE-2022-0843): stale CAN_MERGE flags on a page-cache pipe buffer. Neutralized here by the quoted `buf->flags = 0;` in execution order before publication; the merge path preserves flags only on buffers this function itself installed with flags 0.

`buf->len = bytes;` and `buf->len += bytes;` can truncate/wrap only for bytes at 2^32 scale, which requires the unshown syscall/import layer to hand this helper an iov_iter count above 4 GB (readv totals are capped near 2^31 by unshown code); the harmful use of a wrapped len would occur in unshown pipe consumers, so the impact chain is not instantiated.

`buf->offset = offset;` truncation needs a within-page offset >= 2^32 from the unshown caller; even then the stored offset addresses the same page, producing mispositioned data rather than memory unsafety.

NULL `page` or `i`, or a pipe with ring_size == 0 (which would make `p_mask` UINT_MAX), would crash or misindex, but no statement of this code produces those states; they require unshown caller or allocator invariants to be violated.

verdict.summary: All memory-access sinks in getcmdline_int() (cursor movement reads, the Ctrl-U compaction copy, the NUL sentinel writes, and history/return handling) are guarded in execution order by quotable bounds checks: 'if (ccline.cmdpos >= ccline.cmdlen) break;' caps every cursor-advance iteration, 'ccline.cmdpos > 0 &&' precedes both cmdbuff[cmdpos-1] reads, 'while (i < ccline.cmdlen)' bounds the Ctrl-U copy with reads provably confined to [old_cmdpos, old_cmdlen-1], 'if (depth == 50)' with paired ++/-- bounds recursion, and mb_char2bytes output (max 6 bytes) is far within IObuff. Remaining candidates (wim_flags[wim_index], key-name insertion, register paste, history browsing) have their entire impact chain inside internal callees not shown, so no trigger with a security impact is instantiable from this code.

assumptions: ccline.cmdbuff is maintained NUL-terminated at ccline.cmdbuff[ccline.cmdlen] with the allocation covering index cmdlen; this invariant is upheld by the unshown helpers (init_ccline, put_on_cmdline, cmdline_erase_chars) that this code calls. The K_RIGHT do-while read 'ccline.cmdbuff[ccline.cmdpos] != ' '' relies on it when cmdpos == cmdlen.

ccline.cmdpos <= ccline.cmdlen is a maintained invariant; the Ctrl-U subtraction 'ccline.cmdlen -= j' would underflow only if cmdpos > cmdlen, which no statement in this code can produce (every visible cmdpos write sets it to 0, cmdlen, or a bounded advance).
wim_index stays within the bounds of wim_flags[] as managed by the unshown cmdline_wildchar_complete(); this code only ever sets 'wim_index = 0' and passes &wim_index onward.
limitations: wim_flags[wim_index] is read twice with no local bounds check; an out-of-range index could only be produced inside the unshown callee cmdline_wildchar_complete(), so the impact chain is not instantiated in this code (speculative, callee-side if anything).

put_on_cmdline(get_special_key_name(c, mod_mask), -1, TRUE) and the paste/bracketed-paste/history/nextwild call sites pass raw keystroke-derived data into unshown internal helpers with no local validation; any misuse would occur inside those callees, which are not part of the given code.
The '==' in 'if (depth == 50)' would only be bypassed by a non-unitary depth increment; no statement in this code performs one, so no trigger exists (a '>=' would be strictly equivalent here).

Safe operation of the K_RIGHT read at cmdpos == cmdlen depends on the NUL-termination invariant held by unshown helpers; if that invariant were broken elsewhere the read would touch the terminator byte, still within the allocation under the stated assumption.

verdict.summary: In the tabline drag paths of do_mouse(), mouse_col is used to index the Columns-sized global array TabPageIdxs without any bounds check. The only mouse_col guard in the function, '&& mouse_col < Columns' (line 271), applies solely to the click branch and lacks a lower bound; the drag branches at lines 255-263 and 315-320 read TabPageIdxs[mouse_col] with a completely unvalidated mouse_col. Because in_tab_line persists (static, set only by a previously valid click), an attacker-controlled terminal/multiplexer mouse report (or a resize race) with mouse_col outside [0, Columns) during a drag causes an out-of-bounds heap read whose value is then used in tabpage_move()/goto_tabpage() index arithmetic.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read: TabPageIdxs is indexed with mouse_col on the drag path with no bounds check on any execution path. mouse_col is a terminal-decoded global (full int domain); the only guard in the function ('&& mouse_col < Columns', line 271) is in the sibling click branch and never runs here. Trigger: a valid click on the tabline sets the static in_tab_line (line 273), then a drag report with mouse_col >= Columns (or negative) reaches this line, e.g. mouse_col=200 with Columns=80, reading past the Columns-sized TabPageIdxs array; the OOB value c1 immediately feeds tabpage_move().

Same unguarded sink on the tabline-row drag path: after a prior valid click set in_tab_line, a drag with mouse_row == 0 and mouse_col outside [0, Columns) indexes TabPageIdxs out of bounds. The mouse_col < Columns guard sits only in the click branch (line 271) and is bypassed by the 'if (is_drag)' branch at line 255, so no bound reaches this use in execution order.

assumptions: TabPageIdxs is a global array sized Columns (its allocation in draw_tabline() is not shown); the code's own guard at line 271 ('&& mouse_col < Columns') is the quoted evidence that Columns is the valid index bound.

mouse_row, mouse_col, and mod_mask are globals set by the terminal-input decode layer, which is not shown; per the width-domain rule their surface is the full int domain and they are treated as attacker data (terminal/multiplexer/ssh peer or a resize race can supply values outside [0, Columns)).
tabpage_move(), goto_tabpage(), find_tabpage(), and get_mouse_button() are project-internal callees not shown; their behavior is not relied on to either trigger or protect the read.
limitations: The click-path guard at line 271 also lacks a lower bound, so a negative mouse_col would OOB-read at line 274 (TabPageIdxs[-1]); this is folded into the same root cause (no [0, Columns) validation of mouse_col) rather than emitted as a separate finding, since reachability of negative mouse_col at row 0 depends on the not-shown decode layer.

The value read out of bounds (c1) flows into goto_tabpage(c1), find_tabpage(-c1), and c1 - 1 arithmetic; any secondary misuse inside those not-shown callees is speculative (the local sentinel checks 'tp == curtab' and 'tp != NULL' are quoted and honored).

Whether mouse_col can exceed Columns at runtime depends on the decode layer or a resize race between terminal-reported coordinates and Vim's Columns; per the width-domain rule this is treated as attacker-data, but no specific decoder bug was shown.

verdict.summary: This PCI probe allocation routine consumes device-controlled data (MMIO hw_rev, config-space IDs, IRQ number) but every such value reaches only a sentinel check, width-safe arithmetic, a sizeof-bounded snprintf with a literal format string, or a kernel-validated IRQ request. All allocation and callee failure sentinels are checked before first use in execution order, and all error exits unwind resources in reverse allocation order. No attacker-derived size, index, offset, or pointer is passed into any memory, copy, or injection sink; no primary vulnerability is reachable in this code.

assumptions: iwl_trans_alloc zeroes the allocated memory; the read of trans_pcie->msix_enabled at 'if (trans_pcie->msix_enabled)' depends on the unshown callee iwl_pcie_set_interrupt_capa setting that field, and on zeroed allocation for inta_mask and other fields.
IWL_TRANS_GET_PCIE_TRANS is a container_of-style in-bounds accessor on the allocation returned by iwl_trans_alloc, whose NULL sentinel is checked in this code.
free_percpu treats NULL as a no-op (documented kernel semantic), so the alloc_percpu failure path through out_no_pci is safe.
cfg_trans comes from the driver's static device tables; its fields (gen2, use_tfh, device_family, pcie_l1_allowed) are driver-defined constants, not device-supplied numerics.
limitations: Speculative UAF window: if the unshown callee iwl_pcie_init_msix_handler partially registers devm-managed MSI-X IRQ handlers and then fails, 'goto out_no_pci' calls iwl_trans_free(trans) before devres cleanup releases those handlers, leaving a short window in which a handler could reference freed memory. The partial-registration step is not produced by any quoted statement in this code, so the trigger is not instantiated here.
The trust model treats the PCI device as the trust-boundary party; the MMIO-derived hw_rev is fully in-domain for this code but any downstream misuse of trans->hw_rev would occur in code not shown.

A hypothetical failure of iwl_pcie_set_interrupt_capa to set msix_enabled could cause an uninitialized-value branch, but the producer is not shown and neither branch outcome is a memory-safety sink in this code.

verdict.summary: The overflow guard at line 40 rejects only provider names >= 0xffff0000 bytes, but rrlen is a uint16_t (line 19) that truncates when the size_t sum at lines 45-49 (strlen(provider_name) + 15 + 4*sizeof(struct SignedCert) + 2) reaches 65536. For a provider_name of length 65519 - 4*S (e.g. 65023 when sizeof(struct SignedCert)=124), rrlen wraps to 0, malloc(0) returns a valid pointer, and snprintf(rr, rrlen - 1, ...) at line 55 receives size (size_t)-1 = SIZE_MAX, writing ~65KB of attacker-influenced bytes into a zero-size heap allocation: a heap out-of-bounds write. rrlen == 1 (sum == 65537) similarly leaves rr uninitialized and overflows via strlen(rr) at line 59.

evidence.reason: Missing-check site: this is the only length validation on provider_name, but its bound (~4.29e9) is orders of magnitude above the actual overflow point of the uint16_t rrlen (sum >= 65536, i.e. strlen(provider_name) >= 65519 - 4*sizeof(struct SignedCert)), so the 'integer overflow in rrlen calculation' the comment claims to guard against is not prevented; the (unsigned) cast also truncates a 64-bit size_t.

evidence.snippet:
rrlen = strlen(dnscenv->provider_name) +
                         strlen(ttl_class_type) +
                         4 * sizeof(struct SignedCert) + // worst case scenario
                         1 + // trailing double quote
                         1;
evidence.reason: Truncation origin: the size_t-valued sum (strlen(provider_name) + 15 + 4*sizeof(struct SignedCert) + 2) is stored into uint16_t rrlen, which silently wraps to 0 when the sum equals 65536 (e.g. provider_name length 65023 with a 124-byte SignedCert, which passes the line-40 guard).

Sink: with rrlen == 0, rrlen - 1 promotes to int -1 and converts to size_t SIZE_MAX; malloc(0) (line 50) returned a valid pointer so the !rr check passed, and snprintf writes strlen(provider_name)+16 attacker-influenced bytes into the zero-byte allocation, a heap out-of-bounds write; lines 59/61/70 keep writing with the same underflowed bound.

assumptions: provider_name is a struct field set outside this code (config-derived); per the width-domain rule its full domain (any-length NUL-terminated string) is instantiable, and the code's own attempted length guard at line 40 confirms it is treated as untrusted input.

sizeof(struct SignedCert) is a fixed positive compile-time constant S; for any S there exists a provider_name length L = k*65536 - 17 - 4S (k >= 1) with 0 <= L < 0xffff0000 that passes the line-40 guard and makes the sum wrap (unbound's SignedCert is 124 bytes, giving L = 65023).
malloc(0) returning a valid non-NULL pointer is standard allocator behavior (e.g. glibc); the !rr check at line 51 therefore does not stop the trigger.
limitations: Line 43 'continue' lacks a terminating semicolon as given (syntax error; the unit would not compile). The analysis treats it as the intended 'continue;' — the guard bound it belongs to is ineffective either way.
Truncated-but-nonzero rrlen >= 2 yields silent truncation of the published certificate text (misrepresented local-data) rather than memory corruption; same root cause, lower impact.
Line 71 calls cfg_strlist_insert without checking its return value, unlike the checked call at line 5 — an unhandled allocation/insertion failure path with no corruption consequence shown.

Exploitability requires an operator-supplied (or otherwise boundary-crossing) provider_name of ~65KB with a precise length; the corruption primitive itself (heap OOB write with attacker-influenced content) is fully instantiated in the simulation.

verdict.summary: Off-by-one out-of-bounds write in gopherToHTML: the bounds check `gopherState->len + llen >= TEMP_BUF_SIZE` admits llen up to TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1, and the terminator write `line[llen + 1] = '\0';` then writes one NUL byte past the end of the stack buffer `char line[TEMP_BUF_SIZE]`. A remote gopher server (attacker) triggers it by sending a line whose length makes gopherState->len + llen exactly TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 (or via the clamp path, which produces the same llen). At that value the buffer is also left without an in-bounds NUL terminator, so subsequent strchr/strtok parsing can read past the buffer.
