verdict.summary: sug_filltree() walks a spell-file-supplied trie (sl_fbyts/sl_fidxs) with stack arrays arridx, curi, tword, wordcount sized MAXWLEN, but never bounds depth against MAXWLEN before writing them, and never validates the file-controlled idxs[] values used as indices into byts/idxs. A crafted spell file with a word longer than MAXWLEN, or with an out-of-range idxs entry, yields out-of-bounds stack writes (tword[depth++]=c, arridx[depth]=idxs[n]) and an out-of-bounds heap write (idxs[arridx[depth]]=wordcount[depth]) with attacker-controlled values.

evidence.reason: Stack out-of-bounds write. depth is incremented once per non-NUL byte (line 88) with no comparison of depth against MAXWLEN anywhere in the function (the while at line 37 only checks depth >= 0). A spell file whose case-folded tree chains more than MAXWLEN non-NUL bytes makes depth reach MAXWLEN, so tword[MAXWLEN]=c writes attacker bytes past the stack array and arridx[MAXWLEN]=idxs[n] writes an attacker-chosen int out of bounds, plus curi/wordcount OOB writes.

Heap out-of-bounds write at an attacker-controlled index. arridx[depth] is loaded from the spell file at line 89 (arridx[depth] = idxs[n]) with no check against sl_fbyts_len/sl_fidxs_len on any path (the only bounds check, line 79 'n + 1 < slang->sl_fbyts_len', constrains only the NUL-skip loop's n+1). Line 39 byts[arridx[depth]] is the matching OOB read. A file-supplied idxs value such as 0x40000000 makes this write wordcount[depth] far outside the idxs allocation.

Origin of the tainted data: the trie byte array, index array, and sl_fbyts_len come from the loaded spell file (producer not shown in this code), and this function consumes their contents and indices without any range or depth validation of its own.

assumptions: MAXWLEN is the fixed stack-array dimension (100 in Vim); idx_T is a 32-bit signed int, so idxs[] entries can hold any value in [INT_MIN, INT_MAX].
sl_fbyts, sl_fidxs and sl_fbyts_len are populated from an untrusted spell (.spl) file by code not shown; per the width-domain rule their full byte/index domain is instantiable.

spell_soundfold and tree_add_word internals are not shown; tword is NUL-terminated at line 60 before the spell_soundfold call, and tree_add_word's FAIL sentinel is checked at lines 65-68, so neither is relied upon as a guard for the defects found.
limitations: If the not-shown spell-file loader independently rejects words longer than MAXWLEN and out-of-range idxs entries, the trigger would be blocked there, but no such check is quotable in this code; the in-function bound at line 79 shows length checking was needed and is absent at every other index use.
curi[depth] integer overflow is not treated as a primary defect: per well-formed node it is bounded by the node byte count (<= 256); it is subsumed by the unbounded-depth defect.

verdict.summary: Off-by-one out-of-bounds write in gopherToHTML: the clamp at line 79 permits llen up to TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1, and the sink `line[llen + 1] = '\0';` then indexes line[TEMP_BUF_SIZE], one byte past the TEMP_BUF_SIZE-byte buffer, whenever a gopher line (attacker-controlled server response) is TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 bytes or longer. The line is also mis-terminated (line[llen] is never NUL-ed). A malicious gopher server can trigger this one-byte NUL overflow in the proxy process.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the terminator is written at index llen+1 although llen can reach TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 (both via the unclamped path, since gopherState->len + llen < TEMP_BUF_SIZE admits llen = TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1, and via the clamp path), so this statement writes line[TEMP_BUF_SIZE], one byte past the LOCAL_ARRAY(char, line, TEMP_BUF_SIZE) buffer. Instantiated trigger: a gopher server response line of exactly TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 bytes ending in '\n' with no leftover data makes memcpy fill the whole buffer and this statement write out of bounds; the correct guard (llen <= TEMP_BUF_SIZE-2, or terminating at line[llen]) appears nowhere in the code.

Origin of the too-loose bound: this is the only clamp on llen, but it caps llen at TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 (after `llen += gopherState->len` on the leftover path) while the sink at line 98 requires llen <= TEMP_BUF_SIZE-2; the clamp therefore admits exactly the value that makes line[llen+1] index one past the end of the buffer.

assumptions: gopherState->buf is assumed to be at least TEMP_BUF_SIZE bytes; its declaration is not shown in the given code (the clamp keeps writes to it below index TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1).

gopherState->len is assumed to start in range and to be modified only by this function within the module; its initialization is not shown, but the confirmed trigger uses gopherState->len == 0 and does not depend on this assumption.
TEMP_BUF_SIZE is the size argument of the LOCAL_ARRAY declarations, so `line` and `tmpbuf` are exactly TEMP_BUF_SIZE bytes by construction.
limitations: The CSO branch's atoi(s_code)/atoi(s_recno) NULL-deref possibility was examined and is guarded by the quoted `if (!result) break;` before any atoi call, since strtok returns NULL only at token exhaustion.

The statement also leaves line[llen] unterminated (CWE-170 aspect: one stale byte from a prior line can attach to the parsed line on non-memset paths); it is part of the same defective statement and not counted as an independent primary defect.
Truncation of over-long lines (data loss with a debug message) is functional, with no security impact beyond the confirmed overflow.

verdict.summary: No security vulnerability confirmed. The single anomaly is the unguarded dereference of the parameter prog at 'if (prog->type == AST_LIST)': no NULL check exists anywhere in the code (mention sweep covers lines 1, 4, 5, 7), but the trigger value prog == NULL can only be supplied by the direct caller, whose own same-privilege process is the only crash victim (no corruption, disclosure, bypass, or amplification). The trust-boundary party that controls the AST content (the parsed script's originator) cannot instantiate the pointer value because the parse/call path producing prog is outside this code. Per the NULL-deref robustness carve-out, this is a robustness issue, not a vulnerability. All other inputs (dominify, J) reach no security sink; callees receive only constants and the prog pointer.

assumptions: pstmlist, pstm, and nl are project-internal functions defined in not-shown code; their behavior is not relied on as either a guard or a trigger producer.
The global 'minify' and the constant AST_LIST are declared outside this snippet; js_State and js_Ast types are external.
jsP_dumpsyntax is non-static; per the given code it is treated as an exported entry point, so its parameters were classified attacker-data by default and traced to sinks.
limitations: Robustness (not security): NULL pointer dereference at line 4 ('if (prog->type == AST_LIST)') if a caller passes prog == NULL; the mention sweep found no NULL check on any path. Impact is a crash confined to the caller's own process at equal privilege, and no trust-boundary party can instantiate the NULL pointer value because the producing parse/call path is not part of this code. A defensive fix would be an early return if prog == NULL.

Concurrency: the shared global 'minify' and stdio state would race if jsP_dumpsyntax were invoked from multiple threads; no window (lock release, callback, re-entry point) is exhibited by any statement of this code, so this is speculative.
The dump output (including script-derived tokens) is written to stdout; any log-forging relevance depends on unshown consumers and is not a defect in this code.

verdict.summary: In the MOOF cleanup the guard tests mov->root_ssix but the free deletes mov->seg_ssix (and nulls root_ssix instead of seg_ssix), leaving a dangling pointer that is freed again when the next SSIX box arrives, a double free of an attacker-file-controlled box (CWE-415). Independently, mov->moof->mfhd is dereferenced with no NULL check when the file is opened in GF_ISOM_OPEN_KEEP_FRAGMENTS mode, crashing the parser on a moof lacking an mfhd box (CWE-476).

evidence.reason: Wrong-variable guard: the condition tests mov->root_ssix but the statement frees mov->seg_ssix and clears only root_ssix, so seg_ssix is left dangling. Trigger: with root_ssix non-NULL, a first SSIX box stores a live box in mov->seg_ssix (line 278); a following MOOF runs this block and frees it without clearing the field; the next SSIX box hits 'if (mov->seg_ssix) gf_isom_box_del(mov->seg_ssix);' and frees the already-freed box again, corrupting the heap. The sibling blocks for root_sidx (lines 377-379) and seg_styp (lines 384-387) follow the correct check/free/clear pattern, confirming this block's guard is the missing one.

Second link of the double-free chain: this guard only verifies the field is non-NULL, not that it is live; after the MOOF cleanup freed the box without clearing the field, this statement frees the dangling pointer again, completing the memory corruption triggered by the attacker-supplied sequence of ssix/moof/ssix top-level boxes.

Unchecked NULL dereference: mov->moof->mfhd is populated by child-box parsing of the attacker's moof, and a moof without an mfhd child leaves it NULL; this is the only mention of mfhd in the code, with no NULL check on any path. Trigger: an attacker-supplied fragmented MP4 whose moof lacks mfhd, opened with openMode == GF_ISOM_OPEN_KEEP_FRAGMENTS and not in READ_DEBUG mode, reaches this line and crashes the parsing process (denial of service across the file trust boundary).

assumptions: gf_isom_box_del frees the passed box, per the universal box-manager convention implied by its use for ownership release throughout this code; its behavior on a NULL argument is not shown and was not relied on for any confirmed finding.

mov->root_ssix has no assignment anywhere in the given code; its non-NULL value in the C1 trigger is instantiable only under the width-domain rule for struct fields set by producers not shown. This lowers confidence for CWE-415 specifically.
mov->moof->mfhd is treated as an optional parse result (absent child leaves NULL) since no statement of this code asserts or enforces mfhd presence.
limitations: If no code outside this function ever assigns mov->root_ssix, the block at lines 380-383 is dead code and the double free reduces to a mere seg_ssix leak; the CWE-415 trigger then depends on an external setter that is not shown.

Line 213 'gf_isom_box_del((GF_Box *) mov->brand);' can receive NULL when an 'otyp' box precedes any 'ftyp'; the impact depends on the unshown NULL handling of gf_isom_box_del and could not be instantiated.

The chained dereferences 'trak->Media->information->sampleTable->...' at lines 100-101 are the same NULL-deref class as the mfhd finding but were not promoted because the box parsers that could enforce mdia/stbl presence are not shown.

The JP signature read 'GF_4CC(c[0],c[1],c[2],c[3])' is protected by the short-circuit 'box->dataSize==4'; a NULL data pointer with dataSize==4 would require an unshown allocation failure in the unknown-box parser.
Unchecked return values of gf_list_add at lines 153 and 327 cause at most a box leak on allocation failure, with no security effect.

verdict.summary: In the backward (forward == false) search path, the found handler computes the post-match result string's size as count + (size - 1), but at a backward match count equals the match index j, so the stored size (j + size - 1) exceeds the bytes actually remaining after the match (N - j - size). A one-byte needle matching the last byte yields a post string of length N-1 starting one past the end of the buffer; an empty needle on an empty haystack wraps size - 1 to 0xFFFFFFFF. The resulting string reference extends beyond its allocation, enabling out-of-bounds reads and writes (heap corruption on a writable string) in subsequent string operations.

evidence.reason: Root cause: miscalculated buffer size for the backward search result. At a backward match, count equals the match index j (the loop tests index count with count unchanged), so the stored post size is j + size - 1 while only N - j - size bytes remain after ptr + size (line 42). Instantiated trigger: backward search of a 5-byte writable string "abcde" for "e": size=1, count=4, first loop iteration matches at ptr=start+4, line 42 sets op1->value.bytes=start+5, and this line stores size 4 on a buffer with 0 remaining bytes, producing a string ref extending past the allocation; subsequent get/put on it performs out-of-bounds access. Additionally, when size==0 this expression wraps (0 - 1 = 0xFFFFFFFF), storing a ~4GB size on an empty buffer.

Contributing origin of the second trigger: the empty-needle early jump to found executes before the backward pointer adjustment (line 23), so found is reached with count = r_size(op1) and size = 0; combined with the size - 1 term at the line 43 sink, an empty haystack (count = 0) produces a post string of size 0xFFFFFFFF on an empty buffer.

assumptions: The forward parameter has both values instantiable; a reverse-search operator entry point passing forward=false is presumed to exist (caller not shown), which per the width-domain rule cannot dismiss the backward path but tempers confidence.

Standard Ghostscript operand/ref macros are assumed: check_read_type validates string type and read access; push(2) includes the operand-stack overflow check; r_set_size/r_size manipulate the ref size field.
The PostScript `string` operator creates writable strings, so the oversized post ref supports out-of-bounds writes via later `put` operations, not only reads.
limitations: The actual out-of-bounds access occurs in subsequent interpreter string operations consuming the malformed result ref; within this function only the size field is miscomputed (no direct OOB access in this code). String get/put accessors are characterizable per standard container semantics, so the chain is treated as instantiated.
The forward (classic search) path was verified correct at all boundary values tested (size=0, size=1, size=N-1, size=N, match at first/last position).

Backward matches ending before the string midpoint under-report the post size (in-bounds truncation, semantic error only); the memory-safety direction is a match ending past the midpoint, maximally the first position tested.

verdict.summary: gdImageFillToBorder clamps only the upper bounds of the caller-supplied coordinates (if (x >= im->sx) / if (y >= im->sy)) and never checks y < 0. With any negative y (full int domain at this exported intake point), the row-0 'Below' branch's under-admitting condition if (y < ((im->sy) - 1)) passes, and the function recurses via gdImageFillToBorder(im, i, y + 1, border, color) one row at a time with depth exactly |y|, each level scanning the full image width: an attacker-chosen negative coordinate causes uncontrolled recursion and stack exhaustion (plus O(sx*|y|) work), a denial of service in any process consuming the fill request. Negative y is also handed unvalidated to gdImageGetPixel/gdImageSetPixel (lines 21/24/33/36).

evidence.reason: Recursive sink: when y is negative, the Below guard at line 56 (if (y < ((im->sy) - 1))) passes, and this call re-enters with y+1 still negative (or row 0), producing recursion depth equal to |y| with no lower-bound check anywhere on any path; e.g. y = -1000000 exhausts the stack long before row 0 is reached.

Missing-check site: y is clamped only against its maximum; no if (y < 0) clamp or rejection exists anywhere in the function, so an attacker-supplied negative y (declared int, full domain at this exported API entry) flows unvalidated into the pixel accessors at lines 21/24/33/36 and into the unbounded Below recursion at line 63. The x coordinate is incidentally protected by the if (leftLimit == -1) return, but y has no equivalent.

assumptions: gdImageGetPixel/gdImageSetPixel are libgd's documented bounds-safe accessors (gdImageGetPixel returns -1 for out-of-range coordinates; gdImageSetPixel clips out-of-range writes), which is why the negative row index does not corrupt memory; this documented sentinel behavior (-1 != border, since border >= 0 is enforced at line 8) is also what keeps the seek-left loop painting and leftLimit being set on the negative-y path.
The image is non-empty (sx >= 1, sy >= 1) so the clamps and loops are well-defined.
The color parameter is chosen not equal to -1 (e.g. color = 0) so the sentinel -1 from out-of-range GetPixel does not suppress the recursive spawn at line 63.
limitations: No memory-corruption primitive was instantiated: the out-of-range row accesses at lines 21/24/33/36 are absorbed by the accessors' bounds-safe contract, so the impact is stack exhaustion and CPU amplification (DoS), not an out-of-bounds read/write in this code.
If an embedding caller pre-validates coordinates, the negative-y trigger is not reachable from that caller, but no such contract is quotable here and this function is the public intake point.

Edge case: y = INT_MIN makes y + 1 at line 63 signed-overflow (undefined behavior); practically it wraps and is clamped by line 16 in the recursive frame, so the practical trigger is any moderately large negative y (e.g. -10^6) rather than INT_MIN.

Even for in-bounds coordinates the recursive flood fill's depth scales with attacker-crafted image geometry (bounded by the number of pixels, since a sticking color guarantees paint progress); this is a secondary DoS surface, not the primary defect.

verdict.summary: sug_filltree walks the case-folded trie (sl_fbyts/sl_fidxs loaded from an attacker-supplied spell file) with an unbounded depth variable and unvalidated idx_T indices. A crafted trie whose descent chain exceeds the fixed MAXWLEN-sized stack arrays causes out-of-bounds stack writes (tword[depth++] = c and the following arridx/curi/wordcount stores) with attacker-controlled values; independently, an unchecked idxs[n] value flows into byts[]/idxs[] accesses (idxs[arridx[depth]] is a write) with no comparison against sl_fbyts_len anywhere before use. Memory corruption in the process parsing the .spl file.

evidence.reason: Root cause: depth has no upper bound. Every non-NUL byte in the attacker-controlled trie descends one level, and tword/arridx/curi/wordcount are fixed MAXWLEN-sized stack arrays; the only depth-related checks in the function are 'depth >= 0' and 'depth > 0'. Instantiated trigger: a spell file whose folded tree contains a chain of MAXWLEN+1 non-NUL bytes makes depth reach MAXWLEN, so tword[depth++] = c writes an attacker-chosen byte past tword[MAXWLEN], and the following three statements write past arridx/curi/wordcount — out-of-bounds stack write (CWE-787).

Root cause: arridx[depth] originates from idxs[n] (line 87) with no range check against sl_fbyts_len; n is used to read byts[n] before any validation (the only sl_fbyts_len check, at line 77, guards the later NUL-skip loop only). An idxs entry set to any full-domain idx_T value (e.g. 0x7fffffff) yields byts[n] as an out-of-bounds read at line 54 and byts[arridx[depth]] at line 37, plus an out-of-bounds write idxs[arridx[depth]] = wordcount[depth] at line 40 (CWE-125).

assumptions: MAXWLEN and idx_T are not defined in the given code; the arrays are of fixed size whatever the constant is, so the unbounded-depth overflow holds for any value (in Vim MAXWLEN is 50 and idx_T is a wide signed integer).

sl_fbyts/sl_fidxs/sl_fbyts_len are populated by a spell-file (.spl) reader not shown; per the width-domain rule their contents are attacker-data at full declared width, since no statement in this code narrows them.
spell_soundfold, tree_add_word, wordtree_alloc, line_breakcheck and the got_int global are not shown; their internal safety is their own concern and was not relied on.
limitations: If the not-shown .spl reader provably bounded the trie depth to below MAXWLEN and validated every idxs value against sl_fbyts_len, both triggers would be blocked; no such statement is quotable in this code, so this remains an unverified external precondition, not a guard.

Candidate 2's most damaging form (line 40, idxs[arridx[depth]] write) shares the same missing-validation root cause as the read at line 54; the reported CWE-125 evidence anchors on the first unchecked use.

verdict.summary: All writes to the heap buffer are bounded by snprintf size expressions derived from the same rrlen used for malloc, so no memory corruption is reachable from any trust boundary. The residual defects are a uint16_t truncation of rrlen and a worst-case dropped trailing quote, both triggerable only by the operator's own multi-kilobyte config values, plus unchecked strdup results under OOM.

assumptions: dnscenv->provider_name, signed_certs/signed_certs_count, and rotated_certs/rotated_certs_count are populated from the resolver's own configuration file during dnscrypt env init (code not shown); the config file is operator-authored and not writable by any network peer or unprivileged user, so these values are internal-trusted, not attacker-data.

struct SignedCert is defined elsewhere (not shown); its serial field is assumed to be at least 4 bytes so that memcpy(&serial, cert->serial, sizeof serial) stays in bounds, and its total size S is assumed small (approximately 124 bytes in dnscrypt, so 4*S is far below 65536).
cfg_str2list_insert and cfg_strlist_insert are internal Unbound container-insert helpers whose internals are not shown.
The function's return type is truncated in the given snippet; it is assumed compatible with dnscenv->signed_certs_count.
limitations: uint16_t truncation: rrlen = strlen(provider_name) + 15 + 4*S + 2 is computed in size_t and truncated into uint16_t rrlen. If the operator configures a provider name of tuned length 65536-17-4S (about 65023 bytes for S=124), rrlen wraps to 0; then malloc(0) can return non-NULL, if(!rr) passes, and snprintf(rr, rrlen - 1, ...) receives (size_t)-1 and overflows the 0-byte allocation. rrlen=1 similarly leaves the buffer uninitialized before strlen(rr) and then wraps rrlen - 1 - strlen(rr). Not scored as a vulnerability: the only party that can instantiate the trigger is the operator writing their own config file, which is not across a trust boundary.

Off-by-one truncation: the three snprintf calls use size rrlen - 1 (and rrlen - 1 - strlen(rr)), capping content at rrlen-2 while worst-case content (provider name + 15-char prefix + 4 chars per escaped cert byte + closing quote) is rrlen-1 chars; if every certificate byte requires escaping, the trailing double quote is dropped and a malformed TXT string is inserted into cfg->local_data. Functional defect; the downstream zone-data consumer is not shown, so no security impact is instantiated.

Return values of strdup(dnscenv->provider_name), strdup("deny"), and strdup(rr) are passed to cfg_str2list_insert/cfg_strlist_insert without NULL checks; reachable only under malloc/OOM failure, which no attacker can induce.
If dnscenv->provider_name were NULL (init contract not shown), strdup and strlen would dereference NULL, crashing the operator's own process during startup.
If signed_certs_count or rotated_certs_count were inconsistent with their backing arrays (producer not shown), the loops could read out of bounds; the producer is trusted config.

verdict.summary: The brush-header fields (guint32, set by g_ntohl from file data) are validated against a 64-bit bound (G_MAXSIZE), but the allocation sizes are computed in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic. `size = bh.width * bh.height * bh.bytes` (line 122) and `4 * bh.width * bh.height` (line 165) wrap modulo 2^32 for permitted dimensions (e.g. width=26650, height=80581, bytes=2 gives size=4), producing a 4-byte heap buffer that the subsequent conversion loops (lines 167-177 and 190-206) then write across for width*height iterations, causing massive heap out-of-bounds reads and writes with a 33-byte crafted .gbr file.

evidence.snippet:
size = bh.width * bh.height * bh.bytes;
  brush_buf = g_malloc (size);
evidence.reason: Origin of primary defect: bh.width/height/bytes are attacker-controlled 32-bit fields from the file; the product is evaluated in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic and wraps (26650*80581*2 = 4294967300 mod 2^32 = 4), so g_malloc(4) allocates a 4-byte buffer for an image whose loops assume 2*width*height bytes. The only sanitizer (line 51, `G_MAXSIZE / bh.width / bh.height / bh.bytes < 1`) checks a 64-bit bound and does not prevent the 32-bit wrap.

Out-of-bounds write sink: the loop at line 190 bounds i by bh.width * bh.height (2147483650 for the trigger header) while brush_buf holds only the wrapped size of 4 bytes; at i=4 this writes past the allocation and continues for ~2^31 iterations, sequentially corrupting the heap. Paired with the OOB read at line 200 (`GUINT16_FROM_BE (*buf)`), this is memory corruption triggered by a 33-byte crafted brush file.

Independent second defect: the allocation size `4 * bh.width * bh.height` is computed in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic and wraps for permitted dimensions (4*13325*80581 = 4294967300 mod 2^32 = 4), yielding a 4-byte buffer, while the pattern loop at line 167 iterates ph.width * ph.height = 1073741825 times.

Out-of-bounds write sink for the second defect: with the wrapped 4-byte allocation from line 165, at i=1 read() stores 3 bytes at brush_buf+4, past the end of the buffer; the write at line 177 (brush_buf[i * 4 + 3]) continues the corruption. Trigger requires a ~1GB brush payload plus a matching fake pattern header, all attacker-supplied file content.

assumptions: BrushHeader fields are 32-bit unsigned integers: inferred from the per-field g_ntohl byte-swaps and the comment 'rearrange the bytes in each unsigned int'; the struct definition itself is not shown.
GIMP_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE is the documented GIMP constant 262144; the trigger dimensions (26650, 80581, 13325) are within it, and 262144^2 * bytes far exceeds 2^32, making the wrap reachable.
GBRUSH_MAGIC and GPATTERN_MAGIC are public file-format constants the attacker can embed in a crafted file.
GLib semantics: g_malloc(0) returns NULL, g_malloc/g_new abort the process on allocation failure; read() on a regular file returns the full requested count when the file is large enough.
limitations: Version-1 path: `bh.header_size += 8` with no validation of header_size allows bn_size up to ~2GB (g_new aborts on OOM) and the gint truncation at line 95 can misparse the name offset, but the attacker must supply a correspondingly large file and no memory-unsafety follows; resource-consumption robustness issue only.
Resource leaks on error paths: fd is not closed on the sanitize-failure return (line 58), and brush_buf/fd leak on the unsupported-depth return; minor availability impact.
The bytes==18 sanitize allowance combined with a wrapped size reaching the final default arm leaks brush_buf; minor.

OOB behavior inside not-shown libgimp calls (gimp_pixel_rgn_set_rect reading the undersized buffer) is not counted as a separate finding; the confirmed corruption occurs at in-code sinks (lines 206 and 169) before those calls.

verdict.summary: All attacker-influenced numeric inputs (sampleSize, numRecords) reach arithmetic sinks only behind quoted, correctly-positioned guards: the sharded-path division is protected by the 'numRecords <= 100' early return (denominator >= 5.05 at the first passing value), and the time-series-path division plus the *bucketUnpacker dereferences are protected by 'if (!(bucketUnpacker && numRecords))', which also neutralizes the NaN scenario the code comments describe. Both computed ratios are further clamped into valid ranges via std::min/std::max, and every callee sentinel (getRandomCursor, plan_executor_factory::make status, trialStage null) is tested before first use. No memory-safety, injection, bypass, or amplification impact is instantiable from any input within the declared widths.

assumptions: Behavior of unshown internal callees (getRecordStore()->getRandomCursor, CollectionShardingState::get/getOwnershipFilter, SampleFromTimeseriesBucket, TrialStage, UnpackTimeseriesBucket, plan_executor_factory::make) is not verifiable here; none of them is relied on as a guard and none is relied on to produce a trigger.
expCtx and coll are internal-trusted interface-contract parameters; the collection-lock precondition is documented in this code's comment and enforced by the quoted invariant.
gTimeseriesBucketMaxCount is an operator-set server parameter, not attacker data across a trust boundary.
limitations: Negative sampleSize or numRecords (within the full long long width domain) produce only finite, clamped ratio values on every simulated path; a negative sampleSize passed to the unshown SampleFromTimeseriesBucket callee has no provable impact in this code (impact chain breaks at a discipline-3 unshowable link).

If the operator-set gTimeseriesBucketMaxCount were 0, the time-series ratio could become NaN, affecting only TrialStage plan selection (a performance concern, not a security impact, and not attacker-instantiable).
A potential lifetime concern of '&coll' captured into the executor depends on PlanExecutor semantics not shown; no use-after-free is exhibitible as two ordered operations in this code.
expCtx NULL at 'expCtx->opCtx' would require the internal caller to violate the documented lock-context precondition; treated as an interface contract, not a vulnerability.

verdict.summary: The dynamic CAPABILITY message parser copies a fixed sizeof(struct capability_mp_data) bytes from pnt+3 while its only guards guarantee 3 and hdr->length bytes respectively, so a peer-supplied capability with length < 4 at the message tail causes an out-of-bounds read of up to 4 bytes past the validated message region. Independently, two continue paths (override-capability and invalid afi/safi) skip the loop's only pointer advance pnt += hdr->length + 3, so the while (pnt < end) loop re-parses the same bytes forever, a remotely triggerable infinite-loop denial of service of bgpd.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). The sink copies a fixed sizeof(struct capability_mp_data) (4) bytes from pnt+3, but the only guards bound different quantities: 'if (pnt + 3 > end)' (line 17) guarantees exactly 3 bytes and 'if ((pnt + hdr->length + 3) > end)' (line 41) guarantees hdr->length bytes at pnt+3. Instantiated trigger: a BGP peer sends a dynamic CAPABILITY message of total length 3 with [action=CAPABILITY_ACTION_SET, code, hdr->length=0]; line 41 evaluates pnt+0+3 == end and passes, then the memcpy reads bytes end..end+3, up to 4 bytes past the validated message region (crash/adjacent-memory read), and it executes even for non-MP capability codes.

Infinite loop (CWE-835). This continue (override-capability arm) and the one at line 66 are the only loop exits that re-enter 'while (pnt < end)' (line 14) without executing the loop's sole pointer advance 'pnt += hdr->length + 3;' (line 102) — the mention sweep of pnt (lines 12, 14, 17, 24, 41, 49, 102) shows no statement on this path mutates pnt. All checks re-evaluate identically on unchanged bytes, so the loop never terminates; a 7-byte MP capability from the peer wedges bgpd at 100% CPU. This site requires the peer to be configured with override-capability; the site at line 66 needs no such configuration.

Infinite loop (CWE-835), primary remote trigger. When the afi/safi validity lookup at line 61 misses (an attacker-supplied afi/safi pair from the full 16-bit/8-bit wire domain, e.g. an out-of-range pair — a failure sentinel this code itself tests for), this continue skips 'pnt += hdr->length + 3;' (line 102); pnt never changes, so 'while (pnt < end)' re-parses the same capability forever. A ~9-byte MP capability with invalid afi/safi yields unbounded CPU consumption in the routing daemon with no special configuration — attacker-scalable amplification.

Origin of the tainted data: this non-static function is the intake point for a BGP peer's dynamic CAPABILITY message; pnt, length, and every parsed field (action at line 23, hdr->code/hdr->length at line 24, mpc.afi/mpc.safi at lines 54-55) are network-peer controlled across the trust boundary.

assumptions: bgp_afi_safi_valid_indices (line 61), peer_active_nego (line 91), bgp_announce_route, bgp_clear_route, bgp_notify_send, BGP_EVENT_ADD are internal callees not shown; their semantics are assumptions. In particular the array writes peer->afc_recv[afi][safi], peer->afc_nego[afi][safi] and the read peer->afc[afi][safi] (lines 79-89) are guarded only by the unshown validity lookup at line 61 — no local afi/safi range check, clamp, or mask exists in this code. If that lookup can return true for values outside the arrays' (also unshown) domain, those writes would be out-of-bounds writes (CWE-787); this was not promoted to a primary because the trigger direction (the callee accepting out-of-domain afi 0..65535 / safi 0..255) rests on the same unshown callee, so it cannot be instantiated from the given code.

struct capability_mp_data is assumed 4 bytes (afi u16, reserved, safi u_char) and struct capability_header 2 bytes (code, length), matching the wire format; the out-of-bounds read scales with sizeof(struct capability_mp_data) and triggers whenever it exceeds hdr->length at the message tail.
The allocation geometry of the received message buffer behind pnt..end is not shown; end = pnt + length is treated as the validated data boundary for the out-of-bounds-read judgment.
limitations: Pointer overflow in 'pnt + hdr->length + 3' (line 41) is not attacker-instantiable: hdr->length is a u_char (max 255), so the offset is at most 258 and cannot wrap the pointer.
The infinite-loop site at line 59 requires the operator to have configured override-capability on the peer; the site at line 66 is the unconditional remote trigger.

The out-of-bounds read is at most 4 bytes past the message tail; disclosure potential is limited (the read values feed indices and debug logs), the reliable impact being a crash of bgpd (denial of service).
zlog_debug at line 64 passes more arguments than its format specifiers — cosmetic, no security effect.

verdict.summary: unix_expandpath() copies each readdir() entry name (dp->d_name) into a heap buffer allocated as STRLEN(path) + BASENAMELEN + 5, then appends the remaining path and "/**" — with no check anywhere that the entry-name length fits the buffer's fixed slack. A file planted in a globbed directory whose name exceeds that slack (e.g. macOS NFD UTF-8 names up to ~765 bytes, which this MACOS_CONVERT-enabled build targets) causes an attacker-sized and attacker-content out-of-bounds heap write at STRCPY(s, dp->d_name) and the subsequent STRCPY(buf + len, ...) appends.

evidence.reason: Primary sink: the readdir() entry name is copied into buf with strcpy semantics and no length validation on any path. buf was sized only from STRLEN(path) + BASENAMELEN + 5 (line 32); the mention sweep over every use of dp->d_name (lines 141, 143-144, 146, 148) shows only character compares, a regex match, and a fnamencmp — none bounds STRLEN(dp->d_name). A planted directory entry longer than the fixed slack (e.g. a 600-byte NFD macOS filename against the 507-byte allocation for pattern "**") writes past the heap buffer with attacker-chosen bytes — heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787).

Compounding writes of the same defect: after the oversized d_name is inserted, len = STRLEN(buf) already reflects the attacker-controlled name length, and these strcpy calls write "/**" plus the remaining path at buf+len — beyond the allocation whenever d_name exceeded the BASENAMELEN slack. No remaining-capacity check exists between lines 151 and 164.

Origin of the undersized allocation: the buffer's only slack beyond the path length is the fixed constant BASENAMELEN + 5. The code never re-derives the allocation from, or checks it against, the actual length of the directory entry names it will copy into the buffer, so the allocation is provably insufficient whenever the scanned directory contains an entry name longer than that slack.

assumptions: BASENAMELEN is a compile-time constant whose value is not shown in the given code (500 in Vim); alloc() is a malloc-like allocator returning NULL on failure (NULL checked at line 33).
STRCPY/STRMOVE/STRNCPY are Vim's strcpy/strmov/strncpy wrappers; opendir/readdir have standard POSIX semantics.

wildoff/flags/didstar are derived by internal Vim glob machinery; all recursive call sites shown pass offsets within [0, STRLEN(buf)], and no memory-unsafe use of a wildcard-offset was found in this code.

On Linux the VFS caps entry names at 255 bytes; on the macOS build this code compiles (indicated by #ifdef MACOS_CONVERT), HFS+ readdir historically returned NFD UTF-8 names of up to roughly 765 bytes — which is why the precompose helper exists.
limitations: On platforms where the maximum file-name length is below BASENAMELEN (e.g. Linux, 255-byte names vs 500-byte slack) the simulated writes stay in bounds; the overflow trigger requires a filesystem permitting entry names longer than the fixed slack, which the macOS code path in this function was written to handle.

mac_precompose_path() is not shown; the memmove at line 190 was assumed safe because UTF-8 canonical precomposition does not lengthen a string — its actual contract cannot be verified from the given code.

A negative or huge wildoff could in principle move the backslash-removal loop start (line 78) out of the buffer, but no shown call site passes such a value and the top-level caller is not given; not instantiated.

verdict.summary: In expand_case_fold_string, the character length len = enclen(reg->enc, p) is never clamped to the remaining buffer span end - p. The loop guard `while (p < end)` only ensures at least one byte remains, but onig_node_str_cat(snode, p, p + len) copies len bytes, so a pattern string node ending in a truncated multi-byte character (e.g., a lone 0xF0 lead byte under UTF-8) causes a heap out-of-bounds read of up to len - (end - p) bytes past sn->end; the same unclamped len is also passed to expand_case_fold_string_alt. The read data is stored into the compiled regex AST string node.

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: len is taken from the encoding's lead-byte length with no clamp to the remaining span (no `if (p + len > end) len = end - p` and no len > 0 check follows); the loop guard `while (p < end)` constrains only p, not p + len.

Out-of-bounds read sink: with p = end - 1 and a truncated multi-byte final character (e.g., lone 0xF0 under UTF-8), enclen returns 4 while only 1 byte is in-bounds, so onig_node_str_cat copies 4 bytes from a 1-byte-valid region, reading past sn->end of the pattern buffer; the over-read bytes are retained in the AST string node. The same unclamped len is also forwarded at the expand_case_fold_string_alt call site (line 66).

assumptions: The producer of the string node content (regex parser) is not shown; per the width-domain rule the pattern bytes are treated as attacker-data, so a string node ending in a truncated multi-byte character is instantiable regardless of unquoted parser validation.

enclen(reg->enc, p) is a project-internal macro/function not shown; for multi-byte encodings such as UTF-8 it returns the full character length from the lead byte, which can exceed end - p. The defect stands for any encoding where a lead byte's declared length can exceed the remaining bytes.
limitations: Potential infinite loop if enclen could return 0 (p += len would never advance) is speculative: enclen's minimum return value is not shown in this code and cannot be quoted, so it is not counted as a vulnerability here.

On the `goto err` path, prev_node can leak when it was created but never linked into top_root (onig_node_free(top_root) with top_root == NULL_NODE); the reachable error triggers (allocation failure, n < 0) are not attacker-instantiable from the given code, so this leak is recorded as a robustness issue only.

swap_node(node, top_root) and the node-list helpers are internal callees whose semantics (swap contents, then free old contents) are assumed standard for this codebase per their universally known usage pattern.

verdict.summary: get_recurse_data_length walks attacker-derived compiled-pattern bytecode and uses operand fields as an array index and as a pointer offset with no runtime validation: the 16-bit capture number read by GET2(cc, 1 + LINK_SIZE) indexes common->optimized_cbracket unchecked, and the link offset GET(cc, 1) is added to cc and dereferenced unchecked. The only invariants are SLJIT_ASSERTs, which are compiled out in release builds, so out-of-bounds reads are reachable during JIT compilation of attacker-supplied patterns.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the 16-bit capture-index field read from the bytecode is used directly as an array index with no bounds check, clamp, mask, or error arm anywhere in the function (mention sweep: line 73 is the value's only mention; ccend is never compared against it). Instantiated trigger: GET2(cc, 1 + LINK_SIZE) = 0xFFFF (within the field's declared uint16 width; producer not shown in this code) while optimized_cbracket is sized elsewhere to the capture count, producing an out-of-bounds heap read that also corrupts the computed private-data length.

evidence.snippet:
alternative = cc + GET(cc, 1);
    if (*alternative == OP_KETRMAX || *alternative == OP_KETRMIN)
evidence.reason: Root cause: the link-offset operand GET(cc, 1) is added to the bytecode cursor and the resulting pointer is dereferenced with no validation that it lies within [cc, ccend] (ccend is mentioned only at lines 20 and 199, neither bounds this pointer). Instantiated trigger: GET(cc, 1) = 0xFFFF for an OP_COND opcode makes alternative = cc + 65535, an out-of-bounds read far past the compiled-pattern allocation; the read byte gates length++.

evidence.snippet:
static int get_recurse_data_length(compiler_common *common, PCRE2_SPTR cc, PCRE2_SPTR ccend,
  BOOL *needs_control_head, BOOL *has_quit, BOOL *has_accept)
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted data: cc/ccend delimit the compiled pattern bytecode consumed as raw instruction words; this translation-stage helper receives attacker-influenced operand fields (opcodes, GET/GET2 offsets and indices, cc[1] lengths, PRIVATE_DATA words) whose producers are not shown in this code, and no statement in this function narrows their widths before the sinks at lines 73 and 89.

assumptions: SLJIT_ASSERT is a no-op unless SLJIT_DEBUG is defined (standard sljit behavior), so none of the assertions in this code enforce anything in release builds and none qualifies as a guard.

GET/GET2/PRIVATE_DATA read operand fields from the compiled-pattern bytecode produced by compilation stages not shown in this code; per the width-domain rule these fields are instantiable across their full declared widths (GET2: 0..65535; GET with LINK_SIZE=2: 0..65535).
common->optimized_cbracket is allocated elsewhere sized to the capture count; no quotable bound for it exists in this code.
limitations: next_opcode NULL sentinel (lines 194-195): cc = next_opcode(common, cc) is consumed with only the debug-only SLJIT_ASSERT(cc != NULL); a NULL would be dereferenced at switch(*cc) after the pointer comparison at line 20. However, whether any instantiable opcode value makes the not-shown next_opcode return NULL cannot be exhibited from the given code, so this unchecked-sentinel use is recorded as a robustness defect rather than a primary finding (CWE-476 demoted).

Additional unvalidated-operand uses of the same systemic class were batched with the primary findings rather than listed as separate evidence: line 46 (cc += PRIVATE_DATA(cc + 1), unbounded advance), lines 143-149 (XCLASS size from GET(cc, 1) passed raw to get_class_iterator_size and used as an unchecked advance), lines 164/176 (cc += 1 + 2 + cc[1], unbounded advance).

Under a trust model that treats compiled bytecode as internally consistent by construction of the not-shown pcre2_compile stage, these triggers would additionally require a bug in that stage; this analysis judges the function as the last line of defense per the width-domain rule.
No out-of-bounds write is instantiated inside this function; a corrupted length value propagates into JIT frame layout in code not shown and was not counted as impact.
int length overflow would require roughly 2^31 counted private words, unreachable at realistic pattern sizes.

verdict.summary: jetp3852_print_page pads each trimmed scan line with `memset(end_data, 0, 7)` without bounding end_data against the end of the fixed stack buffer `byte data[DATA_SIZE]`. The only guard, `if (line_size > DATA_SIZE)`, admits line_size == DATA_SIZE (and everything down to DATA_SIZE-6), so a document whose page geometry yields line_size at/near DATA_SIZE and whose scan line has no trailing zero bytes drives end_data to data + line_size, and the memset writes up to 7 bytes past the end of the array — an attacker-triggered out-of-bounds stack write (memory corruption) in the Ghostscript process printing the document.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write sink. end_data can equal data + DATA_SIZE (or data + DATA_SIZE-6..DATA_SIZE) at this point, and the unconditional 7-byte memset then writes at data[DATA_SIZE..DATA_SIZE+6], past the end of the fixed stack array `byte data[DATA_SIZE]` declared at line 10. No statement in the function bounds end_data + 7 against data + DATA_SIZE.

The only bound on line_size, and it is the wrong bound for the memset sink: the `>` operator admits line_size == DATA_SIZE (and all values down to DATA_SIZE-6), so `byte *end_data = data + line_size;` (line 29) can reach the exact end of the buffer while the trailing-zero trim loop (lines 33-34) is skipped by a nonzero last pixel byte. Attacker instantiates this via page width/resolution choice plus a dense (no trailing zero bytes) scan line.

assumptions: LINE_SIZE is a compile-time constant defined outside the given snippet; DATA_SIZE = LINE_SIZE * 8 is therefore a fixed positive array bound.

The attacker (document author) can select device page width/resolution so that gdev_mem_bytes_per_scan_line returns a value in [DATA_SIZE-6, DATA_SIZE], and can render a scan line whose bytes are all nonzero — both are standard Ghostscript setpagedevice/content capabilities.
limitations: A negative line_size would also bypass the upper-bound-only check at line 22 (it tests only `> DATA_SIZE`), making end_data = data + negative and the memset write 7 bytes before the buffer — same missing guard at the same sink; whether width can be negative depends on parameter validation in Ghostscript core, which is not shown, so this secondary trigger is not relied upon for the verdict.

The return value of gdev_prn_copy_scan_lines (lines 30-31) is not checked; on failure the stack array `data` is read uninitialized (line 33 `end_data[-1]`, transpose reads) and can influence output — an in-bounds uninitialized-read (CWE-457) robustness concern, not promoted to a primary finding.
The out-of-bounds bytes written are zeros (memset of 0), so the attacker controls the occurrence and offset/distance of the corruption, not its content.

verdict.summary: This is Lua's parser function for variable references (singlevaraux resolution followed by _ENV-based global access). The only candidate is the reliance on lua_assert(var->k != VVOID) to validate the second singlevaraux lookup: lua_assert is a no-op in release builds, so if the _ENV lookup missed, luaK_exp2anyregup would receive a VVOID expdesc. The trigger is not instantiable: the code documents and asserts the 'this one must exist' contract, the _ENV upvalue is created for the main function by the parser outside this excerpt and cannot be removed by chunk source, and even the hypothetical path yields only invalid bytecode semantics (a stale tagged register used as env) that surface as a runtime type error inside the attacker's own chunk, with no memory corruption, disclosure, or bypass.

assumptions: str_checkname, singlevaraux, codestring, luaK_exp2anyregup, and luaK_indexed are project-internal callees of the same parser/codegen file not shown; their contracts (str_checkname rejects non-name tokens, singlevaraux returns a proper expdesc, luaK_indexed consumes a non-VVOID expdesc) could not be quoted from the given code and are recorded as assumptions.
lua_assert is assumed to follow standard Lua semantics: an active abort when assertions are enabled, a no-op in release builds.
The _ENV upvalue is assumed to be created for the main function at chunk creation outside this excerpt, which is the basis of the code's documented 'this one must exist' invariant.
limitations: Speculative candidate (dismissed): if singlevaraux(fs, ls->envn, var, 1) could return VVOID, the only check is lua_assert(var->k != VVOID), which is compiled out in release builds, and luaK_exp2anyregup would then consume a VVOID expdesc. The precondition (missing _ENV in the function chain) contradicts the contract this code itself documents and asserts, cannot be produced by any statement in this excerpt, and chunk source cannot delete the main function's _ENV upvalue. Even if reached, the impact is a stale tagged register used as the environment, causing a Lua runtime error in the attacker's own chunk (CWE-617-adjacent robustness concern, not a security impact).
No trust-boundary memory sink, injection sink, or allocation sizing appears in this excerpt; the function delegates all memory and table operations to characterizable parser/codegen helpers.

verdict.summary: squashfs_opendir reads directory entries from directory_table + bytes where bytes is advanced by attacker-controlled inode offset (bytes += (*i)->offset) and per-entry sizes (bytes += dire->size + 1) with no bound against the end of directory_table; the only check, while(bytes < size), compares against size = (*i)->data + bytes, an attacker-computed relative value, and is not rechecked inside the while(dir_count--) loop. A crafted squashfs image therefore drives out-of-bounds heap reads whose contents are copied into dire->name and then into dir->dirs[].name (strcpy), yielding heap-memory disclosure into extracted filenames and a reliable crash.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read sink: bytes is attacker-positioned (line 47 adds the unchecked inode offset; line 115 adds attacker dire->size + 1 inside an inner loop with no recheck) and no statement in the function bounds bytes against the end of directory_table. Trigger: crafted image with inode offset = 0x40000000, data = 1 gives bytes = 0x40000000, size = 0x40000001, so while(bytes < size) passes and this memcpy (and lines 56 and 86-87) reads far past the heap buffer.

Taint origin: (*i)->offset and (*i)->data come from read_inode of an attacker-supplied image and are added to bytes without any range check; size is a relative attacker-computed value, not a bound on directory_table, so the while(bytes < size) test at line 50 cannot prevent reads past the buffer.

assumptions: directory_table is a heap buffer of finite size allocated elsewhere; its exact size is not shown, but the absence of any check against it in this code is the defect regardless of the value.
struct dir_ent.name is assumed sized to hold SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN+1 characters; if smaller, the strcpy at line 107 would be an additional OOB write, but the struct is not shown.
limitations: *i = read_inode(...) at line 17 is dereferenced without a NULL check; NULL appears reachable only on allocation failure inside the unshown callee (environment failure, not attacker-instantiable), so it is recorded as a robustness issue rather than a vulnerability.

size = (*i)->data + bytes (line 48) can overflow signed int; this merges with the primary OOB read (it only changes how far past the buffer the loop reads) and does not constitute an independent defect.
check_name and lookup_entry are internal callees whose strictness is not shown; no candidate was dismissed on their behavior.

verdict.summary: Attacker-controlled int attr_len (netlink action parsing) is never validated for sign or magnitude: size_t req_size = NLA_ALIGN(attr_len) can become ~2^64-k for negative (or near-INT_MAX) attr_len, and new_acts_size = max(next_offset + req_size, ksize(*sfa) * 2) truncates that size_t into an int, so the only oversized-request guard (if (new_acts_size > MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE) with its EMSGSIZE arm) is bypassed. Execution continues, (*sfa)->actions_len += req_size wraps actions_len negative, and the following call performs memcpy(acts->actions, (*sfa)->actions, (*sfa)->actions_len) with a negative length converted to a huge size_t and returns a pointer at (*sfa) + negative next_offset that the caller writes through: heap out-of-bounds read/write in the kernel (known as CVE-2022-4337).

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: the 32-bit signed parameter attr_len, whose producer (netlink action parsing) is not shown and whose full int domain is attacker-instantiable per the width-domain rule, is passed through NLA_ALIGN with no sign or magnitude check; for attr_len negative (e.g. -8) or near INT_MAX, req_size becomes ~2^64-k. No statement in the code bounds attr_len or req_size before this point or anywhere else except inside the cap branch bypassed below.

Defect site: the size_t expression next_offset + req_size (huge, ~2^64-k, for negative attr_len) is stored into int new_acts_size, truncating to a small or negative value. The only rejection guard, line 17 'if ((MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE - next_offset) < req_size) ... return ERR_PTR(-EMSGSIZE);', is gated by line 16 'if (new_acts_size > MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE)', which the truncated value fails to trigger, so the guard never executes in execution order. Trigger instantiated with attr_len = -8, actions_len = 0, next_offset = 24: req_size = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF8, new_acts_size = 1024, cap check skipped, line 36 '(*sfa)->actions_len += req_size' wraps actions_len to -8, and the next call reaches line 29 'memcpy(acts->actions, (*sfa)->actions, (*sfa)->actions_len)' with a negative length converted to a huge size_t, an out-of-bounds heap read/write; line 37 likewise returns (*sfa) + negative next_offset for the caller to write through.

assumptions: NLA_ALIGN(n) is ((n) + NLA_ALIGNTO - 1) & ~(NLA_ALIGNTO - 1) with NLA_ALIGNTO = 4; its mask bounds alignment only, never sign or magnitude.
ksize() returns the actual allocated bucket size of the slab object; nla_alloc_flow_actions behaves as a standard allocator (kmalloc or ERR_PTR), which is checked at line 26.
struct sw_flow_actions::actions_len is a signed int and struct sw_flow_actions::actions is the trailing flexible array; next_offset is small (tens of bytes) on a fresh allocation.
MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE is a modest kernel constant (32 KiB in OVS); regardless of its exact value, a truncated negative new_acts_size is always <= it.
Signed overflow in NLA_ALIGN and the size_t-to-int conversions wrap as is standard on kernel targets.
limitations: The concrete caller that instantiates a negative or near-INT_MAX attr_len is not part of the given snippet; per the width-domain rule the full int domain of the parameter is treated as instantiable, which matches the real-world CVE-2022-4337 netlink path.
If every caller in the module could be shown to pass a provably in-range u16-derived attr_len, the trigger would not instantiate; no such narrowing is quotable from this code.
Precise privilege-escalation exploitability (beyond heap corruption/crash) depends on heap layout outside this snippet.

verdict.summary: nft_verdict_init is shown in its hardened form: the netlink payload is validated by a checked parse (lines 11-13), the attacker-controlled 32-bit verdict code is exhaustively enumerated by the switch with rejecting default arms, and the selected chain is guarded on every path by `if (IS_ERR(chain)) return PTR_ERR(chain);` (in the byid branch and again before first dereference), followed by base-chain, bound-chain, and setelem/binding-chain state rejections, before `chain->use++` takes the reference. No sink in this code is reachable with an out-of-domain attacker value; the guards whose absence caused the historical CVE-2024-1086-class defect in this function are present.

assumptions: nft_chain_lookup and nft_chain_lookup_byid (project-internal, not shown) return an ERR_PTR sentinel, not NULL, on failure; this code tests that sentinel with IS_ERR at lines 45-46 and 55-56 before any dereference.
nft_verdict_policy (not shown) enforces attribute types/lengths; nla_parse_nested_deprecated applies it and its error is checked at lines 11-13.
nft_is_base_chain/nft_chain_is_bound and desc->flags are kernel-internal state, not attacker-settable here.
limitations: If an unshown lookup could return NULL (not the kernel error-pointer convention), IS_ERR would not catch it and nft_is_base_chain(chain) would deref NULL; not instantiable from this snippet.

The historical UAF patterns around nft_chain_lookup_byid returning a chain pending deletion in the same transaction batch depend entirely on the callee's transaction-state filtering, which is not shown; the given code contains every locally applicable check (IS_ERR, base-chain, bound-chain, SETELEM/binding rejections).
chain->use is a u32; overflow would require 2^32 verdict references in one table, not attacker-scalable.
