No check, clamp, or u64 widening exists anywhere in this function, so an undersized heap area is allocated while line 15 still passes the unwrapped elem_size and max_entries, causing out-of-bounds writes during freelist population.

Impact sink: the populate call consumes smap->elems as max_entries elements of elem_size bytes each (e.g. elem_size=0x80000012, max_entries=4 into a ~72-byte allocation), writing freelist nodes at offsets far past the allocation and corrupting kernel heap memory; the size mismatch originates in the wrapped multiplication on line 6.

Origin of the tainted size: elem_size is derived from attacker-controlled smap->map.value_size (full u32 domain, producer not shown in this code) into a u32, so no statement of this code narrows it below the wrap threshold; this value feeds the overflowing multiplication on line 6.

assumptions: smap->map.value_size and smap->map.max_entries are set by the not-shown map-creation path from user BPF_MAP_CREATE attributes; per the width-domain rule their surface is the full u32 domain, and no narrowing statement exists in this code.

pcpu_freelist_populate (kernel/percpu_freelist.c, not shown) populates the freelist by writing one node at each of nr_elems offsets of elem_size bytes within buf, i.e. it consumes buf as nr_elems * elem_size bytes; this characterizes the OOB-write impact of the undersized allocation but is not required to locate the defect, which is the wrapped size at the line 6 call site.
bpf_map_area_alloc allocates exactly the requested size and returns NULL on failure; the NULL sentinel is correctly checked at line 8.

verdict.summary: SQClass::NewSlot's member-index growth (the classic Squirrel overflow of the 24-bit member index into the FIELD/METHOD type bits) is bounded by the quoted guard 'if (_members->CountUsed() >= MEMBER_MAX_COUNT) { return false; }', executed before both push_back paths with no bypass; all other indexing uses are sentinel-checked, type-checked, or store-bounded by this code itself. No attacker-instantiable trigger survives.

assumptions: ss->GetMetaMethodIdxByName(key) returns either -1 (checked) or a valid index into _metamethods; the -1 sentinel is tested in this code, and no statement here can produce an out-of-range non-sentinel return.
SQObjectPtr's default constructor leaves 'temp' typed OT_NULL, which the 'sq_type(temp) == OT_NULL' branch relies on when _members->Get misses.
SQTable::Get/NewSlot/CountUsed and SQClass vectors behave as standard container accessors; _members is populated only by this code's guarded inserts (Clone is outside this code).
MEMBER_MAX_COUNT and the _make_*/_member_idx/_isfield macros (24-bit index field plus distinct FIELD/METHOD type bits) are as defined in the Squirrel headers this code is compiled against.
limitations: Hypothetical out-of-range (non -1) return from GetMetaMethodIdxByName would make _metamethods[mmidx] an OOB write, but no statement in this code instantiates it; speculative.
If SQObjectPtr's default constructor left an uninitialized type and _members->Get missed without writing temp, the OT_NULL test would consume garbage; not producible from given code.
The _locked check is intentionally bypassed for closure/static members so statics remain addable after instantiation; this is documented VM semantics, not a security-state misrepresentation.

verdict.summary: e1000_send_packet forwards guest-derived packet data (buf), packet length (size), and a queue pointer (nc) to QEMU net APIs and stats helpers with no local validation (no bounds check, clamp, mask, or NULL test anywhere in the function), but every operation that consumes size, buf, or nc lives inside project-internal callees not shown (qemu_send_packet, nc->info->receive, inc_tx_bcast_or_mcast_count, e1000x_increase_size_stats); no memory, copy, indexing, or allocation sink on attacker-data exists within the quoted code, so no trigger's impact chain can be instantiated. Not vulnerable as given.

assumptions: qemu_get_queue, qemu_send_packet, nc->info->receive, inc_tx_bcast_or_mcast_count, and e1000x_increase_size_stats are QEMU-internal callees whose implementations are not given; per discipline 3 their behavior can neither produce a trigger nor serve as a guard.

Callers of e1000_send_packet (TX descriptor processing, not shown) supply buf pointing to an assembled packet and size as its length; the guest controls packet content and TX descriptor fields, and the loopback branch is guest-selectable via s->phy_reg[PHY_CTRL].
PTCregs has exactly 6 elements (line 3); the mapping from size to an index within 0..5 is performed inside e1000x_increase_size_stats, which is not shown.
limitations: C1 (unvalidated size): the guest-derived int size reaches three callees with zero local validation (mention sweep: size appears only at the parameter declaration and the three call sites on lines 8, 10, and 13; no range check, clamp, mask, or error arm anywhere). A negative or oversized size would be harmful only inside the unshown callees; no size-consuming memory/copy/indexing operation exists in the quoted code, so the impact chain is not instantiated. In the full QEMU source the TX path bounds size and e1000x_increase_size_stats uses bounded branch selection, but that is context not quoted here.

C2 (unchecked lookup return): the result of qemu_get_queue(s->nic) (line 6) is dereferenced at nc->info->receive (line 8) and passed at line 10 without a NULL check. No statement in this code can make the lookup miss, and the callee's failure behavior is not shown, so a NULL-dereference trigger is speculative.

C3 (size-less buffer pass): inc_tx_bcast_or_mcast_count(s, buf) (line 12) receives buf with no length; if it reads a 6-byte destination MAC from a packet shorter than 6 bytes the read would exceed the packet. Both the callee's read extent and buf's allocation size are outside the given code, so the out-of-bounds read is not instantiated here.

C4 (design note): the loopback branch (lines 7-8) invokes nc->info->receive directly, bypassing the queueing/filtering path of qemu_send_packet; no security consequence is quotable from this code alone.

verdict.summary: This BMP decoder validates every attacker-derived field before use: dimensions (width/height/planes checks plus a successful SetImageExtent), bits-per-pixel whitelist, colormap size capped and allocated from the same expression as the read length with a full-read count check, raster buffer stride provably >= per-row consumption for every bits-per-pixel case, a blob-size sanity check on the raster length, full-read count checks on every ReadBlob, offset checks on every SeekBlob, and bounds-checked colormap index access via IsValidColormapIndex. No memory-safety, integer, or injection trigger could be instantiated.

assumptions: IsValidColormapIndex is the standard bounds-checked colormap accessor: it validates the index against image->colors and supplies a safe index through its output parameter; every SetPixelIndex in cases 4 and 8 is preceded by a call to it.

DecodeImage(image,compression,pixels,image->columns*image->rows) respects its size argument; the buffer passed is rows*MagickMax(bytes_per_line,columns+256) which is provably >= columns*rows for every accepted header, so the call site passes in-domain arguments.
QueueAuthenticPixels returns a pixel region of the requested width (image->columns) or NULL, and the code NULL-checks it before use.
AcquireImageColormap(image,image->colors) allocates at least image->colors colormap entries; the subsequent parse loop iterates exactly image->colors times and the code checks the function's return.
limitations: The shift-detection loops permit shift/sample to reach 33 before the `> 32U` break, so `mask << 33` on a 32-bit operand is undefined behavior; the result only feeds color-component arithmetic, never a memory index or size, so no security impact.
The file-size mismatch paths call ThrowMagickException but continue processing; all subsequent reads are still bounded by count checks, so this is non-fatal diagnostics, not fail-open.

For bmp_info.size == 64 the header parser consumes more header bytes than the 64-byte declaration claims (color-management reads span 68+ bytes); this only misaligns sequential reads and the code re-seeks before reading the colormap and raster, so it is a functional nit.

On a second do-while iteration entered through a BA offset, start_position is not refreshed (the `if (bmp_info.ba_offset == 0)` guard skips the update); any resulting mispositioned reads are rejected by the count guards.

Hypothetical 32-bit size_t wrap in bytes_per_line*rows would require the unwrapped product to be allocatable in 64-bit internal arithmetic inside AcquireVirtualMemory, which fails and returns NULL, which the code checks.

verdict.summary: Unsigned 64-bit overflow in the bounds check 'if (needle + 4 < to)' lets the 4-byte read 'r_read_le32 (buf + needle - from)' run up to 3 bytes past the calloc(len,1) heap buffer when the attacker-controlled scan range ends near UT64_MAX; no statement in the code bounds the absolute value of from/to (only their difference, 'st64 len = (st64)(to - from)' checked against ST32_MAX), so the heap out-of-bounds read trigger is fully instantiated.

evidence.snippet:
if (needle + 4 < to) {
			ut32 n1 = r_read_le32 (buf + needle - from);
evidence.reason: The guard 'needle + 4 < to' performs unchecked ut64 addition: with attacker-controlled from = 0xfffffffffffffff0 and to = 0xffffffffffffffff (len = to - from = 15 passes 'len < 1 || len > ST32_MAX'), at needle = to - 3 the expression needle + 4 wraps to 0, which is '< to', so the check passes and r_read_le32 reads buf[12..15] from a 15-byte calloc(len,1) buffer — a heap out-of-bounds read of 1 byte (up to 3 bytes at needle = to - 1). Root cause: integer overflow in the bounds check; consequence: OOB read (CWE-125).

evidence.snippet:
static int string_scan_range(RList *list, RBinFile *bf, int min,
			      const ut64 from, const ut64 to, int type, int raw, RBinSection *section) {
evidence.reason: Taint origin: 'from' and 'to' are ut64 parameters whose producer is not shown in this code; per the width-domain rule their surface is the full 64-bit domain, including values near UT64_MAX that trigger the wrap in the 'needle + 4 < to' check at line 77.

assumptions: r_read_le32 reads exactly 4 bytes little-endian from the given address; r_utf8_decode/r_utf16le_decode/r_utf32le_decode honor the length argument passed as 'to - needle' and read no more than that many bytes; r_utf8_encode writes at most 4 bytes — all characterizable per discipline 3.
The scan range (from, to) derives from the parsed binary or caller-supplied range; its producer is not shown, so both values are treated as attacker-data over the full ut64 domain.
The escape lookup table literal is exactly 93 characters long, matching the 'r < 93' guard, so the tmp[i+1] table indexing is in bounds.
limitations: Charset path (lines 47-53): 'int outlen = len * 4;' truncates to a negative int for scan ranges len >= 2^30 (permitted by the ST32_MAX check), and 'int res = r_charset_encode_str (...)' is consumed by 'for (i = 0; i < res; i++)' and 'len = res' with no sentinel check. Impact is not instantiated: it requires a >= 4 GB successful calloc, an operator-set RABIN2_CHARSET, and semantics of the not-shown internal callee r_charset_encode_str that discipline 3 does not cover. Recorded as an int-truncation/unchecked-return hardening concern, not a confirmed vulnerability.
r_buf_read_at (line 42) return value is unchecked; a short read leaves the calloc-zeroed buffer, which has no memory-safety consequence, only missed strings.

The OOB bytes read into n1 are only tested for zero (skip optimization), so no direct information disclosure of the out-of-bounds bytes to output was instantiated; the impact is the heap out-of-bounds read itself and potential crash on unmapped page adjacency.

All other sinks (w[0]..w[8] detection reads, tmp writes, needle backup 'needle -= 2', WIDE/WIDE32 BOM lookbacks, decode calls) were verified guarded by quoted statements: '(to - needle) > 8 + rc', 'i < sizeof (tmp) - 4', 'runes >= 2', 'str_start - from > 1' / '> 3'.

verdict.summary: add_mtab writes the unvalidated, attacker-supplied strings devname, mountpoint and fstype verbatim into the root-owned /etc/mtab via addmntent. An embedded newline in any of these fields (instantiable by the unprivileged invoker this function is designed for, per its own 'if (uid != 0)' branch) terminates the real record and injects arbitrary forged mount-table records, corrupting the shared table and misleading privileged mtab consumers such as setuid umount's user=-based unmount authorization. No statement in this code validates, canonicalizes, or encodes these fields on any path.

evidence.reason:
Sink: addmntent serializes mountent's fields verbatim into the privileged MOUNTED file. mnt_fsname/mnt_dir/mnt_type hold raw attacker-supplied strings; a '
' inside devname or mountpoint injects forged records into /etc/mtab. Trigger instantiated: unprivileged invoker, mountpoint '/tmp/m
//evil/dev /srv/data cifs rw,user=<self> 0 0
'.

Taint origin in-body: the attacker-controlled parameters devname and mountpoint are assigned to mntent fields with no delimiter/metacharacter validation, canonicalization, or length check anywhere between entry (line 1) and the addmntent sink (line 86).

assumptions: addmntent (glibc mntent) writes mnt_fsname/mnt_dir/mnt_type/mnt_opts fields verbatim without escaping record delimiters — standard documented mntent behavior relied on per callee-semantics rules.

/etc/mtab (MOUNTED) is a root-owned shared system file whose consumers (setuid umount user= authorization, df, mount) trust its records — documented OS behavior, but those consumers are outside this code.

The privileged (setuid-root) execution context is inferred from this code's own statements: writing MOUNTED, locking the mtab, toggle_dac_capability, and recording the invoking user's name when uid != 0.
limitations: If calloc(MTAB_OPTIONS_LEN, 1) at line 61 fails, mnt_opts stays NULL and is passed unchecked to addmntent at line 86 (the line-62 check guards only the strlcat block). Not counted as a vulnerability: allocation failure of a constant size is not attacker-inducible, and glibc-style rendering of NULL %s yields '(null)' rather than corruption.

unlock_mtab is invoked twice on every normal path (explicitly at line 91/53 and again at process exit through atexit registered at line 42). Potentially a lock-lifetime defect, but unlock_mtab's body is not shown, so no harmful effect can be exhibited from this code.

strlcat safely truncates a very long username in the 'user=' option, which could produce a misleading truncated user= record that collides with another user's name; trigger requires an improbable prefix-named account and a near-full options buffer.

strlcat usage is otherwise correct: every size argument matches the calloc size, and calloc's NULL sentinel is checked before all strlcat calls; setmntent/setreuid/sigfillset/sigprocmask/lock_mtab return values are all sentinel-checked.

verdict.summary: The exported netlink handler tc_new_tfilter consumes attacker-supplied netlink attributes (filter kind string, u32 chain index, tcm_* fields), but every data-carrying value that reaches a sink is bounded by a quoted, execution-order-correct guard: the kind string is length-validated by the tested return of tcf_proto_check_kind before any use of the fixed 16-byte buffer 'name', the u32 chain index is rejected above TC_ACT_EXT_VAL_MASK before tcf_chain_get, and all callee failure sentinels (IS_ERR/NULL/negative err) are checked before first use on every path including the EAGAIN replay loop, which re-initializes tp_created and re-executes all guards. No attacker-instantiable trigger reaches an unguarded memory, index, size, or injection sink in this code.

assumptions: Semantics of not-shown internal callees (tcf_proto_check_kind's length validation of the kind string into name[IFNAMSIZ], __tcf_qdisc_find's filtering of qdiscs without cl_ops, tcf_chain_get/tcf_chain_tp_insert_unique reference accounting) were treated per discipline 3; where this code consumes their returns, it checks the failure sentinel locally (IS_ERR, NULL, negative err) at every use site.
TC_ACT_EXT_VAL_MASK is taken as the kernel's defined upper bound for chain indices; the quoted comparison correctly admits the limit itself and rejects one-past-the-limit.
limitations: The expression q->ops->cl_ops->flags in the rtnl-lock condition dereferences cl_ops; non-NULL cl_ops is a contract of the not-shown __tcf_qdisc_find (called with create=false) that cannot be quoted here. Worst case would be a NULL read crash with no demonstrated corruption; the precondition could not be instantiated from this code, so it is speculative, not a vulnerability finding.

Reference-balance on the errout/errout_tp/EAGAIN-replay goto web relies on the refcount semantics of not-shown helpers (tcf_chain_tp_delete_empty, tcf_proto_put, tcf_chain_put); the local guards (tp && !IS_ERR(tp), !tp_created, tp_created reset at replay:) are quoted and consistent, and no imbalance is derivable from this code alone.

All paths are gated by netlink_ns_capable(..., CAP_NET_ADMIN), so triggering any behavior already requires CAP_NET_ADMIN in the target net namespace; even setting that aside, no unguarded attacker-data sink was found.

verdict.summary: reg_match_visual() is a static engine helper with no attacker-parameterized inputs; its two historical memory-safety hazards are explicitly guarded in this code: the cross-buffer/stale-Visual check (rex.reg_buf != curbuf || VIsual.lnum == 0) and the post-getvvcol line refetch with input re-anchoring (rex.line = reg_getline(rex.lnum); rex.input = rex.line + col;). Remaining boundary arithmetic (end - (*p_sel == 'e'), col >= bot.col + (*p_sel != 'e')) is comparison-only, fails closed at the edge values, and reaches no memory, copy, or injection sink.

assumptions: colnr_T is Vim's signed int; VIsual, wp->w_cursor, and curbuf->b_visual positions are editor-maintained in-buffer values whose producers (not shown) keep them within the buffer.

The regex engine (not shown) maintains rex.lnum within the buffer, rex.input within [rex.line, rex.line + line-length], and sets rex.reg_win consistently with rex.reg_buf; no statement in this code can violate these contracts.
getvvcol() computes virtual columns and does not mutate buffer lines, so reg_getline(rex.lnum) cannot return NULL on any path in this code.
p_sel is 'old', 'inclusive', or 'exclusive'; the expression (*p_sel != 'e') evaluates to 0 or 1 as assumed.
limitations: A NULL return from reg_getline(rex.lnum) at the refetch would make rex.input = NULL + col and win_linetabsize dereference it, but instantiating it requires the buffer to shrink or rex.lnum to be out of range due to code not shown (e.g., a callback fired from inside getvvcol); speculative in this code.
If the not-shown engine ever set rex.reg_win to a window whose buffer differs from rex.reg_buf, getvvcol could index the wrong buffer's lines; no such path exists in the given code.

cols > end - (*p_sel == 'e') evaluates to end - 1 = -1 when end == 0 with exclusive selection, rejecting all columns; this is correct fail-closed behavior for an empty exclusive Visual block and affects only match results, not memory safety.

The pre-fix version of this function (without the rex.line refetch and rex.input re-anchor, or without the curbuf check) had a reachable stale-pointer/cross-buffer defect; the given code is the patched form.

verdict.summary: All memory-safety sinks in apprentice_load are guarded by quotable checks: the filearr growth check 'if (files >= maxfiles)' caps indexing, ecalloc/erealloc results are NULL-checked with error arms, and the estrndup length clamp '(mflen > sizeof(mfn) - 1)? sizeof(mfn) - 1: mflen' bounds the duplicate against snprintf's inherent NUL-terminated truncation. The one absent check is an upper-bound test on the snprintf return (only '< 0' is tested), so an overlong path is silently truncated to a same-directory prefix; the truncated path cannot escape the directory (prefix truncation only), causes no out-of-bounds access, and any harmful consequence would require an unshown consumer, so it is recorded as a limitation rather than a vulnerability. Remaining issues (empty-directory efree(NULL)/qsort(NULL,0), OOM-path leaks, stat-then-load TOCTOU, maxfiles overflow at ~2^62 entries) are either unshown-callee semantics, environment-only triggers, or require attacker filesystem access this code never grants.

assumptions: ms is a valid pointer produced by the same module's caller (file_apprentice); no assertion exists in this code, but NULL would crash at memset before any sink.

load_1, coalesce_entries, set_text_binary, set_last_default, magic_entry_free, cmpstrp are unshown project-internal callees; the invariants that mset[j].me holds mset[j].count valid entries and that coalesce_entries transfers ownership before magic_entry_free are module-internal and unquotable here.
PHP allocator semantics (erealloc/efree/estrndup failure and NULL behavior) are not shown; erealloc is treated per its quoted NULL check, efree(NULL) behavior is unknown and cannot produce a trigger.

fn and the directory entries d.d_name are attacker-influenced data per discipline 4; in the PHP fileinfo extension the magic path is userland-settable, which is the basis for treating directory contents as attacker-reachable.
limitations: Missing truncation check: 'if ((mflen = snprintf(mfn, sizeof(mfn), "%s/%s", fn, d.d_name)) < 0)' tests only the negative return; upstream libmagic also rejects mflen >= sizeof(mfn). A path longer than MAXPATHLEN-1 is silently truncated and the truncated same-directory prefix is then stat'd, duplicated, and loaded by load_1. No memory-safety violation results (snprintf bounds and the estrndup clamp keep every access in-bounds) and the truncated path is a strict prefix within fn's directory, so no path escape or other in-code security impact is instantiated; the defect becomes security-relevant only if an unshown consumer mis-handles the misloaded file.

If the opened directory contains no regular files, filearr remains NULL and the code executes qsort(NULL, 0, ...) and efree(NULL); if the PHP allocator crashed on efree(NULL) this would be a local DoS, but that callee behavior is not shown and per discipline 3 cannot be assumed.
The two 'goto out' paths inside the readdir loop (snprintf negative, erealloc NULL) leak filearr and its estrndup'd entries; trigger requires allocation failure no attacker can induce.

TOCTOU: 'if (stat(mfn, &st) == -1 || !S_ISREG(st.st_mode))' validates file type before load_1 later opens the path; an attacker with write access to the magic directory could swap in a FIFO or device between check and open. This code never makes the directory attacker-writable, so the trigger is speculative (STEP 4(d)).
maxfiles = (maxfiles + 1) * 2 and mlen = maxfiles * sizeof(*filearr) can overflow only with roughly 2^62 directory entries, which is not instantiable.

verdict.summary: nft_verdict_init validates every attacker-supplied value at its own sinks: the nested netlink attributes are policy-parsed with the tb array correctly sized for the parse bound, a missing NFTA_VERDICT_CODE is rejected, the verdict code is whitelist-validated against NF_ACCEPT/NF_DROP/NF_QUEUE (masked) and the NFT_* constants, and both chain-resolution paths (name lookup and lookup-byid) funnel into an IS_ERR check that returns before any dereference of chain. The set-element/binding-chain combination is explicitly rejected before chain->use++. The only residual concerns (a hypothetical NULL-returning chain lookup and the permitted jump-from-rule to a binding chain) rest on callee or destruction behavior not present in the given code and could not be instantiated as triggers here.

assumptions: nft_verdict_policy (not shown) declares attribute types/lengths enforced by nla_parse_nested_deprecated, so tb[NFTA_VERDICT_CODE] carries a 4-byte big-endian value as nla_get_be32 requires and tb[NFTA_VERDICT_CHAIN] carries a bounded chain name.

nft_chain_lookup and nft_chain_lookup_byid (not shown) signal a miss with an error pointer, per the IS_ERR/PTR_ERR convention this code itself applies; if their miss sentinel were instead NULL, that would be a defect in the callees, not in this code.
Batch transaction serialization in the caller (not shown) prevents concurrent use of the commit-list chains between the lookup and chain->use++.
limitations: If nft_chain_lookup could return NULL on a missed lookup, the IS_ERR-only checks at lines 42 and 48 would not catch it and nft_is_base_chain(chain)/chain->use++ would dereference NULL (kernel NULL-deref DoS triggered by unprivileged netlink). Dismissed as speculative: the callee's return convention is not shown, and per the analysis rules an unshown callee's behavior can neither produce the trigger nor guard the sink.

The code permits NFT_JUMP/NFT_GOTO to an NFT_CHAIN_BINDING chain when desc->flags lacks NFT_DATA_DESC_SETELEM (the line 52-53 rejection is conditional on it). Any dangling-reference/UAF impact depends on chain destruction and commit logic not present in the given code, so the impact chain is not instantiated here.
chain->use is incremented here without a bound; overflowing it would require roughly 2^32 live verdict references referencing the same chain, which is not attacker-scalable through this interface.

verdict.summary: All attacker-controlled lengths and indices (optlen, exportnamelen, nrinfos, querylen, opt_index) are constrained by on-screen reject-form guards in execution order — optlen > MAX_REQUEST_SIZE, optlen < 6/8, exportnamelen > optlen-6, the exact-length pin optlen != 4+exportnamelen+2+2*nrinfos, and opt_index+4 > optlen — and by validation helpers (check_export_name, check_string) to which this code explicitly passes the remaining-buffer maxima. Allocation is sized from the same expression as the copy length. The only candidate triggers (u32 wrap of opt_index+4 permitting an out-of-bounds memcpy in the meta-context query walk, or exportnamelen-driven over-read) require the unshown validation helpers to ignore the maxima quoted at their call sites, a precondition that cannot be instantiated per the analysis rules.

assumptions: check_export_name (option, buf, len, max) and check_string (option, buf, len, max, ...) enforce len <= max; the maxima are explicitly passed at the quoted call sites (optlen, optlen-6, optlen-8, optlen - opt_index), which is this code's way of documenting that contract.
conn_recv_full fills exactly the requested byte count and returns 0/-1; every call site checks == -1.
send_newstyle_option_reply_info_str treats a length of -1 (SIZE_MAX) as strlen(name); the in-code NBD_INFO_DESCRIPTION call passing 'desc, -1' documents this convention.

MAX_REQUEST_SIZE and MAX_NR_OPTIONS are sane compile-time constants (in upstream nbdkit 64MiB and a small option cap), so optlen+1 and 4+exportnamelen+2+2*nrinfos cannot wrap their u32/size_t arithmetic.

backend_finalize/backend_close tolerate a NULL context (the OPT_INFO tail calls them without the NULL check used on the nearby failure path); finish_newstyle_options is responsible for top_context's state.
send_newstyle_option_reply_exportnames (option, &nr_options) writes the loop countdown (option-budget accounting) and cannot extend negotiation without the attacker paying a round trip per iteration.
limitations: Meta-context query walk: if querylen were accepted by check_string despite exceeding optlen - opt_index, then opt_index += querylen could wrap u32 to >= 0xFFFFFFFC so that the guard 'if (opt_index+4 > optlen)' itself wraps and an out-of-bounds memcpy (&querylen, &data[opt_index], 4) would occur (~4GB past an optlen+1 heap buffer). Trigger requires the unshown check_string to violate the max this code passes it; not instantiable here.

If check_export_name did not enforce exportnamelen <= optlen-8, strndup (&data[4], exportnamelen) and the data[4..] reads could over-read; the call site quotes the max, and the on-screen opt_index+4 > optlen guard additionally contains all non-wrapping cases.

data[optlen] (the malloc'd +1 trailing byte) is never zeroed on-screen; the comment 'Allowing a trailing NUL helps some uses' implies some unshown consumer may treat data as a string — an over-read would occur only inside that unshown callee; all on-screen uses pass explicit lengths.
size_t namelen = -1 (SIZE_MAX) is passed to the unshown send_newstyle_option_reply_info_str; harmless only under the strlen convention.
Repeated NBD_OPT_SET_META_CONTEXT options leak the previous conn->exportname_from_set_meta_context allocation (pointer overwritten without free); bounded by MAX_NR_OPTIONS.
The non-fixed-newstyle reject path continues without draining optlen payload bytes, desynchronizing only the attacker's own connection; no cross-tenant impact.

verdict.summary: Kernel driver teardown routine with no attacker-data inputs. The only security-relevant use, gpio_free, is correctly guarded by gpio_is_valid on the same variable and unit in execution order; teardown ordering (abort, deinit, unregister, free, kfree) is canonical with no visible double-free or UAF. All other dereferences consume driver-internal state pointers under a same-driver caller contract, which no trust-boundary party can instantiate.

assumptions: priv, priv->ndev, priv->ndev->nfc_dev, and priv->config.reset_n_io are set by this driver's registration path (nfcmrvl_nci_register_dev and probe code, not shown) and are passed by in-tree kernel transport callers, not by any trust-boundary party.
nfcmrvl_fw_dnld_abort, nfcmrvl_fw_dnld_deinit, nci_unregister_device, nci_free_device behave per kernel NCI core semantics; none of their return values are consumed here.
limitations: NULL dereference of priv at 'struct nci_dev *ndev = priv->ndev;' (and the line-5 chained deref) would crash if a caller passed NULL, but no trust-boundary attacker can instantiate a kernel pointer parameter of this internal teardown API; it would require a buggy in-tree caller. Robustness concern only.

Potential TOCTOU on 'if (priv->ndev->nfc_dev->fw_download_in_progress)' followed by abort/deinit with no visible locking: the statement that flips the flag and the concurrent firmware-download worker are not shown in this code, so the race window and any use-after-free consequence inside the unshown deinit path cannot be instantiated from the given code.
Whether nfcmrvl_fw_dnld_deinit safely handles the download-in-progress case when the flag flips after the check cannot be verified because the callee is not shown.

verdict.summary: FindEmptyObjectSlot is an internal slot-lookup helper with no attacker-data inputs. The only parameter is an optional output pointer whose NULL case is guarded by the quoted 'if(handle)', and the array index is bounded by the quoted loop condition 'i < MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS', which matches the array's defining constant with the correct operator. The MemorySet size is sizeof of the exact destination type. All statements are defensible under boundary testing; dismissed candidates (concurrency on the slot table, unchecked NULL return by callers, stale slot contents) are speculative because their triggers or impact chains lie in code not shown.

assumptions: s_objects is declared with exactly MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS elements; the loop bound uses the identical constant, so the code is self-consistent by construction (the array declaration is not shown).
TRANSIENT_FIRST is a fixed TPM 2.0 transient-handle base constant small enough that i + TRANSIENT_FIRST cannot overflow UINT32 for any i the loop admits.
MemorySet is a standard memset-equivalent helper that cannot fail.
limitations: Concurrency: the occupied check and MemorySet on a slot would be a check-then-use window if this function ran concurrently on s_objects, but no lock release, callback, or re-entry point exists inside this code, so no window is exhibitable here; single-threaded TPM command execution is assumed.
Callers that use the returned pointer without checking for NULL would dereference NULL on a full object table; the callers are not shown and the sentinel is correctly returned here.

The returned slot's memory beyond 'attributes' (e.g., publicArea, sensitive fields) retains stale contents until the caller initializes the object; any impact depends on consumers not shown in this code.

verdict.summary: FindEmptyObjectSlot indexes the global s_objects array only under the loop bound 'i < MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS', guards the only pointer write with 'if(handle)', and memsets exactly sizeof(*object) bytes into an in-bounds slot; no attacker-controlled value reaches any sink and no guard is missing or mis-operatored.

assumptions: s_objects is declared with exactly MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS elements (internal array/constant pairing; not a trust-boundary value).
TPMI_DH_OBJECT is a 32-bit handle type, so i + TRANSIENT_FIRST cannot overflow for any realistic MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS.
occupied == CLEAR corresponds to a zeroed attributes field, so the whole-object MemorySet leaves the slot read as empty.
limitations: Callers of FindEmptyObjectSlot must NULL-check the returned pointer; an unchecked use in a caller not shown here would be a defect there, not in this function.
handle must point to writable memory of type TPMI_DH_OBJECT when non-NULL; that is the caller's contract and is outside this code's control.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds write in ST21NFCA_EVT_TRANSACTION handling: skb->data[1] is copied into transaction->aid_len and used directly as a memcpy length without any validation against skb->len or the skb->len-2 devm_kzalloc allocation. The only length check (lines 22-24) uses && so both of its conditions must fail to reject, letting a 7-byte skb with aid_len 0xFF pass, which writes 255 bytes into a 5-byte kernel heap allocation (and OOB-reads the skb). The params side (lines 39-41) has the same missing validation, and the tag check at lines 35-36 also indexes skb->data out of bounds.

evidence.reason: Defective validation: the && operator means the request is rejected only when BOTH the length is short AND the tag is wrong, so a skb with len >= 7 passes regardless of tag and a short skb passes whenever data[0] == 0x81. Trigger input skb->len = 7 makes '7 < 7' false and the whole condition false. The check also never constrains aid_len or params_len against skb->len anywhere.

Primary sink: attacker-controlled u8 skb->data[1] (domain 0-255 per width rule) becomes the memcpy length, but the allocation at line 26 is sized skb->len - 2. Simulated trigger: skb->len = 7, data[1] = 0xFF -> devm_kzalloc(5) then memcpy of 255 bytes into a 5-byte kernel heap object, a ~250-byte out-of-bounds write (CWE-787), plus an out-of-bounds read of skb->data[2..256]. No statement anywhere ties aid_len to skb->len or the allocation.

Out-of-bounds read: index aid_len + 2 (up to 257) is never checked against skb->len. At the exact boundary skb->len == aid_len + 2 (e.g. len 7, aid_len 5) this reads skb->data[7], one past the last valid byte.

Second unguarded sink: params_len (u8, 0-255) is read from index aid_len + 3 and used as memcpy length with no check that aid_len + 4 + params_len <= skb->len (read side) or that fields + aid_len + params_len fit in the skb->len - 2 allocation (write side). Simulated trigger: len 260, aid_len 255, params_len 2 -> reads skb->data[259..260] past len and writes past offset 257 of a 258-byte allocation.

assumptions: skb is the raw HCI EVT_TRANSACTION packet delivered to this event-received handler; its content and lengths cross the controller/host trust boundary and are treated as attacker-data per the width-domain rule (each data[] byte domain 0-255, skb->len domain of unsigned int). No statement in this code narrows them except the defective check at lines 22-24.

struct nfc_evt_transaction is not shown; the overflow proof only assumes transaction->aid/params lie within the skb->len-2 allocation, which holds for any layout, and any nonzero field offsets only enlarge the overflow.
NFC_MIN_AID_LENGTH = 5 and the tags are 0x81/0x82 per the in-code ETSI 102 622 comment.
limitations: skb->len < 2 makes skb->len - 2 wrap to a near-UINT_MAX size; devm_kzalloc then fails and the NULL check at line 27 returns -ENOMEM, so that path is contained and not counted as a vulnerability.

On the -EPROTO arms (lines 24 and 37) the devm_kzalloc'd transaction and the skb are never freed; devm memory persists until device unbind, so each malformed event retains skb->len-2 bytes of kernel memory (attacker-scalable retention, CWE-400 class) - secondary, not the primary defect.
Reading skb->data[0] when skb->len == 0 (line 23) reads past the logical skb data area, though typically still within allocated buffer tailroom - minor out-of-bounds read.

verdict.summary: No attacker-instantiable defect. The function is a teardown path with no data content crossing a trust boundary: the only memory-affecting call on an unbounded value, gpio_free(priv->config.reset_n_io), is guarded by the immediately preceding, same-variable check if (gpio_is_valid(priv->config.reset_n_io)); the frees of ndev and priv occur after their last use with no use-after-free on any path visible in this code; the unchecked pointer derefs of priv, priv->ndev and priv->ndev->nfc_dev lack NULL guards but their failure requires the kernel-internal caller to pass a NULL handle and results only in an equal-privilege crash, and the check-then-abort on fw_download_in_progress has no exhibitable race window between its two consecutive statements.

assumptions: nci_unregister_device, nci_free_device, nfcmrvl_fw_dnld_abort and nfcmrvl_fw_dnld_deinit are project-internal callees not shown; per the analysis rules their behavior (including whether nci_unregister_device frees ndev before line 6 re-reads priv->ndev) is an assumption that can neither create nor dismiss a defect here.
gpio_is_valid is treated per its standard kernel semantics: it rejects negative and out-of-range GPIO numbers, including the one-past-limit value.

priv, priv->ndev and priv->ndev->nfc_dev are produced by the device registration path (not shown) and are assumed to be non-NULL pointers created at probe time; this code contains no statement narrowing them.
limitations: Unchecked NULL dereference chain: lines 3 and 6 dereference priv, priv->ndev and priv->ndev->nfc_dev with no NULL guard anywhere in the function (mention sweep found none). A NULL handle from the unregister path would crash the kernel, but the trigger is not instantiable by any trust-boundary party from this code and the impact is an equal-privilege crash only, so it is recorded as a robustness issue rather than a vulnerability.

Check-then-act on priv->ndev->nfc_dev->fw_download_in_progress (line 6 check, line 7 abort): a TOCTOU exists in principle, but the two statements are consecutive with no quoted lock release, callback registration, or re-entry point between them, and the impact of a stale flag decision lands entirely inside unshown callees, so the window and impact cannot be instantiated here.

Potential use-after-free/double-free of ndev (lines 5, 6, 14) would exist only if nci_unregister_device freed ndev before the re-read at line 6; the callee is not shown and its behavior may not be assumed to produce a trigger, so this candidate is speculative.

verdict.summary: ReadTGAImage reads the attacker-supplied TGA comment with an unchecked length: ReadBlob(image,tga_info.id_length,comment) may return fewer bytes than id_length on a truncated file, but the return count is never compared to id_length and the buffer (AcquireQuantumMemory, non-zeroing) is never initialized or NUL-terminated at count; only comment[id_length]='\0' is written. The resulting string contains uninitialized heap bytes and is stored via SetImageProperty(image,"comment",...). Because the final EOF handling uses the non-returning ThrowFileException before returning the image, the poisoned comment property survives, disclosing up to 255 bytes of process heap memory through image metadata.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the ReadBlob return count is not validated against tga_info.id_length and the non-zeroing buffer is terminated at id_length rather than at count, so on a short read (e.g. a file truncated right after the 18-byte header with id_length=255) bytes [count, id_length) remain uninitialized heap, are included in the stored comment string, and reach output as image metadata.

Origin of the uninitialized bytes: AcquireQuantumMemory is a malloc-like allocator that does not zero memory; nothing between this allocation and the SetImageProperty call initializes the [count, id_length) region, so those bytes are attacker-triggerable uninitialized heap disclosure.

assumptions: AcquireQuantumMemory behaves like malloc (no zeroing); ReadBlob returns only the number of bytes actually read (0 at EOF) and does not fill the remainder of the buffer.
SetImageProperty copies the string into the image's comment property, which is exportable image metadata.

ThrowFileException records the exception and does not return (unlike ThrowReaderException), so the truncated-file image with the poisoned comment is still returned by the final return(GetFirstImageInList(image)).

ConstrainColormapIndex bounds indexes against image->colors (bounds-safe helper at the colormap dereference sites), and AcquireImageColormap allocates image->colors entries or returns MagickFalse, which this code checks; both failures are handled by ThrowReaderException paths.
limitations: Raw grayscale index (0-255) is stored via SetPixelIndex for PseudoClass images with colormap_type==0 even when image->colors < 256 (e.g. 2-bpp Monochrome gives colors=4); no memory dereference in this code uses that value, and downstream consumers are not shown, so this is recorded as an integrity issue, not a primary vulnerability.

On 32-bit builds, one << tga_info.bits_per_pixel with bits_per_pixel==32 is undefined behavior; this is width-specific speculation, and on 64-bit the resulting 2^32-entry colormap request fails through the checked AcquireImageColormap error path.

Actual disclosure requires the victim to view or export the image's comment property (standard metadata flow outside the given code); the in-code chain (uninitialized bytes to SetImageProperty) is fully instantiated.

verdict.summary: tipc_crypto_key_rcv() copies an attacker-controlled session key from a TIPC message into a heap buffer allocated from the attacker-controlled message data size, using a key length read raw from the packet (skey->keylen) as the memcpy length, with the only size validation (size != tipc_aead_key_size(skey)) performed AFTER the copies. A network peer sending a key-distribution message with a small data size and arbitrary keylen causes a kernel heap out-of-bounds write with fully attacker-controlled content and length (up to 2^32-1 bytes past a <=64KB allocation); even a zero/small size overflows via the fixed 32-byte alg_name copy and the keylen store at offset 32.

evidence.reason: Heap out-of-bounds write: the copy length skey->keylen is read raw from the attacker-controlled message payload (line 24, no clamp or mask) while the destination was allocated with kmalloc(size) where size = msg_data_sz(hdr) is an independent attacker-controlled u16 (line 6/17). No statement in the code bounds keylen against size before this memcpy; the only sanity check (line 30) runs after the copy. Trigger: first-keyed rx node receives a key message with size=4 and keylen=0x1000 -> memcpy writes 4096 attacker bytes past a 4-byte heap chunk in kernel space.

Origin of the undersized destination: the allocation is sized from the attacker-controlled message data size (u16, domain 0..65535), which is never validated against the minimum TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME + sizeof(__be32) bytes that lines 24-27 unconditionally write. With size < 36 (including size=0, where kmalloc returns non-NULL ZERO_SIZE_PTR that passes the !skey check on line 18), the keylen store at offset 32 and the 32-byte alg_name memcpy on lines 24-25 are themselves out-of-bounds heap writes before any validation.

assumptions: TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME = 32 and struct tipc_aead_key is { char alg_name[32]; unsigned int keylen; char key[]; } per the known kernel header (not shown in the snippet); the keylen field therefore sits at offset 32 of the allocation.
msg_data_sz/msg_data/msg_key_gen/msg_key_mode read fields of the raw TIPC message supplied by a network peer; TIPC bearer traffic is across the trust boundary.
kmalloc(0, GFP_ATOMIC) returns the non-NULL ZERO_SIZE_PTR, so the !skey check on line 18 does not reject a zero-size message.
limitations: The out-of-bounds READ of data + TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME when size < 36 (line 24) is folded into the primary write-overflow finding rather than reported separately.

The sanity check at line 30 (size != tipc_aead_key_size(skey)) is fail-late, not fail-open: it prevents installing the oversized key but executes after the heap corruption has already occurred; it is recorded as the root-cause context, not an independent vulnerability.

Reachability requires TIPC to be configured with a bearer and the receiving node not yet keyed (rx->skey == NULL and generation mismatch); these are ordinary first-key states, and deployment configuration is not a code-level guard.

verdict.summary: ex_retab's memory operations are self-consistent: the allocation size (old_len - col + start_col + len + 1) is computed from the same expressions that bound every memmove and fill write, col is held within [0, old_len] by the NUL test, vcol is capped by the MAXCOL check, and new_ts is range-checked before use, so no out-of-bounds access, overflow, or division defect is reachable from attacker-controlled line content. The three early-return error paths fail to restore curwin->w_p_list, which is a display-state defect, not a security impact.

assumptions: eap->arg, eap->forceit, eap->line1/line2 originate from the operator's own Ex command line, not from a party across a trust boundary; the cross-boundary data in this function is the buffer line content returned by ml_get()
ml_get() returns a NUL-terminated line for lnum in the operator-specified range; range clamping is performed in the Ex command dispatcher, which is not shown

tabstop_set(), tabstop_fromto(), tabstop_count(), tabstop_first(), and set_string_option_direct() are internal callees whose contracts (valid array on success, t/s always written, no frees of curbuf->b_p_vts_array inside set_string_option_direct) could not be quoted from the given code and are recorded as assumptions, not guards
curbuf->b_p_ts and the vartabstop arrays maintain Vim's internal invariants (ts >= 1, arrays NUL/zero-terminated)
limitations: Functional defect: the three early error returns (tabstop_set(...) == FAIL, negative new_ts, new_ts > TABSTOP_MAX) all occur after curwin->w_p_list = 0 and bypass the restore statement curwin->w_p_list = save_list;, so an invalid :retab argument permanently clears the 'list' option until the user resets it; 'list' is a display-only option and does not represent a security state, so this is recorded as a limitation

Speculative: if set_string_option_direct() for "vts" internally reallocates or frees curbuf->b_p_vts_array, the subsequent curbuf->b_p_vts_array = new_vts_array; vim_free(old_vts_ary); could double-free or leak; no statement in the given code exhibits this, and the callee is not shown, so the trigger is not instantiated
If ml_replace() returns FAIL, the newly allocated new_line leaks once; reachable only on out-of-memory with no attacker leverage
Line-range values eap->line1/eap->line2 are assumed clamped by the Ex dispatcher; if a caller passed an out-of-range lnum the defect would be in the dispatcher, not here

verdict.summary: In mbfl_filt_conv_big5_wchar's CP950 PUA handling, the table-scan loop can terminate without a match, leaving k equal to the table entry count; k is then used to index cp950_pua_tbl[k][0..3] with no post-loop bounds check, reading one element past the end of the static table. The out-of-bounds values are folded into w and emitted through the filter's output function, so attacker-supplied CP950 bytes (any pair accepted by the PUA gate but outside every table range) cause an out-of-bounds read with disclosure of adjacent read-only data into the converted output, or a crash of the process performing the conversion.

evidence.reason: Sink: cp950_pua_tbl[k] is indexed with k after the scan loop, but k can equal the table entry count (lookup miss), so these reads are one element past the end of cp950_pua_tbl. The loaded values flow into w and are emitted at the output_function call, turning the OOB read into disclosure of adjacent data in the converted output. No bounds check on k exists between the loop and these uses.

Origin of the harmful value: this loop is a lookup over the PUA range table whose failure sentinel is k == the entry count (loop exits without break when attacker-controlled c2 = c1<<8|c matches no range). The bound k < N constrains k only during iterations; the sentinel k == N is consumed unchecked at line 53.

assumptions: is_in_cp950_pua(c1, c) is a project-internal callee not shown in the given code; its exact acceptance region is unknown, so it is treated as an unquotable contract that can neither guard the table access nor block the trigger.
The contents of cp950_pua_tbl and big5_ucs_table/big5_ucs_table_size are not shown; N is taken from the code's own expression sizeof(cp950_pua_tbl)/(sizeof(unsigned short)*4).
The CK macro is assumed to be a standard error-path wrapper around the output call; it does not affect the table indexing.
filter->cache was verified internal-trusted: it is only set at line 20 to a byte that passed the quoted lead-byte branch c > c1 && c < 0xff.
limitations: The concrete trigger byte pair depends on the unshown is_in_cp950_pua region and table ranges; the miss path is nonetheless in-domain because the loop's break condition (a range match) is conditional and its failure sentinel k == N is always reachable per the lookup-miss rule.
big5_ucs_table[w] at line 38 is safely guarded by the quoted check w >= 0 && w < big5_ucs_table_size; no other candidates survived.

verdict.summary: On the X10-format ('static short') path with padding, read_bitmap_file_data allocates bits with g_malloc (uninitialized) and the version10p loop skips the second byte write at every scanline end ('if (!padding || ((bytes+2) % bytes_per_line)) *(ptr++) = value >> 8;'), so only size-hh bytes are ever written. The full size-byte buffer, including hh uninitialized heap bytes (entire bottom scanlines), is returned to the caller via *data = bits, disclosing heap memory contents through the parsed bitmap data.

evidence.reason: Root cause: in the version10p loop with padding=1 (ww%16 in [1,8]), the second byte write is skipped whenever (bytes+2) % bytes_per_line == 0, i.e., once per scanline. Over hh scanlines only size-hh bytes are written into the size-byte buffer, but the loop terminates on the bytes counter, not the write count, so nothing detects the shortfall. Trigger instantiated: file with '#define b_width 8', '#define b_height 4', 'static short b_bits[] = { 0x12,0x34,0x56,0x78 };' yields bytes_per_line=2, size=8, and only bits[0..3] written; bits[4..7] remain uninitialized and are returned as bitmap data.

Origin of the uninitialized memory: g_malloc does not zero the allocation, and no statement in the function (mention sweep over every use of bits: NULL init, RETURN macro g_free, this allocation, ptr = bits, *data = bits) initializes or zeroes the pad slots that the version10p loop skips, so uninitialized heap bytes reach the output *data = bits.

assumptions: next_int() is a project-internal callee not shown; its return is sentinel-checked (< 0) before use, and its positive values are truncated to guchar on write, so no memory-safety dependence was placed on its range.
g_malloc is assumed to follow documented GLib semantics: it aborts on allocation failure rather than returning NULL, so the unchecked result at line 96 is not a NULL-deref path.
MAX_SIZE is a constant large enough that the sscanf %s token (bounded by strlen(line) <= MAX_SIZE-1) always fits name_and_type[MAX_SIZE].
limitations: Functional over-rejection: a line of exactly MAX_SIZE-1 characters including the newline fills the fgets buffer and is rejected by 'if (strlen (line) == MAX_SIZE-1) RETURN (FALSE);' — over-rejects the exact-fit boundary but cannot under-admit an oversized line.

Transient resource spike: attacker-declared dimensions up to INT_MAX (e.g., width 16, height 2^30-1) pass the quoted overflow check 'if (size / bytes_per_line != hh)' and force a g_malloc of ~2GB before any data is read; the allocation is freed when next_int fails, and abort requires an actual allocation failure, so this is bounded and not promoted to a primary finding.
Hotspot values hx/hy are taken from the file without validating that they lie within [0,ww]x[0,hh]; any consequence depends on the consumer, which is not shown.

For a bare '#define hot ...' name, 'if (type-- == name_and_type || type-- == name_and_type)' decrements type to name_and_type-1 (an out-of-bounds pointer value) before 'continue'; the pointer is never dereferenced on that path, so this is a robustness issue only.

verdict.summary: In inflate()'s gzip EXTRA-field handling, the copy offset len = extra_len - state->length counts input bytes consumed, while extra_len is set directly from the attacker-controlled 16-bit gzip XLEN field with no bound (line 130). When the caller's header buffer (extra_max) is smaller than the declared XLEN, len eventually exceeds extra_max, and the copy length state->head->extra_max - len (line 149) underflows to ~4 GiB, so zmemcpy writes attacker-controlled bytes far past the caller's heap buffer. A crafted gzip stream fed across three or more inflate() calls with a caller using inflateGetHeader (a documented, legitimate configuration) yields a heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787; root cause unsigned underflow CWE-191). This is the zlib CVE-2022-37434 defect, fixed upstream by clamping len to extra_max, a guard absent from this code.

evidence.reason: Sink of the heap out-of-bounds write. len is the number of extra-field input bytes consumed so far (extra_len - state->length) and grows without bound, while the ternary's else-arm state->head->extra_max - len is unsigned and underflows once len > extra_max. Trigger: attacker declares XLEN=500, caller supplies a truthful 100-byte extra buffer; on the third inflate() call len=200 and the copy length becomes 100-200 = 0xFFFFFF9C, so zmemcpy writes ~4 GiB of attacker bytes past the buffer. No clamp of len or extra_len against extra_max exists anywhere in the code.

Origin of the tainted values. hold is the attacker-controlled 16-bit gzip XLEN field (full domain 0..0xFFFF after NEEDBITS(16)); it is stored into state->length and state->head->extra_len with no comparison against state->head->extra_max, which is what later permits len = extra_len - length to exceed the destination buffer size.

assumptions: GUNZIP is defined so the gzip header path (HEAD/FLAGS/EXLEN/EXTRA) is compiled in; the given code textually includes this path and the hbuf declaration under the same guard.

The caller uses inflateGetHeader with head->extra != Z_NULL and a truthful extra_max (a documented, legitimate API usage; the API explicitly permits extra_max smaller than the actual extra-field length).
zmemcpy is memcpy with a 32-bit uInt length; the underflowed value 4294967196 fits and is passed through.
limitations: The overflow requires the gzip input to be delivered across at least three inflate() calls (e.g., a chunked network feed), which the attacker arranges but the caller's buffering pattern must permit; single-call feeds are safe because copy then equals the full remaining length.

All other classic inflate guards were verified present and quoted: nlen>286/ndist>30 check, the state->have + copy > nlen + ndist repeat bound, stored-block NLEN check, COPY clamps, NAME/COMMENT name_max/comm_max guards, MATCH whave/sane window checks, and left==0 tests; no other candidate survived.
This defect corresponds to CVE-2022-37434 in zlib through 1.2.12; the upstream fix adds 'if (len > state->head->extra_max) len = state->head->extra_max;' which appears nowhere in this code.

verdict.summary: addBinding computes the attacker-supplied namespace URI length in a signed int with an unbounded counting loop. A URI of at least 2^31 characters (or an exact-INT_MAX-length URI followed by the separator len++) overflows len to a negative value. Every downstream guard ('len > INT_MAX - EXPAND_SPARE', 'len > b->uriAlloc', the UINT_MAX/SIZE_MAX check) compares against positive bounds only, so a negative len bypasses them all; on the freeBindingList path no allocation or check runs at all and memcpy(b->uri, uri, len * sizeof(XML_Char)) executes with a wrapped ~2^64-scale size, giving an out-of-bounds read (uri[len] at negative indices) and a wild out-of-bounds write, crashing or corrupting the process parsing the attacker's document.

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: uri is the namespace URI string decoded from the attacker-supplied xmlns attribute of the parsed XML document; its full domain is an unbounded NUL-terminated string and no statement in this code bounds its length.

Defect site: len is a signed int with no iteration bound; the loop terminates only on the attacker-controlled NUL. With a >=2^31-character URI, len++ overflows past INT_MAX and wraps negative (the later 'len++' at the m_namespaceSeparator branch overflows identically for an exact-INT_MAX URI). This is the missing guard: no check anywhere rejects len reaching INT_MAX or a negative len.

evidence.snippet:
b->uriLen = len;
  memcpy(b->uri, uri, len * sizeof(XML_Char));
evidence.reason: Sink reached with the wrapped value: for negative len, the reuse-branch gate 'if (len > b->uriAlloc)' is false (negative <= uriAlloc), so the realloc block containing the 'len > INT_MAX - EXPAND_SPARE' overflow check is skipped entirely; memcpy then runs with len converted to size_t (~0xFFFFFFFF80000000 on 64-bit), a wild out-of-bounds write preceded by out-of-bounds reads of uri[len] at negative indices in the counting loop.

assumptions: uri is a NUL-terminated string (the code itself dereferences *uri and loops on the NUL); producers are the parser's internal pools, not shown.
REALLOC/MALLOC/FREE behave as standard allocation functions returning NULL on failure; their NULL sentinels are checked at lines 85, 93 and 112.
EXPAND_SPARE is a small positive constant, so INT_MAX - EXPAND_SPARE is near INT_MAX and the quoted checks are correct for the positive tail.
b->uriAlloc is a non-negative int maintained by the assignments 'b->uriAlloc = len + EXPAND_SPARE' in earlier invocations of this same function.
limitations: prefix->name[1..5] index reads are safe: the short-circuit '&&' chain stops at the first mismatch or NUL, so no read passes the string's terminator.
The memcpy never over-reads the source: with the separator set len == strlen+1, so it copies exactly the string including its NUL.
b->uri[len - 1] at len == 0 cannot occur: the write sits under 'if (parser->m_namespaceSeparator)', the same condition that performed len++, so len >= 1.
A NULL uri would crash at '*uri' (line 30), but uri originates from internal pool code not shown; recorded as a robustness contract issue only.

The wrapped memcpy size is astronomically large and not attacker-precise, so the practical impact of the confirmed corruption primitive is an immediate crash (denial of service of the parsing process) rather than controlled exploitation; triggering also requires an attacker to deliver a >=2 GiB namespace URI attribute value and to have a non-empty free-binding list, both arrangeable within a single crafted XML document.

verdict.summary: In the octet-counting digit branch, processDataRcvd writes the attacker-supplied digit into the message buffer with *(pThis->pMsg + pThis->iMsg++) = c; without any check of iMsg against iMaxLine. The code's own statements (clamp at iMaxLine - pThis->iMsg plus pThis->iMsg += octatesToCopy, and the end-of-frame transition to eAtStrtFram that resets state but never iMsg) can leave iMsg == iMaxLine when a new frame begins, so the first digit writes at pMsg[iMaxLine] and each subsequent digit (up to ~10 before the 200000000 error arm) writes further bytes past the allocation, a remote heap out-of-bounds write with attacker-chosen digit content. Every other pMsg write in the function is guarded (if(pThis->iMsg < iMaxLine) or the memcpy clamp), proving the bound is required and absent only here.

evidence.reason: Root cause: unguarded buffer write. The octet-count digit is stored at pMsg[iMsg] with no local bound on iMsg, although the identical stuffing-mode copy is guarded by if(pThis->iMsg < iMaxLine) (lines 102-104) and the memcpy path is clamped (lines 113-115). Instantiated trigger: a prior octet-counted frame clamps octatesToCopy = iMaxLine - pThis->iMsg and executes pThis->iMsg += octatesToCopy, leaving iMsg == iMaxLine; the end-of-frame path sets inputState = eAtStrtFram with no iMsg reset; the next attacker byte being a digit enters eInOctetCnt and this line writes pMsg[iMaxLine], and each following digit writes one byte further past the allocation — an out-of-bounds write of attacker-chosen digit characters.

Origin of the harmful state: the clamp at lines 113-115 plus pThis->iMsg += octatesToCopy drives iMsg to exactly iMaxLine for an oversized octet-counted frame, and the end-of-frame transition sets inputState = eAtStrtFram without any statement of this code resetting iMsg, so the unguarded digit write on the next frame operates at and past the buffer bound.

assumptions: The allocation size of pThis->pMsg is not shown in this code; it is presumably iMaxLine-based, but the defect holds regardless: the write at index >= iMaxLine violates the bound this code itself enforces at every other pMsg write.
doSubmitMsg, doSubmitMsg's effect on pThis->iMsg, errmsg.LogError, and LogError are internal callees not shown; their behavior cannot be assumed to reset iMsg and therefore cannot guard the sink.

buff and buffLen are supplied by the not-shown receive layer; buffLen is treated as the valid extent of *buff for the read loop at line 74 and the pointer advance at line 121, both of which are bounded by buffLen within this code.
limitations: The emergency-flush path can call doSubmitMsg twice for one logical message (flush at line 81 followed by a delimiter hit at lines 90-96), causing duplicate message submission; this is a logic defect without memory-safety or authorization impact and does not affect the verdict.

The exact exploitation reachability (heap layout, allocator behavior) beyond the out-of-bounds write primitive is not shown in this code; the confirmed primitive is the OOB write of up to ~10 attacker-chosen digit bytes past the message buffer.
The integer growth of iOctetsRemain is safely bounded by the quoted check iOctetsRemain <= 200000000 (max reachable 2000000009 < INT_MAX) and is not a defect.

verdict.summary: check_termcode parses attacker-controlled terminal escape sequences, but every memory access on the input buffer is guarded in this code: a per-iteration NUL sentinel is written at tp[len], all partial-sequence paths return -1 via quoted length checks (len<3, len<slen, len<=modslen, len<j, nr>=tp+len), and all internal callee results are sentinel-tested before use. Residual risks rest on unshown code (typebuf/buf slack for the sentinel write, check_termcode_mouse handling of idx==tc_len with a stale slen, modifiers2keycode sizing of string[]) and could not be instantiated as defects in the given code.

assumptions: typebuf.tb_buf and any caller-provided buf have at least one writable byte at index tb_len/*buflen; the statement tp[len] = NUL writes exactly there. No statement in this code enforces that slack; the allocation code is not shown.
*buflen <= bufsize and typebuf.tb_len are maintained correctly by vim's input layer (producer not shown); this code never validates them against the buffer size.

Internal callees (handle_csi, handle_osc, handle_dcs, check_termcode_mouse, put_string_in_typebuf, getdigits, get_bytes_from_buf, get_long_from_buf, modifiers2keycode, decode_modifiers) honor their documented contracts: scans stop at the NUL sentinel, num_bytes/-1 and FAIL sentinels are respected, and modifiers2keycode returns new_slen small enough that the subsequent 1-3 byte appends fit in string[MAX_KEY_CODE_LEN + 1].
limitations: Deferred-mouse path: when a mouse candidate is remembered via mouse_index_found and the termcodes loop completes without break, idx equals tc_len (one-past-end) and slen still holds the last iterated entry's length, which may exceed len (its len<slen check only runs on a STRNCMP match). These values are passed to the unshown callee check_termcode_mouse; if that callee indexes termcodes[idx] or consumes the stale slen without recomputing, the defect would be there, not in this code, so no trigger could be proven here.

tp[len] = NUL performs a deliberate one-past-length write; it is safe only under the allocation-slack assumption above. If the unshown allocation ever sized the buffer to exactly the tracked length, this would be a one-byte NUL out-of-bounds write (CWE-787), but no statement in this code can produce an oversized tb_len/*buflen.
n = atoi((char *)modifiers_start) is bounded by the NUL sentinel at tp[len], but decode_modifiers (unshown) must mask n; an unmasked large/negative n is only a concern if the callee mishandles it.

verdict.summary: nft_flow_rule_create sizes the flow rule's inline action array from num_actions, which counts only expressions whose ops provide offload_action returning true, but then invokes expr->ops->offload on every expression in the rule. Any expression type that appends a flow action during offload without being counted (no offload_action callback or a false return) causes the action array to be written past its allocation, an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) rooted in the buffer size miscalculation (CWE-131). No bounds enforcement between the counting pass, the offload pass, or nft_flow_rule_transfer_vlan exists anywhere in this function.

evidence.reason: Sink: the offload callback is invoked for every expression in the attacker-configured rule, appending action entries to flow's array, which was allocated for num_actions entries. No statement in this code bounds the number of appended actions to num_actions, so an expression lacking offload_action (or returning false) that still adds an action during offload writes past the allocation. Attacker-chosen expression types instantiate the trigger.

Origin of the miscalculated capacity: num_actions increments only when offload_action exists and returns true, while the subsequent pass calls offload on all expressions; the resulting capacity under-counts the actions actually appended, sizing the buffer at line 21 too small.

assumptions: The rule and its expression list are configured through the nftables netlink interface from userspace, making expression types and their configurations attacker-influenced in an unprivileged-user-namespace context.

nft_flow_rule_alloc allocates the flow rule with an inline action entry array sized by its argument, and the offload callbacks append entries to that array; these callees are not shown in the given code.

The concrete overflow requires at least one expression type whose offload callback appends a flow action while lacking an offload_action callback (or returning false from it); the expression ops tables are not shown, so the specific overflowing expression type is identified from kernel context rather than from the quoted code.
limitations: nft_flow_rule_transfer_vlan (line 46) also consumes flow after the loop and may append or modify actions; its implementation is not shown, so its contribution to the overflow could not be simulated.

The exact nftables expression types available in the target kernel version that trigger the count/append mismatch (e.g., payload set expressions) are outside the given code; the proof rests on the structural mismatch visible in this function plus the absence of any bounds enforcement.

verdict.summary: Integer overflow in `size = bytes_per_line * hh;` with attacker-controlled width/height parsed from the bitmap file: the only check (`if (!ww || !hh)`) rejects emptiness, not magnitude, so the unsigned product wraps (e.g. width=-16, height=8 gives bytes_per_line=536870910 and size=-16) and the wrapped or huge size is passed unchecked to g_malloc, which aborts the process on allocation failure (denial of service) or allocates up to ~2 GB from a sub-100-byte file (resource amplification). The copy loops use the same wrapped `size` as the allocation, so no out-of-bounds write occurs inside this function.

evidence.reason: Root cause: bytes_per_line (up to 536870912, from unbounded guint ww) multiplied by hh (unbounded guint, from a negative %d value) wraps as unsigned and is truncated into int `size`; the wrapped value (e.g. -16 for width -16 / height 8) is passed unchecked to g_malloc, which aborts the process, and in-range products force GB-scale allocations from a tiny attacker file. No range or overflow check on ww/hh exists anywhere; the only guard, `if (!ww || !hh)`, rejects zero alone.

Origin of the tainted value: `value` is parsed from the attacker-supplied file with `sscanf(line, "#define %s %d", ...)` and cast to guint without any clamping, so a negative decimal (full int domain per the width-domain rule) becomes a ~4.29e9 width that drives the overflow at line 87.

assumptions: g_malloc follows documented GLib semantics: it aborts the program on allocation failure and returns NULL only when the requested size is 0 (the NULL case is caught by `if (!bits) RETURN (FALSE);` because neither copy loop runs when size is 0).
`next_int` is an internal helper not shown, but its return value is sentinel-checked (`< 0` → RETURN FALSE) before use, and the stored value is truncated to a byte, a data-only effect.
limitations: No out-of-bounds write inside this function: both copy loops are bounded by the same `size` used for the allocation, and bytes_per_line is provably even in the version10p path (padding=1 exactly when (ww+7)/8 is odd, including the unsigned wrap window), so the bytes+=2 loop never writes past size.

With version10p padding, the loop writes only size − hh bytes (it skips the high byte at each line end), leaving bits[size−hh .. size) uninitialized; this buffer is returned via `*data = bits;`, a potential info leak, but the consuming/rendering code is not shown, so the impact chain is not instantiated here.
A wrapped small positive size makes the function return TRUE with an undersized buffer for the reported width/height; any out-of-bounds consumption would occur in the not-shown caller.

`if (strlen (line) == MAX_SIZE-1) RETURN (FALSE);` over-rejects a complete line of MAX_SIZE-2 chars plus newline; since fgets caps strlen at MAX_SIZE-1, the check cannot under-admit truncated lines — functional over-rejection only.
The hotspot values hx/hy are not validated against width/height; misuse would occur in the not-shown caller.

verdict.summary: st21nfca_connectivity_event_received validates the EVT_TRANSACTION payload with defective arithmetic: the params_len bound ((skb->len - 2) - sizeof(struct nfc_evt_transaction)) is computed in unsigned size_t and wraps to a huge value whenever skb->len - 2 < 24, so the check passes for any params_len up to 255 and the memcpy writes up to 255 attacker-controlled bytes past a small devm_kzalloc allocation (e.g. skb->len=25, aid_len=16, params_len=255 yields a 256-byte heap out-of-bounds write plus an out-of-bounds read of the skb). Additionally, aid_len is never checked against skb->len before the aid memcpy, and the entry check uses && so short frames carrying the AID tag are admitted, producing further out-of-bounds reads/writes with undersized allocations. The event payload originates from the NFC controller/HCI transport, a trust boundary.

evidence.reason: Defective guard: skb->len - 2 (unsigned int) is promoted to size_t and subtracts sizeof(struct nfc_evt_transaction) (=24), wrapping to ~2^64-1 for every skb->len <= 25, so the > test never rejects. Tainted params_len is loaded at line 44 from skb->data[aid_len + 3] (attacker byte). Trigger: skb->len=25, data[1]=16, data[18]=0x82, data[19]=0xFF.

Sink: with the simulated values (alloc = skb->len - 2 = 23 bytes, aid_len = 16, params_len = 255) this writes 255 bytes at transaction offset 24, i.e. ~256 bytes past the 23-byte heap allocation (out-of-bounds write, attacker-controlled length and content), and reads skb->data[20..274] beyond skb->len=25 (out-of-bounds read). No quoted statement on any path bounds params_len against the allocation.

Independent unguarded sink: aid_len (attacker byte, <= 16 per line 33) is never checked against skb->len, nor is the allocation (skb->len - 2) checked to cover the struct. With skb->len=7, data[0]=0x81, data[1]=16: reads skb->data[2..17] out of bounds and writes aid (16 bytes at offset 4) into a 5-byte allocation — 15-byte heap out-of-bounds write.

Boundary defect in the entry validation: the && operator admits short frames (skb->len < 7) whenever data[0] equals the AID tag, so undersized allocations (skb->len - 2 < 5, and < sizeof(struct) for any skb->len < 26) reach the struct writes and memcpys; the correct form (||, or an explicit skb->len floor) appears nowhere in the code.

assumptions: struct nfc_evt_transaction is the kernel's include/net/nfc/nfc.h type: __packed { u32 aid_len; u8 aid[NFC_MAX_AID_LENGTH=16]; u32 params_len; u8 params[]; }, so sizeof = 24, offsetof(aid) = 4, offsetof(params) = 24; the wrap condition skb->len - 2 < 24 and the destination offsets derive from this layout.
NFC_MIN_AID_LENGTH = 5, NFC_EVT_TRANSACTION_AID_TAG = 0x81, NFC_EVT_TRANSACTION_PARAMS_TAG = 0x82 (kernel NFC headers).

skb->len is unsigned int and the skb payload is produced by the not-shown ST21NFCA HCI transport (controller event); per the width-domain rule its full surface (any len, any data bytes) is instantiable attacker-data at this intake-point handler.
devm_kzalloc returns NULL on failure (checked at line 27); allocations of the small positive sizes used in the simulations are assumed to succeed.
limitations: skb->len < 2 makes skb->len - 2 wrap to ~4 GiB, so devm_kzalloc fails and the function returns -ENOMEM — memory-safe path (but the skb is not freed).

All early error returns (-EPROTO/-EINVAL/-ENOMEM) skip kfree_skb(skb), leaking the skb, and the devm allocation is retained until device unbind — resource retention only, not memory corruption; not counted as a primary finding.
nfc_se_transaction()/nfc_se_connectivity() internals are not shown; the out-of-bounds writes occur before these calls, so the impact does not depend on them.
The ZERO_SIZE_PTR behavior of kmalloc(0) for skb->len == 2 was not relied on; undersized positive allocations (skb->len 3..6) already instantiate the overflow.

verdict.summary: No attacker-instantiable defect found. All memory/index/count sinks are either covered by quoted guards (qfl/qf_start NULL check, qfp NULL break, qftf_str and qftf_li sentinel checks with the invalid_val latch) or consume values that stay in-domain by the code's own construction (lnum is an iteration counter bounded by successful line additions, not a raw attacker offset; NULL qftf_str is the code's own default-path argument). The potential use-after-free if 'quickfixtextfunc' frees the quickfix list, and the NULL deref of buf on the incremental path, both require unshown caller/callee/config contracts and are not attacker-triggerable.

assumptions: qf_buf_add_line() (not shown) accepts qftf_str == NULL and adds exactly one line per successful call; this is consistent with this code's own usage, which passes qftf_str == NULL on the default path and keeps the comment 'Add one line for each error'.
ml_delete() handles out-of-range line numbers safely and sets ML_EMPTY when a buffer becomes empty, so the delete-all loop terminates.
call_qftf_func() returns NULL on failure and a valid list otherwise; the code checks the NULL sentinel before use.
list item links (li_next) are NULL-terminated, so the qftf_li walk cannot run past the list.
limitations: Potential use-after-free: if the 'quickfixtextfunc' callback invoked through call_qftf_func frees or replaces the quickfix list qfl, the subsequent loop dereferences of qfp (qfp->qf_fnum, qfp->qf_next) would use freed memory; no refcount or re-validation appears in this code. The callback is operator configuration (vimscript), so no trust-boundary attacker can instantiate this trigger.

NULL-pointer deref: on the old_last != NULL path, buf is dereferenced (buf->b_ml.ml_line_count) without a NULL check; the buf != curbuf guard only covers the old_last == NULL path. A NULL buf would require the unshown caller (qf_update_buffer) to violate its contract.
The invariant that the incremental path's lnum equals the index of old_last is maintained by callers (qf_update_buffer) and cannot be verified from this snippet.

Long-file boundary note: the final ml_delete(lnum + 1) has no explicit written bounds check; its safety rests on the one-line-per-iteration invariant established by qf_buf_add_line returning OK only after adding a line.

verdict.summary: suggest_trie_walk() writes into fixed-size stack buffers (compflags[MAXWLEN], tword[MAXWLEN], stack[MAXWLEN]) using walk counters ts_complen, ts_twordlen and depth that are never bounds-checked against MAXWLEN anywhere in the function. An attacker-controlled spell file (.spl/.aff: sl_nobreak, sl_compminlen, sl_compmax, sl_compsylmax, compound-flagged words) combined with crafted buffer text drives ts_complen past MAXWLEN-1 (the NOBREAK path at line 485 forces try_compound with no count cap, and the sl_compsylmax < MAXWLEN disjunction at line 471 bypasses the compmax cap entirely), causing compflags[ts_complen + 1] = NUL and tword[ts_twordlen++] = c to write out of bounds into adjacent stack memory (memory corruption in the editor process).
