missing top-level key: evidence

verdict.summary: ReadCINImage copies attacker-derived bytes-per-row into the quantum pixel buffer without any local bounds check. The per-channel bits_per_pixel byte read from the file (0-255) is assigned directly to image->depth with no whitelist, clamp, or range test, and length=GetBytesPerRow(columns,3,depth,pad) scales with that raw depth. ReadBlobStream(image,length,pixels,&count) then writes up to length file-controlled bytes into the buffer allocated by AcquireQuantumInfo, which is sized far smaller for non-standard depths. The code even computes the correct extent (GetQuantumExtent) and discards it with '(void) extent;', so a crafted CIN file (e.g. depth=255, columns=1000, rows=1) produces an out-of-bounds heap write of tens of kilobytes of attacker data.

evidence.reason: Sink: up to 'length' bytes of file data are copied into 'pixels', the buffer returned by GetQuantumPixels(quantum_info) at line 386, whose allocation (AcquireQuantumInfo, line 371) is never compared against 'length' on any path. Instantiated trigger: bits_per_pixel=255, pixels_per_line=1000, lines_per_image=1 gives length ~= 95,625 bytes for a buffer sized for a clamped quantum depth, producing a heap out-of-bounds write of attacker-controlled file data.

Origin of the tainted value: the per-channel bits_per_pixel byte read from the attacker's file at line 134 (full 0-255 domain of its unsigned char width) is assigned to image->depth with no range check, whitelist, clamp, or mask anywhere between this line and the GetBytesPerRow calls at lines 379/383, so depth=255 directly scales the copy length used at the line 395 sink.

assumptions: GetBytesPerRow, AcquireQuantumInfo, GetQuantumExtent, GetQuantumPixels, and ReadBlobStream are project-internal callees not shown in this snippet; per the analysis rules their sizing relationship cannot serve as a guard, and the unvalidated attacker-derived size passed into the copy at line 395 is the defect at the call site.
sizeof(cin.*) field arrays are assumed smaller than MaxTextExtent for the CopyMagickString calls (struct definition not shown); this does not affect the primary finding.
limitations: Degenerate inputs depth=0 or columns=0 yield length=0 and zero-byte reads; any resulting misbehavior would be inside the not-shown quantum helpers, so no local impact is instantiated.

The file-size sanity check at line 348 (columns*rows/8 > blob size) under-approximates the data needed for depths above 8 bits, but short files are caught by the count check at line 396; this weakens the filter without itself enabling the overflow.
The return value of SetQuantumPad (line 385) is unchecked, but the pad argument is the constant 0, so no attacker-influenced failure path exists.

verdict.summary: cgroup1_parse_param stores the attacker-controlled release_agent path (ctx->release_agent = param->string) with no capability or namespace check anywhere in the function. The cgroup v1 release_agent is executed by the kernel with root privileges in the initial namespaces when the cgroup becomes empty, so a caller holding only namespaced CAP_SYS_ADMIN (e.g., container root) can set an arbitrary path and achieve host-level code execution as root — the pre-fix condition of CVE-2022-0492, whose fix added an ns_capable(&init_user_ns, CAP_SYS_ADMIN) check to this arm.

evidence.reason: Sink stores attacker-supplied param->string (full string domain, producer not shown) into ctx->release_agent, the documented cgroup-v1 path that the kernel executes via call_usermodehelper with root credentials on cgroup release. The only mention-swept guard in the arm is the duplicate check at line 55 ('if (ctx->release_agent)'), which guards respecification, not privilege; no capable/ns_capable, param->type, or content validation exists on any path (contrast the 'source' arm's type check at line 11 and the 'name' arm's whitelist at lines 70-76). Trigger: namespaced-privileged attacker passes release_agent=<arbitrary path> through fsconfig/mount; opt == Opt_release_agent; line 55 passes (first specification); line 57 stores the path; kernel later runs it as root — privilege escalation / container escape.

assumptions: fs_parse's internal type enforcement for string-typed parameters is not shown and is therefore an assumption; the analysis judges this code as the last line of defense.

The downstream consumption of ctx->release_agent (kstrdup into the cgroup root at mount time and execution via the release path) is not shown; the release_agent execution semantics are treated as characterizable, universally documented kernel behavior (call_usermodehelper with root credentials).

Attacker model requires the cgroup v1 filesystem to be reachable for a caller with namespaced CAP_SYS_ADMIN (the standard CVE-2022-0492 container scenario); the mount permission check that does exist runs against the caller's namespaced context, which is the incorrect context.
limitations: Secondary candidate dismissed: the Opt_release_agent arm, unlike the 'source' arm, performs no param->type != fs_value_is_string check, so a NULL param->string could reach ctx->release_agent; the harmful dereference would occur entirely in not-shown mount/lookup code and depends on unshown fs_parse type matching — speculative, recorded here.

No memory-safety defect found in the Opt_name path: line 67 'if (param->size > MAX_CGROUP_ROOT_NAMELEN - 1)' was edge-tested at sizes 0, 63, and 64 and both bounds behave correctly; the loop at line 70 reads exactly param->size bytes of the same variable and unit that was checked.
The 'source' arm is type- and duplicate-checked (lines 11-14) with correct ownership transfer (param->string = NULL); no defect observed.

verdict.summary: kvmppc_rtas_hcall copies a guest-authored struct rtas_args into a host kernel stack buffer and computes args.rets = &args.args[be32_to_cpu(args.nargs)] using the fully guest-controlled 32-bit nargs field with no bounds validation anywhere in the function. A guest can set nargs (e.g. 0x10000) so that rets points far past the stack buffer, and the registered token handler invoked at line 35 then writes RTAS status words through that pointer, giving a guest-triggered out-of-bounds write (memory corruption) in the host kernel.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds pointer formation at the sink: args.nargs is a guest-controlled __be32 (full 0..0xFFFFFFFF domain) copied from guest memory, used as an index into the fixed-size stack array args.args with no bounds check, clamp, or mask anywhere in the function (mention sweep: nargs is mentioned nowhere else). The resulting pointer is passed to d->handler->handler(vcpu, &args), which writes RTAS return words through it, producing an attacker-controlled-offset out-of-bounds write in host kernel stack memory. Instantiated trigger: guest issues the RTAS hypercall with nargs = 0x10000 and any registered token.

Origin of the tainted value: this read copies the guest-authored rtas_args block, including the unvalidated nargs (and nret) fields, into the host stack struct that line 28 then indexes with. The return value is checked (line 18) but the content is never validated, making this the intake point for the guest-controlled index.

assumptions: struct rtas_args contains a fixed-size array args[] (16 x u32 in the known kernel definition, including separate nargs/nret/token fields); the exact array size is not shown in this code, but no fixed-size array can contain any 32-bit index, so the defect does not depend on the constant.

The registered RTAS token handlers (d->handler->handler) follow the documented RTAS convention of writing status/return words through args->rets; these callees are not shown, but per the call-site rule the defect stands at line 28/35 where the unbounded pointer is formed and passed.
KVM_PAM masks only the top 4 bits of the args GPA; kvm_read_guest/kvm_write_guest validate the GFN and their failure sentinels are checked with 'if (rc) goto fail;'
limitations: args.nret is likewise never validated (handlers may write up to nret words through rets); it shares the same missing guard as nargs and is folded into the primary finding.

Impact of reading sizeof(args) where the struct embeds a host pointer field: the size matches the stack object, and the rets field round-trips the guest's own value back, so no host-address disclosure was instantiated.

verdict.summary: qh_help consumes attacker-controlled socket data only through strcmp tests and %s arguments with literal format strings; the one callee sentinel it consumes (qh_find_handler's NULL return) is checked with 'if (qh == NULL)' before the only member dereference. No memory, size, index, injection, or authorization sink is reachable from attacker input in this code.

assumptions: qh_find_handler(buf) returns either a pointer into the internally-registered qhandlers list or NULL; the NULL sentinel is the only failure mode and is checked locally at 'if (qh == NULL) {'.

nsock_printf/nsock_printf_nul interpret their first string argument as a format string and write to the socket descriptor; their internal bounds behavior is not shown but they receive only literal format strings here.
Registered query handlers have non-NULL handler, name, and next_qh fields, set by the daemon's own registration path (not shown, not attacker-reachable).
limitations: Speculative: if the unseen query-socket dispatcher can pass buf == NULL, '!*buf' at the first use dereferences NULL; the pointer value is produced by the caller, not by attacker-controlled content, so the trigger is not instantiated in this code.

Speculative: if the dispatcher passes a non-NUL-terminated buf, the %s uses at the 'No handler named' print read out of bounds; the unused 'len' parameter suggests the caller supplies a bounded buffer, but neither the termination contract nor its violation is shown in this code.
The 'len' parameter is never used; passing it to a precision-bounded output call ('%.*s') would harden the string uses, but its absence is a hardening note, not an instantiated defect.

verdict.summary: qf_fill_buffer validates every locally checkable sentinel (NULL list, NULL old_last->qf_next, NULL string returns from tv_get_string_chk, FAIL from qf_buf_add_line, NULL qf_next) with correctly positioned guards, keeps lnum bounded by qfl->qf_count with no truncation or overflow, and contains no injection, format, path, crypto, or authz sink. The only defects found require either an internally inconsistent quickfix list (qf_start == NULL with qf_count > 0, producible by no statement in this code, impact limited to an equal-privilege crash) or the operator's own quickfixtextfunc callback freeing the list across the call_qftf_func re-entry point (trigger outside this code and outside any trust boundary Vim defines for parsed content). Neither is an instantiated vulnerability in this code.

assumptions: qf_buf_add_line, call_qftf_func, ml_delete, and check_lnums are project-internal callees not shown; their standard documented semantics (append a line, invoke the user-configured text function, delete a memory line returning FAIL when out of range) are relied upon for the safe-path analysis.

The invariant that qfl->qf_start is non-NULL whenever qfl->qf_count > 0 (and that qf_count matches the linked-list length) is maintained by the not-shown quickfix module; no statement in this code enforces it, but no statement in this code can violate it either.

The 'quickfixtextfunc' user function is treated as operator configuration (same trust level as .vimrc/plugins), not as data originating from a trust-boundary party, since nothing in this code derives it from parsed file or quickfix content.
Ownership/refcount semantics of the list returned by call_qftf_func are unshown; whether its cleanup belongs to this function cannot be determined from the given code.
limitations: NULL-dereference candidate: if qfl->qf_start were NULL while qfl->qf_count > 0, the first loop iteration would dereference NULL at 'prev_bufnr != qfp->qf_fnum' because the only guard 'if (qfp == NULL) break;' executes after the uses. The precondition is an internal invariant violation of a not-shown producer and the impact is a crash of the user's own editor process at equal privilege, so it is recorded as a robustness limitation, not a vulnerability.

Re-entrancy hazard: qfp and qfl are captured before 'call_qftf_func(...)', which invokes an operator-configured VimL function (a re-entry point), and 'while (lnum < qfl->qf_count)' together with 'qfp = qfp->qf_next' reads them afterward with no re-validation anywhere in this code. If that function freed or replaced the quickfix list, this would be a use-after-free. The trigger requires code outside this file executing a freeing command and requires control of editor configuration, so the impact chain is not instantiated here; hardening this path (re-checking the list identity after the call) would still be worthwhile upstream.

If call_qftf_func transfers ownership of the returned list, the absence of any free/unref statement for qftf_list is a per-update memory leak; refcount semantics are not shown, so this remains unconfirmed.

When old_last != NULL, old_last->qf_next == NULL, and the buffer line count is below qfl->qf_count, the loop re-emits the old_last entry once (qfp = old_last), producing a duplicated display line; cosmetic only.

verdict.summary: Guest-controlled RTAS args are handled safely: the nargs bounds check `be32_to_cpu(args.nargs) >= ARRAY_SIZE(args.args)` correctly rejects the one-past-limit value before the pointer fixup, keeping args.rets and rets[0] in bounds; args_phys is masked by KVM_PAM and consumed only by memslot-validated kvm_read_guest/kvm_write_guest with constant lengths whose failure sentinels are checked before any use of the copied data.

assumptions: kvm_read_guest/kvm_write_guest follow standard KVM semantics: they validate the guest physical address against memslots, copy exactly the constant sizeof(args), and return nonzero on failure; both sentinel checks are quoted in the code.

ARRAY_SIZE(args.args) reflects the actual declared length of the args.args array in struct rtas_args (definition not shown); the check and the sink use the same array, so the bound is self-consistent for any length.

The RTAS handlers invoked via d->handler->handler are not shown; the quoted comment documents that they must validate nargs and nret, and this code independently guarantees rets[0] is in-bounds, so it passes only in-domain arguments to that callee.
limitations: nret is not validated in this function; a hypothetical handler that trusted nret and wrote multiple rets entries without checking could write out of bounds, but that use would occur entirely inside the not-shown callee, and this code both passes in-domain pointers and documents the handler contract.
If a handler were found by token yet malformed, the guest only receives what the handler writes into rets[0], which is in-bounds; no impact link inside this code is affected.

verdict.summary: In mbfl_filt_conv_big5_wchar, the CP950 PUA lookup loop (for (k = 0; k < sizeof(cp950_pua_tbl)/(sizeof(unsigned short)*4); k++)) can exit by exhaustion when c2 = c1<<8|c is not covered by any table range; k then equals the table length and the subsequent cp950_pua_tbl[k][2] read (and the w computation using it) accesses memory past the end of the const table. The second-byte check 'c > 0x39' admits bytes 0x3a-0x3f, which are not valid Big5 second bytes and fall below the 0x40/0xa1-style range starts, making exhaustion reachable from attacker-supplied input bytes (e.g. '\x81\x3a' in CP950 input). The out-of-bounds-derived value can flow into the conversion output, giving a read/info-leak primitive.

evidence.reason: Unguarded use of k after the search loop: when no table range contains c2, the loop at lines 51-55 exits without break with k == sizeof(cp950_pua_tbl)/(sizeof(unsigned short)*4), so cp950_pua_tbl[k][2] reads past the end of the table; no bounds check, clamp, or unmatched-c2 error arm exists on any path. The read value also feeds w (lines 58/61) which is passed to filter->output_function, leaking out-of-bounds memory into the converted output.

Origin of the trigger: attacker controls both bytes (c1 from filter->cache set at line 20, c is the stream byte); the PUA condition at lines 45-49 admits c in [0x3a,0x7e] (check 'c > 0x39' under-admits invalid second bytes 0x3a-0x3f), so c2 values such as 0x813a lie below every table range start (ranges start at low byte 0x40 or 0xa1 per the line-57 discriminator and the line-61 else branch), guaranteeing loop exhaustion and k == table length.

assumptions: cp950_pua_tbl contents are not shown; the claim that its range entries start at low byte 0x40 or 0xa1 (so c2 with low byte 0x3a-0x3f misses) is inferred from the code's own discriminator '(cp950_pua_tbl[k][2] & 0xff) == 0x40' and the linear else-branch formula, not from quoted data.
big5_ucs_table_size is assumed to match the actual extent of big5_ucs_table; the line-37 check 'w >= 0 && w < big5_ucs_table_size' is the only guard for that index.
MBFL_WCSGROUP_MASK / MBFL_WCSPLANE_MASK are assumed to bound w to its output domain; their widths are not shown.
filter->status/filter->cache are assumed initialized by the filter framework before this handler runs.
limitations: Loop exhaustion (the OOB trigger) requires at least one c2 value inside the line 45-49 PUA domain that is outside every cp950_pua_tbl range; the table data is not shown, so this is inferred from the 0x40/0xa1 range-start structure rather than quoted. Per the single-anomaly rule, the unshown table cannot serve as a guard against the missing post-loop check.
Impact is limited to an out-of-bounds read of adjacent static const data with a narrow info-leak path into the conversion output; no out-of-bounds write primitive was found.
A negative or >255 value of c is treated as reachable per the width-domain rule; all such paths are masked (lines 22, 68, 76) and safe.
If filter->status could be 1 with filter->cache never set (init not shown), c1 would be uninitialized; this is speculative and not counted.

verdict.summary: r_bin_java_inner_classes_attr_new reads the 2-byte number_of_classes field at buffer offset 6 (R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT on line 14) before any check that the attribute size sz is at least 8 bytes. The only bounds check in the function, `if (offset + 8 > sz)`, sits inside the parsing loop and thus executes after the read. An attacker-crafted class file with an InnerClasses attribute of size < 8 drives an out-of-bounds read of 2 bytes past the attribute buffer while parsing untrusted input.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read sink: with offset = 6 (set at line 8), R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT(buffer, offset) reads buffer[6..7] unconditionally. Trigger: attacker supplies an InnerClasses attribute with sz < 8 (e.g., sz = 0, in-domain for the ut64 parameter); default_attr_new returns non-NULL (callee shown nowhere to reject small sz, and per the code's own model at line 19, sz is the valid extent of buffer), so the read executes past the end of the buffer. No check on any path in this code constrains sz before this line.

The only bounds check on sz in this function executes inside the loop (line 17), i.e., after the number_of_classes read at line 14 and only on iterations of a loop whose count is the very value read out of bounds. It correctly guards the four USHORT reads at lines 27-33 but cannot guard the initial read at line 14 when sz < 8; the missing one-line guard `if (sz < 8) return attr;` before line 14 is the defect.

assumptions: R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT(buffer, offset) reads exactly buffer[offset] and buffer[offset+1] (standard radare2 big-endian ushort macro).
sz is the valid byte extent of buffer, per the code's own bounds model at line 19 (`offset + 8 > sz`).
r_bin_java_default_attr_new may return a non-NULL attr for sz < 8; the callee is not shown and therefore cannot serve as a guard for the read at line 14.
limitations: A failed constant-pool lookup returns NULL obj (lines 39/45); the code logs but does not reject it and passes the possibly-NULL obj to r_bin_java_get_item_name_from_bin_cp_list (lines 43, 49). If that unshown callee dereferences obj, this is a NULL-deref crash; the callee is not shown and the code's own fallback handling suggests it tolerates NULL, so the impact chain is not instantiated here.
Line 53 frees icattr while leaking icattr->name (line 51) and icattr->flags_str (line 35); a bounded, non-security memory leak.
curpos = buf_offset + offset (line 18) can wrap ut64, but the value is stored only as metadata (file_offset) with no memory-safety use.

verdict.summary: ax25_release calls ax25_destroy_socket(ax25), which frees the ax25 control block (paths: SOCK_DGRAM else-branch, SEQPACKET state 0, and SEQPACKET states 1/2 without SOCK_DESTROY), then unconditionally falls through to the trailing cleanup block guarded only by 'if (ax25_dev)' — a NULL test on the cached device pointer, not on the control block — and dereferences the freed ax25 in five del_timer_sync calls. A local unprivileged user closing an AF_AX25 socket reaches this use-after-free, giving a kernel memory read/write (del_timer_sync manipulates timer list fields inside freed slab memory).

evidence.reason: UAF sink: the guard 'if (ax25_dev)' tests the cached device pointer for NULL, not whether the ax25 control block is still allocated; del_timer_sync then dereferences 'ax25', which ax25_destroy_socket has already freed on the fall-through paths. Trigger: local user closes a bound SOCK_DGRAM (or SEQPACKET in state 0/1/2) AF_AX25 socket.

Free site (origin of the dangling 'ax25') on the non-SOCK_SEQPACKET path; the equivalent frees on the SEQPACKET paths are at lines 22 and 32, all of which fall through to the dereference at lines 77-81.

assumptions: ax25_destroy_socket, not shown, is treated as the AX.25 control-block destructor (it removes the cb and drops its reference so the struct is freed), per its universally-known destroy/free role and the documented pre-fix upstream behavior of net/ax25/af_ax25.c; this is what makes lines 22/32/74 free sites.

sk_to_ax25(sk) returns the sk_protinfo control block set at socket creation (accessor), so 'ax25' is non-NULL at entry; ax25_dev is separately refcounted (bind-held reference, dropped only at line 83 here), so the line 82 use of the cached ax25_dev pointer is not itself a UAF.
limitations: The 'default:' arm of the state switch (lines 67-68) leaves the control block un-destroyed while the trailing block still stops timers and drops device references, which can leak the cb on an out-of-range state; no security impact shown.
A NULL ax25->ax25_dev dereference at line 40 (states 3/4) is not instantiated: those states require a connected, hence bound, socket.

Exploitation impact beyond the UAF (controlled reallocation of the freed slab between L74 and L77) depends on allocator timing not exhibited as ordered statements here; the direct UAF read/write on the freed cb is itself the confirmed primitive.

verdict.summary: cgroup1_parse_param validates attacker-supplied mount options correctly: the name loop is bounded by quoted emptiness and maximum-length checks with the correct comparison operators, size and string arrive through the fs_context string-parameter API contract, ownership transfers are paired with NULL resets, and all fs_parse error sentinels are returned. No sink is reachable with an out-of-domain value inside this code.

assumptions: fs_parse and the fs_context parameter API are system framework callees with documented semantics: for fsparam_string options (name, release_agent), param->string is NUL-terminated and param->size equals its strlen; fs_parse returns a negative error (handled by the quoted 'if (opt < 0) return opt;') on type mismatches, so param->string is non-NULL when the Opt_release_agent/Opt_name arms run.

MAX_CGROUP_ROOT_NAMELEN is 64 and downstream consumers of ctx->name use buffers of that same constant, so the quoted size <= MAX_CGROUP_ROOT_NAMELEN - 1 check (admitting at most 63 characters plus NUL) fits every copy site.
for_each_subsys bounds i to the compiled-in subsystem count, which fits the u16 subsys_mask.
limitations: Opt_release_agent stores an arbitrary unvalidated path string; its security-relevant consumption (execution via call_usermodehelper on the cgroup release path) happens entirely in code not shown, and its historical privilege gating (cf. CVE-2022-0492) also lives outside this function, so no impact chain is instantiated here.

char c = param->string[i] followed by isalnum(c) passes a possibly signed char to the kernel ctype helper; a user byte >= 0x80 would be sign-extended, and if kernel isalnum indexes its table without an unsigned-char cast this is a fixed-offset out-of-bounds read of adjacent kernel rodata whose value only gates accept/reject of a name character and is never disclosed. Upstream-identical behavior; no corruption, disclosure, or bypass chain quotable in this code.

A hypothetical size decoupled from strlen(param->string) would make the Opt_name loop read out of bounds, but no statement in this code constructs struct fs_parameter; the VFS core (vfs_parse_fs_string) always binds size to the string length, so that trigger requires violating the framework contract and is not instantiated in this code.

verdict.summary: All memory-access sinks in parse_command_modifiers are locally bounded or sentinel-checked: the visual-range memmoves are confined by 'if (eap->cmd > cmd_start)' to the original string extent (verified at both bounds m=1 and m=7), tab numbers are fully range-checked, and pointer reads (p[1], n[1], p[-1], eap->cmd[-1]) are covered by quoted short-circuit or match guards. The only write that can pass the original string terminator (STRCPY(orig_cmd + len, "'<,'>+") in the use_plus_cmd arm), plus an atoi-based int overflow into cmod_verbose and assignments of string literals to eap->cmd, all lack a locally instantiated security impact because the command-line buffer's allocation, the later consumers, and the verbose level's uses lie in code not shown.

assumptions: checkforcmd_noparen/checkforcmd_opt advance the passed pointer past the matched command name (minimum the given length argument) and return nonzero only on match; skip_range/skipwhite/comment_start/ends_excmd/ends_excmd2 have their conventional Vim semantics; these internal callees are not shown and their behavior is treated as consistent with how this code uses them.
The command line (eap->cmd) is NUL-terminated by the caller (ex parser); this code's pointer walks (ASCII_ISALPHA loop, atoi, STRNCMP) rely on that terminator.
skip_vimgrep_pat_ext sets *reg_pat when it returns non-NULL (unshown callee contract); the local sentinel checks cover its NULL return.
limitations: use_plus_cmd arm with a Visual range: STRCPY(orig_cmd + len, "'<,'>+") writes 7 bytes where the original string occupied len+6 bytes including its NUL, i.e. one byte past the old terminator, reachable by typing "'<,'>silent" + Enter in ex mode with the cursor not on the last line. Whether this leaves the allocation depends on the line-buffer sizing in the unshown ex-mode getline callee (chunked/fixed buffers with slack in Vim), so a heap overflow is not provable from this code alone; a capacity check at this use site would be the hardening fix.

cmod->cmod_verbose = atoi((char *)eap->cmd) + 1 can overflow int for very long digit prefixes (e.g. ':99999999999verbose'); no clamp exists, but the only shown impact is a wrong verbose level, with no memory or index use of cmod_verbose in this code.

eap->cmd is assigned read-only string literals ("'<,'>+" and "+") on the use_plus_cmd paths; any later in-place write to the command line by do_one_cmd (not shown) would fault on them. The vulnerable consumer, if any, is outside this code.

On error paths after modifiers were parsed (e.g. "'<,'>silent" alone, non-ex mode), eap->cmd is returned pointing past the "'<','>" prefix without restoration; caller error handling is not shown and no corruption is produced here.

verdict.summary: reg_match_visual() passes the bot position, whose .lnum comes from stale per-buffer Visual state (curbuf->b_visual.vi_end/vi_start, producer not shown) and is never bounded, into getvvcol(), which resolves that line in buffer memory. The only check, `lnum < top.lnum || lnum > bot.lnum`, bounds the match line lnum, not bot.lnum; a stale Visual-block end (selection made, then lines below it deleted) makes bot.lnum exceed the buffer line count and the lookup reads an invalid line (out-of-bounds read / NULL dereference in the callee).

evidence.reason: Sink: bot.lnum is never validated against the buffer's line count on any path. The only guard, `lnum < top.lnum || lnum > bot.lnum` (line 48), constrains lnum, not bot (top is transitively bounded since top.lnum <= lnum <= line count; bot is unbounded above). Trigger instantiated: block selection vi_start={10,c}, vi_end={1000,c}, mode Ctrl_V, lines 950-1000 deleted (949 lines remain), regex match at line 20 passes line 48, and getvvcol is called with bot.lnum=1000, an out-of-bounds line index passed into a memory-indexing callee.

Origin of the unbounded value: b_visual.vi_end.lnum is set outside this code and can be stale (selection recorded, then lines below it deleted); it enters bot with no local bounds check, and its full linenr_T domain is instantiable per the width-domain rule.

assumptions: colnr_T is signed int and linenr_T is long (Vim typedefs, not shown in the snippet); bot.col + 1 and end - 1 are signed arithmetic.
getvvcol/getvcol/ml_get_buf are project-internal callees not shown; their behavior on invalid lnum is treated per the call-site rule (defect at the call site) and is not used as a guard.
rex.line/rex.lnum/rex.reg_firstlnum are regex-engine invariants: rex.line is the content of line lnum, so lnum at line 47 is a valid buffer line at match time.
limitations: Signed underflow at `cols > end - (*p_sel == 'e')` (line 69): with 'selection' exclusive and the block bottom at column 0 of an empty line, getvvcol yields end == 0, end - 1 == -1, so `cols > -1` is always false and the block-column test passes for any column — a fail-open in the Visual-area test. Not promoted: the party writing the \%V pattern already controls pattern matching, so no cross-trust-boundary consumer of the bypassed test is shown.

`bot.col + (*p_sel != 'e')` (line 55) could overflow signed colnr_T if bot.col == MAXCOL, but in charwise Visual mode bot.col is a real in-line column, so MAXCOL is not instantiable there; effect would be over-rejection (return FALSE), functional only.

top.lnum == 0 from a zeroed b_visual would also pass `lnum < top.lnum` (0 < 0 false), but a zeroed b_visual carries vi_mode == 0, so the Ctrl_V branch (the only memory-dereferencing path) is unreachable in that state; line 14 also requires VIsual.lnum != 0.

verdict.summary: In g_socket_client_connected_callback, the success path dereferences the local `data` pointer without a NULL check. The code itself documents that `attempt->data` is NULL once the async task is completed (comment `/* data is NULL once the task is completed */`) and the winning attempt sets `attempt_entry->data = NULL` for every sibling attempt. When two connection attempts to a multi-address host both succeed (any normal server accepting both connections), the first invocation completes the task and NULLs the sibling's `data`; the sibling's already-queued callback then falls through the `if (data && g_task_return_error_if_cancelled (...))` guard (which is pass-through when data is NULL), gets TRUE from connect_finish, and executes `data->socket = g_steal_pointer (&attempt->socket);` with data == NULL, crashing the client process. A remote peer controls the connection timing that triggers this, making it a denial-of-service vulnerability.

evidence.reason: NULL-pointer dereference (CWE-476). `data` is `attempt->data`, which this code documents can be NULL once the task is completed and which the sibling-cancellation loop sets to NULL. The only checks on `data` before this sink are `if (data && g_task_return_error_if_cancelled (data->task))` (pass-through when data is NULL) and `if (data)` (error path only, lines 37-43); neither reaches the success path. Trigger: two parallel connection attempts both succeed; the first callback runs the loop that sets the second attempt's `data = NULL`; the second callback then falls through every check and writes through NULL at line 48, crashing the process (network-peer-triggerable DoS).

Origin of the NULL value: when one connection attempt succeeds, this loop cancels every sibling attempt and sets its `data` field to NULL, while the sibling's own callback may already be queued with a successful connect result. Cancellation cannot retroactively fail an established connection, so the sibling's callback subsequently reaches the unguarded `data->socket = ...` sink with data == NULL.

assumptions: connection_attempt_ref/unref helpers are not shown; it is assumed the callback's user_data holds its own reference so that the loop's unref (line 56) plus the unref at line 60 are balanced. If the list held the only reference, lines 56 and 60 would be a double-unref, but this cannot be proven from the given code.

g_proxy_address_get_protocol is assumed to return a non-NULL string owned by data->proxy_addr (which stays alive for the function's duration), so the `protocol` uses in the hash-table lookup and g_set_error are safe.
Internal helpers (set_last_error, clarify_connect_error, enumerator_next_async, connection_attempt_remove) are assumed to behave as their names indicate; their internals are not shown.
limitations: Line 31 `clarify_connect_error (error, data->connectable, attempt->address);` also dereferences `data` without a NULL check, and the nearby `if (data)` at line 37 executes after this first use. However, the only shown NULLing site cancels the attempt's cancellable first, so reaching line 31 with data == NULL and an uncancelled cancellable requires the unshown timeout path; the trigger was not fully instantiated from the given code, so it is recorded here as sharing the same root cause rather than as a separate finding.
The crash is a denial of service (write through a NULL pointer at a small struct offset); no attacker-controlled out-of-bounds write beyond the NULL dereference is part of the simulated trigger.

The timeout_source callback's behavior (whether it completes the task and how it treats sibling attempts) is not shown; this only affects the secondary error-path candidate, not the primary success-path trigger.

verdict.summary: keylen is taken from the unshown make_key producer (full int domain instantiable per the width-domain rule) and used unchecked as the read length for the fixed stack buffer key[MAX_MAILBOX_PATH+1] at read_old_value, cyrusdb_delete and cyrusdb_store; the buffer is sized for a mailbox path alone while the key embeds mboxname+uid+entry+userid, with attacker-controlled unbounded entry/userid strings and no local range check, clamp, or dynamic sizing anywhere on any path, yielding an out-of-bounds read (and potential stack overwrite in the key builder) reachable from client-supplied annotation data.

evidence.snippet: keylen = make_key(mboxname, uid, entry, userid, key, sizeof(key));
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: unbounded attacker-influenced strings (entry, userid) plus mboxname are packed into the fixed stack buffer key[MAX_MAILBOX_PATH+1] (line 12), which is sized for a mailbox path alone; the returned keylen (int, producer not shown, full int domain instantiable) is never range-checked against sizeof(key) on any path.

evidence.snippet: r = cyrusdb_store(d->db, key, keylen, data.s, data.len, tid(d));
evidence.reason: Sink: the db layer reads keylen bytes from the MAX_MAILBOX_PATH+1 stack buffer; with keylen instantiated outside [0, sizeof(key)] (e.g. larger than the buffer, or negative) this is an out-of-bounds read of stack memory in the privileged imapd process, triggered by client-controlled annotation entry/userid names. The twin unchecked uses at lines 30 and 68 share the same missing guard.

assumptions: cyrusdb_store, cyrusdb_delete and read_old_value consume (key, keylen) as a byte range and access key[0..keylen-1] — characterizable container/db semantics per discipline 3; the out-of-bounds access they induce lands inside the callee but the defect is the unchecked call-site pair, per the impact-chain rule.
entry and userid originate from IMAP ANNOTATE client commands reaching this *_write-shaped helper; no statement of this code bounds their lengths.

value->s/oldval.s are struct buf fields assumed internally consistent (len matches allocation) for the memcmp at line 34; oldval.len is locally produced by read_old_value whose failure is checked at line 31.
limitations: make_key's implementation is not shown: if it provably truncates to sizeof(key) and returns the truncated non-negative length, the out-of-bounds read cannot occur; per the width-domain rule its return's full int domain is treated as instantiable, which is why confidence is moderate rather than high.

The maywrite permission check (lines 44-47) is skipped when mailbox == NULL (server-annotation path); whether that creates an authorization gap depends on caller-side permission checks not shown, so it is speculative.
The DEBUG-only syslog at lines 87-88 formats value->s which may be NULL; DEBUG is compiled out and printf-style %s NULL is non-corrupting — not a vulnerability.
Line 46 'if (r) goto out;' immediately after 'r = IMAP_PERMISSION_DENIED;' is always true; redundant but harmless.

verdict.summary: In source_from_buf mode, buf[ga.ga_len++] = NUL terminates the line but advances ga_len past the terminator, so the shared len computation len = ga.ga_len + STRLEN(buf + ga.ga_len) scans uninitialized heap memory (and can run past the allocation entirely). The indeterminate len then serves as the index for buf[len-1] reads, the buf[len-1] = NUL and buf[len-2] = '\n' writes, and ga.ga_len bookkeeping, enabling out-of-bounds reads and potential out-of-bounds writes while sourcing attacker-supplied lines. No statement in the code initializes or NUL-terminates the region at buf + ga_len on this path.

evidence.reason: Sink. In source_from_buf mode, ga_len points one past the NUL written at line 31 (the only initialized terminator), so STRLEN scans uninitialized growarray memory and can read past the allocation when no zero byte exists in the remaining space. The resulting indeterminate len is used at lines 44-46, 57, 60, 76 and 103 as a read index and as the index of the writes buf[len-1] = NUL and buf[len-2] = '\n', corrupting the growarray length and enabling out-of-bounds access on attacker-supplied sourced lines. No guard on any path establishes a terminator or bounds len.

Origin. This statement places the line terminator at index ga_len and increments ga_len past it, leaving buf[ga_len] uninitialized when the shared len computation at line 40 runs. In fgets mode ga_len correctly points at the freshly read, fgets-terminated segment, which is why the same line is safe there; the mode mismatch leaves the buf path unguarded.

assumptions: ga_concat and ga_grow are internal callees not shown in the given code; the analysis relies only on the given code's own termination statement (buf[ga.ga_len++] = NUL) and treats any claimed clearing/termination inside those callees as unverifiable and not a guard.

source_from_buf mode is selected by the not-shown sourcing machinery; the given code fully implements and dispatches on this mode (if (sp->source_from_buf)), and the buflines content it consumes is attacker-supplied sourced script content.
buflines entries are treated as arbitrary-length byte strings per the width-domain rule; no statement of this code bounds their length before use.
limitations: The fgets (file) path was fully traced and is guarded: ga_grow(&ga, 120) before each fgets bounds the copy size, fgets NUL-terminates, and every buf[len-1]/buf[len-2] access is guarded by len>=1/len>=2 in that path; the escaped-NL parity with c = -1 and the CTRL-Z len==1 edge were boundary-tested and found correct.

The out-of-bounds write (buf[len-1] = NUL at line 103) requires stale heap bytes at the uninit-derived index to match specific values ('\n'), so it is a conditional consequence of the certain uninitialized out-of-bounds read at line 40, not an unconditionally reachable write.

The exact reachability of ga_len == ga_maxlen at line 40 (read starting one byte past the allocation) depends on the internal growth arithmetic of ga_grow, which is not shown; the uninitialized-memory defect at line 40 stands independently of that boundary case.

verdict.summary: The octet-counted TCP framing parser accumulates the attacker-supplied frame length in a signed int with no bound (line 33: `pThis->iOctetsRemain = pThis->iOctetsRemain * 10 + c - '0';`). A network peer sending a digit string whose value exceeds INT_MAX (e.g. "4294967291 ") wraps the count negative. The `if(pThis->iOctetsRemain < 1)` validation at line 40 only logs an error and does not reject the frame; control falls through to `pThis->inputState = eInMsg;`, so the wrapped negative count reaches `memcpy(pThis->pMsg + pThis->iMsg, *buff, octatesToCopy);` (line 108). Both size caps (`if (buffLen < octatesToCopy)` and `if (octatesToCopy + pThis->iMsg > iMaxLine)`) are false for a negative value, and memcpy's size_t parameter converts it to a near-2^64 length, producing a massive out-of-bounds read and write (memory corruption) in the log-receiving daemon. Positive oversize counts are correctly truncated, so the missing guard is specifically the rejection/clamp of an out-of-range (wrapped negative) octet count.

evidence.reason: Sink: octatesToCopy is memcpy's size but can be a negative int inherited from the wrapped octet counter. With octatesToCopy = -5: line 100 `if (buffLen < octatesToCopy)` is false (positive buffLen vs negative value) and line 103 `if (octatesToCopy + pThis->iMsg > iMaxLine)` is false (-5 + 0 > iMaxLine fails), so no cap applies and the negative converts to (size_t)0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFB, causing an out-of-bounds write into pMsg and out-of-bounds read from the receive buffer. No non-negativity guard exists on any path (mention sweep of lines 16, 33, 40, 45, 98, 100, 103, 105, 110, 112 found none).

Origin: the octet count is accumulated in a signed int from an unbounded run of attacker-supplied digits with no overflow check, clamp, or digit-count limit. Parsing "4294967291" wraps past INT_MAX and yields iOctetsRemain = -5, which is stored in session state and consumed on the next invocation.

Fail-open validation: the `< 1` test correctly detects the wrapped negative/zero count, but the arm contains only log calls — no state reset, no FINALIZE, no return — and execution continues to `pThis->inputState = eInMsg;` (line 53), admitting the invalid negative count into the octet-counting copy path. This missing rejecting error arm is the single guard whose absence constitutes the defect.

assumptions: pMsg is allocated with at least iMaxLine bytes and iMsg <= iMaxLine is maintained; this is consistent with the code's own bounds (`if(pThis->iMsg < iMaxLine)` at line 92 and `iMaxLine - pThis->iMsg` at line 105).
doSubmitMsg is a project-internal callee not shown; its behavior (e.g., resetting iMsg) is not relied upon for any verdict.
The driver calls processDataRcvd once per received character, advancing *buff, with buffLen = bytes remaining in the network receive buffer.

bSuppOctetFram (octet-counted framing support) is a listener configuration flag; when enabled the attack path is active. Signed overflow at line 33 is formally UB but wraps to the computed negative value on all relevant target compilers.

Potential int overflow of `octatesToCopy + pThis->iMsg` (line 103) would require buffLen near 2^31, which no statement in this code can produce (line 100 caps octatesToCopy by buffLen); speculative.
Return values of doSubmitMsg are not checked; the callee is not shown and cannot be evaluated.
Octet-stuffing write path is properly guarded by `if(pThis->iMsg < iMaxLine)`; large positive oversize octet counts are correctly truncated by lines 103-105.

verdict.summary: The exported syscall handler validates its attacker-controlled inputs correctly and in the right execution order: 'resource' is bounds-checked (resource >= RLIM_NLIMITS) before the only array index computed from it, copy_from_user is failure-checked, the cur<=max invariant is enforced, raising the hard limit requires CAP_SYS_RESOURCE, and RLIMIT_NOFILE is capped at NR_OPEN even for privileged callers. The RLIMIT_CPU remap of rlim_cur 0 to 1, the unlocked single-word reads of old_rlim->rlim_max and it_prof_expires, and the acknowledged absence of an error code on the RLIMIT_CPU path are either documented self-limiting behavior or require a same-credential sibling thread of the caller's own process, so no trust-boundary party can instantiate a memory-safety, authorization, or security-state impact.

assumptions: security_task_setrlimit, cputime_to_secs, secs_to_cputime, and set_process_cpu_timer are internal kernel callees whose implementations are not shown; their return/parameter contracts were not relied on to dismiss any memory-safety or authorization candidate — the only unchecked call results consumed are capable() (boolean) and the timer setters, neither of which is a bounds/size/index sink in this code.

RLIM_NLIMITS, RLIMIT_NOFILE, NR_OPEN, and RLIM_INFINITY are taken as the standard kernel constants; RLIM_INFINITY is the exact all-ones sentinel compared with ==, so no near-miss value bypasses the exclusion.
limitations: Setting RLIMIT_CPU with rlim_cur=0 and rlim_max=0 passes the cur>max check (0>0 is false) and the remap new_rlim.rlim_cur=1 then stores cur=1 with max=0, breaking the cur<=max invariant; impact is limited to the caller's own soft limit (documented 'cheat' in the code comment) and is not attacker-amplifiable across a trust boundary.

old_rlim->rlim_max is read for the capability check outside task_lock, and it_prof_expires is read outside siglock; a racing sibling thread of the same process (shared credentials) could interleave, but every writer to these fields is this same syscall run by the caller's own equally-privileged threads, so no external or lower-privileged party can exploit the window.

secs_to_cputime of a near-RLIM_INFINITY attacker-chosen rlim_cur could wrap a narrow cputime_t on some configurations, causing the caller's own CPU timer to expire early (self-inflicted DoS at equal privilege); no memory-unsafety results at any quoted statement in this code.

The syscall returns 0 even in the case the in-code comment describes as a historically rejected RLIMIT_CPU request; this misreports no security state to any verifier (the request is in fact handled by remapping cur to 1).

verdict.summary: win_redr_status appends a space and status tags to the fixed-size global NameBuff without any capacity check on len. When the translated buffer name occupies MAXPATHL-1 bytes (an attacker-influenced file path, with a flag such as read-only or modified triggering the append), the statement *(p + len++) = ' ' overwrites the sole NUL terminator and advances len to MAXPATHL, so subsequent STRLEN(p + len), mb_string2cells and screen_puts accesses read past NameBuff (out-of-bounds read with disclosure of adjacent global memory into the status line), and a second appended tag turns the negative MAXPATHL - len into a huge size_t for vim_snprintf, producing an out-of-bounds write.

evidence.reason: Root cause: unchecked append to the fixed-size NameBuff. With len == MAXPATHL-1 (boundary length of the translated buffer name, set at line 46), this statement overwrites the only NUL terminator and increments len to MAXPATHL; no statement in the function compares len with MAXPATHL before this first use, so every later p + len and MAXPATHL - len use is out of bounds. Trigger: attacker-supplied buffer whose translated name reaches 1023 bytes and whose read-only/changed/help/preview flag selects a tag.

evidence.snippet:
vim_snprintf((char *)p + len, MAXPATHL - len, "%s", _("[RO]"));
	    len += (int)STRLEN(p + len);
evidence.reason: Executed with len == MAXPATHL after the unchecked append: p + len is one past NameBuff[MAXPATHL], so STRLEN(p + len) is the instantiated out-of-bounds read of adjacent global memory (whose bytes are then rendered in the status line); when len > MAXPATHL (two appended tags with a non-NUL byte run after the buffer), the size argument MAXPATHL - len is negative and widens to a huge size_t, making the vim_snprintf call an out-of-bounds write.

Origin of the tainted length: the attacker-influenced buffer name (file path) fills the global NameBuff whose capacity this code itself treats as MAXPATHL, and len = STRLEN(p) can reach the boundary value MAXPATHL-1; nothing in this code narrows len before the append at line 54.

assumptions: NameBuff is the Vim global buffer of MAXPATHL bytes; its capacity is implied by this code's own bound expressions (MAXPATHL - len) although the declaration is outside the given snippet.

get_trans_bufname (unshown internal callee) fills NameBuff with the translated buffer name; buffer names are attacker-influenced file paths, and even under the charitable contract that it truncates to MAXPATHL-1, the boundary length 1023 is still produced for any sufficiently long name.
vim_snprintf follows snprintf-style truncation semantics (writes nothing when the size argument is 0); the defect at the call site (out-of-bounds p + len pointer) stands either way.
screen_puts/screen_fill clip to screen columns; they guard display geometry, not NameBuff memory.
bt_help, bufIsChanged, b_p_ro are standard Vim predicates; b_p_ro reflects file permissions, bufIsChanged modification state.
limitations: The out-of-bounds WRITE variant (negative MAXPATHL - len widened to size_t in vim_snprintf, or the '<' written past the buffer in the non-mbyte truncation branch) additionally requires a non-NUL byte run adjacent to NameBuff and/or a second appended tag; this cannot be proven from the given code alone, so the confirmed primitive is the out-of-bounds read.
ru_col and Columns are unshown globals, but this_ru_col is locally clamped by quoted statements and never indexes NameBuff, so no separate defect arises there.

verdict.summary: A correctly error-checked syscall binding: mkdir(2) exposed to Scheme with a documented path contract, fail-closed error handling (SCM_SYSERROR on rv != 0), and a mode argument converted by scm_to_uint, which raises on out-of-domain values. The only defect-shaped construct, the umask(0)/umask(mask) save-restore pair, opens a process-wide umask-zero window, but its impact chain (a concurrent thread creating an overly permissive file) lies entirely in code not shown and cannot be instantiated here.

assumptions: STRING_SYSCALL is Guile's documented wrapper that converts the Scheme string to a NUL-terminated C string or raises a wrong-type-arg error; this macro's body is not shown in the given code.
scm_to_uint raises (does not return a sentinel) for non-exact-integer or out-of-range arguments, per documented Guile semantics; the body is not shown.
umask() never fails and returns only bits within 0777, per POSIX; therefore 0777 ^ mask equals 0777 & ~mask.
limitations: Thread-safety window: between 'mask = umask (0);' and 'umask (mask);' the process umask is 0, so a concurrent thread in the same process creating a file during this window would obtain default 0666 permissions instead of its intended umask-masked mode (CWE-362/367 pattern). The window is two consecutive statements in this code, but the victim's file creation is not part of the given code and the attacker's ability to control that thread's timing and privilege is unproven, so the impact is not instantiated.

mode_t width truncation: scm_to_uint yields an unsigned int while mode_t is 16 bits on some platforms (e.g. Darwin), so high bits of a caller-supplied mode are dropped; the caller already directly controls all permission bits, so truncation grants no capability it did not have.

Scheme strings containing embedded NUL characters would truncate at the NUL inside mkdir's C-string path, creating a directory at a different path than the full Scheme string suggests; the Scheme caller is the same principal that supplied the string, so this is a self-inflicted confusion, not a cross-boundary defect.

verdict.summary: The authorization gate 'if (!maywrite) { r = IMAP_PERMISSION_DENIED; ... }' is executed only after the identical-value short-circuit. When an unauthorized requester submits an annotation value that happens to equal the stored value, 'goto out' returns r==0 (success) without ever evaluating maywrite, bypassing the permission check and converting it into a value-equality oracle for annotation contents; no other authorization check exists on any path in this code.

evidence.snippet:
if (oldval.len == value->len && (!value->len || !memcmp(oldval.s, value->s, value->len)))
        goto out;
evidence.reason: Attacker-chosen value bytes control this equality test; when they match the stored annotation, 'goto out' exits with r==0 (set by the successful read_old_value at line 29) before the maywrite authorization gate at lines 36-38 ever executes, presenting success for an unauthorized write request.

This is the only authorization enforcement in the function (maywrite is mentioned nowhere else except its declaration), and its execution order places it after the line 34 early exit, so the equal-value path bypasses it entirely; no statement between line 34 and the return re-checks authorization.

assumptions: make_key (line 26) is an unshown internal callee; this code passes the exact bound sizeof(key) as its size argument and the safety of the write into key[MAX_MAILBOX_PATH+1] rests on the callee honoring that bound; the returned keylen is consumed unchecked at lines 29, 47, and 58.
read_old_value (line 29) is assumed to leave oldval consistent (s != NULL when len > 0) when returning r==0; its failure sentinel is checked at line 30 before first use.
quota_t arithmetic at line 41 (value->len - (quota_t)oldval.len) is assumed not to wrap; a wrap would require a value->len near 2^63, which cannot be instantiated by any allocatable input.
The annotate_begin/annotate_putdb transaction pairing on error paths is assumed to be handled inside those unshown callees.

The client-visible effect of the bypass (an OK vs PERMISSION_DENIED response distinguishing equality) additionally depends on the unshown caller mapping r==0 to success, which is the universal convention of this code's own return value (0 vs its own IMAP_PERMISSION_DENIED).
limitations: Line 33 memcmp dereferences value->s whenever value->len > 0 and lengths match; the code's own later check 'value->s == NULL' (line 51) shows {len>0, s==NULL} was considered possible, but the trigger requires an internal caller to construct a malformed struct buf on this static, non-intake function — the pointer field is not client-controllable content, so the NULL-deref trigger is not attacker-instantiable (robustness note).
The quota difference at line 41 can only wrap at unallocatable ~2^63-scale lengths, so no quota bypass is instantiable.

The 'if (!userid) goto out;' path at line 52 returns success without writing; the in-code comment marks this as an intentional compatibility no-op for past API abuse, though it is another silent success-without-write path.
The DEBUG syslog at lines 55-57 uses value->s as a %s argument, but is compiled out by default and its format string is fixed; not a vulnerability as given.

verdict.summary: This is a thin, correct syscall binding for mkdir(2). The path parameter is converted by STRING_SYSCALL into a valid NUL-terminated C string (throwing on non-strings) before the only sink, mkdir(c_path, c_mode); the mode parameter is either the constant 0777 or converted by scm_to_uint and passed by value into a syscall that masks it to permission bits. Error handling is fail-closed (rv != 0 raises SCM_SYSERROR). The code asserts no path-confinement contract, and directory-creation policy is enforced by kernel DAC checks; an unvalidated path reaching mkdir is the designed capability of a language primitive, not a defect in this code. Any path-traversal impact would require a confining caller application that is not part of this code.

assumptions: STRING_SYSCALL converts the SCM value 'path' into a heap-allocated, NUL-terminated C string and throws a Scheme error for non-string input before the syscall executes; the macro body is not shown in the given code.

scm_to_uint (mode) throws an out-of-range error for Scheme values that do not fit in unsigned int; scm_to_uint is a Guile-internal callee not shown in the given code. Even if it returned garbage, the value is passed by value to mkdir(2), which masks it to permission bits, so no memory-safety consequence follows.
limitations: Candidate C1 (CWE-22 path traversal): the 'path' parameter flows unvalidated into mkdir(2), so a Guile application that passes externally sourced paths to (mkdir ...) could create directories at unintended locations within process permissions. Dismissed because this code defines a general-purpose language primitive with no confinement contract; the impact requires a confining caller application not given, and the kernel's permission checks are the actual security policy at this sink.

Candidate C2: the docstring states that when 'mode' is given the permissions are 'set to the value specified', but the kernel applies the process umask to mkdir regardless; the resulting permissions can only be more restrictive than documented, never more permissive, so this is a documentation inaccuracy with no security effect.

Candidate C3: if scm_to_uint did not range-check 'mode', a truncated or garbage value would still only influence directory permission bits after kernel masking; no memory-corruption or privilege primitive is reachable.

verdict.summary: The allocation-size expression `elem_size * smap->map.max_entries` computes a u64 product from two unvalidated u32 map fields (value_size-derived elem_size and max_entries) with no overflow or range check anywhere in the function. With in-width inputs (value_size = 0xFFFFFFFF, max_entries = 0xFFFFFFF2, elem_size = sizeof(struct stack_map_bucket) + 0xFFFFFFFF), the product wraps u64 to a ~4 GiB value, so bpf_map_area_alloc succeeds with a buffer far smaller than elem_size * max_entries; pcpu_freelist_populate then carves max_entries elements at elem_size strides into that undersized buffer, writing out of bounds from element 1 onward (kernel heap/vmalloc out-of-bounds write, memory corruption).

evidence.reason: Integer overflow (u64 wraparound) in the allocation-size computation: elem_size (up to 2^32 + sizeof(struct stack_map_bucket)) times max_entries (up to 2^32 - 1) can reach/exceed 2^64 with full-domain u32 field values (e.g. value_size = 0xFFFFFFFF, max_entries = 0xFFFFFFF2 yields a wrapped size of 0xFFFFFF2E), producing an undersized allocation. No overflow/range check guards this multiplication anywhere in the function (mention sweep: lines 3-4 are pure arithmetic, line 9 checks only NULL, lines 12-14 check an unrelated error code), so the undersized buffer is returned as valid.

Impact call site: elem_size and smap->map.max_entries (whose product exceeded the wrapped allocation size) are passed into a memory-initializing callee that carves max_entries elements of elem_size bytes from smap->elems; with the simulated values (elem_size = 0x10000000F, max_entries = 0xFFFFFFF2, buffer = 0xFFFFFF2E bytes) element 1 already begins at offset 0x10000000F, past the end of the allocation, producing a kernel out-of-bounds write. Per the call-site rule, the defect stands here even though the corrupting write lands inside the callee.

Origin of the tainted factor: smap->map.value_size is a u32 map field set by a not-shown map-creation path from user-supplied attributes; its full u32 domain (up to 0xFFFFFFFF) flows unbounded into elem_size, and no statement in this code narrows it.

assumptions: sizeof(struct stack_map_bucket) is assumed >= 3 bytes (structurally certain: it contains at least a freelist node and a count), which is required for the product elem_size * max_entries to be able to reach 2^64 within the u32 domain; the concrete simulation uses 16.

smap->map.value_size and smap->map.max_entries originate from the BPF map-creation path (not shown); per the width-domain rule they are treated as carrying the full u32 domain, and validation in unshown caller code is not credited.

bpf_map_area_alloc is relied on only for its characterizable alloc-or-NULL semantics; pcpu_freelist_populate is relied on for its argument-determined carve semantics (buf, elem_size, nr_elems), consistent with the call-site rule.
limitations: The smallest wrapped allocation size achievable is roughly 2^32 minus a small constant (~4 GiB), so triggering the out-of-bounds write additionally requires the host to complete a ~4 GiB vmalloc-backed allocation; on memory-constrained hosts the allocation returns NULL and the path fails harmlessly with -ENOMEM.
An invalid smap->map.numa_node (full int domain) is passed to bpf_map_area_alloc as a placement hint; its internal use is not shown and not characterizable, so no impact could be instantiated for it.

max_entries = 0 would request a zero-size allocation and populate nothing; value_size = 0 keeps elem_size small; these boundary values do not wrap and cause no defect, confirming the wrap lives only in the near-maximum corner of the u32 domain.

verdict.summary: The attacker-controlled ticket length is pinned to the received message length by the exact-equality check 'if (ticklen + 6 != n) ... goto f_err;' (with the earlier 'if (n < 6)' minimum-length guard), so the memcpy and EVP_Digest read exactly the message body; the destination is allocated from the same ticklen and the allocation result is checked for NULL before first use. No unguarded sink on any path.

assumptions: s->method->ssl_get_message is the well-known OpenSSL message-receive helper: on ok it returns the received message length n in s->init_msg, a buffer holding exactly n bytes, and enforces the passed max of 16384. The local consistency check 'ticklen + 6 != n' makes the copy in-bounds for any n this contract can deliver, so the code does not depend on the 16384 cap for memory safety.

s->session and s->session_ctx are non-NULL and internally consistent as maintained by the SSL state machine; the 'if (s->session->session_id_length > 0)' branch only affects cache bookkeeping and the session replacement, which is followed by reassignment before any read of s->session fields.
EVP_Digest with EVP_sha256()/EVP_sha1() into session_id fits: SHA-256 writes 32 bytes and SHA-1 writes 20 bytes, both within the SSL_SESSION session_id field size of 32.
limitations: The return value of EVP_Digest is not checked; if it ever failed, the session_id and session_id_length would retain the values from the duplicated session and the function would still return success. No input in this code instantiates an EVP_Digest failure for a valid digest implementation, so this remains speculative.

If ssl_get_message were changed to deliver an n inconsistent with the actual init_msg buffer size, the consistency check would not help; that would be a defect in the callee, not in this code as written.
malloc(0) returning NULL when the server sends exactly n = 6 (empty ticket) leads only to a clean error path (SSL_ST_ERR, return -1); no memory-safety effect.

verdict.summary: The caller-supplied unsigned int *count is used without any validation to size a t_malloc buffer and to drive a subsequent memset and memcpy. The expression *count + auth_count wraps modulo 2^32 for large *count (e.g. 0xFFFFFFFF), producing a small undersized allocation, while the following memset uses *count * sizeof(*tab) (about 2^32 * 16 bytes) as its length, causing a massive heap out-of-bounds write. No overflow check, clamp, or bound exists anywhere in the function.

evidence.snippet:
tab = ret_tab = t_malloc((*count + auth_count) * sizeof(*tab));
	memset(tab, 0, *count * sizeof(*tab));
evidence.reason: Root cause: unchecked unsigned integer overflow at the sink. With *count = 0xFFFFFFFF (full domain of the unsigned int parameter of this exported function), *count + auth_count wraps mod 2^32 to auth_count - 1, so t_malloc allocates only (auth_count - 1) * sizeof(*tab) bytes, while the very next statement memsets *count * sizeof(*tab) bytes (at least 2^32 * 16 on 64-bit) into that undersized buffer, an instantiated heap out-of-bounds write. No statement in the code checks, clamps, or masks *count before this use.

Origin of the tainted value: *count is a caller-set unsigned int whose producer is not shown in this code, so per the width-domain rule its surface is the full unsigned int range 0..0xFFFFFFFF; it flows unvalidated into the allocation size at line 15 and the memset length at line 16.

assumptions: auth_count = N_ELEMENTS(auth_request_var_expand_static_tab) is not shown; the code writes tab[0] through tab[33] unconditionally, and it is assumed the static table has at least 34 entries plus a terminating NULL entry (the comment at lines 13-14 suggests this). The primary trigger does not depend on the exact value of auth_count.

t_malloc is an internal allocator not shown; standard allocator semantics are assumed (a small wrapped allocation of (auth_count - 1) * sizeof(*tab) bytes succeeds). Dovecot's t_malloc never returns NULL for small sizes, so the trigger does not depend on a NULL-return path.
escape_none (line 11) is an internal callee not shown; assumed to be a no-op escaping function.
limitations: If auth_request->user were NULL, strchr(auth_request->user, '@') at the tab[2] assignment would be a NULL dereference, but no statement in this code can produce user == NULL, so that trigger is speculative and not counted.

The writes tab[0]..tab[33] rely on the unshown static table containing at least 34 entries; if it were smaller, the memcpy at lines 20-21 would also be an out-of-bounds read source, but the table definition is not given.

In the upstream project the callers of this exported helper pass small counts (typically 0 or the number of extra fields), which limits practical reachability; per the width-domain rule this unquoted caller contract does not demote the defect, but it lowers real-world exploitability.

verdict.summary: All attacker-influenced values reaching memory sinks in this ctrl handler are bounded by quoted, correctly-operatored guards in execution order: SET_TAG/GET_TAG lengths are checked against POLY1305_BLOCK_SIZE, SET_IVLEN against CHACHA_CTR_SIZE, the TLS1_AAD length is checked to equal EVP_AEAD_TLS1_AAD_LEN before the 13-byte copy, and the decrypt-side subtraction is preceded by 'if (len < POLY1305_BLOCK_SIZE) return 0;', eliminating the historical payload-length underflow. Allocation results from OPENSSL_zalloc and OPENSSL_memdup are NULL-checked. Remaining issues (NULL actx dereference if ctrl is called before EVP_CTRL_INIT, and consumption of nonce_len/tls_payload_length/tag_len by the not-shown cipher routine) are caller-contract or out-of-scope and not attacker-instantiable in this code.

assumptions: Struct definitions are not shown; tls_aad, tag, and nonce buffer sizes, and the values of CHACHA_CTR_SIZE, POLY1305_BLOCK_SIZE, and EVP_AEAD_TLS1_AAD_LEN (taken as 16, 16, and 13 per the universally known OpenSSL headers) are assumed from the guard constants the code itself quotes.

aead_data(ctx), Poly1305_ctx_size(), and CHACHA_U8TOU32 are internal helpers whose semantics are assumed standard (return the cipher's AEAD state, the Poly1305 context size, and a little-endian 32-bit load respectively).
The consumers of actx->nonce_len, actx->tls_payload_length, actx->tag_len, and actx->tag (the chacha20_poly1305_cipher routine) are not shown; their handling of these values cannot be judged here.
limitations: Robustness, not attacker-triggerable: in the EVP_CTRL_AEAD_SET_IVLEN, SET_IV_FIXED, SET_TAG, GET_TAG, and TLS1_AAD cases, actx is dereferenced without a NULL check (only INIT and COPY test it). A NULL dereference crash occurs only if the operator's own application calls EVP_CIPHER_CTX_ctrl before initialization, which no trust-boundary party can induce; later OpenSSL hardening added explicit actx == NULL checks for defense in depth.
EVP_CTRL_COPY with actx == NULL returns 1 without duplicating state, leaving the destination context's cipher_data unset; same caller-contract class as above.

EVP_CTRL_AEAD_SET_TAG with ptr == NULL is a successful no-op that does not set tag_len; whether that can produce a fail-open decrypt depends on the not-shown MAC-verification code in the cipher routine, so no impact chain is instantiated in this code.

nonce_len may be set up to CHACHA_CTR_SIZE (16) while the nonce array is presumably 12 bytes in the (unshown) struct; no use of nonce_len exists in this code, so any overflow would have to occur in the not-shown consumer.

verdict.summary: In ex_retab's inner scanning loop, col is advanced by mb_ptr2len(ptr + col), which for a truncated multibyte lead byte returns a length that steps over the line's NUL terminator. The only loop-exit guard, 'if (ptr[col] == NUL) break;', is then never satisfied at the skipped NUL index, so col walks past the end of the line buffer. All subsequent ptr[col] reads and chartabsize(ptr + col, ...) calls are out-of-bounds reads past the allocated line, and if the bytes past the terminator form white space, the retabulation path computes old_len - col + 1 as negative (col > old_len) and casts it to size_t in mch_memmove, yielding a near-SIZE_MAX copy length that reads far out of bounds and writes out of bounds into the undersized new_line buffer. A file line consisting of a space followed by a multibyte lead byte (e.g. 0xff) with no continuation instantiates the trigger.

evidence.reason: The mb_ptr2len advance can move col past the NUL terminator of the line (a truncated multibyte lead byte yields a length > 1 that skips the NUL index), so the NUL check on the next iteration reads out of bounds and never breaks. Root cause: no validation that the multibyte character length keeps col within the line. Trigger: line ' \xff' — col goes 1 -> 3, skipping the NUL at index 2; every later ptr[col] and chartabsize is an out-of-bounds read.

Escalation sink: when col has walked past the NUL terminator (col > old_len), old_len - col + 1 is negative and the later mch_memmove(new_line + start_col + len, ptr + col, (size_t)(old_len - col + 1)) casts it to size_t, producing a near-SIZE_MAX copy length: massive out-of-bounds read from ptr+col and out-of-bounds write into the small new_line buffer. old_len is STRLEN(ptr) which stops at the NUL col already skipped.

assumptions: FEAT_VARTABS is enabled in the analyzed build (the VARTABS branches are taken); the defect exists in both build variants since the scanning loop is common.
eap->arg (the :retab argument) is ex-command parser output; tabstop_set/getdigits validate it, treated as contract data rather than direct attacker file content.
has_mbyte is true and mb_ptr2len returns >= 2 for an invalid/truncated lead byte such as 0xff without stopping at NUL, consistent with Vim's documented multibyte layer semantics.
limitations: The out-of-bounds WRITE variant requires the heap bytes immediately after the line's NUL terminator to form white space (for :retab with !) or a tab run, so it is heap-layout dependent; the out-of-bounds READ walk past the terminator is deterministic from the trigger line alone.

Candidate dismissed as functional, not security: ml_get can return a short allocation when swap-file reading of :retab-modified lines is interrupted; the code's NULL break handles it, and the cause is allocator/swap behavior, not an attacker-instantiated value.

eap->line1/line2 come from the ex command range parser (not shown); no local validation exists, but their producer is Vim's own command parser, not file content; recorded as an unquotable contract rather than a vulnerability.

verdict.summary: All attacker-influenced indices (cur_match, tagstackidx, count-derived offsets, prompt_for_number result) are clamped or range-checked by quoted statements before every memory access; the candidate off-by-one paths (negative tagstackidx after stack-full compaction, cur_match beyond num_matches on the NOTAGFILE retry loop) are provably unreachable or re-clamped on every iteration.

assumptions: Internal callees find_tags, parse_match, jumpto_tag, prompt_for_number, vim_strsave are assumed to honor their standard vim semantics; their return values are nevertheless consumed only after local sentinel/range checks quoted in the analysis.
TAGSTACKSIZE and MAXCOL are assumed to be modest positive constants per their usage as array bound and clamping ceiling.
limitations: Storing w_tagstackidx == w_tagstacklen at end (comparison 'tagstackidx <= curwin->w_tagstacklen') may be a functional off-by-one in stack-position semantics but has no memory-safety effect; recorded as functional.

The tagfunc ('tagfunc' callback) can invalidate state during find_tags; the quoted 'tagstack != curwin->w_tagstack' check covers the window-close case in this version, but re-entrancy effects deeper inside unshown callees are out of scope.
prompt_for_number returning an out-of-range value combined with got_int is handled; pure-UI crash robustness of other emsg paths assumed benign.

verdict.summary: Unsigned integer underflow of dataLeft in SProcXkbSelectEvents: the bounds check at line 53 uses size=1 for XkbBellNotify/XkbActionMessage/XkbCompatMapNotify events, but the else branch at line 64 overrides size to 2 before lines 66-67 advance the pointer and decrement dataLeft by 4. When dataLeft is 2 or 3, the subtraction wraps to a huge unsigned value, causing subsequent loop iterations to pass the now-meaningless check and perform out-of-bounds reads and writes via swaps/swapl calls at lines 56-61.

evidence.reason: The else branch overrides size from 1 to 2 AFTER the bounds check at line 53 (`if (dataLeft < (size * 2))`) already passed using the pre-override value of 1 (requiring only dataLeft >= 2). The subsequent `dataLeft -= (size * 2)` at line 67 subtracts 4 when only 2 bytes were verified, causing unsigned underflow when dataLeft is 2 or 3. The wrapped dataLeft passes the check on the next loop iteration, enabling out-of-bounds swaps/swapl calls. Trigger: any X client sending a SelectEvents request selecting a size=1 event (e.g., XkbCompatMapNotify) followed by a size=2 event (e.g., XkbAccessXNotify) with only 2 bytes of trailing data.

assumptions: Exact numeric values of XkbBellNotify, XkbActionMessage, XkbCompatMapNotify, XkbAccessXNotify constants are not shown in this snippet; assumed to be distinct indices matching the switch cases such that a size=1 event can precede a size=2 or size=4 event in bit order.
The swaps/swapl functions are assumed to read and write 2/4 bytes at the given pointer (standard X server byte-swap semantics).
limitations: The initial dataLeft computation at line 23 is properly guarded by REQUEST_AT_LEAST_SIZE at line 6, so no underflow occurs at initialization.
The post-loop check at line 69 (`dataLeft > 2`) would catch the wrapped value, but only after OOB swaps have already occurred in the loop body.

verdict.summary: No memory-safety, bounds, injection, or validation defect is present. All pointer dereferences are guarded by quoted, execution-order-correct checks (NULL checks at lines 10, 61, 91; type-discriminator check at line 19; lookup-sentinel check at line 93), and the function consumes only internal optimizer structures; no attacker-derived size, index, offset, or content value reaches any dangerous sink in this code. The residual issues (LEX/JOIN state not restored on early error returns, and a possibly-NULL explain pointer passed to the unshown save_union_explain callee) have impact chains outside this code and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: un->thd, un->thd->lex, and sl->select_lex are assumed non-NULL executor invariants; their construction is not shown in this code.

un->item, subquery_predicate->fixed, substype(), is_jtbm_merged, const_item(), and sl->join are produced by the parser/resolver (not shown); they are consumed here only behind quoted guards and never as memory sizes or indices.

save_union_explain is a project-internal callee not shown; its tolerance of a NULL Explain_query argument is unknown from this code (the author's own NULL test of thd->lex->explain at the later use suggests NULL is a normal in-domain state).
limitations: Error-path state non-restoration: 'if ((res= inner_join->optimize())) return TRUE;' (lines 74-75) and the save_union_explain failure return (lines 44-45) return before restoring 'un->thd->lex->current_select= save_select' and 'inner_join->select_options= save_options' (restored only at lines 84-85). A failing optimize() leaves stale current_select and possibly SELECT_DESCRIBE-laden select_options. Any harmful consequence depends on the (unshown) statement error-recovery code that runs after this return, so the impact is not instantiated in this code.

Possibly-NULL 'un->thd->lex->explain' is passed unchecked to 'un->save_union_explain(un->thd->lex->explain)' (line 44), while the later use of the same field is NULL-tested ('if ((eq= inner_join->thd->lex->explain))', line 91). If the unshown callee dereferenced the argument, a NULL dereference would be possible; the callee's behavior is not quotable here, so this remains an unproven, callee-dependent robustness concern.
The check 'if (res) return TRUE;' following the explain block is dead code because res is already tested at line 74; this is a cosmetic redundancy with no security effect.

verdict.summary: All attacker-derived values (netlink attributes, tcm fields, chain_index) are validated at their uses: capability gate at entry, chain_index bounded by TC_ACT_EXT_VAL_MASK, NULL and IS_ERR checks on every lookup result before first use, and no unbounded copy or indexing exists in this function.

assumptions: Internal helpers (tcf_proto_check_kind, __tcf_qdisc_find, __tcf_block_find, tcf_chain_tp_find, tcf_proto_create, tcf_chain_tp_insert_unique, tfilter_put) are not shown; their contracts are assumed to match upstream kernel semantics, per discipline 3 internal callees are otherwise unjudgable.
TC_ACT_EXT_VAL_MASK is assumed to be 0xFFFFFFFF per upstream; under that value the u32 chain_index check rejects nothing, but no consumer in this code is harmed by any u32 value.
nlmsg_parse_deprecated is assumed to initialize the tca array and validate attribute payloads against rtm_tca_policy before this code reads them.
limitations: On failure of tcf_chain_tp_insert_unique, the newly created tp_new is not explicitly released at errout_tp (tp holds the error pointer so the errout_tp put is skipped); potential reference leak of a tcf_proto, but no corruption, disclosure, or attacker-scalable retention is shown and cleanup paths outside this code are not visible.

The err == -EAGAIN replay loop depends on chain->flushing being set concurrently; unbounded replay would require a concurrent flusher to win indefinitely against rtnl_lock, a race window not exhibitable as two ordered operations in this code.
