A distractor-level inconsistency exists where goto errout is used inside the tp == NULL branch after mutex_unlock, but tp is non-NULL non-error on every path reaching it, so no lock imbalance occurs; noted only as a robustness observation.

verdict.summary: All attacker-reachable size and index sinks in this EVP ctrl handler are guarded by exact-constant or range checks quoted in the code (arg==12 for the fixed IV, 0<arg<=CHACHA20_POLY1305_MAX_IVLEN for nonce_len, 0<arg<=POLY1305_BLOCK_SIZE for tag get/set, arg==EVP_AEAD_TLS1_AAD_LEN for the TLS AAD copy, and len<POLY1305_BLOCK_SIZE rejection before the tag-discount subtraction). The unsigned len arithmetic cannot wrap (minimum 16 at subtraction), all fixed offsets stay within the 16-byte tls_aad buffer, and allocation/memdup failure sentinels are checked before use. The remaining concerns (NULL actx if EVP_CTRL_INIT is skipped, and caller-provided ptr buffer sizes) rest on contracts with code not shown and would only crash the caller's own process at equal privilege, so they are recorded as limitations, not vulnerabilities.

assumptions: The EVP_CHACHA_AEAD_CTX struct fields (tag[POLY1305_BLOCK_SIZE], tls_aad[POLY1305_BLOCK_SIZE], nonce storage sized for CHACHA20_POLY1305_MAX_IVLEN) and the helpers aead_data() and Poly1305_ctx_size() are defined outside the given code; the in-code constant-based bounds are consistent with those definitions.
The EVP framework is assumed to invoke EVP_CTRL_INIT before other ctrl commands; this sequencing contract is not shown in the given code.
limitations: Cases other than EVP_CTRL_INIT dereference actx without a NULL check; if a caller skipped EVP_CTRL_INIT, actx would be NULL and e.g. memcpy(actx->tag, ptr, arg) would crash. The triggering party is the operator's own application at equal privilege, the NULL value is not produced by any statement of this code, and the sequencing contract lives in the EVP layer (not shown), so this is a robustness issue, not an instantiated vulnerability.

The ptr-based copies (SET_TAG read of arg bytes, GET_TAG write of arg bytes, SET_IV_FIXED read of 12 bytes, TLS1_AAD read of 13 bytes) trust the caller to supply a sufficiently large buffer; this code enforces only the internal-buffer side of each bound. A short caller buffer crashes or corrupts the caller's own process at equal privilege with no trust boundary crossed.

EVP_CTRL_COPY does not free a pre-existing dst->cipher_data (potential memory leak) and, when actx is NULL, returns 1 leaving dst->cipher_data unset; neither path has a security effect within this code.
EVP_CTRL_AEAD_SET_TAG returns 1 when ptr is NULL without updating tag_len; harmless no-op semantics with no memory effect.

verdict.summary: g_socket_client_connected_callback releases the current ConnectionAttempt twice on the success path (once inside the data->connection_attempts cleanup loop at lines 48-53, since no connection_attempt_remove precedes it there, and again at line 56), and on the cancelled paths (lines 14-15, 38-39) it releases the attempt without removing it from data->connection_attempts, leaving a dangling list member that a later success-path iteration dereferences (line 51) and releases again (line 52). Only the failure path at line 32 removes the attempt first. The result is reference-count underflow, premature free, and use-after-free in the client process; a network peer controlling which of several parallel (Happy Eyeballs) connection attempts succeeds or fails, and the ordering of cancellations, can trigger the double release.

evidence.reason: Second release of the same ConnectionAttempt on one execution path: the loop at lines 48-53 already executed connection_attempt_unref (attempt_entry) for every member of data->connection_attempts, which still contains the current attempt because this path never calls connection_attempt_remove (attempt) (contrast line 32 on the failure path) and takes no ref before the loop. One release at line 52 plus this release at line 56 is a double unref / premature free (UAF), reachable when a connection attempt succeeds while it remains in the attempt list, which a remote peer controls by accepting one of several parallel connections.

Consuming sink for dangling list members: entries released but never removed from data->connection_attempts by the cancelled paths (lines 14-15 and 38-39) are dereferenced here (attempt_entry->cancellable) and released a second time when a later attempt succeeds, producing a use-after-free read plus a second unref on freed memory.

Cancelled-failure path releases attempt without connection_attempt_remove (attempt), unlike the sibling failure path at line 32 which does remove it, so the attempt stays in data->connection_attempts after its release and becomes the dangling entry later consumed at lines 51-52; the branch also unrefs data->task with no local ref or clear.

First branch releases the attempt without removing it from data->connection_attempts (no connection_attempt_remove call, contrast line 32), leaving a dangling list member; with multiple cancelled attempts this branch also unrefs data->task repeatedly.

assumptions: connection_attempt_unref, connection_attempt_remove, task_completed_or_cancelled, set_last_error, clarify_connect_error, enumerator_next_async, g_socket_client_async_connect_complete, and g_socket_client_tls_handshake are project-internal callees not shown; their exact refcount/free semantics cannot be quoted, so per discipline 3 they may not serve as guards for the release sites in this code.

Attempts are created and appended to data->connection_attempts by unshown enumerator code; membership being the managed norm is inferred from this code's own line 32 connection_attempt_remove (attempt) and from the per-member unref at line 52.
The free inside connection_attempt_unref is assumed to occur at refcount zero (standard refcount convention); the in-code double/dangling release pattern itself is fully quoted.
limitations: Candidate C (data->task double-unref across multiple cancelled callbacks at lines 14 and 38) depends on unshown task-completion and data-free bookkeeping, so the landing point of the premature free could not be instantiated from the given code; recorded as speculative.
The non-TCP branch (lines 80-82) sets data->last_error without g_clear_error, unlike line 105, potentially leaking a prior GError; minor resource leak, no security impact shown.

protocol from g_proxy_address_get_protocol (line 70) is not NULL-checked before use as a hash-table key (line 86) and as a %s argument (line 107); GLib surfaces this as a critical warning and a literal, a robustness issue rather than memory corruption.
Severity of exploitation (controlled corruption vs. crash) depends on allocator state and the unshown ConnectionAttempt free path; the double-release trigger itself is fully instantiated.

verdict.summary: Off-by-one bounds check in rpa_read_buffer: `if (p > end)` admits p == end (fully consumed buffer), so `len = *p++` reads one byte past the end of the attacker-supplied buffer. The code's own `*data += 1 + len;` can leave *data == end after a successful parse, so a subsequent call instantiates a 1-byte heap out-of-bounds read, crashing the process that parses untrusted input (DoS) when end sits at a page/allocation boundary.

evidence.reason: The only guard before the read uses `>` instead of `>=`, so it admits p == end; `len = *p++;` then dereferences the exclusive end pointer, a one-byte out-of-bounds read of the attacker-supplied buffer. The later check `if (p + len > end || len == 0)` runs after the dereference and cannot protect it.

Origin of the trigger state: when p + len == end is permitted by the line-11 check, this statement leaves *data == end; a subsequent rpa_read_buffer call in the caller's parse loop then enters with p == end and passes the insufficient `if (p > end)` guard, instantiating the out-of-bounds read at line 10.

assumptions: `end` is the exclusive one-past-the-end pointer of the buffer; this is implied by the code's own check `p + len > end` permitting consumption up to exactly end, and by full consumption leaving *data == end.

The caller parses the attacker-supplied message in a loop / successive field reads, so rpa_read_buffer is invoked again after the buffer is fully consumed; the caller is a protocol parse path (intake point per discipline 4).
limitations: Unchecked p_malloc sentinel: if the allocation fails, `memcpy(*buffer, p, len)` dereferences NULL. Since len is bounded to 255 and allocation failure is environment-induced rather than attacker-controllable, this is a robustness issue, not a counted vulnerability.

The out-of-bounds byte read at p == end is discarded (p becomes end+1 and `p + len > end` always returns 0), so the direct impact is a potential crash of the parsing process (denial of service), not information disclosure.

If a caller passed *data == NULL or *data > end by more than pointer arithmetic allows, other misbehavior could occur, but such states are not producible by this code's own flow and are caller-contract questions.

verdict.summary: All attacker-controlled inputs from the TIFF directory entry (tdir_type, tdir_count, tdir_offset) are bounded by quotable guards before reaching any sink: the maxcount clamp and the two 2147483647 sanity checks cap target_count64 at 2147483647/typesize, so the uint32 truncation at *count and the multiply datasize=(*count)*typesize cannot overflow; the heap buffer is allocated from the same expressions as every later copy/read length; the inline memcpy paths are bounded by datasize<=4 (classic) and datasize<=8 (BigTIFF) against an >=8-byte union; and the malloc NULL and TIFFReadDirEntryData error sentinels are checked before *value is published. The only locally unchecked value, desttypesize, is a contract parameter of a static internal helper with no attacker-reachable instantiation of 0.

assumptions: TIFFDataWidth returns one of {0,1,2,4,8} for any uint16 tdir_type, with 0 for unknown types (standard libtiff table); the typesize==0 early return covers the failure sentinel.
_TIFFCheckMalloc allocates count*typesize bytes or returns NULL; even without its internal overflow check, the quoted 2147483647/typesize bound already caps the product at 2147483647.

TIFFReadDirEntryData reads at most the requested datasize bytes from the file into the supplied buffer and returns a failure sentinel on error; the buffer is exactly datasize bytes, so no callee-side overflow is induced by this code.
Callers of this static helper pass sizeof()-derived constants for desttypesize and check the returned error code before consuming *value; these callers are not shown.
limitations: Division by zero at (uint64)(2147483647/desttypesize) if a caller passes desttypesize==0. No statement in this code can produce that value, the function is static and not a trust-boundary intake point, and the impact would be a same-process crash; recorded as speculative, not a vulnerability in this code.

*value is not initialized on the TIFFReadDirEntryErrSizesan, TIFFReadDirEntryErrAlloc, and TIFFReadDirEntryData error return paths; any harmful use of the uninitialized output pointer would occur in caller code not shown, so the impact chain is not instantiated here.

A malformed file can request an allocation approaching 2GB before the read is attempted; this is bounded by the code's own documented 2GB sanity cap and the malloc-failure path, so it is not attacker-scalable amplification.
The assert((tmsize_t)datasize>0) is compiled out in NDEBUG builds, but the invariant datasize>=1 holds by construction (count>=1, typesize>=1), so nothing depends on the assert.

verdict.summary: Query-planning helper for $sample. The attacker-influenced inputs (sampleSize, namespace choice) reach only floating-point ratio comparisons, clamped divisions, and internal stage-construction arguments; all division denominators are guarded by quoted early returns ('numRecords <= 100' or the ratio checks), and every failure sentinel this code's own calls produce (rsRandCursor, execStatus) is checked before first use. The only unguarded use is the double dereference of the boost::optional 'bucketUnpacker' with no engagement check anywhere in this code; however, no attacker-reachable statement of this code can set that optional to its harmful (disengaged) state — it is produced entirely by a caller not shown — so no trigger with a security impact is instantiated. Residual robustness notes: NaN trial ratio when sampleSize and numRecords are both 0 (plan-selection bias only) and a negative sampleSize would pass all ratio checks if upstream parsing allowed it.

assumptions: The caller of createRandomCursorExecutor passes an engaged bucketUnpacker whenever expCtx->ns is a time-series buckets collection; this contract is not documented, asserted, or checked anywhere in the given code.
Upstream $sample parsing rejects negative sizes; the parser is not shown in this code.
numRecords is a non-negative record count from the record store and gTimeseriesBucketMaxCount is a positive server parameter; both producers are outside this code.
The collection lock asserted by 'invariant(opCtx->lockState()->isCollectionLockedForMode(coll->ns(), MODE_IS))' is held for the duration, so no concurrent-drop race is considered.
limitations: Speculative (CWE-476-shaped): '*bucketUnpacker' is dereferenced twice with no has_value()/invariant check anywhere in this code. If the unshown caller ever passed a disengaged optional for a time-series buckets collection, this would be undefined behavior (crash of the mongod process). The trigger requires an internal caller-contract violation; no statement in this code can be driven to it by request data, so it is not counted as a vulnerability here, but a defensive invariant would be cheap.

Functional: with sampleSize = 0 and numRecords = 0 on a time-series buckets collection whose record store supports random cursors, 'std::min(sampleSize / (kCoefficient * numRecords * gTimeseriesBucketMaxCount), 1.0)' computes 0/0 = NaN and NaN propagates through the subsequent std::max into minAdvancedToWorkRatio; this only biases TrialStage toward the backup plan over an empty collection, with no memory-safety or security effect.

Uncharacterizable downstream: a negative sampleSize (within the full long long parameter domain, since upstream validation is not shown) passes every ratio check in this code and flows into the SampleFromTimeseriesBucket constructor; that stage's use of the value is not shown, so no impact link can be instantiated.

verdict.summary: Stack out-of-bounds write in spell_suggest(): the suggestion-list loop copies sug.su_badlen - stp->st_orglen bytes to wcopy + stp->st_wordlen into the fixed stack array char_u wcopy[MAXWLEN + 2] with no upper bound on either the offset or the length. The bad-word length is computed unbounded (e.g., a single-line Visual selection, lines 40-45) and is never capped to MAXWLEN before use, so a bad word longer than MAXWLEN (or any callee-supplied st_wordlen/su_badlen beyond the array) writes attacker-influenced buffer bytes past the array, corrupting the stack.

evidence.reason: Root cause: unbounded stack write. wcopy is char_u[MAXWLEN + 2] (declared line 5); the destination offset stp->st_wordlen and the copy length sug.su_badlen - stp->st_orglen are never bounded against MAXWLEN + 2 anywhere in the function — the check at line 134 is only a lower bound (length >= 1) and the MAXWLEN in the preceding vim_strncpy bounds only the first copy, not this offset/length. Simulated trigger: a 600-byte single-line Visual selection on a crafted 1000-byte line gives badlen = 601 (lines 40-45, no cap), reaching this sink with su_badlen = 601, st_orglen = 5, st_wordlen = 4, writing wcopy[4..600] into a 256-byte stack array — a stack out-of-bounds write with attacker-crafted content (CWE-787).

Origin of the tainted length: the Visual-selection branch computes badlen as the raw column difference (+1) with no clamp to MAXWLEN; it is passed unmodified into spell_find_suggest at line 88 and flows into sug.su_badlen, the copy length at the sink. A crafted file with a very long line makes this difference exceed MAXWLEN + 2, instantiating the overflow.

assumptions: MAXWLEN is 254 (Vim spell.h), so wcopy is 256 bytes; MAXWLEN is not defined in the given snippet.
vim_strncpy(dst, src, len) copies up to len bytes, stopping at the source NUL, and writes a terminating NUL: at most len + 1 bytes at dst.

sug.su_badlen, sug.su_badptr, stp->st_word, stp->st_wordlen and stp->st_orglen are produced by spell_find_suggest / the suggestion machinery, which is not shown; per the width-domain rule their surface is the full domain of their declared int width. The concrete story that the callee stores the unbounded badlen as su_badlen is plausible but not quotable from the given code.
sps_limit, Rows, prompt_for_number and did_set_spelllang behave per normal Vim semantics; Rows < 2 only makes limit negative, with no security effect in this code.
limitations: Replacement block: if st_orglen > STRLEN(line), the size expression STRLEN(line) - stp->st_orglen + stp->st_wordlen + 1 underflows in size_t, but the huge allocation fails and the quoted guard `if (p != NULL)` skips the memmove/STRCPY/STRAT writes; no corruption path was instantiated there. A heap write at STRCPY would additionally require the unshown callee to be internally inconsistent (STRLEN(st_word) != st_wordlen), which no statement of this code instantiates.

Secondary same-root candidates: repl_from = vim_strnsave(sug.su_badptr, sug.su_badlen) and AppendToRedobuffLit(p + c, stp->st_wordlen + sug.su_badlen - stp->st_orglen) can read past the end of the line copy when su_badlen exceeds the bytes remaining after su_badptr (the `++badlen` can even count one past the last byte of the line). These are out-of-bounds reads of the same unbounded su_badlen family, reached only after the primary stack write and only when a replacement is applied; they are subsumed by the primary finding.

The verified-good guards were: selected > 0 && selected <= sug.su_ga.ga_len before SUG(sug.su_ga, selected - 1) (correct at both bounds), all IObuff writes bounded by vim_snprintf with IOSIZE, and the first vim_strncpy(wcopy, stp->st_word, MAXWLEN) writing at most MAXWLEN + 1 bytes at offset 0.

verdict.summary: fix_dl_name reads dl->str + dl->length - so_ext_len with no check that dl->length >= so_ext_len; when the parsed library name is shorter than ".so" (e.g. length 0-2), the size_t subtraction underflows and my_strcasecmp reads out of bounds before the buffer, causing an OOB read and potential crash (DoS) of the server processing attacker-supplied SONAME/plugin names.

evidence.reason: The expression dl->str + dl->length - so_ext_len is computed without any check that dl->length >= so_ext_len. dl->str/dl->length are attacker-influenced parsed data (LEX_STRING produced outside this code). Trigger: dl->length = 2, dl->str = "ab" gives pointer dl->str - 1 (size_t underflow 2-3 = SIZE_MAX, pointer wraps one byte before the buffer); with dl->length = 0 the read starts at dl->str - 3. my_strcasecmp then reads up to 3 bytes outside the allocation before the string (heap metadata or an unmapped page at an allocation start, causing a segfault of the higher-privileged server process). No mention of dl->length anywhere in the function (lines 3-11) constitutes a minimum-length guard, clamp, or mask.

assumptions: SO_EXT is a string literal such that so_ext_len = sizeof(SO_EXT) - 1 = 3; the underflow defect holds for any so_ext_len >= 1.
my_strcasecmp has standard case-insensitive compare semantics: it reads bytes from both arguments until a difference or NUL, so it dereferences the computed pointer.
dl->str/dl->length arrive from a parser/caller not shown; per the width-domain and intake-point rules they are treated as attacker-data, and this function is judged as the last line of defense.
limitations: Secondary candidate (not primary): alloc size dl->length + so_ext_len + 1 (line 7) can wrap if dl->length is near SIZE_MAX, yielding a small buffer followed by memcpy(s, dl->str, dl->length) with the huge length (heap overflow, CWE-190/CWE-787). Not counted as primary because no realistic parse can instantiate a string length of ~SIZE_MAX; the precondition could not be instantiated.
Unchecked alloc_root return at line 7 consumed by memcpy at line 8: NULL only on allocation failure (OOM), not attacker-instantiable environment failure; would be a NULL deref, no corruption.

Reachability of fix_dl_name from a specific SQL statement (e.g. INSTALL PLUGIN ... SONAME) is inferred from the function's shape and signature; the call site is not shown, but its arguments carry parsed, trust-boundary-crossing content per the intake-point rule.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds write in the macro-expansion path of compileRule: substituted macro-argument characters are appended to the stack-resident tmpFile.line buffer with no bound on tmpFile.linelen. The only capacity check in the function ("else if (tmpFile.linelen >= MAXSTRING)") guards the definition-character copy but not the argument-substitution loop, so a table file can overflow the buffer with attacker-controlled content and attacker-scalable length (repeatable argument references).

evidence.snippet:
for (int j = 0; j < arg.length; j++)
								tmpFile.line[tmpFile.linelen++] = arg.chars[j];
evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The loop copies macro-argument characters into tmpFile.line (a stack-local FileInfo buffer whose capacity the code itself fixes at MAXSTRING via the "else if (tmpFile.linelen >= MAXSTRING)" check on line 157) without testing tmpFile.linelen or arg.length. An exhaustive mention sweep shows lines 157 and 155-156 are the only statements bounding linelen and neither is executed in this loop. Trigger (instantiated): a table-file macro whose definition references an argument is invoked with an argument token of length A; each substitution appends A attacker-controlled widechars at tmpFile.linelen, and multiple references accumulate linelen past MAXSTRING (e.g. A=1500 with three references writes ~2450 widechars past the buffer). Even a single reference overflows when linelen is at MAXSTRING, since the line-157 guard lets linelen reach MAXSTRING and the argument copy then writes at index MAXSTRING.

Origin of the tainted value: the macro argument is read as a token directly from the attacker-supplied table file, so its content and length (up to the CharsString container width) are attacker-controlled and flow unchecked into the unbounded copy at lines 169-170.

assumptions: MAXSTRING is the capacity of FileInfo.line; this is anchored on the code's own bound check at line 157 ("else if (tmpFile.linelen >= MAXSTRING)"), which treats MAXSTRING as the write limit for tmpFile.line.
getToken fills a CharsString whose chars-array capacity bounds any single argument's length; the trigger uses multiple substitution references so it does not depend on the exact token cap.

A macro whose definition references arguments has substitution_count >= 1; line 166 ("if (subst < m->substitution_count)") treats substitutions as an ordinary macro property, and line 37 shows macros are defined from the same attacker-supplied file. The macro path requires a build with ENABLE_MACROS and macros in scope (line 107).
limitations: Unchecked malloc at lines 127-128 ("CharsString *arguments = malloc(...)"): NULL is not tested before the writes at lines 131 and 168; reachable impact requires allocation failure, so it is recorded, not counted as primary (CWE-476).

arguments[m->substitutions[2 * subst + 1] - 1] (line 168) and the definition offsets m->substitutions[2 * subst] / m->definition[i++] (lines 141, 145) are not validated in this code; their safety depends on the unshown compileMacro, so an out-of-bounds read trigger could not be instantiated here.

CTO_Match/CTO_BackMatch ignore the return values of getCharacters/getRuleCharsText/getRuleDotsPattern and then consume ptn_before.chars[0], .length, ruleChars and ruleDots; whether the structs are left uninitialized on failure depends on unshown callee semantics, so the uninitialized-value impact is not instantiated.

CTO_ExactDots reads ruleChars.chars[0] with no length check and computes scratchPad.length = ruleChars.length - 1 (negative for an empty operand); CTO_Replace reads ruleDots.chars[1] and memmoves with ruleDots.length-- after an unchecked getRuleDotsText; both depend on unshown parse callee behavior.
CTO_RepEndWord appends ',' and y.chars to ruleDots.chars; a one-past write at MAXSTRING is conceivable only with maximal tokens and unshown parseDots expansion ratios, so it was not instantiated.
Without ENABLE_MACROS the primary macro path is dead code; the vulnerability applies to macro-enabled builds, which is the feature's intended configuration.

verdict.summary: qtm_decompress fails to clamp the match-copy extent to the decompression window: in the window-wrap branch the copy loops write match_length bytes at window[window_posn] with no bound against qtm->window_size (the non-wrap branch has exactly this clamp), and frame_end is likewise never clamped to window_size. An attacker-controlled compressed stream (e.g. a wrap match with match_offset = window_size at window_posn = window_size-1, match_length = 3) writes attacker-chosen decoded bytes past the end of the heap-allocated window buffer, yielding heap memory corruption in the process decompressing the untrusted archive.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write (root cause). The wrap-branch copies write i = match_length bytes starting at rundest = &window[window_posn] with no clamp of i to window_size - window_posn; the only guard, 'if (j > (int) qtm->window_size)' (line 98), bounds the SOURCE index (runsrc), not the destination extent. Instantiated trigger: window_posn = W-1 (admitted by 'while (window_posn < frame_end)'), selector 4 with match_length = 3 and attacker-chosen extra bits making match_offset = W = qtm->window_size: j = 1 passes the guard, the first run copies 1 byte, then 'while (i-- > 0) *rundest++ = *runsrc++;' writes window[W] and window[W+1] past the heap window buffer with attacker-controlled decoded bytes. The non-wrap branch at lines 112-113 contains the missing clamp ('if(i > (int) (qtm->window_size - window_posn)) i = qtm->window_size - window_posn;'), proving its absence here is the defect.

Origin of the secondary unbounded index: frame_end is clamped only to the frame boundary (frame_start + QTM_FRAME_SIZE), never to qtm->window_size. When frame_start + QTM_FRAME_SIZE exceeds the window size (unaligned or small window), the inner loop 'while (window_posn < frame_end)' lets window_posn reach and pass window_size, so even the literal write 'window[window_posn++] = sym;' (line 59) and the match copies write out of bounds. Additionally, 'window_posn += match_length;' (line 116) advances past window_size unclamped, making 'qtm->o_end = &window[window_posn];' (line 120) point beyond the buffer and enabling out-of-bounds reads in the mspack_write flush paths (lines 137-138, 153-154).

assumptions: QTM_RESTORE_BITS, QTM_STORE_BITS, QTM_GET_SYMBOL, QTM_READ_BITS, QTM_REMOVE_BITS macros and the qtm init/lookup tables (position_base[], extra_bits[], length_base[], length_extra[]) are not shown; their outputs (selector, sym, extra, match_offset, match_length) are therefore treated as attacker data at the full width of their expressions, with no narrowing assumed.
The window buffer is qtm->window_size bytes; this is supported by the code's own else-branch clamp 'qtm->window_size - window_posn' (lines 112-113), which treats window_size as the buffer extent.
QTM_FRAME_SIZE and the admissible window_size values are constants defined elsewhere; the wrap-branch overflow (primary evidence) does not depend on their exact values.
mspack_write and cli_dbgmsg semantics assumed per standard library/documentation conventions; mspack_write return values are checked at every call site in this code.
limitations: Line 131: 'do { QTM_READ_BITS(i, 8); } while (i != 0xFF);' may loop indefinitely on a malformed stream if the unshown QTM_READ_BITS macro does not error out on input exhaustion; potential unbounded-consumption DoS, but the macro's exhaustion behavior cannot be verified from the given code.

The overshoot check at lines 123-127 ('if ((window_posn - frame_start) != QTM_FRAME_SIZE) ... return qtm->error = CL_EFORMAT;') catches some window_posn overshoots from the clamped else branch, but it runs only after the inner loop and only on completed frames; it does not cover the wrap-branch write itself, which is the primary defect.
Exact exploitability of the frame_end path (second evidence) depends on the unshown relationship between QTM_FRAME_SIZE and window_size; the wrap-branch trigger is independent of it.

verdict.summary: In the 'code not in table' branch, lzw_decode consumes ctx->previous_code without any bounds validation and uses it as the dictionary chain-walk index (code_out). previous_code is a uint32_t context field whose producer (lzw_init/lzw__clear_codes) is not shown, so its surface is the full uint32_t domain; no statement in this code bounds it before 'table + code_out' indexes the dictionary and '*stack_pos++ = entry->last_value' copies the out-of-bounds-read byte into the decode output. A malformed compressed stream whose first code equals current_entry reaches this branch immediately, causing an out-of-bounds read with disclosure and, as the garbage-driven loop iterates past the stack buffer, an out-of-bounds write. The same unvalidated value is also stored into the dictionary at line 52 (entry->previous_entry = ctx->previous_code), poisoning later chain walks.

evidence.reason: Root cause: ctx->previous_code (uint32_t, producer not shown in this code, full width domain) is assigned to the chain-walk index code_out with no bounds, range, or sentinel check anywhere on any path; the else-branch is reachable whenever the attacker-supplied code equals current_entry, including on the first decode call.

Sink: with code_out unbounded (e.g. 0xFFFFFFFF), 'table + code_out' indexes far out of bounds; entry->last_value is an out-of-bounds read whose byte is disclosed through the decode output stack, and each loop iteration advances stack_pos with no capacity check, becoming an out-of-bounds write once iterations exceed the stack buffer.

Secondary use of the same unvalidated value: the out-of-domain previous_code is stored into the dictionary, so even if the immediate walk halts, a later chain walk that reaches this entry sets code_out to the poisoned value and re-instantiates the out-of-bounds access at lines 73-74.

assumptions: LZW_CODE_MAX is assumed to be 12, so '1 << LZW_CODE_MAX' = 4096; the guards at lines 32 and 48 imply the table holds at least 4096 entries.

ctx->stack_base capacity is not shown in this code; in the fully guarded in-table path, the write count is bounded by this code's own logic (each entry's previous_entry, stored at line 52 from a code_new that passed the line-28 check, is strictly less than its own index, so chains strictly decrease), keeping writes within roughly current_entry - clear_code + 1.

lzw__next_code, lzw__clear_codes, lzw_init, and the struct lzw_ctx layout are not shown; previous_code has no quoted producer in this code, which per the width-domain rule leaves its input surface the full uint32_t domain.
limitations: The code-size increase at line 57 compares the stale pre-increment local current_entry against ctx->current_code_size_max; this appears to be a decode-timing/correctness issue only, since lines 28 and 32 still bound every table index reachable from code_new.

If the unshown initializer (lzw_init or lzw__clear_codes) provably sets previous_code to an in-range value before lzw_decode can first execute the not-in-table branch, the out-of-bounds trigger would be blocked by code outside this snippet; that unquoted external contract cannot serve as a guard for this code, but it is the one external fact that would neutralize the finding in the full source tree.

The root entries (indices <= clear_code) read at line 77 depend on initialization performed by the unshown lzw__clear_codes routine; if those were left uninitialized it would be an additional uninitialized-read defect of the same unshown-producer class.

verdict.summary: pax_decode_header consumes the return values of find_next_block() without any NULL sentinel check, at 'p = blk->buffer;' and inside COPY_BUF at 'src = b->buffer;'. A truncated or crafted sparse PAX archive (sparse_major > 0 with no following data block) makes find_next_block return NULL, and the immediate dereference crashes tar while it processes the attacker-supplied archive: denial of service.

evidence.reason: Unchecked failure sentinel: blk is assigned from find_next_block(), an archive-block lookup that returns NULL when the archive holds no further block (truncated archive), and 'p = blk->buffer;' dereferences it with no 'if (!blk)' test anywhere on any path. Trigger instantiated: sparse_major > 0 with the archive ending after the member header → blk == NULL → NULL dereference → SIGSEGV in tar processing the attacker's file (DoS).

Same missing guard inside the COPY_BUF macro: when a sparse-map number spans past the end of the current block ('if (src == endp)'), find_next_block() is called and its return is immediately dereferenced as 'src = b->buffer;' with no sentinel test; a truncated archive makes b == NULL and crashes the process mid-copy.

assumptions: decode_num returns false on parse failure and, on success, yields u not exceeding its max argument (TYPE_MAXIMUM(size_t)/TYPE_MAXIMUM(off_t)); its false-return IS checked at lines 42/57/65 before u is used, but the on-success range contract is internal and not shown.
xcalloc (gnulib) aborts the process on allocation failure or size overflow; its behavior is not part of the given code.

find_next_block returns NULL when the archive contains no further block (its miss sentinel); per the analysis rules, a return of an unshown internal callee consumed without a local sentinel check is a defect at the use site.
limitations: Memory-exhaustion vector (secondary, not primary): a one-line PAX header can set sparse_map_size up to TYPE_MAXIMUM(size_t), driving xcalloc(size, sizeof(struct sp_array)); with gnulib xalloc-die semantics tar exits cleanly on failure, but a large-but-satisfiable size under memory overcommit can OOM the host — impact depends on unshown xcalloc behavior and environment, so it is not counted as a primary finding.
The NULL dereference is a read through a NULL base ('blk->buffer' / 'b->buffer'), so the direct impact is a crash (DoS), not memory corruption.

No memory-corruption sink was found: the COPY_BUF write path is bounded by the quoted guard 'if (dst == buf + UINTMAX_STRSIZE_BOUND -1)' followed by 'return false;', verified at both boundaries (write at index BOUND-2 allowed, index BOUND-1 rejected before the write).

verdict.summary: Stack-based out-of-bounds write in the suggestion-listing loop of spell_suggest(): the second vim_strncpy writes sug.su_badlen - stp->st_orglen bytes at offset stp->st_wordlen into the fixed stack buffer char_u wcopy[MAXWLEN + 2], with no statement anywhere bounding the offset-plus-length to the buffer size. badlen is clamped only to the remaining line length (lines 49-50), so a single-line Visual selection longer than MAXWLEN passes a bad-word length to spell_find_suggest that returns as sug.su_badlen far exceeding the buffer, and a partial-replacement suggestion (st_orglen < su_badlen, the case the code itself designs for at lines 135-138) makes the copy run past the end of wcopy with line-content bytes, corrupting the stack.

evidence.reason: Unguarded out-of-bounds write: vim_strncpy writes up to (sug.su_badlen - stp->st_orglen) + 1 bytes at wcopy + stp->st_wordlen, but wcopy is the fixed stack array char_u wcopy[MAXWLEN + 2] (line 5). The if only gates when the copy happens, not how much. No statement in the code compares st_wordlen, or su_badlen - st_orglen, or their sum, against MAXWLEN/sizeof(wcopy) (mention sweep: lines 5, 137, 138-141, and the later read of wcopy are the only mentions). Trigger: with a 400-byte line and a Visual selection of 300 bytes, lines 40-50 compute badlen=300 (the clamp at 49-50 bounds it only to the line), line 92 passes 300 to spell_find_suggest, and for a split suggestion with st_orglen=40, st_wordlen=80 the copy writes ~261 bytes at wcopy[80] into a 102-byte stack array — ~240 bytes past the end, source bytes being the line text (file content). st_wordlen/st_orglen/su_badlen are callee-set int fields with no quoted narrowing; the width-domain rule makes the oversized combination instantiable, and no unquoted callee contract may dismiss it.

evidence.snippet:
if (badlen > STRLEN(line) - curwin->w_cursor.col)
	    badlen = STRLEN(line) - curwin->w_cursor.col;
evidence.reason: Origin of the oversized tainted length: badlen (from the Visual selection, line 40, ++ at line 45) is clamped to the remaining line length only — never to MAXWLEN, the capacity of the stack buffer that derivatives of this value later fill. A line can be thousands of bytes, so badlen can exceed MAXWLEN+2 by an arbitrary margin; it is then passed as the bad-word length at line 92 (spell_find_suggest(line + curwin->w_cursor.col, badlen, &sug, limit, ...)) and returns as sug.su_badlen, which the sink at lines 139-141 consumes with no local bound.

assumptions: MAXWLEN is the vim spell constant (100); the exact value does not affect the analysis since no check anywhere references it at the sink — only wcopy's fixed size MAXWLEN+2 matters.
vim_strncpy semantics per discipline 3: copies at most len bytes from src and always NUL-terminates, writing at most len+1 bytes at the destination.

sug.su_badlen, stp->st_wordlen and stp->st_orglen are int fields set inside the unshown spell_find_suggest; per the width-domain rule their surface is the full int domain, and no statement of this code narrows them.

The badlen value passed at line 92 propagating to sug.su_badlen is assumed (callee unshown); per disciplines 1/3 this cannot dismiss the candidate — the value 300 is produced by this code's own lines 40-50.
limitations: Stale VIsual position beyond end-of-line could make STRLEN(line) - curwin->w_cursor.col (size_t) wrap to a huge value at line 49, bypassing the clamp entirely; this requires an editor state that this code's own statements never exhibit, so it is speculative.

The exact-fit allocation at the replacement site (alloc(STRLEN(line) - stp->st_orglen + stp->st_wordlen + 1) with STRCPY/STRCAT) is safe only if st_wordlen == STRLEN(st_word) and st_orglen <= remaining line length — unquoted callee contracts; if violated it is a heap overflow, but the stack overflow at lines 139-141 fires first in the same iteration and is the primary defect.

AppendToRedobuffLit(p + c, stp->st_wordlen + sug.su_badlen - stp->st_orglen) performs an OOB read if sug.su_badlen exceeds the remaining line length; on the Visual path the quoted clamp prevents it, on the word path it depends on the unshown callee.
If Rows < 2, limit becomes <= 0 and is passed as maxcount to spell_find_suggest; no memory operation in this code consumes it, so at most a functional issue.

Candidates (2)-(4) of STEP 3 share the same root cause (callee-derived lengths consumed without local bounds) but were not counted as independent primary defects; the single named guard whose absence is decisive is the missing bound of stp->st_wordlen + (sug.su_badlen - stp->st_orglen) to sizeof(wcopy) before line 139.

verdict.summary: In the gzip EXTRA header field handling, inflate() dereferences state->head->extra_len at line 144 before the NULL test at line 145, so an attacker-supplied gzip stream with the FEXTRA flag crashes (NULL-pointer read) any decompressing process when state->head is Z_NULL, the documented default state this code itself handles elsewhere. The NULL/sentinel checks exist but are placed after the first use, so they never guard it in execution order.

evidence.reason: Root cause: state->head is dereferenced (read of head->extra_len) before the only NULL sentinel check, which appears on the following lines and therefore never covers this first use in execution order. Trigger: attacker gzip stream 1f 8b 04 ... with FEXTRA set makes EXLEN set state->length=1, then EXTRA runs with state->head == Z_NULL (a state the code explicitly supports, e.g. 'if (state->head != Z_NULL)' at lines 52, 129, 169) and copy=1, executing this line and crashing the victim process. The sibling NAME/COMMENT cases perform their head NULL checks before the analogous dereference, isolating EXTRA as the defect.
Origin of the tainted value: the attacker-controlled XLEN field sets state->length, which drives the EXTRA case into the copy branch that reaches the unguarded dereference at line 144.

assumptions: Macros LOAD, RESTORE, INITBITS, NEEDBITS, PULLBYTE, BITS, DROPBITS, BYTEBITS, CRC2, CRC4 and the struct inflate_state layout are not shown; standard zlib semantics assumed.

inflateStateCheck, inflate_table, inflate_fast, updatewindow, fixedtables are not shown; their arguments are validated at the quoted call sites (nlen<=286, ndist<=30, ret sentinels checked) and standard semantics are assumed.
GUNZIP is assumed compiled in, since the vulnerable extra-field path exists only in that branch and the given code includes it.
limitations: A heap-buffer-overflow escalation via unsigned underflow of extra_len - length requires the application to replace state->head with a fresh struct between inflate() calls mid-extra-field; that caller behavior is an unquoted contract, so the overflow variant is speculative. Only the NULL dereference is instantiated from the given code.
The nlen/ndist bound check 'if (state->nlen > 286 || state->ndist > 30)' is compiled only when PKZIP_BUG_WORKAROUND is not defined; in the given configuration it is present.
The INFLATE_ALLOW_INVALID_DISTANCE_TOOFAR_ARRR zero-fill path is compiled only with that macro and is bounded by the quoted clamps as written.
INFLATE_STRICT distance check 'state->offset > state->dmax' is optional; window bounds are still enforced by the whave/sane checks quoted in STEP 2.

verdict.summary: All memory sinks in this function are locally sentinel-guarded in execution order: clone NULLs are checked before the placement new, the eq pointer is checked with a short-circuit before push_back, right_item is NULL-checked before its dereferences, and the iterator's NULL sentinel terminates both loops before any use of item. The one concrete anomaly is that `left_item= item;` executes before the pushdown checker runs, so if the checker rejects every field the exhausted loop leaves left_item pointing at a checker-rejected item and `if (!left_item)` (a NULL-only test) lets it through; an equality built from that rejected item is then appended to `equalities`. That is a pushdown-correctness logic defect, but every claimed security consequence (wrong pushdown into a derived table or storage engine, wrong results, engine-side assert) occurs in caller code not shown, so the impact is not instantiated in this code and the candidate is recorded as a limitation, not a vulnerability.

assumptions: Item_equal_fields_iterator, get_const(), build_clone(), List::push_back, and the Pushdown_checker callback are internal callees not shown; however, every return value this code consumes from them (item, right_item, clones, eq, push_back result) is locally sentinel-checked before first use, so memory safety here does not rest on their contracts.

Items in the Item_equal ultimately originate from user SQL, but this function performs no arithmetic on attacker-derived sizes, indices, or offsets and passes only locally NULL-checked pointers to callees.
Placement new on thd->mem_root can return NULL under OOM; the code tests it (`if (!eq || ...`) before use.
limitations: Stale anchor defect: in the first loop, `left_item= item;` runs before `if (checker && !((item->*checker) (arg))) continue;`. If a non-NULL checker rejects every field, the iterator exhausts without `break`, left_item holds the last REJECTED item, and the NULL-only guard `if (!left_item) return false;` does not catch it. Simulated trigger: one field F1, checker rejects F1, get_const() non-NULL → equality F1 = const is pushed into `equalities` even though F1 failed the pushdown check, and the function reports success (return false). No guard of any form (found-flag, post-check assignment, re-test, early return) exists in the mention sweep. Not scored as a vulnerability because every claimed consequence (incorrect condition pushdown, wrong query results, engine assert) happens in the unshown caller that consumes `equalities`; the impact link leaves this code.
Error-path partial output: the second loop can `return true` after already having pushed some equalities into the caller's list; whether the caller discards the list on error is not shown.

First-branch clones do not get `set_item_equal(NULL)` (only second-loop clones do); any stale item_equal back-pointer consequence depends on Item_equal/clone lifetime management not shown in this code.

verdict.summary: The sys_setrlimit implementation contains all necessary security guards: resource is bounds-checked against RLIM_NLIMITS before pointer arithmetic, user input is validated by copy_from_user with EFAULT on failure, soft limit is enforced not to exceed hard limit, raising the hard limit requires CAP_SYS_RESOURCE, RLIMIT_NOFILE is capped at NR_OPEN, and the LSM hook return value is checked. The RLIMIT_CPU timer path handles the zero and infinity sentinel values correctly. The only theoretical issues (TOCTOU between the capability check read and the task_locked write, and potential unsigned overflow in secs_to_cputime) are confined to threads of the same process sharing the same credentials, do not cross a trust boundary, and produce no memory corruption, privilege escalation, or injection.

assumptions: RLIM_NLIMITS matches the declared array size of current->signal->rlim (kernel invariant, not shown in this snippet)
cputime_t and the secs_to_cputime/cputime_to_secs macros follow standard kernel definitions (architecture-specific, not shown)
security_task_setrlimit follows the standard LSM hook contract of returning 0 on allow or a negative errno on deny (implementation not shown)
limitations: TOCTOU race: the read of old_rlim->rlim_max in the capability check is outside task_lock while the write *old_rlim = new_rlim is inside it. Exploitation requires two threads of the same process to hold different capability sets simultaneously (racing a credential transition), which is an application-level race within a single trust domain, not a cross-boundary attack. Later kernel versions moved the check inside the lock as a correctness fix.

secs_to_cputime(rlim_cur) can overflow unsigned long for very large rlim_cur values (e.g., multiples of 2^62 with HZ=100 on 64-bit), causing the CPU timer to wrap or be zero. Impact is limited to the calling process own timer behavior (self-inflicted, equivalent to setting RLIM_INFINITY which is permitted), with no memory corruption or system-wide effect.

The code comments note a long-standing API error: the kernel does not return an error code when it rejects a user attempt to set RLIMIT_CPU. This is a documented functional/compatibility issue, not a security vulnerability.

verdict.summary: In gst_flxdec_chain's FLX_FRAME_TYPE path, the attacker-controlled parsed chunk size is used as `flxfh.size - FlxFrameChunkSize` without any lower-bound check. A crafted FLIC file with a frame chunk whose size field is smaller than FlxFrameChunkSize (e.g., 0) slips past the only nearby check (`if (avail < flxfh.size)`, which compares against available bytes, not against the chunk header size), making the subtraction underflow to a huge unsigned byte count. gst_adapter_take then returns NULL, and chunk is dereferenced unchecked at FLX_FRAME_TYPE_FIX_ENDIANNESS ((FlxFrameType *) chunk) and ((FlxFrameType *) chunk)->chunks, crashing the process decoding the attacker-supplied file (remote denial of service). The missing guard is a `flxfh.size < FlxFrameChunkSize` check (or a NULL test on the take result), which appears nowhere in the code.

evidence.reason: Origin of the defect: flxfh.size is parsed straight from the media file (memcpy at line 98, byte-swapped at line 99) and its full 16-bit domain is instantiable by the file author. With flxfh.size in 0..5, the only check on this path, `if (avail < flxfh.size)` at line 105, passes because the loop condition already guarantees avail >= FlxFrameChunkSize, so the subtraction underflows to a negative int that converts to a huge unsigned byte count passed to gst_adapter_take. No lower-bound check, clamp, or mask on flxfh.size exists anywhere in the code.

Sink: gst_adapter_take returns its documented failure sentinel NULL when the requested byte count exceeds the available data, so chunk is NULL for the underflowed length, yet it is dereferenced here without any NULL check (the mention sweep over chunk at lines 96, 111, 113, 114, 128-129, 158 finds no sentinel test). Concrete trigger: state PLAYING, chunk header with size 0 and id FLX_FRAME_TYPE, avail >= FlxFrameChunkSize; the result is a NULL pointer dereference that crashes the victim's process decoding the attacker-crafted media file (denial of service).

assumptions: FlxFrameChunk/FlxFrameType struct layouts and the FLX_*_FIX_ENDIANNESS macro bodies are not part of the given code; the trigger value flxfh.size = 0 is representable in any integral width the field could have, so the underflow trigger does not depend on the exact declaration. The endian-fix macro is assumed to read and swap fields of the pointed struct, as its name and every use indicate.

gst_adapter_take is treated per its documented library semantics: it returns NULL when the requested number of bytes is not available (and for a request of 0). FlxFrameChunkSize is sizeof of the non-empty chunk-header struct used as a positive copy length at line 98, hence a positive constant greater than 0.
limitations: When the file header's depth is greater than 8, the converter is only created under `if (flxh->depth <= 8)` (lines 67-69) yet flx_colorspace_convert is called unconditionally at line 140 with the possibly-NULL converter; the callee is not shown, so whether this crashes or is handled cannot be characterized from the given code.

`out = gst_buffer_new_and_alloc (flxdec->size * 4)` (line 124) can overflow a 32-bit flxdec->size field (width*height reaches 4294836225) and yield an undersized output buffer that the colorspace conversion then fills; the declared width of flxdec->size is not shown in the given code, so this overflow remains speculative.

For flxfh.size in [7,13] the take buffer is smaller than FlxFrameTypeSize: with flxfh.size == 7 the shown read ((FlxFrameType *) chunk)->chunks over-reads a 1-byte heap allocation by one byte, and chunk + FlxFrameTypeSize (line 129) points past the allocation into flx_decode_chunks; the write primitives live in the endian macro and flx_decode_chunks, neither of which is part of the given code, so no corruption impact could be fully instantiated from the shown statements alone.

The wrong_type error path calls gst_object_unref (flxdec) on the element itself from within its own chain function; whether this drops the final reference and causes a use-after-free depends on pipeline refcounts not shown, so it is not counted as a primary finding.
The `return GST_FLOW_ERROR` at line 132 and the need_more_data goto skip g_free (chunk) on some paths, which is a memory leak without security impact.

verdict.summary: In the DEC_MOUSE digit-scanning loop, getdigits(&nr) consumes digit bytes with no length bound before the only bounds check (if (nr >= tp + len) return -1;) executes, so a terminal response whose digits run to the end of the input buffer causes getdigits to read one byte past the end of the buffer (buf[*buflen] on the buf != NULL path) before the guard runs.

evidence.reason: getdigits(&nr) advances nr through consecutive digit bytes reading each one, including the first non-digit terminator, with no length limit; the sole bound `if (nr >= tp + len) return -1;` executes only AFTER getdigits has already consumed. With buf = "ESC[1234567890", *buflen = 13, offset = 0 (len = 13, tp = buf) and a termcodes entry "ESC [" named KS_DEC_MOUSE, the first iteration calls getdigits, which reads buf[2]..buf[12] (all digits) and then buf[13] — one byte past the buffer — before the check at line 171 runs. Root cause: bounds check placed after the unbounded read; no pre-scan bound or length argument exists anywhere in the loop.

assumptions: getdigits is treated as a digit-consuming advance helper that reads each byte it advances over (standard vim idiom); it is not shown, but the read of the terminating non-digit byte is inherent to any digit-scan implementation, so the one-past read does not depend on unknown internals.

modifiers2keycode's return (used as the index into string[MAX_KEY_CODE_LEN + 1]) is not shown; no local bound on new_slen exists, but overflow depends entirely on the callee's maximum — recorded as assumption, not a finding.

put_string_in_typebuf, handle_csi, handle_osc, handle_dcs, check_termcode_mouse, get_bytes_from_buf, get_long_from_buf are internal callees not shown; the first four receive len and their returns are sentinel-checked at the call sites, so no defect is claimed at those call sites.
limitations: KS_VER_SCROLLBAR/KS_HOR_SCROLLBAR loops read tp[j], tp[j+1], tp[j+2] with j only bounded by the content (`tp[j] == CSI && tp[j+1] == ... && tp[j + 2] != NUL`), allowing reads at tp[len..len+2]; however reaching these branches requires a termcodes[] entry whose key name is KS_VER_SCROLLBAR/KS_HOR_SCROLLBAR, which no statement in this code or attacker input can create (names come from the builtin termcap key table), plus GUI build without USE_ON_FLY_SCROLL — trigger not instantiable here.

The buf == NULL path's overread lands within typebuf.tb_buf's allocation slack (reads past tb_len but likely inside the buffer), so the cleanest past-allocation read is the buf != NULL path whose exact buffer sizing is the caller's (not shown).
Single-byte out-of-bounds read whose value is used only for a comparison; disclosure impact is minimal, but it is a terminal-attacker-reachable memory-safety defect in the parsing process.

verdict.summary: The NewSessionTicket parser is memory-safe: the exact-equality guard `if (ticklen + 6 != n)` binds the 16-bit parsed ticket length to the remaining message bytes, the destination buffer is allocated from the same expression as the copy length, and the malloc NULL sentinel is checked before first use; all remaining candidates (malloc(0), unchecked EVP_Digest return, lifetime hint validation) fail closed or lack an attacker-instantiable trigger.

assumptions: The internal callee `ssl_get_method->ssl_get_message` returns ok=1 with `s->init_msg` pointing at an n-byte message body and n bounded by the 16384 max-size argument; this framework contract is not shown in the given code but the `ticklen + 6 != n` equality makes the copy bound independent of the 16384 cap.
`s->session` is non-NULL while the handshake state machine runs this stage.
`SSL_SESSION::session_id` is the fixed 32-byte array (SSL_MAX_SSL_SESSION_ID_LENGTH), which exactly contains the 32-byte SHA-256 digest output written by EVP_Digest.
limitations: The return value of `EVP_Digest` is not checked; a failure would leave `session_id`/`session_id_length` stale, but the failure sentinel (EVP_sha256 unavailable) is not instantiable by attacker input or by any statement in this code, so this is a robustness nit, not a vulnerability.
`ticklen == 0` leads to `OPENSSL_malloc(0)`, whose result is platform-dependent; both possible behaviors (unique non-NULL pointer or NULL) are handled fail-closed by the existing sentinel check.
`tlsext_tick_lifetime_hint` (a fully attacker-controlled 32-bit value) is stored without range validation; any downstream misuse would occur in code not shown here.
`d` in `p = d = (unsigned char *)s->init_msg;` is a dead store with no security effect.

verdict.summary: The bounds check `if (p > end)` admits p == end, so the subsequent `len = *p++` dereferences one byte past the buffer end (one-past-the-limit input, produced e.g. by this code's own `*data += 1 + len` advancing *data exactly to end). Off-by-one guard (should be `p >= end`); 1-byte out-of-bounds read in an attacker-supplied authentication message parser.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read sink: when *data == end (attacker message content controls field consumption; the code's own `*data += 1 + len` can advance *data exactly to end), the only preceding check `if (p > end)` passes for equality and this statement reads one byte past the buffer.

Root cause: the guard uses `>` instead of `>=`, under-admitting the exactly-at-limit value p == end for a dereference that requires p < end (end is one-past-the-end, as proven by the exact memcpy bound `if (p + len > end)` permitting p + len == end).

assumptions: `end` is a one-past-the-end pointer (exclusive bound), inferred from the code's own exact check `if (p + len > end)` permitting p + len == end for a len-byte memcpy from p; under an inclusive reading that same check would over-reject the last valid byte, contradicting the code.
p_malloc is Dovecot's pool allocator that aborts on allocation failure rather than returning NULL; sizes are bounded by len ≤ 255 so allocation size is not attacker-scalable.
limitations: The out-of-bounds byte read at p == end is never disclosed or otherwise used: after the read, `if (p + len > end)` always fails (p = end+1), so the function returns 0; impact is limited to a potential crash if end lands at an unmapped page boundary.

len == 0 is a valid parse (empty buffer) but returns 0, the same value as the failure sentinel, and calls p_malloc(pool, 0); the caller's handling and p_malloc(0) semantics are not shown, so any impact there is speculative.
p + len cannot wrap the address space because len is derived from a single byte (0..255) and p ≤ end points into a mapped buffer.

verdict.summary: The HTTP log-view handler is not vulnerable as written: the only memory sink (buf[n] = 0) is bounded by the fread count argument sizeof(buf) - 1 (n <= 511 into char buf[512]), fopen is NULL-checked before use, the privilege check is_readonly(req) rejects before any output, and all StringBuffer_append calls use literal '%s' format strings. The one anomaly observed is that raw log-file bytes are embedded into the HTML response without escaping, but the log's writer is not part of this code and no statement here lets a trust-boundary party choose log content, so an XSS trigger cannot be instantiated; it is recorded as a hardening limitation.

assumptions: is_readonly(req) is an internal credential-classification callee whose implementation is not shown; this code correctly gates all output behind its result at line 2.
StringBuffer_append is assumed to be a printf-style formatting helper whose '%s' consumption is safe, per its usage pattern throughout this code.
Run.flags and Run.files.log are set from the operator's configuration at process startup; no statement in this code allows a network peer to alter them.
STRERROR expands to a system errno message string, which does not carry attacker-composed content.
limitations: HTML injection (potential CWE-79): line 11 embeds raw log-file bytes into the HTML response with no escaping (no escape/filter/encode call exists anywhere in the function per the mention sweep). If the unshown logging subsystem ever writes attacker-influenced strings (e.g., client-supplied request data, service program output) into the log file, a privileged-viewer XSS would result. The trigger precondition — attacker-chosen bytes in Run.files.log — cannot be instantiated from this code because no statement here writes the log or makes it attacker-writable, so this is speculative hardening guidance, not a confirmed vulnerability.

Buffering the entire log file into res->outputbuffer (lines 9-11) can consume memory proportional to log size, but the requester must be an authenticated full-privilege user and log size is operator-governed, so this is not attacker-scalable amplification.

Authentication itself is not performed in this function; it is assumed to occur in the HTTP dispatch layer (not shown). If this handler were reachable without prior authentication, that would be a defect outside the code given.

verdict.summary: No security vulnerability found. All krb5 callee failure sentinels (init_context, kt_resolve, kt_default, sname_to_principal, kt_get_entry) are checked in execution order before use; cleanup at the exit label is fully NULL-guarded in correct order (keytab, principal, context last); the uninitialized 'entry' variable is never read on any path before being written by krb5_kt_get_entry. The only unguarded input is a potential NULL kssl_ctx dereference, which is crash-only with no corruption, disclosure, bypass, or amplification, and is classified as robustness. The KRB5_KT_NOTFOUND arm returning rc=1 is intentional semantics (keytab FILE availability, not key availability) with no security-state misrepresentation at this function's boundary.

assumptions: krb5_kt_get_entry zeroes and does not populate the output entry parameter on error returns (per MIT krb5 and Heimdal documented implementation behavior), so skipping krb5_kt_free_entry on the NOTFOUND and error arms does not leak.

kssl_ctx->keytab_file and kssl_ctx->service_name are set by the server application configuration (not derived from network input) in the intended OpenSSL deployment; this code itself does not narrow their content.
limitations: kssl_ctx is not NULL-checked before dereference at line 13 ('if (kssl_ctx->keytab_file)'); a NULL argument causes a process crash. This is a robustness issue (CWE-476 class) with no memory corruption or other security impact, not classified as a vulnerability here.

The KRB5_KT_NOTFOUND arm sets rc=1, meaning the function reports the keytab as available when the specific service principal key is absent. This is intentional (checking file availability, not key availability); any downstream security impact would depend on how callers interpret the return value, which is outside this code.
If a caller sets kssl_ctx->keytab_file to an attacker-influenced string, krb5_kt_resolve would process it; no such path is visible in this code and no impact chain from it is instantiated here.

verdict.summary: In the first field-selection loop, `left_item= item;` is executed before the caller-supplied Pushdown_checker gate, so when the checker rejects every field of the multiple equality, left_item retains the last REJECTED item; the subsequent `if (!left_item)` guard tests only NULL-ness and cannot reject it, and the function clones that item, builds Item_func_eq from it, and returns success with an equality the admissibility gate explicitly refused. The mirrored second loop gates before use, proving the intended contract; the bypassed gate lets an unvalidated expression cross the pushdown trust boundary the checker exists to protect.

evidence.reason: Root cause: left_item is committed before the admissibility check runs. If the checker (attacker-influenced items come from parsed SQL) rejects every field, `continue` skips the gate each iteration but never retracts left_item; the loop exits with left_item holding the last checker-REJECTED item, which then passes the NULL-only guard `if (!left_item) return false;` and flows to the output list — a validation-gate bypass (CWE-20).

Sink: the equality built from the clone of the checker-rejected item is pushed into the pushable-equalities output list and the function returns success, so a condition the admissibility gate explicitly refused crosses the pushdown trust boundary.

assumptions: The fields iterated by Item_equal_fields_iterator derive from attacker-controlled SQL (database client is the trust-boundary party), so their content and which ones a given checker rejects are attacker-influenceable.

The concrete Pushdown_checker body and the consumer of the `equalities` list are not shown; the contract that only checker-accepted items may be pushed is inferred from this function's name and from the mirrored, correct gate-before-use pattern in the second loop (line 42).

build_clone/placement-new/push_back failure sentinels are assumed reachable (standard allocator semantics) and are all locally checked in this code (lines 29, 34, 47, 54), so no memory-safety defect arises from them.
limitations: The exact downstream impact (which engine or derived-table pushdown consumes the emitted equalities, and whether an unpushable item causes wrong filtering, disclosure of rows that should be filtered, or an engine-side crash) is outside the given code and could not be simulated; the confirmed defect is the in-code bypass of the caller-supplied admissibility gate and the emission of a gate-rejected item as a pushable equality.

The trigger requires a checker that rejects every field of the equality; any item instantiable in the equality is attacker-chosen via the SQL query, but the concrete checker implementation was not shown, so the specific query shape that makes all fields non-pushable is characterized by the gate's purpose rather than quoted code.
No memory-corruption primitive was found: all clone/allocation/push_back sentinels and the right_item NULL check are guarded in this code.

verdict.summary: This MSG_CRYPTO key-receive handler is the post-CVE-2021-43267 fixed form: every attacker-controlled length and offset is cross-validated before use. The min-size check (line 11) bounds the packet data region before the keylen field is read at data+32, and the exact-match/maximum checks (lines 19-20) force size == keylen + sizeof(struct tipc_aead_key) with keylen <= TIPC_AEAD_KEY_SIZE_MAX, so kmalloc(size) at line 32 is sized from the same validated expression that bounds both memcpys (32-byte alg_name fits the >=36-byte allocation; the key memcpy at lines 41-42 exactly fills the allocation and the claimed data region). 32-bit wrap of keylen + sizeof(...) is rejected by the keylen > TIPC_AEAD_KEY_SIZE_MAX clause. The kmalloc NULL sentinel is checked before first use, shared state is written under spin_lock, and per-message resource use is bounded. No unguarded sink is reachable.

assumptions: The buffer behind data = msg_data(hdr) actually contains the size = msg_data_sz(hdr) bytes the message header claims; this skb/message correspondence is enforced by the TIPC receive path (not shown) and is the one interface contract this code relies on. Within this code, every access is bounded by the cross-validated values.

sizeof(struct tipc_aead_key) equals TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME (32) + sizeof(__be32) (4) = 36, matching the copy offsets data + TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME and data + TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME + sizeof(__be32) used at lines 16 and 41.

TIPC_AEAD_KEY_SIZE_MAX and TIPC_AEAD_KEYLEN_MIN are small positive constants (AEAD key-length bounds defined with this code); the analysis holds for any MIN >= 0 and any MAX far below 2^32, which the keylen > TIPC_AEAD_KEY_SIZE_MAX clause requires to reject 32-bit wrap values.
limitations: skey->alg_name is filled with 32 attacker-controlled bytes (line 40) without enforcing NUL termination; a downstream consumer (not shown) that treats it as a C string without a bound could over-read. The impact lands entirely in unshown code, so it is not instantiated here.

skey->keylen = keylen stores the host-order (already ntohl-converted) length into the __be32-annotated field (line 39); within this code the memcpy at line 42 consumes the identical stored value (in-bounds), but a downstream consumer applying ntohl() again would see a byte-swapped length. Consumer behavior is not shown, so no in-scope impact.

If queue_delayed_work() at line 55 fails, the function returns false while rx->skey retains the allocated key; the allocation remains referenced by rx->skey (attachable later), so no confirmed leak or corruption results.

An attacker flooding MSG_CRYPTO keys with fresh generations can repeatedly trigger small (<= MAX+36 byte) allocations and deferred work, but per-message cost is bounded by the validated sizes and duplicates are rejected at line 26; this is ordinary protocol load, not a notable amplification.

verdict.summary: The S3 GET response path passes the raw, Range-driven offset and length pair (bl_ofs, bl_len) straight into a copy-to-socket sink, dump_body(s, bl.c_str() + bl_ofs, bl_len), with no local validation against the bufferlist's actual extent anywhere in the function. Any off_t value pair is in-domain at this virtual handler, so an inconsistent (bl_ofs, bl_len) versus bl reads past the bufferlist and transmits out-of-bounds heap bytes to the requesting client or crashes the gateway worker.

evidence.snippet: int r = dump_body(s, bl.c_str() + bl_ofs, bl_len);
evidence.reason: Root cause: raw pointer arithmetic bl.c_str() + bl_ofs plus unvalidated copy length bl_len handed to a memory-copy sink. The mention sweep over the whole function shows bl_ofs, bl_len and bl are mentioned only at their declarations (lines 1-2), the flag test if (get_data && !op_ret) (line 204), and this sink; bl.length() is never computed and no check, clamp, mask, or error arm bounds bl_ofs/bl_len on any path. Trigger: an S3 GET whose read pipeline invokes this overridden virtual method with a (bl_ofs, bl_len) pair exceeding bl's extent (e.g. bl_len=4096 while bl holds 1024 bytes, or negative bl_ofs); dump_body then reads past the bufferlist, leaking adjacent heap bytes to the client or crashing the worker.

Origin of the tainted values: bl_ofs (and bl_len on the next line) enter here as off_t parameters of this virtual response handler, driven by the client-controlled Range header through the unshown read pipeline; no statement of this code narrows their full signed-64-bit domain before they reach the dump_body sink at line 205.

assumptions: dump_body(ptr, len) is characterized as a copy-to-output that consumes exactly len bytes from ptr (analogous to fwrite/memcpy semantics); the OOB read occurs because the source region is read past the bufferlist's extent, and per the impact rules the defect sits at this call site even though the faulting access lands inside the callee.
dump_header/dump_end_header are header-emission helpers whose internal sanitization is not shown; attrs content is treated as attacker-controlled (set by the object writer).

bl_ofs and bl_len are produced by the unshown RGW read pipeline from the client-supplied Range header (members start/end); because no local statement bounds them, their input surface is taken as the full off_t domain per the width-domain rule.
limitations: In normal operation the unshown caller slices bl to match (bl_ofs, bl_len); exploiting the missing local check additionally requires a caller-side inconsistency (short read at EOF, truncated or encrypted-object chunk, partial range read) which cannot be exhibited from this code alone. This caveat does not demote the finding per the width-domain rule, but it bounds realistic exploitability.

Potential HTTP response-header injection (CWE-113) via query-string values stored into response_attrs (line 116) or user metadata values (line 152) reaching dump_header depends on sanitization inside the not-shown dump_header; it can be neither confirmed nor dismissed here.
s->auth.identity->is_anonymous() (line 112) would NULL-deref if identity were NULL; the auth pipeline that populates it is not shown, so the trigger is speculative.

obj_tags.count() (line 161) is dumped even when decode throws (catch at lines 158-160), reporting a possibly partially decoded count on a decode-failure path; whether count is default-initialized depends on the not-shown RGWObjTags definition, so this is at most a robustness/misreporting issue.

verdict.summary: Optimizer code traversing internal query-plan structures. Every pointer that can be NULL in a valid plan is checked before first use (subquery_predicate, sl->join, explain objects), callee failure sentinels are tested, the iteration over a mutating list captures the next pointer before exclude_level(), and res is assigned before any read. The remaining observations (LEX state left unrestored on two early error returns, no local NULL check on un->thd/lex, SELECT_DESCRIBE not removed from sl->options) are either state hygiene with no instantiated impact inside this code or rest on server structural invariants; no memory, injection, or validation sink consuming attacker data is present.

assumptions: SELECT_LEX_UNIT::thd and thd->lex are non-NULL for every unit this loop visits; this is a server structural invariant set at unit construction in code not shown, so it is an assumption, not a quotable guard in this code.
An object whose substype() == Item_subselect::IN_SUBS is genuinely an Item_in_subselect (constructor-set subtype invariant), making the C-style downcast safe.
exclude_level() mutates list linkage but does not free the unit or the captured next pointer, so traversal remains valid.

Calless not shown (optimize, set_limit, save_union_explain, empty_result, update_correlated_cache, no_rows_in_result) operate on the same plan objects and do not invalidate the local pointers sl, un, inner_join between their uses.
limitations: On the early error returns (save_union_explain failing, or inner_join->optimize() returning nonzero), un->thd->lex->current_select is left pointing at the subquery SELECT_LEX and inner_join->select_options is not restored, because the returns happen before the restore statements. A security impact would require a consumer of the stale current_select after the error return; no such consumer is present in this code, and statement error handling in the server re-initializes LEX state, so the impact is not instantiated.

sl->options keeps the SELECT_DESCRIBE bit after the loop (only inner_join->select_options is restored); this occurs only within EXPLAIN processing where describe flags are expected and has no memory-safety consequence.

A NULL dereference of un->thd or un->thd->lex would be a server crash reachable in principle from client SQL, but producing a unit with a NULL thd requires a defect in the parser or unit construction, neither of which is in this code; the trigger is therefore speculative here.
The trailing 'if (res) return TRUE;' is dead code because res is always 0 at that point after the earlier 'if ((res= inner_join->optimize())) return TRUE;'; it is a readability defect only.

verdict.summary: No instantiable security defect in this function. All memory sinks (tmp_tables[cnt], fields_for_table[cnt], tmp_table_param+cnt, map2table[tablenr]) are consumed with server-internal values produced by earlier prepare/optimizer stages; the allocation sentinels that matter are present and correctly ordered (NULL checks on the mem_root Item and on create_tmp_table's result before use). The only locally missing validations (a bound on table_ref->shared, non-emptiness of fields) protect against states excluded by this code's own documented contract and by the SQL parser, and no attacker-input value, callee failure sentinel, or statement in this code can produce those states.

assumptions: table_ref->shared (uint cnt) is assigned within [0, number of updated tables) by the multi-update prepare stage, and tmp_tables / fields_for_table / tmp_table_param are allocated to the same count in that stage, which is not shown in this snippet.

update_tables, leaves, fields, check_option and map2table are executor structures already validated and resolved by the parser/fix_fields/JOIN::make stages; this function is an internal executor stage, not a protocol intake point.
TABLE::alias is NUL-terminated (table-open invariant), so strlen(field_name.str) is safe.
fields->head() resolves to an Item_field after fix_fields for UPDATE field lists; the unchecked C-style cast to Item_field* relies on that resolution stage.
limitations: DBUG_ASSERT(fields->elements) is compiled out in release builds; if the SET list were ever empty at this point, ((Item_field *) fields->head())->field->table would be a NULL dereference. The precondition is documented in the comment above it and enforced by the SQL grammar (UPDATE requires at least one assignment), which is not shown, so the trigger is speculative.

An out-of-range table_ref->shared would cause out-of-bounds reads/writes at fields_for_table[cnt] and tmp_tables[cnt], but producing it requires a defect in the unshown prepare code that assigns shared and sizes the arrays; no in-code instantiation exists.
item->fix_fields(thd, 0) has its return value ignored; a hypothetical resolution failure would surface later as a robustness issue, with no memory-corruption or bypass chain in this code.

The while ((tbl_ref= ti++) && unupdated_tables) loop could in principle leave a table of the CHECK OPTION unaccounted for if it were absent from leaves, but check_option->used_tables() is built from the same resolved table set; the consequence would be a missing rowid field, not a security impact.

verdict.summary: add_mtab passes attacker-controlled devname, mountpoint, and fstype strings into the /etc/mtab record without any validation or escaping of record delimiters (newline) or field delimiters (whitespace). addmntent serializes mntent fields verbatim, so a mountpoint or device string containing a newline injects fully attacker-forged entries into the privileged mount table, misrepresenting system mount state to every consumer of mtab.

evidence.reason: Sink: addmntent writes the mntent record verbatim to /etc/mtab. mountent.mnt_fsname/mnt_dir/mnt_type carry the raw attacker-supplied devname/mountpoint/fstype with no special-element (newline, whitespace) sanitization on any path, so a mountpoint such as "/mnt/a\n/dev/sda9 / ext3 rw 0 0\n" injects forged mount-table records under the process's privileges.

Origin: the attacker-data parameters (char* devname, char* mountpoint, const char* fstype of the non-static add_mtab entry point) are assigned directly into the record fields. These three lines and the addmntent call are the only mentions of these variables in the code; no check, clamp, mask, or escaping guard exists between origin and sink.

assumptions: MOUNTED designates /etc/mtab and is a real writable file on the target (on systems where it is a /proc/self/mounts symlink the append fails and the error path at line 52 handles it).
glibc/libc addmntent serializes mntent fields verbatim without escaping whitespace or newlines, per its documented behavior.
Internal callees getusername, toggle_dac_capability, lock_mtab, unlock_mtab, my_endmntent, and the SAFE_FREE macro are not shown; their semantics are not relied on for the primary finding.
limitations: If calloc(MTAB_OPTIONS_LEN, 1) at line 79 returns NULL, the quoted `if (mountent.mnt_opts)` skips option assembly but line 104 still calls addmntent with mnt_opts = NULL, an unchecked allocation sentinel at a use (CWE-476-shaped). The trigger is allocation failure of a fixed-size buffer that no attacker can induce, so it is a robustness issue, not a vulnerability in this code.
