verdict.summary: pps_id is parsed as an unsigned Exp-Golomb value into a signed s32; ue values >= 2^31 truncate to negative, pass the 'pps_id > 255' check, and index avc->pps out of bounds, producing an out-of-bounds write ('si->pps->id = pps_id;') in the process parsing attacker-supplied H.264/SVC slice data.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write. pps_id (s32) is assigned from the unsigned Exp-Golomb parse at line 10; a ue codeNum of 0xFFFFFFFE truncates to pps_id = -2, which passes the signed check 'if (pps_id > 255)' (no lower-bound arm exists), so &avc->pps[-2] is out of bounds and 'si->pps->id = pps_id;' writes an attacker-chosen negative value outside the array. The slice_group_count check at line 15 runs after the write and cannot prevent it.

Origin of the tainted value and the defective guard: the unsigned Exp-Golomb result (u32 domain) is stored into s32 pps_id, truncating values >= 2^31 to negative; the sole check 'pps_id > 255' only bounds the positive direction and admits every negative index.

assumptions: gf_bs_read_ue_log is the standard unsigned Exp-Golomb reader returning a full-width unsigned value; per the width-domain rule its u32 domain (values >= 2^31 encodable with 31 leading zeros plus a 31-bit suffix) is instantiable, and no statement in this code narrows it.
The declaration/size of avc->pps and AVCState is not shown; the negative-index out-of-bounds condition holds for any array size or placement, so the primary trigger does not depend on it.
limitations: Line 17 indexes avc->sps with si->pps->sps_id + GF_SVC_SSPS_ID_SHIFT with no local check; sps_id's field width, the sps array size, and any validation in the not-shown PPS parse cannot be quoted, so an independent OOB read there is plausible but not provable from this code alone.

si->sps->log2_max_frame_num and log2_max_poc_lsb are only checked for zero (lines 18, 35) before being used as bit counts in gf_bs_read_int_log; the callee's behavior for counts > 32 is not shown, so no impact is instantiated.
si->slice_type (line 7) has the same signed-truncation shape past the '> 9' check, but it is not used as a memory index in this function; misuse by callers is outside the given code.

si->nal_unit_type / si->NalHeader.idr_pic_flag are caller-set from the NAL header and used here only to gate a read; no guard is quotable, but the values control parsing order only, with no direct security impact in this function.

verdict.summary: The do_viewlog handler is memory-safe and fail-closed as written. The log-read loop is bounded: fread is capped at sizeof(buf) - 1 = 511 items into char buf[512], so buf[n] = 0 writes at most buf[511], and the buffer is NUL-terminated before escapeHTML consumes it on every iteration. Log content is passed through escapeHTML before embedding in the <textarea>, preventing markup breakout within this code. Authorization fail-closes: read-only users receive SC_FORBIDDEN and return before any output is produced. Remaining risk (exactness of is_readonly, the authentication layer, and the escapeHTML implementation) lies in code not shown and cannot produce an instantiated trigger here.

assumptions: is_readonly(req) correctly reports the requester's privilege level; its implementation and the dispatcher's authentication enforcement are not shown, so the authorization strength of this handler rests on that unshown layer.

escapeHTML(res->outputbuffer, buf) escapes markup-significant characters (<, >, &, quotes); its implementation is not shown. The call itself is quoted in this code and runs before the closing </textarea> is appended.
StringBuffer_append is a printf-style, dynamically growing accumulator (literal format strings are used here, so no format-string risk regardless), and STRERROR expands to a strerror-family call.
Run.flags and Run.files.log are operator configuration set by the daemon at startup, not writable by a trust-boundary party through any statement of this code.
limitations: XSS in the log view (CWE-79) would require attacker-controlled markup inside the Monit logfile (e.g., a literal </textarea><script> sequence). The statements that write that file are not in this code and this code never makes the path attacker-writable, so the trigger precondition is not instantiable; within this code the content is escaped via the quoted escapeHTML call.

An authorization bypass would require is_readonly to return false for a read-only requester, or the unshown HTTP dispatcher to route unauthenticated requests to this handler. Both depend on unshown callees/callers and cannot be instantiated from the given code; the visible check itself is fail-closed.
Reading the entire logfile into the response buffer is bounded only by the operator's log size and rotation policy; it is not attacker-scalable from small input, so it is not classified as CWE-400.

If Run_Log is set while Run.files.log is NULL, fopen would receive a NULL path; per the flag-setting code (not shown) this state is not producible, and the failure would be a NULL-path fopen on operator configuration, not attacker data.

verdict.summary: SafeToRemoveIdentity resolves the attacker-named input node with node_map_->GetNode(NodeName(node.input(0))), a lookup that can miss on malformed or dangling references in an attacker-supplied GraphDef, and handles the nullptr sentinel with CHECK(input != nullptr), which aborts the host process. A model-file author can crash the process that loads their model (denial of service); no graceful rejection exists anywhere in the function.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the lookup of the attacker-controlled input name (node.input(0)) can return its failure sentinel nullptr for a dangling or unresolvable reference in a malicious GraphDef, and the only local handling is a CHECK that aborts the process instead of returning false. Instantiated trigger: Identity node with input(0) naming a node absent from the node map → GetNode returns nullptr → CHECK fires → process abort (DoS of the victim loading the model).

Taint origin: the node parameter is graph data whose content (names, input strings) is set by the model-file author, a party across a trust boundary; no statement in this code narrows the string passed to NodeName/GetNode.

assumptions: node_map_->GetOutputs is assumed to return non-null consumer pointers pointing at stored NodeDefs; no statement in this code can produce a null consumer, so the unguarded dereferences at lines 28 and 32 have no locally instantiable trigger.

IsIdentity/IsIdentityN/IsRetval/IsMerge/IsSwitch/NodeName/AsControlDependency semantics are taken as standard TensorFlow helpers per universally known project conventions; their exact behavior is not shown.

Reachability of a GraphDef with a dangling input reference to this optimizer stage depends on upstream loading paths not shown; per the analysis rules this unquoted contract cannot dismiss the candidate.
limitations: The early 'return true' for non-Identity nodes is a caller-contract quirk: if a caller invoked this on arbitrary non-Identity nodes and removed them, semantics could break, but no caller is shown and no security impact link is instantiable in this code.

The input_size() > 1 Retval/Merge branch and the Switch control-dependency loop affect only graph-rewrite decisions (optimizer correctness), with no memory-safety, injection, or security-state sink in this function.

If upstream validation guaranteed every input name resolves to an existing node, the CHECK would be unreachable; that guarantee is not quotable from the given code, so the finding stands only on the in-domain lookup-miss sentinel.

verdict.summary: In change_indent(), when VREPLACE mode is active, the final cursor column is computed from the entry cursor column without any check against the line length (new_cursor_col = entry_col - first_non_blank + new_first_non_blank at lines 39/41/81, assigned unchecked at line 134). The subsequent write `new_line[curwin->w_cursor.col] = NUL;` (line 194) then truncates a heap buffer allocated by vim_strsave (strlen+1 bytes) at an unbounded index. With an entry cursor column beyond the end of the line (a colnr_T-domain editor state, e.g., a past-EOL cursor position), this is a heap out-of-bounds write (memory corruption), reachable from indent-changing operations in virtual-replace mode.

evidence.reason: Heap out-of-bounds write: new_line is a vim_strsave copy of the current line (strlen+1 bytes, allocated at line 189), but curwin->w_cursor.col is never bounded against that length anywhere in the function (mention sweep: lines 24, 36, 39, 41, 47, 50, 79, 81, 110, 131, 134 contain no length comparison). With an entry cursor column past the end of the line, e.g., col=40 on line "ab" in gR (VREPLACE) mode with INDENT_SET, the simulation yields new_cursor_col = 40 - 0 + 2 = 42 at line 81, col = 42 at line 134, and new_line[42] = NUL writes 38 bytes past the 5-byte allocation.

Origin of the tainted value: new_cursor_col carries the raw entry cursor column (copied at line 39, offset-preserving accumulation at line 81) whose producer is not shown and whose declared colnr_T domain is unbounded; the only check here is the sign test `new_cursor_col <= 0`, so any positive out-of-range column is assigned to curwin->w_cursor.col and consumed by the write at line 194 with no bounds guard on any path.

assumptions: vim_strsave is treated as strdup (allocates strlen+1, NUL-terminates) and alloc returns NULL on failure; both are characterizable standard behaviors.

set_indent/shift_line preserve the text after the indent, so the Case A mapping itself does not push the column past the line when the entry column is in range; the overflow arises from the unbounded entry column.
beginline(BL_WHITE) repositions the cursor but operates on the cursor state, not on the already-copied new_cursor_col offset; it is not a guard for the copied value.
limitations: Walk loop (lines 95-103): the index new_cursor_col advances through ptr = ml_get_curline() with no `ptr[new_cursor_col] == NUL` termination test; an overread would require curwin->w_virtcol (derived from get_indent()) to exceed the width accumulated by lbr_chartabsize() over the whole line. That requires a mismatch between two unshown internal callees, so the trigger cannot be instantiated from this code alone (speculative, not counted toward the verdict).

Replace-stack pop loop (lines 161-165): popping start_col - col entries via replace_join(0) could exceed the stack depth if the entry cursor column exceeds it; the depth invariant and replace_join's behavior on an empty stack are not shown, so impact is not characterizable here.

Parameters amount, round, and replaced flow only into internal callees (set_indent, shift_line, replace_push) with no local memory or indexing use in this code; any misuse would occur entirely inside callees not shown.

The primary trigger assumes the editor can present a cursor column beyond the current line length (e.g., a past-EOL position under virtual editing); this state is not produced by this code but is within the declared colnr_T domain of cursor state whose producer is not shown.

verdict.summary: No attacker-instantiable memory-safety or security defect found. All writes into NameBuff are bounded by quoted guards (len < MAXPATHL - 1 before the space append; MAXPATHL - len snprintf sizes; the p[i] != NUL loop bound plus i > 0 before the '<' write; len > this_ru_col - 1 in the byte branch). The one concrete anomaly — the space-append condition includes bufIsChanged() while the [+] append arm excludes bt_terminal(), leaving NameBuff without a NUL terminator for a changed terminal buffer — requires a user-set state ('modified' on a :terminal buffer) that no trust-boundary party can induce, and its impact degrades to rendering stale in-buffer bytes on the same user's status line, with the out-of-bounds read link not producible by any statement in this code.

assumptions: Internal callees not shown behave per their Vim contracts: get_trans_bufname NUL-terminates within NameBuff[MAXPATHL]; vim_snprintf NUL-terminates within its size argument; mb_ptr2len never advances past the terminating NUL; mb_string2cells counts cells until NUL; get_keymap_str NUL-terminates within the passed MAXPATHL; screen_puts/screen_fill/screen_putchar clip columns to the screen.
fillchar_status()/fillchar_vsep() set *attr on every path that later consumes attr (standard by-address initialization pattern).
ru_col is maintained by unshown redraw code to sane window-geometry-derived values; its unbounded upper side is covered only by the clipping assumption, not by any statement in this code.
limitations: Speculative: with FEAT_TERMINAL compiled, if a terminal-typed buffer has the changed flag set (user runs :setlocal modified on a :terminal buffer) while help/preview/readonly are all false, the statement `*(p + len++) = ' ';` overwrites the NUL terminator and no tag snprintf re-terminates NameBuff (the [+] arm carries `&& !bt_terminal(wp->w_buffer)` but the space condition does not). mb_string2cells and the truncation loop then scan stale bytes from previous NameBuff use. The state is not producible by attacker data (file content cannot make a buffer terminal-typed or modified), and the OOB-read link requires a NUL-free stale tail no statement here can produce, so impact is same-user garbage/misdisplay only. Not counted as a vulnerability.

this_ru_col = ru_col - (Columns - wp->w_width) is clamped only on the low side; a large stale ru_col passes an unvalidated column to screen_fill/screen_puts, whose clipping behavior is not shown in this code.

The multibyte truncation loop condition `clen >= this_ru_col - 1` consumes a string whose remaining width exactly equals the available width, collapsing the display to "<" (functional over-truncation, non-security).
The static busy flag is not restored if control unwinds abnormally between `busy = TRUE;` and `busy = FALSE;` (e.g., an interrupt), leaving subsequent redrawstatus calls ignored — robustness only.

verdict.summary: The ELF parser trusts every offset, index, and size field of the parsed file. Section/program header tables are computed from unchecked e_shoff/e_phoff and indexed with unchecked e_shstrndx/e_shnum/e_phnum without any relation to the mapped file size; the dynamic-section pointer and loop count come from unchecked sh_offset/sh_size; string pointers used at strcmp/printf %s/snprintf %s sinks (segment mapping, .dynstr/.dynamic search, DT_NEEDED) are never validated, so out-of-bounds reads occur and read memory is disclosed in printed output. Independently, dynstr/dynamic are declared uninitialized and used as section indices when no .dynstr/.dynamic section exists.

evidence.reason: e_shoff, e_phoff, and e_shstrndx are raw attacker-file fields with full declared-width domains and no bounds check against st.st_size anywhere in the code; the mention sweep found only display statements (PRINT_HEADER lines) and the uses themselves. Trigger: a 64-byte ELF32 file with e_shoff = 0xFFFFFF00 and e_shstrndx = 0xFFFF makes line 178 read far outside the mapping (out-of-bounds read, CWE-125); the copied shstrtab fields then steer further reads and are printed.

dynstr and dynamic are declared without initializers and are assigned only inside conditional strcmp matches (lines 339-344); an ELF file whose section names include neither .dynstr nor .dynamic leaves them indeterminate, and they are then used as section-header indices (CWE-457), producing an out-of-domain index at the first use.

The dynamic-section pointer is computed from the attacker-controlled sh_offset and the loop count from sh_size with no validation against st.st_size and no sentinel check on the possibly uninitialized dynamic index (origin: uninitialized declarations at lines 334-335). Trigger: sh_offset = 0xF0000000 and sh_size = 0xFFFFFFFF in a crafted file give an out-of-bounds pointer and a count of 0x1FFFFFFF iterations reading dyn[i] outside the mapping, with the read values emitted by PRINT_DYN (out-of-bounds read with disclosure and attacker-scalable amplification, CWE-125).

evidence.snippet:
name = elf_map + shdr[dynstr].sh_offset + dyn[i].d_un.d_val;
                    snprintf(value, 50, "Shared library: [%s]", name);
evidence.reason: For a DT_NEEDED entry the string pointer is elf_map plus the attacker-controlled sh_offset and the full-width d_val, with no validated_offset call or any other guard on any path (validated_offset is used only at line 184, inside a different, earlier loop). Trigger: d_val = 0x41414141 makes snprintf's %s read and print process memory at an arbitrary offset from the mapping, an out-of-bounds read with information disclosure (CWE-125). The same unguarded pattern affects the name pointers at lines 323/326 and 338-342.

assumptions: get_elf_class, validated_offset, flag2str, flag2str_sh, and the PRINT_*/INFO/ERROR macros are project-internal and not shown; only the quoted call sites of validated_offset (line 184 and its 64-bit twin) are relied on, and only for the name pointer in the first section-header loop.

Whether validated_offset also verifies NUL termination cannot be quoted; if it only range-checks the start pointer, strlen(name) at line 258 can read past the end of the mapping for a name placed near the file end with no NUL.
limitations: strcpy(&name[15 - 6], "[...]") writes indices 9..14 only, and the guard strlen(name) > 15 ensures at least 16 readable non-NUL bytes precede the write, so this write is bounded by the code as written.
snprintf(value, 50, ...) always bounds the 50-byte destination; strcpy(flag, "   ") writes exactly 4 bytes into flag[4] and fits.
flag2str and flag2str_sh write into the 4-byte flag buffer inside a callee that is not shown; their bounds cannot be verified here.
Out-of-bounds reads will often terminate in SIGSEGV (denial of service); the %s and PRINT_DYN sinks additionally disclose the read memory in the tool's output when the pages are mapped.
ELF pathological conventions (e_shnum == 0 with real count in shdr[0].sh_size, e_shstrndx == SHN_XINDEX) are not handled; that is a functional correctness gap, not the security defect.

verdict.summary: SetUnknownShape consumes the attacker-domain int output_port (and the raw node pointer) by passing them to GetUnknownOutputShape at line 3 before any validation: the only bounds check, `if (output_port < 0 || output_port >= ctx->num_outputs())`, and the only null/context check execute at lines 5-7, after the first use. Any out-of-range port (negative or >= num_outputs) reaches the internal per-output shape lookup unvalidated; the check's rejection arms run too late to protect that use.

evidence.reason: Root cause: use-before-validation. output_port (full int domain, attacker-data per width-domain rule) and the unvalidated node pointer are passed into the index-shaped lookup GetUnknownOutputShape here, before the function performs any checks. Trigger: output_port = -1 (or any value >= ctx->num_outputs()) reaches this call with no guard on any path; the bounds test at line 7 and the ctx null test at line 5 execute only after this use, so their rejection arms cannot protect it.

The only guard on output_port in the entire function. Its operators are correct at both bounds (rejects -1 and rejects exactly num_outputs), and it correctly protects the later sink ctx->set_output(output_port, shape) at line 12, but in execution order it runs after the first use at line 3, so it does not cover that use.

assumptions: GetUnknownOutputShape and GetContext are project-internal callees whose bodies are not shown; their indexing and null-handling behavior is an assumption. Per the call-site rule, passing the unvalidated port is a defect at the call site regardless of where the failure lands.

node is a const NodeDef* drawn from a GraphDef processed by shape-inference utilities; graph/model content is treated as attacker-influenced data, and the pointer/parameter surface is its full declared domain since no statement in this code narrows it.
limitations: The concrete out-of-bounds access (if any) would occur inside the unshown callee GetUnknownOutputShape; from the given code alone the impact is a validated index consumed at an unguarded call site, not a quotable OOB read/write, hence CWE-20 rather than CWE-125/787 and medium severity.
The shown code's own memory sink, ctx->set_output(output_port, shape), is correctly guarded by the line-7 check (both bounds edge-tested) and is not a defect.
A NULL node dereference inside the callees is possible in principle but both consumers are unshown; it is folded into the same entry-validation defect rather than claimed as a separate vulnerability.

verdict.summary: send_control_msg memcpy's a fixed-length control message into elem.in_sg[0] without verifying elem.in_sg[0].iov_len >= len or elem.in_num >= 1. A malicious guest controls the virtqueue descriptors, so it can supply a writable buffer smaller than len (or none at all); the raw memcpy then writes past the guest-declared buffer, and with the buffer placed at the end of the guest RAM block the write escapes the mapped region into host-process memory (guest-to-host OOB write).

evidence.reason: Root cause: missing bounds guard before the copy. elem is populated by virtqueue_pop from guest-written descriptors, so in_sg[0].iov_len and in_num are attacker-controlled. The code never compares in_sg[0].iov_len with len nor checks in_num >= 1 (mention sweep covers lines 3, 10, 14, 16: only queue-ready and pop-failure are checked). Trigger: guest posts a 1-byte writable descriptor at the end of guest RAM; with len = 12 (control-message size), the memcpy writes 12 bytes, corrupting 11 bytes past the guest-declared buffer and potentially past the host-mapped region.

assumptions: len and buf originate from callers not shown; callers in virtio-serial pass sizeof(struct virtio_serial_control) (~12 bytes) as len, but the defect triggers even with that fixed value, so no caller contract is relied upon.
virtqueue_pop is a standard QEMU helper: it fills elem from guest descriptors and returns false on failure; its success return is treated per discipline 3.
limitations: If the guest places the short buffer away from the end of the RAM region, the overwrite lands inside guest RAM only (guest self-corruption); the host-memory-escape variant requires the descriptor at the region edge, which the guest can freely choose, so the corruption primitive stands.

verdict.summary: This Hermes constant-folding helper dispatches only on typed IR literal kinds and performs IEEE-defined double negation; it contains no memory, copy, size, index, injection, or authorization sink reachable by trust-boundary data. The only failure modes (NULL operand dereference at operand->getKind(), and llvm_unreachable in the TypeofKind default arm) require compiler-internal contract violations (a NULL or non-Literal pointer passed as the Literal* parameter) that no statement in this code produces and no external party can instantiate, and would at worst crash the compiler at the input supplier's own privilege.

assumptions: LiteralNumber::getValue() returns a double (Hermes IR convention); negation of any double is well-defined IEEE754 behavior with no wrap or overflow.
evalIsTrue/evalIsFalse are internal helpers whose behavior on typed Literal operands is total; they receive no raw attacker sizes or indices here.

The TypeofKind switch enumerates the complete set of Literal subclasses of Hermes IR (GlobalObject, LiteralBool, LiteralNumber, LiteralString, LiteralUndefined, LiteralNull), so the default llvm_unreachable arm is unreachable for well-typed callers.
limitations: NULL dereference candidate: operand->getKind() is called without a NULL check; trigger requires the caller to pass nullptr, which no statement in this code produces and which a JS-source author cannot instantiate — speculative, robustness only.

llvm_unreachable("Invalid literal kind.") in the TypeofKind default arm is undefined behavior in release builds if a non-Literal Value were passed as operand; trigger requires a caller type violation outside the given code — speculative.
The dead break; following the exhaustive TypeofKind switch is cosmetic with no security effect.
Fallthrough return of nullptr is a sentinel whose consumers are not shown; no impact chain exists in the given code, so no finding is derived from it.

verdict.summary: qh_help treats the attacker-supplied, length-delimited query buffer 'buf' as a NUL-terminated C string: it receives 'len' but never uses it, and calls strcmp (lines 5, 12) and %s formatting echoed to the socket (lines 25, 29) without any termination or bounds check, allowing an out-of-bounds read whose bytes are sent back to the attacker.

evidence.reason: First unguarded use: strcmp reads buf until a NUL byte, but the accompanying len parameter is never consulted and no statement in the code validates buf[len] == '\0' or bounds the read. An attacker-supplied non-terminated query buffer causes an out-of-bounds read starting at this line and continuing through the %s echo on line 25 (nsock_printf_nul(sd, "No handler named '%s' is registered\n", buf)), which discloses memory past the buffer back over the socket.

evidence.snippet: static int qh_help(int sd, char *buf, unsigned int len)
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: buf is a data-carrying parameter of a query-handler entry point, and the len parameter declared here is never read anywhere in the body, evidencing that buf is length-delimited data whose NUL-termination is never established or enforced by this code.

assumptions: qh_find_handler is an internal callee not shown; it is assumed to consume buf as a string and return NULL when no handler matches, and its NULL result is properly checked on line 23.
qh->name is assumed non-NULL and NUL-terminated by the internal registration code that populates the qhandlers list, which is not shown; qh->description is explicitly NULL-checked on line 15.
nsock_printf_nul / nsock_printf are treated as print-to-socket helpers with literal format strings only; no attacker-controlled format string exists in this code.
limitations: No format-string, command-injection, SQL, or path sink exists; all format strings are string literals, so CWE-134 does not apply.
The qh->handler indirect call on line 27 passes only fixed in-domain arguments (sd, "help", 4) and its NULL sentinel on qh is checked on line 23, so no defect at that call site.

verdict.summary: No instantiated vulnerability in this code. All callee failure sentinels (ArgNumType, AddItem) are checked; the size_t-to-int narrowing of arg_index is caught by the quoted invariant check at the top of each loop iteration, which fails closed before the value is written into the node; the loop bound is enforced by construction. The one unvalidated write — attacker-supplied FunctionDef arg attrs (lines 41-42) copying over the reserved 'T' and 'index' node attributes with no name filter — has its security impact in downstream graph consumers that are not part of this code, so it is recorded as a limitation, not a confirmed defect.

verdict.summary: MulConvPushDown dereferences the results of node_map_->GetNode(conv_node->input(0)/(1)) without a nullptr check. A model file crafted with a Mul node whose Conv2D child references a nonexistent input name makes GetNode return nullptr, and IsReallyConstant(*conv_left_child) dereferences it, crashing the process that loads/optimizes the untrusted model (denial of service). The function null-checks the identical GetNode pattern for the mul children but omits it for the conv children.

evidence.snippet:
const bool conv_left_is_constant = IsReallyConstant(*conv_left_child);
  const bool conv_right_is_constant = IsReallyConstant(*conv_right_child);
evidence.reason: NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476): conv_left_child/conv_right_child come from node_map_->GetNode on attacker-controlled Conv2D input names (lookup that can miss and return nullptr, a sentinel this code itself tests for the mul children at line 18), and they are dereferenced here with no nullptr check anywhere on the path. Trigger: crafted GraphDef where the Conv2D node's input(0) names a node absent from the node map.

evidence.snippet:
NodeDef* conv_left_child = node_map_->GetNode(conv_node->input(0));
  NodeDef* conv_right_child = node_map_->GetNode(conv_node->input(1));
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted pointers: GetNode is a lookup that returns nullptr when the attacker-chosen input name does not resolve to a node in the map; the failure sentinel flows unchecked to the dereference on lines 48-49.

assumptions: node_map_->GetNode returns nullptr for names not present in the map (lookup failure sentinel), corroborated by the code's own nullptr test of the same call at line 18
The optimized GraphDef originates from an untrusted model file, so node input names, ops, devices, and attrs are attacker-data
limitations: conv_node->attr().at("data_format") can throw on a crafted Conv2D node missing the attribute, but reaching that line requires non-empty inferred shape properties for such a malformed node, which depends on unshown shape-inference behavior; trigger not fully instantiated
Impact is denial of service (process abort on NULL dereference), not memory corruption or disclosure

verdict.summary: startSslClient loads a CA trust store and sets validation parameters but never enables peer certificate verification (no SSL_CTX_set_verify with SSL_VERIFY_PEER and no SSL_get_verify_result check). With the OpenSSL client default of SSL_VERIFY_NONE, SSL_connect completes even when the server presents a self-signed, untrusted, or hostname-mismatched certificate, and the function then sets isssl = true and returns 0, presenting an unverified connection as a secure one. A network man in the middle can intercept and rewrite all traffic on the channel.

evidence.reason: The only check on the handshake result is rc < 0 (transport failure). Because the code never sets SSL_VERIFY_PEER on ctx, the documented OpenSSL client default SSL_VERIFY_NONE applies, so a man in the middle presenting any certificate (self-signed, untrusted chain, or hostname mismatch) yields a completed handshake with rc >= 0 and falls through to the success path. The verification parameters set at lines 66, 75, and 97 never take effect because certificate verification is never performed; on the OpenSSL < 1.1.0 branch (line 95) there is no hostname pin at all.

Fail-open success presentation: after an unverified handshake, the socket is flagged as an SSL connection (isssl = true) and 0 (success) is returned to the caller, misrepresenting the security state of an unauthenticated channel (CWE-451 flavor of the same defect). No SSL_get_verify_result or peer-certificate check exists between SSL_connect and this return on any path.

The only hostname-binding statement in the code is conditional on OpenSSL >= 1.1.0 and only records the expected DNS name in the verify param; it is evaluated solely during certificate verification, which this code never enables, so it cannot authenticate the peer. The empty #if branch (line 95) leaves the legacy path with no hostname expectation whatsoever.

assumptions: String (the hostname parameter type) is assumed to be a std::string-like wrapper whose c_str() returns a NUL-terminated C string; no definition is shown in this code.

log_ssl_errors is assumed to be a printf-style logging helper that consumes the constant format strings shown; all format arguments are passed as %s values, so no format-string injection exists in this function.
OpenSSL semantics are relied on per standard documentation: client-side default verify mode is SSL_VERIFY_NONE, and without it SSL_connect succeeds regardless of certificate verification errors.
limitations: ssl = SSL_new(ctx) at line 87 is not checked for NULL before SSL_set_options at line 88 dereferences it. Triggering requires SSL_new to fail (allocation failure or context error), which an attacker cannot instantiate at will; recorded as a robustness issue, not a vulnerability.
SSL_set_tlsext_host_name and SSL_set_fd return values are unchecked; both are non-fatal for memory safety here.
On OpenSSL < 1.1.0 the code additionally lacks any hostname pin, but this is subsumed by the primary defect since peer verification never runs on either branch.

verdict.summary: TfLiteIntArrayGetSizeInBytes computes an allocation size as sizeof(dummy) + sizeof(dummy.data[0]) * size with no validation of the exported function's int parameter. For attacker-supplied values within the full int domain (e.g., size = 2^30 the product wraps and truncates to 4; size = -2 yields -4; size = -1 yields 0), the returned byte count is negative, zero, or orders of magnitude too small for the declared element count, turning every allocation sized from this helper into an undersized heap buffer and enabling out-of-bounds writes in its consumers. No range check, clamp, or overflow-safe arithmetic exists on any path.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the attacker-controlled int parameter size is multiplied by sizeof(dummy.data[0]) as size_t and the sum is truncated into the int computed_size with no range or overflow check. Simulated trigger: size = 1073741824 (2^30, in-domain for a 32-bit int) gives 4*2^30 + 4 = 0x100000004, truncated to 4, so the function declares that an array of 2^30 int elements needs 4 bytes; size = -2 gives -4; size = -1 gives 0. The returned size is consumed directly for heap allocation sizing, producing undersized buffers and hence out-of-bounds writes in the consumers of this exported helper.

Origin of the tainted value: size is a data-carrying parameter of a non-static exported function with declared type int, so its input surface is the full 32-bit signed domain (-2^31 .. 2^31-1) per the width-domain rule. No statement in the function documents a precondition, asserts a range, or otherwise narrows it, so the wrap-producing values used in the trigger are instantiable by any trust-boundary caller (e.g., model-file parsing).

assumptions: The definition of TfLiteIntArray is not included in the snippet; the universally known TFLite layout (int size; int data[];) gives sizeof(dummy) = 4 and sizeof(dummy.data[0]) = 4 was assumed for the numeric simulations. The defect does not depend on this exact layout: for any element width >= 4 bytes the undersize trigger at size = 2^30 holds, and the negative-size truncation (e.g., size near INT_MAX or negative values producing negative computed_size) holds for any nonzero element width.

size_t is assumed to be wider than int (64-bit targets); the simulation used standard two's-complement conversion of negative int to size_t and truncating assignment to int, both characterized per standard conversion semantics.
limitations: The heap out-of-bounds write that completes the impact chain occurs in consumers of this helper (e.g., an array-create function that mallocs the returned byte count and then writes size entries); those statements are not part of the given code. Within the given code the fully instantiated impact is the wraparound itself: an allocation size of 0, negative, or ~2^30 times too small returned for an in-domain attacker value, which is the memory-corruption enabler at this use site. Per the width-domain rule the missing overflow guard on attacker-data at this exported size-computation sink is the defect in this code regardless of the unshown consumer.
The #if defined(_MSC_VER) subtraction (lines 5-8) is a platform workaround and not an independent defect; on MSVC it merely adjusts an already-unvalidated computed_size.

verdict.summary: The only bound on numTriggeredTopics is `if (numTriggeredTopics == 64) { drain(); }`, executed once at function entry with `==`. A single publish() call increments numTriggeredTopics many times (once per matched terminatingWildcardChild per segment at line 29, once per recursive frame, and once after the loop at line 53), so an attacker-published topic with enough segments walking a trie containing untriggered terminating wildcard children drives the index past the array capacity and writes a Topic* out of bounds at `triggeredTopics[numTriggeredTopics++]`.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write sink. No bounds check on numTriggeredTopics exists inside the loop or before this indexed write; the index can exceed the array capacity within a single call (e.g., entry numTriggeredTopics==64 drains to 0, then a topic of 65+ segments each matching an untriggered terminatingWildcardChild writes at index 64 and beyond), corrupting memory adjacent to the fixed triggeredTopics array.

Origin of the defect: this is the only bound-related statement in the code, and it is defective in both directions and position — it uses `==` instead of a per-write `>=` capacity check and executes only once at function entry, before the loop that can increment numTriggeredTopics arbitrarily many times (line 29 per segment, line 53 after the loop, plus recursive frames via line 36).

Second instance of the same unguarded indexed write: a topic that matches wildcard children along the way and then matches exactly adds a further entry after the loop with no capacity check, overflowing triggeredTopics when the per-call adds exceed the remaining capacity.

assumptions: triggeredTopics is a fixed-capacity array of 64 entries and drain() resets numTriggeredTopics: the declarations of these members and drain() are not shown; the capacity of 64 is inferred from this code's own comment (line 2) and check (line 3). Independently of the exact capacity C, the entry-only `== 64` check cannot bound numTriggeredTopics to C because a single call can add an unbounded number of entries.

The trie containing terminatingWildcardChild and wildcardChild nodes is assumed buildable by the same trust-boundary party (subscriber and publisher are the typical MQTT broker clients); without wildcard children at many levels the per-segment adds at line 29 do not occur.
limitations: Secondary candidate (not primary): exponential/unbounded recursion at line 36 (`publish(iterator->wildcardChild, ...)`) can amplify a long published topic into 2^N recursion paths when the trie has wildcard children at many levels, exhausting the stack (CWE-400). The code's own comment acknowledges the mitigation is partial. Dismissed as primary only because it needs a cooperatively built wildcard trie; it remains an attacker-scalable amplification risk.

drain() semantics (whether it resets numTriggeredTopics and how it delivers messages) are not shown; the trigger is instantiated either way — with or without a reset, one call's adds can exceed the capacity since the check never re-runs mid-call.

verdict.summary: multi_update::initialize_tables uses table_ref->shared as the index cnt into the pre-allocated tmp_table_param, fields_for_table and tmp_tables arrays without any bounds check; a prepared UPDATE whose update_tables entry carries an out-of-range shared value drives out-of-bounds pointer arithmetic at tmp_table_param+cnt and an out-of-bounds pointer write at tmp_tables[cnt]=create_tmp_table(...), corrupting mysqld memory from client-supplied SQL.

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted index: cnt is taken from table_ref->shared, a prepare-layer field shaped by the client's UPDATE/VIEW statement, with full uint domain and no narrowing statement anywhere in this function.

First unguarded use: out-of-bounds pointer arithmetic on the pre-allocated tmp_table_param array; the subsequent writes tmp_param->quick_group/field_count/func_count (lines 134-136) then write out of bounds.

Primary sink: attacker-derived cnt indexes tmp_tables with no bound on any path (mention sweep: lines 31, 93, 127, 141, 145, 147; line 145 checks the stored value, not the index, and runs after the write), producing an out-of-bounds pointer write and memory corruption in the server process.

assumptions: tmp_tables, tmp_table_param and fields_for_table are pre-allocated by the multi_update constructor / prepare layer, which is not shown; their element counts and the assignment of table_ref->shared are unquoted contracts, so cnt is treated as attacker-data with full uint surface per the width-domain rule.
join->map2table is sized by join setup code not shown; indexing it with tablenr (lines 48, 116) is likewise unvalidated in this code and shares the same root-cause class as the primary defect.
fields list elements are Item_field pointers by parser construction (line 25 downcast); this code documents the non-emptiness invariant via DBUG_ASSERT(fields->elements) at line 18.
limitations: C3 (unchecked (Item_field*) fields->head() downcast and deref at line 25): emptiness is blocked only by the debug-only DBUG_ASSERT at line 18 plus an unshown parser invariant; recorded as contract, not a vulnerability.
C4 (unchecked return of item->fix_fields(thd, 0) at line 122): failure sentinel can occur essentially only under allocation failure, not attacker-instantiated input; robustness issue.

C2 (join->map2map indexing via tablenr at lines 48/116): same unvalidated-index class as the confirmed defect; tablenr is assigned by not-shown table-open code within parser-enforced table limits, so it is folded into notes rather than emitted as an independent primary finding.
has_vers_fields is assigned only on the update-on-the-fly branch (line 43); its initialization in other paths depends on constructor code not shown.

verdict.summary: IsSimplifiableReshape consumes an attacker-authored GraphDef. node_map_->GetNode(node.input(1)) returns nullptr for an input naming a node absent from the map, and the result is dereferenced at IsReallyConstant(*new_shape) with no null check (NULL dereference, DoS on the process loading the model). Independently, the else arm reads the shape constant with flat<int64_t>() for every dtype other than DT_INT32 (e.g. a float/bool Const), a type-confused out-of-bounds heap read whose values can surface in the error DebugString. Additionally, TF_CHECK_OK around TensorShapeUtils::MakeShape turns attacker-supplied negative/oversized dims into a fatal abort.

evidence.reason: GetNode is a lookup that returns nullptr when node.input(1) names a node not present in node_map_; node.input(1) is attacker-controlled content of an untrusted GraphDef. The pointer is dereferenced at first use (*new_shape) with no null check anywhere on lines 11-24, so a malformed saved model crashes the loading process (CWE-476, NULL pointer dereference / DoS).

The only dtype guard is '== DT_INT32' at line 52; the else arm is taken for every other dtype (DT_FLOAT, DT_BOOL, ...). flat<int64_t>() on e.g. a float constant with N elements reads 8N bytes from an 4N-byte buffer (the dtype DCHECK is a no-op in release builds), an out-of-bounds heap read whose values reach new_dims.DebugString() in the line-70 error message (CWE-125, type-confusion OOB read).

shp is filled with raw values read from an attacker-supplied Const tensor with no range validation in the loop body; a negative dim (e.g. -1) makes MakeShape return an error status, and TF_CHECK_OK converts that into a fatal process abort, giving the model author a controlled denial of service.

assumptions: Standard TensorFlow semantics: NodeMap::GetNode returns nullptr for a name absent from the map; TF_CHECK_OK aborts the process on a non-OK status; Tensor::flat<T>() enforces dtype only through a DCHECK, which is compiled out in release builds.

EvaluateNode's contract (ok status implies outputs populated with valid TensorValue entries) is not shown in this code; if it could push a null tensor with an ok status, outputs[0] derefs would be an additional defect, but that producer behavior cannot be quoted here.
The GraphProperties for the node are assumed inferable in the normal optimization flow; an attacker crafting the graph controls whether lines 34-49 pass.
limitations: The error message at lines 7-9 says 'must have at most 2 inputs' while the check '2 > node.input_size()' actually requires at least 2; the check itself correctly guards index 1, so the wrong text is cosmetic only.
The OOB read in candidate B requires a release build for silent over-read; in debug builds the DCHECK aborts, which still yields a crash (DoS) on the model-loading process.
The info-leak channel for candidate B is coarse: leaked dimension values surface only through new_dims.DebugString() inside an error status message that may be logged or propagated.

verdict.summary: In ImmutableExecutorState::Initialize, the outputs_required heap buffer is sized n->num_outputs() but the edge output index e->src_output() (attacker-controlled int from the parsed graph) is guarded only by a lower-bound check 'if (e->src_output() >= 0)'. Any src_output >= n->num_outputs() passes and causes an out-of-bounds read at line 145 and an out-of-bounds heap write of 'true' at line 147 at an attacker-chosen offset.

evidence.reason: Root cause: outputs_required is allocated as new bool[n->num_outputs()] (line 139), so the index must satisfy 0 <= src_output < n->num_outputs(); the only guard is 'e->src_output() >= 0', which constrains the lower bound only. Instantiated trigger: a graph whose node has an out-edge with src_output() >= num_outputs() (any non-negative int is in the declared int domain of the edge field, whose producer is not shown) passes the guard and writes 'true' out of bounds on the heap (and reads out of bounds at line 145) at an attacker-chosen offset.

assumptions: EnsureFrameInfo, BuildControlFlowInfo, GraphView::Initialize, GetMaxPendingCounts, CreateHandle, GetNodeAttr internals are not shown; per discipline 3 they are treated as neither producing triggers nor serving as guards.

FrameInfo default construction (fields of frame_info_[frame_name] created by operator[] at line 83) is not shown; the outer frame_info used at line 131 comes from cf_info frame names, whose nodes allocation at lines 8-11 depends on the unshown BuildControlFlowInfo.
limitations: Line 83 'frame_info_[frame_name].get()' can create a FrameInfo whose nodes vector is never allocated (allocation only occurs for names in cf_info.unique_frame_names at lines 8-11); in this code the pointer is only stored to enter_frame_info_[id] (line 101), and any nodes dereference happens in executor code not shown, so no impact is instantiated here.
Line 171 'e.input_slot += dst_item->input_start;' can overflow int only with roughly 2^31 accumulated graph inputs; the trigger scale is not exercised by the code as written.

The attacker-controlled 'parallel_iterations' attribute (lines 85-87) is stored into frame_info->parallel_iterations with no validation (e.g., zero or negative values), but its consumption occurs in executor code not shown.

'new bool[n->num_outputs()]' with an attacker-huge num_outputs would at worst throw bad_alloc (DoS), requiring a graph of that scale to be constructible; treated as resource-consumption hardening, not a confirmed primary defect.

verdict.summary: Stack buffer overflow in gf_text_get_utf8_line: the UTF-8/latin conversion loop writes into the fixed 2048-byte stack buffer szLineConv through index j that is never bounded (no check of j or len against sizeof(szLineConv) anywhere), while the input line length is attacker-controlled via the parsed file (up to lineSize-1 bytes, with a 2:1 expansion for non-UTF8 high-bit bytes). A crafted text line of ~1366 bytes overflows szLineConv by hundreds of bytes with attacker-influenced content; for lineSize values below the direct overflow threshold, strcpy(szLine, szLineConv) instead overflows the caller's lineSize-byte buffer with the oversized converted string. The function is the trust-boundary intake point for the parsed file, so the missing bounds checks are the vulnerability.

evidence.reason: Primary OOB write sink: j is incremented (lines 19, 26, 35, 44, 47, 54) with no bound against the 2048-byte stack buffer declared at line 5 (char szLineConv[2048;]). The only loop bound, line 14 'for (i=0; i<len; i++)', constrains i, not j; len is attacker-controlled (strlen of the attacker's file line, up to lineSize-1) and the line 17-21 branch doubles the output (writes at both line 18 and line 53 per input byte). Instantiated trigger: unicode_type==0, a file line of repeating 0x80 0x41 pairs; each pair emits 3 bytes, so 683 pairs (1366 input bytes) drive j to 2049 and a full 2047-byte line drives j to ~3070, writing ~1KB of attacker-influenced bytes past szLineConv into the stack frame (memory corruption of saved state/return address region).

Origin of the attacker data: gf_fgets reads a line from txt_in (the parsed text/subtitle file, originating across the trust boundary) into szLine with attacker-controlled content of up to lineSize-1 bytes; combined with line 13 'len = (u32) strlen(szLine);' this value feeds the unbounded conversion loop and, when the converted length exceeds lineSize, the unchecked strcpy at line 57 'strcpy(szLine, szLineConv);' overflows the caller's lineSize-byte buffer for any lineSize where the direct szLineConv overflow does not fire first.

assumptions: gf_fgets is assumed to have standard fgets semantics (writes at most lineSize-1 bytes plus a NUL terminator, returns NULL on EOF/error); the NULL return is checked at line 10.

gf_utf8_wcstombs is a project-internal callee not shown; its return semantics (range, error sentinel, whether it can return exactly its 2048 size limit) are unknown and were not relied on to either trigger or dismiss any candidate.
limitations: Line 79 'szLineConv[i] = 0;' consumes the gf_utf8_wcstombs return from line 78 without a local sentinel check; if that unshown callee returns (size_t)-1 on an invalid UTF-16 sequence, the (u32) cast yields 0xFFFFFFFF and the write lands far out of bounds, and a return of exactly 2048 would be a one-past write. The trigger depends on the unshown callee's behavior, so it is recorded rather than confirmed.

Minor OOB read: when the final byte of a completely full line (len == lineSize-1) begins a 3- or 4-byte UTF-8 sequence, the in-body i++ increments make lines 42/45 read szLine[lineSize] and szLine[lineSize+1], up to 2 bytes past the caller's buffer; dominated by the confirmed OOB write on the same path.

The strcpy at lines 57 and 80 can overflow szLine for any lineSize < 2049 whenever the converted string is longer than the caller's buffer; treated as the same root cause (unbounded conversion length vs. destination sizes) rather than a second independent CWE.

verdict.summary: The RPL_WHOREPLY (352) handler bounds-checks every argv/argv_eol index against argc with correct strict operators in execution order ('if (argc < 8) return', '(argc > 9)', '(argc > arg_start + 1)', '(argc > arg_start + 2)'), checks the malloc sentinel ('if (str_host)') before use, sizes the host buffer from the same expression passed to snprintf, uses a literal format string with attacker data only in %s positions, and frees/reassigns nick->realname without double-free or UAF. No attacker-reachable memory-safety, injection, or fail-open defect was instantiated.

assumptions: The callback framework supplies argc/argv/argv_eol such that argv and argv_eol each contain exactly argc entries (WeeChat's documented callback contract; the parser is not shown). All index guards in this code are written against that same argc, so the guards hold for whatever argc the parser yields.
IRC_PROTOCOL_MIN_ARGS(5) is a macro that returns early when argc < 5; not relied upon, since the quoted 'if (argc < 8)' check is stricter and covers every index used.

Internal callees (irc_channel_search, irc_nick_search, irc_nick_set_host, irc_nick_set_away, irc_msgbuffer_get_target_buffer, irc_protocol_tags) accept the well-formed, NUL-terminated strings this code passes; no raw attacker index/size/offset is passed to any of them.
limitations: Theoretical int overflow in 'length = strlen (argv[4]) + 1 + strlen (argv[5]) + 1;' requires a ~2 GiB single IRC line (upstream receive cap not shown). Even if instantiated, malloc and snprintf both consume the same wrapped length, so the write remains bounded by the allocation — no heap overflow chain exists; worst case is truncation or a failed huge allocation handled by the quoted 'if (str_host)'.

Pointer arithmetic '+1' on argv[arg_start] and argv[arg_start+1] would point one past the NUL only if the parser could emit an empty parameter; WeeChat's message splitter (not shown) never produces empty argv elements, so no trigger could be instantiated here.

strdup(pos_realname) failure is not checked, but the consequence is only ptr_nick->realname becoming NULL, which no statement in this code dereferences; at worst a downstream consumer would display an empty realname.

verdict.summary: In gopherToHTML, the line terminator is written at line[llen + 1] (line 97) while the only bounds logic (lines 75-77) permits the final llen to reach TEMP_BUF_SIZE - 1. A gopher server response containing a line of at least TEMP_BUF_SIZE - 1 bytes makes the code write a NUL byte at line[TEMP_BUF_SIZE], one byte past the end of the TEMP_BUF_SIZE-element stack buffer line — a network-reachable off-by-one out-of-bounds stack write (the clamp reserves one headroom byte but the terminator index needs two).

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write sink: the NUL terminator is placed at index llen + 1, but llen can equal TEMP_BUF_SIZE - 1 (both via the clamp at line 77 and via an unclamped line of exactly TEMP_BUF_SIZE - 1 bytes, which passes the >= test at line 75), so this statement writes line[TEMP_BUF_SIZE] — one byte past the end of the stack array line (LOCAL_ARRAY(char, line, TEMP_BUF_SIZE)). Trigger: a malicious gopher server sends a line of at least TEMP_BUF_SIZE - 1 bytes ending in '\n'; with gopherState->len == 0, llen = TEMP_BUF_SIZE - 1, the check 0 + (TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1) >= TEMP_BUF_SIZE is false, memcpy(line, pos, TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1) fills indices 0..TEMP_BUF_SIZE-2, and line[llen+1] writes the out-of-bounds NUL.

Origin of the boundary value: this is the only guard on llen, and it caps the copy length so the final llen is TEMP_BUF_SIZE - 1 (the clamp sets llen = TEMP_BUF_SIZE - gopherState->len - 1 and line 92 then adds gopherState->len back). It reserves exactly one headroom byte, but the sink at line 97 writes at index llen + 1, which requires two. No other statement in the function bounds llen or the terminator index.

assumptions: TEMP_BUF_SIZE is the size of both the stack buffer line (LOCAL_ARRAY(char, line, TEMP_BUF_SIZE)) and gopherState->buf; the clamp's invariant gopherState->len + llen <= TEMP_BUF_SIZE - 1 keeps the memcpy at line 84 in bounds only under this sizing, which is not shown in the given code.
gopherState->len starts at 0; the only writers shown are lines 85 and 93, so the invariant gopherState->len <= TEMP_BUF_SIZE - 1 is maintained by this code.
limitations: The terminator is placed at line[llen + 1] rather than line[llen], so line[llen] can retain a stale non-NUL byte from a previous longer line between iterations; this lengthens the parsed line by stale data but stays in bounds (data confusion only, no memory-safety impact).
port[2] at the '0 means none' check can be computed only when port[1] != 0, which short-circuits the && before any out-of-range read when port sits at the very end of the terminated string.
The CSO path's strtok/atoi sequence is safe: if (!result) break; precedes both atoi calls, and a non-NULL result implies non-NULL s_code and s_recno by strtok semantics.

verdict.summary: This is the specialized NIST P-256 modular reduction routine. All memory offsets (rp + n - 4, rp + n - 3, rp[n-2], rp[2], rp[3]) are bounded by the quoted loop condition 'for (; n >= p->size; n--)', which confines n to [p->size, 2*p->size-1] at every iteration entry, keeping every access inside the 2*p->size limb buffer. Attacker-influenced limb content (full 64-bit domain per the width-domain rule) flows only into value arithmetic: q2 is provably in {0,1} for all limb values (1 + (2^64-1) + 1 ≡ 1 mod 2^64), so the assert invariant holds and the cnd_sub_n/cnd_add_n conditions are always in-domain; mpn_submul_1 accepts any 64-bit multiplier. Unsigned wraparound in limb arithmetic is the intended multi-precision semantics. The only out-of-bounds paths require p->size ≠ 4 (e.g., p->size = 1 gives rp + n - 4 = rp - 3), but the modulus descriptor is an operator-fixed constant of the module — no trust-boundary party can supply it, and the function body (hardwired rp[2]/rp[3], 0xffffffff masks, the 2^96-1 comment) documents the 256-bit/4-limb specialization — so that trigger is a caller-contract misuse, not an attacker-instantiable vulnerability.

assumptions: p is the fixed 256-bit P-256 modulo descriptor with p->size == 4 and 64-bit limbs; the snippet contains no check enforcing p->size == 4, so this is a caller contract recorded here rather than relied on as a guard.
rp points to a buffer of 2*p->size (8) limbs; the extent is a caller allocation contract not checked in this snippet.
The two low limbs of p->m equal 2^96 - 1, as the code's own comment states; the arithmetic specialization depends on it.
assert may be compiled out under NDEBUG; the q2 < 2 invariant was verified to hold for the full 64-bit limb domain, so the assert is an invariant, not a load-bearing guard.
p->m is at least 2 limbs long (consumed by mpn_submul_1/cnd_sub_n/cnd_add_n with count 1 or 2).
limitations: Speculative candidate (not a vulnerability in this code): a caller passing a struct ecc_modulo with p->size < 4 (e.g., p->size = 1 makes 'rp + n - 4' = rp - 3, an out-of-bounds write inside mpn_submul_1, and p->size <= 0 makes 'rp[--n]' an out-of-bounds read) would corrupt memory. No such caller is instantiable by a trust-boundary party: the modulus is a compile-time constant of the module, and the function's hardcoded rp[2]/rp[3] stores and 2^96-1 specialization document the 4-limb contract. The missing one-line guard would be an entry check such as 'if (p->size != 4) return;', which appears nowhere in the snippet.
Signed overflow of n = 2*p->size requires p->size near SIZE_MAX/2 — same non-instantiable contract path as above.

The 32-bit shifts and 0xffffffff masks assume GMP_NUMB_BITS == 64; on a 32-bit-limb build this variant would be wrong, but that is build-time configuration of the module, not a runtime input any attacker controls.

If the assert fires in a debug build under some unproven input class, the crash would affect only the process performing its own crypto computation; the q2 invariant computation shows no such input exists within the 512-bit input domain.

verdict.summary: startSslClient establishes a TLS client session without ever enabling peer certificate verification: no SSL_set_verify(SSL_VERIFY_PEER), no SSL_get_verify_result check, and no hostname verification (line 94 only sets the SNI extension), so the default SSL_VERIFY_NONE lets a MITM complete the handshake with any certificate and the function marks the socket secure (isssl = true, return 0). Independently, the guard 'if (rc < 0)' at line 101 fails to reject SSL_connect's documented return value 0 (fatal handshake failure, e.g. a peer-sent fatal alert), so a failed handshake is also presented as a fully established SSL connection.

evidence.reason: Missing-check site for CWE-295: this is the only hostname-related statement in the function and it only sets the SNI extension; the full mention sweep of the function shows SSL_CTX_load_verify_locations (line 32) and SSL_CTX_set_default_verify_paths (line 42) only load the CA store, and the X509_VERIFY_PARAM carries only X509_V_FLAG_TRUSTED_FIRST (line 66). No SSL_set_verify/SSL_VERIFY_PEER, SSL_get_verify_result, or X509_VERIFY_PARAM_set1_host exists anywhere, so with OpenSSL's default SSL_VERIFY_NONE a MITM presenting a self-signed certificate completes the handshake (rc = 1), passes 'if (rc < 0)', and reaches 'isssl = true; return 0;' on lines 115/117 — the socket is presented as a secure verified channel while the peer is unauthenticated.

CWE-451 fail-open: SSL_connect is documented to return 1 on success, 0 on fatal handshake failure (e.g. the network peer sends a fatal TLS alert), and <0 on retryable/IO errors. The guard 'rc < 0' is the only rc test in the function (mention sweep: lines 100, 101, and the NETDEBUG log at 104) and under-admits rc == 0, so a fatally failed handshake falls through to line 115 'isssl = true;' and line 117 'return 0;', presenting a secure, established SSL connection on an error path that a hostile peer can trigger at will.

Security-state presentation sink: reached both when the peer was never verified (no SSL_VERIFY_PEER anywhere in the function, so rc = 1 with a MITM certificate) and when the handshake fatally failed (rc == 0 passes 'if (rc < 0)' at line 101). In both cases the function marks the socket as a fully set-up secure SSL connection and returns success.

assumptions: log_ssl_errors is an unshown internal callee treated as printf-like; all its format strings in this code are literal constants with matching %s arguments (e.g. line 102), so no format-string injection depends on it.
The String type provides c_str() returning a NUL-terminated buffer used by SSL_set_tlsext_host_name and the log calls; String is not shown.
stopSsl() (line 4) and getFD() (line 93) are unshown internal members assumed to release the prior session and return the socket descriptor.

certificate_path is a caller-supplied trust-anchor path; if any deployment derives it from attacker input, the caller hands the attacker the choice of CA store, compounding the CWE-295 finding. No statement in this code narrows it.
limitations: C3 (robustness, not counted): line 87 'ssl = SSL_new(ctx);' is consumed at line 88 without a NULL check — no if-test exists in the mention sweep of ssl (lines 87-108). A NULL from SSL_new would be dereferenced by SSL_set_options, but the trigger requires an allocation failure no attacker input reaches (ctx is already NULL-checked at line 14), so it is a robustness issue (CWE-476-class), not an attacker-instantiated vulnerability.

SSL_set_fd's return value (line 93) is ignored, but an invalid descriptor leads to SSL_connect failing at line 100 and the -3 cleanup path (except the rc==0 nuance covered by the CWE-451 finding); no independent impact.

On the rc == 0 path, subsequent SSL_read/SSL_write on the failed handshake return errors rather than transmitting cleartext, so the direct impact is the misrepresentation of the connection state and return code, not plaintext data flow in this function.

verdict.summary: gf_text_get_utf8_line copies an attacker-controlled file line of up to lineSize-1 bytes into a fixed 1024-byte stack buffer szLineConv with no bound on the output index j (which can grow to 2*len via the CP1252 branch), performs an unbounded UTF-16 byte-swap loop that reads and can write past the caller's szLine buffer when the line fills it, and indexes szLineConv with the unchecked return of gf_utf8_wcstombs, allowing out-of-bounds stack writes from parsed file content.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds stack write (CWE-787): j is never compared to sizeof(szLineConv)=1024 or to lineSize anywhere (mention sweep: only j=0 at line 12, increments at 19/26/32/35/41/44/47/54, writes at 18/24/30/33/39/42/45/53/56). In the branch at lines 17-21 j gains 2 per input byte, so with unicode_type=0 and a file line of 513+ bytes of 0xC0 (lineSize>=514), j reaches 1024 and this sink writes past szLineConv[1023]; the write at line 18 overflows first, and szLineConv[j]=0 at line 56 overflows again. Trigger fully instantiated from parsed file content.

Out-of-bounds read and potential write past the caller's szLine buffer (CWE-125): the loop only stops on an in-buffer NUL pair and never checks i+1 < lineSize (mention sweep for i: lines 67, 70, 71, 72, 73, 74 only). When the attacker's UTF-16 line is longer than the buffer, gf_fgets fills it exactly (len = lineSize-1), the final in-bounds pair fails the break test, i advances to lineSize, and line 70 reads szLine[lineSize] and szLine[lineSize+1] out of bounds; lines 71-73 then write szLine[lineSize+1] if the adjacent bytes are non-zero. Trigger instantiated for any lineSize by supplying a sufficiently long line.

Unchecked failure sentinel used as a stack buffer index (CWE-787): gf_utf8_wcstombs is a conversion routine that returns -1 on an illegal UTF-16 sequence (e.g., an unpaired 0xD800 surrogate in the attacker-supplied line); the cast yields i = 0xFFFFFFFF and szLineConv[i] = 0 becomes a wild out-of-bounds write. Even on the success boundary, a conversion producing exactly 1024 bytes returns i = 1024 and line 79 writes one past szLineConv. No sentinel or range check exists between the call and the use (mention sweep for i: lines 78-79 only).

assumptions: The doubling overflow at lines 17-21 requires the caller's lineSize to be at least 514 (any line reader buffer at or above the function's own 1024-byte szLineConv satisfies this, and even unicode_type==1 with lineSize>1024 overflows with a plain long line); lineSize is caller-provided and not shown, but the code never relates lineSize to sizeof(szLineConv), which is itself the defect.

gf_utf8_wcstombs is not shown; standard wcstombs-family semantics (return -1 on illegal input, at most n bytes on success) are assumed. Per the unchecked-sentinel rule the missing local test at line 79 is the defect regardless of callee behavior.
limitations: strcpy(szLine, szLineConv) at lines 57 and 80 can overflow the caller's szLine when the converted string is at least lineSize bytes and lineSize < 1025; this is folded into the primary szLineConv overflow rather than reported separately because the overflowed content originates from the same unbounded conversion.
The read szLine[i+1] at line 17 when i=len-1 touches the NUL written by gf_fgets and is in-bounds; not a defect.
unicode_type values outside 0..3 skip all conversion branches and cause no out-of-bounds access; not a defect.

verdict.summary: MulConvPushDown dereferences NodeMap::GetNode() results without any NULL check (lines 19-20, 45-46) and calls conv_node->attr().at("data_format") without an existence check (line 80). A crafted GraphDef whose Mul node input(0)/input(1) is a control-input name (e.g. "^c0") or a dangling node name makes GetNode return nullptr, causing a NULL dereference crash; a Conv2D node missing the data_format attribute triggers an unhandled out_of_range exception/abort. Both crash the process optimizing the attacker-supplied model (denial of service).

evidence.snippet:
const bool left_child_is_constant = IsReallyConstant(*mul_left_child);
  const bool right_child_is_constant = IsReallyConstant(*mul_right_child);
evidence.reason: Root cause: unchecked NULL dereference. mul_left_child/mul_right_child come from node_map_->GetNode(node->input(0/1)) (lines 16-17), a name lookup that returns nullptr on a miss; no NULL check exists on any path (mention sweep of lines 16, 19, 24-25, 29-30, 72-73 found only uses, no guards). Instantiated trigger: a crafted GraphDef Mul node with inputs ["^c0", "Const/1", "Conv/1"] passes the line-14 count check (which verifies only the count of non-control inputs, not resolvability), GetNode("^c0") returns nullptr, and the first use at line 19 dereferences it, crashing the process.

evidence.snippet:
NodeDef* mul_left_child = node_map_->GetNode(node->input(0));
  NodeDef* mul_right_child = node_map_->GetNode(node->input(1));
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted pointers: attacker-controlled input-name strings from the parsed GraphDef are passed to the NodeMap lookup, whose miss sentinel (nullptr) is consumed without a check at lines 19-20. The minimal absent guard is: reject if either GetNode result is nullptr before the first use.

evidence.snippet:
const bool conv_left_is_constant = IsReallyConstant(*conv_left_child);
  const bool conv_right_is_constant = IsReallyConstant(*conv_right_child);
evidence.reason: Same defect class, independent use site: conv_left_child/conv_right_child (lines 43-44) are GetNode results on attacker-controlled conv-node input names; the line-36 input_size()<2 check guards only the proto indices, not lookup resolvability, and no NULL check precedes the first-use dereference here.

Root cause: improper check for exceptional conditions. attr().at("data_format") throws/aborts when the key is absent, and no contains/count/Find guard exists anywhere in the function. Instantiated trigger: a crafted Conv2D node in the attacker-supplied GraphDef that omits the data_format attribute reaches this line after passing the op-name and shape checks, terminating the optimizing process with an unhandled out_of_range exception.

assumptions: NodeMap::GetNode is a by-name lookup whose documented failure sentinel is nullptr on a miss (standard lookup semantics); the code tests no other sentinel for it.

IsReallyConstant, IsConv2D/IsConv3D, NumNonControlInputs/NumNonControlOutputs, AddPrefixToNodeName, MaybeRemoveControlInput/MaybeAddControlInput, and IsValidConstShapeForMulConvPushDown are project-internal callees not shown; their behavior is not relied on to produce or block any trigger — the dereference of the null argument occurs at the call site.

The GraphDef being optimized originates outside the operator's trust boundary (e.g., a shared or downloaded model file), so node names, input strings, and attributes are attacker-controlled content per the width-domain rule.
limitations: Impact is limited to process crash / denial of service of the process loading the crafted model; no memory corruption, disclosure, or bypass primitive was found in the given code.

The name-swap and node_map_ update block (lines 99-115) uses stale map keys after set_name(); this is graph-rewrite bookkeeping with no demonstrated memory-safety consequence in this code and is not treated as a vulnerability.

Whether an upstream graph-construction stage validates input-name resolvability or required attributes before grappler runs cannot be quoted from this code and is not credited; this code is judged as the last line of defense.

verdict.summary: updateHandshakeState consumes only cipher/transport-parameter availability from the handshake layer, and every consumed value is guarded: each cipher is installed only under a presence check, the transport-params optional is sentinel-checked with a throw before dereference, duplicate 1-RTT write-cipher installation is rejected, HandshakeDone is idempotent via conn.sentHandshakeDone, and the anti-amplification writable-bytes limit is cleared only when the 1-RTT read cipher is derived (post-CFIN, i.e., after client address validation), never on the 0-RTT path. No attacker-data value reaches a memory, size, index, or injection sink in this function. The remaining CHECK assertions and unchecked conn.readCodec dereferences depend on invariants established in code not shown and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: conn.readCodec is non-NULL for the lifetime of the connection: it is set during connection construction (code not shown) and never cleared in this function; a null value cannot be produced by any statement here.
conn.serverHandshakeLayer is non-NULL: it is connection infrastructure established outside this function; no statement here can null it.
The fizz handshake layer exports the 1-RTT read cipher only after a validated client Finished (CFIN) is processed, as the code's own comments state; the export-ordering code itself is not shown.
The transport-parameter content is fully attacker-controlled, but its parsing and validation occur inside processClientInitialParams, which is not shown and therefore outside this analysis.
limitations: CHECK(handshakeReadHeaderCipher) crashes the server process if the handshake layer ever derives a handshake read cipher without a matching header cipher. The producing code is not shown, so no attacker-reachable trigger could be instantiated here; if such a path exists it would be a CHECK-abort denial of service rooted in the unshown handshake layer.

CHECK(conn.oneRttWriteCipher) crashes if isHandshakeDone() returns true while no 1-RTT write cipher was ever installed. The state combination depends on unshown handshake-layer logic; trigger not instantiable from this code.

processClientInitialParams receives attacker-authored QUIC transport parameters after only a presence check on the optional. Any bounds or validation defect in consuming those parameters would live in that callee, which is not given; the impact chain cannot be traced in this analysis.

Read-side ciphers and header ciphers lack the duplicate-derivation check that the 1-RTT write cipher has, but re-installation in this code only overwrites a moved-from slot with no corruption primitive; treated as benign asymmetry, not a defect.

verdict.summary: gopherToHTML parses attacker-controlled gopher server responses. Two confirmed defects: (1) an off-by-one out-of-bounds write at `line[llen + 1] = '\0';` — the only bound (`gopherState->len + llen >= TEMP_BUF_SIZE`, which clamps the total to exactly TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1) admits llen == TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1, so the NUL terminator is written at line[TEMP_BUF_SIZE], one byte past the LOCAL_ARRAY(char, line, TEMP_BUF_SIZE) buffer; triggered by a gopher response line whose length (including leftover from the previous call) is exactly TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 bytes. (2) A NULL-pointer dereference of `port` in the telnet branch: `port = strchr(host, TAB)` can return NULL for a menu line lacking a third TAB, the `if (port)` block guards only the junk-chop code, and the telnet snprintf dereferences `*port`, remotely crashing the proxy process (denial of service).

evidence.reason: Off-by-one out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). `line` is `LOCAL_ARRAY(char, line, TEMP_BUF_SIZE)` with valid indices 0..TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1, but the terminator index is llen+1. The only bound, `if (gopherState->len + llen >= TEMP_BUF_SIZE)` (line 77) and its clamp `llen = TEMP_BUF_SIZE - gopherState->len - 1` (line 79), cap the COPY total at exactly TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1, so after `llen += gopherState->len` (line 94) llen can equal TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 and this statement writes line[TEMP_BUF_SIZE] — one byte past the buffer. Trigger instantiated: a gopher server (or cleartext MITM) returns a menu line of exactly TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 bytes ending in '\n' (or leftover bytes from a previous call plus a line completing the same total), e.g. with gopherState->len==0 and llen==TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 the line-77 check is false (T-1 >= T fails), memcpy fills indices 0..T-2, and the NUL lands out of bounds.

Origin of the boundary value: this guard uses `>=`, so the exact-limit case gopherState->len + llen == TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 passes unclamped, and even the clamped path produces a total of exactly TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 — the maximum that line 99 turns into the out-of-bounds index TEMP_BUF_SIZE. No statement anywhere in the code bounds llen to <= TEMP_BUF_SIZE-2 or terminates at line[llen].

NULL-pointer dereference (CWE-476). `port = strchr(host, TAB)` (line 130) returns NULL when the attacker-supplied menu line has no third TAB; the `if (port)` block (line 132) only guards the junk-chop code and control falls through to the telnet branch, where `*port` and `port` are dereferenced/passed here with no NULL check on any path. Trigger instantiated: a gopher menu line of the telnet gtype (the GOPHER_TELNET arm at line 195 of this code's own switch) with exactly two TABs, e.g. "8name\tsel\thost\n", causes *NULL to be read in the Squid worker — a remotely triggered crash (denial of service) of the proxy process. Line 233 contains the mirrored deref in the empty-selector branch.

Origin of the NULL: the strchr lookup can miss (attacker controls the presence of the third TAB), and the `if (port)` guard covers only the port-chopping statements inside lines 132-154; nothing resets port or rejects the entry when it is NULL before the first use at line 230.

assumptions: `gopherState->buf` is assumed to be at least TEMP_BUF_SIZE bytes; its allocation is not shown in this code, so the guard at line 77 (`gopherState->len + llen >= TEMP_BUF_SIZE`) was judged against TEMP_BUF_SIZE, the only size this code quotes.

`len` is treated as the actual byte count of attacker response data delivered by the caller (the gopher state machine); the off-by-one at line 99 triggers with ordinary small values of len, so no assumption about extreme len is needed.
TEMP_BUF_SIZE's numeric value is not shown; all arithmetic was verified symbolically against the bound this code itself uses.

rfc1738_escape_part, html_quote, mimeGetIconURL, xstrdup, gopherHTMLHeader, and StoreEntry methods are internal callees not shown; they are relied on only for their return-a-string/append semantics, not for any bounds enforcement.
limitations: Integer overflow of `gopherState->len + llen` (line 77) or of `int left` would require the caller to deliver len near INT_MAX in one call; the read-chunking code is not shown, so this speculative wrap path was not counted as a vulnerability.
A gopherState->buf smaller than TEMP_BUF_SIZE would make the memcpy at line 86 overflow, but the allocation is not in the given code; judged as guarded per the only quotable bound.
The `line[llen]` byte is left stale between the copied data and the terminator at line[llen+1]; worst case string functions read one stale byte, in-bounds and non-security-relevant.

Practical exploitability of the one-byte NUL overflow at line 99 depends on the memory adjacent to the LOCAL_ARRAY storage (likely the sibling tmpbuf array, which is memset before each use); per the analysis rules the memory-corruption primitive itself is the confirmed defect regardless of adjacent layout.

verdict.summary: In the IRC 352 (WHOREPLY) handler, arg_start is set to 9 when argv[8] equals "*", but argv[arg_start][0] is dereferenced without any argc > arg_start check; a malicious IRC server sending a 9-argument 352 message whose 8th parameter is "*" causes a one-past-the-end read of the argv array (NULL/wild-pointer dereference, remote crash, possible memory disclosure via the who display).

evidence.reason: Root cause: with argc == 9 (valid indices 0..8, per 'if (argc > 8)') and argv[8] == "*", the ternary selects arg_start = 9 and the very next statement dereferences argv[9][0], one past the end of the argv array. Instantiated trigger: server sends ':s 352 me #chan u h srv n *' → argc=9, arg_start=9, out-of-bounds read/crash. No argc > arg_start check precedes this use anywhere in the code.

The code itself uses the exact guard the sink requires ('argc > arg_start') but only at line 24, after the first unguarded use of argv[arg_start] at line 21 (and the unguarded assignment pos_attr = argv[arg_start] at line 29) — a sentinel check placed after the first use does not cover it.

assumptions: argc, argv and argv_eol are produced by the IRC message splitter, which is not shown; per the width-domain rule argc is any count and argv[i] any string, and argv has exactly argc valid entries (indices 0..argc-1).
IRC_PROTOCOL_MIN_ARGS(5) is taken to enforce argc >= 5 by name; it does not affect the trigger, which uses argc == 9.
IRC protocol callback parameters are attacker-data by default (network peer originates the 352 message).
limitations: The layout of memory just past argv[argc-1] is not shown: if the splitter NUL-terminates the array, the impact is a NULL-dereference crash (CWE-476-style) rather than a wild read; either way the one-past-the-end index at line 21 is out of bounds.

Info disclosure via lines 29/97-101 (OOB argv[9] value flowing into weechat_printf %s) is possible only if the OOB element dereference at line 21 does not itself fault; the crash/DoS impact is unconditional.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds read of TabPageIdxs array via unchecked mouse_col index in drag event paths.
