evidence.reason: Sink: the chain-walk loop writes one byte per iteration into ctx->stack_base with no bound on stack_pos and no upper-bound validation of code_out (the only comparison is the lower bound `code_out > clear_code`). code_out is seeded from the unvalidated ctx->previous_code and refreshed from entry->previous_entry, so an out-of-domain (full uint32_t surface, producer not shown) or cyclic chain makes `*stack_pos++` run past the end of the stack buffer (out-of-bounds write) and `table + code_out` an out-of-bounds read. Trigger instantiated by an attacker code_new == current_entry, which the quoted `code_new > current_entry` check admits.

Origin: in the code-not-in-table branch (reached when attacker-supplied code_new == current_entry), code_out is seeded from ctx->previous_code, a uint32_t context field whose value at the first decode call and after a clear is produced by code not shown in this function. No statement of this code checks previous_code against current_entry or the table size before it is used as a table index (line 69) and as the seed of the unbounded *stack_pos++ write loop; line 48 also stores this unvalidated value as entry->previous_entry, poisoning the chain.

assumptions: ctx->table has (1 << LZW_CODE_MAX) entries, matching the quoted write guard `if (current_entry < (1 << LZW_CODE_MAX))`, so the guarded table[code_new] and dictionary-add accesses are in range.

lzw__next_code returns codes of at most ctx->current_code_size bits, with current_code_size capped at LZW_CODE_MAX by the quoted `if (ctx->current_code_size < LZW_CODE_MAX)`, so code_new is bounded to [0, 4095].

The capacity of ctx->stack_base is not shown in this code, and no statement in this function relates the number of stack writes to that capacity; the write bound would have to be the maximum chain length, which itself depends on entries written elsewhere (init) and on clear handling not shown.
limitations: The infinite-cycle variant of the trigger additionally depends on lzw__clear_codes resetting ctx->current_entry without resetting ctx->previous_code (callee not shown); per the width-domain rule the unvalidated use at lines 39/69-71 remains the defect regardless, since no statement of this code documents or enforces a contract on previous_code.

If every consumed previous_code/previous_entry were provingly < its own table index and stack_base were sized at (1 << LZW_CODE_MAX), per-call writes would be bounded (~4094) and fit; those bounds are not established by any quoted statement of this code.

The code-size increase at line 53 tests the pre-increment local current_entry while ctx->current_entry may already be current_entry+1, which can shift the code-size increase by one code relative to a post-increment check; this affects decode accuracy only, no memory-safety impact was found.

verdict.summary: example_labels tensor is flattened and indexed with example_id up to num_examples derived from example_weights.size(), with no check that example_labels has at least num_examples elements, allowing an out-of-bounds heap read via a mismatched example_labels input tensor.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read sink: example_id ranges to num_examples-1 derived from example_weights.size() (line 46), but example_labels is never size-checked (mention sweep: lines 48, 49, 65 only); an attacker passing example_weights with 100 elements and example_labels with 1 element makes example_labels(example_id) read past the 1-element tensor for example_id 1..99.

Origin of the tainted value: the attacker-controlled example_labels tensor is fetched and flattened with no accompanying length validation against num_examples or example_weights.size(), unlike every other input list which is size-checked (lines 11, 19, 28).

assumptions: CreateSparseFeatureRepresentation / CreateDenseFeatureRepresentation are project-internal callees not shown; their indexing behavior is not relied on for the primary finding.
num_sparse_features, num_sparse_features_with_values, num_dense_features are op-level configuration ints treated as internal-trusted; their producer bounds are not visible in this code.
limitations: dense_features_inputs (line 53) is never size-checked against num_dense_features while the sibling sparse lists are; the resulting out-of-bounds list indexing would occur inside the unshown CreateDenseFeatureRepresentation callee, so it is a real validation gap but not counted as a primary here.

num_features_ = num_sparse_features + num_dense_features (line 6) can overflow int if the two configuration ints are large; no guard exists, but the achievable input scale is not quotable from this code.
Calling flat<float>() on a tensor of a different dtype triggers a CHECK failure inside TensorFlow (crash of the op process only), a robustness issue rather than corruption.

verdict.summary: All attacker-influenced dimensions (decode.width, decode.height from the PNG IHDR) are validated before any use: the quoted guard block performs truncation round-trip casts, rejects non-positive values, bounds each dimension below 2^27 and the product below 2^29 via a returning OP_REQUIRES. With decode.channels confined to 1-4 by libpng's documented color-type mapping, every derived size expression fits its int arithmetic (max element count 4*(2^29-1) = 2^31-4, strides < 2^30 bytes), allocation and decode stride stay consistent, the CommonInitDecode return is sentinel-checked before first use, and the cleanup lambda frees decode exactly once on every path. No guard exists locally for decode.channels, but no value outside 1-4 is instantiable from this code's input surface.

assumptions: png::CommonInitDecode, CommonFinishDecode and CommonFreeDecode are project-internal callees not shown; per libpng's documented semantics, a PNG's channel count derived from its color type is confined to 1-4, and decode.width/decode.height are png_uint_32 IHDR fields.

OP_REQUIRES and OP_REQUIRES_OK expand to statements that set the context status and return from the function, so every early exit unwinds through the gtl::MakeCleanup lambda exactly once (no double free or use-after-free of decode).

The kernel attributes channels_, data_type_ and op_type_ are fixed at graph construction; the op registration constrains the DecodeGif variant to uint8 output and the channels attribute to its documented values (enforcement outside this code).
png::DecodeContext is assumed to use default member initializers (TF's definition does) so that a failed CommonInitDecode leaves a state CommonFreeDecode can safely handle.
limitations: decode.channels has no local range check in this code. An out-of-range value (>= 5) is reachable only through a non-default channels_ graph attribute surviving constructor validation not shown here and an unshown CommonInitDecode passing it through; the DT_FLOAT path's 'new uint16[height * width * decode.channels]' int arithmetic could then overflow. However, a wrap to a small positive count requires height*width*channels >= 2^32, which forces a >= 16 GB allocate_output (int64 true size, 4 bytes/element) to succeed first, and a wrap to negative converts to a huge size_t and fails allocation. Trigger not instantiable from the code's input surface; recorded as a defense-in-depth gap.

If op_type_ were 'DecodeGif' together with data_type_ DT_FLOAT, the 4-D output would be indexed via output->tensor<float, 3>(), a shape mismatch that at worst crashes the process; the combination is barred by op registration outside this code.
The leftover debug statement 'std::cerr << "Cleanup called...\n"' writes a fixed string with no attacker data to stderr; a code-quality issue, not a security defect.

verdict.summary: Unsanitized configuration name (booth_conf->name) is used in lockfile path construction via snprintf without validation for path traversal characters, allowing the PID file to be written to an arbitrary location if the configuration content is attacker-influenced.

evidence.reason: booth_conf->name, set by read_config() from the configuration file, is interpolated into a filesystem path without any sanitization for path traversal sequences (/, ..). An attacker who can influence the config file content can cause the lockfile/PID file to be constructed at an arbitrary filesystem path outside BOOTH_RUN_DIR.
The configuration file content, including booth_conf->name, enters this code via read_config() with no subsequent validation of the name for path safety before its use in lockfile path construction.

assumptions: find_site_by_name is assumed to set the 'local' pointer to a valid non-NULL value when it returns non-zero; the implementation is not shown in this code.
booth_conf->name is assumed to be a NUL-terminated string within the buffer allocated by read_config(); read_config() is not shown.
BOOTH_RUN_DIR is assumed to be a compile-time constant string representing the intended PID file directory.
The exploitability of the path traversal depends on whether the configuration file is attacker-influenced; in a typical root-owned deployment this requires a separate access vector.
limitations: The gcry_control(GCRYCTL_DISABLE_SECMEM, 0) call disables secure memory for libgcrypt, meaning the authkey may be stored in swappable memory. This is a hardening concern (CWE-316 adjacent) rather than a directly exploitable vulnerability, as it requires an attacker with the ability to read process memory or swap space.

In the else branch, find_myself() is called without checking its return value (comment says 'ignoring errors'). If find_myself fails to set the 'local' pointer, subsequent code using 'local' (e.g., check_config) could dereference NULL. However, no dereference of 'local' is visible in this function in the else path, making the impact chain incomplete from this code alone.
The snprintf uses sizeof(cl.lockfile)-1 as the size limit, which is one byte more conservative than necessary but safe (snprintf always NUL-terminates within its size parameter).

verdict.summary: In the no-password branch of callback_glewlwyd_user_auth, an attacker holding any valid session can supply an arbitrary username (with password absent or empty) and the code passes it to user_session_update with flag 0 without verifying credentials or that the username is already authenticated in that session — the only guard is that the session itself exists (get_users_for_session == G_OK). This enables switching the session's default user to a victim, i.e., authentication bypass/account impersonation if the callee accepts the update.

evidence.snippet: if (user_session_update(config, u_map_get(request->map_cookie, config->session_key), u_map_get_case(request->map_header, "user-agent"), issued_for, json_string_value(json_object_get(j_param, "username")), NULL, 0) != G_OK) {
evidence.reason: Root cause: this call passes the attacker-controlled username to user_session_update with new_session flag 0 on a path that performs no credential verification (no auth_check_user_credentials) and no check that the username belongs to the validated session. Trigger: attacker sends their own valid session cookie plus {"username":"victim_user"} with no password; get_users_for_session returns G_OK for the session and the victim username is installed as the session default, impersonating the victim.

Origin of the missing guard: the code fetches the session's user list and checks only the G_OK sentinel; it never inspects j_result to confirm the requested username is among the session's authenticated users before reaching the line-53 sink.

assumptions: user_session_update is a project-internal callee not shown; per analysis rules its possible internal username-membership validation cannot be quoted and therefore cannot serve as a guard for the line-53 sink.
get_session_id is assumed to return the cookie value or NULL without transformation; the raw u_map_get cookie passed at line 53 is treated as equivalent to session_uid on this path.
o_free/json_decref are assumed NULL-safe, matching their documented library semantics.
limitations: Final impact depends on whether the unshown user_session_update independently rejects usernames not already in the session; the missing local validation at the call site is the defect regardless.
Session cookie is set with http_only=0 (lines 27, 57) — a hardening weakness (CWE-1004) noted but not primary.
Username/IP are interpolated into log messages (CWE-117 log forging) — low severity, not primary.

Existing session IDs are reused across re-authentication rather than regenerated (session-fixation prerequisite, CWE-384), but exploitation requires an external cookie-planting vector not present in this code — speculative.

verdict.summary: This GetSessionHandle-style op kernel contains no unguarded security sink. The session_state pointer is NULL-checked via OP_REQUIRES, the allocate_output result (handle) is guarded by OP_REQUIRES_OK, which returns before the handle writes on failure, and attacker-influenced tensor content is only stored and passed by value with no length, index, or copy arithmetic in this code. The only unchecked pointer, ctx->tensor_store() at the AddTensor call, has a trigger (a NULL tensor store) that is not instantiable from any statement in this code or attacker-supplied input; it depends on the graph executor's context wiring, which is not shown.

assumptions: OP_REQUIRES and OP_REQUIRES_OK have their standard documented TensorFlow semantics: on a non-OK status they cause Compute to return before subsequent statements, so handle is non-NULL at lines using it and session_state is non-NULL at GetNewId.
The op's registered output dtype is either DT_RESOURCE or a string dtype, so the else-arm's flat<tstring>() dtype check succeeds; this is fixed by op registration, not attacker-selectable at runtime.
Session-state/tensor-store accessors on OpKernelContext are framework-supplied interface members whose wiring is established by the graph executor, not by attacker-supplied data values.
limitations: ctx->tensor_store() is dereferenced at the AddTensor call without a NULL check, unlike the analogous session_state pointer which is explicitly checked. If an execution path existed where the OpKernelContext is built without a tensor store while still scheduling this op, this would be a NULL dereference (CWE-476). No statement in the given code can produce that state and no attacker input selects it, so the trigger is speculative and rests on executor behavior not shown; a defensive OP_REQUIRES on tensor_store would still be good hardening.

verdict.summary: The only memory-write sink, memcpy(data, ch->sample->data, ch->sample->dataLength), is guarded on every path: the destination buffer is allocated from the character-identical length expression (gf_filter_pck_new_alloc(ch->pid, ch->sample->dataLength, &data)) and the allocation result is NULL-checked before the copy, so the copied length can never exceed the allocation. All lookup/parse sentinels (prop, subs_buf, tfrf, finfo.seg_start_plus_one) are tested before first use, list indices are bounded by gf_list_count, and unsigned subtractions are guarded by nonzero checks. No attacker-reachable memory-safety, injection, or validation defect is present in this function.

assumptions: gf_filter_pck_new_alloc (GPAC framework allocator) is treated per standard library semantics: on success it sets *data to a buffer of exactly the requested size, on failure it returns NULL — relied on only as the discipline-3 contract of a universally known project framework function.

isor_reader_get_sample / isor_reader_get_sample_from_item / isor_reader_check_config / gf_isom_* are internal callees not shown; their effects on ch->sample were not assumed in either direction (they neither narrow nor enlarge dataLength for purposes of the memcpy analysis, which depends only on the quoted same-expression allocation).
ch (ISOMChannel*) returned by gf_list_get was assumed non-NULL for provably in-range indices, as count bounds the loop and i is not modified in the body.
limitations: If a not-shown internal reader could pair a non-NULL ch->sample->data pointer with a dataLength larger than the actual sample buffer, the memcpy would read out of bounds — but per the width-domain/assumption rules that producer behavior is unquotable here, and the alloc/length equality in this code still prevents any overflow of the destination.

sample_dur = ch->au_duration; sample_dur *= ch->sample->nb_pack can wrap u32, but the result only feeds packet duration metadata (gf_filter_pck_set_duration) — no memory or size use, so no security impact.

min_offset_plus_one = 1 + ch->last_valid_sample_data_offset could wrap only if the sample offset reached UINT64_MAX, which requires an unreachable input scale; the wrap result 0 is handled as 'unset'.

verdict.summary: This GetSessionHandle-style op kernel stores the caller-supplied tensor under a server-generated id and returns a handle. Every fallible call (AddTensor, allocate_output) is dominated by OP_REQUIRES_OK, the output allocation uses the constant scalar shape TensorShape({}), and no attacker-derived size, index, offset, or pointer reaches any memory, copy, or injection sink in this code. The dtype branch is consistent with the allocation dtype on both arms. No vulnerability found in the given code.

assumptions: allocate_output sets the output pointer and returns OK on success; OP_REQUIRES_OK returns from Compute on any non-OK status, so handle is valid at both use sites (framework contract of OpKernelContext).
MakeResourceHandle<Tensor> returns a well-formed ResourceHandle (possibly default-constructed on internal error); assigning it into a scalar<ResourceHandle> is memory-safe.
The instantiable output dtypes of this kernel are fixed by the op registration layer (not shown) to DT_RESOURCE and DT_STRING, matching the two branch arms.
limitations: If this kernel could ever be instantiated with an output dtype other than DT_RESOURCE or DT_STRING, handle->flat<tstring>() in the else arm would fail a CHECK and abort the process (possible DoS for a shared TF serving process). The trigger requires an unregistered dtype signature, which cannot be instantiated from any statement in the given code, so this is recorded as a robustness/speculative concern, not a vulnerability here.

No validation is performed on the contents of the input tensor before it is stored in the tensor store; whether stored tensors are later consumed unsafely is outside this code and cannot be judged from this snippet.

verdict.summary: In string_number_format, the thousand-separator size computation ((integral-1)/3) * thousand_sep.size() is evaluated in 32-bit int and can wrap to a small positive value (e.g. 42,107,523 * 102 = 4,294,967,346 wraps to +50). The only overflow check, 'integral + thousand_sep.size() * ((integral-1) / 3) < integral', tests only the addition for wraparound and passes when the product has already wrapped positive, so integral/reslen are set from the wrapped value and the result buffer is allocated far too small. The copy loop then executes memcpy(t + (1 - thousand_sep.size()), thousand_sep.data(), thousand_sep.size()), writing the full multi-megabyte attacker-controlled separator tens of megabytes below the undersized heap buffer: an attacker-controlled heap out-of-bounds write (root cause: integer overflow CWE-190 flowing to an out-of-bounds write CWE-787) reachable from a scripting-language builtin with string_number_format(1e308, 0, '.', str_repeat('A', 42107523)).

evidence.reason: Sink: with thousand_sep.size() = 42,107,523 and integral wrapped from 309 to 359, resbuf holds only 359 bytes; the first loop iteration calls memcpy at resbuf+356-42,107,523 for 42,107,523 attacker-controlled bytes, a massive heap out-of-bounds write below the undersized buffer (repeated ~102 times per call).

Origin of the undersized length: the 32-bit int product ((309-1)/3) * 42,107,523 = 4,294,967,346 wraps to +50, so integral becomes 359 instead of 4,294,967,655; the check on line 62 ('integral + thousand_sep.size() * ((integral-1) / 3) < integral') evaluates the same wrapped product (309+50=359) and cannot detect the multiplication overflow, making the destination allocation at line 88 (String resstr(reslen, ReserveString)) undersized relative to the bytes actually copied at line 128.

assumptions: String::size() returns a 32-bit int and String::mutableData() on a ReserveString(n) construction yields at least n+1 writable bytes, per the code's own comment 'This actually means 63 bytes for characters + 1 byte for the '\0'; snprintf(tmpbuf, 64, ...) therefore stays in bounds.
raise_error aborts control flow (throws), so the existing overflow checks are treated as terminal when they fire; the defect is that the line-62 check does not fire for a positive-wrapped product.
Signed 32-bit overflow in the product technically has C++ undefined behavior but wraps in practice on all target ABIs (32-bit int, 64-bit size_t) used by this engine.

integral is bounded by 309 because the largest finite double (~1.8e308) formats to 309 integer digits under '%F'; INF/NAN/leading non-digit outputs exit early at the isdigit(tmpbuf[0]) checks on lines 29 and 39.
thousand_sep of ~42MB is instantiable by a script (e.g. str_repeat) since string length is not bounded anywhere in this code.
limitations: reslen += dec (line 73) has no overflow check, but a pure-dec overflow is unreachable because reslen = integral + dec <= tmplen - 1 <= INT_MAX (snprintf returns -1 beyond INT_MAX, exiting at lines 28/38); overflow becomes arithmetically possible only by combining a large legitimate (non-wrapped) separator byte count with dec ~2e9, which first requires a successful ~2GB temporary allocation (line 35) and then depends on the unshown behavior of String(negative, ReserveString) at line 88, so no concrete memory-safety impact is instantiated here.

Very large dec (up to INT_MAX-309) drives snprintf to produce and copy a ~2GB string: attacker-influenced resource amplification (CWE-400) bounded by INT_MAX and allocation limits; not counted as a primary memory-safety defect.

The tmpbuf == nullptr tests on lines 29 and 39 occur only after snprintf has already dereferenced tmpbuf, but mutableData() on a ReserveString is documented by the adjacent comment to return a valid buffer, so no concrete trigger.

Same-root-cause secondary writes: with the wrapped integral, the per-digit stores *t-- = *s-- (line 124) and the t -= thousand_sep.size() (line 129) are also out of bounds; they are part of the single primary defect, not independent findings.

verdict.summary: The overridden handler Compute consumes the attacker-controlled scalar tensor input (full 32-bit int domain), widens it to std::size_t with no validation (negative values wrap to huge values), and passes the raw index into the indexing operation buf->Peek(index, &tuple) with no bounds check on any path. An out-of-range index (e.g. -1 becoming SIZE_MAX, or any value beyond the buffer's occupancy) produces an out-of-bounds read inside the buffer lookup, crashing or corrupting the host process; the defect is the missing local bounds validation at the call site.

evidence.reason: Unvalidated use: the attacker-derived index (no range, clamp, mask, or sign check exists anywhere in this code) is passed into the indexing operation buf->Peek. OP_REQUIRES_OK checks only the returned Status, not the index. Trigger: attacker feeds scalar int -1 (index becomes SIZE_MAX) or any value beyond the buffer's occupancy; the out-of-bounds access at this call site is the defect.

Origin of the tainted value: the content of input tensor 0 (runtime-fed data crossing the op trust boundary) is read as a signed int whose full domain is instantiable by the attacker, then implicitly widened to std::size_t with no check, so negative values wrap to huge out-of-range indices.

assumptions: OP_REQUIRES_OK / OP_REQUIRES return from Compute on non-OK status, so buf is valid after line 3 and the set_output loop only runs when tuple.size() equals num_outputs() (quoted line 12); these macro semantics are relied on as characterizable framework behavior.

Buffer::Peek is a project-internal callee not shown; its behavior is not relied on as either a guard or a trigger producer. Per the call-site rule, passing the raw unvalidated index to this indexing operation is a defect in this code regardless of Peek's internals.
Buffer::Tuple is assumed to be a container supporting size() and operator[] with standard semantics; the loop at lines 16-17 is guarded by the quoted size-equality check.
limitations: The actual out-of-bounds access executes inside Buffer::Peek, which is not part of the given code; if Peek contained an internal range check returning an error Status, OP_REQUIRES_OK would return cleanly. No such check can be quoted, so the missing local validation at the call site remains the defect.

ctx->input(0).scalar<int>()() on a non-scalar or wrong-dtype input relies on TensorFlow-internal tensor accessor semantics not shown; any resulting failure is a robustness concern of the framework, not a primary finding here.

verdict.summary: The FractionalMaxPool kernel never validates that pooling_ratio_[0] (batch) and pooling_ratio_[3] (channel) equal 1. The only in-code check, `input_size[i] >= pooling_ratio_[i]`, admits any ratio in (1, input_size[i]] and any ratio < 1. With pooling_ratio_[0] > 1, output_size[0] = floor(input_size[0]/pooling_ratio_[0]) is smaller than the batch loop bound `b < input_size[0]`, so out_offset indexes past out_mat's columns and `out_mat.col(out_offset) = ...` performs a heap out-of-bounds write of attacker-influenced values (memory corruption). With pooling_ratio_[3] < 1, output_size[3] exceeds input_size[3], so the cwiseMax reads coefficients past the input tensor's column into adjacent heap memory and stores them into the attacker-readable output tensor (out-of-bounds read with information disclosure).

evidence.reason: The batch loop is bounded by the INPUT batch (input_size[0]) while the output tensor was allocated with output_size[0] = floor(input_size[0]/pooling_ratio_[0]) batches (lines 46-50, 68). The only ratio check, `input_size[i] >= pooling_ratio_[i]` (line 19), permits pooling_ratio_[0] > 1 (e.g. 2.0 with batch 4), so b indexes beyond out_mat's column count; this missing bound is the root cause of the out-of-bounds write at line 114.

Primary sink. With pooling_ratio_ = {2.0,2.0,2.0,1.0} and input shape [4,4,4,4]: output_size = {2,2,2,4}, out_mat has 8 columns (32-element buffer), but for b=2,hs=0,ws=0, out_offset = (2*2+0)*2+0 = 8, so out_mat.col(8) writes 4 elements starting one past the heap buffer (up to out_offset 15 for b=3) — out-of-bounds write of cwiseMax results computed from attacker-controlled input values (CWE-787). Independently, with pooling_ratio_[3] = 0.5, output_size[3] = 8 > input_size[3] = 4, so this same assignment iterates i < 8 and reads in_mat.col(in_offset) coefficients i = 4..7, past the input tensor buffer at the last column; the maxed values land in the attacker-readable output tensor (CWE-125).

Origin of the divergent geometry: nothing in the code forces pooling_ratio_[3] == 1 (the line-19 check admits e.g. 0.5), so output_size[3] = floor(4/0.5) = 8 exceeds input_size[3] = 4; the channel-length mismatch between out_mat (line 67) and in_mat (line 64) then makes the cwiseMax at lines 114-115 read out of bounds of the input tensor.

assumptions: pooling_ratio_ is the op attribute taken from the graph definition; under the untrusted-model threat model it is attacker-controlled, and nothing in this code narrows it beyond `input_size[i] >= pooling_ratio_[i]`.
Tensor shapes are supplied at runtime by whoever feeds the op; Compute is the intake point and must validate them itself.
Eigen Maps/Blocks perform no runtime bounds checks in release (NDEBUG) builds, and the assignment `block = expr` iterates the destination's size — standard Eigen semantics, analogous to memcpy.

GeneratePoolingSequence (callee not shown) returns a non-decreasing sequence of at least 2 non-negative entries when output_size >= 1; this is needed only for reachability of the sink loops, not for either defect, and both triggers use ordinary, well-formed sequences.
OP_REQUIRES aborts the op on failure; DCHECK is a no-op in release builds.
limitations: hs/ws loop bounds (`height_cum_seq.size() - 1`, `width_cum_seq.size() - 1`) and the unclamped starts `height_start`/`width_start` rest entirely on the unshown GeneratePoolingSequence contract — no local statement ties the sequence length to output_size[1]/[2] or clamps starts to >= 0; these are latent unguarded uses but not instantiable from this code alone.
`height_cum_seq.size() - 1` would wrap (size_t) if the callee returned an empty sequence; callee-dependent, not instantiable here.
pooling_ratio <= 0 leads to an inf/negative static_cast or a negative TensorShape dimension (CHECK failure / UB); crash-only robustness impact, no corruption demonstrated.

`input_size[2] * input_size[1] * input_size[0]` and the output analogue are int multiplications that overflow for tensors with >= 2^31 elements, but the in/out offsets remain int64 and within the real buffers, so no out-of-bounds access is demonstrated from that overflow alone (and it requires multi-GB allocations).
`DCHECK_GT(output_size[i], 0)` is a release no-op but cannot fire anyway when the ratio is positive, given the line-19 check.

Validation might exist in the unshown op registration/shape function (the comment at lines 27-28 only claims the floor formula matches); per the analysis rules an enforcement that cannot be quoted does not exist for this code.

verdict.summary: FractionalMaxPoolV2's pooling-sequence loops bound out_offset using the generated sequence length rather than the output tensor's allocated dims, so when a sequence exceeds output_size[1]/[2] (e.g. ratio 1.0) out_mat.col(out_offset) indexes past the output buffer: out-of-bounds heap read and write with attacker-scaled offset (input H·W).

evidence.reason: out_offset is bounded by sequence sizes (hs < height_cum_seq.size()-1, ws < width_cum_seq.size()-1), but out_mat is sized output_size[0..2]·output_size[3]; nothing ties sequence length to output_size[1]/[2] (mention sweep: output_size assigned lines 26–31 from input/ratio; height/width_cum_seq only constrained to input_size by comment), so out_offset exceeds row/col count → OOB col() read+write on out_mat.
Origin: sequences' only guaranteed bound (per comment) is ≤ input_size[1]/[2]; with pooling_ratio = 1.0 the sequences can exceed output_size[1]/[2], instantiating the OOB out_offset.

assumptions: GeneratePoolingSequence is project-internal; its exact length bound is unquoted, but its own comment ('must not be greater than input size') plus output_size = floor(input/ratio) with ratio=1.0 makes longer-than-output sequences achievable within the attacker's parameter surface (attribute pooling_ratio is attacker-supplied op config).
limitations: The `- 1` in `hs < height_cum_seq.size() - 1` (line 116) skips the last interval of each sequence (size_t truncation makes it benign for size≥2); functional, not security.
in_offset bounds (height_max/width_max clamps) verified in-bounds; no OOB on the input tensor.

DCHECK_GT(output_size[i], 0) is compiled out in release; with ratio > input dim, output_size[i] = 0 → zero-size output allocation while sequences have size ≥ 2; that additionally yields sequence size > output_size[i], reinforcing the primary trigger.

verdict.summary: mrb_remove_method is guarded at its only memory-consuming sink: 'if (h && mt_del(mrb, h, mid)) return;' null-checks the method table before the delete and consumes the callee result as the branch condition; the failure path raises NameError (fail-closed). The two residual candidates - a missing NULL check on the class pointer 'c' and the unvalidated symbol domain of 'mid' - cannot be instantiated by a trust-boundary party (a script cannot forge an RClass* and symbol interning produces domain-valid ids) and their impact chains land entirely inside callees not shown, so neither is a vulnerability in this code.

assumptions: mt_del(mrb, h, mid) (internal callee, not shown) returns truthy on successful deletion and false when the key is absent; the code's own use as the if-branch condition documents this boolean contract.
mrb_name_error (internal callee, not shown) raises a NameError exception and does not return; no code after line 7 relies on it returning.
MRB_CLASS_ORIGIN(c) (macro body not shown) only rewrites i-class pointers to their origin class and dereferences c->tt.
Symbol interning in the unshown producing layer yields valid mrb_sym ids; the width-domain surface of mid is nevertheless treated as full uint32 in the analysis.
limitations: NULL-pointer dereference candidate: 'MRB_CLASS_ORIGIN(c); h = c->mt;' dereferences c with no NULL check anywhere in the snippet (mention sweep found no guard). Trigger requires a caller to pass NULL; the only caller is the interpreter's own Ruby-level remove_method handler (not shown), which passes a live class object, so no trust-boundary party can instantiate it; worst case is an equal-privilege process crash. Robustness/contract issue, not a vulnerability in this code.

Unvalidated symbol id: mid is passed to mt_del and to mrb_name_error's '%n' format without any domain check. mt_del is a masked hash delete (safe for any uint32 key), and any out-of-bounds access for an out-of-range id would occur inside mrb_name_error/mrb_sym_name, which are not shown and not characterizable; the impact link is not instantiated in this code.

The snippet alone cannot show the full call path from script-level remove_method; reachability judgments for c and mid rest on the interpreter's argument-resolution layer, which is outside the given code.

verdict.summary: The Compute kernel reads attacker-supplied tensors with epsilon_t->scalar<float>()() and num_streams_t->scalar<int64>()() without validating that the inputs are non-empty scalars of the expected dtype. The only checks present (OP_REQUIRES_OK on input existence, epsilon > 0, num_streams >= 0) run after the reads and never constrain shape or dtype. Feeding an empty (shape {0}) tensor makes the scalar element read access a 0-byte allocation (out-of-bounds read whose garbage value then reaches the epsilon check and the resource constructor); feeding a wrong-dtype tensor aborts the host TF process consuming the untrusted input. The same defect exists at both scalar reads.

evidence.reason: Root cause: unvalidated scalar element read on an attacker-fed tensor. Trigger: the op input kEpsilonName is fed as Tensor(DT_FLOAT, shape {0}); OP_REQUIRES_OK passes (input exists), then this statement reads element 0 from a 0-byte buffer, an out-of-bounds read. No shape/emptiness/dtype guard exists on any path (mention sweep: line 7 fetch only, no other mentions).

Same missing-validation defect, second instantiation: an empty shape-{0} tensor fed for kNumStreamsName passes the OP_REQUIRES_OK existence check on line 14 and is consumed here as a scalar, yielding an 8-byte out-of-bounds read; a wrong-dtype feed aborts the process.

assumptions: Semantics of the TensorFlow framework accessors were relied on per discipline 3: Tensor::scalar<T>()() reads the single element of the tensor's buffer and performs no runtime narrowing of shape or element count quoted in this code; a wrong dtype triggers the accessor's abort. If the framework accessor did enforce scalar shape at runtime, the impact would reduce to a fail-closed error rather than an OOB read.
Ownership of `result` on the ALREADY_EXISTS path rests on the in-code comment 'If one already exists, it unrefs the new one.'
max_elements_ is a member whose producer is not shown; its full domain is unknown and it is consumed only by the not-shown constructor.
limitations: num_streams is checked only as num_streams >= 0 (line 16): values 0 through INT64_MAX are admitted with no upper bound. Any proportional allocation would occur inside the not-shown QuantileStreamResource constructor, so an OOM/amplification impact is not instantiated in this code; recorded as a hardening gap (an explicit upper bound or num_streams >= 1 check would be advisable).

epsilon is bounded only below (epsilon > 0): +inf and denormal positives are admitted, so the comment's performance rationale is not fully enforced; the performance effect lives in the not-shown callee.
Potential leak of `result` if CreateResource fails with a status other than ALREADY_EXISTS without taking ownership; no contract for that arm is quoted in this code, so the trigger is speculative.
Any upstream op shape-function enforcement of scalar inputs is not shown and was not treated as a guard.

verdict.summary: This TensorFlow shape-inference function performs no raw memory, allocation, copy, or injection operations. Its only indexing use, c->Dim(c->input(0), 1), is guarded by the quoted preceding statement TF_RETURN_IF_ERROR(c->WithRank(c->input(0), 2, &unused)), which enforces rank 2 (or sets an unknown rank to 2) and returns on the error path before the use on every execution path; the remaining calls (UnknownDim, Matrix, Vector, set_output) are handle-based shape constructors that accept unknown-dimension sentinels safely. No attacker-reachable failure mode exists in this code.

assumptions: The semantics of TensorFlow's InferenceContext methods (WithRank, Dim, Matrix, Vector, UnknownDim, set_output) are taken as documented framework behavior: they operate on managed ShapeHandle/DimensionHandle values, WithRank returns an error Status on a known-rank mismatch and TF_RETURN_IF_ERROR propagates it before the subsequent Dim call, and the Shape::dim accessor returns an unknown-dimension sentinel for out-of-range indices rather than performing an unchecked memory read.

The InferenceContext pointer c is supplied by the TensorFlow graph-construction framework; the declared shapes within it are attacker-influenced when an untrusted graph/SavedModel is loaded, and the analysis treats the rank of c->input(0) as attacker-data with an unknown-rank sentinel in its domain.
limitations: Dismissed candidate: an out-of-bounds dimension access at c->Dim(c->input(0), 1) if input(0) had rank < 2 was considered, but the quoted guard TF_RETURN_IF_ERROR(c->WithRank(c->input(0), 2, &unused)) blocks it in execution order for all boundary values tested (rank 1, rank 2, unknown rank, larger rank), and the framework accessor itself returns an unknown-dimension sentinel for out-of-range indices as defense in depth.

The function validates only input(0); the op's other inputs (values, dense_shape, weights) are not rank-checked here, but nothing in this code consumes or indexes them, so this is a semantic scope observation with no security effect in this code, not a vulnerability.

verdict.summary: All memory, sentinel, and size sinks in setup_config are covered by quoted guards in execution order: read_config/read_authkey/check_config failure sentinels are tested with 'if (rv < 0) goto out;' before any fall-through, the pointer write 'local->local = 1' is preceded by the find_site_by_name failure arm 'return -EINVAL', and the only buffer write is a sizeof-bounded snprintf that truncates safely. The two observed weaknesses (gcry_control(GCRYCTL_DISABLE_SECMEM, 0) and the ignored find_myself return) have impact chains that depend entirely on code not shown, so neither is an instantiated vulnerability in this code.

assumptions: read_config (unshown) populates the global booth_conf when it returns >= 0; this code's only quoted contract is the 'if (rv < 0) goto out;' sentinel test, which is the documented failure mode it relies on at line 9.
cl.site, cl.configfile, and cl.lockfile are NUL-terminated by the unshown command-line parser; line 25 tests only cl.site[0] for emptiness, not termination, before the %s use at line 27.
find_site_by_name (unshown) sets *local when it returns nonzero; the code's own '!find_site_by_name(...)' test at line 26 defines nonzero as success.
check_config (unshown) validates the configuration, including the 'local' site, when find_myself errors are deliberately ignored at line 33; its failure sentinel is checked at lines 37-38.

The static function's caller in the same translation unit passes a type constant consistent with the cl.type global set by command-line parsing; the line 25 branch on cl.type versus the type parameter assumes that consistency.
limitations: Line 19 'gcry_control(GCRYCTL_DISABLE_SECMEM, 0);' disables libgcrypt secure memory whenever an authfile is configured, so key material handled in standard heap could be exposed through swap or core dumps; the exposure link depends on the unshown read_authkey's allocation behavior, so this is recorded as a hardening weakness, not an instantiated vulnerability.

Line 33 discards find_myself's return value (the comment on line 24 documents this); if find_myself fails for a daemon, 'local' may remain NULL, but any dereference would occur in the unshown check_config or daemon loop, so the trigger's impact is not instantiated in this code.

Lines 44-45: a long booth_conf->name truncates the default PID-file path at sizeof(cl.lockfile)-1; the result remains under the BOOTH_RUN_DIR prefix with a guaranteed NUL, so this is functional truncation with no memory-safety or path-traversal effect.
If built without HAVE_LIBGCRYPT while an authfile is configured, the key is loaded but libgcrypt is never initialized here; any authentication consequence would occur in unshown code.
Line 29 'return -EINVAL;' bypasses the out: label, but out: contains no cleanup (only 'return rv;'), so behavior is equivalent to the goto pattern used elsewhere.

verdict.summary: DoCompute passes attacker-controlled index values from the indices tensor directly into the scatter write functors (ScatterScalarFunctor at lines 42-43 and ScatterFunctor at lines 60-61) without any bounds validation on those values anywhere in this code. The only relevant check, OP_REQUIRES(c, bad_i < 0, ...), executes after the scatter call has already run, so it merely reports an error after the fact, and its reliability depends entirely on the unshown internal functor. An index value such as 7 (or -1) against a params tensor with dim_size(0) == 4 produces an attacker-controlled out-of-bounds heap write (offset and written data both attacker-chosen), i.e., memory corruption.

evidence.snippet:
const Index bad_i = functor(c, c->template eigen_device<Device>(),
                                    params_flat, update, indices_flat);
evidence.reason: Root cause: unvalidated attacker index values (indices_flat, full Index width domain, from c->input(1)) are handed to the scatter write primitive that mutates params_flat at those indices. No statement in this code bounds the values against params->dim_size(0) before this call; the OP_REQUIRES(c, bad_i < 0, ...) on line 44 runs after the write and only reports. Instantiated trigger: params shape [4], indices [1] value {7}, scalar update → scatter writes params_flat(7), out of bounds.

evidence.snippet:
const Index bad_i = functor(c, c->template eigen_device<Device>(),
                                    params_flat, updates_flat, indices_flat);
evidence.reason: Same unguarded sink in the non-scalar branch, with an additional gap: the rank check (lines 9-17) and the prefix check (TensorShapeUtils::StartsWith, lines 51-52) never verify that updates' trailing shape equals params.shape[1:], so updates_flat (shaped {N, num_updates / N} at line 57) can have a different inner extent than params_flat; combined with unvalidated index values this reaches the same out-of-bounds write with attacker-chosen offset and data.

assumptions: The bodies of ScatterScalarFunctor/ScatterFunctor are not shown; their behavior (including any internal bounds checking that sets bad_i) is an assumption and, per GUARD ANCHORING, may not serve as a guard for the sinks at lines 42-43 and 60-61.
OP_REQUIRES/OP_REQUIRES_OK are assumed to have standard TensorFlow macro semantics (set error status and return from the function on failure).
Index is assumed to be a signed integer type (TF convention, typically int32); the analysis only relies on it admitting values outside [0, params->dim_size(0)).
limitations: Speculative secondary: at lines 46-47 and 64-65 the error path evaluates SliceDebugString(indices.shape(), bad_i) and indices_flat(bad_i) with bad_i tested only for bad_i < 0 and never for bad_i < N; an out-of-range bad_i returned by the unshown functor would cause an out-of-bounds read, but the trigger depends on unshown callee behavior, so it is recorded here rather than confirmed.

The exact faulting store of the primary defect executes inside the unshown functor; per the call-site rule the defect is located at the passing statements (lines 42-43, 60-61), which pass raw unvalidated indices into a memory-writing primitive.
Checks at lines 21-22 and 28-29 were edge-tested and found sound (correct variable, bound, and operator); no boundary defect there.

verdict.summary: No attacker-reachable memory, allocation, copy, or injection sink exists in this JIT compiler routine. The bytecode (cc) it consumes is produced by the same-process pattern compiler, so the values are governed by an interface contract rather than a trust boundary, and no statement in this code validates or needs to validate them against an external attacker. The single concrete anomaly found is an always-false condition, 'if (*cc == PT_CLIST && *cc == XCL_PROP)' (PT_CLIST and XCL_PROP are distinct constants, so the PT_CLIST min/max refinement is dead code), which only loosens the computed min/max to the full character range (min=0, max=READ_CHAR_MAX) — a conservative, safe-direction bound that cannot cause min > max or any out-of-range read at the read_char call site.

assumptions: The XCLASS bytecode (cc) is produced by PCRE2's own same-process pattern compiler (pcre2_compile), which is treated as an interface-contract producer, not an attacker: the pattern author controls pattern text, not raw bytecode, so opcode validity (XCL_SINGLE/RANGE/PROP/NOTPROP/END), compares > 0, XCL_END termination, and bounded property indices (cc[1] for PT_GC/PT_PC/PT_SC/PT_SCX/PT_BOOL/PT_BIDICL/PT_CLIST) are assumed validated at parse time in code not shown. If a hostile party could inject arbitrary compiled bytecode, the unchecked cc[1] indices into PRIV(ucp_typerange), PRIV(ucd_caseless_sets), PRIV(ucd_boolprop_sets), and PRIV(ucd_script_sets) would become out-of-bounds reads.

read_char, compile_char1_matchingpath, optimize_class, add_jump, set_jumps, GETCHARINCTEST, SET_CHAR_OFFSET, and SET_TYPE_OFFSET are project-internal callees/macros not shown; their memory safety is assumed per standard JIT compiler design and cannot be verified here.

PT_CLIST, XCL_PROP, and other opcode constants are assumed to be pairwise distinct values, making 'if (*cc == PT_CLIST && *cc == XCL_PROP)' always false (in upstream PCRE2 this reads 'cc[-1] == XCL_PROP').
SLJIT_ASSERT and SLJIT_UNREACHABLE are debug-only in release builds; the invariants they state (compares > 0, opcode domain, sorted caseless sets) are assumed maintained by the bytecode contract.
limitations: The condition 'if (*cc == PT_CLIST && *cc == XCL_PROP)' is always false (it almost certainly should read 'cc[-1] == XCL_PROP' as in upstream PCRE2). Effect: the PT_CLIST min/max refinement in the scanning loop is dead and PROPs always set min=0, max=READ_CHAR_MAX. This is a safe-direction bug (bounds loosened, never inverted; min > max cannot arise), affecting only optimization precision, so it is recorded as a code defect without security impact rather than as a vulnerability.

A class consisting solely of property tests in code paths where the PT_CLIST branch was intended could, in the upstream-intended logic, produce tighter min/max; in the given code no min > max inconsistency is reachable, and even a hypothetical min > max would flow only into the not-shown read_char callee, whose behavior cannot be verified here.

The compares counter transiently reaches -1 in the main generation loop for single-element PT_SC/PT_SCX classes (compares-- at loop top before the PT_SC arm's compares++), mirroring upstream structure; any residual off-by-one would only misroute a jump between the 'list' and 'backtracks' jump lists (match-semantics correctness), not memory safety.

SLJIT_ASSERT/SLJIT_UNREACHABLE compile out in release builds, so malformed bytecode (unreachable per the interface contract) would fall through switch defaults with no error arm; this is defense-in-depth advice, not a reachable defect.

verdict.summary: The Rabin-Williams private-key inversion contains no memory, size, injection, or authorization sink reachable by attacker data. The only attacker-influenced input, the value x to invert, flows exclusively through arbitrary-precision modular arithmetic that reduces it into bounded domains, and every possible computational failure path (degenerate Jacobi-symbol cases, halving adjustments, ModularSquareRoot failure) is neutralized by the unconditional fail-closed verification `if (ApplyFunction(y) != x) throw Exception(...)` before any result is returned. Out-of-domain x values (0, negative, >= n) cause the equality check to fail and throw rather than produce or accept an incorrect result.

assumptions: DoQuickSanityCheck(), MultiplicativeInverse(), Jacobi(), ModularSquareRoot(), CRT(), and ApplyFunction() are project-internal callees not shown; their semantics were not relied upon to dismiss any candidate — the only guard used (the ApplyFunction(y) != x check plus throw) is quoted in this code.
Private key members m_n, m_p, m_q, m_u are treated as internal-trusted operator key material; no statement in this code reads attacker data into them.
The rng parameter is a caller-supplied RandomNumberGenerator per the library's documented API contract.
limitations: Degenerate private keys (e.g., m_n <= 2, making the Randomize range at `r.Randomize(rng, Integer::One(), m_n - Integer::One())` empty or inverted) could cause undefined behavior or an infinite retry loop in the `do { ... } while (rInv.IsZero())` loop. The trigger requires corrupt key material that no attacker-data path in this code can instantiate, so it is speculative here.

If ModularSquareRoot() returns a failure sentinel or throws on a non-residue, the behavior depends on the not-shown callee; either outcome is still caught by the final ApplyFunction verification or propagates as an exception (fail-closed).

The branch at `if (Jacobi(cp, m_p) * Jacobi(cq, m_q) != 1)` performs a same-shift halving of both cp and cq; if this adjustment were mathematically incorrect for some edge case, the result would be rejected by the final check with an exception, which is a functional DoS of a single signing operation initiated by the operator, not a security bypass.

verdict.summary: The packet-memory reads (q->type, q->dnsclass) are guarded by the verified bounds check 'if (p + 4 > max) return PJLIB_UTIL_EDNSINSIZE;', which is correct at both boundary values (p+4==max admitted and safe; p+4==max+1 rejected) and precedes the first use in straight-line execution order with no bypass. Both parser callees are called with the packet end pointer 'max' and their failure sentinels are locally checked ('if (status != PJ_SUCCESS) return status;'). The name buffer allocation 'pj_pool_alloc(pool, name_len+4)' and the offset 'start + name_part_len' carry no local range validation, but their harmful values are producible only by a success-path contract violation of the not-shown same-module helper get_name_len, which no statement of this code instantiates.

assumptions: get_name_len (not shown, same-module static helper) is assumed to return, on PJ_SUCCESS, a non-negative name_len (expanded name length) and name_part_len (consumed byte count) bounded by max-start; its failure sentinel is locally checked via 'if (status != PJ_SUCCESS) return status;'.
The same-file caller (pj_dns_parse_packet) is assumed to pass pkt/start/max pointing into one received DNS message with start <= max; this ordering is not asserted in the given code.

get_name (not shown) is assumed to write into q->name.ptr no more than the name_len+4 bytes allocated from the same parser's computation; no length parameter is passed to it, so this consistency is a cross-callee contract.
pj_pool_alloc is assumed not to return NULL on packet-scale (tens of KB) requests; on failure pjlib pools raise the no-memory exception rather than yielding a NULL that get_name would dereference.
limitations: Speculative (not a vulnerability in this code): if get_name_len could report PJ_SUCCESS while returning name_len < -4 or name_len > INT_MAX-4, the allocation 'pj_pool_alloc(pool, name_len+4)' would be undersized or overflowed and get_name would perform a heap out-of-bounds write; no local check on name_len exists, but the harmful value requires misbehavior of the not-shown helper on its success path.

Speculative: if get_name_len could return a negative name_part_len on success, 'p = (start + name_part_len)' would point before the packet and the lower bound is unchecked locally (only the upper bound 'p + 4 > max' is guarded), giving an out-of-bounds read in the memcpy; same uninstantiable precondition.
The unchecked result of pj_pool_alloc would be a NULL dereference inside get_name, but only under allocation failure no attacker can induce; robustness note, not a vulnerability.

verdict.summary: The main memory-safety sink (memcpy of sample data) is guarded: the destination buffer is allocated with the same expression used as the copy length (gf_filter_pck_new_alloc with ch->sample->dataLength) and the allocation's failure sentinel is checked before the copy. Other sinks (channel-list indexing, purge offset, subsample buffer, tfrf pointer) are bounded by locally quoted checks. Remaining candidates (NULL channel entries, sai_buffer_size assert, uninitialized finfo fields, non-decrementing continue in the stsd-mismatch arm) all depend on the behavior of internal reader/parser callees not shown in this code, so their triggers cannot be instantiated from the given code.

assumptions: isor_reader_get_sample / isor_reader_get_sample_from_item advance ch->sample_num and set/clear ch->sample; their internal behavior is not shown in this code.
gf_isom_sample_is_fragment_start fills all consumed fields of finfo when returning TRUE; the callee body is not shown.
read->channels never contains NULL entries and is not shrunk during a single process() invocation; channel creation/removal code (isoffin_setup, isoffin_configure_pid internals) is not shown.
ch->sai_buffer and ch->sai_buffer_size are consistently set together by the (unshown) sample reader before use here.
isoffin_push_buffer and isoffin_purge_mem manage read->mem_blob allocation/clamping internally; their bodies are not shown.
limitations: Speculative: NULL dereference of ch (from gf_list_get) at the three channel loops would require a NULL entry or mid-invocation list shrink, producible by no statement in this code; robustness note.

Speculative: assert(ch->sai_buffer_size) followed by PROP_DATA(ch->sai_buffer, ch->sai_buffer_size) — under NDEBUG the size is unchecked, but a non-NULL buffer with zero/unset size is only producible by unshown reader code, and the site performs no memory operation with the size; robustness note.

Speculative (CWE-457 shape): GF_ISOFragmentBoundaryInfo finfo is stack-uninitialized and its fields (moof_template, moof_template_size, sidx_start/end, frag_start, mdat_end) are consumed when gf_isom_sample_is_fragment_start returns TRUE; whether the callee initializes all fields on success is unquotable here.

Speculative (CWE-400 shape): the stsd-mismatch arm uses continue without decrementing nb_pck; an unbounded loop would require isor_reader_get_sample to return samples without advancing, which the unshown callee contract prevents from being either claimed or excluded.
Functional: sample_dur *= ch->sample->nb_pack can wrap u32 for large nb_pack values, corrupting only a duration metadata value with no memory sink in this code.
Functional: dep_flags shifts (u8 isLeading<<2|dependsOn<<2|dependedOn<<2|redundant) truncate through integer promotion; worst case is a wrong dependency-flag property value, not memory corruption.

verdict.summary: gf_hinter_finalize consumes the return value of gf_isom_get_esd(file, odT, 1) (line 66) and gf_isom_get_esd(file, sceneT, 1) (line 105) without any NULL check, then dereferences it (esd->decoderConfig, esd->OCRESID, esd->URLString, gf_list_add). An attacker-crafted MP4 containing an OD or SCENE track registered in the root OD but with a missing/invalid ESD makes gf_isom_get_esd return NULL (the same sentinel this code tests for elsewhere at line 144: 'if (!esd) continue;'), causing a NULL-pointer dereference (e.g., at line 98/99 or 134/135) and a crash of the process hinting the untrusted file - a denial of service.

evidence.reason: Origin: the return value of this internal lookup/parse call is assigned to esd with no sentinel test, although the same call is NULL-checked later in the function (line 144).

evidence.snippet:
if (remove_ocr) esd->OCRESID = 0;
			else if (esd->OCRESID == esd->ESID) esd->OCRESID = 0;
evidence.reason: Sink: first unconditional dereference of esd on every path through the if (odT) block. With an OD track whose ESD is invalid, esd == NULL here, so esd->OCRESID is a NULL-pointer read/write - instantiable crash triggered solely by the attacker-supplied file.
Origin: second unchecked lookup; a SCENE track with a missing/invalid ESD yields esd == NULL (sceneT is guaranteed nonzero by the check at line 47).

evidence.snippet:
if (remove_ocr) esd->OCRESID = 0;
		else if (esd->OCRESID == esd->ESID) esd->OCRESID = 0;
evidence.reason: Sink: mirrored dereference of the possibly-NULL esd from line 105 (also reached via esd->decoderConfig at line 121); executed on every ISMA path, including when gf_isom_get_sample_count != 1, so no intervening statement can repair esd.

assumptions: gf_base64_encode(..., buf64, 2000) is assumed to honor its outSize argument (callee not shown); if it does not, the samp->data-derived base64 output could overflow buf64[5000], but that behavior is not provable from the given code.
gf_hinter_can_embbed_data(samp->data, samp->dataLength, ...) is assumed to bound samp->dataLength before the base64/sprintf use; its threshold is not shown.

gf_isom_get_esd returning NULL on a missing/invalid ESD is treated as the standard failure sentinel of a lookup/parse call (discipline 3); the code's own 'if (!esd) continue;' at line 144 corroborates that NULL is a reachable return.
limitations: Potential stack overflow of buf64[5000]/sdpLine[5100] via gf_base64_encode writing more than 2000 bytes is SPECULATIVE: it depends on the unshown callee ignoring outSize and on gf_hinter_can_embbed_data's unknown size threshold; no trigger could be instantiated from the given code alone.
esd->URLString = gf_malloc(...) results are used without NULL checks (lines 90-91, 126-127); this is allocation-failure-only, not attacker-inducible.

When is_ok == 0 (sample too large), the OD/scene esd is still added to the IOD and the function returns GF_OK; functional inconsistency with the 'ISMA disabled' log message, no direct security impact shown.

verdict.summary: This Eval callback validates all tensor pointers it consumes via GetInputSafe/GetOutputSafe whose error sentinels are tested with TF_LITE_ENSURE_OK before any use, and its type dispatch has a rejecting default arm. The only in-code statements consuming attacker-influenced values are guarded; all remaining candidates (discarded EvalDiv return value, dispatch on output->type only, opaque params/data pointers) have both trigger and impact located inside EvalDiv/EvalQuantized/Prepare, none of which are shown, so no defect is instantiated in this code.

assumptions: GetInputSafe/GetOutputSafe are framework safe accessors whose error status is the failure sentinel tested by TF_LITE_ENSURE_OK; on success the output pointers are set to valid tensors.
The return type of EvalDiv (status vs void) is not shown; the sibling EvalQuantized call is wrapped in TF_LITE_ENSURE_OK, suggesting a status return, but this is inferred, not quoted.

node is a valid TfLiteNode pointer supplied by the interpreter framework; node->builtin_data and node->user_data are produced by registration/Prepare code not shown, and are only cast (never dereferenced) in this code.
kernel_type is a template parameter whose value does not influence any memory-safety decision visible in this snippet.
limitations: Line 14 discards the return value of EvalDiv<kernel_type>(...) while the sibling EvalQuantized call on lines 16-17 is checked with TF_LITE_ENSURE_OK. If EvalDiv returns TfLiteStatus and can fail, Eval would report kTfLiteOk on a failed sub-evaluation (fail-open). Both premises require unshown callee behavior, so this is not confirmed here.

The dispatch on lines 13-15 checks only output->type; input tensor types are never validated in this code. A model declaring mismatched types (e.g., uint8 inputs with a float32 output) reaches the float evaluator, but any resulting out-of-bounds read would occur inside the not-shown EvalDiv, and it is unprovable whether the not-shown Prepare rejects such models. Impact chain not instantiated.

params (from node->builtin_data) and data (from node->user_data) are passed to callees without null checks; any null-dereference would land inside EvalDiv/EvalQuantized, whose code is not given. Not instantiable from this snippet.
This function alone cannot be the last line of defense for tensor-shape or type consistency; that responsibility sits in Prepare and the evaluators, neither of which is part of the given code.

verdict.summary: In ReadTGAImage, the TGA comment read 'count=ReadBlob(image,tga_info.id_length,(unsigned char *) comment);' (line 152) never checks that the requested id_length bytes were actually read. On a truncated file, ReadBlob returns less than id_length (e.g. 0), leaving bytes [count, id_length-1] of the freshly AcquireQuantumMemory-allocated heap buffer uninitialized; comment[tga_info.id_length]='\0' then terminates only the end, and SetImageProperty(image,"comment",comment,exception) persists the uninitialized heap bytes as the image's comment metadata, an information disclosure when image properties are read or written out.

evidence.reason: Unchecked short read: ReadBlob's return count is never compared to id_length before the buffer is NUL-terminated only at index id_length and passed to SetImageProperty. A file truncated after the 18-byte header with id_length=255 yields count=0, so 255 uninitialized heap bytes are stored as the image 'comment' property (CWE-908, heap info disclosure).

Origin of the tainted data: the comment buffer is freshly allocated heap memory with indeterminate contents; nothing in the code initializes it, so any short ReadBlob leaves uninitialized bytes that line 154 persists as image metadata.

assumptions: ConstrainColormapIndex is treated as ImageMagick's documented checked accessor that returns an in-range colormap index or raises an exception; all direct colormap indexing in this code goes through it.
AcquireQuantumMemory returns non-zeroed heap (standard allocator semantics); NULL is the only failure sentinel and is checked at line 150.
SetImageProperty retains a copy of the string as the image's named property, which is the universal documented behavior of that API across all ImageMagick coders.

AcquireImageColormap is assumed to reject color counts exceeding MaxColormapSize (and zero), which bounds the 1<<bits_per_pixel (bpp up to 32) and colormap_index+colormap_length (up to 131070) color counts; both call sites check its MagickFalse sentinel.
limitations: Latent out-of-range colormap index (CWE-125, downstream impact only): for Monochrome/RLEMonochrome images with colormap_type==0 and bits_per_pixel 2..7, 'index=(Quantum) ReadBlobByte(image);' in case 8/default is never constrained (ConstrainColormapIndex is used only in the colormap_type!=0 branch and case 15/16), so indexes up to 255 (or 65535 on EOF) are stored into a PseudoClass pixel cache whose colormap has only 1<<bpp entries. The write location itself is in-bounds and no out-of-bounds access occurs within this function; the harmful colormap[index] lookups happen in consumers not shown (e.g. SyncImage/export paths), so the impact chain is not instantiated in this code.
Dead check inside the pixel loop: 'if (status == MagickFalse) ThrowReaderException(...)' tests the stale SetImageExtent/SetImageProgress status; functionally inert, no security effect.

The interleave walk (offset/base) was proven to keep the row index in [0, rows-1] by iteration-count arithmetic; the historical overflow at this site is fixed by the quoted reset 'if (offset >= image->rows) { base++; offset=base; }'.

verdict.summary: SparseFillEmptyRowsOpImpl validates each tensor's shape individually but never checks the consistency between the indices matrix's second dimension (indices_t.dim_size(1)) and the dense_shape vector's length (dense_shape_t.NumElements()) before passing both tensors into the fill functor at the sink. An attacker invoking the op with, e.g., indices of shape [2,5] and dense_shape of shape [3] bypasses every quoted OP_REQUIRES_ASYNC check (IsMatrix, IsVector, IsScalar, dim_size(0) equality, NumElements()!=0), and the memory-consuming fill routine then indexes one tensor using the other's extent, causing a heap out-of-bounds access. The code's own TODO comment (lines 43-44) admits the shape checks are missing; the single absent guard is indices_t.dim_size(1) == dense_shape_t.NumElements(), which appears nowhere in the code.

evidence.snippet:
FunctorType()(context, default_value_t, indices_t,
                                     values_t, dense_shape_t, done),
evidence.reason: Sink: the fill functor is invoked with indices_t and dense_shape_t whose extents are never checked against each other on any path. Trigger instantiated: attacker passes indices matrix [2,5] and dense_shape vector of length 3; all local checks (lines 20, 24, 28, 33, 39, 45) pass; the routine indexes rank columns of indices against dense_shape's length, producing a heap out-of-bounds access. Root cause: missing rank-consistency guard before this call.

Origin of the attacker-controlled tensors: shapes and contents of indices_t and dense_shape_t are chosen by the op invoker across the trust boundary, and both reach the line 51 sink with no local check relating indices' column count to dense_shape's element count.

assumptions: The framework's op registration enforces input dtypes matching the template types T and Tindex; this enforcement is not shown in the given code but is the standard contract of TensorFlow kernels and no local dtype check is customary.

The functor functor::SparseFillEmptyRows performs the actual fill, consuming indices_t's column extent and dense_shape_t's element count together (the standard semantics of this operation); its internal code is not shown.
limitations: The exact primitive (out-of-bounds read vs write) inside the unshown functor is not provable from the given code; the CWE is therefore reported at the container class CWE-119 rather than CWE-787/CWE-125.

dense_shape element contents (int64, including negative or zero values) also reach the functor without local range validation, and index values within indices are not locally checked against dense_shape; these are the same intake-point validation gap but their consuming arithmetic lies entirely in the unshown functor, so they are folded into the primary finding rather than reported separately.

verdict.summary: SparseFillEmptyRowsOpImpl validates only each tensor's individual rank (vector/matrix/scalar) and never validates consistency among indices_t, values_t, and dense_shape_t before passing them to the SparseFillEmptyRows functor. An attacker supplying, e.g., an indices matrix with more rows than values_t has elements, or a dense_shape length different from the indices matrix's second dimension, passes every quoted check; the unvalidated tensors then drive out-of-bounds heap accesses in the op implementation (the known TensorFlow SparseFillEmptyRows heap buffer overflow). The in-code TODO comment explicitly admits the missing cross-shape checks.

evidence.snippet:
OP_REQUIRES_OK_ASYNC(context,
                       FunctorType()(context, default_value_t, indices_t,
                                     values_t, dense_shape_t, done),
                       done);
evidence.reason: The sink: attacker-controlled tensors indices_t, values_t, and dense_shape_t are passed to the SparseFillEmptyRows functor with no consistency validation on any path. No statement checks indices_t.shape().dim_size(0) == values_t.NumElements() or indices_t.shape().dim_size(1) == dense_shape_t.NumElements(), so mutually inconsistent shapes (e.g., indices [3,1] with values of length 1) reach the functor and cause heap out-of-bounds access. This is the missing-validation defect; the upstream fix added exactly these wrapper checks.

Origin of the tainted data: op-kernel tensor inputs whose shapes and contents are attacker-controlled across the TF runtime trust boundary (reachable through the raw op API). These values flow unmodified through the per-tensor rank checks at lines 19-41 to the unguarded sink at lines 44-47.

assumptions: The body of functor::SparseFillEmptyRows is not shown; its consumption of the tensors (per-op semantics: one value per index row, one coordinate per dense rank, row-indexed marker array sized from dense_shape) is inferred from the op contract and the known upstream vulnerability rather than quoted from the given code.
Template context (Device, T, Tindex) and OpKernelContext/TensorShapeUtils are taken as standard TensorFlow machinery with their documented semantics.

The mention sweep found the in-code TODO at lines 37-38 ('add shape checks between values, indices') documenting that the cross-shape checks are absent; it is treated as proof of absence, not as a guard.
limitations: The precise primitive (out-of-bounds write to the row-marking array vs out-of-bounds read of values/indices) depends on the unshown functor body; the read (values(i) for each index row) is guaranteed by the op's semantics, while the write to a buffer sized from dense_shape(0) indexed by attacker row values matches the known upstream heap-buffer-overflow advisory.
Negative or huge dense_shape element values (also unvalidated here) would additionally cause failed allocations/CHECK aborts; that path is a denial-of-service note rather than the primary defect.
The null `done` callback is safely handled by lines 5-7 and is not a defect.

verdict.summary: saveAs only inspects the first path component for '.'/'..' before prepending the upload path, so attacker-supplied filenames with intermediate '..' components (or leading '..') escape the upload directory: directories are created outside the root via create_directories and the uploaded file is written to an arbitrary location by saveTo (arbitrary file write with attacker-controlled content).

evidence.reason: The only confinement guard compares just the FIRST path component (*fsFileName.begin()) against '.' and '..'. An attacker-supplied fileName such as 'subdir/../../../tmp/pwn' has first component 'subdir', passes the test, gets the upload path prepended lexically (operator/ does not normalize '..'), and resolves outside the upload root. A leading '..' also bypasses: the branch is false, no prefix is added, and the path is used as-is. No statement checks intermediate components, normalizes the path, or re-confines it to the upload root.

Unguarded sink: fsFileName, tainted by the attacker-supplied fileName parameter (line 1) and only partially validated by the first-component check, is passed to saveTo with no traversal or confinement validation on any path in this code, yielding a file write outside the intended upload directory (e.g. fileName='subdir/../../../tmp/pwn' writes to /tmp/pwn after create_directories at line 18 creates directories above the root).

assumptions: utils::toNativePath is a separator-conversion helper and does not normalize or reject '..' components (callee not shown; nothing in this code suggests otherwise).
saveTo writes the uploaded file's (attacker-controlled) content to the given path, which is the documented purpose of HttpFileImpl::saveAs/saveTo; its internals are not shown.
HttpAppFrameworkImpl::instance().getUploadPath() returns a fixed configured directory (internal-trusted).
limitations: An absolute fileName (e.g. '/etc/x') is used verbatim with no prepend; this may be intended API surface for application code choosing a destination, but if the value is attacker-derived it is a full confinement bypass sharing the same root cause as the primary finding.
assert(!fileName.empty()) is compiled out under NDEBUG; an empty fileName would then attempt to save to the upload directory itself — robustness only, no distinct security impact.

Actual exploitability depends on how the application obtains fileName (e.g., from a multipart upload's client-supplied filename) and on the process's filesystem permissions; per the analysis rules the parameter is treated as attacker-data at this intake point.

verdict.summary: The return value of the by-index track lookup gf_isom_get_track(movie->moov, i+1) is never checked against NULL before being dereferenced at writer->mdia = trak->Media. A malformed track in an attacker-originated ISO/MP4 file (e.g. a trak box without a usable mdia) makes the lookup miss and return NULL, and the very next dereference crashes the process rewriting the file (denial of service).

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: the return of a lookup over attacker-constructed tracks (parsed file content) is consumed without any sentinel check; a lookup can miss and return NULL for a malformed track, and this failure sentinel is never tested anywhere in the function.

Sink: first dereference of the unchecked trak pointer. With trak == NULL from the malformed attacker-supplied track, trak->Media at line 18 dereferences NULL and crashes the process that ingested the file. No NULL check on trak exists on any path (mention sweep covered lines 13, 18, 19, 20, 23 and the sample_groups block); the code checks the sentinels of GF_SAFEALLOC and gf_isom_box_new but not this lookup, so the missing 'if (!trak)' after line 13 is the single absent guard.

assumptions: gf_isom_get_track is a by-index lookup over the parsed trackList and can miss (return NULL) for a malformed track lacking Media/mediaHeader; per lookup-can-miss semantics its return domain includes NULL. The code never locally validates it, so its safety cannot rest on this assumption either way.

mw and writers are valid internal caller state; behavior of unshown internal callees (CleanWriters, Media_SelfContainedType, Media_IsSelfContainedType, gf_isom_box_new, gf_isom_box_array_del_parent) is not relied on to produce or block the trigger.
limitations: Same-class unchecked parsed-structure dereferences (writer->stbl, stbl->SampleSize, stbl->TimeToSample, stbl->ChunkOffset, mdia->information at lines 19, 31, 33, 42, 57) depend on which fields gf_isom_get_track guarantees; they share the missing-local-validation root cause but were not simulated independently.

The error returns at lines 41 and 47 (gf_isom_box_new failure) skip the exit label and CleanWriters, leaking the current TrackWriter and abandoning partially built writers; a one-shot allocation-failure leak with no attacker-scalable impact.
The constant_dur/constant_size reset logic (lines 33-38) is functionally odd but has no security effect.
Impact is a crash of the process handling the attacker's file; no memory corruption or disclosure was instantiated, so severity is limited to denial of service.

verdict.summary: HttpFileImpl::save joins the attacker-controlled uploaded filename (fileName_, sourced from the multipart Content-Disposition) into the file-write path without any traversal or absolute-path validation: the only guards are 'if (fileName_.empty())' (line 4, wrong invariant) and a traversal check that applies solely to the developer-supplied 'path' argument (lines 7-9, mentions fsPath only). At line 27 the path 'fsPath / fsFileName' reaches saveTo unguarded; a filename such as '../../x' escapes the intended directory and an absolute filename ('/etc/cron.d/x') replaces the entire computed directory per std::filesystem operator/ semantics, yielding an arbitrary file write with attacker-controlled upload content.

evidence.reason: Unguarded sink: the file-write path is built from fsFileName, which originates from the attacker-controlled uploaded filename, with no check anywhere in the function rejecting '..' components or absolute prefixes. Trigger: an attacker uploads a multipart file with filename '/etc/cron.d/x' (absolute RHS replaces fsPath entirely per std::filesystem operator/) or '../../x' (traversal escapes the upload directory), and the uploaded attacker-chosen content is written outside the intended directory. The traversal check at lines 7-9 constrains only the developer-supplied fsPath, never fsFileName.

Origin of the tainted value: fileName_ is the uploaded file's name set by the multipart parser from the HTTP Content-Disposition header (producer not shown; full std::string domain per the width-domain rule). It is converted here with no sanitization for path separators, '..' components, or absolute paths, and flows directly to the saveTo sink at line 27.

assumptions: fileName_ is populated by the multipart/form-data request parser from the HTTP request's Content-Disposition filename field (code not shown); per the width-domain rule and the intake-point shape of HttpFileImpl (HTTP upload handler), it is treated as attacker-controlled data with the full string domain.
utils::toNativePath is assumed to be a path-separator conversion utility only; it is an internal callee not shown and cannot serve as a sanitization guard.

saveTo (internal, not shown) writes the uploaded file content to the supplied path; per discipline 3, passing the unvalidated attacker-derived path at the call site makes the defect local to this code even though the write lands inside the callee.
limitations: The relative-path check on the 'path' parameter (lines 7-9) inspects only the first component ('fsPath.begin()'), so a developer-supplied path like 'a/../../..' would also escape; this argument is developer-supplied rather than attacker-data, so it does not drive the verdict.
TOCTOU between filesystem::exists (line 16) and create_directories (line 20) — no attacker-reachable race window is exhibited within this code.
assert(!path.empty()) is inactive under NDEBUG; the guarded value is the developer-supplied path, not attacker data.
Exploitation is bounded by the server process's filesystem permissions; the write itself (arbitrary location, attacker-controlled content) is the confirmed primary defect.

verdict.summary: btrfs_rm_device drops uuid_mutex around btrfs_shrink_device (lines 55-59) while the device is still on dev_list (list_del_rcu is deferred to line 92). A concurrent invocation of the same ioctl-reachable entry point can look up and pass all checks for the same device during this window, so both contexts execute the removal tail: the second context performs list_del_rcu on freed memory, decrements counters of freed fs_devices, and calls btrfs_free_device/free_fs_devices a second time, producing use-after-free writes and double frees (memory corruption).
