No re-validation, state bit, refcount, or lock covers the window anywhere in the code.

evidence.reason: TOCTOU window: uuid_mutex is released while the target device is still registered (list_del_rcu at line 92 runs only after the relock), so a second concurrent caller of this entry point passes btrfs_find_device_by_devspec and all state checks for the same device and proceeds to remove and free it a second time; no statement re-validates device ownership after the relock.

UAF write sink: executed by the second context after the first context already executed btrfs_free_device(device) at line 126, performing list_del_rcu on freed memory; the synchronize_rcu() at line 125 does not protect a mutex-holding context that captured the pointer during the unlocked window.

Double-free sink: with both contexts holding the same device pointer obtained before the window, this statement frees the same object twice (and free_fs_devices(cur_devices) at line 131 is likewise executed twice), giving attacker-triggerable memory corruption.

assumptions: btrfs_shrink_device, btrfs_find_device_by_devspec, btrfs_num_devices, and the ioctl entry path are not shown; their internal locking (e.g., any dev_mutex inside shrink) is not treated as a guard, since no statement in this code enforces single-ownership of the device across the unlocked window.
Mount-time validation of super_copy fields is not shown and was not assumed when classifying on-disk metadata values.
limitations: Line 111, `num_devices = btrfs_super_num_devices(fs_info->super_copy) - 1;`, underflows to 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF if the mounted image's superblock num_devices is 0 (full u64 domain of attacker-controlled on-disk metadata, no local bound); the corrupted count is stored at line 112, but its harmful consumption occurs in mount/scan code not given, so the impact chain is not instantiated in this code.

The cur_devices->open_devices == 0 branch (lines 128-132) would free the top-level fs_devices when cur_devices == fs_devices; reachability of that state for the main (non-seed) fs_devices depends on mount-state invariants enforced outside this code, so it is recorded as speculative on its own.
A potential lock-order issue between uuid_mutex and fs_devices->device_list_mutex was not analyzed further as no deadlock chain is exhibited within this code.

verdict.summary: In the macro-expansion path of compileRule, macro arguments are appended into the fixed-size line buffer of a stack-local FileInfo (tmpFile.line) with no bounds check: 'tmpFile.line[tmpFile.linelen++] = arg.chars[j];'. The only MAXSTRING guard (tmpFile.linelen >= MAXSTRING) applies solely to the macro-definition copy loop and has exited before the argument-copy loop runs. A table-file author who places a substitution after a definition segment that fills the line buffer (or supplies arguments pushing linelen past MAXSTRING) writes attacker-chosen widechar content past the end of the array on the stack — memory corruption in the process compiling the table.

evidence.snippet:
for (int j = 0; j < arg.length; j++)
	tmpFile.line[tmpFile.linelen++] = arg.chars[j];
evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). tmpFile is a stack-local FileInfo whose line array is bounded by MAXSTRING; the code's own invariant appears at line 157 ('else if (tmpFile.linelen >= MAXSTRING)'), but that guard is inside the definition-copy 'while (i < next)' loop, which has terminated before this argument-copy loop executes. Instantiated trigger: a macro whose definition segment since the last newline is exactly MAXSTRING chars (loop exits with linelen == MAXSTRING without triggering the guard, since i == next) followed by a substitution whose argument has length L >= 1; the loop then writes tmpFile.line[MAXSTRING .. MAXSTRING+L-1] with attacker-chosen characters from the table file, corrupting memory adjacent to tmpFile in compileRule's stack frame.

Origin of the tainted values: macro arguments are read as tokens directly from the attacker-authored table file and later copied at line 170 into tmpFile.line with no length accounting against MAXSTRING, enabling the out-of-bounds write at the sink.

assumptions: CharsString buffers are MAXSTRING-sized and the unshown token/line parsers (getToken, getRuleCharsText, getCharacters, parseChars) cap token and line lengths at MAXSTRING; this underpins dismissing several secondary copy sites (CTO_ExactDots scratchPad, CTO_MultInd, CTO_RepEndWord) as in-bounds.

Macro structure fields (definition, substitutions, argument_count) are produced by the unshown compileMacro from attacker-authored table text; the definition content, newline placement, substitution placement, and argument tokens used in the primary trigger are directly attacker-chosen, so the trigger needs no assumption about compileMacro's grammar.

The expansion block (lines 104-186) is outside the '#ifdef ENABLE_MACROS'; reachability of the macro path requires a build with ENABLE_MACROS and a non-NULL inScopeMacros (table-file compilation context, per the quoted check at line 107).
limitations: Line 168: 'arguments[m->substitutions[2 * subst + 1] - 1]' indexes the argument array (allocated with 'malloc(m->argument_count * sizeof(CharsString))') with no validation that the macro's substitution argument number lies in [1, m->argument_count]; an index of 0 yields arguments[-1]. Trigger depends on whether the unshown compileMacro can store out-of-range or zero indices, so it is not fully instantiated here; the missing local validation at the use site remains a hardening gap.

Line 128: the malloc result for 'arguments' is not checked for NULL; the size is attacker-influenced but small (argument_count * sizeof(CharsString)), so failure requires an environment condition an attacker cannot reliably induce (robustness issue).

CTO_Match/CTO_BackMatch ignore the return of getCharacters(file, &ptn_before/&ptn_after) and then read ptn_before.chars[0] and pass ptn_before.length into _lou_pattern_compile although the local CharsString is uninitialized when the operand is missing (CWE-908 risk); the out-of-bounds-read impact chain passes through the unshown _lou_pattern_compile, so it is recorded rather than confirmed.

CTO_SeqAfterExpression writes (*table)->seqAfterExpression[0..ruleChars.length] with no size check, unlike its sibling cases which quote guards against LETSIGNSIZE / SEQPATTERNSIZE / EMPHMODECHARSSIZE; the declared size of seqAfterExpression is not quotable from the given code, so overflow cannot be proven here.

verdict.summary: SparseCountSparseOutputShapeFn reads dimension 1 of input 0's shape (c->Dim(c->input(0), 1)) without any rank validation. The shape of input 0 is attacker-controlled: a malicious GraphDef/SavedModel or raw_ops call can supply a scalar, rank-1, or unknown-rank tensor as the 'indices' input. Shape inference then indexes one-past-the-end of the shape's dimension vector, causing an out-of-bounds read (or CHECK/DCHECK failure abort) in the host process that loads the attacker's model, and the out-of-bounds-derived DimensionHandle is propagated into the constructed output shapes.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the attacker-controlled shape of input 0 (the 'indices' input of the graph being inferred) is indexed at dimension 1 with no rank guard of any form in the function (no WithRank/WithRankAtLeast/rank check; the sole return path is 'return Status::OK();' so no error arm can reject). Instantiated trigger: a malicious model giving input 0 rank 0, rank 1, or unknown rank makes this a one-past-the-limit (or further) out-of-bounds read of the shape's dimension vector in the process loading the model; the garbage DimensionHandle is then consumed by c->Matrix(nvals, rank) and c->Vector(rank) on lines 4 and 6.

assumptions: InferenceContext::Dim's implementation is not shown; per TensorFlow semantics it indexes the shape's internal dimension vector with bounds enforced only by DCHECK (compiled out in release builds), so the actual out-of-bounds access occurs inside the callee — under the call-site rule the defect remains at line 2, which passes the unvalidated attacker-controlled shape into an indexing operation.

The op registration for SparseCountSparseOutput (not shown) declares input 0 as 'indices: int64' with no rank constraint, and the framework does not pre-validate input ranks before invoking a shape function; no quotable contract narrows the shape's rank below its full domain (any rank >= 0 or unknown).
limitations: The exact runtime effect (CHECK-failure abort in debug builds versus silent out-of-bounds read of vector storage in release builds) depends on the TensorFlow build type; either way the host process loading the attacker-supplied model crashes or reads out of bounds.

The Python-level wrapper tf.sparse.count_sparse_output constructs rank-2 indices via SparseTensor, but raw GraphDef/SavedModel import and tf.raw_ops.SparseCountSparseOutput reach this shape function with attacker-chosen input shapes, so reachability of the trigger does not depend on the wrapper.

verdict.summary: SetupWriters dereferences parser-populated box pointers without NULL checks: the mandatory-box validation at the top of the loop covers stbl, SampleSize, ChunkOffset and SampleToChunk but omits stbl->TimeToSample and trak->Media->mediaHeader. A crafted MP4 whose stbl lacks a stts box (or whose mdia lacks mdhd) reaches the dereferences at lines 39 and 26 and crashes the process ingesting the file (NULL pointer dereference, denial of service).

evidence.reason: NULL pointer dereference: stbl->TimeToSample is set by the (unshown) file parser and is not covered by the validation 'if (!stbl || !stbl->SampleSize || !stbl->ChunkOffset || !stbl->SampleToChunk)' at line 17; a mention sweep shows TimeToSample is touched nowhere else in the function. Trigger: attacker-crafted track whose stbl contains stsz/stco/stsc but no stts box passes the line 17 check, and 'writer->stbl->TimeToSample->nb_entries' dereferences NULL, crashing the process handling the attacker's file.

Independent NULL pointer dereference: trak->Media->mediaHeader appears exactly once in the function and is never checked; the line 16 guard constrains only trak->Media and trak->Media->information. Trigger: attacker-crafted track whose mdia carries minf/stbl (satisfying the line 17 checks) but no mdhd box reaches this read of NULL->timeScale, crashing the process.

assumptions: gf_isom_get_track(movie->moov, i+1) is a 1-based indexed accessor over movie->moov->trackList; with the quoted loop bound 'for (i = 0; i < trackCount; i++)' and 'trackCount = gf_list_count(movie->moov->trackList)' the argument is in range, so the unchecked return at line 14 is treated as valid.

TimeToSample->entries is assumed allocated with at least nb_entries elements by the unshown stts parser; the entries[0] access at line 40 is bounded by the quoted 'nb_entries==1' test only if that allocation contract holds.
Behavior of unshown internal callees Media_SelfContainedType, Media_IsSelfContained, gf_isom_box_new, and CleanWriters is assumed to match GPAC library semantics.
limitations: Early returns 'return GF_ISOM_INVALID_FILE;' (line 18) and 'return GF_OUT_OF_MEM;' (lines 47, 53) leak TrackWriter objects already added to the writers list and the current writer; this is a resource leak on error/OOM paths with no attacker-scalable impact shown.

The unchecked return of gf_isom_get_track at line 14 could crash if the callee returned NULL, but the quoted loop bound over the same list makes the index provably in-domain for a list accessor, so this trigger is not instantiated.
An out-of-bounds read of entries[0] would require the unshown stts parser to under-allocate the entries array relative to nb_entries; no statement in this code produces that condition.

verdict.summary: Examples::Initialize validates every sparse input list against its count (quoted checks at lines 11, 19, 28) but never validates num_dense_features against dense_features_inputs.size(). The unbounded, attacker-domain count sizes per-example dense_vectors_ allocations (line 68), enabling attacker-scalable unbounded allocation/OOM from a tiny op call, and is passed together with the dense list to CreateDenseFeatureRepresentation (lines 78-80), which indexes the list per the count, producing a heap out-of-bounds read of Tensor pointers.

evidence.reason: Primary sink: the unvalidated attacker-domain count num_dense_features is passed together with dense_features_inputs, whose size is never checked against it anywhere in this code; the builder consumes the list indexed by the count, so any count exceeding the actual list size (e.g., num_dense_features=3 with a 1-element list) yields a heap out-of-bounds read of Tensor pointers dereferenced downstream — the defect sits at this call site.

Allocation-sizing sink: num_dense_features has no bound, clamp, or comparison anywhere in this code (mention sweep: declaration line 5, uses lines 6, 68, 79, 82 — no guard); with num_dense_features = INT_MAX and num_examples = 1 the loop allocates INT_MAX * sizeof(DenseVector) bytes from an op call carrying two tiny tensors — attacker-scalable unbounded retention (OOM), CWE-400.

Missing-check site: the dense input list is fetched but its size() is never compared to num_dense_features, in contrast to the three quoted sparse checks (lines 11, 19, 28); this asymmetry is the single missing guard whose absence is the root cause.

Origin of the tainted value: num_dense_features enters as an int parameter whose producer is not shown; its input surface is the full int domain (width-domain rule), and no statement in this code narrows it before the sinks at lines 68 and 78-80.

assumptions: The original TensorFlow op derives num_dense_features from the dense input list size before calling Initialize (caller code not shown); this unquoted contract cannot act as a guard for this analysis.

The bodies of CreateSparseFeatureRepresentation, CreateDenseFeatureRepresentation, and ComputeSquaredNormPerExample are not shown; their consumption of the passed count/list pair is inferred from their signatures and treated per the call-site impact rule.
OpKernelContext::input/input_list and Tensor::flat semantics follow the TensorFlow framework's documented behavior.
limitations: Signed overflow at line 6 (num_features_ = num_sparse_features + num_dense_features) requires num_sparse_features near 2^31, but the quoted check at line 11 pins it to the physically supplied sparse tensor count, so the overflow is not realistically instantiable by an attacker.

flat<float>() enforces dtype with a CHECK and tensorflow_cpu_worker_threads() returns NULL on non-CPU devices; both are guarded by op-registration/framework constraints outside the shown code, so any residual crash there is speculative.
The check at line 39 (>= INT_MAX) slightly over-rejects exactly INT_MAX, where static_cast<int> would still be representable — harmless over-rejection, no under-admission at any bound.

verdict.summary: The per-channel loop is bounded by depth = input_max.NumElements() (line 6), but nothing in this code validates that input's channel (last) dimension equals depth. transposed_input.chip<0>(i) therefore indexes the input tensor buffer out of bounds for any i >= input.dim_size(input.dims()-1), a heap out-of-bounds read reachable by an attacker who supplies the model with mismatched tensor shapes. A second, independent defect: the guard 'input_min.dim_size(0) == depth' checks the wrong quantity, so a rank-2 input_min of shape [depth, 0] passes validation while its flat buffer holds 0 elements, making input_min_data[i] an out-of-bounds/null read.

evidence.reason: Primary defect (sink): the loop bound is depth, taken from input_max.NumElements(), but transposed_input's dimension 0 is input's last dimension (flat_inner_dims + shuffle({1,0})). No statement in the code ties these together, so chip<0>(i) reads past the input buffer. Instantiated trigger: input shape [1,1], input_min shape [100], input_max shape [100] passes both OP_REQUIRES checks; at i=1 chip<0>(1) reads past the 4-byte input allocation (and up to depth-1 elements further), an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

Origin of the tainted loop bound: depth is derived solely from input_max's element count, an attacker-chosen graph shape decoupled from input's channel dimension; every downstream use (loop bound, ranges sizing, min/max indexing) inherits this unvalidated value.

Secondary defect (sink): input_min_data points at input_min's flat buffer, whose size is input_min.NumElements(), yet the only validation checks dim_size(0) == depth. With input_min shaped [depth, 0] (dim_size(0) == depth passes, NumElements() == 0), the flat buffer is empty and input_min_data[i] for i in [0, depth) is an out-of-bounds/null read induced purely by attacker-controlled tensor shapes.

evidence.snippet:
OP_REQUIRES(
        ctx, input_min.dim_size(0) == depth,
        errors::InvalidArgument("input_min has incorrect size, expected ",
                                depth, " was ", input_min.dim_size(0)));
evidence.reason: Missing/incorrect guard site: the check constrains input_min's first dimension only, not the total element count of its flat buffer (and not input's channel dimension at all). At the boundary value shape [depth, 0] it passes while the consumed buffer has 0 elements, so the check fails to keep input_min_data[i] inside its required domain.

assumptions: Tensor shapes and contents are attacker-controlled: this op kernel is an intake point executing a node of a possibly untrusted model/graph, so input, input_min, and input_max (including their ranks and dim sizes) fall under the width-domain rule.
Release builds of Eigen used by TensorFlow omit the debug bounds assertion inside chip(), so the out-of-range chip index performs the out-of-bounds read rather than aborting.
limitations: The data races on is_non_negative (written inside the OpenMP parallel loop without a reduction clause) and on out_min_max on the _MSC_VER pragma path are correctness issues with no direct security impact.

std::vector<float> ranges(depth) with an enormous attacker-chosen depth can throw std::bad_alloc, but the attacker must first allocate an equally large input_max tensor, so this is self-limiting rather than amplification.
Calling dim_size(0) on a rank-0 input_min is undefined behavior in TensorFlow's TensorShape internals; it is not independently exploitable beyond the defects already reported.

verdict.summary: The sparse-dense binary op kernel iterates over the sparse entry count using a 32-bit signed loop counter: 'for (int i = 0; i < nnz; ++i)' where nnz is the 64-bit attacker-controlled row count of sp_indices (const int64_t nnz = indices_t->dim_size(0)). No check anywhere bounds nnz below INT_MAX. With nnz = 2^31 (a valid, allocatable tensor size on 64-bit hosts), ++i overflows int, wraps negative, and the loop continues; indices_mat(i, d) then reads out of bounds and dense_gathered_flat(i) = rhs_ref.coeff(idx) writes out of bounds (heap corruption). The per-dimension FastBoundsCheck guard on idx is correct and executes before the sink, but it validates idx, not the loop counter i.

evidence.reason: Root cause: 32-bit signed loop counter i compared against 64-bit nnz (attacker-controlled row count of sp_indices). When nnz > INT_MAX, ++i overflows and wraps negative while i < nnz still holds, so subsequent iterations index with negative i. No statement in the code bounds nnz below 2^31 (mention sweep: dim-equality check, shape-length check, NumElements>0 check, and the two allocations sized from nnz — none caps it).

Sink: with the wrapped counter (e.g., i = -2147483648 after nnz = 2^31 iterations), this is an out-of-bounds heap WRITE (and indices_mat(i, d) at line 92 an out-of-bounds read). The FastBoundsCheck at line 93 validates only idx[d], not i, so it cannot prevent this.

Origin of the tainted value: nnz is the first dimension of the attacker-supplied sp_indices tensor, a full-domain 64-bit count with no range check before it is consumed as a loop bound against a 32-bit counter.

assumptions: FastBoundsCheck(idx, limit) implements index >= 0 && index < limit (standard TF helper semantics); the guard at line 93 with the OP_REQUIRES return at lines 97-100 was verified to run before the coeff sink each iteration and is correct at both bounds.
Tensor dtypes (sp_indices/sp_shape int64, sp_values/dense of type T) are enforced by op registration at dispatch; vec<int64_t>()/matrix<int64_t>() would otherwise CHECK-fail on mismatched dtypes.
Eigen TensorMap flat/matrix accessors perform no release-mode bounds checking, so negative indices read/write out of bounds rather than trapping.
limitations: Negative or overflowing dimensions in sp_shape are passed unchecked into TensorShape(shape_vec) at line 42; if the constructor CHECK-fails on negative dims this is a crash-only DoS, but the callee's behavior on negative input is not shown and not a standard-library semantic, so it is recorded as speculative rather than confirmed.

Exploitability of the confirmed defect requires the process to successfully allocate tensors of roughly 2^31 elements (tens of GB); this is an environment resource constraint, not a code guard, and TF explicitly supports tensors of that size on 64-bit hosts.

The OOB write at line 101 additionally requires the OOB-read index value at line 92 to pass FastBoundsCheck; adjacent heap contents include the attacker's own large input tensors, making this attacker-influenceable but not fully deterministic; the OOB read at line 92 occurs unconditionally once i wraps.

verdict.summary: The DeleteSessionTensor kernel validates only the SHAPE of input 0 (IsScalar) but never its dtype before calling handle.scalar<tstring>()(). An attacker supplying a scalar tensor of a non-string dtype (e.g., int64/double) causes the tensor's small raw buffer to be reinterpreted as a tstring object, a type confusion that reads beyond the allocation and treats attacker-supplied bytes as string pointer/size fields, which are then dereferenced during the session-state lookup in DeleteTensor. Impact: memory corruption class (out-of-bounds/arbitrary read) in the host process triggered by untrusted graph input; fixed upstream only by adding an explicit DT_STRING check that is absent here.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the only check on `handle` is a shape check (IsScalar), which constrains dimensionality but not dtype; line 5 then unconditionally reinterprets the tensor buffer as tstring. Instantiated trigger: attacker feeds a scalar int64/double tensor whose 8 bytes become the tstring's pointer field, so the dereference in session_state->DeleteTensor(name) (line 10) performs an out-of-bounds/arbitrary read. No dtype check exists anywhere in the function (mention sweep: handle appears only at lines 2, 3, 5).

assumptions: `session_state->DeleteTensor(name)` is a standard map-lookup-style callee; its internal behavior is not shown, but the harmful reinterpretation and the OOB read of the type-confused tstring occur at line 5 and at the line-10 call site in this code.

In release builds, Tensor::scalar<T>() does not enforce the dtype at runtime (its type assertion is a DCHECK), so the reinterpretation reaches the sink; in the analyzed code no runtime dtype guard is present in any build configuration.
limitations: The null-session-state and DeleteTensor-status checks are correctly implemented and are not defects.
A missing input-0 (no tensor fed) is handled by the framework outside this code and was not evaluated.

verdict.summary: In php_wddx_pop_element, the __wakeup invocation discards the return value of call_user_function_ex and unconditionally executes zval_ptr_dtor(&retval) on a stack zval that was never initialized. When the attacker-chosen deserialized class has no __wakeup method (e.g. stdClass or the incomplete-class fallback), the call fails and leaves retval with stale stack contents; the subsequent zval_ptr_dtor consumes this uninitialized value, branching on a garbage type byte and, when the refcounted flag is set, decrementing/freeing through a garbage pointer. The result is memory corruption or, at minimum, a remotely-triggered crash in the process deserializing the attacker's wddx packet.

evidence.reason: retval is declared without an initializer (line 41) and the return value of call_user_function_ex is discarded; the call provably fails (FAILURE, retval untouched) when the deserialized object's class lacks __wakeup, a class the attacker selects via the packet's php_class_name value. zval_ptr_dtor(&retval) then consumes the uninitialized zval, reading a garbage type and possibly decrementing/freeing through a wild pointer (memory corruption) or crashing the process. The minimal guard — initializing retval (ZVAL_UNDEF) or testing the call's SUCCESS return before the dtor — appears nowhere in the code (retval is mentioned only at lines 41, 45, 48).

assumptions: wddx_stack_top returns the element at stack->top-1 and succeeds for top >= 1; this code's quoted guard 'if (stack->top == 0) { return; }' (line 11) and the guarded decrements (lines 24, 52) keep every deref of ent1/ent2 in range.
The not-shown start-element handler pushes st_entries, estrdup's varname as a NUL-terminated string, and sets stack->varname; strlen(ent1->varname) at line 106 relies on that termination contract.
php_base64_decode in non-strict mode returns a valid (possibly empty) zend_string, never NULL, so ZVAL_STR at line 36 cannot store a NULL string.

zend_call_function/call_user_function_ex leave fci->retval untouched when returning FAILURE for a non-callable __wakeup; this is the documented API contract relied on per callee-semantics rules, not a statement of the given code.
limitations: The EL_FIELD branch (lines 120-124) pops and efree's the top stack entry without the 'stack->top > 1' guard used elsewhere and without destroying ent->data/ent->varname; a crafted packet like '<struct><field/></struct>' frees the container under construction and leaks its zval tree, desynchronizing the parser. Within the given code the freed entry is never dereferenced (top is decremented together with the free), so the corruption impact would depend on the not-shown wddx_deserialize result extraction; recorded as a leak/desync issue, not promoted.

Several pop paths (lines 58, 113, and the fall-through when ent2->data is neither array nor object) efree the st_entry without zval_ptr_dtor on its data, leaking memory proportional to the attacker's input size; no unbounded amplification was shown.

verdict.summary: The scalar validation for the requested_output_max input re-checks input_requested_min.NumElements() == 1 instead of validating input_requested_max, so a zero-element requested_output_max tensor reaches input_requested_max.flat<float>()(0) (line 34), causing a heap out-of-bounds read whose 4-byte value is then written to the readable output_max tensor (information disclosure) or a null dereference.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read: element 0 is indexed without any check that input_requested_max has at least 1 element. Triggered by supplying requested_output_max as a 0-element float tensor; the leaked float is later stored to the caller-readable output_max tensor.

Origin of the defect: the guard intended to validate requested_output_max instead re-checks input_requested_min (copy-paste of the requested_min check at lines 23-25), leaving input_requested_max.NumElements() unvalidated anywhere in this code.

assumptions: Op registration code is not shown; it presumably constrains input dtypes so that flat<qint32>()/flat<float>() type mismatches are rejected by the framework before Compute — an unquoted contract, relied on only for excluding CHECK-fail crashes, not for the primary finding.
Release-build Eigen TensorMap operator() performs no bounds assertion on flat()(index); debug builds may instead abort.
limitations: The QINT8 validation checks input_requested_min_float < 0.0f while the error message names requested_output_max — a functional/message bug with no memory-safety impact.

The loop counter int i compared against size_t depth can overflow only if depth > INT_MAX, which requires a >8 GB input_min_vec tensor already materialized by the framework; proportional, not an amplification primitive.

std::vector<float> scales(depth) can throw std::bad_alloc for a huge depth; the catch clause only handles mkldnn::error, so an uncaught exception aborts the process — DoS at equal privilege requiring the attacker to already allocate a correspondingly huge tensor.
Division by a zero requested_min_max yields IEEE inf/NaN in the scales, not a memory-safety fault.
Passing a tensor with a wrong dtype would trigger a CHECK failure inside Tensor::flat<T>() (controlled abort); this is a framework-contract question since the op's type registration is not shown.

verdict.summary: gf_hinter_finalize consumes the return of gf_isom_get_esd without a NULL check: a crafted MP4 whose scene or OD track is referenced in the root OD but has a missing/malformed esds makes gf_isom_get_esd return NULL, which is then dereferenced at esd->OCRESID (and esd->decoderConfig / gf_list_add), crashing the process that consumes the untrusted file. The code itself proves this call can return NULL (it tests 'if (!esd) continue;' later at another call site), but no NULL guard exists on any path between the assignments and the first dereferences.

evidence.snippet:
if (remove_ocr) esd->OCRESID = 0;
		else if (esd->OCRESID == esd->ESID) esd->OCRESID = 0;
evidence.reason: Unconditional NULL-pointer dereference: esd comes from gf_isom_get_esd (line 105) with no NULL check; a malformed scene-track esds makes esd NULL and this read crashes the process. Triggered purely by crafted file content during ISMA hinting.

Origin of the tainted value: an internal lookup/parse call whose NULL failure sentinel is proven in-domain by the code's own test 'if (!esd) continue;' at line 144 for the same call; its result is consumed here without any sentinel check.

evidence.snippet:
if (remove_ocr) esd->OCRESID = 0;
			else if (esd->OCRESID == esd->ESID) esd->OCRESID = 0;
evidence.reason: Identical unguarded dereference of the odT-instance esd from gf_isom_get_esd(file, odT, 1) (line 66); a malformed OD-track esds yields NULL and this statement crashes.
Origin of the odT-instance tainted value: unchecked failure-sentinel-bearing return consumed at lines 84, 98-99 and 102.

assumptions: Behavior of unshown internal callees is treated as assumptions in both directions per discipline 3: gf_base64_encode's honoring of dstLen=2000, gf_hinter_can_embbed_data's size limit, and gf_isom_get_esd's NULL-on-miss (the NULL sentinel itself is established by this code's own 'if (!esd) continue;' at line 144).
The root OD and track/ESD layout come entirely from the parsed file and are treated as attacker-controlled content.
limitations: Potential stack overflow at lines 80-82/117-119/172-176 (buf64[5000]/sdpLine[5100] vs gf_base64_encode with dstLen 2000) could not be verified: it requires gf_base64_encode to ignore its dstLen parameter, and that callee is not shown; with any dstLen-honoring implementation the arithmetic fits (max ~2050 bytes into 5100).
gf_malloc results at lines 90 and 126 are not checked before strcpy; trigger requires allocation failure the attacker cannot induce.

GF_SLConfig slc (line 5) is used partially uninitialized in the sceneT path when InitSL_NULL (line 70) never ran (odT==0 or OD sample not embedded); the uninitialized fields flow into gf_isom_set_extraction_slc, an unshown callee, so the impact chain is not instantiated (CWE-908 precursor).
sprintf uses '%d' for the u32 bandwidth at line 15; output is at most ~11 characters into a 5000-byte buffer, so no overflow is reachable.

verdict.summary: This libpq connection state machine validates every server-controlled byte it consumes: the message type byte is restricted to 'R'/'E', the message length word is range-checked per type (8..2000 for auth requests, 8..30000 for errors) before any buffer sizing, the buffered-body check `avail < msgLength` plus the checked `pqCheckInBufferSpace` sentinel ensure complete messages, negotiation bytes ('S'/'N'/'E', 'G'/'N'/'E') are handled by fully-enumerated switches with rejecting default arms, and all PGresult accessor uses are preceded by explicit NULL/status/tuple checks. No memory-safety, injection, or trust-boundary defect is reachable from a malicious server in this code.

verdict.summary: pgpPrtParams walks attacker-supplied PGP packets using fields (pkt.body, pkt.blen) filled by the unshown decodePkt callee and never bounds-checks them: it passes pkt unvalidated into the memory-consuming pgpPrtPkt (line 22) and advances p by the raw sum (pkt.body - pkt.head) + pkt.blen (line 25) with no comparison against pend on any path, so an out-of-range blen/body (full declared-width domain, producer not shown) yields a heap out-of-bounds read of attacker-scalable size and moves p past the buffer.

evidence.reason: Sink: pkt (raw pkt.body pointer and pkt.blen size, produced by unshown decodePkt at line 11) is passed to the memory-reading pgpPrtPkt with no local check that pkt.body + pkt.blen lies within [pkts, pend]; the mention sweep (lines 5, 10, 11, 15, 18, 22, 25, 30) contains no bound, clamp, mask, or sentinel test on these fields, so a width-domain blen exceeding the remaining buffer instantiates a heap out-of-bounds read (crash landing inside the callee does not break the chain).

Origin of the tainted values: decodePkt (project-internal, not shown) fills pkt.head, pkt.body, pkt.blen and pkt.tag from attacker-controlled packet bytes; only its return sentinel is checked, and the length argument pend - p bounds what is handed to the callee, not the fields it stores, so pkt.body/pkt.blen reach lines 22 and 25 with their full declared-width surface and no local validation.

Unguarded pointer advance consuming the same unvalidated fields: no statement verifies the sum stays within pend - p (the while (p < pend) at line 10 tests only the current p, and line 30 runs after the uses), so an oversized or sign-confused pkt.body - pkt.head + pkt.blen moves p beyond the buffer; the one-line guard whose absence is the defect (break if pkt.body + pkt.blen > pend before lines 22/25) appears nowhere in the code.

assumptions: struct pgpPkt's definition is not given; pkt.blen is treated as an unsigned/size_t-width field whose full declared-width domain is instantiable per the width-domain rule, and pkt.body/pkt.head as pointers with no quoted ordering constraint.

decodePkt, pgpPrtPkt, pgpDigParamsNew and pgpDigParamsFree are project-internal callees not shown; their behaviors are assumptions that per the analysis rules can neither protect the sinks nor block the trigger, and the absent local validation at lines 22/25 is the defect.
pkts/pktlen are assumed to be a matching pointer+length pair from the caller (standard C interface); this code forms and consistently uses pend from them.
limitations: digp from pgpDigParamsNew (line 18) is not NULL-checked before pgpPrtPkt(&pkt, digp) at line 22 (potential CWE-476), but the only in-domain trigger is allocation failure, which an attacker cannot induce — environment-triggered robustness issue, not a vulnerability.

A wraparound of p at line 25 followed by decodePkt reading through the wild p would require a near-maximum pkt.blen (field width not shown); recorded as speculative in addition to the confirmed OOB-read path through line 22.

pkts == NULL with pktlen > 0 makes pend = pkts + pktlen and enters the loop with a NULL p; this requires the caller to violate the pointer/length interface contract rather than attacker-controlled content, so it is not counted as a trigger.

If the advance at line 25 merely overshoots pend without the fields themselves being out of range, the function fails closed (rc = -1, digp freed) — the instantiated security impact is the out-of-bounds read through line 22, not the status path.

verdict.summary: This hardened ImageMagick GetEXIFProperty parses attacker-supplied EXIF data, but every memory sink is guarded by a quotable check in execution order: entry reads are bounded by 'if (q > (exif+length-12)) break;', value-data windows by the dir_offset triple check ending in 'if (((size_t) dir_offset+number_bytes) > length) continue;', the fixed-size directory stack by 'level < (MaxDirectoryStack-2)' (max write index 14 of 16), multiplication overflow by 'if (number_bytes < components) break;', and buffer formatting by the per-iteration clamp 'if (length >= (MaxTextExtent-1)) length=MaxTextExtent-1;'. The in-bounds q+8 inline path, duplicate-tag pointer comparison, and unchecked AcquireString/NewSplayTree returns are functional or allocation-failure-only issues with no instantiated security impact.

assumptions: ReadPropertyByte/Short/Long read 2- or 4-byte width-bounded values and ReadPropertyByte advances the pointer/decrements the remaining length; these are the documented semantics of these ImageMagick helpers.

FormatLocaleString follows snprintf semantics (bounded write with NUL, returns the would-be length); the macro clamp 'if (length >= (MaxTextExtent-1)) length=MaxTextExtent-1;' makes the buffer writes safe under either return-value convention, including a negative error return.
AcquireString allocates strlen(source)+MaxTextExtent bytes, so the subsequent FormatLocaleString(key,MaxTextExtent,...) writes fit; this is the canonical ImageMagick idiom.
GetValueFromSplayTree/AddValueToSplayTree on a NewSplayTree result behave as documented (NULL sentinel on miss); the code tests the sentinel ('== q' and 'if (p == (const char *) NULL)').
limitations: The duplicate-tag check 'for (i=0; i < level; i++) if (directory_stack[i].directory == (exif+tag_offset1))' compares against the fixed base exif+0 or exif+0x10000 rather than the newly pushed exif+offset, so it does not detect revisiting an arbitrary sub-IFD offset. This is functionally wrong but has no security effect here: the q-keyed splay tree prevents any directory entry from being processed twice, and level is hard-capped, so no unbounded loop or stack growth is reachable.

key=AcquireString(property) and exif_resources=NewSplayTree(...) results are not NULL-checked; a NULL would be dereferenced on the following FormatLocaleString/SubstituteString calls. Only reachable through allocation failure, which no attacker input value instantiates, so this is robustness, not a vulnerability.

Computing q=(directory+(12*entry)+2) and directory+2+(12*number_entries)+4 can form pointers beyond one-past-end of the profile object before the comparison rejects them (theoretical UB), but no read or write occurs through those pointers; the comparisons still correctly gate every subsequent dereference.

A pushed sub-IFD directory pointer with offset == length-1 passes its own validation but is rejected by the loop-top check 'directory > (exif+length-2)' before the 2-byte entry-count read on the next iteration; confirmed safe at the boundary.

verdict.summary: All memory-sizing and indexing uses are internally consistent: memset lengths exactly match their allocations, and the loop bound m_ucCount provably matches the m_ppDownsampler allocation size, with no integer overflow possible at UBYTE width (max 16320 bytes). The only concrete anomaly, unchecked AllocMem returns passed to memset, can only trigger on allocation failure of a small (<=16KB) request, which no attacker can induce; remaining concerns rest on unshown internal callees (ComponentOf, CreateDownsampler) and are speculative.

assumptions: m_pEnviron->AllocMem is assumed to be the library's allocator; whether it throws or can return NULL is not shown in this code.
m_ucCount, m_ulPixelWidth, m_ulPixelHeight are member fields whose producers are not shown; their consistency with m_pFrame's actual component count and dimensions is an unshown contract.
The semantics of ComponentOf, SubXOf/SubYOf, CreateDownsampler, TablesOf, isDownsamplingInterpolated, and PrepareForEncoding are not shown.
limitations: Unchecked allocation sentinel: m_pEnviron->AllocMem return is not NULL-checked before memset(m_ppEncodingMCU,0,...) and memset(m_ppDownsampler,0,...). If AllocMem can return NULL, this is a NULL dereference; trigger requires allocation failure for a <=16KB request, which is environment-induced, not attacker-induced — robustness, not a vulnerability here.

Unchecked internal callee return: comp = m_pFrame->ComponentOf(i) is dereferenced (comp->SubXOf()) without a sentinel check; triggerable only if ComponentOf returns NULL for i < m_ucCount, a behavior not shown in this code.

Raw sizes m_ulPixelWidth/m_ulPixelHeight and subsampling factors sx,sy are passed to the unshown DownsamplerBase::CreateDownsampler without local validation; any harmful use would occur inside that callee, whose implementation is not given.
The entire body compiles only under #if ACCUSOFT_CODE; with that macro undefined the function is empty.

verdict.summary: btrfs_rm_device dereferences the unvalidated pointer parameter device_path in strcmp(device_path, "missing") whenever the device lookup fails with -ENOENT, although devid-based removal legitimately supplies NULL and no NULL check exists anywhere in the function; additionally, the explicit uuid_mutex drop around btrfs_shrink_device creates a check-to-use race window in which a concurrent invocation can re-validate and remove the same device object, leading to a double rw_devices decrement, use-after-free, and double free of the btrfs_device.

evidence.reason: device_path is a pointer parameter of a non-static exported entry point whose producer is not shown; its full domain includes NULL (devid-based removal passes no path). When btrfs_find_device_by_devspec returns ERR_PTR(-ENOENT) — the exact failure sentinel this line itself anticipates — strcmp dereferences NULL with no guard. Mention sweep over the whole function shows device_path appears only at line 18 (pass-through) and here; the one-line guard `device_path &&` exists nowhere. Instantiated trigger: btrfs_rm_device(fs_info, NULL, devid) with lookup miss → kernel NULL dereference (CWE-476), crashing a higher-privileged process on attacker-supplied data.

All validation (raid minimum, device lookup, swapfile/replace/last-writable checks) happens under the first uuid_mutex hold, then the mutex is explicitly dropped across btrfs_shrink_device and re-taken after — an exhibited check-to-use window. A second concurrent caller can lock uuid_mutex, find and validate the same still-listed device, execute `device->fs_devices->rw_devices--;` (line 51) a second time for the same device, and then operate on it after the first caller's `btrfs_free_device(device)` at line 126 — use-after-free at lines 68/72/90/139 and double free at line 126. No membership recheck, REMOVING bit, or per-device serialization exists between the unlock and the free on any path.

Terminal free of the shared device object reached without any re-validation after the uuid_mutex window at lines 55-59. In the simulated interleaving, the losing thread subsequently executes btrfs_rm_dev_item(device) / clear_bit(&device->dev_state) / list_del_rcu(&device->dev_list) / btrfs_reada_undo_remove_dev(device) on this freed object and calls btrfs_free_device(device) again — use-after-free writes and a double free (CWE-416), memory corruption in kernel context triggered by two concurrent attacker-initiated device-removal requests.

assumptions: btrfs_find_device_by_devspec and all other project-internal callees are not shown; per the width-domain rule their parameter and return domains are taken in full (device_path may be NULL; the return may be any ERR_PTR including -ENOENT, the sentinel the given code itself tests at line 21).

The ioctl entry point supplying device_path/devid is not shown; per discipline 4 the data-carrying parameters of this non-static intake function are attacker-data, and unshown privilege gating (e.g. CAP_SYS_ADMIN) cannot demote a candidate.
btrfs_num_devices and the superblock device count are assumed to reflect a mounted filesystem (at least 1); this is not instantiable to 0 from the given code.
limitations: Potential free of the live fs_devices at lines 128-131 when cur_devices == fs_devices and open_devices reaches 0: requires a mounted filesystem with zero open devices; the precondition could not be instantiated, recorded as a robustness concern only.
num_devices - 1 at line 14 and btrfs_super_num_devices(...) - 1 at line 111 can wrap only if the mounted fs reports 0 devices; trigger precondition not instantiable from the given code.
device_path NUL-termination depends on the unshown caller; judged under the width-domain rule together with the NULL-pointer finding rather than as a separate candidate.

Any per-device serialization inside the unshown btrfs_shrink_device could narrow the race window in practice; per discipline 3 it can neither produce nor block the trigger, so the defect is judged on this code alone.

verdict.summary: The kernel validates only the RANK of updates (updates.dims() == indices.dims() + params->dims() - 1) and that indices.shape is a PREFIX of updates.shape, but never checks that the trailing dimensions of updates.shape match params.shape[1:]. An attacker-supplied updates tensor with a wider (or narrower) innermost extent than the variable's row width reaches the scatter functor (params_flat vs updates_flat with mismatched row widths), producing an out-of-bounds write into (or out-of-bounds read of) the params buffer with attacker-controlled values.

evidence.snippet:
const Index bad_i = functor(c, c->template eigen_device<Device>(),
                                    params_flat, updates_flat, indices_flat);
evidence.reason: Sink: the scatter functor is handed params_flat (row width = product of params dims 1:) and updates_flat (row width num_updates / N, fully attacker-controlled via updates.shape) with no check that the two widths match; e.g. params [10,3], indices [4] with valid values {0,1,2,3}, updates [4,64] passes every check in this function, and the scatter of a 64-element row into a 3-element row writes out of bounds of the params buffer with attacker-controlled update values (mirrored direction, updates [4,2], yields an out-of-bounds read).

Root cause: this check (whose own error message claims 'Must have updates.shape = indices.shape + params.shape[1:]') compares only the number of dimensions, never the sizes; combined with the prefix-only StartsWith check at line 58, the trailing extent of updates.shape is never reconciled against params.shape[1:], so the mismatched-width trigger reaches the functor call at lines 66-67 unguarded.

assumptions: The bodies of functor::ScatterFunctor / ScatterScalarFunctor are not shown; per the analysis rules their internal bounds behavior cannot serve as a guard, and the defect is judged at the call site in this code that passes the mismatched, attacker-derived matrices. Under any scatter implementation that applies all update elements (the semantics its name and this code's error message describe), at least one mismatch direction yields an out-of-bounds access; only an unquoted internal clamp to min(width) would neutralize it.

ValidateInput<T>, LookupResource, and the op's registered shape-inference function are not shown; none can be relied on (resource-variable shapes are not knowable to shape inference at graph-build time).
Op-kernel inputs (tensor contents and shapes) are treated as attacker-data per the intake-point rule; the concrete trigger needs only ordinary in-domain op inputs.
limitations: Row-index VALUES (indices contents, full int32 domain) are passed raw into the functor calls (lines 48-49 and 66-67); the only validation is the functor's bad_i return, consumed by the post-hoc OP_REQUIRES at lines 50/68 which runs after the functor. Safety here rests on the unshown functor's check-before-write contract, so it is recorded as a contract dependence rather than a proven in-code guard.
A rank-0 params tensor makes params->dim_size(0) at line 29 CHECK-fail: an equal-privilege abort with no corruption, robustness only.
The division-by-zero guard at lines 36-38 applies only to the CPU device; on GPU a zero update under DIV yields inf/undefined numerics, no memory-safety impact.
The variable's tensor is mutated without holding the variable mutex; a concurrent-modification race is plausible but no window is exhibited as two ordered operations in this code.
num_updates % N divisibility is implied by StartsWith plus the rank check (num_updates = N * suffix elements), so the shaped() call at line 63 cannot CHECK-fail on a non-divisible split.

verdict.summary: This function is a pure type-dispatcher for the TFLite GatherNd kernel. The only attacker-influenced value it directly consumes, params->type, is handled by a fully-enumerated switch whose default arm fails closed (ReportError + kTfLiteError). No offset, size, index, or pointer arithmetic is computed here; tensor pointers are forwarded unmodified, so any index-validation defect (the well-known GatherNd negative-index class) resides in the not-shown GatherNd/GatherNdString callees, not in this code.

assumptions: EvalGatherNd is invoked by the TFLite framework with context/params/indices/output pointers that conform to the framework's TfLiteTensor interface; the tensor objects themselves are trusted framework objects, while their contents (types, shapes, index values) are model-controlled.
TfLiteTypeGetName is the standard TFLite API returning a constant name string for every type value, including a named default for undefined types, so the %s argument is never NULL.
IndicesT is a template parameter fixed by the enclosing kernel instantiation; it is not attacker-selectable through this function.
limitations: The templated callees GatherNd<T, IndicesT> and GatherNdString<IndicesT> are not shown. The historically vulnerable GatherNd logic (failure to reject negative or out-of-range indices before computing element offsets, enabling out-of-bounds reads in the params tensor) would be instantiated entirely inside those callees. Since this dispatcher passes no computed offsets, sizes, or indices, any such defect is not locatable in the given code; audit the callee implementations for index sign/range validation.

Speculative robustness note: if TfLiteTypeGetName were to return NULL for some future type value, the '%s' in the fixed ReportError format would dereference NULL on the error path — a same-process crash on an error path with no corruption or disclosure; standard TFLite semantics currently preclude this.

verdict.summary: GetDeviceForInput is defensively written: every pointer use is either NULL-guarded (quoted ternaries and short-circuit checks), status-checked via TF_RETURN_IF_ERROR, or bounds-guarded by the NumElements()==0 rejection before the flat<ResourceHandle>()(0) access. The only fully attacker-controlled value, the resource handle's device string, flows solely into ctx.FindDeviceForInput, a fail-closed lookup whose failure returns an error. All remaining candidates (unchecked absl::get<Device*>(op.Device()) variant alternative, unset out-params from Tensor()/FindDeviceFromName(), NULL HostCPU) require unshown internal callees to violate their set-on-OK or type contracts; none is instantiable from this code, and the sole crash-shaped candidate is a clean terminate with no corruption. No trigger with a security impact is instantiated.

assumptions: TensorHandle::Tensor sets *t and EagerContext::FindDeviceFromName sets *device on OK status (standard TF out-param contract; producers not shown in this code).
EagerContext::HostCPU() returns a non-null Device* (TF context always owns a host CPU; not shown).
For LOCAL handles, TensorHandle::dtype matches the underlying Tensor's dtype, so flat<ResourceHandle>() does not hit its dtype CHECK (construction invariant, not shown).

op.Device() returns an absl::variant whose Device* alternative is guaranteed for non-function eager ops; the guard !op.is_function() appears to be the alternative discriminator but this cannot be confirmed from the given code.
tensor_handle and result are non-null (internal TF caller contract; no NULL checks exist in this function).
limitations: device = absl::get<Device*>(op.Device()); would terminate (abort under -fno-exceptions) if op.Device() held a non-Device* alternative for a non-function op. The variant's state is produced by unshown EagerOperation lifecycle code, so the wrong-alternative state cannot be exhibited here; impact would be crash/DoS only, no corruption. Speculative.

const Tensor* tensor; is consumed (tensor->NumElements()) without a NULL check; if Tensor() ever returned OK without setting *t, an uninitialized pointer would be dereferenced. Requires callee contract violation; not instantiable from given code. Speculative.

Device* input_device; is consumed (*result = input_device) after only a status check; if FindDeviceFromName returned OK without setting it, an uninitialized Device* would propagate to the caller. Same contract caveat. Speculative.
cpu_device (ctx.HostCPU()) is dereferenced (cpu_device->name()) and returned without a NULL check; a null HostCPU would crash. Internal malfunction required; speculative.
device_name assigned in the Type() != LOCAL branch is a dead store (never used on that path); no security effect.

tensor->flat<ResourceHandle>() would CHECK-abort if the handle's declared dtype (DT_RESOURCE) disagreed with the underlying Tensor's dtype; the construction invariant preventing this is not shown in this code.

verdict.summary: BinaryBroadcastFiveFold drives all pointer arithmetic and loop bounds from params.broadcast_shape with no local size validation (the RuntimeShape parameters are never read), but this code itself documents the exact precondition that makes every access safe ('input1.shape.FlatSize = y0 * y1 * y2 * y4, input2.shape.FlatSize = y0 * y2 * y3 * y4'), and simulation shows the accumulated pointer offsets exactly match all three flat sizes under that contract with no off-by-one at any boundary (y4==1 scalar path, y4>1 general path, negative or zero dims yielding zero iterations). Every out-of-bounds trigger requires the caller to violate that documented precondition; the function is an internal computation helper, not an intake point, so the candidates are speculative contract questions rather than vulnerabilities in this code.

assumptions: elementwise_f and scalar_broadcast_f are internal callees not shown; assumed to process exactly y4 / y3 elements respectively from the pointers passed, staying in bounds whenever the documented flat-size contract holds.
The caller kernel computes broadcast_shape and broadcast_category consistently with the input/output tensor shapes, per the flat-size equations documented in this code's comments.
Input/output buffers are allocated by the runtime to match the declared tensor flat sizes.
limitations: Out-of-bounds read/write is reachable if a caller sets params.broadcast_shape inconsistently with the actual buffer sizes: this code performs no local validation, and the unswitched_input1_shape, unswitched_input2_shape, and output_shape parameters are dead (never read). The trigger requires violating the documented caller precondition, so it is speculative for this code.

The general branch (y4 > 1) has no NULL check on input1_data/input2_data/output_data; the check 'else if (input1_data_ptr != nullptr)' guards only the y4<=1 path. A NULL input with y4>1 would dereference NULL inside the callee, but only on caller contract violation.

When y4 <= 1 and input1_data is NULL, the function silently writes nothing, leaving the output tensor uninitialized for downstream consumers (CWE-908 flavor); impact depends on consumers not shown and on a caller passing NULL, so it is not instantiated.
Accumulated pointer offsets could overflow int-scale arithmetic for extremely large dimensions, but only at flat sizes beyond what the documented contract and the runtime's allocation can produce.

verdict.summary: The RequantizePerChannel kernel validates input_max_vec with only 'input_max_vec.dim_size(0) == depth' (leading dimension) instead of its element count, so a max vector of shape [depth, 0] passes validation while holding zero readable floats; the scaling loop then reads input_max_vec_data[i] for i in [0, depth), a heap out-of-bounds read of attacker-controlled length. Additionally, input_requested_min/max are read at flat<float>()(0) with no non-emptiness check, allowing an OOB read from a shape-[0] tensor.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read sink: with input_min_vec of shape [8] (depth=8) and input_max_vec of shape [8, 0] (dim_size(0)=8, NumElements=0), all guards pass and input_max_vec_data[i] reads 8 floats from a zero-element buffer; the read length depth is attacker-scalable.

evidence.snippet:
OP_REQUIRES(
          ctx, input_max_vec.dim_size(0) == depth,
          errors::InvalidArgument("input_max has incorrect size, expected ",
                                  depth, " was ", input_max_vec.dim_size(0)));
evidence.reason: The only guard on input_max_vec checks the leading dimension dim_size(0), the wrong unit for the sink, which requires max_vec to hold at least depth readable floats (NumElements). The named missing guard is an OP_REQUIRES on input_max_vec.NumElements() == depth, which appears nowhere in the code.

Independent primary defect: element (0) is read from input_requested_min without any check that the tensor is non-empty; an attacker-supplied float tensor of shape [0] yields an out-of-bounds read of a zero-element buffer (same pattern applies to input_requested_max at lines 15-16).

assumptions: mkldnn/oneDNN is treated as a standard library per discipline 3: it validates primitive descriptors and throws mkldnn::error on bad arguments, which this code catches and converts to an error status, so the mkldnn call sites are not treated as unguarded memory sinks.

TF Tensor/Eigen flat<float>().data() returns the underlying buffer of NumElements() floats; TF shape semantics (dim_size(0) is the leading dimension, NumElements() the product of all dims, zero-sized dims representable) are treated as known framework semantics.
Attacker model: a party controlling the graph and the content/shapes of the tensors fed to this op kernel (malicious SavedModel/graph), the standard TF op-kernel trust boundary.
limitations: int i (signed 32-bit) vs size_t depth loop comparison: overflow at i=INT_MAX requires depth > 2^31, i.e., an 8GB+ input_min_vec; before the wrap, reads stay within min_vec's own NumElements, so no separate OOB is instantiated; recorded as a hardening concern.
requested_min_max == 0.0f produces NaN/Inf scales (division by zero) but no memory-safety impact; functional robustness only.
The DCHECK on input_requested_min_float < 0.0f (line 32) is debug-only and post-hoc; in release builds it constrains nothing.

The values read out of bounds feed only the per-channel scale computation; no direct exfiltration path is shown in this code, so impact is the OOB read primitive itself (crash/heap overread), not a demonstrated disclosure.

verdict.summary: No guardable defect in this code. The node-type switch is fully enumerated with rejecting defaults; the argument count n is provably bounded to [0,15] by quoted statements (gen_values max 13/14, n<0 clamped to 15, 13/14 boxed via OP_ARRAY, final increment capped at 15); lv_idx's result is guarded by 'if (idx > 0)'. Remaining candidates (NULL deref on malformed AST, register-range or stack-imbalance via internal callees) require a not-shown parser or callee to misbehave and are not instantiable from this code's own statements.

assumptions: Internal callees not shown (gen_values, gen_hash, gen_move, lv_idx, gen_setupvar, gen_massignment, nsym, nint, new_sym, attrsym, genop_1/2/3, genjmp2_0, dispatch, cursp/push/pop macros, codegen_error, MRB_OPSYM_2) are assumed to follow standard mruby codegen semantics: gen_values honors its max-slot argument, gen_hash pushes exactly one slot, lv_idx returns 0 for not-found, genop_* grow the code buffer safely.
The parser (not shown) is assumed to emit well-formed AST nodes where every node type referenced here has the car/cdr structure the code dereferences; this contract is unquotable from the given code.
sp is a stack register index supplied by codegen-internal callers whose domain is not documented in this snippet; it is used only as a move source and forwarded to internal helpers.
limitations: Potential NULL dereferences (e.g., nsym(tree) when tree->cdr is NULL, or tree->cdr->car in the CALL case) would crash the compiler process, but producing such a malformed AST requires the not-shown parser to violate its node-construction invariants; per the trigger rules this precondition cannot be instantiated, so these are robustness/speculative, not vulnerabilities in this code.

Stack-balance correctness of the keyword-argument accounting ultimately rests on gen_values/gen_hash honoring their max-slot and push-count contracts (not shown); all local arithmetic on n was edge-tested at 0, 13, 14, 15 and the negative sentinel and stays consistent, but a callee-side violation could not be verified from this snippet.
The 'n == 14' arm of the keyword-argument check is unreachable when keyword arguments are present (gen_values is capped at 13 in that case); it is harmless over-coverage, not a boundary defect.

verdict.summary: EvalGatherNd validates only the lower bound of attacker-controlled gather_nd indices (`indices_values[i] < 0`); no check anywhere in the code bounds index values against params->dims before the tensor is passed whole to GatherNd/GatherNdString. Any large positive index within the declared width of IndicesT passes the sole guard and causes an out-of-bounds read of the params buffer, with the disclosed value written into the attacker-readable output tensor.

evidence.reason: This is the only validation applied to the attacker-controlled indices tensor, and it enforces only non-negativity. An index value such as INT32_MAX (full declared-width domain of IndicesT) passes `indices_values[i] < 0` as false and the TF_LITE_ENSURE succeeds; no statement in this code compares any index against params->dims or params->bytes, so out-of-range positive indices reach the gather kernel unguarded (missing upper-bound check).

evidence.snippet:
case kTfLiteFloat32:
      return GatherNd<float, IndicesT>(params, indices, output);
evidence.reason: Sink: the unvalidated indices tensor is passed whole to GatherNd, which by gather semantics computes a flat offset from the index values and reads params_data at that offset (same for every dispatch arm and GatherNdString). With index 2147483647 against a 2-element params buffer, the only guard in the code (negativity) has passed, producing an out-of-bounds read of process memory whose value is written to the attacker-readable output tensor.

assumptions: GatherNd/GatherNdString callee bodies are not shown; the OOB-read conclusion rests on the universally-known gather_nd semantics (index params by the index tuple, write result to output) per discipline 3 — an unshown callee cannot be credited with a bounds check either.

indices tensor content is treated as attacker-data per the width-domain rule since this function is the op eval intake point; indices->bytes and params->type are framework-set and taken as internal-trusted.
limitations: The `indices_values[i] < 0` check is dead code for unsigned IndicesT instantiations; this is subsumed by the primary missing-upper-bound defect and is not counted separately.

GetTensorData<IndicesT>(indices) could in principle return NULL on a type mismatch; the framework contract for evaluated op tensors makes this unreachable in this code's flow, so it is not counted as a defect.

verdict.summary: Off-by-one in the DEFI chunk handler of ReadOneMNGImage: the bound check `if (object_id > MNG_MAX_OBJECTS)` admits object_id == MNG_MAX_OBJECTS, and its overflow arm clamps larger ids to exactly MNG_MAX_OBJECTS. Since the per-object MngInfo arrays are valid only for indices 0..MNG_MAX_OBJECTS-1 (as proven by the code's own `for (i=1; i < MNG_MAX_OBJECTS; i++)` loops and the mirrored `if ((i < 0) || (i >= MNG_MAX_OBJECTS)) continue;` checks in the CLIP/MOVE handlers), a malicious MNG file with a DEFI chunk carrying object id 256 (or any id > 256) causes one-past-the-end out-of-bounds reads and writes, including writes of attacker-chosen bytes (`mng_info->invisible[object_id]=p[2];`) and attacker-chosen 32-bit values (`mng_info->x_off[object_id]`, `mng_info->y_off[object_id]`), plus a 16-byte `object_clip[object_id]` struct write, corrupting heap memory adjacent to those arrays. The corrupted index also persists into the later IHDR path (`mng_info->exists[object_id]=MagickTrue;`, `image->page.x=mng_info->x_off[object_id];`, `mng_info->object_clip[object_id]` in the crop code), extending the corruption to further reads and writes.

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: object_id is built from raw attacker-controlled chunk bytes, giving it the full 0..65535 domain. Nothing before or after narrows it below MNG_MAX_OBJECTS on the DEFI path.

Missing-guard site (off-by-one): the check uses `>` instead of `>=`, so object_id == MNG_MAX_OBJECTS passes unclamped, and the overflow arm itself clamps to object_id = MNG_MAX_OBJECTS, the first out-of-bounds index. The mirrored checks in the CLIP and MOVE handlers (`if ((i < 0) || (i >= MNG_MAX_OBJECTS)) continue;`) prove the valid domain is [0, MNG_MAX_OBJECTS). ThrowMagickException does not return, so flow continues to the array uses with the corrupted index. Instantiated trigger: a DEFI chunk with id bytes 0x01 0x00 yields object_id = 256.

Out-of-bounds write sink: with object_id == MNG_MAX_OBJECTS from the simulated DEFI chunk, this writes the attacker-chosen byte p[2] one past the end of the invisible[] array, corrupting adjacent MngInfo members. The same tainted index also drives the OOB writes `mng_info->exists[object_id]=MagickTrue;` (line 406), `mng_info->x_off[object_id]`/`y_off[object_id]` with attacker-chosen 32-bit values (lines 416-420), and the 16-byte `mng_info->object_clip[object_id]=mng_read_box(...)` write (line 435).

assumptions: The not-shown MngInfo struct declares exists[], frozen[], invisible[], viewable[], x_off[], y_off[], object_clip[] with exactly MNG_MAX_OBJECTS elements. This is established within the given code by the init/iteration loops `for (i=0; i < MNG_MAX_OBJECTS; i++)` (lines 114, 326), `for (i=1; i < MNG_MAX_OBJECTS; i++)` (SAVE), and the mirrored rejection checks `if ((i < 0) || (i >= MNG_MAX_OBJECTS)) continue;` in the CLIP and MOVE handlers, all of which treat [0, MNG_MAX_OBJECTS) as the valid index domain.

ThrowMagickException records an exception but does not return or longjmp; execution continues to the clamped object_id uses (consistent with the code's own flow, e.g. the jhdr/dhdr/magn warning counters incremented after the call).

The loop bookkeeping arrays (loop_active/loop_jump/loop_count/loop_iteration) are sized at least 256 in the not-shown struct; `loop_level=chunk[0]` is bounded to 0..255 by the byte read, so those indices stay in domain.
limitations: DISC handler passes a raw attacker index (up to 65535) to the unshown internal callee with no local validation: `i=p[j-1] << 8 | p[j]; MngInfoDiscardObject(mng_info,i);`. The mirrored CLIP/MOVE bound checks show the code's own domain requirement, but the harmful use lands entirely inside the not-shown MngInfoDiscardObject, so per discipline 3 the impact chain is not characterizable from the given code; it is a strong hardening candidate (would be CWE-787/125 if the callee indexes exists[id] unchecked).

TERM chunk: `repeat == 3` leads to `mng_get_long(&p[2])` and `mng_get_long(&p[6])` with only `length != 0` verified; for length < 10 these read bytes past the chunk data but still inside the `AcquireQuantumMemory(length+MagickPathExtent,...)` allocation (uninitialized reads, CWE-908), not a heap out-of-bounds.

FRAM handler: after the `(p-chunk) < (ssize_t) (length-4)` check, the change_delay/change_timeout/change_clipping fields can collectively consume up to 25 bytes where as few as 5 remain, reading uninitialized bytes within the +MagickPathExtent allocation padding (CWE-908), not past the allocation.

MAGN magnification: `magnified_width/height` png_uint_32 arithmetic (e.g. `(png_uint_32) ((image->rows-3)*(mng_info->magn_my-1))`) can wrap for image->rows above roughly 65540 combined with magn factors up to 65535, potentially desynchronizing the `yy` accumulator from large_image->rows (assert/OOB path). Trigger depends on image dimensions produced by the unshown ReadOnePNGImage exceeding that scale and on GetAuthenticPixels/assert behavior not quotable here, so it is not promoted to a primary finding.

The chunk fill loop breaks on EOF (`if (c == EOF) break;`) leaving the allocation tail uninitialized, which later chunk parsers consume (uninitialized read, CWE-908) when the declared length exceeds the bytes actually present.
The early-EOF, TERM, FRAM, and MAGN items are secondary observations; they do not affect the verdict, which rests solely on the fully instantiated DEFI off-by-one primary candidate.

verdict.summary: DecodePngV2 returns early on attacker-triggerable error paths (dimension-size rejection, DecodeBmp/DecodeAndCropJpeg rejections) without releasing the decode state allocated by png::CommonInitDecode; the only release, 'if (!status.ok()) png::CommonFreeDecode(&decode);', is bypassed by these returns. An attacker supplying a tiny PNG header claiming width >= 2^27 (or width*height >= 2^29) makes the op leak the png decoder allocations on every request, giving unbounded memory retention and eventual exhaustion of the decoding process.

evidence.reason: Root cause: this early return fires for attacker-chosen dimensions (e.g. width = 2^27 claimed in a ~30-byte PNG header) without freeing the decode state allocated at line 5; no png::CommonFreeDecode call exists on this path (the only one, line 55, executes after the return), so each request permanently retains the decoder allocations, enabling memory-exhaustion DoS. The sibling op_type_ rejections at lines 44-52 have the same missing free.

Origin of the leaked resource: png::CommonInitDecode allocates the decode context (the code's own paired cleanup at line 55 proves the free obligation belongs to this function), and every early return between this line and line 55 bypasses it.

assumptions: OP_REQUIRES(context, false, ...) sets an error status and returns from the function when the condition is false (standard TensorFlow macro semantics).
png::CommonInitDecode allocates heap state owned by the caller and requiring png::CommonFreeDecode, inferred from the paired free call at line 55 of this code.

decode.width/height are 32-bit values taken from the attacker-supplied PNG header; decode.channels is in the PNG-legal range (1-4), which per callee-semantics discipline cannot be instantiated outside that range.
limitations: The op_type_-dependent leak paths (DecodeBmp at lines 44-47, DecodeAndCropJpeg at lines 48-52) additionally require the deployed graph to instantiate that op type; the primary size-check leak has no such precondition.
If png::CommonInitDecode fails, or png::CommonFinishDecode fails after a successful decode, whether cleanup happens internally is not shown; those potential leaks are not counted as evidence.
If data_type_ were neither DT_UINT8, DT_UINT16, nor DT_FLOAT, the output tensor would be returned uninitialized, but the op's dtype attribute is constrained by op registration code not shown here.

All width/height arithmetic was verified sound: the quoted check at lines 18-20 bounds width, height < 2^27 and width*height < 2^29, so height*width*decode.channels <= (2^29-1)*4 = 2^31-4 fits int, and strides fit without wrap; no overflow candidate survived.
Large-but-legal allocations up to the designed ~2^29-pixel bound are inherent to the op's size limits, not a defect.

verdict.summary: The Compute handler reads an attacker-influenced session-tensor name from input 0 and passes it to a keyed map-style delete. The only pointer dereference (session_state) is guarded by a quoted NULL check, and the callee's failure sentinel is checked with OP_REQUIRES_OK at the use; the code contains no memory, copy, indexing, size, format, path, or injection sink parameterized by attacker data. The unvalidated tensor shape/dtype at handle.scalar<tstring>()() and the effect of deleting an arbitrary session tensor both have their impact chains entirely inside callees and consumers not shown in this code, so they remain speculative.

assumptions: The TF runtime enforces input(0)'s dtype (DT_STRING per the op registration) before invoking Compute; that enforcement is not shown in this code and is treated as an assumption, not a guard.

Tensor::scalar<tstring>() and TensorShape handling are project-internal callees whose internals are not shown; their behavior on non-scalar or zero-element tensors is an assumption that cuts both ways and cannot confirm or dismiss the OOB-read candidate.

session_state->DeleteTensor(name) is assumed to be a keyed map erase; its internals are not shown, but the code passes only a string key (no raw offset, size, or index) and checks its Status sentinel with OP_REQUIRES_OK.
limitations: Speculative: handle.scalar<tstring>()() is called with no local check that input(0) is a scalar with at least one element; an attacker feeding a zero-element or non-scalar DT_STRING tensor could cause an out-of-bounds read or CHECK failure inside the unshown Tensor::scalar/Eigen accessor. The impact chain breaks at the unshown callee, so it is not provable in this code. A fix would be an OP_REQUIRES TensorShapeUtils::IsScalar(handle.shape()) check, which appears nowhere in the given snippet.

Speculative: the attacker-chosen name lets the op delete any tensor in the session state (e.g., one another op depends on), but all consumers of session tensors are outside this code, the state is same-session in-process state at equal privilege, and no bypass, corruption, or disclosure is instantiable from the given statements.

verdict.summary: This Compute method consumes attacker-controlled ragged tensor splits and values, but the only reachable out-of-domain use, indexing nested_splits at position 0 when the split list is empty, is prevented by the quoted guard OP_REQUIRES(context, ragged_nested_splits_len > 0, ...) which executes before the access and is not bypassed on any path; the non-batched early-return path never dereferences splits. The output copy loop is bounded by the same expression that sizes the output tensor, num_components is checked and never reused, and remaining edge behaviors (vec<SPLIT_TYPE> dtype CHECK, negative TensorShape from a wrapped unbatched size) are abort-only with graph-author-level or multi-terabyte preconditions and no memory corruption, disclosure, or bypass.

assumptions: UnbatchRaggedZerothDim and RaggedTensorVariant methods (set_values, append_splits, splits, mutable_nested_splits) are internal callees not shown in this code; their internal handling of attacker-controlled split values (negative or non-monotonic entries) is outside this analysis.
OpKernelContext::input and allocate_output are standard TensorFlow framework callees: they validate indices and shapes with errors or CHECK aborts rather than out-of-bounds access.
limitations: Historical CVE pattern (empty rt_nested_splits reaching splits(0) out-of-range) is fixed here by the quoted OP_REQUIRES guard; if this code were the pre-patch version without that check, the defect would be CWE-125/129 class.
batched_splits_top_vec.size() (64-bit) is narrowed into int num_components, but num_components is only consumed by the >= 0 check and never used as a size or index, so truncation has no sink.

int output_size = unbatched_ragged_input.size() can truncate only for >2^31 unbatched components (requires multi-gigabyte attacker inputs and 2^31 constructed variants); a negative result reaches TensorShape and aborts/errors via OP_REQUIRES_OK with no memory corruption, so this is speculative and crash-only.

vec<SPLIT_TYPE>() CHECK failures on dtype or rank mismatch are abort-only and require the graph author to construct a mismatched kernel/attr pairing; classified as robustness, not a security vulnerability.

verdict.summary: The per-effect color chain validates only the -1 sentinel and lower thresholds (<0x10 ... <0xe0) but never bounds the attacker-controlled pattern effect value (a file-derived short) above 0xff or below 0 before indexing member color tables: a negative value other than -1 reaches fxColors[<negative>] and any value >= 0x100 falls into the bare else and indexes extFxColors[value-0xe0] with an index up to 32543. The garbage enum read is then used as a second-stage index into uiColors, producing a far out-of-bounds read (likely SIGSEGV) when rendering a crafted song file.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the final else of the effect-color chain indexes extFxColors with the raw, unvalidated effect cell value minus 0xe0. The whole chain tests only lower thresholds (== -1 sentinel, then <0x10..<0xe0); no statement bounds pat->data[i][index] above 0xff or rejects out-of-range values. Trigger: a crafted song file sets an effect cell to 0x7FFF (short domain), simulation: data[0][4]=32767 != -1, all <0xNN tests false, index becomes 32767-224=32543 into a member array sized for the 0xe0..0xff domain, then the garbage enum is used as uiColors[...] -> out-of-bounds read and likely crash.

Mirror of the same missing bound: the ==-1 sentinel at line 194 handles exactly one value, so any negative short other than -1 (e.g. -2 from a crafted file) passes 194, satisfies the <0x10 lower-threshold test, and indexes fxColors with a negative index -> out-of-bounds read before the array, then the garbage value indexes uiColors. No clamp/mask/range check exists anywhere on this path (mention sweep: lines 194, 198, 199-215, 200, 218 contain no upper or lower bound).

Origin of the tainted data: the attacker-controlled pattern cells (file-derived shorts, full -32768..32767 domain) are bound to pat here and consumed at pat->data[i][index] in the effect loop without any range validation of the cell values in this code.

assumptions: fxColors and extFxColors are GUI member color-mapping arrays sized for the intended effect domains (0x00..0x0f and 0xe0..0xff) established by the code's own comparison constants; their exact declarations are not shown in this snippet, but any value >= 0x100 (index up to 32543) or negative exceeds them by construction.

DivPattern::data is a fixed-dimension short array (declared in project headers, not shown); the guard if (i<0 || i>=e->song.patLen) is safe only if the song loader caps patLen at the array's row count (e.g. 256) - enforced outside this code.

chans and patCache are supplied by the same-file GUI caller from the engine's channel count; the engine is assumed to cap the channel count to the sizes of chanShow/chanCollapse/patChanX, none of which are shown here.
noteName() is a project-internal callee not shown; its return-string length is unknown, so the sprintf into static char id[32] cannot be proven overflowing or safe from this code alone.
e->song.ins[pat->data[i][2]] is assumed non-NULL for in-range indices by engine invariant (unshown).
