g_strlcat silently truncates the outgoing CAP REQ when an attacker floods the CAP LS list with whitelisted capabilities; the result is a malformed truncated request line (functional robustness), not memory corruption or injection.
Impact is a process crash (denial of service) with no memory corruption; no privilege boundary is crossed beyond the server-to-client trust boundary already exploited for the crash.

verdict.summary: In Compute, the fill loop indexes row_id_present[i] for i in [0, num_rows_) and col_id_present[j] for j in [0, num_cols_) without ever validating that those vectors are large enough. Their sizes are produced only by the unshown RemapVectorToMap (whose status, not container size, is checked), and the one explicit sizing statement in the code, col_id_present.resize(num_cols_, true), is bypassed whenever remap_cols is true and never applies to row_id_present. When the remapping input leaves a present-vector smaller than num_rows_/num_cols_ (e.g., row_remapping = [-1,-1,-1], the all-missing-rows case this fill loop exists to handle), std::vector<bool>::operator[] performs a heap out-of-bounds read spanning an attacker-chosen number of rows, and the out-of-bounds bit also decides whether output cells are left uninitialized.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read sink: row_id_present and col_id_present are indexed by i < num_rows_ and j < num_cols_ (loop bounds at lines 211-212), but no statement in this code checks row_id_present.size() >= num_rows_ or col_id_present.size() >= num_cols_. The mention sweep shows row_id_present's only other mentions are its declaration (line 5) and the unshown RemapVectorToMap producer (line 13); col_id_present's resize to num_cols_ (line 51) exists only in the !remap_cols branch, bypassed when remap_cols is true. Instantiated trigger: row_remapping = [-1,-1,-1] with num_rows_=3 passes the size check at line 9, and the resulting present-vector, sized solely by the unshown callee, is smaller than num_rows_, so the first iteration reads row_id_present[0] out of bounds (std::vector<bool> word access), a heap OOB read whose garbage bit also gates whether output cells are left uninitialized.

Origin of the tainted container: row_id_present's contents and size are produced solely by RemapVectorToMap, a project-internal callee not shown in this code; only its return status is checked, never the resulting vector's size, even though i later ranges over [0, num_rows_) at line 211. The mirrored column origin is line 47 (RemapVectorToMap(col_remapping, &col_id_present, ...)), whose output size likewise goes unchecked on the remap_cols path because the resize at line 51 is skipped.

assumptions: RemapVectorToMap is not shown; per the width-domain rule its output vector sizes are treated as full-domain attacker-controllable values, and only its status return is verified in this code (lines 13-14, 47-48).
BundleReader, LookupSlice, LookupDtypeAndShape, TensorSlice::set_start/set_length/SliceTensorShape are unshown project-internal callees; only their return statuses are checked.
All op input tensors (row_remapping, col_remapping, ckpt_path, old_tensor_name, initializing_values) are runtime-feedable and therefore attacker-data per discipline 4.
limitations: Speculative (not counted in verdict): signed integer overflow at lines 116-117, 'max_old_row - row_start + 1', when row_remapping contains INT64_MAX (no statement bounds old row IDs against tensor_shape.dim_size(0)); it wraps to INT64_MIN and can drive an unbounded tensor_slices.push_back loop (CWE-190/CWE-400), but the impact chain passes through the unshown TensorSlice::set_length and SliceTensorShape, whose behavior on negative/zero lengths cannot be characterized per discipline 3.

Speculative: ckpt_path and old_tensor_name are attacker-supplied strings passed to the unshown BundleReader (lines 69-75); an arbitrary-file-read impact is not instantiated because BundleReader enforces its own checkpoint-bundle format, which is not shown.

Verified safe, not defects: the output-matrix write guard at lines 185-187 uses strict '<' against num_rows_/num_cols_ and '>= 0', correctly rejecting both one-past-the-limit and negative values immediately before the write at line 194; the initializing_values guard at lines 214-215 is correct and precedes the first use; FindOrNull sentinels are checked at lines 161 and 176 before dereference.

Negative num_rows_/num_cols_ attributes are rejected by the quoted checks at lines 9, 43 and 93 (tensor/vector sizes are never negative), so allocation-shape abuse via negative dimensions is not reachable.

verdict.summary: Test-harness callback for parsing backing-store strings. All data originates from the test suite's own static fixture tables (no trust boundary); every internal sentinel path (NULL src, NULL expect, NULL xml from virBufferContentAndReset) is guarded by quoted checks in correct execution order, and no memory, copy, index, injection, or arithmetic sink consumes unvalidated external data.

assumptions: args points to a struct testBackingParseData fixture authored in the same test file (standard libvirt virtTestRun callback pattern); the producer is not shown, so fields were treated as potentially NULL during the sweep.
virStorageSourceNewFromBackingAbsolute returns -1 and leaves src NULL on failure; its internal behavior is not shown, but both rc and src are locally checked before every use.
limitations: data->backing is never NULL-checked before being used as a %s fprintf argument (lines 16-17) and passed to the parser (line 10). A NULL fixture would cause undefined behavior in the test binary, but the fixture author is the test developer, not a trust-boundary party, so the trigger is not attacker-instantiable; recorded as a robustness note only.

The src && !data->expect branch at line 21 is a defensive safety net; on standard callee semantics it is unreachable with src set, but it correctly intercepts the hypothetical rc==-1-with-src-set case.

verdict.summary: No attacker-instantiable vulnerability. Both callee failure sentinels are checked in execution order (kzalloc NULL via 'if (!a)', dma_get_sgtable failure via 'if (ret < 0)' before publication), and the list node is initialized before attachment->priv publishes it. The unchecked dmabuf->priv dereference has no reachable trigger: the attacker can invoke attach but cannot author the dma_buf/priv pair, which is produced by this driver's own export path not shown.

assumptions: FASTRPC_PHYS(buffer->phys) is a project macro that extracts the physical address; its semantics are not shown and were not relied on for any guard.
buffer->lock and buffer->attachments are initialized at buffer creation (not shown); mutex_lock/list_add rely on that.
The detach counterpart (not shown) removes a->node under the same lock and calls sg_free_table/kfree; the pre-publication INIT_LIST_HEAD makes a partially published node safe to list_del.
dma_buf_attach is called by the kernel framework on dma_bufs exported by this driver with priv set to the fastrpc_buf; the attacker triggers attach but does not construct these structs.
limitations: NULL-deref candidate: 'buffer = dmabuf->priv' (line 5) is dereferenced at lines 12-13, 15, 24-25 with no local NULL check (mention sweep found none). Speculative: instantiating priv==NULL requires the not-shown export path to fail, which no attacker-reachable statement, standard sentinel, or code statement here produces. Recorded as speculative, not a vulnerability.

Race candidate: attachment->priv is published at line 22 before list_add at line 25, creating a theoretical window; a concurrent detach of the same attachment before attach returns is a caller contradiction, and INIT_LIST_HEAD at line 21 already neutralizes the stale-node hazard. Not instantiable.
The error path returns -EINVAL instead of the dma_get_sgtable errno (line 17) — loss of diagnostic precision only, no security effect.

verdict.summary: No guard defect instantiated: state machine inputs are bounded by the entry NULL check and callee contracts; the recv mutex is provably released on every error path by the quoted exit sequence; the multithread pendResp lifecycle and wait_again loop rest on callee behavior not shown in this code.

assumptions: MqttClient_RespList_Find, MqttClient_HandlePacket, MqttClient_DecodePacket, and MqttPacket_Read are internal callees not shown in this code; their sentinel semantics (return of negative rc on failure, bounds enforcement during decode) are assumed per standard project convention and cannot be verified here.
The MqttPendResp packetProcessing/packetDone ownership handshake between threads is enforced by code outside this function.

*mms_stat (the caller's packet_obj state) is only ever assigned the enum literals MQTT_MSG_WAIT, MQTT_MSG_READ, MQTT_MSG_READ_PAYLOAD, MQTT_MSG_BEGIN shown here plus values set by the not-shown callee MqttClient_HandlePacket.
limitations: C-LOCK (mutex kept on wm_SemLock failure): trigger simulated, but the quoted exit sequence 'if (readLocked) { wm_SemUnlock(&client->lockRecv); }' releases the lock on every rc<0 return in all build configurations, so the hang is not instantiated; the MQTT_CODE_CONTINUE early return intentionally holds the lock per the in-code comment.

goto wait_again forms an unbounded read loop while non-matching packets keep arriving; this is protocol wait semantics gated by timeout_ms passed to MqttPacket_Read, not attacker-amplifiable unbounded work (no CWE-400).

waitMatchFound is not set when a multithread pending-response lookup matches an incoming packet (waitMatchFound = 0), forcing another loop pass; behavior is per the cross-thread design and any lifetime risk depends on the not-shown RespList implementation.

PENDRESP pointer reacquired via MqttClient_RespList_Find is dereferenced after wm_SemUnlock in other threads' contexts; a UAF would depend on the not-shown RespList_Remove implementation honoring packetProcessing, which cannot be verified from this code.

verdict.summary: DecodeImageAPNG reads APNG fcTL frame-control fields at fixed offsets 12-33 of chunk.p (png_get_uint_32/png_get_uint_16 at chunk.p+12..+30, byte reads at chunk.p[32]/[33], and memcpy source chunk.p+12) without validating chunk.size. A well-formed fcTL chunk with declared data length 0 (or any length < 22) produces a heap buffer of only 12-33 bytes, so these reads run up to 22 bytes past the allocation. The only chunk-size check in the function (`chunkIHDR.size == 25`) applies to the IHDR chunk only, and the w0/h0/x0/y0/dop/bop validation at lines 153-155 executes after the out-of-bounds reads have already occurred, so it does not cover the first use. Any attacker who can feed a crafted PNG/APNG file to the decoder triggers a heap out-of-bounds read (crash/DoS of the decoding process, with heap contents flowing into parsed frame geometry).

evidence.reason: Root cause: out-of-bounds heap read. The fcTL frame-control fields are read at fixed offsets 12-33 of chunk.p with no check that chunk.size covers those offsets; the mention sweep of every chunk.size reference (lines 39, 176, 181, 183, 192) shows the only size validation (`chunkIHDR.size == 25`, line 39) applies to the IHDR chunk, and the geometry checks at lines 153-155 run after these reads. Instantiated trigger: a well-formed fcTL chunk with declared length 0 gives chunk.size = 12 (a 12-byte heap allocation) while the reads span offsets 12-33, reading up to 22 bytes past the buffer.

Origin of the tainted value: chunk.p/chunk.size are filled by read_chunk from attacker-controlled file bytes; the only local checks are that the returned id is non-zero and an assert on chunk.p being non-null (which may be compiled out in release builds) - nothing ties chunk.size to the offsets later consumed at lines 142-149 and 161.

assumptions: read_chunk, processing_start/finish/data, isAbc, and the CHUNK/Reader/APNGFrame definitions are not shown; read_chunk is assumed to return a complete chunk (length+name+data+CRC, so chunk.size = declared_length + 12 >= 12) with a non-zero id only for a complete chunk - the most conservative reading, under which the fcTL trigger at chunk.size = 12 is still fully attacker-instantiable via the declared length field.
cMaxPNGSize is a constant whose value is not shown in the given code.

JXL_ASSERT(chunk.p != nullptr) at line 66 is the only NULL check on chunk.p and assertions may be disabled in release builds; a NULL chunk.p with non-zero id could not be instantiated from the given code.
The reads at lines 187-188 (isAbc(chunk.p[4..7])) are treated as covered because a non-zero id is derived from the 4 name bytes, implying they were read.
limitations: fdAT unsigned underflow (line 181, `png_save_uint_32(chunk.p + 4, chunk.size - 16)` with no `chunk.size >= 16` check): with a well-formed zero-length fdAT (chunk.size = 12) the subtraction wraps to 4294967292 and is written in-bounds as a fake IDAT length, but the impact chain was not instantiated as memory corruption - libpng (known behavior) rejects chunk lengths above 2^31-1 and png_process_data only consumes the bytes handed to it per call. An OOB write via `memcpy(chunk.p + 8, "IDAT", 4)` would require chunk.size < 12 with a non-zero id, which depends on unshown read_chunk truncation semantics. Recorded as a CWE-191 risk pending that contract, not counted for the verdict.

`imagesize = h * rowbytes` (line 54) is computed in 32-bit unsigned int from w,h bounded only by the unshown constant cMaxPNGSize; if cMaxPNGSize >= 2^15 (the upstream libjxl value is 1,000,000), w*h*4 >= 2^32 wraps, `new unsigned char[imagesize]` under-allocates, and the row pointers `frameRaw.p + j*rowbytes` (line 58) place libpng row writes outside the buffer (heap overflow). The trigger precondition (the constant's value) is not quotable from the given code, so this is recorded here rather than counted for the verdict.
Memory leak: chunk.p is not deleted on the IEND break path (lines 137-139) - at most one chunk leaked per file, no security impact.
`io->dec_pixels += w0 * h0` (line 103) can wrap in 32-bit arithmetic for large frames - accounting only, no security effect in the given code.

The OOB-read values w0/h0/x0/y0 are subsequently bounded by the checks at lines 153-155, so downstream allocations and row accesses stay in bounds; the defect's impact is the out-of-bounds read itself (crash/DoS, heap data influencing parsed geometry).

verdict.summary: All attacker-controlled reads of in_data are guarded by quoted, correctly ordered length checks (in_len >= 1, in_len < 8, in_len != 16), all output writes fit their allocations, all allocation/parse/lookup sentinels are checked, and the 64-bit wrap check on offset+length is correct. The only unguarded arithmetic is a potential uint32 truncation of labels_data_count in FSCTL_GET_SHADOW_COPY_DATA, which requires roughly 43 million shadow-copy volumes to trigger and cannot be instantiated by a trust-boundary party, so it is recorded as a limitation, not a vulnerability.

assumptions: SMB_VFS_GET_SHADOW_COPY_DATA (not shown) fills shadow_data->num_volumes and shadow_data->labels consistently, i.e., the labels array holds num_volumes entries; this code does not validate that relationship, but the producer is a project-internal backend scanning server-side snapshot directories.

SHADOW_COPY_LABEL and its sizeof are consistent between the labels_data_count computation, the srvstr_push length, and the cur_pdata advance, so the per-volume write size equals the per-volume allocation size.
fsp->file_id, fsp->conn and fsp->fsp_name are valid internal state; st_ex_size is valid because vfs_stat_fsp's failure arm returns before use.
limitations: Speculative: labels_data_count = (num_volumes * 2 * sizeof(SHADOW_COPY_LABEL)) + 2 is a truncating uint32 assignment of a size_t product; a num_volumes of about 43 million would truncate labels_data_count, undersize the talloc_zero_array allocation (12 + labels_data_count bytes), and the subsequent loop (bounded by the untruncated num_volumes) would write 2*sizeof(SHADOW_COPY_LABEL) bytes per iteration past the buffer, a heap overflow. Not judged a vulnerability because instantiating it requires tens of millions of snapshot directories where the (not shown) shadow-copy backend scans, a location no statement of this code makes attacker-writable, plus gigabytes of label storage.

FSCTL_CREATE_OR_GET_OBJECT_ID sets *out_len = max_out_len when max_out_len < 64 while always allocating and writing a 64-byte buffer (the code's own comment flags this: 'Hmmm, will this cause problems if less data asked for?'). All writes stay within the 64-byte allocation, so this is a protocol/interoperability question, not a memory-safety defect.

If the shadow-copy backend returned NULL entries in shadow_data->labels, the DEBUGADD %s would print an indeterminate pointer; this depends entirely on the not-shown producer and was not instantiated.

verdict.summary: load_buffer leaks attacker-triggered memory on its error paths: the RBuffer reference taken with r_buf_ref(buf) is never released on the early !main_mach0 return, and RRebaseInfo allocated from attacker-controlled chained-fixup data is never freed on any beach path (all gotos occur before the ownership transfer at obj->rebase_info = rebase_info). A crafted kernelcache file that fails prelink-range extraction makes the leak reachable on every load.

evidence.reason: The r_buf_ref(buf) taken at line 2 is never released before this return. Trigger: an attacker-crafted file that passes the plugin's format check but fails MACH0_(new_buf) makes load_buffer return here, permanently retaining the RBuffer reference (and its backing data) with no statement on this path dropping it — a per-load memory leak of parsed untrusted input.

The beach cleanup block frees fbuf and main_mach0 but contains no release of rebase_info, allocated at line 10 from attacker-controlled chained-fixup data. All four gotos (lines 15, 21, 31, 41) precede the ownership transfer at line 46 (obj->rebase_info = rebase_info), so every error path leaks rebase_info. Trigger: a crafted kernelcache with chained fixups but no prelink info makes get_prelink_info_range_from_mach0 return NULL, jumping to beach with a live, non-NULL rebase_info that is never freed.

Origin of the leaked value: this allocation builds rebase lists from attacker-supplied Mach-O chained-fixup data; on every beach path taken after this line the allocation is retained with no free anywhere in the function (verified by mention sweep: rebase_info appears only at lines 10, 46, 58 — the free at 46 is unreachable from beach).

assumptions: Semantics of unshown internal callees (MACH0_(new_buf), r_rebase_info_new_from_mach0, get_prelink_info_range_from_mach0, r_cf_value_dict_parse, swizzle_io_read) are not quoted in this code; their failure sentinels (NULL returns) are treated as in-domain per standard allocation/parse semantics, and the leak findings do not depend on any assumed caller or callee contract.

r_cf_value_dict_parse is assumed to read via the bounds-checked RBuffer accessors; the prelink offset/size passed at lines 26-27 are attacker-derived from Mach-O headers but reach a parse call, not a raw memory/copy/index operation in this code.
limitations: R_FREE(prelink_info) at line 40 frees an RCFValueDict with plain free(), leaking the nested parsed value tree, but that path requires r_list_new() to fail (allocation failure an attacker cannot induce), so the trigger is environment-only; recorded as a latent leak, not a primary finding.

The if (obj) { obj->cache_buf = NULL; } arm at lines 67-69 is dead code: obj is NULL on every path that reaches beach (verified per path), so no double-free of fbuf exists between line 48 and line 66.

No memory-corruption, out-of-bounds, injection, or authz primitive was found; the confirmed impact is attacker-triggered memory retention (DoS surface in long-lived processes that parse untrusted files), not corruption. Severity is accordingly low.

verdict.summary: The function checks input1's type but not input2's type or shape compatibility, and passes unvalidated tensor shapes and data pointers to internal comparison routines. However, no out-of-bounds access is directly instantiated within this code: input_dtype is constrained to 1-byte types by the entry check, no tensor element type is smaller than 1 byte, so type confusion cannot exceed allocated buffers. The potential OOB from shape mismatch depends entirely on the unshown callee's iteration behavior and an unshown caller's requires_broadcast computation, neither of which is quotable or characterizable.

assumptions: input_dtype is a 1-byte integer type (uint8_t or int8_t) based on the entry check accepting only kTfLiteUInt8 and kTfLiteInt8; if instantiated with a wider type, GetTensorData<input_dtype>(input1) would read OOB, but this is a compile-time developer choice, not runtime attacker-controllable.
QuantizeMultiplier is assumed to be a pure math function that safely handles any float input including 0, negative, NaN, and infinity, writing only to its local out-parameters.
GetTensorShape and GetTensorData are standard TFLite accessors that return the tensor's runtime shape and reinterpret its raw data pointer respectively, without performing bounds validation.

reference_ops::ComparisonWithScaling and reference_ops::BroadcastComparison4DSlowWithScaling are standard TFLite reference implementations whose internal iteration logic is not shown and is treated as an assumption in both directions per discipline 3.
limitations: Missing input2->type validation: the code checks input1->type at line 4 but never checks input2->type. A malicious model defining input2 as a non-quantized type (e.g., kTfLiteFloat32) would cause type confusion — input2's buffer would be read as input_dtype (1 byte/element) producing wrong comparison results and reading potentially uninitialized quantization params. However, since input_dtype is 1 byte and no tensor type is smaller, this does not produce an out-of-bounds access. Impact is correctness/uninitialized-read, not memory corruption.

Missing shape compatibility validation: in the non-broadcast path (requires_broadcast=false), no check ensures input1 and input2 have the same shape. If a caller passed requires_broadcast=false with mismatched shapes AND the unshown callee iterates using input1's flat size while indexing input2, an OOB read would occur. Both the trigger condition (caller passing false with mismatched shapes) and the impact (callee's iteration behavior) depend on code not shown, so this is speculative.

Missing NULL checks on tensor pointers: if input1, input2, or output were NULL, the function would crash at the first dereference. In standard TFLite flow, tensor pointers come from the runtime's internal tensor array and are never NULL, so this is not attacker-instantiable.

Missing else branch: if input1->type is neither kTfLiteUInt8 nor kTfLiteInt8, the function silently returns without writing to output. The output tensor would contain stale or uninitialized data. This is a robustness issue if the caller dispatches incorrectly, but the caller is not shown.

No output->type check: the function writes bool values to output without verifying output->type is kTfLiteBool. If output is a wider type, fewer bytes are written than allocated — within bounds but semantically wrong.

verdict.summary: The header length check `if (length < sizeof(bh))` takes the size of the pointer variable (8 bytes on LP64) instead of the blobheader struct (at least 10 bytes given the fields the code dereferences), so a blob as short as 8 bytes passes validation; the subsequent reads of bh->min_version/version/hdrsize/flags then read past the end of the attacker-supplied buffer.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the only bound on `length` applies sizeof to the pointer variable bh (8 on LP64, 4 on ILP32) instead of the struct *bh, which must be at least 10 bytes (uint32 totlen + uint16 hdrsize + uint16 flags + uint8 version + uint8 min_version). Instantiated trigger: an attacker-supplied state file of length 8 with totlen = htonl(8) passes this check and the totlen equality check, so the struct field reads execute on an 8-byte buffer.

Sink: with length = 8 (totlen = 8), the header fields at struct offsets >= 8 (version, min_version at line 22, or flags/hdrsize depending on layout — the 10 bytes of referenced fields cannot all fit below offset 8) are read beyond the caller's buffer; the out-of-bounds bytes flow into *hdrversion/*hdrflags and are returned to the caller with TPM_SUCCESS.

assumptions: blobheader's definition is not shown; its minimum size is derived from the fields this code dereferences (10 bytes plus padding), which exceeds sizeof(pointer) on both LP64 (8) and ILP32 (4) for any field ordering.
`data` points to exactly `length` readable bytes (the contract the line-7 check exists to enforce); the out-params dataoffset/hdrflags/hdrversion point to valid caller storage.
logprintf writes formatted output to a file descriptor and its return value is ignored on error paths only.
limitations: Line 32 sets *dataoffset = ntohs(bh->hdrsize) (domain 0..65535) without checking it against `length`; a header with hdrsize > length returns TPM_SUCCESS with an out-of-range offset, but the harmful use (indexing data + dataoffset) occurs in a caller not shown, so the impact is not instantiated here (hardening: reject if hdrsize > length).
Casting possibly-unaligned `data` to blobheader* (line 5) can fault on strict-alignment targets — robustness only.
The log argument htonl(bh->totlen) (line 18) prints the value already equal to ntohl(bh->totlen) — cosmetic only; all format strings are constants, so no format-string or log-injection issue.

verdict.summary: In the error path of load_buffer, the beach label unconditionally executes 'obj->cache_buf = NULL;' while obj is NULL (or already freed by R_FREE). Every goto beach carries an invalid obj: obj is initialized NULL and never assigned before the first two gotos, and R_NEW0/r_cf/r_list failure paths free obj before jumping. An attacker-supplied Mach-O file that makes get_prelink_info_range_from_mach0 return its NULL failure sentinel reaches this line and crashes the parsing process with a NULL-pointer write (denial of service on the untrusted-file intake path).

evidence.reason: NULL-pointer write. On every path reaching beach, obj is invalid: it is NULL after lines 11/18-19 and freed-and-nulled by 'R_FREE (obj)' on the prelink_info and pending_bin_files failure paths. No NULL or validity check guards this dereference anywhere in the function, so the error handler itself crashes the process.

Trigger origin: get_prelink_info_range_from_mach0 parses the attacker-supplied Mach-O and returns its NULL failure sentinel (explicitly anticipated by this check) for a file lacking the expected prelink layout, transferring control to beach with obj still NULL (line 11), where line 67 dereferences it.

assumptions: get_prelink_info_range_from_mach0 and r_cf_value_dict_parse are project-internal callees not shown; the NULL return of get_prelink_info_range_from_mach0 is treated as a reachable parse failure sentinel because the code itself tests it at line 14.

R_FREE is assumed to free and NULL its argument (radare2 macro); if it does not NULL the pointer, paths through 'R_FREE (obj)' turn the line-67 defect into a use-after-free write instead of a NULL dereference, which is strictly worse and does not change the verdict.
limitations: Lines 26-27 pass attacker-derived prelink_range->range.offset and range.size into the unshown internal parser r_cf_value_dict_parse with no local bounds validation; any out-of-bounds consequence would land inside the callee, which is not characterizable from the given code, so no trigger was instantiated here.

Minor resource leak: the early return at lines 6-8 returns without r_buf_free(fbuf) after r_buf_ref took a reference (line 2), leaking one buffer reference per malformed Mach-O that fails MACH0_(new_buf); bounded per file, not classified as a primary security impact.
rebase_info (line 10) is never freed on the beach paths; same bounded-leak class.
The R_NEW0 failure path (lines 18-22) also reaches the defective line 67, but allocation failure is environment-induced; the attacker-data trigger via prelink_range does not depend on it.

verdict.summary: This is a libvirt unit-test callback whose inputs come from static test fixtures in the same trust domain; no trust-boundary party can influence them. Every sink is guarded by quoted statements: src is initialized NULL and exited on via 'if (!src) return 0;', the format call is checked with '< 0', and virBufferContentAndReset is NULL-checked before xml is used, so data->expect cannot reach STRNEQ as NULL under standard parse failure semantics. The remaining quirks (a vacuous pass when contradictory fixture data supplies rv=-1 with non-NULL expect, and a hypothetical NULL deref requiring the unshown callee to populate *src while returning -1) are test-quality or speculative, not security vulnerabilities.

assumptions: virStorageSourceNewFromBackingAbsolute follows the libvirt convention: returns 0 on success and -1 on failure, and only populates *src on success; the quoted 'g_autoptr(virStorageSource) src = NULL;' means a standard failure leaves src NULL.
args points to a static testBackingParseData fixture registered with the test harness in the same source suite; no external trust-boundary party can set backing, expect, or rv.
STRNEQ is libvirt's strcmp-based string inequality macro.
virBufferContentAndReset returns a NUL-terminated string or NULL, and its NULL case is checked in the given code.
limitations: Speculative NULL deref: STRNEQ(xml, data->expect) with expect == NULL requires the unshown callee virStorageSourceNewFromBackingAbsolute to populate *src and still return -1; under standard failure semantics src stays NULL and 'if (!src) return 0;' exits first. Precondition could not be instantiated.

Test-logic fail-open (not security): 'if (!src) return 0;' ignores data->expect, so contradictory fixture data (rv == -1 with non-NULL expect) makes the test pass vacuously; impact is limited to test coverage of the developer's own process.
If args were NULL, 'int erc = data->rv;' would deref NULL and crash the test binary; the harness (not shown) is the only caller and this is a same-privilege self-crash at most.

The fprintf at the STRNEQ failure path passes data->backing and data->expect to %s; if a fixture ever set these NULL the print would be undefined, but the format string itself is a literal and no injection exists.

verdict.summary: ga_concat_shorten_esc safely walks a NUL-terminated string: clen is derived from the same in-bounds character decode that advances s, the inner loop re-tests *s != NUL before every s += clen advance, and the only fixed-size buffer write (vim_snprintf into buf of NUMBUFLEN with %d) is size-bounded and NUL-terminated. No unguarded memory, copy, or format sink exists on any path.

assumptions: NUMBUFLEN (65 in Vim) is sufficient for any int rendered with %d, and vim_snprintf honors the size argument and always NUL-terminates.

mb_cptr2char_adv and mb_ptr2char decode one character without reading past the NUL, return length 1 for malformed or truncated sequences, and accept no overlong encodings, so equal characters always have equal byte lengths.
ga_concat/ga_concat_esc grow the garray internally and fail safe on allocation errors, copying only the requested in-bounds byte counts.
limitations: A theoretical overread at s += clen would require an encoding where the same codepoint has encodings of differing byte lengths (overlong forms); Vim's supported encodings do not, so the trigger is not instantiable.
The else branch advances p by one byte for a multibyte character, re-decoding continuation bytes; this is a display inaccuracy in the shortened representation, not a memory-safety or security defect.

verdict.summary: UnsortedSegmentJoin consumes the attacker-controlled scalar num_segments with no sign/range validation: the only checks are tensor-emptiness (NumElements() != 0) and a per-element bound of segment values against num_segments. By supplying an empty segment tensor (e.g. input shape [0], segment_ids shape [0]) together with a negative num_segments, the per-element validation loop executes zero times, so a negative segment count flows unvalidated into GetOutputShape and allocate_output, where it is used as an output dimension; TensorFlow's shape construction CHECK-fails on negative dimensions, aborting the process (denial of service). The missing one-line guard is a num_segments >= 0 check at the point of consumption.

evidence.reason: Unvalidated use: attacker-controlled num_segments is consumed as the leading output dimension/allocation count with no sign check in this code; with num_segments = -1 and an empty segment_ids tensor (shape [0], input shape [0]) every preceding check passes and the per-element validation loop at lines 42-49 runs zero iterations, so the negative count reaches shape construction and causes a CHECK-failure crash. Root cause: missing num_segments >= 0 validation at this call site.

Origin of the tainted value: the scalar is read from an attacker-supplied tensor whose only preceding check is num_segments_tensor.NumElements() != 0 (tensor emptiness), never the value's sign or range; its full declared-width domain, including negative values, is instantiable at this op's trust boundary.

assumptions: GetOutputShape, GetStrides and GetFlattenedRelativeOffsets are project-internal and not shown; their stride/offset contracts were used neither to trigger nor to guard any sink, so the bounds of output_flat(output_index), flat_input(offset) and flat_segment_id(i) for i < relative_offset_set.size() could not be verified from this code alone and are not claimed as defects.

The concrete abort (CHECK failure on a negative dimension in TensorFlow's TensorShape::AddDim inside GetOutputShape/allocate_output) lands in framework code not shown; per the analysis rules the defect is the unvalidated out-of-domain argument passed at the quoted call site.
Behavior of Tensor::scalar<NUM_SEGMENTS_TYPE>() for a non-scalar num_segments tensor (possible internal CHECK) is unverified.
limitations: Loop counters use 32-bit int (int i, auto start_offset = 0) against 64-bit size(); signed overflow requires tensors with more than 2^31 elements (multi-GB allocations) and was not counted as a primary finding.
The error message in the dimension check prints input_dims instead of input_shape.dim_size(i); the comparison itself uses the correct value, so this is cosmetic only.

A potential out-of-bounds read of flat_segment_id(i) when relative_offset_set.size() exceeds the segment tensor size could not be triggered or excluded without the unshown stride/offset helper implementations.

verdict.summary: In njs_object_iterate_reverse, the byte-string and UTF-8 iterator paths compute the starting pointer from args->from (an int64_t from the caller's iterator args) without ever checking it against the string length: p = string_prop.start + from (and njs_string_offset(start, end, from)). Any from outside [0, length) — the full int64 domain is instantiable per the width-domain rule, and the only bounds check in the function, from < array->length, executes solely on the array branch — yields an out-of-bounds pointer whose bytes are copied by njs_string_new and passed to the handler (out-of-bounds read with disclosure to script-land), while the loop then walks p-- far past the buffer for up to from-to iterations, adding memory-unsafe amplification.

evidence.reason: Root cause: raw, unvalidated args->from (int64_t, full declared-width domain) is added to the string buffer start with no comparison against string_prop.size/length anywhere on the string path (the only length guard, from < array->length, is inside the array branch). Trigger: a 1-byte string with from = 0x7fffffff, to = 0 makes p point ~2GB past the buffer; njs_string_new(vm, &character, p, 1, 1) then reads out of bounds each of ~2^31 iterations (p--), disclosing OOB bytes to the handler — OOB read with amplification.

Origin of the tainted value: args->from is consumed with no local validation (no range check, clamp, or mask on any path except the array branch), so per the width-domain rule any int64_t value is instantiable at this iterator engine's entry.

assumptions: njs_string_new copies exactly the requested byte count from the given pointer (standard njs semantics per discipline 3); the OOB read and disclosure conclusion rests on that.

njs_string_prop returns the string's byte size in string_prop.size and character length in length, as the branch comment 'Byte or ASCII string' and the (size_t) length == string_prop.size test indicate.

args->from/args->to are set by callers (iterator setup, e.g. for-in/slice over attacker-controlled objects); their producers are not shown, so both are treated as attacker-data with full int64 domain per the width-domain rule.
limitations: The UTF-8 path sink p = njs_string_offset(string_prop.start, end, from) shares the same unvalidated-from root cause; it is batched with the primary finding rather than emitted as a second evidence entry.

from - to in njs_fast_object(from - to) can overflow int64_t for extreme from/to, but njs_fast_object is a not-shown macro and the subsequent key filtering (idx < to || idx > from) uses values bounded by actual object property indices; trigger impact could not be fully instantiated.
If from is within [to, length] the code behaves correctly; the defect requires the caller-supplied range to exceed the actual string length, which no statement in this code prevents.

verdict.summary: The MNG CLIP chunk handler reads first_object/last_object (0..65535) from attacker-controlled chunk bytes and loops i from first_object to last_object indexing MngInfo arrays (exists[], frozen[], object_clip[]) whose valid domain is 0..MNG_MAX_OBJECTS-1, with no bounds check on any path, producing an out-of-bounds read (exists[i], frozen[i], object_clip[i]) and an out-of-bounds write (mng_info->object_clip[i]=mng_read_box(...), a 32-byte MngBox at an attacker-chosen offset with attacker-derived contents) — heap memory corruption from a crafted MNG file. A second, independent off-by-one in the DEFI handler (if (object_id > MNG_MAX_OBJECTS) should be >=, and the clamp object_id=MNG_MAX_OBJECTS is itself one-past the domain established by this code's own loops) yields a one-past out-of-bounds read/write of exists[] and peer arrays.

evidence.reason: CLIP chunk bytes p[0..3] (attacker data, domain 0..65535) set first_object/last_object; the loop index i is used to index exists[]/frozen[] with no bounds check versus MNG_MAX_OBJECTS anywhere on this path (the mention sweep found the identical check only in the MOVE handler). First OOB access executes on the first iteration for any first_object >= MNG_MAX_OBJECTS, e.g. bytes 01 2C FF FF give i=300.

Out-of-bounds write sink: object_clip[] has valid domain 0..MNG_MAX_OBJECTS-1 (per this code's loops 'for (i=0; i < MNG_MAX_OBJECTS; i++)'), but i ranges to 65535; the guard '(p-chunk) < (ssize_t) (length-17)' bounds the chunk-data read &p[1], not the array index. With a CLIP chunk of length 22 and payload 01 2C FF FF plus filler, mng_info->object_clip[300] is written with a MngBox parsed from attacker bytes — heap memory corruption.

Off-by-one: the only bound, 'if (object_id > MNG_MAX_OBJECTS)' (line 384), under-admits object_id == MNG_MAX_OBJECTS (256 > 256 is false), and its clamp sets object_id to MNG_MAX_OBJECTS, itself one past the valid domain 0..MNG_MAX_OBJECTS-1. A DEFI chunk with payload 01 00 (object_id=256) reaches 'if (mng_info->exists[object_id])' and 'mng_info->exists[object_id]=MagickTrue;' (line 406) one element out of bounds.

assumptions: MngInfo member array capacities are not shown; the valid index domain 0..MNG_MAX_OBJECTS-1 is inferred from this code's own loops (initialization 'for (i=0; i < MNG_MAX_OBJECTS; i++)' and the SAVE handler 'for (i=1; i < MNG_MAX_OBJECTS; i++) if (mng_info->exists[i])').

mng_info is allocated by a caller not shown; writes past member arrays still corrupt adjacent MngInfo fields consumed later in this code (e.g. image->page.x=mng_info->x_off[object_id]) or, for large indices, memory beyond the struct.
Preprocessor state (MNG_INSERT_LAYERS, MNG_LOOSE, MNG_OBJECT_BUFFERS, JNG_SUPPORTED) is unknown; the confirmed findings do not depend on any optional block.
limitations: DISC handler passes attacker object ids (0..65535, 'i=p[j-1] << 8 | p[j]; MngInfoDiscardObject(mng_info,i);') with no local bounds check; safety depends on the unshown internal callee MngInfoDiscardObject, so the harmful use cannot be located in the given code.

LOOP/ENDL: loop_count taken from the chunk (up to 0xFFFFFFFF) with SeekBlob back on each ENDL permits up to 2^32-1 re-parses of a tiny chunk span — large but bounded CPU amplification (CWE-400-type), not driving the verdict.

TERM reads p[2..9] guarded only by 'length != 0', DEFI length>27 reads 17 bytes from &p[12] needing length >= 29, and the chunk-fill loop breaks on EOF leaving the tail unset: all reads remain inside the length+MagickPathExtent allocation (uninitialized data, CWE-908), not out-of-bounds.
PLTE: the AcquireQuantumMemory result for global_plte is not NULL-checked before mng_info->global_plte[i] writes — trigger requires allocation failure only.
If MNG_LOOSE were defined, the PLTE fallback loop 'for ( ; i < 256; i++)' uses i uninitialized and possibly a NULL global_plte when length is 0 or >= 769 — conditional-compilation path only.
LOOP/ENDL use loop_level=chunk[0] (0..255, narrowed by byte width) to index loop_active/loop_jump/loop_count/loop_iteration arrays whose declared sizes are not shown — not provably out of bounds.

verdict.summary: In _gnutls_server_select_suite, the initial SCSV-scanning loop iterates with bound `i < datalen` while reading two bytes (data[i] and data[i+1]) per iteration. When the attacker-controlled ClientHello cipher-suite list has odd length datalen, the last iteration has i == datalen-1 and reads data[datalen], one byte past the end of the buffer. The code's own evenness guard (`if (datalen % 2 != 0) ... return GNUTLS_E_UNEXPECTED_PACKET_LENGTH`) exists but executes only after this loop, so it cannot prevent the out-of-bounds read. The OOB byte is compared against the renegotiation- and fallback-SCSV minor values, feeding attacker-triggered security logic (safe-renegotiation extension handling or a fallback alert) from out-of-bounds memory.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read sink: with odd attacker-controlled datalen, the loop reaches i == datalen-1 and reads data[i+1] == data[datalen], one byte past the buffer. Same defect exists at the data[i + 1] read on line 17. Trigger: datalen = 3, data = {0x56, 0x41, 0x00} (or last byte 0x56 for this branch); line 16 matches data[2]==0x00 (or data[2]==0x56 here), so line 30 reads data[3] out of bounds.

Faulty loop bound: it constrains only i < datalen while the body consumes two bytes (data[i], data[i+1]); for odd datalen this admits i == datalen-1, making the second byte index one-past-the-limit. The code's evenness check `if (datalen % 2 != 0)` appears only later in execution order (after three callee calls), so no statement before or inside this loop bounds i+1 against datalen.

assumptions: `data` points to a buffer of exactly `datalen` bytes containing the attacker-supplied ClientHello cipher-suite list; `datalen` is an unsigned int parameter whose producer is not shown, so its full width domain (including odd values) is instantiable per the width-domain rule.

GNUTLS_RENEGO_PROTECTION_REQUEST_MAJOR is 0x00, GNUTLS_FALLBACK_SCSV_MAJOR is 0x56, and the MINOR constants are 0xff and 0x00 respectively (standard TLS SCSV values); the trigger requires only that data[i] equal the respective MAJOR constant on the last iteration, which the attacker controls.
limitations: cipher_suites_size is taken from the internal callee _gnutls_remove_unwanted_ciphersuites and used as a loop bound over the stack array cipher_suites[MAX_CIPHERSUITE_SIZE] with only a `ret <= 0` sentinel check and no local upper-bound test; if that unshown callee ever returned a size larger than the buffer filled by _gnutls_supported_ciphersuites, further OOB reads would occur, but this cannot be instantiated from the given code.
Odd datalen is also passed to the unshown internal callee server_find_pk_algos_in_ciphersuites before the evenness check; any defect inside that callee cannot be assessed from this code.

The OOB read is a single byte compared against fixed SCSV constants; worst direct impact is a crash or a one-bit side channel on adjacent heap contents influencing renegotiation/fallback decisions, not a direct memory-corruption write.

verdict.summary: Kernel test-driver encoder initializer with no runtime attacker input surface. The only pointer dereference sink (args.head traversal) is guarded by 'if (args.head)'. Remaining candidates (unchecked vzalloc and kstrdup returns, unvalidated src_buf_sz) require OS allocation failure or a misbehaving in-module caller/unshown encode callback to trigger, so no trust-boundary party can instantiate them.

assumptions: This function is called only by the in-module vidtv bridge driver at device initialization with compile-time constant arguments (name, es_pid) and an in-module synthesized src_buf; it is not an exported, ioctl, callback, or packet-handler entry point.

The consumers of e->name, e->encoder_buf, and e->src_buf_sz (vidtv_s302m_encode, destroy path) are outside the given code; no statement in this code uses those values as copy lengths, indices, or dereferences.
limitations: e->encoder_buf = vzalloc(VIDTV_S302M_BUF_SZ) does not check for NULL; under kernel OOM the encoder callback would later operate on a NULL buffer. Robustness issue, not attacker-triggerable.
e->name = kstrdup(args.name, GFP_KERNEL) does not check for NULL; under OOM e->name is NULL (kfree(NULL) is safe, and no dereference of e->name exists in this code).
args.src_buf_sz is stored without local validation; safety of its consumption depends on the unshown vidtv_s302m_encode callback and the in-module caller sizing src_buf consistently.
The args.head traversal loop has no cycle detection; an infinite loop requires the in-module caller to build a cyclic list, which no statement in this code produces.

verdict.summary: Module-internal kernel encoder constructor. All allocation results are NULL-checked (kzalloc, vzalloc, ctx) and the only caller-supplied pointer dereference (args.head->next) is guarded by `if (args.head)`. The unchecked kstrdup result (e->name) is never dereferenced in this code, and the unvalidated src_buf/src_buf_sz pair is only stored here; its harmful use would occur in the not-shown encode function. No trust-boundary party can reach this entry point with attacker data, so no trigger is instantiated in this code.

assumptions: This function is treated as module-internal: it is the constructor of the vidtv test driver, invoked from within the same module with driver-defined constant arguments, so no trust-boundary party (userspace, network, file parser, guest) can influence args.
kfree(NULL) is safe per standard kernel semantics, so the unchecked e->name on the cleanup path causes no harm in this code.
The src_buf/src_buf_sz pairing contract (sz describes the buffer) is honored by the same-module caller; this code cannot verify it and does not use the pair in any memory operation itself.
limitations: kstrdup(args.name) result is stored without a NULL check (`e->name = kstrdup(args.name, GFP_KERNEL);`). On allocation failure e->name is NULL; kfree(NULL) is safe here, but any later dereference of e->name in the not-shown encode/debugfs/destroy paths could NULL-deref. Trigger requires environmental allocation failure and an unshown use site, so not a vulnerability in this code.

src_buf_sz is not validated against the actual extent of src_buf at the store site (`e->src_buf_sz = (args.src_buf) ? args.src_buf_sz : 0;`). If a caller ever passed a size larger than the buffer, the out-of-bounds read would occur inside vidtv_s302m_encode, which is not shown; the defect would live at the read site, not here.

`while (args.head->next) args.head = args.head->next;` loops forever if the caller-supplied list is circular; no statement of this code can create a cycle, and the reachable caller builds an acyclic list, so this is at most an init-time robustness concern.

verdict.summary: ljpeg_start never checks the return value of any fread (lines 10, 13, 17). When the attacker-supplied file ends after a marker segment, every subsequent fread fails and leaves the stale segment bytes in data[], so tag = data[0]<<8|data[1] is recomputed to the same constant value on every iteration. Since the only loop exits are tag <= 0xff00 (line 16) and tag == 0xffda (line 40), a file such as FF D8 FF C0 00 04 FF C0 00 02 followed by EOF makes the do-while loop spin forever with zero file consumption: an unreachable-exit infinite loop (denial of service) triggerable by any party that can supply the parsed image file.

evidence.reason: The fread return value is not checked; on a failed or short read at EOF, data[0..1] retain the previous segment's bytes, so tag is recomputed as the same constant on every loop iteration. With the remaining exit tests being only 'if (tag <= 0xff00) return 0;' (line 16) and 'while (tag != 0xffda)' (line 40), a crafted file whose last in-buffer tag bytes are e.g. FF C0 (0xffc0, which passes the >0xff00 check and is not 0xffda) yields an infinite, CPU-bound loop: an unreachable-exit-condition denial of service instantiated by a roughly 9-byte attacker file.

The loop's only exit conditions are this test and the tag <= 0xff00 return. Once every fread fails at EOF, no statement in the function writes data[] (the switch cases only read it), so tag is frozen at a value that is neither <= 0xff00 nor 0xffda and the loop never terminates.

assumptions: struct jhead is not shown; huff[]/free[] are assumed to have at least 6 slots (line 43 accesses jh->huff[5]) and at least 4 (lines 30-31 use indices 0..3, which the loop guard '(c = *dp++) < 4' provably bounds).
merror() is a project-internal callee not shown; assumed to abort on a NULL allocation, otherwise the calloc at line 48 result is consumed unchecked.
make_decoder_ref() is not shown; its parsing semantics (how far it advances dp and how many bytes it reads) are unknown and were not relied on to admit or dismiss any candidate.
dng_version, ifp and zero_after_ff are globals set outside this function; their producers are not shown.
jh is an output pointer parameter; a NULL jh would crash the memset at line 8, but that is an unquotable caller contract.
limitations: Uninitialized/stale stack reads (CWE-908): when a segment is shorter than the fields consumed, data[7] (line 20, needs len >= 8), data[0..5] (lines 22-25, needs len >= 6) and data[1+data[0]*2]/data[3+data[0]*2] (lines 34-35, up to index 513) read bytes never filled by fread; only the 0xffc4 walk is bounded ('dp < data+len', line 30). These values reach jh->bits/high/wide/clrs/psv, the branch at line 42 and the calloc sizing at line 48, but all accesses stay in-bounds (buffer is 65536 bytes, max index 513) and the harmful use of the garbage values would occur in the not-shown ljpeg_row/decode stages, so no impact link inside this code was instantiated.

len underflow (CWE-191) at line 15: a length field of 0 or 1 wraps ushort len to 65534/65535, but the computed maximum (65535) still fits the 65536-byte data buffer, so fread at line 17 and the dp walk at line 30 remain in-bounds; no out-of-bounds access results in this code.

Line 42 admits jh->clrs == 0 and jh->wide == 0 (only clrs > 6 is rejected), so calloc(0*wide, 4) at line 48 can produce a zero-size row that is returned as success; any resulting out-of-bounds write would occur inside ljpeg_row, which is not shown.

make_decoder_ref(&dp) is called with dp in-bounds (dp < data+len <= data+65535), but the callee may read the 16 huffman-count bytes past the end of data[] when dp is near data+65535 (reachable with the wrapped len); that out-of-bounds read would occur entirely inside the not-shown callee, so it is not attributed to this code.

A NULL jh parameter would crash memset at line 8, but that trigger requires a caller violating an unquotable precondition and produces only a same-privilege crash; recorded as robustness, not a vulnerability.

verdict.summary: In ImmutableExecutorState::Initialize, the outputs_required heap array is allocated with n->num_outputs() elements (line 140), but the edge source-output slot e->src_output() is validated only against the lower bound ('if (e->src_output() >= 0)', line 145) before being used as an array index (read at line 146, write of 'true' at line 148). An attacker-authored graph containing an edge whose src_output exceeds the source node's num_outputs() causes a heap out-of-bounds read followed by an out-of-bounds write of a fixed non-zero byte at an attacker-chosen offset, i.e., memory corruption during executor initialization.

evidence.reason: The array outputs_required is sized n->num_outputs() (line 140), but the index e->src_output() — an int derived from the attacker-supplied graph's edge metadata — is checked only for the lower bound ('e->src_output() >= 0'). No statement in the code upper-bounds it against n->num_outputs(), so any slot value from num_outputs() up to INT_MAX performs an out-of-bounds read at line 146 and, when the read byte is zero, an out-of-bounds write of 'true' at line 148 at an attacker-chosen heap offset. Trigger instantiated by simulation: node with num_outputs()==1 and an edge with src_output()==3 writes 3 bytes past a 1-byte heap allocation.

assumptions: BuildControlFlowInfo, EnsureFrameInfo, GetMaxPendingCounts, gview_ internals, and params_.create_kernel are not shown; their contracts were treated as unquoted assumptions that neither guard nor trigger any sink in this code.
The Graph object arrives fully constructed from attacker-authorable GraphDef content; per the width-domain rule, e->src_output() can hold any int value since no statement in this code narrows it.
limitations: Line 84 'FrameInfo* frame_info = frame_info_[frame_name].get();' followed by the deref at line 90 could yield a NULL dereference if an Enter node's attacker-controlled 'frame_name' attribute is not a key in frame_info_; however, instantiating the mismatch requires BuildControlFlowInfo (not shown) to compute a frame name different from the very attribute it derives frame names from for Enter nodes, and an assumption cannot produce a trigger. Speculative.

Line 132 'frame_info->nodes->push_back(item)' dereferences a pointer set only for names in cf_info.unique_frame_names (lines 8-11); a mismatch between cf_info.frame_names and unique_frame_names would cause a NULL dereference, but that mismatch is only producible by the unshown BuildControlFlowInfo. Speculative.

Integer accumulation in 'frame_info->total_inputs += n->num_inputs()' (line 47) and 'e.input_slot += dst_item->input_start' (line 172) could overflow int only at graph scales no quoted statement of this code can produce; speculative.
The NULL-deref candidates, if ever instantiated by a mismatched-graph bug elsewhere, would crash the process loading the untrusted graph (denial of service) without a corruption primitive.

verdict.summary: The frame index is used to read gif->frames[frame].display at the very first executable statement, before the only bounds check (frame > gif->frame_count_partial), which runs too late and is itself off by one (> instead of >=), admitting frame == frame_count_partial. With frame being an unvalidated unsigned int parameter of a decode entry point, any value in the width domain (e.g. 0x10000) produces an out-of-bounds heap read, and the admitted boundary value consumes an unparsed entry's uninitialized frame_pointer in pointer arithmetic.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read: the array index frame (full unsigned int domain, unvalidated at this point) is dereferenced as gif->frames[frame] before any range check executes; with frame = 0x10000 the load reads far past the frames array. No statement in the code bounds frame before this line.

The only frame bound executes after the first use at line 19 (too late to guard it), and its operator is wrong for count semantics: > admits frame == frame_count_partial, the one-past-the-parsed-limit entry, whose uninitialized frame_pointer is then used in pointer arithmetic at gif_data = gif->gif_data + gif->frames[frame].frame_pointer.

Origin of the tainted value: frame is a data-carrying parameter of a non-static *_decode_* intake function; no shown caller or in-code statement narrows it, so its input surface is the full unsigned int domain per the width-domain rule.

assumptions: The gif_animation struct (frames array capacity, local_colour_table/global_colour_table being fixed 256-entry arrays so that byte indices colour and background_index stay in-bounds) and the bitmap buffer being gif->width*gif->height pixels are not shown; their sizing is assumed, which is why the colour_table[...] reads are not primary findings.

Internal callees gif_skip_frame_extensions, lzw_decode_init, lzw_decode, gif_interlaced_line and the bitmap callbacks are not shown; their return-value contracts (e.g. gif_interlaced_line returning a row < height, stack_pos staying within [stack_base, stack_base+capacity]) are unquoted assumptions and cut both ways.
limitations: Unbounded recursion through the GIF_FRAME_RESTORE path (each recursive call decrements the frame index by at least 1, depth up to the frame count) can plausibly exhaust the stack with a GIF containing tens of thousands of RESTORE frames; it is a potential denial of service but was not simulated to completion here.

The memset in the (frame == 0 || decoded_frame == GIF_INVALID_FRAME) branch and the burst-write loop were verified in-bounds only relative to the assumed bitmap dimensions; a mismatch in the unshown bitmap_create sizing would be outside this code.

colour_table[colour] with colour up to 255 is only safe if the colour tables are 256-entry arrays as in the upstream struct; if they were sized to a smaller colour_table_size elsewhere, that read would be out of bounds, but no such sizing is visible in the given code.

verdict.summary: snd_pcm_oss_sync uses the return value of snd_pcm_format_physical_width(format) as a divisor without checking it: that helper returns 0 (its failure sentinel) for an invalid format, so a format value outside the valid snd_pcm_format_t range reaching line 25 produces width == 0 and a division by zero at line 30 (and mirrored at line 44), causing a kernel divide-error oops. The function is an intake point for OSS ioctl data and no statement in this code validates the format or the width, so an unprivileged local user with audio-device access can crash the kernel.

evidence.reason: Division sink: width is used as a divisor with no zero check on any path. width comes from snd_pcm_format_physical_width, whose documented failure sentinel is 0 for an invalid format; the invalid format value arrives from snd_pcm_oss_format_from(runtime->oss.format) at line 24, an unshown producer whose return domain (snd_pcm_format_t) includes invalid values. When runtime->oss.buffer_used > 0 (ordinary attacker action: write a partial period, then close), this statement divides by zero, producing a kernel #DE oops (local DoS). The same unchecked divisor appears at line 44.

Origin of the tainted value: the failure sentinel (0) of the format-width lookup is consumed without any local sentinel check and flows directly to the divisions at lines 30 and 44. No statement in the code tests width, tests format validity, clamps, or masks the value.

assumptions: snd_pcm_oss_format_from and snd_pcm_oss_make_ready are internal callees not shown; their behavior was not used as a guard or a trigger producer, and their return surfaces were taken as the full declared-type domains per the width-domain rule.
The trigger path assumes make_ready succeeds and params_lock is acquired (the normal path for an opened playback stream), both of which are ordinary outcomes, not attacker-favoring failures.
substream->runtime is non-NULL whenever substream is non-NULL (kernel invariant, not shown).
limitations: Integer underflow candidates at line 30 (period_bytes - buffer_used) and line 41 (period_bytes - period_ptr) would yield a huge frame count into snd_pcm_format_set_silence (OOB write, CWE-191/787), but the harmful state buffer_used > period_bytes or period_ptr > period_bytes cannot be produced by any statement in this code and the write path that maintains these counters is not shown; trigger precondition not instantiated here.

Modulo by zero at line 53 (appl_ptr % runtime->period_size) would require period_size == 0, a state no statement in this code can produce and which earlier unshown hardware-configuration stages reject; speculative.

Real-world exploitability depends on whether the unshown format-setting path can ever store a value that snd_pcm_oss_format_from maps to an invalid snd_pcm_format_t; within the given code that producer is unquoted, so per the width-domain rule the trigger is treated as instantiable.

verdict.summary: The attacker-sized stack writes (argument copy at lines 38-40 and receiver write at line 45) are guarded by the quoted allocation `mrb_stack_extend(mrb, len+2)` at line 35, which is sized from the same expression as the copy (len+2 slots cover maximum touched index len+1) and executes before every write on the only reaching path; all remaining candidates (ci[1] out-of-array write, MRB_PROC_ENV NULL dereference, len+2 overflow, ci->n truncation, GC window on `a`) require states produced only by code not shown and are speculative.

assumptions: fiber_check(mrb, self) raises for a non-Fiber self and returns the fiber's context; mrb_stack_extend(mrb, room) guarantees `room` usable slots from the current ci->stack (raising via longjmp on allocation failure); mrb_get_args-style argc `len` is a non-negative count of materialized arguments matching the size of `a` — all documented semantics of known mruby APIs (discipline 3).

For a MRB_FIBER_CREATED fiber, ci->stack == stbase and cibase->proc == ci->proc with a non-NULL REnv (set by unshown fiber_init); the vmexec 'dummy callinfo' popped at line 42 was pushed by the unshown VM entry stub.
fiber_result(mrb, a, len) consumes exactly len elements of a (in-domain arguments).
limitations: Line 50 `c->ci[1].stack[0] = value;` has no local bound against the ci-array end in this code; an out-of-bounds ci[1] would require a suspension state (ci at the last allocated callinfo) produced by unshown fiber_yield/vm.c code, so the trigger is not instantiable here.

Line 44 `c->cibase->n = len;` would truncate if callinfo n is a narrow bitfield (width not shown); the wrapped count stays <= len while the stack holds len args (extend used len+2), so only argument-count misbehavior, no memory-safety impact, follows.

Line 45 dereferences MRB_PROC_ENV(c->cibase->proc)->stack[0]; the NULL check at line 32 tests c->ci->proc, not cibase->proc nor the env; a NULL env/proc is only producible by unshown fiber_init/machinery.
`mrb_stack_extend(mrb, len+2)` could overflow mrb_int only for len near MRB_INT_MAX, which requires materializing ~2^63 argument values before entry — no statement of this code produces that scale.

A GC triggered inside mrb_stack_extend could in principle invalidate `a` (caller stack) if the old context were unmarked; both the GC trigger and the marking of old contexts reside in unshown gc.c, so this window cannot be exhibited here.

verdict.summary: set_fflags_platform consumes attacker-influenced set/clear flag values and a file path, but every sink is safe: the ioctls write only into valid local ints of the kernel-expected width, the kernel itself validates flag bits (EPERM/EINVAL paths are handled and reported as ARCHIVE_WARN), there is no use-before-initialization, and fd ownership at close is correctly tested against the original fd parameter. The silent ARCHIVE_OK on open() failure, the benign unsigned long to int truncation of set, and a TOCTOU window on open(name) are recorded as limitations because their impact chains terminate in code not shown.

assumptions: The behavior of __archive_ensure_cloexec_flag is not shown; its ignored return value is not consumed by any security sink in this code.

The kernel ioctl semantics for FS_IOC_GETFLAGS/FS_IOC_SETFLAGS and EXT2 equivalents are relied upon per discipline 3: they read/write exactly an int through the user pointer, validate flag bits, and return EPERM/EINVAL on permission/bit errors.
The producer of the name path is the archive extractor (not shown); this code opens it O_RDONLY with no create/truncate mode, so the open itself cannot create or modify files via the path.
limitations: Fail-open reporting: if the caller passes fd < 0 and open(name) fails, the function returns ARCHIVE_OK (the statement 'if (myfd < 0) return (ARCHIVE_OK);'), silently skipping requested file flags, whereas an ioctl failure yields ARCHIVE_WARN. The consequence is an unreported skipped metadata operation; no consumer in this code relies on the flags having been applied, so the impact is not instantiated here.

Width truncation: 'newflags = (oldflags & ~clear) | set;' truncates the 64-bit unsigned long set/clear into the 32-bit int newflags. Simulated with set = 0x100000000, the high bits are silently dropped; the surviving low bits are validated by the kernel ioctl, so no memory-safety, bypass, or state-misrepresentation impact results.

TOCTOU: open(name) by path after the caller created the file leaves a symlink-swap window; the two ordered operations bounding that window (file creation and this open) are in the caller, not in this code, so the race cannot be exhibited here.

Values of set/clear that request root-only flags (immutable, append, journal) are gracefully degraded through the sf_mask subset retry and reported as ARCHIVE_WARN, which is the intended behavior, not a defect.

verdict.summary: No exploitable defect found in this snippet. Attacker-influenced unsigned long set/clear values are truncated into the int newflags, but the only consumer is an ioctl that reads exactly sizeof(int) from a declared int and whose callee (the kernel FS_IOC_SETFLAGS) validates all flag bits; O_NOFOLLOW guards the open() sink against final-component symlink substitution. The open-failure path returning ARCHIVE_OK is a deliberate best-effort skip of optional metadata, and the intermediate-component path race is not instantiable from the given code.

assumptions: Parameter 'a' (struct archive_write_disk *) is a non-NULL internal context supplied by the same translation unit's set_fflags caller; used only for archive_set_error.
fd >= 0 callers pass a descriptor referring to the same file described by 'name' and 'mode'; ownership contract enforced locally by 'if (fd < 0) close(myfd);'.
__archive_ensure_cloexec_flag tolerates a -1 fd (it is called immediately after open() without a sentinel check between them in this snippet).
limitations: Width truncation: 'newflags = (oldflags & ~clear) | set;' narrows unsigned long attacker-derived set/clear into an int with no local mask; impact is limited to silently dropping bits >= 32, because FS_IOC_SETFLAGS reads sizeof(int) and rejects unknown flag bits (EINVAL), so no memory-safety or privilege effect.

Fail-open: 'if (myfd < 0) return (ARCHIVE_OK);' reports success when the file could not be opened for flag setting, while later ioctl failures yield ARCHIVE_WARN; inconsistent but limited to optional metadata restoration, not a security-state presentation.

TOCTOU: 'mode' is checked from the entry while the object is later re-opened by 'name'; O_NOFOLLOW protects only the final path component, so a local attacker racing an intermediate directory could redirect the ioctl. The window requires unshown caller-side creation/validation statements and yields at most setting standard file flags on one file; not instantiable as a vulnerability from this code.

verdict.summary: In the FSCTL_GET_SHADOW_COPY_DATA branch, labels_data_count is computed with 32-bit unsigned arithmetic: 'labels_data_count = (shadow_data->num_volumes * 2 * sizeof(SHADOW_COPY_LABEL)) + 2;'. num_volumes is a uint32 field filled by an unshown VFS backend with no local bound; when num_volumes = 0x80000000, 'num_volumes * 2' wraps to 0 and labels_data_count truncates to 2, so *out_len = 18 and the check 'if (max_out_len < *out_len)' passes (it compares the wrapped value). The buffer is allocated with talloc_zero_array(ctx, char, *out_len) = 18 bytes, but the label loop then iterates num_volumes times writing 2 * sizeof(SHADOW_COPY_LABEL) bytes per iteration at cur_pdata, producing an out-of-bounds heap write with attacker-influenced label content on the first iteration. The missing guard is an overflow-checked (64-bit) size computation or a bound on num_volumes before allocation; no such statement exists anywhere in the code.

evidence.reason: Root cause: 32-bit integer overflow/truncation. shadow_data->num_volumes is an unbounded uint32 set by the VFS backend; 'num_volumes * 2' is evaluated in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic and the result is stored into uint32 labels_data_count. With num_volumes = 0x80000000 the product wraps to 0, labels_data_count becomes 2, *out_len becomes 18 (line 133), and the 'max_out_len < *out_len' check at line 136 compares the wrapped value and passes, so the subsequent allocation is undersized relative to the loop that writes num_volumes labels.

Origin of the tainted value: this call populates shadow_data->num_volumes and shadow_data->labels via a backend not shown in this code. Only the return sentinel is checked; num_volumes is consumed afterwards with no local range check, clamp, or overflow-safe size computation, so per the width-domain rule its input surface is the full uint32 domain.

Sink: the loop bound is the unwrapped num_volumes while the buffer (cur_pdata, allocated as talloc_zero_array(ctx, char, *out_len) at line 143 with the wrapped *out_len = 18) holds only 18 bytes. In the simulated trigger the first srvstr_push writes up to 2 * sizeof(SHADOW_COPY_LABEL) bytes at cur_pdata = buf + 12, an out-of-bounds heap write with attacker-influenced label content, iterated 0x80000000 times.

assumptions: shadow_data->num_volumes and shadow_data->labels are populated by SMB_VFS_GET_SHADOW_COPY_DATA, a project-internal callee not shown; per the width-domain rule num_volumes is treated as instantiable over its full uint32 domain and the missing local bound is treated as the defect in this code.
sizeof(SHADOW_COPY_LABEL) is a positive compile-time constant; the trigger (num_volumes = 0x80000000 wrapping 'num_volumes * 2' to 0) is independent of its exact value.
srvstr_push is taken to write at most its dest_len argument bytes at dest, per its standard Samba semantics; the overflow arises because the underlying allocation, not dest_len, is undersized.
limitations: FSCTL_SET_SPARSE, FSCTL_FIND_FILES_BY_SID, and FSCTL_QUERY_ALLOCATED_RANGES were examined and their guards ('in_len >= 1', 'in_len < 8' before 'MIN(in_len - 4, SID_MAX_SIZE)', 'in_len != 16', 'max_out_len < 16', 'offset + length < offset' wrap check) are correct at both bounds; no candidates there.
The non-atomic static bool vfswrap_logged_ioctl_message could race between threads, causing at worst a duplicated debug log line; no security effect.

Practically reaching num_volumes near 2^31 requires an implausible number of snapshot labels from the backend; per the analysis rules this does not demote the defect, but it lowers exploit likelihood in real deployments.

verdict.summary: fname_match performs no memory copy, size arithmetic, or indexing on attacker-derived data. Both potentially-NULL pointers (name and the return of home_replace_save) are explicitly checked before their only uses, and the allocated string is freed on all paths. No guard is missing.

assumptions: vim_regexec and home_replace_save are project-internal functions whose implementations are not shown; standard Vim semantics (safe regex execution, NULL-able allocation return) are assumed per discipline 3.
p_fic is a global configuration flag set by the user's 'fileignorecase' option; treated as trusted configuration.
limitations: The regex pattern inside regmatch_T is compiled by the caller (not shown). If the caller ever compiles an attacker-supplied pattern, catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS) could occur inside vim_regexec; this function does not and cannot validate the pattern. No evidence in this code that the pattern crosses a trust boundary.
The subject string name (a filename) is matched against the pattern but never used for memory operations, so its content cannot cause memory corruption here.

verdict.summary: This promise-reaction handler resumes a suspended async function after await. The only trust-boundary-derived input is the content of the fulfilled value (args[1]); every use of it is a fixed-size njs_value_t copy (error type test, scope-slot write, vm->retval assignment, call arguments), and the arg fetch goes through njs_arg, the engine's bounds-checked accessor, so no attacker-derived size, index, offset, or pointer reaches any sink. All pointer-valued inputs (ctx, ctx->await, ctx->index, ctx->pc, ctx->capability, frame fields) are produced by njs's own await and compiler machinery inside the same trust boundary and cannot be driven out of domain by an external party. Remaining issues (unchecked ctx dereferences, a ctx leak on the fatal memory-error path, an ignored reject-call result) are robustness defects without an attacker-instantiable security impact.

assumptions: njs_arg(args, nargs, 1) is njs's bounds-checked argument accessor: it returns &args[i] only when i < nargs and &njs_value_undefined otherwise; its definition is not shown, but nargs is fixed by the engine's own reaction-invocation machinery, not by any trust-boundary party, so the boundary case (nargs <= 1) yields the undefined sentinel rather than an OOB read.

ctx (= vm->top_frame->function->context), ctx->await, ctx->index, ctx->pc and ctx->capability are set by the not-shown njs_vmcode_await / async-invocation machinery: ctx is never NULL, ctx->await points at the suspended continuation frame, ctx->index is a compiler-generated scope index valid for exactly the frame scopes this function installs (async->local, njs_function_closures(async->function), async->temp), and ctx->capability holds callable resolve/reject builtins. None of these is influenceable across the trust boundary njs defends (external input reaching engine internals).
njs_vmcode_interpreter returns only NJS_OK, NJS_AGAIN or NJS_ERROR; other return values (which would skip njs_async_context_free at 'return ret;') are not producible.

Promise single-settle semantics in the unshown reaction machinery mean exactly one of fulfilled/rejected runs per ctx, so njs_async_context_free(vm, ctx) executes at most once per context; a second invocation would require the not-shown promise code to violate its own semantics.
limitations: No NULL checks on ctx, ctx->await or ctx->capability: if the await machinery ever registered a reaction with a NULL context, the dereference of ctx->await would crash the VM process. Equal-privilege crash with no trust-boundary party able to instantiate it; robustness only.

The memory-error path 'if (njs_is_memory_error(vm, &vm->retval)) { return NJS_ERROR; }' returns without calling njs_async_context_free(vm, ctx), leaking the async context on a fatal out-of-memory path. No corruption, disclosure, bypass, or attacker-scalable amplification, and the VM is aborting anyway; robustness, not a vulnerability.

The failed path ignores the result of the reject call ('(void) njs_function_call(vm, njs_function(&ctx->capability->reject), ...)'): if that call itself failed, the async function's outer promise would remain pending, though the NJS_ERROR return still propagates the failure. Fail-silent robustness issue, not a security-state misrepresentation.

A double-free or use-after-free of ctx would require the unshown promise reaction machinery to invoke this handler (or its rejected twin) twice for the same ctx, violating single-settle semantics; no statement in this code instantiates that, so the scenario is speculative.

verdict.summary: In CONNECTION_CHECK_WRITABLE and CONNECTION_CHECK_STANDBY, the result of PQgetvalue(res, 0, 0) is used as the first argument to strncmp without any NULL check and without validating the result's field count. The local guard only tests res, PQresultStatus(res) == PGRES_TUPLES_OK, and PQntuples(res) == 1; a server (or MITM on a non-SSL connection) can return a TUPLES_OK result with one row and zero fields, making PQgetvalue return NULL, so strncmp(NULL, ...) dereferences NULL and crashes the client process (denial of service induced by the network peer).

evidence.reason: First use of val with no sentinel check. val comes from `char *val = PQgetvalue(res, 0, 0);` (line 1477), and the only guard, `if (res && PQresultStatus(res) == PGRES_TUPLES_OK && PQntuples(res) == 1)` (lines 1474-1475), checks the tuple count but not the field count; with a server-supplied PGRES_TUPLES_OK result of 1 row and 0 fields, PQgetvalue returns NULL (documented out-of-range sentinel) and strncmp(NULL, "on", 2) dereferences NULL, crashing the client. Trigger fully instantiated: CONNECTION_CHECK_TARGET sends "SHOW transaction_read_only" (line 1315), status becomes CONNECTION_CHECK_WRITABLE (line 1319), and the attacker-controlled reply reaches this strncmp on the next poll.

Identical defect in CONNECTION_CHECK_STANDBY: val from `char *val = PQgetvalue(res, 0, 0);` (line 1544) is unchecked before its first use; the guard at lines 1541-1542 tests only res, resultStatus, and PQntuples(res) == 1, never the field count, so a malicious server answering "SELECT pg_catalog.pg_is_in_recovery()" (sent at line 1376) with a zero-column single-row result makes strncmp(NULL, "t", 1) dereference NULL, crashing the client application.

assumptions: PQgetvalue, PQgetResult, PQresultStatus, PQntuples, PQgetvalue semantics are taken as documented libpq behavior: PQgetvalue returns NULL for an out-of-range field index; PQgetResult/PQntuples/PQresultStatus behave per the public API.

Macros and helpers not shown (UNIXSOCK_PATH, IS_AF_UNIX, pg_getaddrinfo_all, getHostaddr, pqGetErrorNotice3, pqGetc/pqGetInt/pqGetErrorNotice3 buffer handling) are assumed to behave per their documented/project contracts; the getaddrinfo-derived ai_addrlen values are treated as in-domain for sockaddr_storage (system callee guarantee, plus the quoted `if (strlen(portstr) >= UNIXSOCK_PATH_BUFLEN)` bound for AF_UNIX).

conn->last_sqlstate is assumed to be NUL-terminated and initialized by the unshown pqGetErrorNotice3 before the strcmp at line 1103; if a server omitted the SQLSTATE field and the writer left the array unwritten, the impact would still be limited to a stale comparison, not memory unsafety.
limitations: areq, a fully server-controlled 4-byte value, is passed unvalidated to pg_fe_sendauth(areq, msgLength, conn) at line 1182; msgLength is provably bounded (8..2000 checked at line 1032, then -4 and -4), but areq has no local validation.
