The harmful use, if any, occurs entirely inside the not-shown callee, so the impact is not instantiated in this code; a local whitelist of authentication request codes at this call site would be defense-in-depth.

The confirmed NULL-dereference defects cause a deterministic crash (client-side denial of service) with no memory corruption or disclosure; severity is therefore low and requires the client to be connecting to a hostile or man-in-the-middle server (or an SSL-less connection under sslmode=prefer).

No overflow exists in the msgLength path: the quoted range checks `msgLength < 8 || msgLength > 2000` (line 1032) and `msgLength < 8 || msgLength > 30000` (line 1040) keep every subsequent subtraction and the (size_t) cast within [0, 29996], and the availability check `if (avail < msgLength)` precedes any body consumption.

verdict.summary: r_bin_java_bootstrap_methods_attr_new reads the 2-byte num_bootstrap_methods field at offset 6 (R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT (buffer, offset)) without verifying that sz >= 8. sz is attacker-controlled (attribute size from an untrusted Java class file), so a truncated attribute with sz < 8 causes an out-of-bounds read past the buffer. The code's only bounds check, `if (offset >= sz)`, is inside the loop and executes after the header read, so no guard covers it.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read: R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT reads buffer[6] and buffer[7] after `offset += 6`, with no check that sz >= 8. Trigger: attacker supplies a truncated BootstrapMethods attribute with sz = 7 (or any sz < 8 with a valid attr), so buffer[7] is read one byte past the buffer. The only sz bound in the code, `if (offset >= sz)`, is at line 14 inside the loop and runs strictly after this read in execution order.

evidence.snippet: R_API RBinJavaAttrInfo *r_bin_java_bootstrap_methods_attr_new(RBinJavaObj *bin, ut8 *buffer, ut64 sz, ut64 buf_offset) {
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted values: buffer (raw attribute bytes of an untrusted Java class file) and sz (its size, full ut64 domain, never validated in this code before the read at line 9).

assumptions: r_bin_java_default_attr_new returns a non-NULL attr for at least sz >= 6, mirroring this code's own `offset += 6` consumption; its internal validation is not shown and was not relied on to demote the finding.
r_bin_java_bootstrap_method_new parses within the size argument passed to it; its internals are not shown.
R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT performs a raw 2-byte big-endian memory read at buffer+offset with no bounds checking.
limitations: When offset == sz-1 passes the line-14 guard, the callee r_bin_java_bootstrap_method_new receives a 1-byte grant; any overread past that grant would be a defect inside the not-shown callee, since this call site passes an in-bounds pointer and an exact remaining size.

offset += bsm->size could theoretically wrap ut64 if bsm->size were near 2^64, but no statement in this code can produce such a value and the next iteration's `offset >= sz` check would catch any overshoot.
attr->size = offset may record a misparsed size consumed by later parsing stages not shown here; no impact chain is instantiated in this code.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds read of 1 byte past the cipher suite buffer when a TLS client sends a ClientHello with an odd-length cipher suite list. The loop at line 13 permits i = datalen-1 when datalen is odd, making data[i+1] at lines 17 and 30 read data[datalen], one byte past the buffer. The datalen % 2 validation exists at line 78 but is positioned after the first loop has already executed.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read: when datalen is odd (attacker-controlled via ClientHello cipher suite list length), the loop bound 'i < datalen' at line 13 permits i = datalen-1, so data[i+1] reads data[datalen], one byte past the buffer. The attacker sets data[datalen-1] to GNUTLS_FALLBACK_SCSV_MAJOR to pass the short-circuit and trigger the OOB read. No guard exists before this loop; the datalen % 2 check is at line 78, after the loop has already executed.

The loop condition 'i < datalen' does not bound 'i + 1 < datalen'. When datalen is odd, the final iteration has i = datalen-1, making data[i+1] at line 17 read data[datalen], an out-of-bounds access. This is the origin of the defective iteration pattern; the same issue repeats at line 30.

The odd-length validation for datalen exists but is positioned at line 78, AFTER the first loop (lines 13-39) has already performed the out-of-bounds read. In execution order, this guard does not protect the data[i+1] accesses at lines 17 and 30. Had this check been placed before line 13, the OOB read would be prevented.

assumptions: The value of GNUTLS_FALLBACK_SCSV_MAJOR is a specific constant (likely 0x56 per RFC 7507) that the attacker can set in the last byte of data to trigger the OOB read via short-circuit evaluation.
server_find_pk_algos_in_ciphersuites (line 43) also receives potentially odd datalen before validation, but its internal behavior is not shown; it may or may not have its own OOB issue.

The caller of _gnutls_server_select_suite passes data and datalen from a parsed TLS ClientHello; per the width-domain rule, datalen's full unsigned int domain (including odd values) is treated as instantiable.
limitations: The server_find_pk_algos_in_ciphersuites callee also receives unvalidated odd datalen (line 43) before the line 78 check; if that callee has its own i+=2 loop accessing data[i+1], it would have the same OOB issue, but this cannot be confirmed without seeing its code.

The 1-byte OOB read value is used only in comparisons against constants; direct information disclosure is limited to inferring whether the adjacent byte equals those specific constants. Primary impact is memory safety violation and potential crash at page boundaries.

verdict.summary: No trust-boundary-reachable defect. The only concrete anomalies are in the localhost_number block: expand_string(host_number_string) result is used in Ustrtol without the NULL check present at all three sibling expansion sites (NULL deref, crash-only at config parse), and the bound check 'if (n > LOCALHOST_MAX)' omits a lower bound, admitting negative values. Both triggers require writing the configuration file, which the quoted owner/mode guard restricts to root; the command-line (-C) path runs with privilege already given away per the code's own comment, so an unprivileged user could only crash their own unprivileged process. Config errors are operator-side robustness issues, not security vulnerabilities.

assumptions: The comment 'unless it was specified on the command line, in which case privilege was given away at the start' is taken as this code's documentation that command-line-supplied configurations are parsed by a privilege-dropped process; no unprivileged crash of a higher-privileged process is reachable from this code as given.
string_nextinlist(&list, &sep, big_buffer, big_buffer_size) is assumed to bound the copied filename within big_buffer per its buffer+size calling convention (project-internal callee not shown).
hostdata->h_name is assumed non-NULL on a successful gethostbyname/gethostbyname2 lookup (standard resolver semantics).
expand_string returning NULL is treated as in-domain because this code itself checks 'if (s == NULL)' after the spool_directory, log_file_path, and pid_file_path expansions.
limitations: Unchecked sentinel: 'uschar *s = expand_string(host_number_string); long int n = Ustrtol(s, &end, 0);' has no NULL check (siblings have one); a configuration whose localhost_number expansion fails causes a NULL-dereference crash at daemon/invocation startup. Trigger is instantiable only by the root owner of the config (enforced by the quoted fstat owner/mode guard), so it is a robustness/availability issue for the operator, not a trust-boundary vulnerability.

One-sided bound: 'if (n > LOCALHOST_MAX)' admits negative values from Ustrtol base-0 parsing (e.g. localhost_number = -5 sets host_number = -5); any harmful consequence depends on host_number consumers not present in this code, so the impact chain is not instantiated.

Under CONFIGURE_FILE_USE_NODE/CONFIGURE_FILE_USE_EUID builds, sprintf at 'uschar *suffix = filename + Ustrlen(filename)' appends up to ~278 bytes past the filename inside big_buffer; overflow would require a config_main_filelist entry nearly big_buffer_size long, but that list is a compile-time constant, so no runtime party can instantiate it.
Error messages after the fancy filename block (fstat failure, wrong owner/mode) print big_buffer, which may contain the filename with a suffix appended; cosmetic log-message inaccuracy only.

verdict.summary: In cvtchar, the '^' escape arm reads the character after '^' (c = UChar(*++sp)) and then unconditionally sets len = 2, without the terminator check that every other arm performs (case '\0': c = '\\'; len = 1, and the ternaries at lines 33/47). When the attacker-supplied source string ends in '^', sp[1] is the terminating NUL; the function consumes the terminator and returns len = 2 although only one character remains. The caller advances sp += 2, stepping one byte past the end of the string, and its translation loop then reads (and copies) out-of-bounds heap memory until an incidental NUL. Off-by-one (CWE-193) causing an out-of-bounds read on untrusted terminfo/termcap source.

evidence.reason: Off-by-one: when *++sp is the terminating NUL (input string ends with '^'), c becomes 0 and len is still set to 2, so the returned length counts the string terminator as consumed. The caller advances sp += len past the end of the buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read of attacker-originated source data. The mirrored backslash arm (case '\0': c = '\\'; len = 1) proves the intended invariant that the terminator must never be counted; no terminator check exists anywhere on the '^' path.

Taint origin: sp points into attacker-controlled termcap/terminfo source text being converted to terminfo push sequences; every byte it references, including a string ending in '^' followed by the terminator, is attacker-instantiable.

assumptions: save_string/save_char and the global dp are unshown internal helpers; their buffer-sizing and append semantics are assumed correct since no local statement contradicts that.
UChar is assumed to be the standard ncurses mask/cast ((unsigned char)(x)), bounding all arithmetic through it to 0-255.

The caller consumes len as a character-advance count (sp += len) and loops on the source string; this contract is inferred from the function's own uniform len computation in every other arm (lines 15, 19, 25-28, 33, 47) and from its documented purpose, not from shown caller code.
limitations: A NULL sp would crash at switch (*sp) (line 7), but the caller's non-NULL precondition is unquotable in this code; robustness issue only.
The octal arm consumes an unbounded number of digits and c wraps modulo 256 in unsigned char (defined behavior); len remains exact, so this is a functional quirk, not a memory defect.
The out-of-bounds read itself materializes in the caller's advancement loop (not shown); the defect proven here is the off-by-one returned length that provably consumes the string terminator.

verdict.summary: print_media_desc validates the output buffer only against m->desc.media.slen + m->desc.transport.slen + 36 bytes, then copies the attacker-controlled format list (m->desc.fmt[i], up to m->desc.fmt_count entries) into the buffer with no check against the buffer end, so a remote SDP peer supplying long format tokens causes an out-of-bounds write of arbitrary length and content past the caller's buffer.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write sink: copies fmt[i].slen attacker-controlled bytes (parsed from a remote peer's SDP 'm=' line; producer not shown, so full declared-width domain applies) into the output buffer without any check that p + fmt[i].slen stays within 'end'. Simulated trigger: media.slen=5, transport.slen=7, fmt_count=1, fmt[0].slen=5000, len=1024 passes the L9 check (48 <= 1024), and this memcpy writes buf+22..buf+5021, ~3998 bytes past the 1024-byte buffer, with attacker-controlled content.

Origin of the failure: the only length validation in the function accounts for media.slen + transport.slen + 36 bytes of fixed overhead (spaces, port digits, '/', port_count digits, CRLF) but omits every byte of the format list copied at L29, and 'end' is not consulted again until after the fmt loop (L37/46/55). Even at the check's exact boundary (len == media.slen+transport.slen+36) a single format token longer than the ~14-byte slack overflows the buffer.

assumptions: m points to a pjmedia_sdp_media populated by the SDP parser from a remote peer's SDP (producer not shown); per the width-domain rule its fields (media.slen, transport.slen, fmt_count, fmt[i].slen, port, port_count) are treated as attacker-controlled across the network trust boundary.

buf and len come from a caller not shown; this code's own design (end = buf+len, end-p passed to section printers, 'return -1' on printed < 0) establishes len as a hard bound this function is responsible for enforcing at every write, so caller-side sizing cannot excuse the missing fmt check.

print_connection_info, print_bandw, print_attr, pj_utoa, and pj_memcpy are treated per their standard/documented semantics; the section printers receive the remaining space (end-p) and their negative failure sentinel is checked at the call site, so those sections are guarded with respect to the visible contract.
limitations: The L9 bound expression can additionally be wrapped by extreme slen values near the width maximum, producing a huge memcpy for media/transport as well; this is the same root cause (trusting an arithmetic expression over attacker slen values) and is folded into the primary finding rather than reported separately.
Exploitability (code execution vs. crash) depends on where the caller places buf (stack/heap) and adjacent object layout, which are not shown; the confirmed impact is the out-of-bounds write itself.

If deployed callers always sized the buffer to hold the entire original SDP packet, practical triggering would be harder, but this code neither documents nor enforces that contract, and its own -1-on-overflow design shows undersized buffers are expected inputs.

verdict.summary: ip6gre_err() reads the GRE flags via `flags = p[0];` where `p = (__be16 *)(skb->data + offset)` BEFORE the only length check in the function (`if (!pskb_may_pull(skb, grehlen))`), so a crafted ICMPv6 error whose embedded packet is shorter than offset+4 bytes (or a negative offset) causes an out-of-bounds read in kernel memory; the unchecked flags value also controls grehlen and the subsequent tunnel-lookup key derivation.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read sink: p was formed as skb->data + attacker-controlled offset (line 5) with no validation, and this 2-byte read executes before the function's only bounds check, pskb_may_pull at line 22. Trigger instantiated: attacker sends a truncated ICMPv6 error embedding an ip6gre packet with skb->len = 40 and offset = 40 (or any offset with offset + 4 > skb->len, or a negative offset per the full int domain), so p[0] reads past the packet data into adjacent kernel memory; the read value then controls grehlen and the lookup key.

Taint origin: the attacker-controlled `offset` parameter (full int domain; no contract or validation quoted anywhere in this code) is used directly in pointer arithmetic and in grehlen with no clamp, mask, or range check; this is where the unvalidated value enters the data flow that reaches the unguarded read at line 10.

assumptions: ip6_tnl_parse_tlv_enc_lim (not shown) is an internal callee; its return value teli is used as an index into skb->data after the sentinel check `if (teli && teli == be32_to_cpu(info) - 2)`, and its in-range contract could not be quoted from this code.

The ICMPv6 dispatch layer that calls this handler with `offset`/`info` is not shown; no precondition on offset is documented or asserted in this code, so offset is treated as attacker-data over its full declared int width.
pskb_may_pull, ip6gre_tunnel_lookup, and be32_to_cpu semantics relied on per standard kernel documentation (sentinels 0/NULL, both checked at lines 22 and 27).
limitations: In the ICMPV6_PKT_TOOBIG arm, `mtu = be32_to_cpu(info) - offset;` can wrap to a huge unsigned value when the attacker-chosen `info` is smaller than `offset`; the clamp `if (mtu < IPV6_MIN_MTU)` guards only the low bound, so an oversized value can be assigned to t->dev->mtu. The security consequence materializes in MTU-dependent transmit paths not shown in this code, so it is recorded here rather than as a primary finding.

The lookup call site reads the key at `*(((__be32 *)p) + (grehlen / 4) - 1)` after pskb_may_pull; the byte offset (grehlen/4 - 1)*4 is provably < grehlen, so it stays within the pulled region, but grehlen itself was computed from the out-of-bounds flags read, making this a consequence of the primary defect rather than an independent one.

verdict.summary: In the error path of _gdContributionsAlloc, the cleanup loop is entered with u == 0 and executes 'u--', wrapping the unsigned counter to 0xFFFFFFFF. The subsequent loop 'for (i=0;i<=u;i++) gdFree(res->ContribRow[i].Weights);' then iterates up to 4294967296 times, reading res->ContribRow[i] far out of bounds of the line_length-element array and passing uninitialized/out-of-bounds pointers to gdFree, causing heap corruption and an unterminating loop. The trigger is instantiated with attacker-influenced size parameters (line_length = 1, windows_size >= 0x10000000, e.g. from extreme image scale ratios): overflow2 flags windows_size * sizeof(double) at iteration 0 (or the 2 GB gdMalloc fails), the error arm runs at u == 0, and no statement in the code checks u > 0 before the decrement or bounds i against line_length.

evidence.reason: Root cause: 'u--' executes when u == 0 (the first loop iteration, i.e. whenever the overflow2 flag or a failed gdMalloc occurs at u = 0), wrapping the unsigned int to 0xFFFFFFFF. The cleanup loop then uses 'i<=u' with no bound against line_length, so 'res->ContribRow[i].Weights' is read out of bounds and its value (uninitialized on the overflow_error path, where line 26 never assigned it) is passed to gdFree. Concrete trigger simulated: line_length = 1, windows_size = 0x10000000 → overflow2(windows_size, sizeof(double)) returns 1 at iteration 0 → error arm at line 28 → u = 0xFFFFFFFF → gdFree of uninitialized ContribRow[0].Weights, then OOB reads/invalid frees at i = 1, 2, ... with no loop termination. No guard of any form (u>0 test, corrected loop bound, clamp, early return) exists anywhere on the path.

assumptions: overflow2 is libgd's documented overflow predicate returning nonzero when the product of its arguments would overflow; this assumption is not load-bearing for the defect, because with windows_size >= 0x10000000 the else-branch gdMalloc(windows_size * sizeof(double)) requests ~2 GB, whose NULL failure sentinel (always in-domain for an allocation per standard semantics) reaches the same error arm at u == 0.

gdMalloc behaves as a standard allocator: returns pointer or NULL, contents uninitialized; every returned pointer is NULL-checked in this code, but the uninitialized content of res->ContribRow is what line 32 frees on the overflow_error path.

Callers are not shown; line_length and windows_size are treated as attacker-data under the width-domain rule (full unsigned int domain), consistent with their origin in libgd's image-scaling path where they derive from attacker-supplied image dimensions.
limitations: The secondary uninitialized-value issue (res->ContribRow[u].Weights never assigned on the overflow_error branch, then freed at line 32) is folded into the primary defect's impact chain rather than reported as an independent CWE-457 finding.
Memory-safety of the line 17 and line 26 allocation sizings was verified as guarded by the quoted overflow2 checks at lines 13 and 23 respectively; no separate finding arises there.

verdict.summary: luaG_runerror is the Lua VM's internal error-reporting helper. Its only external-content parameter, the format string fmt, is produced solely by the VM's own error paths (none shown in this code), so no attacker-instantiable format-string trigger exists here; the remaining data (L->ci, L->top, msg) are interpreter-internal values or returns of an unshown internal formatter whose failure modes are not characterizable from the given snippet. No memory-safety, injection, or fail-open defect is instantiable from the statements shown.

assumptions: luaO_pushvfstring, luaG_addinfo, luaG_errormsg, luaC_checkGC, isLua, ci_func, getcurrentline, and setobjs2s are project-internal callees not shown; their semantics (formatter directive handling, non-NULL return, exactly-one-value push, noreturn behavior) are assumed per the Lua core, not quoted from this code.
L is a valid lua_State and L->ci points to a valid CallInfo per the interpreter's internal contract; no boundary-crossing party can supply these directly.
Callers of luaG_runerror are the VM's internal error paths, which pass literal format strings; the Lua script author controls the values substituted into the message, not the format.
limitations: Format-string candidate (CWE-134 shape) at 'msg = luaO_pushvfstring(L, fmt, argp);': dismissed as speculative because the trigger requires an unseen caller to pass attacker-authored text as fmt, and the impact additionally depends on the unshown formatter's directive semantics; no such caller or path appears in the given code.

Unchecked-return candidate at 'luaG_addinfo(L, msg, ci_func(ci)->p->source, getcurrentline(ci));': msg is consumed without a NULL check, but no failure sentinel for the unshown luaO_pushvfstring can be established from this code, so the trigger precondition cannot be instantiated.

Stack-adjustment candidate at 'setobjs2s(L, L->top - 2, L->top - 1);': an underflow would require the unshown formatter to push a count other than one; that behavior is not exercisable from the given statements.

verdict.summary: njs_await_fulfilled consumes only one attacker-influenced datum (the fulfilled promise value), which flows solely through fixed-width njs_value copies and an njs_is_error type test. Frame-state mutations are symmetric and their restore provably executes before every return branch. Remaining NULL-deref and leak candidates depend on engine invariants (context set by await setup, promise settles once) that no statement in this code can violate, and the leak occurs only on an OOM path.

assumptions: vm->top_frame->function->context is a non-NULL njs_async_ctx_t set by the not-shown await-setup code; this code quotes no assertion, but no statement here can produce a NULL context either.

ctx->await, ctx->index, ctx->pc and ctx->capability are engine-recorded fields (compiler-generated index, promise capability with function-valued resolve/reject); producers are not shown in this code.
The promise machinery invokes this onFulfilled reaction at most once per settlement and with the reaction frame it constructed, so ctx is freed exactly once by njs_async_context_free.
limitations: If the await-setup code ever registered this callback with a frame whose function->context is NULL, or if a double fulfillment of the underlying promise were possible, async_frame = ctx->await would dereference NULL and njs_async_context_free would double-free; both require violating promise settle-once semantics or engine invariants not shown in this code, so the trigger is not instantiable here.

On the memory-error early return (return NJS_ERROR after njs_is_memory_error), njs_async_context_free is not called, leaking ctx; this requires an allocation failure the attacker cannot deterministically induce and is a bounded leak on an abort path, not a vulnerability.

A return value from njs_vmcode_interpreter other than NJS_OK/NJS_AGAIN/NJS_ERROR would fall through to return ret without resolve/reject; the interpreter is characterizable as returning only those three sentinels.

verdict.summary: All attacker-derived offsets and lengths in this parser are guarded before their memory-consuming uses: the header read is covered by 'if (offset + 8 > sz)' (sz >= 14 before reading 2 bytes at offset 6), and the per-iteration 'if (offset >= sz) { break; }' runs before 'r_bin_java_bootstrap_method_new (buffer + offset, sz - offset, ...)', so the callee always receives an in-buffer pointer and a positive remaining length, and no ut64 underflow of sz - offset is reachable. The unchecked callee-produced 'bsm->size' can move 'offset' arbitrarily but every subsequent use of offset is either the same guard or a metadata store ('attr->size = offset'), so no out-of-bounds access is reachable in this code.

assumptions: r_bin_java_default_attr_new and r_bin_java_bootstrap_method_new are internal callees not shown; their internal bounds handling cannot be verified here. This code passes them the raw buffer with its true size and, for the latter, a verified in-buffer pointer and positive remaining length (guarded by 'if (offset >= sz) { break; }').
bsm->size is produced by the unshown callee; its declared width is unknown. Even assuming the full ut64 domain, no use of offset in this code escapes the loop guard.
r_list_newf failure and r_list_append behavior on a NULL list are treated per standard allocation semantics (failure returns NULL); only an allocation-failure path could reach an unchecked list.
limitations: The return of r_list_newf is not NULL-checked before r_list_append; triggerable only by allocation failure, which an attacker cannot induce, so it is a robustness issue, not a vulnerability.

If the unshown r_bin_java_bootstrap_method_new parses attacker 16-bit fields without checking against the length argument it receives, an out-of-bounds read would exist inside that callee; per the analysis rules the defect would be located there, not at this call site, since this code passes in-domain arguments.

The initial bound 'offset + 8 > sz' requires sz >= 14 where only 2 bytes are subsequently read (offset 6..7); this over-rejects buffers of size 8..13, a functional over-rejection with no security effect.
A NULL bsm return leaves offset unadvanced for that iteration, causing up to num_bootstrap_methods (max 65535) repeated identical calls; bounded, no amplification beyond a small constant factor.

verdict.summary: No exploitable vulnerability found. All memory accesses in this Vim regexp matching loop are guarded: reg_getline results are NULL-checked before use (RS_STAR_LONG and RS_BEHIND2 paths), regstack_push and ga_grow failure sentinels are tested at every call site, unknown opcodes are rejected by the default arm, and pattern memory consumption is capped by the p_mmp checks and the FEAT_RELTIME timeout. The MULTIBYTECODE byte-comparison loop, when simulated at the end-of-line boundary, cannot read past the NUL because it stops at the first mismatching byte and all previously matched bytes are non-NUL content bytes by construction. The remaining unchecked value (len written by the not-shown match_with_backref callee before 'rex.input += len') rests on an unquoted internal contract and is recorded as an assumption, not a defect in this code.

assumptions: match_with_backref (callee not shown) writes a sane length into *len before this code executes 'rex.input += len'; no local sentinel check on len exists, but per discipline 3 an unshown internal callee can neither produce the trigger nor serve as a guard, so this is recorded as an unquoted contract rather than a confirmed defect.

cstrncmp adjusts its *len argument to the number of bytes actually compared, bounding the subsequent 'rex.input += len' in the EXACTLY, BACKREF and ZREF cases; this is the documented Vim internal semantics.

rex.reg_startpos/reg_endpos columns are set by this engine during forward matching such that endpos.col >= startpos.col within a line; the BACKREF single-line subtraction 'rex.reg_endpos[no].col - rex.reg_startpos[no].col' relies on that ordering.

The compiled regexp program (scan, OPERAND nodes, BRACE limits) is well-formed because it was produced by the not-shown regcomp; the 'default:' arm of the switch rejects any out-of-domain opcode at runtime.
limitations: Hypothetical program corruption (e.g. via the unvalidated 'scan = OPERAND(rp->rs_scan) + 4' pointer arithmetic in RS_BEHIND1/RS_BEHIND2) would require a separate memory-safety defect in code not shown; no such trigger could be instantiated from the given code.

A negative or inverted column pair in BACKREF (endpos.col < startpos.col, e.g. through unusual \ze placement) would pass a negative len to cstrncmp, but the engine's MOPEN-before-MCLOSE program ordering prevents instantiation from the given code.

The MULTIBYTECODE non-composing loop 'for (i = 0; i < len; ++i) if (opnd[i] != rex.input[i])' performs no explicit NUL check on rex.input; simulation showed the read is content-bounded (first non-matching byte, which is the NUL at end of line, terminates the loop), so no out-of-bounds read was provable.

verdict.summary: The NE entry-table parser contains two attacker-triggerable heap out-of-bounds reads. First, after off++ on line 37, bundle_type is dereferenced on line 38 with no recheck of tableat + off < r_buf_size, so a file whose last byte is a non-zero bundle_length causes a one-past-the-end read. Second, in the moveable path the inner-loop guard on line 42 reserves only 4 bytes while r_read_le16 on line 62 consumes bytes at off+4 and off+5, so a file ending at tableat + off + 5 leaks one heap byte into entry->paddr, which radare2 later displays to the user. Both are reachable from a crafted NE binary.

evidence.reason: Missing bounds check after increment: the guard at line 30 (tableat + off >= r_buf_size) covers only the pre-increment off, and no statement between off++ and this dereference rechecks either bound. Trigger: r_buf_size == tableat + 1, EntryTableLength > 0, byte at tableat non-zero — the read lands at buf + r_buf_size, one byte past the heap buffer (out-of-bounds read).

Insufficient reservation for moveable entries: the inner-loop guard at line 42 (tableat + off + 4 >= r_buf_size) reserves only 4 bytes, but the moveable path advances off by 4 and then r_read_le16 reads two bytes, consuming 6. The check at line 59 (off > EntryTableLength) guards against the wrong bound with the wrong operator and cannot prevent this. Trigger: bundle_type == 0xff, EntryTableLength >= off, r_buf_size == tableat + off + 5 — the second byte of segoff is read at buf + r_buf_size and flows into entry->paddr (line 64), an information leak into displayed output.

Origin of the insufficient bound for the second defect: this reservation covers only 4 bytes from the inner-loop start, while a moveable entry (bundle_type == 0xff) reads through relative offset +5; the constant should be +6 for the moveable path.

assumptions: The allocation layout of bin->entry_table is not shown; the vulnerabilities are reachable whether it is a pointer into bin->buf at tableat (bound r_buf_size) or a separately allocated buffer of EntryTableLength bytes — in the latter case off == EntryTableLength passes the line-59 > check and reads past that buffer instead.
bin->segment_entries is assumed to contain SegCount elements, consistent with the guarded indices segnum - 1 < SegCount and bundle_type - 1 < SegCount.
limitations: Memory leak: at the inner-loop break statements in the moveable (line 60) and fixed (line 68) arms, the RBinAddr allocated at line 45 is not freed — a resource leak, not the primary memory-safety defect.
The csEntryPoint path is safe: r_list_get_n returns NULL for out-of-range indices and the code handles it with (s? s->paddr: 0).
The fixed-entry path (lines 67-70) is correctly bounded: the line-42 reservation of 4 bytes covers its 3-byte read, and line 67 uses the proper >= operator against EntryTableLength.

verdict.summary: This is the standard Lua core error-reporting helper. The three plausible sinks (unvalidated format parameter fmt at line 7, unchecked internal callee return msg used at line 10, and the ci pointer captured at line 2 and used after luaC_checkGC at line 5) are all unguarded in this snippet, but none of their trigger preconditions or impact chains can be instantiated from the given code: no shown caller feeds trust-boundary data into fmt, luaO_pushvfstring is an internal formatter whose failure sentinel is not characterizable here, and any finalizer-induced invalidation of ci happens in GC/stack code not shown. The candidates are speculative, not vulnerabilities of this code.

assumptions: L is a valid non-NULL lua_State pointer and L->ci is a valid current CallInfo; these are VM invariants maintained in code not shown.
luaO_pushvfstring pushes the formatted string on the Lua stack and returns it, or raises the Lua error (longjmp) on failure; this internal callee's semantics are not shown in the given code.
luaC_checkGC is a conditional GC step that may run __gc finalizers (arbitrary Lua/C code) before returning; its macro definition is not shown.
isLua(ci), ci_func(ci) and getcurrentline(ci) are ldebug.h/lstate.h macros with their usual meanings; their definitions are not shown.

In the Lua VM, every in-core call site of luaG_runerror passes a fixed literal format string with script-controlled data only as %-arguments; no such call site is included in the given code, so this cannot be treated as a quoted contract.
limitations: Potential format-string misuse (CWE-134): fmt is consumed at line 7 with no narrowing statement anywhere in the snippet. If any caller (not shown) ever forwarded attacker-influenced text as fmt, that caller would create the vulnerability. Dismissed only because no boundary-reaching call path is shown and the formatting callee is not characterizable; a local fix would be an explicit format literal such as luaO_pushvfstring(L, "%s", fmt) at call sites handling raw data.

Unchecked callee return: msg is assigned at line 7 from luaO_pushvfstring and used at line 10 with no sentinel test. A NULL-return failure mode for this internal function is not established by the given code, so the NULL-deref trigger is not instantiated; in stock Lua this function either returns a valid string or longjmps.

Stale ci across GC: ci is captured at line 2 and dereferenced at line 10 after luaC_checkGC at line 5, which can run __gc finalizers. CallInfo lifetime management (stack shrink, frame free) is entirely in code not given, so a use-after-free window cannot be exhibited as two ordered operations here.

va_end(argp) at line 8 is skipped if an error longjmps out of luaC_checkGC, luaO_pushvfstring, luaG_addinfo or luaG_errormsg; this is a platform-specific va_list hygiene quirk with no demonstrated security effect.

verdict.summary: In the allocation-failure cleanup path, the unsigned loop counter u is decremented (u--) before and inside 'while (u >= 0)', a tautological bound for unsigned int. When the error arm is entered at u == 0 (or after freeing down to 0 from any row), u wraps to 0xFFFFFFFF and res->ContribRow[u].Weights is read massively out of bounds, with the garbage pointer then passed to gdFree, repeating for decreasing out-of-bounds indices: an out-of-bounds read feeding an invalid free (heap corruption / crash). Trigger is instantiated by attacker-controlled line_length/windows_size plus the always-in-domain gdMalloc NULL sentinel.

evidence.reason: u is declared 'unsigned int u = 0;' (line 3), so after 'u--' from 0 (or the final decrement after freeing row 0) it wraps to 0xFFFFFFFF, and 'while (u >= 0)' is always true. Simulated trigger: windows_size = 0x10000000 makes gdMalloc(windows_size * sizeof(double)) at line 26 return NULL at u = 0; line 28's check enters this arm; u becomes 0xFFFFFFFF; line 31 reads res->ContribRow[0xFFFFFFFF].Weights far out of bounds and gdFree()s the garbage pointer, continuing OOB with each iteration. No statement anywhere bounds u below zero (mention sweep: lines 3, 22, 29, 30, 31, 32 only; line 22's 'u < line_length' applies solely to the for loop).

assumptions: overflow2() is an internal helper not shown; its exact overflow threshold is unknown. The confirmed trigger does not depend on it: it relies only on the width-domain of the unsigned parameters and the gdMalloc NULL failure sentinel, which is always in-domain per standard allocation semantics.

line_length and windows_size are produced by callers not shown (typically image-scaling geometry); per the width-domain rule their surface is the full unsigned int domain, and no statement in this code narrows them at entry.
limitations: Secondary non-primary issue: on the error path, res->ContribRow and res themselves are never freed after the cleanup loop (leak of two heap blocks on every failure) — a resource defect, not the memory-safety primary.
The runaway loop's practical outcome beyond the first out-of-bounds access depends on heap layout; the first OOB read plus invalid free alone already establishes the memory-corruption primitive.

verdict.summary: njs_object_iterate_reverse uses args->from (an int64_t iteration range whose producer is not shown, hence attacker-controlled per its full declared width) as a raw byte offset into string data without any bounds check: `p = string_prop.start + from;` (line 80, byte-string branch) and `p = njs_string_offset(string_prop.start, end, from);` (line 103, UTF-8 branch) then copy bytes from `p` into a character handed to the handler. With from larger than the string size (e.g. a fromIndex of 1000 on "abc"), the loop reads out-of-bounds heap memory one byte per iteration and the resulting character values (and handler comparison results) are observable by the script, yielding an out-of-bounds read with information-disclosure potential. No statement in this code bounds, clamps, or masks `from` on the string path.

evidence.reason: Sink: from (args->from, int64_t, attacker-data per width-domain rule) is added to the string data pointer with no bound against string_prop.size or length; the following loop (njs_string_new at line 86 copies 1 byte from p each iteration) reads out-of-bounds whenever from exceeds the string size, e.g. from=1000, to=0 on "abc" (size 3): p = start+1000, i = 1001, first iteration reads start[1000].

evidence.snippet:
p = njs_string_offset(string_prop.start, end, from);
            p = njs_utf8_next(p, end);
evidence.reason: Second sink, UTF-8 branch: same unvalidated from is passed to njs_string_offset, walking the pointer past end for from > codepoint count; njs_utf8_prev/njs_string_new (line 112) then read out-of-bounds bytes. The only mention of from on this path besides the offsets is the loop counter i = from + 1 (line 106); no comparison, clamp, or mask of from vs length exists anywhere on the path.

Origin of the tainted values: from and to are loaded from the caller-supplied iterator args struct with no local range validation; their declared width is int64_t and no statement in this code narrows them before the string-branch pointer arithmetic.

assumptions: args->from/args->to are produced by iterator setup code not shown; per the width-domain rule their input surface is taken as the full int64_t domain, and any caller-side clamping is an unquotable contract that cannot demote the finding.

njs_string_offset and njs_utf8_next are treated per their characterizable accessor semantics (advance by index/codepoint); their bounds behavior is not shown, but the byte-string branch (line 80) needs no callee to reach out-of-bounds memory.
limitations: Array branch secondary candidate: the guard at line 27 (`from < array->length`) checks only the upper bound; a negative from (in-domain for int64_t) passes and indexes array->start[from] out of bounds at line 30. Recorded as the same CWE-125 class; the string-branch defect is used as the primary since even its positive range is unchecked.

Object-branch fast path (lines 136, 164-167) iterates from..to without bound checks, but the handler (njs_iterator_object_handler) performs property lookups itself; no memory sink is visible in this code, so no separate candidate is raised.
Exact disclosure utility depends on which handler is bound (e.g. lastIndexOf comparison results vs. value materialization); the OOB read itself is fully instantiated in this code.

verdict.summary: TOCTOU race in pxa3xx_gcu_write: the free-list emptiness check `if (!priv->free)` runs outside the spinlock (lines 21-25), so two concurrent writers sharing the device can both pass it. The first drains the last free buffer at lines 31-32; the second then executes `priv->free = buffer->next` with buffer == NULL, dereferencing NULL in the kernel while holding the spinlock with IRQs disabled. The only under-lock NULL guard that would prevent this exists nowhere in the code. Impact: local denial of service of the kernel by an unprivileged writer of the device node.

evidence.reason: Sink: the batch is popped from the free list under the spinlock with no NULL re-check. After the unlocked check at line 21, a concurrent writer can drain the last free buffer, so `buffer = priv->free` yields NULL and `buffer->next` is a NULL pointer dereference inside the kernel, executed while holding the spinlock with IRQs saved (oops / potential system-wide deadlock). Trigger fully simulated: two threads on the same fd, free list = {B0}; T1 pops B0, T2 pops NULL.

Origin of the defect: the free-list emptiness test is performed without the spinlock held, so it cannot protect the locked pop at lines 31-32. A second context of this same write handler interleaves between this check and the spinlock acquisition, emptying the list; the code never re-validates priv->free (or buffer) under the lock, and pxa3xx_gcu_wait_free's return is checked only for ret < 0, never for list emptiness.

assumptions: PXA3XX_GCU_BATCH_WORDS is a positive constant and buffer->ptr points to an allocation of at least that many 32-bit words, per the comment 'Last word reserved for batch buffer end command' (line 16); the exact value and allocation are not shown in the given code.
pxa3xx_gcu_wait_free and run_ready are not shown; their return/behavior contracts are used neither as guards nor as trigger-blockers.
The attacker has write access to the pxa3xx_gcu device node (deployment permission is outside the given code).
limitations: Line 9, `int words = count / 4`, truncates size_t into int: count >= 0x3FFFFFFFC yields words = -1, which passes the line 17 bound check. Not a vulnerability here: the kernel VFS caps write() count at about 2^31 (MAX_RW_COUNT), and even if instantiated the copy at line 37 receives a near-SIZE_MAX length, fails, and the -EFAULT path returns the buffer before line 49 is reached; no memory corruption results.

Lines 13-14 and 67: priv->shared fields (num_writes, num_words, hw_running) are updated/read without locking; the code itself documents the statistics as racy (lines 11-12). Whether userspace can mmap and write `shared` is not shown, and the effect of a forged hw_running inside run_ready is not shown, so no security impact is instantiated.

The primary trigger requires concurrent execution by two contexts of this write handler; the race window is exhibited inside the given code as the unlocked line 21 check versus the locked lines 31-32 use.

verdict.summary: Balloc(int k) indexes the global freelist with the fully unvalidated int parameter k: no range check, clamp, mask, or error arm exists anywhere in the code, so any k outside freelist's extent performs an out-of-bounds read at line 7 (and a conditional out-of-bounds write plus a write-through of the garbage pointer at lines 8/16), while negative or >=31 k also makes '1 << k' undefined. Independently, the MALLOC result is dereferenced at line 12 without any NULL check, so an allocation failure (attacker-forced via huge k or ordinary OOM) is a NULL dereference.

evidence.reason: freelist is indexed directly with k, an int parameter whose full domain (negative through 2^31-1) is instantiable at this entry point. The mention sweep over every statement touching k (lines 7, 8, 10, 12) finds no bounds check, clamp, mask, or rejection arm, and freelist's extent is not bounded by any quotable statement, so line 7 is an out-of-bounds read at an attacker-controlled offset; when the out-of-bounds slot is non-NULL, line 8 additionally writes a pointer out of bounds and line 16 writes through the garbage pointer (memory corruption). Trigger: Balloc called with any k outside the freelist extent, e.g. a large positive or negative int.

Origin of the tainted value: k is an unvalidated int parameter whose producer is not shown in this code; per the width-domain rule its input surface is the full int range, and this code contains no statement narrowing it before the freelist index, the shift, or the allocation-size computation.

The allocation result rv is consumed without any sentinel check: MALLOC can return NULL (the standard allocation failure sentinel, always in-domain), and the very next statement dereferences it with rv->k = k, followed by rv->maxwds = x and rv->sign = rv->wds = 0. No NULL test on rv exists anywhere between the allocation and the first use. Trigger: allocation failure, which an attacker can force by supplying a k that makes (1<<k)*sizeof(Long) a multi-gigabyte request, causing a NULL dereference (denial of service).

assumptions: freelist is a fixed-extent global array whose declaration and size are not shown; no quotable bound on k exists, so any representable int k is treated as capable of indexing outside it.
MALLOC is assumed to wrap the standard allocator and return NULL on failure (semantics of malloc per discipline 3); its definition is not shown.
k's caller is not shown; since this code neither documents nor checks a precondition on k, k is classified as attacker-data with the full int domain rather than as a contract argument.
limitations: The out-of-bounds write at line 8 and the write-through of the garbage pointer at line 16 require the out-of-bounds freelist slot to contain a non-NULL value, which the given code cannot instantiate; the unconditionally guaranteed primitive is the out-of-bounds read at line 7, so the primary CWE is recorded as CWE-125 rather than CWE-787.
The undefined behavior of '1 << k' for negative k or k >= 31, and the unbounded allocation size, are consequences of the same missing bound on k and are not counted as separate defects.

Upstream gdtoa contains the guard 'if (k <= Kmax && (rv = freelist[k]))' which is absent from this code; its absence is the single decisive fact, but that upstream text is outside the given snippet and is cited only as context, not as evidence.

verdict.summary: pxa3xx_gcu_write checks buffer availability with 'if (!priv->free)' outside the spinlock, then pops the free list under the lock with 'buffer = priv->free; priv->free = buffer->next;' and no NULL test on the popped pointer. Two concurrent writers (the function is an exported file write handler; nothing prevents multiple opens) race past the unlocked check, one drains the free list, and the other executes line 32 with buffer == NULL, dereferencing NULL+offset in kernel context (oops/panic under panic_on_oops): a local denial-of-service triggered by attacker input. The words-count bounds check guarding the copy and end-command stores is correct at both boundaries and is not the defect.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the popped buffer is dereferenced ('buffer->next') with no NULL check, no in-lock re-test of priv->free, and no validation of the wait result's success contract. Trigger: a second concurrent caller that passed the unlocked 'if (!priv->free)' check drains the free list first, so this pop yields buffer == NULL and the store loads from NULL + offsetof(next) in kernel space.

Origin of the stale value: the availability check on priv->free executes without the spinlock, so its result is invalid by the time the pop at lines 31-32 runs under the lock; a concurrent writer can empty the free list (or consume the buffer the wait was woken for) inside this exhibited window.

assumptions: The allocation size of buffer->ptr (PXA3XX_GCU_BATCH_WORDS words) is not shown; the in-bounds verdict for the copy and the end-command store rests on the code's own comment '/* Last word reserved for batch buffer end command */' together with the line 17 guard.

The semantics of pxa3xx_gcu_wait_free are not shown; only the '< 0' test at line 23 is relied upon, and a ret == 0 with priv->free == NULL would reach the same sink even single-threaded — this only strengthens the finding.

Device-node permissions and the possibility of multiple concurrent openers are deployment context not shown; per the analysis rules this may not demote the candidate, so the write handler is treated as a trust-boundary intake point.
limitations: The corruption at the sink is a NULL-pointer dereference at a small fixed struct offset (kernel oops, denial of service), not an attacker-addressed out-of-bounds write; no arbitrary-write primitive was found.

The single-threaded variant of the trigger (wait_free returning 0 without a free buffer) depends on an unshown callee and was not counted as a separate trigger; the concurrent-writer race instantiates the defect on its own.
The non-atomic statistics updates at lines 13-14 are explicitly documented in-code as non-atomic and have no security effect.

verdict.summary: virtbt_rx_handle dereferences skb->data[0] without checking that the device-supplied skb contains at least one byte. A malicious or misbehaving virtio bluetooth device can deliver a zero-length receive buffer, making the read at the sink out of bounds relative to skb->len (and reading an uninitialized byte that then drives the packet-type switch), after which the failed skb_pull leaves a zero-length skb that is passed to hci_recv_frame with a claimed HCI packet type. No statement in this function validates skb->len on any path.

evidence.reason: Primary sink: one byte is read from skb->data with no check that skb->len >= 1. The skb comes from the virtio receive queue, so its length is device-controlled and can be 0; with skb->len == 0 this read is out of bounds relative to the valid data window and yields an uninitialized byte that reaches the switch at line 8, and the subsequent skb_pull(skb, 1) fails without modifying the skb, leaving a zero-length skb to be passed as a typed HCI packet. The mention sweep of every statement touching skb (lines 5, 6, 13, 14, 17) found no length, NULL, or emptiness check anywhere before the read.

evidence.snippet: static void virtbt_rx_handle(struct virtio_bluetooth *vbt, struct sk_buff *skb)
evidence.reason: Origin of attacker-data: skb is populated by the virtio device backend across the VM trust boundary; its content and length (including length 0) are device-controlled and enter this intake function unvalidated.

assumptions: The caller passes a non-NULL skb whose data pointer is valid; only the skb's content and length are treated as attacker-controlled (caller construction code is not shown).
skb_pull is relied on per its standard kernel semantics: it returns NULL and leaves the skb unmodified when the requested length exceeds skb->len.
hci_recv_frame is a project-internal callee not shown; per the analysis rules its internal length validation could neither dismiss nor protect the defect at the call site on line 14.
limitations: The downstream consequence of passing a zero-length, typed skb into hci_recv_frame depends on HCI core code not shown, so only the out-of-bounds/uninitialized read at line 5 and the unchecked call-site pass at line 14 are claimed as impact; no deeper HCI-core corruption is asserted.

Whether the byte read at skb->len == 0 is stale heap memory within the backing allocation or past it depends on the caller's skb allocation strategy (not shown); either way the read exceeds the skb's valid data window and the value is not device-provided data.

verdict.summary: This directory parser contains the complete post-2015 hardening set: the quoted length guard 'if(dire->size >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN)' executes before both the name read and the NUL write and, together with the buffer sized 'sizeof(squashfs_dir_entry_3) + SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN + 1' from the same constant, provably bounds every admitted copy length and terminator index; 'if(dir_count > SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT)' bounds the inner loop; every read_directory_data result is sentinel-checked before use; mallocs are checked; and names are validated by check_name/check_directory. The only local gap, consuming the read_inode return without a NULL check, cannot be instantiated from the given code (callee behavior not shown) and would at worst be a same-privilege crash of the image-parsing tool itself.

assumptions: squashfs_dir_header_3/squashfs_dir_entry_3 field widths, SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN/SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT values, and the semantics of read_inode, read_directory_data, check_name, check_directory, squashfs_closedir, and the SQUASHFS_SWAP_* macros are external to the given code; however, the safety of the name read/NUL write does not depend on the constant's value because the quoted guard 'dire->size >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN' and the quoted buffer allocation 'sizeof(squashfs_dir_entry_3) + SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN + 1' are self-consistent: the worst admitted copy length is SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN and the worst NUL index is SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN, both within the SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN + 1 byte name region.

The int counters 'bytes' and 'dir->dir_count' can only overflow after roughly 2^31 bytes of successfully read directory data supplied in the image; they feed only the 'bytes < size' loop comparison, TRACE output, and a count, with no memory, index, or size sink, so no security impact is instantiated.
limitations: '*i = read_inode(block_start, offset);' is consumed without a NULL check ('dir->mode = (*i)->mode;' is the first dereference). Whether read_inode has a NULL-returning error path cannot be established from the given code, so the trigger is speculative; and even if it fired, the impact would be a NULL dereference crashing only the unsquashfs process run by the party that supplied the image, at equal privilege, with no corruption, disclosure, or bypass — a robustness issue, not an established vulnerability here. Adding a local NULL test after read_inode would still be sound defensive practice.

The 'if(dire->size >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN)' check may be unreachable dead code if size is an 8-bit bitfield (max 255); it is harmless either way, and the buffer allocation independently contains the maximum possible copy length and terminator index.

verdict.summary: hw_atl_utils_fw_rpc_wait consumes a firmware-controlled message length (fw.len) read from a device register and, with no upper-bound check anywhere in the function, uses it as the dword count for hw_atl_utils_fw_downld_dwords copying into the fixed-size embedded buffer &self->rpc. A malicious/compromised NIC presenting a length up to the field's full representable range (the code itself treats 0xFFFF as a retry escape, so 0xFFFE is in-domain) drives an out-of-bounds write of firmware-controlled data past self->rpc into adjacent kernel memory.

evidence.snippet:
err =
		hw_atl_utils_fw_downld_dwords(self,
					      self->rpc_addr,
					      (u32 *)(void *)
					      &self->rpc,
					      (fw.len + sizeof(u32) -
					       sizeof(u8)) /
					      sizeof(u32));
evidence.reason: Sink: fw.len, sliced from a device-register value (attacker-data across the device trust boundary), is used unvalidated as the copy length (rounded up to dwords) into the fixed-size buffer &self->rpc. The only mentions of fw.len in the code are an equality test against 0xFFFFU (line 24, triggering a retry), a loop condition excluding exactly 0xFFFF (line 29), and a nonzero test (line 32); none bounds fw.len against sizeof(self->rpc), so any firmware-supplied length larger than the buffer is copied past its end. Instantiated trigger: firmware sets fw.tid == sw.tid and fw.len = 0x8000 (≠ 0xFFFF), loop exits, (0x8000+3)/4 = 8192 dwords are written into the fixed struct, an out-of-bounds write with firmware-controlled length and content.

Origin of the tainted value: fw.val (containing fw.len and fw.tid) is filled by hw_atl_utils_rpc_state_get, which reads a device RPC-state register controlled by NIC firmware. No statement in this code masks, clamps, or range-checks fw.len after this read, so the full representable width of the length field reaches the copy-length sink at lines 33-40.

assumptions: fw.len is a bitfield of the unshown union struct aq_hw_atl_utils_fw_rpc_tid_s; its width is not declared in this code. The code's own comparison with 0xFFFFU (treated as a protocol retry escape) proves the field spans at least 16 bits, so lengths up to 0xFFFE are representable and in-domain.

sizeof(struct hw_atl_utils_fw_rpc), the type of the fixed embedded buffer self->rpc, is not shown; it is assumed to be far smaller than the maximum representable fw.len (an RPC message struct, not a 64KB buffer). If it were at least 65538 bytes the write would stay in bounds.

hw_atl_utils_fw_downld_dwords (callee not shown) is taken, per its name and argument shape, to copy the given dword count from device registers into the destination buffer; self->rpc_addr (set elsewhere, unshown) is assumed to be the register source address.
limitations: Line 25 passes raw firmware-derived sw.len to hw_atl_utils_fw_rpc_call with no validation; in the known driver this callee writes the value into a control register rather than a memory sink, and the callee is not shown, so no memory-safety impact is instantiated here.

If fw.len's declared width were the full 32 bits, (fw.len + sizeof(u32) - sizeof(u8)) could wrap for lengths near 0xFFFFFFFF, producing an undersized copy that leaves stale buffer contents; with the at-least-16-bit domain evidenced by the 0xFFFF escape handling this is not exercised, and it would be an information-reuse issue only.
The poll timeout (100000 us) bounds how long the loop spins, so no unbounded resource consumption is claimed.

Triggering requires a malicious, compromised, or buggy NIC firmware on the device side of the trust boundary; a purely host-local software attacker without control of device registers cannot instantiate the OOB write.

verdict.summary: virtbt_rx_handle consumes a device-supplied skb but the switch over the attacker-controlled pkt_type byte has no default arm and no other statement frees the skb: for any of the 252 packet-type values outside the four handled HCI constants (e.g. 0x00), the function returns without releasing the buffer, leaking one skb per malicious packet and enabling unbounded kernel memory exhaustion (DoS) by an untrusted virtio Bluetooth device/backend.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the switch over attacker-controlled pkt_type has no default arm and the function contains no free of skb on any other path (mention sweep of skb: lines 5, 6, 13, 14 — the only disposal is the ownership transfer at hci_recv_frame inside the matching cases). Instantiated trigger: device posts a packet with first byte 0x00 and used length 1; line 5 sets pkt_type=0x00, line 6 pulls the byte, the switch matches no case, control reaches line 16, and the skb allocation is retained without release — repeatable per packet for unbounded memory exhaustion.

Origin of the tainted value: pkt_type is read directly from the device-supplied skb payload byte, whose full __u8 domain (0-255) is attacker-instantiable per the width-domain rule; the value drives the switch that decides whether skb is freed or leaked.

assumptions: skb and its length are produced by the driver's rx-completion path, which is not shown; the rx-handler shape of this function marks it as an intake point for device DMA data, so skb contents and skb->len are treated as attacker-controlled per the width-domain rule.
vbt->hdev is assumed to be registered by the driver probe path (not shown); no NULL check exists here, but instantiating hdev==NULL requires unshown state.
limitations: Secondary candidate (not primary): line 5 reads skb->data[0] with no length guard, and the implicit length check inside skb_pull (line 6) runs after the read; if the device supplies a zero-length buffer, data[0] is an uninitialized heap byte that selects the switch branch (CWE-908). Its impact beyond branch selection is not instantiated because hci_recv_frame is project-internal and not shown.

skb_pull's NULL return sentinel (failure when skb->len < 1) is ignored at line 6, so a short skb reaches hci_recv_frame un-pulled; the consequence lands inside code not shown, so it is not counted as a primary defect.

The leak's exploitability presumes the standard kernel rx-handler ownership convention that this function consumes the skb; no caller statement in the given code reclaims it, and no quoted contract could be found to dismiss the candidate.

verdict.summary: lprn_is_black indexes lprn->ImageBuf with fully unvalidated attacker-domain values: the parameter bx (its only mention is the sink line) and the derived row offset y0, which the signed remainder in 'y0 = (r + h - bh) % maxY' can make negative (C99 '%' keeps the dividend's sign) and which is never wrapped for y0+y, so both a large bx and a negative y0 produce an out-of-bounds read at p[x]. Additionally 'BlockLine / nBh' and '% maxY' divide by zero when nBh == 0 or BlockLine < nBh, crashing the process. No bounds, sign, range, NULL, or zero check exists anywhere in the function.

evidence.reason: Primary out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). The index into ImageBuf consumes the unvalidated parameter bx (full int domain of a non-static function; mention sweep shows bx appears only on this line, with no bounds check, clamp, or mask anywhere) and y0, which can be negative. Simulated trigger: lprn_is_black(pdev, 0, 32, 1000000) with nBh=32, nBw=4, BlockLine=96, bpl=100 gives y0=0 and p=&ImageBuf[4000000] against a ~9600-byte buffer; p[x] on lines 14-15 reads far out of bounds. A second trigger with r=0, h=1 gives y0=-31 and a read before the buffer.

Taint origin for the sink and a CWE-369 site. In C99 the result of '%' keeps the dividend's sign, so r+h < bh (e.g., r=0, h=1, bh=32, maxY=96) yields y0 = -31, which flows unchecked into the ImageBuf index on line 13 as a negative byte offset. The modulo also bounds only y0, never y0+y, so blocks near the top of the ring are not wrapped. Furthermore, when BlockLine < nBh (e.g., 5/10*10=0) or BlockLine==0, maxY is 0 and '% maxY' is a division by zero that aborts the process.

Division by zero (CWE-369). The divisor lprn->nBh is a struct field set outside this code; per the width-domain rule its surface is the full int domain, and the mention sweep of nBh (lines 5, 9, 11, 12) shows no zero or positivity check. With nBh == 0 this statement is an integer division by zero (SIGFPE), crashing the process that consumes the data.

assumptions: The caller of this externally visible helper and the code that sets lprn->nBh, nBw, BlockLine, and allocates ImageBuf are not shown; per the width-domain rule all their values are treated as full-domain attacker data and no contract they might enforce may demote a candidate.
gdev_mem_bytes_per_scan_line(pdev) is a project-internal callee not shown; its return bpl is consumed without a sentinel check and is treated as an unvalidated multiplier.
limitations: The row-overrun variant (y0+y reaching maxY-1+bh-1 because the loop lacks a '(y0+y) % maxY' wrap) shares the line-13 sink but its out-of-bounds extent depends on the unquoted ImageBuf allocation size; it is recorded as supporting evidence for the same primary defect, not as an independent finding.

The information-disclosure channel of the OOB read is a coarse oracle (a single 'any byte nonzero' bit per call via return 1); the primary demonstrated impact is out-of-bounds read/crash denial of service, with no write primitive in the given code.

verdict.summary: mobi_decode_infl consumes an attacker-controlled rule string and a caller-supplied decoded_size, and both memory sinks (memmove at lines 32 and 49) plus the indexed accesses at lines 33 and 45 are fully guarded by the quoted checks at lines 28 and 41, which bound pos >= 0, l >= 0, and the one-past-the-end pointer (decoded + *decoded_size + 1) to within decoded + INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX. Edge testing at negative pos, pos == *decoded_size, *decoded_size == SIZEMAX exactly, *decoded_size < 0, and *decoded_size == INT_MAX shows every case is either rejected or lands on a valid index; the checks also precede the first use in execution order on every iteration and in both branches. Residual issues (signed overflow of pos after ~2^28 seek codes, debug_print %s on a possibly non-terminated buffer) have no instantiated memory-safety impact and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: The decoded buffer is at least INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX bytes; this is a caller contract not quotable in the given code, but the local guards bound all accesses to indices < INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX given that size.
debug_print is a project macro not shown in the given code; its release-mode behavior is assumed to be a no-op or stderr print, per the libmobi convention.
limitations: Signed integer underflow of pos at 'pos -= c - 10' (line 20) is reachable with a rule string of roughly 2^28 or more seek codes (bytes 11-19), causing signed-overflow UB (CWE-190). No memory-unsafe effect is instantiated: after any wrap, the insert and delete guards reject via pos < 0 or l < 0 before any memmove or indexed access, so the only realized consequence is undefined behavior in arithmetic with no corruption, disclosure, bypass, or amplification.

debug_print calls at lines 29, 42, and 46 pass decoded as a %s argument although the caller's buffer may not be NUL-terminated (potential over-read up to INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX in debug builds); the macro is not shown, debug builds are not the release path, and the data is the attacker's own file content, so no security impact is instantiated.

The pointer formations decoded + pos (lines 25, 26, 38, 39) are computed before the guards evaluate; forming an out-of-object pointer is formally UB for negative or oversized pos, but the pointers are never dereferenced unless the guard at line 28 or 41 passes first, so no access occurs.

verdict.summary: The attacker-controllable frame index is used to dereference the frames array at line 25 ('gif->frames[frame].display') before the code's only range check ('if (frame > gif->frame_count_partial)', line 30) executes, so any out-of-range frame value causes an out-of-bounds read in the process decoding the attacker-supplied GIF.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read: the attacker-data parameter 'frame' (unsigned int, full-width domain, no narrowing statement in this code) indexes gif->frames here as the very first use, before any range validation. Instantiated trigger: gif_internal_decode_frame(gif, 0x7FFFFFFF, false) with an initialised GIF reads gif->frames[0x7FFFFFFF].display outside the allocation, crashing or influencing the return path (GIF_OK vs GIF_INSUFFICIENT_DATA) from out-of-bounds memory.

This is the only bound on 'frame' in the entire function, and it executes after the first dereference at line 25, so it cannot protect that use; its '>' operator also admits frame == frame_count_partial, whose safety cannot be verified from the shown code.

assumptions: gif_interlaced_line(height, y) (internal callee, not shown) returns a value < height; the decode_y computation depends on this.
The bitmap_get_buffer callback returns a buffer of gif->width * gif->height * 4 bytes; frame buffer writes rely on this unshown contract (its NULL sentinel is checked).
gif->local_colour_table and gif->global_colour_table hold at least 256 entries, matching colour_table_size = 2 << (flags & mask) <= 256.
GIF_COLOUR_TABLE_SIZE_MASK is 0x07, bounding colour_table_size to 256; the quoted gif_bytes checks then cover all descriptor and colour-table reads.
The extent of the gif->frames allocation is set in gif_initialise() (not shown); it is not relied upon for the primary finding.
limitations: Line 30's '>' vs '>=' boundary: frame == frame_count_partial passes the check and flows into gif->frames[frame] uses including writes (virgin/opaque) at the exit label; whether that index is out of bounds cannot be proven because the frames-array allocation size is not shown — at worst an uninitialized-field read (CWE-908), left unconfirmed.

The early returns at lines 21, 26 and 31 bypass the exit-label cleanup (bitmap callbacks, buffer_position restore); buffer_position is not yet modified at those points, so this is functional, not a security defect.
Impact of the primary OOB read is a single out-of-bounds load whose value gates an early return; no out-of-bounds write occurs on the out-of-range path because line 31 returns first.

verdict.summary: Balloc validates only the upper bound of k. The single check, `if (k > Kmax)`, admits every negative value down to INT_MIN, so any negative k reaches the sink `if ((rv = freelist[k]))` and indexes the global freelist array out of bounds: an OOB read, and on the non-NULL branch an OOB write `freelist[k] = rv->next` plus writes through the OOB-derived pointer at `rv->sign = rv->wds = 0` — memory corruption from a negative array index.

evidence.reason: Sink: k is a parameter whose producer is not shown (full int domain per width-domain rule); no statement in the code rejects k < 0, so a negative k (e.g., -1) reaches these lines and both reads and writes freelist[-1] — an out-of-bounds access on the global pointer array; when the OOB slot is non-NULL, line 12 is an out-of-bounds write and line 24 (`rv->sign = rv->wds = 0`) writes through the OOB-loaded pointer.

The only guard on k. It correctly enforces the upper bound (rejects Kmax+1, admits Kmax) but places no lower bound: every negative k passes this test and flows unvalidated to the freelist indexing at lines 11-12. The missing `k < 0` rejection is the defect.

assumptions: freelist is declared as a Kmax+1 element array (declaration not shown), which makes `k > Kmax` correct at the upper bound (k=Kmax in bounds, k=Kmax+1 rejected).
Kmax is a small non-negative constant (< 31), so `x = 1 << k` is well-defined for the admitted non-negative range 0..Kmax.

zend_error(E_ERROR, ...) is PHP's documented fatal error and performs a bailout without returning, so both error arms terminate execution; consequently the failed-MALLOC path cannot NULL-deref at `rv->k = k`, and k > Kmax cannot reach the freelist indexing.
Bigint's fields k, maxwds, sign, wds precede the w[] array, so lines 20-21 and 24 are in-bounds for a fresh allocation.
limitations: Reachability of a negative k depends on internal dtoa callers not shown in this code; per the width-domain rule the parameter's full int domain is treated as instantiable at this entry point, but no concrete caller path producing k < 0 is exhibited here.

The out-of-bounds write branch requires the memory preceding freelist to hold a non-NULL pointer; that state is not shown in this code, so only the unconditional out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) is fully instantiated, with the write as a realistic escalation.

`x = 1 << k` with negative k is undefined behavior whose concrete effect is target-dependent; an int overflow of `1 << k` for admitted k would require Kmax >= 31, and Kmax's value is not shown, so that variant remains speculative.

verdict.summary: outlen/inlen are computed as (sizeof(req) + stream_len) in size_t arithmetic but stored in __u16 locals (line 12-13), silently truncating when the true parameter size exceeds 65535. The chunk is then allocated from the truncated values (line 15, SCTP_PAD4(outlen) + SCTP_PAD4(inlen)) while sctp_addto_chunk subsequently appends sizeof(req) + stream_len bytes (lines 26/29/37/40). With e.g. out=true and stream_num=32767 (within the full __u16 domain): stream_len=65534, outlen truncates to 14, only 16 bytes are allocated, and the code appends 16 + 65534 bytes, a heap out-of-bounds write of ~64KB with attacker-influenced content. No range check, clamp, or cap on stream_num exists anywhere in the function.

evidence.snippet:
outlen = (sizeof(outreq) + stream_len) * out;
	inlen = (sizeof(inreq) + stream_len) * in;
evidence.reason: Root cause: truncating assignment into __u16 locals. For stream_num=32767, out=true: sizeof(outreq)+65534 = 65550 wraps to outlen=14, so the allocation at line 15 (SCTP_PAD4(14)=16 bytes) no longer covers the 65550 bytes later appended; trigger value is within the full declared __u16 domain of stream_num.

Sink: copies stream_len (65534) bytes into a chunk allocated with only SCTP_PAD4(outlen)=16 bytes of payload (line 15) after 16 bytes were already consumed at line 26, producing a heap out-of-bounds write of ~64KB; the 'if (stream_len)' zero-test does not bound the copy against the allocation and no guard exists on any path.

assumptions: sizeof(struct sctp_strreset_outreq)=16 and sizeof(struct sctp_strreset_inreq)=8 (struct definitions not shown); the truncation triggers for any header size >= 2 bytes when stream_len is near 65534, so the defect does not depend on the exact sizes.

sctp_make_reconf allocates parameter payload per the length argument and sctp_addto_chunk appends that many bytes to the chunk buffer (kernel-internal callees not shown); the allocation-vs-copy mismatch is nevertheless fully established by quoted statements in this code.
The caller's stream_list buffer is sized for stream_num * 2 bytes; stream_len <= stream_num*2 in all cases, so the copy source read is in-bounds.
limitations: The stream_len truncation alone (stream_num >= 32768 without outlen/inlen truncation, e.g. stream_num=40000) yields allocation and copy sizes that remain consistent (outlen=14480 vs writes 16+14464) and is only a functional under-reporting, not a memory-safety defect.

When the true outlen is exactly 65536 (stream_num=32760, out=true), outlen truncates to 0 and the 'if (outlen)' branch is skipped, emitting an empty RECONF chunk; protocol error but no memory-safety impact.

If the unshown callee chain (sctp_addto_param/skb_put) contains a BUG_ON on insufficient tailroom, the impact degrades from silent corruption to a kernel panic (denial of service); the defect at this call site stands either way.

verdict.summary: squashfs_opendir consumes the return of read_inode (a parse of attacker-supplied filesystem image data) without any NULL/failure-sentinel check; when read_inode fails to read the inode at the attacker-controlled block_start/offset, the first dereference dir->mode = (*i)->mode crashes the process parsing the malicious image (denial of service).

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: the result of read_inode, a parse over attacker-controlled filesystem image data whose block_start/offset parameters are attacker data at full 32-bit domain, is stored without any NULL or failure-sentinel check, unlike every read_directory_data result in this function which is guarded by 'if(res == FALSE) goto corrupted;'.

Sink: first unchecked dereference of *i. Trigger: a crafted squashfs image whose directory inode location fails to read makes read_inode return its NULL failure sentinel (always in-domain for a parse call); execution reaches this line with *i == NULL and dereferences it, crashing the image-parsing process. Mention sweep of *i (lines 17, 25-29, 32, 41-43) contains no guard; the minimal fix 'if(*i == NULL) return NULL;' appears nowhere in the code.

assumptions: read_directory_data returns TRUE/FALSE and fails at the end of the finite directory table; this is used only to bound the speculative candidates below, never to dismiss the primary finding.
MEM_ERROR terminates the process, so the checked malloc failures are safe arms.

SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN and SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT are compile-time constants; the name-buffer safety argument holds for any value of SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN because the buffer reserves SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN + 1 bytes for the name and the check admits at most size = SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN - 1.
limitations: Inner loop 'while(dir_count--)' does not re-check 'bytes < size', so a header whose count exceeds the directory's declared size causes parsing of adjacent directory-table bytes as extra entries; all reads remain size-bounded and termination is guaranteed by the quoted 'if(res == FALSE) goto corrupted;', so no memory-safety impact.

If dirh.count were a full 32-bit field, 'dirh.count + 1' >= 0x80000001 stored into int dir_count would be negative and pass 'dir_count > SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT'; the resulting long loop still performs only bounded, guarded reads and ends at the first read failure, so it yields no out-of-bounds access.

Integer overflow of the 'bytes' accumulator would require roughly 2^31 bytes of successfully read directory-table data; no quoted statement produces such a table, and the read-failure check ends the loop at the table's end.
The NULL-deref impact is a crash of the parsing process with no memory corruption; it is reported as an attacker-triggered denial of service, not corruption.

verdict.summary: cvtchar parses an attacker-supplied terminfo escape string, but every read (switch (*sp), *++sp, the digit loop) is bounded by the string's NUL terminator, with the quoted guard while (isdigit(UChar(*sp))) testing before the advancing read. Every character value passed to the unshown save_string/save_char helpers is provably confined to the unsigned char domain by the UChar narrowing casts and the mask c &= 0x1f. The octal accumulator 8 * c + (*sp++ - '0') wraps modulo 256 on long digit runs, but the wrapped value stays in-domain and reaches only correctly encoded, in-range output, so it is a parsing-accuracy note, not a memory-safety defect. The len=0 return at end-of-string, the absent NULL check on sp, and the unchecked save_* return values all depend on unshown caller/callee behavior and cannot be instantiated in this code.

assumptions: sp is assumed to point into a NUL-terminated string; this code quotes no NULL check or length parameter for it, so a NULL sp would fault at switch (*sp) — a caller-contract issue, not locally checkable.
UChar is assumed to be the standard ncurses cast macro ((unsigned char)(ch)); with it, the octal accumulator's maximum (8*255+9 = 2049) reduces mod 256 and stays inside the unsigned char domain.

save_string and save_char are not shown; this code passes only constant strings and in-domain 0-255 character values to them, never a raw size, index, or offset, so no defect attaches to these call sites under the given analysis rules.
dp is a global initialized outside this code; its buffer sizing is not shown.
limitations: Octal escape wrap: for inputs like \7777 the accumulation c = UChar(8 * c + (*sp++ - '0')) wraps modulo 256 (defined behavior), producing a terminfo character value different from a naive reading of the digits. The value remains 0-255 and the emitted %{N} encoding is consistent, so this is a semantic/parsing-accuracy issue with no memory-safety consequence in this code.

len = 0 is returned only when *sp == '\0' (quoted: len = (c != '\0') ? 1 : 0;). An unshown caller that advances sp by cvtchar's return without a NUL check could loop forever; a while (*sp) caller never reaches that state. Trigger depends entirely on unshown caller behavior.

Return values of save_string/save_char are consumed without sentinel checks (dp = save_char(dp, ...)). If those helpers could fail (e.g. an exhausted fixed buffer behind dp), a bad pointer would propagate; no such failure mode, buffer size, or reachable exhaustion is exhibit in the given code.
