verdict.summary: vhost_user_get_inflight_fd takes num_queues and queue_size directly from the vhost-user GET_INFLIGHT_FD message payload with no range or sanity check, multiplies them into mmap_size (up to tens of gigabytes with 16-bit maxima), allocates that region and fully memsets it, then retains the mapping in dev->inflight_info. A message peer can force the backend process (e.g., OVS-DPDK) to allocate and touch tens of gigabytes of host memory per request, causing memory-exhaustion denial of service, with no bound anywhere in the function.

evidence.reason: Origin of the taint: both values are copied from the socket message payload into uint16_t locals with no validation; the full uint16 domain (up to 65535 each) is instantiable by the vhost-user peer.

evidence.snippet:
mmap_size = num_queues * pervq_inflight_size;
	addr = inflight_mem_alloc(dev, "vhost-inflight", mmap_size, &fd);
evidence.reason: Unguarded sink: attacker-controlled num_queues and queue_size (through pervq_inflight_size) are multiplied into mmap_size (up to ~60+ GB with 0xFFFF/0xFFFF, no uint64 wrap) and passed straight to the allocation; the mention sweep shows no check of num_queues, queue_size, or mmap_size against any limit on any path.

Impact materialization: the entire attacker-sized region is written byte by byte, forcing tens of gigabytes of physical host memory to be consumed per message (and retained in dev->inflight_info at lines 69-70 until the next request) — a peer-triggered memory-exhaustion denial of service against the backend process.

assumptions: get_pervq_shm_size_packed/split and inflight_mem_alloc are project-internal callees not shown; the analysis assumes the former returns at least header + queue_size*sizeof(desc) (page-aligned) and the latter performs ftruncate/mmap of the passed size and returns NULL on failure (sentinel checked at line 52).
vq_is_packed(dev), dev->nr_vring, dev->virtqueue, and dev->inflight_info state are produced by not-shown vhost-user handlers and are treated as internal state.
The ~60-100 GB mmap_size estimate uses public rte_vhost.h struct sizes (~14-24 bytes per inflight desc); exact values vary, but no uint16 inputs produce a uint64 overflow.
limitations: Speculative candidate: line 23-24 checks dev->nr_vring > 0 but then dereferences dev->virtqueue[0]; if the not-shown queue allocation code could set nr_vring > 0 while virtqueue[0] is NULL, this is a NULL dereference crashing only the backend's own process. The trigger state is not producible by any statement in this code, so it is recorded as speculative.

No memory-corruption defect was found in this function: memset and the packed init loop (lines 76-84) are bounded by the same pervq_inflight_size/mmap_size expressions used for the allocation, and num_queues * pervq_inflight_size cannot wrap uint64_t.

The maximum attacker-forced allocation actually succeeding depends on host overcommit/ftruncate limits; an attacker can binary-search below the ceiling and still force multi-gigabyte memsets, so the DoS trigger remains instantiated.

verdict.summary: jfs_evict_inode indexes bmap->db_active with ji->active_ag guarded only by a '!= -1' sentinel check; no range check, clamp, or mask bounds the index to the array domain, so an active_ag value set out of range by allocation/mount code consuming a crafted filesystem image causes an out-of-bounds read-modify-write (atomic_dec) in kernel memory.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write: the index ji->active_ag is a struct field produced outside this code (set from allocation-group values derived from the mounted, attacker-craftable filesystem image); the only guard is the sentinel test 'if (ji->active_ag != -1)' at line 34, which excludes exactly one value and admits every other 32-bit index. With active_ag = 200, the address computed is 800 bytes past the 128-entry (512-byte) db_active array, and atomic_dec performs a read-modify-write there, corrupting adjacent kernel heap memory. No range check, mask, modulo, clamp, or checked accessor for active_ag exists anywhere in the function.

assumptions: ji->active_ag is a 32-bit integer field of struct jfs_inode_info and db_active is a fixed-size array (MAXAG = 128) member of struct bmap, per JFS kernel headers not shown in the snippet; the analysis only requires that the array bound be far smaller than the 32-bit index domain.

ji->active_ag is assigned by allocation code not shown in this snippet, from allocation-group numbers derived from on-disk filesystem metadata; per the width-domain rule its full declared-width domain is treated as instantiable.
limitations: Dereferencing 'bmap' at line 36 without a NULL check is a potential NULL dereference, but no statement of this code can produce a NULL bmap and a mount with a NULL bmap succeeding is an unshown-producer inconsistency; trigger not instantiated here — robustness concern only.
BUG_ON(!list_empty(&ji->anon_inode_list)) at line 31 is a deliberate kernel assertion; if reachable from crafted images it is a panic/robustness issue, not memory corruption.
If ipimap or i_imap is NULL, diFree is skipped and the inode number leaks — a resource-accounting issue with no corruption impact.

Real-world reachability of an out-of-range active_ag additionally depends on the (not shown) producer code and mount-time sanitization; this analysis judges the given code as the last line of defense at the use site.

verdict.summary: In ip6gre_err, the ICMPV6_PKT_TOOBIG path computes `mtu = be32_to_cpu(info) - offset` using the raw attacker-supplied 32-bit ICMPv6 MTU field. When info < offset (e.g. info = 0, offset = 40), the __u32 subtraction wraps to ~0xFFFFFFD8, and the only guard, `if (mtu < IPV6_MIN_MTU)`, lower-bounds mtu alone, so the wrapped huge value passes and is written to t->dev->mtu. A single spoofed ICMPv6 Packet Too Big error persistently corrupts the shared ip6gre tunnel device's MTU to an impossible value, blackholing tunnel traffic (remote unauthenticated denial of service on a kernel forwarding path).

evidence.reason: Unsigned subtraction `be32_to_cpu(info) - offset` underflows whenever the attacker-crafted ICMPv6 MTU field is smaller than the GRE header offset; the clamp `if (mtu < IPV6_MIN_MTU)` checks only the lower bound (4294967256 < 1280 is false), so the wrapped value reaches `t->dev->mtu = mtu` and corrupts the tunnel device MTU. Trigger: ICMPv6 type 2 with info = htonl(0), offset = 40 → mtu = 0xFFFFFFD8 → t->dev->mtu = 4294967256.

evidence.snippet: u8 type, u8 code, int offset, __be32 info)
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: `info` is the raw 32-bit field of the attacker-crafted ICMPv6 error (for Packet Too Big, the claimed MTU) delivered to this protocol error handler; its full 32-bit domain reaches the subtraction at line 67 with no validation on any path in this code.

assumptions: pskb_may_pull(skb, len) guarantees that the first len bytes of skb->data are accessible, per documented kernel semantics; this was used to verify the GRE header, protocol, and key reads are in bounds (exact fit: key read spans [key_off, key_off+4) = [offset+grehlen-4, offset+grehlen)).
ip6gre_tunnel_lookup returns a tunnel pointer or NULL; the code checks the sentinel (`if (!t) return;`), so that consumption is guarded.

The caller (icmpv6_notify, not shown) invokes this handler for ICMPv6 errors with type/code/offset/info derived from the attacker's ICMPv6 message; `info` content is fully attacker-chosen, which is the basis for the trigger input value.
limitations: Potential out-of-bounds read at line 56 (`tel = (struct ipv6_tlv_tnl_enc_lim *) &skb->data[teli]`): no statement in this code bounds `teli` against the pulled length. Safety rests on the not-shown ip6_tnl_parse_tlv_enc_lim returning in-skb offsets; its 0 miss-sentinel is checked (`if (teli && ...)`), but no concrete trigger producing an out-of-range teli could be instantiated from this code alone, so it is recorded here rather than promoted to a primary finding.

Potential out-of-bounds read of ipv6h->daddr/saddr at line 31: the second pull only guarantees offset+grehlen bytes, and no statement here ensures 40 bytes are pulled; safety depends on the not-shown caller passing offset >= 40, which cannot be quoted from this code.
The downstream consequence of the corrupted MTU (tunnel traffic blackhole) depends on tx-path behavior outside this code; the direct in-code impact is the out-of-domain write to t->dev->mtu.
err_count (line 75) can only wrap after 2^31 attacker packets and is stats-only; no security effect.

verdict.summary: In do_arg_all(), the second loop indexes AARGLIST(alist)[i] (line 252) with i bounded only by the stale snapshot opened_len (old ARGCOUNT), never against the live alist->al_ga.ga_len. The code itself documents (lines 48-50 and 177) that autocommands fired by its own calls (win_close, do_ecmd) change the argument list size mid-function. An autocommand that shrinks the arglist (e.g., :argdel or :args) makes i exceed ga_len on the next iteration, producing an out-of-bounds (or freed-memory) read of the growarray; alist_name() then dereferences the garbage ae_fname read out of bounds and passes it to do_ecmd() as a filename. The first loop guards the identical access with 'if (i < alist->al_ga.ga_len' (line 84); the second loop has no equivalent check anywhere.

evidence.reason: Unguarded sink: AARGLIST(alist)[i] is indexed with no bound against the current alist->al_ga.ga_len. Simulated trigger: arglist ['a','b','c'], ':all' with count=0 so count=opened_len=3; at i=0 do_ecmd fires a BufNew/BufEnter autocommand that runs ':args z' (ga_data freed, ga_len=1); at i=1 the loop condition 'i < count' (stale 3) passes, opened[1]==0, and the read at line 252 indexes entry 1 of a length-1 growarray — out-of-bounds (use-after-free in the :args variant) read; alist_name() dereferences the garbage ae_fname from that OOB entry and do_ecmd() consumes it as a filename. The mention sweep over the whole second loop found no ga_len bound, clamp, mask, or re-snapshot on any path.

Origin of the stale bound: count is clamped to opened_len, the ARGCOUNT snapshot taken at line 43 before any autocommand runs, and is never re-clamped to the live alist->al_ga.ga_len for the loop at line 196, so i can exceed the current argument list length after an autocommand shrinks it — exactly the mutation this code itself documents at lines 48-50 ('We still have to watch out for its size to be changed') and 177 ('ARGCOUNT may change while doing this, because of autocommands').

assumptions: AARGLIST(alist) expands to alist->al_ga.ga_data (standard Vim macro) and alist_name() dereferences aep->ae_fname, as implied by the identically-guarded call at line 86.

do_ecmd(), win_close(), autowrite(), win_split(), and win_enter() fire user autocommands; this re-entrancy is acknowledged by this code's own comments at lines 48-50 and 177, so the mid-loop arglist mutation is a documented, in-domain state, not an external assumption.
limitations: opened[i] at line 200 is safe: i < count <= opened_len and the allocation at line 44 uses the same opened_len expression.
The first loop's accesses at lines 85-86 are guarded by the quoted check at line 84, re-evaluated each iteration.

The 'continue' at line 240 can skip the matching '++autocmd_no_enter' at line 258 after the '--' at line 232, skewing the autocommand-suppression counter when the last split fails during ':tab drop'; no concrete security impact was instantiated, so it is recorded as functional only.

Whether the OOB read hits still-allocated memory (:argdel truncate) or freed memory (:args replace) depends on the shrinking command; both are out-of-bounds reads of the growarray, the freed-memory variant adding a use-after-free flavor to the same unguarded index.

verdict.summary: get_lisp_indent() scans attacker-controlled line content, but every pointer-advance loop is bounded by an explicit NUL-terminator test in its own condition (string/escape skips, quote/paren counting, column walk), the findmatch() NULL failure sentinel is checked before any use of pos, and amount is assigned on every path. No out-of-bounds access, overflow with attacker-instantiable trigger, or other memory-safety or validation defect is reachable.

assumptions: ml_get_curline() returns a NUL-terminated in-memory buffer line with no embedded NULs (characterizable buffer-accessor semantics).

findmatch() returns either NULL (checked at both call sites) or a position within the buffer (lnum >= 1, col <= line length); this code checks the NULL sentinel but performs no local range validation of pos->lnum/pos->col.
lbr_chartabsize_adv()/lbr_chartabsize() advance the line pointer by one multibyte character and never past the terminating NUL; lisp_match(), linewhite(), get_indent() consume only valid positions.
limitations: C2 (speculative): pos->lnum/pos->col from findmatch are consumed without local range checks (cursor assignment and loop bound at 'curwin->w_cursor.lnum = pos->lnum' / 'while (--curwin->w_cursor.lnum >= pos->lnum)'; the col walk is nevertheless locally bounded by the '*that' term of 'while (*that && col)'). No statement in this code can produce an out-of-range position and findmatch's NULL sentinel is checked, so the trigger is not instantiable here.

C3 (functional, not security): int amount can in principle overflow (signed overflow, UB) if 'tabstop'/'vartabstop' is set near its 9999 maximum and a line contains on the order of 10^5 tab characters; 'tabstop' is operator configuration rather than data crossing this function's trust boundary, and the overflowing value feeds only tab-width modulo arithmetic and the returned indent amount, with no memory access consuming it, so no memory-safety impact is instantiated.

If a buffer line could ever lack its NUL terminator (corruption produced outside this code), the '*that' loops would read out of bounds; producing such a line is not possible from any statement in this code.

verdict.summary: This v3 networkstatus parser is the trust-boundary intake point, but every memory/index/size sink it contains is preceded by a quoted, execution-order-verified local guard: hex digest decodes require strlen == HEX_DIGEST_LEN and a non-negative base16_decode return before use, ports are parsed with tor_parse_long range [0,65535] plus an ok check before the uint16 cast, the signature object size is bounded to [128,512] before tor_memdup, the voters smartlist is proven non-empty and (for non-consensus) exactly length 1 before smartlist_get(ns->voters, 0), and ordering loops guard i-1 accesses. Signature state is not fail-open: good_signature is set only after check_signature_token succeeds, at least one signature is enforced, vote identity is bound to the certificate via tor_memneq, and a consensus with zero voters or unsorted routerstatuses is rejected. The remaining candidates (NULL/abort when required header tokens are absent, time_t overflow in valid_after + MIN_VOTE_INTERVAL, a potentially non-advancing routerstatus parse loop, and vote signatures being checked against the SHA-1 digest regardless of the declared algorithm) all require behavior of unshown project-internal callees to instantiate, so they are recorded as limitations rather than vulnerabilities.

assumptions: tokenize_string (not shown) enforces its token table's argument-count rules, so tok->args[k] exists whenever the quoted code indexes it (e.g. tok->args[2] in the 3-argument directory-signature branch after tor_assert(tok->n_args >= 2) plus the n_args == 2 branch split, and tok->args[0] for the optional legacy-dir-key/client-versions tokens with no local n_args check).
Token arguments are NUL-terminated strings within the memarea, which strlen, strcmp, tor_strdup and escaped depend on; this is the tokenizer's contract, not a check in the shown code.
tok->object_body actually contains tok->object_size bytes; the shown code bounds only the size, not the buffer, and the buffer/length consistency is the tokenizer's contract.

find_by_keyword (not shown) is assumed by the code's own convention (tor_assert(tok); after the first call) to never return NULL for required keywords; whether it asserts internally or returns NULL is not shown.

find_start_of_next_routerstatus never returns NULL and stays within s; routerstatus_parse_entry_from_string advances *s past each entry even on failure; parse_iso_time produces in-range time_t values; authority_cert_parse_from_string sets end_of_cert to a position within the input.
Tor allocator wrappers (tor_malloc_zero, tor_memdup, memarea_new) abort on allocation failure rather than returning NULL, so allocation sentinels are not attacker-instantiable here.
limitations: Results of find_by_keyword for K_PUBLISHED, K_VOTE_STATUS (tok->n_args deref), K_VALID_AFTER, K_FRESH_UNTIL, K_VALID_UNTIL, K_VOTING_DELAY and K_KNOWN_FLAGS are consumed without a local NULL check; only the K_NETWORK_STATUS_VERSION lookup is followed by tor_assert(tok). A hostile directory document missing a required line would crash the parsing process (NULL deref or assert abort, at most a denial of service, CWE-476), but instantiating it requires the unshown tokenize_string to accept a document missing required tokens and the unshown find_by_keyword to return NULL rather than abort, so it stays speculative under the framework.

The checks ns->valid_after + MIN_VOTE_INTERVAL > ns->fresh_until and ns->valid_after + MIN_VOTE_INTERVAL*2 > ns->valid_until perform unchecked signed time_t addition; overflow (which would wrap negative and under-admit) requires parse_iso_time (unshown) to produce near-TIME_MAX values, which is not instantiable from the given code.

The while (!strcmpstart(s, "r ")) loop frees a failed vote_routerstatus_t without locally advancing s, so an unshown routerstatus_parse_entry_from_string that fails without advancing *s would produce an infinite loop; the callee's advance-on-failure contract is not shown, so this is a potential CPU-spin issue only.

Vote signature verification passes ns_digests.d[DIGEST_SHA1] and DIGEST_LEN to check_signature_token regardless of the algorithm name parsed into sig->alg, so a vote signature declaring a non-SHA1 algorithm is checked against the SHA-1 document digest; since the signature still must be a valid signature by ns->cert->signing_key over that digest and check_signature_token is not shown, no verification bypass is instantiated (at worst an algorithm-label mismatch).

Impact of any triggered crash in this parser is limited to denial of service of the process parsing a hostile directory document; no memory-corruption, disclosure, or authorization-bypass primitive is reachable in the shown statements.

verdict.summary: In the S4U2Self fast path (b->kdc_options.enc_tkt_in_skey set), the encrypted part of the user-to-user additional ticket t = &b->additional_tickets->val[0] is decrypted into the stack-local EncTicketPart adtkt. On the constrained-delegation path the code guards with '&& b->kdc_options.enc_tkt_in_skey == 0', so the same adtkt is not reused there; however on the S4U2Self path with enc_tkt_in_skey, the KDC builds the reply with s = &adtkt.cname and r = adtkt.crealm while ekey = &adtkt.key is attacker-selected (matched against attacker-supplied b->etype). adtkt was memset to zero and its contents are only filled after krb5_decrypt_ticket succeeds with a key fetched for the ADDITIONAL ticket's realm; the KDC never validates that the decrypted cname/crealm (used as s/r for the server principal sp) belong to a realm this KDC is authoritative for, and never cross-checks the second ticket's sname realm against our_realm — the only realm check, get_krbtgt_realm(&t->sname), is performed BEFORE decryption and only asserts the ticket 'looks like' a krbtgt principal name. An attacker who controls any TGS request can therefore steer the subsequent _kdc_db_fetch and referral logic with a cname/crealm decrypted under a key type they choose from b->etype. The deeper concrete defect: ekey = &adtkt.key is used to sign/encrypt the reply after tgs_make_reply while adtkt's storage is a stack EncTicketPart zero-initialized once; on the constrained-delegation path adtkt is RE-decrypted (krb5_decrypt_ticket ... &adtkt) after already holding the u2u ticket, overwriting it without free_EncTicketPart, leaking and aliasing memory, then free_EncTicketPart(&adtkt) at out: frees the constrained-delegation contents only — double-state confusion, but the single decisive defect is the missing validation of adtkt's origin realm against the KDC's own realm before using adtkt.cname/adtkt.crealm/adtkt.key as trusted request identity, leaving the KDC to issue tickets vouched under a second-ticket identity it never authenticated.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled request body fields sname/realm are captured and later conditionally REPLACED by values decrypted from an attacker-supplied additional ticket with no realm-of-authority validation quoted anywhere in the function.

After decrypting the attacker-provided second ticket with an etype chosen from the attacker's b->etype list, the KDC adopts the decrypted cname/crealm as the service identity (s/r) without any check tying them to a realm this KDC issued the ticket for; the only pre-decrypt check, get_krbtgt_realm(&t->sname), is performed before decryption and only on the outer ticket sname.

ekey points into the stack EncTicketPart adtkt populated solely from the attacker-supplied additional ticket; the only acceptance test is an enctype match against the attacker's list — no realm, kvno, or principal binding of adtkt.key is enforced in this function before ekey is used to derive the reply's encryption path.

assumptions: Callee semantics of krb5_decrypt_ticket, _kdc_db_fetch, hdb_enctype2key, check_PAC, check_KRB5SignedPath, check_s4u2self, and tgs_make_reply are taken per their names as enforcing Kerberos KDC semantics; their internal validation cannot be quoted here.
verify_flags is assumed to check only ticket validity flags/times on the decrypted adtkt, not realm authority, based on its call sites.
b->etype, b->sname, b->realm, b->additional_tickets, b->kdc_options, tgt cname/crealm are attacker-controlled request fields (TGS-REQ body decoded from the network peer) under the width-domain rule.
limitations: A memory-corruption trigger inside tgs_make_reply/check_PAC from adtkt reuse could not be simulated because those callees are not shown; the finding rests on the identity/trust misuse at the given sink lines, not on a demonstrated OOB write.

The re-decrypt of adtkt on the constrained-delegation path (krb5_decrypt_ticket ... &adtkt after it may already hold the u2u ticket) is a state-reuse smell, but the enc_tkt_in_skey == 0 condition makes the two populations mutually exclusive on any single path, so no double-free was instantiated.
If internal callees (not shown) enforce that the additional ticket's realm equals this KDC's realm, the impact degrades to nothing; that enforcement is not quotable here, hence confidence below high.

verdict.summary: warnf formats a warning message into a 256-byte stack buffer but uses vsnprintf's unclamped return value (the full required length, which exceeds 255 on truncation) as the loop bound, compounded by an off-by-one in the accounting (`ptr += cut+1` vs `len -= cut`). The pointer marches past print_buffer while len remains positive, so `ptr[cut]` and `fwrite(ptr, cut+1, 1, config->errors)` read out of bounds and dump stack bytes to the error stream: out-of-bounds read with information disclosure, reachable whenever a formatted warning exceeds the buffer.

evidence.snippet:
ptr += cut+1; /* skip the space too */
        len -= cut;
evidence.reason: Off-by-one accounting: ptr advances by cut+1 but len is decremented by only cut, so each iteration ptr drifts one byte ahead of the consumed count. After enough iterations (or whenever len from line 11 exceeds the truncated 255-byte content), ptr passes the end of print_buffer while `len > (int)WARN_TEXTWIDTH` still holds, and the `while(!ISSPACE(ptr[cut]) && cut)` scan plus `fwrite(ptr, cut+1, 1, config->errors)` read past the 256-byte buffer, disclosing stack memory to the error stream. Trigger instantiated: a warning message whose formatted length exceeds 255 (vsnprintf's documented truncation return), or ≥81 iterations of short words at length ≤ 255.

Origin of the unbounded value: vsnprintf returns the number of characters that WOULD have been written (not counting NUL) when the output is truncated, so len can be any value up to INT_MAX while print_buffer holds only 255 characters plus NUL. No clamp to sizeof(print_buffer) exists anywhere in the code (mention sweep: only `while(len > 0)` and `if(len > (int)WARN_TEXTWIDTH)` test len, neither against the 256-byte bound), so the loop at lines 15-38 uses an attacker-influenceable unbounded length to drive reads of a fixed 256-byte stack buffer.

assumptions: WARN_TEXTWIDTH is a compile-time constant on the order of 80 (not shown in the given code); the exact value does not affect the defect, only the iteration count needed.
ISSPACE is the standard ctype whitespace test; config->errors is a valid FILE* provided by the caller.

The format string fmt is a caller literal, but the substitution values (URLs, server-supplied strings, option arguments in the curl tool that uses this helper) carry attacker-influenceable content and unbounded length; any formatted length up to INT_MAX is within the width domain of the vsnprintf return.
limitations: Lines 9-10 call va_start(ap, fmt) twice without an intervening va_end, which is undefined behavior per the C standard; on common ABIs it merely re-initializes ap and does not contribute to the primary out-of-bounds chain.
A negative vsnprintf return (encoding error) is safely skipped by `while(len > 0)`; a NULL config->errors would only crash the tool's own process at equal privilege (robustness, not security).

The else-branch `fputs(ptr, config->errors)` (line 35) can additionally expose uninitialized in-buffer bytes (CWE-908) once ptr has drifted past the NUL; this shares the same root cause and is covered by the primary finding.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds write in the xml:lang handling: the buffer is sized from the unescaped language length (buf_length = 10 + lang_len + 1), but the pointer p is then advanced by the return value of raptor_xml_escape_string, which expands special characters (including the quote char the code explicitly asks to escape) into multi-byte entities. The unchecked advanced p is written with a closing quote and NUL with no bounds check anywhere, so any xml:lang value containing a character requiring escaping makes the writes land past the end of the allocation, at an attacker-scaled distance.

verdict.summary: mcba_usb_start_xmit copies cf->len bytes into the fixed 8-byte data member of the stack-allocated usb_msg without any local bounds check on cf->len; since cf->len is a u8 frame field under the sender's control (domain 0-255), a CAN frame with dlc > 8 causes a kernel stack buffer overflow (and an out-of-bounds read of cf->data) at the memcpy.

evidence.reason: Root cause: cf->len (u8, attacker-controlled via the transmitted CAN frame, full domain 0-255) is assigned to usb_msg.dlc and used directly as the memcpy length into the fixed 8-byte usb_msg.data array with no bounds check, clamp, or mask on any path in this code. Trigger: a locally sent CAN frame with dlc = 255 reaches this line and the memcpy writes 255 bytes into the 8-byte stack buffer, corrupting kernel stack memory.
Taint origin: the attacker-supplied skb data is reinterpreted as struct can_frame; its unvalidated len and data fields flow to the memcpy at line 45.

assumptions: The size of usb_msg.data is taken from the driver's struct mcba_usb_msg_can definition (data[MCBA_DLC_MAX], MCBA_DLC_MAX = 8), which is not shown in the given snippet; the overflow claim depends on this fixed 8-byte size.
cf->len is a u8 field of struct can_frame (domain 0-255), consistent with the post-rename kernel CAN frame definition.
limitations: In the actual mainline kernel, can_dropped_invalid_skb is documented to also validate the frame DLC against the frame type (dropping classical CAN frames with dlc > CAN_MAX_DLEN); that enforcement lives outside the given code and, per the analysis rules, cannot serve as a guard here. If that callee behavior is credited, the trigger is blocked and the finding becomes speculative.
Triggering requires the ability to transmit on a CAN socket (e.g., CAP_NET_RAW) or to inject frames into the networking stack; it is a local-user primitive, not remotely reachable by itself.

verdict.summary: jfs_evict_inode indexes bmap->db_active with ji->active_ag after validating only the -1 sentinel (`if (ji->active_ag != -1)`), never bounding the value against the array length. active_ag is a 32-bit int recorded by unshown allocation code from allocation-group state of a mounted (attacker-suppliable) filesystem image, so an out-of-range AG number reaches `atomic_dec(&bmap->db_active[ji->active_ag])` and performs an out-of-bounds read-modify-write of kernel heap memory.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the only guard on the index is a sentinel test (`!= -1`) that never bounds active_ag above or below into [0, MAXAG); the sink `atomic_dec(&bmap->db_active[ji->active_ag])` is an out-of-bounds read-modify-write (CWE-787) whenever active_ag holds any value other than -1 outside the array range. Trigger: active_ag is set by unshown JFS allocation code from allocation-group state of the mounted filesystem image, so a crafted image yielding an AG number >= MAXAG (or a negative value other than -1) instantiates the trigger with no check, clamp, mask, or corrected comparison anywhere on the path.

assumptions: bmap->db_active is a fixed-length array sized to the maximum allocation-group count (MAXAG per the not-shown struct bmap in fs/jfs/jfs_bmap.h); its length is not quoted in the given code.
ji->active_ag is a signed int recorded by JFS allocation code (jfs_bmap.c, not shown) from allocation-group state derived from the mounted image's metadata.
The inode pointer supplied by the VFS is valid, and bmap/ipimap are non-NULL for a live mounted filesystem.
limitations: Line 30 `BUG_ON(!list_empty(&ji->anon_inode_list))` can panic the kernel if internal JFS state leaves anonymous inodes referenced, but the state that triggers it is produced by not-shown code; recorded as a robustness issue, not an instantiated vulnerability.

If the not-shown allocation code provably restricts active_ag to [0, MAXAG) for all images, practical reachability drops; that contract cannot be quoted here, so the missing local bound at the use site remains the defect under last-line-of-defense analysis.
A NULL bmap dereference would require a mounted sb with NULL bmap, which is not instantiable through this code.

verdict.summary: eval_string() sizes its output buffer from a first-pass heuristic (extra += 5 per special-key escape) and performs the real decode in a second pass. The only bounds check, if (end >= rettv->vval.v_string + len) iemsg(...), runs after trans_special() has already written at end and is non-aborting, so it detects rather than prevents overflow. However, the code's own comment bounds the worst case at 9 output bytes for at least 4 consumed characters, and 5 + (4 - 2) = 7 >= 9's excess is not provable from quoted code: 9 <= 5 + consumed - 2 holds for consumed >= 6, and single-character key names (consumed 4) produce far fewer than 9 bytes. A concrete overflowing escape cannot be instantiated without assuming the not-shown trans_special() exceeds the documented estimate, so the post-hoc check is a latent robustness/ordering flaw rather than a demonstrable out-of-bounds write in this code.

assumptions: trans_special() and find_special_key() are project-internal callees not shown; their maximum output for special-key escapes is characterizable only through the code's own comment ("produces up to 9 characters" from a form that "occupies at least 4 characters"), which the reservation of 5 plus the consumed-input slack provably covers for all consumed lengths >= 4.
*arg points to NUL-terminated Vimscript source; the parser loop at line 7 stops at NUL or '"', so no unbounded first pass.
alloc(len) returns NULL on failure; the NULL check at line 51 covers it.
limitations: Candidate 1 (heap out-of-bounds write via \<x> special-key escapes): the only bounds check, if (end >= rettv->vval.v_string + len) iemsg("eval_string() used more space than allocated"), is executed AFTER the writing call trans_special(&p, end, flags, FALSE, NULL) and does not return, break, or repair end, so it can only report an overflow already in progress. This check-after-write ordering is a genuine design defect and the author's own error message shows the invariant was known to be at risk. The trigger was not instantiated because proving that trans_special's output exceeds len requires the not-shown callee to exceed the code's own documented estimate (up to 9 bytes from at least 4 consumed characters, covered by the 5-byte reservation plus consumed-input slack); per discipline 3 an unshown internal callee can neither produce the trigger nor excuse it, so the candidate is recorded as latent rather than confirmed. If trans_special can emit more than consumed + 3 bytes for any escape, this becomes a heap buffer overflow (CWE-787) with the guard absent by construction.

The >= comparison in that check is evaluated against one-past-the-end (v_string + len), so it fires only once end has already reached or passed the end; even a corrected operator would remain post-write.

len is declared int while p - *arg is a pointer difference (line 48); a source string longer than INT_MAX would truncate, but allocation and copy both use the same truncated value, so no overflow results from the truncation alone, and reaching it requires a multi-gigabyte script line.

Octal, \x, \u and \U escapes were verified to fit the per-escape headroom (produced bytes <= consumed - 2) by computing their maxima from the code's own digit counts (3 octal digits, 2 hex, 4 hex, 8 hex).

verdict.summary: In get_lisp_indent(), the column loop advances the pointer 'that' one full multibyte character per iteration while decrementing 'col' (a byte offset from pos->col) by one, so with multibyte characters before the matched paren 'that' can land on the line's NUL terminator instead of on the paren. The else branch then executes 'that++' (line 114), moving one byte past the end of the line buffer, and 'VIM_ISWHITE(*that)' (line 118) plus subsequent '*that' loops dereference and scan heap memory beyond the allocation. Triggered by crafted file content (e.g. a line 'é(' whose '(' is matched by findmatch) when lisp indenting runs.

evidence.reason: Root cause: 'that' is incremented unconditionally in the else branch. When the preceding 'while (*that && col)' loop exits with *that == NUL (reachable when multibyte characters before the matched paren make the per-character advance outpace the per-byte 'col' decrement), this statement moves 'that' one byte past the line's NUL terminator; the next dereference 'while (VIM_ISWHITE(*that))' at line 118 performs an out-of-bounds heap read. No check of *that != NUL, clamp, or re-anchor exists between the loop exit and this increment anywhere in the function.

Origin of the faulty state: 'col' is set from pos->col (line 86), a BYTE offset of the matched paren, but lbr_chartabsize_adv advances 'that' by one full (possibly multibyte) character per iteration while 'col' decreases by exactly one. Simulated trigger with line 'é(' (bytes C3 A9 28 00) and pos->col = 2: iteration 1 advances past the two-byte é (col 2->1), iteration 2 advances past '(' (col 1->0), leaving that pointing at the NUL terminator; the loop's own guard permits this exit, feeding the unguarded 'that++' at line 114.

assumptions: lbr_chartabsize_adv advances the char_u* argument by one full multibyte character (MB_PTR_ADV semantics); this is also implied by the code itself, which pairs it with separate byte-wise increments (++that, that++) at lines 42, 48, 62, 121.
findmatch returns a position whose col is a byte index within the line and whose lnum is a valid line number (NULL return is checked in this code at lines 17, 22-23, 26).
ml_get_curline() returns a NUL-terminated line buffer in which the NUL is the final byte.
limitations: 'amount' (int) could in theory overflow by accumulating per-character widths over a roughly 270-million-character line; this is not exercised under realistic line sizes and is treated as speculative.
The escaped-quote handling (e.g. a line ending in \"\"\") stops scanning the line early; this is a functional misparse with no memory-safety effect.
The confirmed defect is an out-of-bounds read: the bytes read beyond the buffer influence only the computed indent or cause a crash; no path in this code exfiltrates those bytes to the attacker.

verdict.summary: The bracketed-paste handler safely bounds all buffer access. The key invariant: a write iteration is entered with idx <= STRLEN(end)-1 (because the only path preserving idx is the continue branch, which requires buf to remain a proper prefix of the end code and end[idx] != NUL, and no written byte is ever NUL), and the guard 'if (end != NULL && STRLEN(end) >= NUMBUFLEN) end = NULL;' caps that length below NUMBUFLEN. Maximum reachable idx is NUMBUFLEN-2+MB_MAXBYTES, two slots inside the buffer 'char_u buf[NUMBUFLEN + MB_MAXBYTES]'. The end[idx] access and STRNCMP read stay within the end string because an interior mismatch against the terminator provably occurs first. The PASTE_EX copy is guarded by ga_grow(gap, idx + 1) == OK with the allocation sized from the same expression as the copy, reserving the NUL slot the in-code comment documents as the caller's responsibility. All break paths restore no_mapping, allow_keys and 'paste'. No guard is missing for any attacker-reachable value.

assumptions: MB_MAXBYTES (used both in the buffer declaration and as the maximum mb_char2bytes output) and NUMBUFLEN (used both in the declaration and in the STRLEN guard) are the same compile-time constants, so the sizing and the bound are consistent by construction.
find_termcode returns a NUL-terminated string or NULL; its NULL sentinel is checked at every use in this code.
mb_char2bytes never writes a zero byte, so buf cannot contain an interior NUL within the accumulated prefix; this is relied on when reasoning about STRNCMP termination.
limitations: PASTE_EX leaves the NUL termination of gap->ga_data to the caller ('add one for the NUL that is going to be appended'); if any unshown caller uses gap->ga_data as a string without appending that NUL, the defect would be in that caller, not here. Capacity for the NUL is reserved and the copy is properly bounded in this function.

Speculative (not instantiated here): 'end' points into the termcodes storage; if a termresponse or an autocommand running during vgetc() or set_option_value() modified t_PE mid-loop, 'end' could dangle. No statement in this code mutates termcodes inside the loop, so no race window is exhibited within the given code.

The 'STRLEN(end) >= NUMBUFLEN' check conservatively rejects an end code of exactly NUMBUFLEN bytes, which analysis shows would still be safe; this is a functional over-rejection with no security effect.
If end == NULL, the loop consumes typeahead as long as vpeekc() != NUL; since vgetc blocks on the terminal, worst-case consumption equals what the terminal sends, with no amplification.

verdict.summary: getsistring allocates exactly len bytes (cli_malloc(len)) but, after the in-place UTF-16 halving loop, writes a NUL terminator at name[i/2] where i is the first post-loop value >= len. When the attacker-controlled length is len==1, the loop exits with i==2 and the terminator is written at name[1] of a 1-byte heap buffer: a one-byte heap out-of-bounds write (null-byte off-by-one) triggered by the parsed SIS file. No clamp, index bound, or len+1 allocation exists anywhere on any path.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write sink: after the loop `for (i = 0 ; i < len; i+=2)` exits, i is the first value >= len. With attacker-data len==1, i==2, so name[1] is written although the buffer allocated at line 7 is only 1 byte. Simulated trigger: len=1 (within uint32_t domain, passes `if (!len)` and `if (len>400)`), cli_malloc(1) succeeds, fread of 1 byte succeeds, loop runs once (i=0) then exits at i=2, and this statement writes '\0' one byte past the heap buffer — heap memory corruption driven by the parsed file.

Origin of the undersized buffer: the allocation is sized exactly len with no room for the terminator written at line 19 (needed size is (len+1)/2 + 1, which exceeds len only when len==1, but the code guarantees no slack for that case). The allocation expression is not derived from an expression covering the terminator index, and no later statement clamps i/2 below len.

assumptions: The caller of this static helper is not shown; per the width-domain rule, ptr and len are treated as attacker-data with the full uint32_t domain (SIS archive fields), so len==1 is instantiable.
cli_malloc is a conventional allocation wrapper returning NULL on failure; its sentinel is checked at `if (!name)`.
limitations: fseek(f, ptr, SEEK_SET) return value is unchecked; a failed seek only changes which bytes fread reads, and fread stays bounded by len, so this is a robustness issue without a security impact.
The overflow triggers only at len==1; for every len >= 2 the exit value of i gives i/2 < len, so the terminator stays in bounds.
The out-of-bounds byte is always a single NUL at name[1] of a 1-byte allocation; exploitability depends on allocator layout, but the out-of-bounds write itself is a memory-corruption primitive.

verdict.summary: In extract_arg, the return value of r_type_func_args_name (an internal type-info lookup that can miss and return NULL, with content driven by the analyzed binary's parsed type data) is passed directly to strdup without any sentinel check. All sibling lookups in the same block are checked (if (!tp) break; / if (fname)), but no statement on any path validates this one, so strdup(NULL) dereferences NULL and crashes the analyst's radare2 process while it processes an attacker-supplied binary (denial of service).

evidence.reason: Unchecked failure sentinel consumed at the use site: r_type_func_args_name is a lookup that can miss and return NULL (its result depends on type/debug info parsed from the attacker's binary), and the NULL is fed directly into strdup, which requires a non-NULL string (UB, SIGSEGV). The mention sweep shows this is the only call site and that no NULL test, fallback, or error arm exists anywhere on the path, in contrast to the checked sibling lookups tp (line 117) and fname (line 103). Trigger: attacker binary with a named function whose arg i has a type entry but no name entry; frame_off = 0 (ptr == fcn->stack, passes the quoted maxstackframe guard at line 90), get_stack_var misses, sum_sz == frame_off at i, lookup misses, strdup(NULL) crashes.

assumptions: strdup(NULL) is undefined behavior that crashes in libc (discipline-3 documented semantics of strdup require a non-NULL NUL-terminated string).

r_type_func_args_name is a lookup call that can miss and return NULL (discipline-3 lookup semantics); nothing in this code documents or enforces that a type entry at index i implies a name entry at index i.
The sdb_types type/name metadata is populated from the analyzed binary's type/debug information, so its content is attacker-influenced (radare2 parses untrusted binaries).
limitations: size_t underflow in the stack_rev loop: with to == 0 (r_anal_cc_max_arg returning 0, callee not shown), the loop condition 'stack_rev ? i >= to : i < to' can never be false for size_t and 'i--' at i == 0 wraps to SIZE_MAX; termination and any memory effect then depend entirely on the unshown callee missing at the wrapped index, so no impact link inside this code is instantiated.

*sign is dereferenced (delta > 0 && *sign == '+'; if (*sign == '+')) although the r_return_if_fail at function entry omits sign; a NULL deref would require an internal caller passing NULL, an unquoted contract, so it is speculative.

Division by zero in 'bit_sz / 8' / R_ROUND(sum_sz, bytes) requires bytes == 0, i.e. both fcn->bits and anal->bits below 8; the ternary on line 114 handles fcn->bits == 0 but no quoted statement bounds anal->bits, and R_ROUND's definition is not shown, so this trigger is not instantiated.

Signed overflow in 'ptr - fcn->stack' / 'ptr + fcn->bp_off' is UB when r_num_get yields extreme st64 values, but the resulting frame_off is immediately bounds-checked by the quoted maxstackframe test on both branches, so no memory-unsafe use was demonstrated.
The comparison 'sum_sz == frame_off' promotes a possibly negative st64 frame_off to ut64, so negative frame offsets never match; functional quirk, no security effect shown.

verdict.summary: Use-after-free in atusb_disconnect: ieee802154_free_hw(atusb->hw) at line 17 frees the memory allocation containing the atusb struct (since atusb = hw->priv resides in the same allocation), and usb_put_dev(atusb->usb_dev) at line 20 subsequently dereferences the freed atusb pointer to read the usb_dev field. On SMP systems, concurrent kernel allocations can reuse the freed slab between the free and the read, causing a corrupted pointer to be passed to usb_put_dev for refcount decrement on arbitrary kernel memory.

evidence.reason: ieee802154_free_hw(atusb->hw) at line 17 kfree's the single allocation containing both struct ieee802154_local (which embeds hw) and hw->priv (which is atusb). After this statement, the local variable atusb is dangling. Line 20 then dereferences atusb to read atusb->usb_dev and passes the result to usb_put_dev. No statement between line 17 and line 20 saves the usb_dev pointer or reorders the operations. The trigger is a device disconnect (attacker-controlled event via unplugging the USB device), and the freed slab can be immediately reused by any concurrent kernel allocation, turning the read into a fetch of attacker-influenced heap content that is then passed as a pointer to usb_put_dev.

assumptions: ieee802154_free_hw kfree's the allocation containing hw->priv; this is the standard ieee802154_alloc_hw/ieee802154_free_hw pattern where hw and hw->priv share one allocation.
usb_get_intfdata returns a non-NULL atusb pointer on disconnect; the USB core calls disconnect only after a successful probe, so this is a framework contract.
limitations: No NULL check on usb_get_intfdata return at line 3; if the USB core ever called disconnect without a successful probe this would be a NULL dereference, but this is a framework contract and not a security defect in this code.

The practical race window between kfree at line 17 and the read at line 20 is narrow (two statements), making reliable exploitation difficult on single-CPU systems, but the UAF remains a genuine memory-safety defect on SMP systems where slab reuse is immediate.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. All reachable memory sinks in regmatch are either guarded by explicit limits, sentinel-checked, bounds-checked, or protected by the compiler invariant over opcode paths. The curly-brace brace_count indices, MULTIBYTECODE program operands, and star-loop regstack memory all have enforceable safety properties within the provided code; REG_MULTI backref comparisons and BHPOS checks are value-only, with no reachable memory defect.

assumptions: regmatch does not parse user input into the program directly; program compilation is assumed to happen in code not shown. Because a compiled program cannot be created in an invalid state (e.g. a BACKREF+n operand with an unmatched MOPEN+n), the translation step must honor the `MOPEN + 0` ... `MOPEN + 9` and `BACKREF + 1` ... `BACKREF + 9` case enumerations. No attempt is made to analyze reachability of regmatch from a specific caller.

`regnext`, `regrepeat`, `regstack_push`, `ga_grow`, `reg_save`, `reg_restore`, `reg_match_visual`, `match_with_backref`, `cstrncmp`, `reg_getline`, `getmark_buf`, `mb_ptr2len`, `mb_head_off` and the remaining unshown helpers/macros (OP, OPERAND, OPERAND_MIN, OPERAND_MAX, WITH_NL, ADVANCE_REGINPUT, PTR2CHAR, MB_CPTR_ADV, MB_PTR_BACK, reg_save_equal, save_se, restore_se, save_subexpr, restore_subexpr, cleanup_subexpr, cleanup_zsubexpr, regstack_pop, re_num_cmp, fast_breakcheck, profile_passed_limit, win_linetabsize, reg_prev_class, mb_get_class_buf, vim_iswordc_buf, vim_iswordp_buf, vim_isIDc, vim_isfilec, vim_isprintc, ri_digit, ri_hex, ri_octal, ri_word, ri_head, ri_alpha, ri_lower, ri_upper, VIM_ISDIGIT, VIM_ISWHITE, cstrchr, utf_ptr2char, utfc_ptr2len, utf_iscomposing, UTF_COMPOSINGLIKE, MB_ISUPPER, MB_TOLOWER) are assumed to have documented, correct semantics; they are not analyzed.

Global/struct state (rex fields, regstack/backpos arrays, brace_count/min/max, bl_minval/bl_maxval, behind_pos, re_extmatch_in, p_mmp, enc_utf8, has_mbyte, curwin) is assumed to be initialized and maintained correctly by code not shown.

`match_with_backref` is assumed to compute `len` as the total length to advance in whole-line units when comparing across multiple lines, so that `rex.input += len` remains in-bounds; this function is not shown.

`getmark_buf` is assumed to return a pos_T* with lnum >= 0 for a mark set in reg_buf, or NULL otherwise; not shown. `reg_getline` is assumed to return NULL for out-of-range lines and a NUL-terminated string otherwise.
limitations: REG_MULTI backref comparisons (`rex.line + rex.reg_startpos[no].col`, `rex.reg_endpos[no].col - rex.reg_startpos[no].col`) operate on column values stored by save_se/cleanup_subexpr in code not shown; if those could be negative or exceed the current line length, this would be an out-of-bounds read. save_se/cleanup_subexpr could not be analyzed.

RE_MARK passes the compiled program byte `OPERAND(scan)[0]` to `getmark_buf` and computes `reg_getline(pos->lnum - rex.reg_firstlnum)` in the `pos->col == MAXCOL` arm; neither the program byte nor the mark line is validated here, and getmark_buf's behavior for out-of-range marks is unknown, so an invalid mark could cause an unvalidated line access.
RS_STAR_LONG calls `reg_getline(rex.lnum)` without an explicit NULL check after `--rex.lnum` (regrepeat is assumed to keep rex.lnum in range); inconsistent state could dereference NULL.

fast_breakcheck/got_int and the p_mmp regstack cap do not bound total match time; the timeout check runs once per 100 outer-loop iterations, so a pathological pattern can consume significant CPU before the cap trips.

`internal_error("BRACE_LIMITS")` and `iemsg(_(e_corrupted_regexp_program))` report corruption but fail soft rather than hard; if a corrupted program were somehow reachable these paths would not abort, but no reachable corruption was found.

verdict.summary: All locally-decidable reads and writes in cdf_read_property_info are covered by exact, execution-ordered quoted guards: offs is bounded, the section header and section extent are validated against the stream, the property type read requires left >= 4, the CDF_VECTOR nelements read requires left >= 8, and the string loop requires o4 + 4 <= left before each length read and o4 + l <= left before storing (s_buf, s_len), keeping all consumed data inside [q, e). Loop indices are bounded by sh_properties <= CDF_PROP_LIMIT, allocation growth is NULL-checked with cleanup on failure, and cdf_copy_info results are sentinel-checked. Residual risks rest on unshown internal callees (cdf_get_property_info_pos bounding the 8-byte property table entries and q within [p, e], cdf_grow_info capacity semantics, cdf_copy_info honoring its e limit), on 32-bit size_t platforms, and on CDF_DEBUG builds; none can be triggered from statements visible in this code, so no vulnerability is instantiated here.

assumptions: cdf_get_property_info_pos (not shown) returns NULL when the property-table entry or the property position is invalid; its non-NULL return is consumed only after the quoted sentinel check `if ((q = cdf_get_property_info_pos(sst, h, p, e, i)) == NULL) goto out;` — this code's chosen checked-accessor form. Whether it also bounds the table read `CDF_GETUINT32(p, i << 1)` against the stream end is not quotable here.
cdf_grow_info (not shown) is assumed to allocate room for *maxcount + inc entries and to return NULL on failure; both call sites quote the NULL error arm (`if (inp == NULL) goto out;`).

cdf_copy_info (not shown) is assumed to reject copies where src + len exceeds its e argument; its 0-return is consumed by `if (!cdf_copy_info(...)) goto unknown;`, an error arm that memsets and continues.
cdf_check_stream_offset is assumed to validate pointer + length against the stream allocation; every call site consumes its -1 sentinel with a quoted `goto out`.
CDF_PROP_LIMIT and CDF_SHLEN_LIMIT are assumed to be sane small constants (upstream 256 and 0x40000000); their values are not visible in the given code.
DPRINTF is assumed compiled out unless CDF_DEBUG is defined (standard file idiom), so the `%s` on the non-NUL-terminated s_buf is inert in release builds.

The inductive invariant *count <= *maxcount across repeated calls for successive sections is maintained by this function's own statements (grow by sh.sh_properties each call, write fewer than sh.sh_properties entries), given count == maxcount == 0 on first call.
limitations: The property-table read `inp[i].pi_id = CDF_GETUINT32(p, i << 1);` has no check in this code tying p + 8*i + 4 to the section end e or to the stream allocation; a section with small sh_len and large sh_properties (e.g., sh_len = 12, sh_properties = 200) would make this read pass e and, if the stream is small, potentially past the allocation. The trigger's reachability depends entirely on the unshown cdf_get_property_info_pos validation, so it cannot be instantiated (nor dismissed) from the given code; if that helper under-validates, this would be an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) at that line.

`left = CAST(size_t, e - q);` underflows to a huge size_t if the unshown helper ever returns q > e; all downstream left-based guards would then pass. Not instantiable without assuming the callee misbehaves.

On 32-bit size_t platforms, `if (o4 + l > left) goto out;` can wrap (e.g., o4 = 8, left = 0x64, l = 0xFFFFFFFC gives 4 <= left) and store s_len = 0xFFFFFFFC with an in-range s_buf; exploitation falls to downstream consumers of pi_str, which are not shown. Speculative on this code as written.

l = 0xFFFFFFFF wraps to 0 in `if (l & 1) l++;` on the hypothetical path where the preceding `o4 + l > left` guard passes; on 64-bit that guard rejects it (o4 + 0xFFFFFFFF > left for any realistic left), so the wrap is unreachable on the widths the code exercises.
In CDF_DEBUG builds the DPRINTF `%s` prints inp[i].pi_str.s_buf, which is length-prefixed and not NUL-terminated — a potential over-read limited to debug builds.
Freeing and nulling *info on the out path discards property data from previously parsed sections on a malformed later section; this is an error-handling/design choice with no security effect shown.

verdict.summary: The archive extractor passes the raw attacker-controlled symlink target to g_file_make_symbolic_link with no validation, unlike entry pathnames and hardlink targets which are routed through _g_path_get_relative_basename_safe. A crafted archive first creates a symlink pointing outside the destination (e.g. 'd' -> '/etc'), then later entries (regular file or directory) resolve through it in g_file_query_exists/g_file_replace/g_file_make_directory, writing attacker-chosen paths and content outside the extraction directory. Independently, g_error_free (local_error) at line 98 leaves local_error dangling, and the same iteration later dereferences the freed GError in g_error_matches/g_error_copy after g_file_make_directory/g_file_make_symbolic_link fails, a use-after-free read.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the attacker-controlled symlink target from archive_entry_symlink is used unvalidated to create a symbolic link inside the destination. The mention sweep shows archive_entry_symlink appears exactly once and no statement constrains the target, whereas pathname (line 45) and hardlink (line 142) are passed through _g_path_get_relative_basename_safe. Trigger: archive with entry1 (pathname 'd', AE_IFLNK, target '/etc') creates dest/d -> /etc; entry2 (pathname 'd/cron.d/bd', AE_IFREG) then has g_file_replace (line 202) write attacker content to /etc/cron.d/bd by resolving through the symlink, an arbitrary out-of-destination file write (CWE-59).

Use-after-free read: when g_file_query_info (line 61) fails with NOT_FOUND, line 98 calls g_error_free (local_error) without resetting the variable; within the same iteration, g_file_make_directory receives &local_error (dangling), fails (e.g. ENOTDIR because a same-named earlier entry is a regular file), and g_error_matches/g_error_copy dereference and deep-copy the freed GError. Same pattern at lines 220-222 for symlinks. Trigger fully instantiated when skip_older or no-overwrite extraction options are active (CWE-416).

Origin of the dangling pointer: local_error is freed here but never set to NULL; no reassignment exists between this line and the later dereferences at 191-193 and 220-222, confirmed by the mention sweep (lines 32, 61, 93, 94, 98, 191-194, 220-223).

assumptions: _g_path_get_relative_basename_safe and extract_data_get_extraction_requested are project-internal callees not shown; their exact filtering behavior is unknown. They cannot be credited as guards, but no candidate relies on them producing a harmful value: the escaping write in the symlink attack is carried by the raw symlink target, which never passes through the helper.

g_file_make_symbolic_link, g_file_replace (G_FILE_CREATE_REPLACE_DESTINATION), g_file_query_exists and g_file_make_directory follow standard GIO semantics: symlink creation with an arbitrary target string, resolution of intermediate symlink directory components, and temp-file-then-rename writes in the containing directory.
limitations: The g_object_unref (info) at line 95 executes with info == NULL and g_object_unref (parent) at line 123 can receive NULL; GLib's g_return_if_fail turns these into critical warnings rather than memory corruption in default builds, so they are recorded as robustness issues only.

fullpath is leaked on the continue paths at lines 46-49 and 143-147 (the latter also leaks file); attacker-controlled entry count makes this a bounded linear memory leak, not promoted to a vulnerability.
n_files_to_extract can be decremented below zero when files are skipped, which only affects progress bookkeeping.
Path traversal via pathname itself could not be evaluated because the sanitizing helper is not shown; no candidate was promoted or demoted on its presumed behavior.

verdict.summary: The ut32 accumulator total_slide_infos wraps when summing per-subcache slide-info counts read from the file (total_slide_infos += n_slide_infos[i] has no overflow check), so the allocation at RZ_NEWS0(RzDyldRebaseInfosEntry, total_slide_infos) is undersized while the inner loop is still bounded by the unwrapped counts. The writes at infos[k].start/end/info then run past the end of the heap buffer (k has no bound against the allocation before first use), giving a heap out-of-bounds write with attacker-influenced values to any process parsing a malicious dyld shared cache. Root cause: integer overflow in the buffer size calculation.

evidence.reason: Heap out-of-bounds write sink. k is incremented once per valid entry (line 60) with no comparison against the allocated entry count anywhere before these writes (the only k-vs-total check, at line 70, executes after the loop). Trigger: two subcache headers carrying n_slide_infos[0]=0xFFFFFFFE and n_slide_infos[1]=4 wrap total_slide_infos to 2, so line 24 allocates 2 entries, while the loop at line 47 still runs up to 0xFFFFFFFE iterations; the third valid entry makes j=2 write infos[2] one past the 2-entry allocation, and k keeps advancing writing attacker-influenced fileOffset/size/pointer values further out of bounds.

Origin of the tainted size: unchecked ut32 accumulation of file-derived counts (each read at line 14 with full 0..0xFFFFFFFF domain). The sum wraps modulo 2^32 (e.g. 0xFFFFFFFE + 4 = 2), and the wrapped value is the only quantity used to size the infos allocation at line 24, while the loop bounds at line 47 retain the unwrapped per-header counts. This missing overflow check is the root-cause defect (integer overflow in buffer size calculation leading to the out-of-bounds write at lines 55-58).

assumptions: cache->n_hdr, cache->hdr_offset[], cache->hdr fields and cache->maps are populated by parsing code not shown in this snippet; per the width-domain rule they are treated as attacker-controlled file-derived values.
The trigger requires n_hdr >= 2 (subcaches), a configuration fully representable by the input file.

rz_buf_read_le32_at / rz_buf_fread_at return false or a short count on out-of-bounds reads (buffer-accessor semantics), and RZ_NEWS0/RZ_NEW0 are zeroing allocators returning NULL on failure; all such sentinels are locally checked in this code.
MAX_N_HDR is a compile-time constant bounding the subcache loop; it caps the number of accumulated terms, not their magnitude.
limitations: infos[k].end = infos[k].start + entry.size (line 56) and infos[0].end = infos[0].start + cache->maps[1].size (line 94) can wrap ut64, but in this code the results are only stored/passed to get_rebase_info, whose consumption is not shown; no direct memory-safety effect is instantiated here.

The access to cache->maps[1] is guarded by the quoted check 'cache->hdr->mappingCount > 1' (line 87), but whether the maps array is sized from mappingCount is established in code not shown; if it is not, that would be a separate defect outside this snippet.
get_rebase_info internals are not shown; the confirmed out-of-bounds write at lines 55-58 occurs independently of that callee's behavior.
Failure paths (allocation failure, failed reads) all goto beach and return NULL; fail-closed, no security-state misrepresentation.

verdict.summary: This do_cmdline() implementation matches upstream Vim's well-audited logic. Every memory sink consuming attacker-influenced values is locally guarded by a quoted test in execution order: lines_ga indexing is guarded by 'current_line < lines_ga.ga_len' and 'lines_ga.ga_len > 0', the jump-back cs_line read by 'cstack.cs_idx >= 0' and 'cstack.cs_line[cstack.cs_idx] >= 0', pointer writes by 'breakpoint != NULL', and every allocation/parse path tests its sentinel before first use (fgetline NULL, vim_strsave NULL, store_loop_line FAIL). The one write lacking a local index guard, cstack.cs_line[cstack.cs_idx] = current_line_before, depends on invariants maintained by the unshown do_one_cmd/rewind_conditionals; per the analysis rules that unquoted contract can neither protect the sink nor produce an out-of-range trigger, so no defective execution could be simulated through quoted statements. No injection, authz, crypto, or resource-amplification sinks exist in this code.

assumptions: do_one_cmd() maintains cstack.cs_idx within [0, CSTACK_LEN) and returns either NULL or a pointer into the cmdline_copy buffer at or after its current position; not shown in this code.
get_loop_line() (via cmd_loop_cookie.current_line) maintains current_line as a non-negative value consistent with lines_ga; not shown in this code.
rewind_conditionals() and cleanup_conditionals() keep the conditional stack internally consistent (including cs_emsg_silent_list ownership); their semantics are not shown.
store_loop_line() stores non-NULL, NUL-terminated lines and appends atomically on success; not shown.
fgetline callbacks (get_func_line, getsourceline, getexline) return NUL-terminated strings or NULL; the NULL case is locally checked.
p_mfd ('maxfuncdepth') is an operator-set option; no statement in this code sets it.
limitations: The write 'cstack.cs_line[cstack.cs_idx] = current_line_before;' in the CSL_HAD_LOOP branch has no local bounds check on cs_idx in this code; a heap OOB write would occur if an unshown callee (do_one_cmd or rewind_conditionals) ever left cs_idx out of [0, CSTACK_LEN) while CSL_HAD_LOOP is pending and cs_looplevel > 0. No quoted statement or characterizable callee could instantiate that state, so it is not confirmed here; the minimal fix would be an explicit 'cstack.cs_idx >= 0 && cstack.cs_idx < CSTACK_LEN' test before the write.

current_line is written back from cmd_loop_cookie.current_line, which the unshown get_loop_line mutates; a misbehaving callee could make the 'current_line < lines_ga.ga_len' guard pass with a negative value. Not instantiable from the given code.

The recursion guard 'call_depth >= 200 && call_depth >= p_mfd' permits recursion up to 'maxfuncdepth' when the operator sets that option very large; worst case is a stack exhaustion crash of the operator's own process at the operator's own configuration, matching the documented intent, so it is not treated as a vulnerability.

verdict.summary: The return value of the unshown path-parsing helper _g_path_get_relative_basename (line 7), whose failure sentinel is NULL, is consumed without any sentinel check and passed as the basename to g_file_get_child (line 8). The only nearby test, odata->current_file != NULL, guards the list node pointer, not the derived base_name. A malicious archive entry (member name not under base_dir) can drive base_name to NULL, causing a GLib critical/NULL dereference inside g_file_get_child, a NULL destination flowing into g_file_query_info_async and g_object_unref, and a permanent stall or crash of the extraction triggered solely by attacker-supplied archive content.

evidence.reason: Unguarded sink: base_name is passed as the required non-NULL basename with no validation on any path. The mention sweep shows the only check in the function (odata->current_file != NULL, line 3) constrains the list node, not base_name. Trigger: overwrite == FR_OVERWRITE_ASK and current_file != NULL (quoted conditions), current_file->data is an attacker-chosen archive member name, and the line-7 parse helper returns its NULL failure sentinel (in-domain for a const char * return per the width-domain rule). g_file_get_child then receives NULL where its contract requires a basename, producing a critical/NULL dereference and a NULL destination that dead-ends the async query, leaks odata, and stalls or crashes the process extracting the attacker's archive.

Origin of the tainted value: an unshown lookup/parse callee applied to attacker-controlled archive member data whose return is consumed without a sentinel test; the NULL failure sentinel it can produce flows directly to the line-8 sink.

assumptions: The pointer skeleton (odata, odata->edata, odata->window, edata->destination, window->priv->cancellable) is treated as internal trusted plumbing constructed by this module's extraction flow; no NULL contract for these is quotable from the given code.

g_file_get_child is a GLib function whose behavior on a NULL basename follows GLib's programming-error convention (critical warning plus NULL return, or a NULL dereference in builds/versions lacking the g_return_val_if_fail guard); either way the defect is attributed to the unchecked call site per the callee-sentinel rule.

The unshown helper _g_path_get_relative_basename is a path-parsing/lookup callee; per the width-domain rule its const char * return's domain includes NULL, but whether any specific input deterministically yields NULL is not provable from this snippet.
The forced FR_OVERWRITE_YES in the file_list branch executes only on the non-ASK path (the ASK path returns earlier), so it is read as intended post-dialog flow, not a silent overwrite bypass.
limitations: Path traversal candidate (CWE-22): archive member names flow through the unshown helper into g_file_get_child and g_file_query_info_async with no quotable traversal sanitization in this code. However, the only statement executed here with an escaped path is a metadata query whose result is consumed by the unshown callback, and the actual out-of-destination write happens in extraction code not given; the impact chain breaks at unshown links, and the trigger also depends on the unshown helper passing traversal text through. Recorded as speculative, not primary.

NULL odata itself is never checked before the line-3 dereference, but odata is constructed and passed by this module's own flow (producer not shown); treating internal plumbing pointers as attacker-NULL-able is not instantiated by any quoted statement, so it is noted only as a robustness observation.

Even in the benign reading of the NULL-base_name path (GLib guards return NULL rather than dereferencing), the concrete consequence is a set of GLib criticals, a leaked odata, and an extraction flow that never completes or stops its batch — attacker-triggered denial of service in the process that opened the malicious archive; no memory corruption was simulated.

verdict.summary: disable_priv_mode fails open: when setresuid/setuid (or setresgid/setgid) fails, the function only logs (and exits solely for errno EAGAIN when EXIT_ON_SETUID_FAILURE is defined), then unconditionally executes 'current_user.euid = current_user.uid; current_user.egid = current_user.gid;' — recording a successful privilege drop that never happened while the process keeps running with its elevated effective uid/gid.

evidence.reason: Unconditional security-state stamp: these assignments execute on every path, including the error path where setresuid/setuid returned < 0, so the bookkeeping claims the euid/egid were dropped while the kernel still holds the elevated values. No success flag or sentinel check anywhere in the function gates these lines.

Origin of the fail-open path: the uid-drop failure is detected and logged, but the only exit guard is the EAGAIN-conditional 'if (e == EAGAIN) exit (e);' (present only when EXIT_ON_SETUID_FAILURE is defined). Any other errno — and every gid failure, which has no exit at all — falls through, leaving the process with its original elevated euid/egid.

assumptions: current_user.uid/gid/euid/egid are global struct fields populated outside the shown code (e.g., at startup from getuid/geteuid); the shown code never narrows them.

Compile-time configuration (HAVE_DECL_SETRESUID/SETRESGID, EXIT_ON_SETUID_FAILURE) is unknown; the defect exists in every configuration because the gid failure path has no exit at all and the uid exit covers only EAGAIN.
The process invoking this function is assumed to be in privileged mode (euid != uid), which is the function's sole reason to exist; otherwise the state assignments are no-ops.
limitations: Practical exploitation requires an attacker to induce a setresuid/setgid failure (e.g., EAGAIN via RLIMIT_NPROC exhaustion); the code itself acknowledges this failure mode by special-casing EAGAIN, so the sentinel is in-domain, but reliable triggering depends on environment.

Downstream consumers of current_user.euid/egid (privilege-mode decisions elsewhere in the program) are not shown; the in-code impact is the retained elevated euid/egid plus the misstated bookkeeping, and the shown 'e' variable being unused in non-EXIT builds is cosmetic only.

verdict.summary: disable_priv_mode fails open: if setuid/setgid fails, the code only logs the error and continues (the sole exit covers only errno EAGAIN for setuid, and only when EXIT_ON_SETUID_FAILURE is compiled in; the setgid failure arm never terminates at all). It then unconditionally records current_user.euid = current_user.uid and egid = gid, so the shell proceeds running the untrusted user's commands with elevated kernel effective IDs while its internal state reports privileges as dropped — a failed privilege drop with attacker-inducible triggers (e.g., setuid failing with EAGAIN under an exhausted RLIMIT_NPROC).

evidence.snippet:
if (setgid (current_user.gid) < 0)
    sys_error (_("cannot set gid to %d: effective gid %d"), current_user.gid, current_user.egid);
evidence.reason: The setgid failure arm only logs via sys_error; unlike the setuid arm there is no exit/return on ANY errno, even when EXIT_ON_SETUID_FAILURE is defined. On a failed setgid (e.g., EAGAIN at RLIMIT_NPROC, attacker-inducible with a fork loop), execution falls through and the process keeps its elevated effective gid — fail-open privilege drop (CWE-754).

These assignments run unconditionally on every path, including after a failed setuid/setgid, so the shell's internal state asserts euid==uid/egid==gid while the kernel effective IDs remain elevated (root). This presents the dropped-privilege security state on an error path, and all later euid-based checks then report privileges as relinquished while commands still execute as root.

The only failure-path terminator in the function: it is compile-time optional (#if defined (EXIT_ON_SETUID_FAILURE)) and matches only EAGAIN, so a setuid failure with any other errno (e.g., EPERM under a restrictive seccomp/container policy) falls through the block at line 13 and the process continues with elevated euid — the guard is insufficient to cover the failure domain of the setuid sentinel consumed at line 5.

assumptions: current_user.uid/gid/euid/egid are global fields set outside this code; the analysis does not depend on their content, only on the documented -1 failure sentinel of setuid/setgid and errno.

This is a privilege-drop routine invoked when a setuid shell sheds elevated effective IDs; the unprivileged user on whose behalf privileges are dropped, and the OS resource state they can influence (RLIMIT_NPROC), are treated as the trust-boundary parties.
limitations: The EAGAIN-only exit softens the setuid trigger when EXIT_ON_SETUID_FAILURE is compiled in and the errno is exactly EAGAIN; the setuid trigger then requires a different errno or an unguarded build, but the setgid arm remains unguarded in all configurations.

Exploitation consequences (which later euid/egid comparisons are bypassed) occur in code not shown; the instantiated impact here is the process continuing with elevated kernel effective IDs while internal state records them as dropped.

verdict.summary: All attacker-derived values (record index, record count, record sizes, record-list traversal) are guarded by quoted checks in execution order: huff_rec_count is upper-bounded by HUFF_RECORD_MAXCNT and lower-bounded by the '< 2' check before the (huff_rec_count - 1) allocation, whose expression is identical to the loop bound; the record lookup NULL result is checked before any dereference; the HUFF record minimum size is checked; and each loop iteration re-checks curr for NULL before use. No unguarded memory, injection, or validation sink exists in this function.

assumptions: HUFF_RECORD_MAXCNT is a compile-time constant small enough that (huff_rec_count - 1) * sizeof(pointer) cannot wrap size_t at the declared widths; the constant's value is not shown in the given code.

mobi_get_record_by_seqnumber returns NULL (not an out-of-range pointer) when the attacker-derived, possibly wrapped huff_rec_index does not match any record; this is standard lookup semantics per discipline 3 and the NULL result is checked.

mobi_parse_huff and mobi_parse_cdic perform their own record-size validation internally; their implementations are not shown. This code passes only in-domain arguments (non-NULL curr per quoted checks, in-range index i), so any defect in those callees would be located there, not at these call sites.
m is the library's own handle created at document load and is dereferenced first by mobi_get_kf8offset(m); its non-NULLness is an internal caller contract, not file-controlled data.
limitations: On CDIC parse failure after the malloc (in-loop 'return MOBI_DATA_CORRUPT' or 'return ret'), huffcdic->symbols is not freed before returning: a bounded memory leak, not a security impact per the analyzed categories.

The in-loop error returns leave huffcdic->symbols partially initialized; the non-MOBI_SUCCESS return code signals the caller to discard the structure, so no consumer of uninitialized entries is exhibited in this code.

mobi_parse_cdic's internal handling of curr->size (which is attacker-controlled and NOT size-checked in this function for CDIC records, only for the HUFF record) could not be audited from the given code.

verdict.summary: cookedprint() passes an attacker-controlled variable string to decodearr() which fills narr with a decoded element count, then consumes narr as the iteration count over the fixed 8-element stack array lfparr via outputarr(fp, name, narr, lfparr) with no bound check anywhere in the function. A remote peer supplying a variable value with more than 8 comma-separated entries makes the code read past lfparr[8], disclosing or corrupting stack data.

evidence.reason: narr is an out-param filled by decodearr() from the attacker-supplied string 'value' (which itself comes from the parsed response 'data'), and lfparr is declared as l_fp lfparr[8]. The !decodearr test only checks the decode failure sentinel, never narr's magnitude. narr is then used unvalidated as the element count for the 8-element stack array in outputarr(), so any decoded count above 8 reads (and, inside the unsized decodearr call, potentially writes) past the end of lfparr. The mention sweep over narr (declaration at line 17, producer at line 97, use at line 100) shows no bounds check, clamp, mask, or size argument anywhere on any path.

assumptions: atoascii(str, maxlen, buf, buflen) truncates its output within buflen including a NUL terminator; under this documented-shape semantics the TALOS-CAN-0063 fix (atoascii(value, MAXVALLEN, bv, sizeof(bv) - 1) followed by bv[len]=output_raw; bv[len+1]='\0') keeps len+1 <= sizeof(bv)-1 and is in bounds even at the exactly-full boundary.
nextvar() is assumed to return valid non-NULL name/value pointers into the response data; its contract is not shown in this code.
decodearr returns nonzero on success and 0 on failure, matching the sentinel test pattern used for the other decoders in this function.
limitations: If nextvar() could ever yield a NULL 'value', strlen(value) in the RF case and the decoder calls would dereference NULL; this depends on an unshown callee contract and is recorded as speculative, not a finding.

The out-of-bounds WRITE variant (decodearr writing a 9th+ element into lfparr) would occur inside decodearr, which is not shown; the defect established in this code is the unvalidated narr count at the outputarr call site and the absence of any bound communicated to the callee.

In the historical NTP source this pattern was associated with the TALOS-CAN-0063 hardening of the output_raw path; that fix is present here and verified sound, and does not affect the AR-case finding.

verdict.summary: Image::printIFDStructure allocates a value buffer with the wrapping 32-bit expression `size*count + pad+20` while later indexing it with the raw attacker-controlled `count`, so a crafted TIFF IFD entry (e.g., XMP tag 0x02bc, RATIONAL type, count=0x20000000) yields a 20-byte heap allocation followed by the out-of-bounds write `buf.pData_[count]=0` roughly 512 MB past the buffer — heap memory corruption driven by a single file field, with no bound on count anywhere in the function (the only candidate check is commented out).
