No statement in this code can produce that state, and the writer that maintains the invariant is not shown, so this trigger is not instantiated here.

A further consequence may exist in code not shown: pcl_status_write could append into the dangling pcs->status.buffer without reallocating (UAF write), but that impact chain lies outside the given code and does not affect the verdict.

The very first call on a fresh state (buffer NULL, positions 0) also reaches line 10; if the allocator did not tolerate freeing NULL this would be a separate crash, but the primary double-free trigger uses the post-drain state and does not depend on that behavior.

verdict.summary: cgroup release_agent write handler correctly requires init-userns privilege (opener's f_cred->user_ns checked plus capable(CAP_SYS_ADMIN)) before accepting the write, and copies the attacker-controlled buffer with strlcpy bounded by exactly sizeof(release_agent_path), whose capacity is compile-time asserted >= PATH_MAX. Both the historical CVE-2022-0492 authorization bypass and any buffer overflow are prevented by quoted statements in execution order.

assumptions: buf arrives NUL-terminated within a single zeroed page, per the standard kernfs write machinery (caller contract not shown in this code); strlcpy's destination-derived bound means no source value can cause an out-of-bounds write regardless.
cgroup_kn_lock_live and cgroup_kn_unlock are project-internal helpers; the NULL sentinel of the former is explicitly checked at 'if (!cgrp) return -ENODEV;' before first use.
limitations: nbytes is not validated against buffer capacity, but it is never used as a copy length; strlcpy's bound is destination-derived, so oversized writes are silently truncated by design, not a defect.
strstrip mutates the caller's write buffer in place (trailing whitespace NULed); harmless since the buffer is a scratch write page.

verdict.summary: This function is a thin dispatch handler that passes the received chunk pointer unmodified to sctp_sf_abort_violation along with a static error string and its exactly-matching sizeof. It performs no memory access, indexing, sizing, or copy on attacker-derived data, so no exploitable sink exists in this code; any mishandling of the attacker-controlled chunk length would occur inside the callee, which is not shown.

assumptions: sctp_sf_abort_violation is a project-internal callee not shown; its handling of the chunk pointer (arg), the error string, and the length parameter cannot be analyzed here and is treated as an assumption, not a guard.
The ep/asoc/commands parameters are internal SCTP state-machine objects supplied by the dispatcher; their validity is a framework contract outside this code.
limitations: The chunk pointer arg carries attacker-derived packet content, and historical SCTP flaws (misuse of the attacker-controlled chunk_hdr->length when constructing the ABORT in sctp_sf_abort_violation) would live in the callee, which is not part of the given code; this analysis cannot confirm or exclude defects there.

sizeof(err_str) is 40 bytes (including the NUL terminator). If the callee expected the string length without the terminator (39), a semantic mismatch could exist, but the callee's length semantics are not shown, so this remains unverified.

This handler is invoked after a chunk-length violation has already been detected upstream; any missing validation of the malformed length is attributable to the dispatcher or the callee, not to statements present in this snippet.

verdict.summary: simplestring_addn performs an unvalidated signed length addition and copies attacker-controlled add_len bytes: a negative add_len (or an int overflow in target->len + add_len + 1) bypasses the only size test at line 6, skipping realloc, and reaches memcpy(target->str + target->len, source, add_len) where add_len converts to a huge size_t, causing a heap out-of-bounds write/read (memory corruption).

evidence.reason: Sink: memcpy length is the signed parameter add_len with no non-negativity or overflow validation; with add_len = -1 (in-domain for an exported function's int parameter) the implicit int-to-size_t conversion yields SIZE_MAX, copying unbounded bytes into the heap buffer — heap out-of-bounds write. The if(add_len) test checks only non-zero, not non-negative.

The only check touching add_len. It is bypassed by the instantiated trigger: with target->len = 0 and add_len = -1 the sum is 0, so no growth is performed; with large add_len the signed sum wraps negative (signed overflow) and the check is again false. It never constrains add_len >= 0, so the defective copy at line 20 is reachable with an unbounded length.

assumptions: simplestring_init_str (line 4) is an internal callee not shown; its effect on target->str/size is unknown and was not relied upon for any guard.
SIMPLESTRING_INCR is not shown; the comment 'align to SIMPLESTRING_INCR increments' suggests the original intent, but the code actually uses incr = target->size * 2.
limitations: Division by zero at line 12 (newsize % incr when incr = target->size * 2 == 0) requires size == 0 with str != NULL; the only shown producer of size = 0 (line 15, realloc failure) co-occurs with str = NULL, which routes through the init at line 3/4 on the next call, so this trigger could not be instantiated from the shown statements alone.

int overflow of incr = target->size * 2 (line 9) requires target->size > 2^30, i.e., roughly a 1 GB string already accumulated; possible in principle (no quoted bound caps accumulation) but dominated by the primary negative-length trigger.

On realloc failure (line 13) the original buffer pointer is lost when NULL is assigned to target->str — a memory leak; the copy itself is safely skipped by target->size = target->str ? newsize : 0 and if(target->str).

OOB read of source when a positive add_len exceeds the readable bytes at source is a caller-contract question; the write-side corruption trigger (negative/overflowing add_len) already instantiates the defect.

verdict.summary: This SCTP state-function only forwards its arguments to sctp_sf_abort_violation along with a compile-time-constant error string whose length (sizeof(err_str), including the NUL) is derived from the same declaration that defines the buffer, so no out-of-domain value can reach any sink in this code. The attacker-influenced chunk pointer (arg) is never dereferenced, sized, or indexed here; it is passed through as a handle. No defect exists within the given code.

assumptions: sctp_sf_abort_violation (callee, not shown) is assumed to handle the forwarded chunk handle (arg), the command sequence, and the err_str/len pair (len = 44, the full buffer including NUL) safely; its internal behavior cannot be audited from the given code.
err_str is NUL-terminated by C string-literal semantics and sizeof(err_str) equals the exact array size; this is enforced by the declaration itself, not by a runtime check.
limitations: The historical SCTP parameter-length handling defects (e.g., insufficient validation of chunk/parameter lengths) live in the callee sctp_sf_abort_violation and in the dispatch code that populates arg, neither of which is shown; any such defect is outside the auditable scope of this snippet and is not recorded as a finding.

If the not-shown callee mishandles err_str's length (for example by treating it as NUL-terminated-variable or by copying a fixed larger size), the defect would be in that callee, not in this forwarding function.

verdict.summary: pfkey_register consumes one attacker-controlled value, hdr->sadb_msg_satype (8-bit). The quoted range check 'if (hdr->sadb_msg_satype > SADB_SATYPE_MAX) return -EINVAL;' bounds it to [0,15] on every path before all bitmap shifts (1<<satype, max 32768, in-domain for the int 'registered' field), the allocation sentinel is checked with correct bitmap rollback, and no other attacker-derived size, index, offset, or pointer reaches a memory or injection sink in this code.

assumptions: SADB_SATYPE_MAX = 15 and SADB_SATYPE_UNSPEC = 0, per RFC 2367 and include/uapi/linux/pfkeyv2.h (header not shown in given code).
pfk->registered is declared as int (32 bits) in struct pfkey_sock, so shift amounts 0..15 are in-domain; the struct definition is not shown.

hdr points to a fully present sadb_msg validated by the unshown PF_KEY dispatch layer (pfkey_rcv/pfkey_process); the given code dereferences hdr->sadb_msg_satype at line 6 with no local length check, so pointer validity rests on that unquoted caller contract.

compose_sadb_supported and pfkey_broadcast are internal callees not shown; this code passes them only a struct pointer and a freshly allocated skb, and checks compose_sadb_supported's NULL sentinel at line 21.
limitations: Functional off-by-one candidate: 'if (hdr->sadb_msg_satype > SADB_SATYPE_MAX)' admits satype == 15 (an RFC-2367-unused satype; the upstream kernel hardening used >=). Tested at both bounds: satype 15 yields 1<<15 = 32768, bit 15 of a 32-bit int bitmap — memory-safe, no UB, no OOB, no security impact; recorded as functional over-admission, not a vulnerability.
Speculative: NULL/short hdr dereference would require the unshown dispatch layer to pass an invalid header; not producible by any statement in this code.
Speculative: concurrent races on pfk->registered cannot be exhibited as two ordered operations with a re-entry window inside this code.
Denial-of-service via compose_sadb_supported allocation failure is handled by the -ENOBUFS error path; no unbounded attacker-amplified work occurs in this function.

verdict.summary: The attacker-controlled thread name length from the on-disk catalog record is bounded by the quoted check 'be16_to_cpu(tmp.thread.nodeName.length) > 255' before being consumed by the key builder, and the record type is validated against thread constants. The only residual defect (uninitialized trailing name units when a record is physically shorter than its declared length) produces only an in-bounds garbage lookup key with no instantiated memory-safety, disclosure, or bypass impact, so the code is not vulnerable.

assumptions: hfsplus_cat_build_key_uni, not shown, is assumed to write at most 255 UTF-16 units into fd->search_key, whose standard struct hfs_find_data layout reserves a key buffer large enough for parentID plus 255 units; the quoted 255 check enforces that bound at the call site.
hfs_brec_read, not shown, is assumed to copy at most the requested sizeof(hfsplus_cat_entry) bytes into tmp, which caps all subsequent reads from tmp within its own extent.
limitations: If an on-disk thread record declares nodeName.length larger than the number of unicode units physically stored in the record, the trailing units of tmp remain uninitialized stack (hfs_brec_read copies only the actual record length) and are read in-bounds when building the search key. This is an uninitialized-value use with no out-of-bounds access, no kernel-to-user disclosure path, and no control-flow effect demonstrated in this code, so it is recorded as a robustness issue rather than a vulnerability.
The > 255 comparison was edge-tested at 0, 255, 256, and 65535; it under-admits nothing and over-rejects nothing for the key buffer bound, so it is a correct bound, not an off-by-one.

verdict.summary: jp2_decode builds dec->chantocmptlut from the attacker-supplied CMAP box without constraining the stored component numbers to the decoded image's component count: the DIRECT branch stores the raw channel number (line 272), an unrecognized map value leaves the slot uninitialized, and jas_image_depalettize's return is ignored. These values are then passed unchecked as component indices to jas_image_setcmpttype (lines 313-314, 321), producing an out-of-bounds write when the CMAP declares more channels than the code stream has components (the sanity loop at lines 240-250 validates only the ents[].cmptno and ents[].pcol fields, never numchans or the LUT values). Independently, the BPCC consistency loop (lines 179-182) is bounded by the code-stream component count while indexing the bpcs array sized from the BPCC box, and the count mismatch is only warned about (lines 172-174), yielding an out-of-bounds read.

evidence.reason: Sink: chantocmptlut values are used as component indices with no validation against jas_image_numcmpts(dec->image). The CMAP sanity loop (lines 240-250) checks only ents[].cmptno and ents[].pcol, never numchans, so a CMAP with numchans=3 of DIRECT entries over an image with 1 component stores LUT={0,1,2}; this loop then calls jas_image_setcmpttype with component indices 1 and 2, which index past the image's component array and write the type through the resulting out-of-bounds pointer — heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) triggered entirely by attacker box content.

Origin of the tainted index: the raw channel number channo (attacker-controlled via cmap numchans) is stored as a component number with no comparison against the image's component count anywhere in the code (the only related checks are ents[].cmptno at line 240 and the LUT-index check at line 309, neither of which bounds this value). An ents[].map value outside {JP2_CMAP_DIRECT, JP2_CMAP_PALETTE} also leaves this slot uninitialized (jas_alloc2 does not zero memory), another unvalidated index reaching the same sink.

The loop is bounded by the code-stream component count while indexing the bpcs array, which is sized from the BPCC box's own numcmpts. The code acknowledges the two counts can diverge at lines 172-174 but only prints a warning and continues (fail-open). A BPCC box declaring 1 component paired with a code stream of 2 differently-typed components (samedtype false) makes this loop read bpcs[1] one past the allocated array — heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) on attacker-controlled data.

assumptions: Box payload fields (cmap.numchans, ents[].map/.cmptno/.pcol, pclr.numchans/.numlutents, bpcc.numcmpts, cdef.numchans) arrive from jp2_box_get with the full width domain of their declared types; the parser (not shown) is not treated as narrowing any of them.

jas_image_setcmpttype is a component-array indexing accessor: it indexes the image's per-component array with the supplied component number and writes the type, so an out-of-range index is an out-of-bounds memory access.
jas_alloc2 has malloc semantics: it returns a pointer or NULL and does not zero the allocation.
The per-box arrays (cmap ents, pclr lutdata/bpc, bpcc bpcs) are sized by their box's own count fields, consistent with the loops this code runs over them.
limitations: Line 274: lutents = jas_alloc2(pclrd->numlutents, sizeof(int_fast32_t)) is not NULL-checked and lutents[i] is written at line 276, a NULL-deref write if the allocation fails; forcing failure depends on the unshown width of numlutents, so the trigger is not fully instantiated here.

Line 268: cdefd = &dec->cdef->data.cdef; executes with a possibly NULL dec->cdef — formally undefined behavior, but the address computation performs no load and cdefd is referenced only inside the #if 0 block, so no runtime impact.
Line 212: assert(dec->image->cmprof_) can abort if jas_cmprof_createfromiccprof fails (allocation failure path) — robustness only, no corruption or bypass.
Potential integer overflow in cmapent->pcol + i * pclrd->numchans (line 276) could not be evaluated because the field widths are not shown.

verdict.summary: The bound check 'if (authkey->sca_keylength > optlen)' compares the attacker-supplied key length against the entire kmalloc(optlen) allocation instead of the bytes remaining after the struct sctp_authkey header, so a keylength in (optlen - sizeof(struct sctp_authkey), optlen] passes validation and sctp_auth_set_key consumes that many bytes from authkey->sca_key, reading up to sizeof(struct sctp_authkey)-1 bytes past the heap allocation (kernel heap out-of-bounds read).

evidence.reason: Defective guard: sca_keylength (attacker-controlled __u16 from optval) is validated against optlen, the full kmalloc(optlen) allocation size, rather than optlen - sizeof(struct sctp_authkey), the bytes actually available after the header. Trigger: optlen=9, sca_keylength=9 passes 9 > 9 as false, so an oversized key reaches the sink.

Sink: the callee consumes authkey->sca_keylength bytes starting at the key field inside a kmalloc(optlen) allocation; with keylength=9 and optlen=9 it reads up to 8 bytes past the 9-byte allocation (heap out-of-bounds read).
Origin of the tainted data: the setsockopt caller fully controls optval contents, including sca_keylength, copied into an optlen-sized heap buffer.

assumptions: sizeof(struct sctp_authkey) is 8 bytes (assoc_id __u32, keylength __u16, padding), matching the upstream sctp.h definition, so the key data begins at offset 8 of the allocation.
sctp_auth_set_key consumes authkey->sca_keylength bytes from authkey->sca_key, per the struct's documented meaning and the upstream fix that changed this check to 'optlen - sizeof(*authkey)'.
limitations: sctp_id2assoc(sk, 0) can return NULL (no association); line 30 only rejects NULL asoc when sca_assoc_id != 0 and the socket is UDP-style, so a NULL asoc may reach sctp_auth_set_key. Whether that is harmful depends on the unshown callee's handling of a NULL association; recorded as a candidate I could not fully instantiate.

The over-read is bounded by sizeof(struct sctp_authkey) (~8 bytes) past the requested allocation; because kmalloc rounds up to slab sizes, on many configurations the read stays within the slab, limiting practical disclosure (the upstream fix described this as a kernel infoleak).

verdict.summary: mobi_buffer_move validates its memmove bounds with additive size_t expressions (buf->offset + aoffset + len and buf->offset + len) that wrap modulo 2^64, so attacker-sized offset/len values (e.g. offset=1, len=SIZE_MAX-buf->offset) pass the checks and drive memmove to perform a massive out-of-bounds read and write past buf->data (CWE-190 root cause, CWE-787 consequence at the memmove sink).

evidence.reason: The only positive-branch bound check adds attacker-derived size_t values (aoffset, len) to buf->offset; the sum wraps mod 2^64 (e.g. 0 + 1 + (SIZE_MAX) = 0), so it compares 0 > maxlen, passes, and the unbounded len reaches the memmove at line 19.
Mirrored defect in the negative branch: buf->offset + len wraps the same way (B + (SIZE_MAX - B + 1) = 0), bypassing the end-of-buffer check before the memmove.

Sink: with offset=1 and len=SIZE_MAX-buf->offset (both within the declared int/size_t domains of the exported function's parameters), both guards wrap and pass, and this memmove copies ~2^64 bytes, reading and writing far past buf->data+buf->maxlen (instantiated out-of-bounds read/write).

assumptions: buf->data, buf->offset and buf->maxlen are initialized by code not shown; buf->offset is treated as carrying the full size_t domain per the width-domain rule, and the simulated trigger works for any buf->offset B and any maxlen M >= 0.
abs(INT_MIN) is formally undefined behavior at line 2; on real platforms it yields (size_t)INT_MIN, which the negative-branch check (buf->offset < aoffset) then rejects.
limitations: buf is never NULL-checked before line 3 dereferences it, but a NULL handle from the caller is an equal-privilege crash with no corruption, a robustness issue only.
No entry check of buf->error means a buffer already in error state is operated on; no quotable corruption link, robustness only.

In the full libmobi library, callers typically derive len from 32-bit record fields, which cannot reach SIZE_MAX-scale values on 64-bit targets; per the width-domain rule this analysis judges the exported function's declared size_t parameter as the input surface, which is why the trigger is instantiated here.

verdict.summary: All memory sinks in esp6_output_head are guarded by quoted, positionally-correct checks: the in-place trailer write is bounded by 'tailen <= skb_tailroom(skb)', the page-frag trailer write is bounded by skb_page_frag_refill(ALIGN(tailen)) with a checked failure sentinel, the frag descriptor index is bounded by 'nr_frags < MAX_SKB_FRAGS', and the COW path checks the skb_cow_data return before use. Residual issues (unsigned overflow of skb->data_len + tailen at ~4GiB scale, and the unverified cross-field invariant tailen == tfclen + plen + 2 established by the not-shown same-file caller) have no instantiable trigger from any attacker-reachable entry point.

assumptions: esp->tailen, esp->tfclen, esp->plen and esp->proto are produced by the not-shown same-file caller (esp6_output/esp6_output_tail); the invariant that the trailer fill writes exactly tailen bytes is established there and could not be quoted from the given code. assumptions: The CLIWandExceptionBreak/CLIWandExceptArgBreak macros break out of the enclosing do-while loop, per their consistent 'Break' naming and use sites; their expansions are not shown.

ExpandFilenames returns a freshly allocated argv vector (so the RelinquishMagickMemory at line 115 frees heap memory, not the stack address '&arg1' assigned at line 93) and returns MagickFalse on allocation failure.
RelinquishMagickMemory/DestroyString tolerate NULL, so the post-break cleanup DestroyString(NULL) calls are safe.
limitations: Line 112 passes the unchecked return of ReadImages/PingImages (which can be NULL on unreadable input) to AppendImageToList; the crash or corruption would occur inside a callee whose NULL tolerance is not shown, so the impact chain is not instantiated here.

The 'set' branch calls InterpretImageProperties with a possibly-NULL arg1n, and the 'clone' branch calls IsSceneGeometry with a possibly-NULL arg1; the behavior of these unshown internal callees on NULL input cannot be characterized, so no trigger is instantiated for them.

Memory leaks (CWE-401): in the 'set' and 'clone' branches, a previously percent-escaped heap copy of arg1/arg2 can be overwritten without being destroyed (e.g. 'arg1=InterpretImageProperties(...)' in the set branch and 'arg1=AcquireString("-1")' in clone); bounded per-option leaks, not amplification.

FormatLocaleString at line 140 can truncate the 'cache:%s' registry key for very long filenames, causing DeleteImageRegistry to delete a truncated key that does not match the WriteImages output; functional consistency issue only.
The write-branch NULL dereference is a crash (DoS) primitive only; no memory corruption or disclosure was found in this code.

verdict.summary: In ins_bs(), the only start-of-buffer guard is wrapped as '!revins_on && ((curwin->w_cursor.lnum == 1 && curwin->w_cursor.col == 0) || ...)', so when reverse-insert mode is active a backspace at the very start of the buffer is not rejected. The delete-newline branch then executes '--Insstart.lnum;' and 'Insstart.col = (colnr_T)STRLEN(ml_get(Insstart.lnum));' with no lower-bound check anywhere, passing line number 0 (and, on the mirrored path, cursor line 0 into ml_get_buf/do_join and -1 into u_save) — an out-of-bounds/invalid line access (CWE-125).

evidence.reason: Sink: Insstart.lnum is decremented with no lower-bound check and then passed directly to the memline container accessor ml_get(). A mention sweep of every Insstart.lnum / cursor.lnum statement in the function shows no 'Insstart.lnum > 1', clamp, or error arm on any path, so Insstart.lnum reaches 0 (e.g. insert started at line 1, revins_on set, empty first line so inc_cursor() moves the cursor to (2,0), the '|| revins_on' at line 82 admits the block, 1-1=0) and ml_get(0) indexes the memline outside its [1, line_count] domain — out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

Origin of the defect: the sole statement that prevents backing up at the very start of the buffer, '(curwin->w_cursor.lnum == 1 && curwin->w_cursor.col == 0)', is conjoined behind '!revins_on &&', so when the revins_on global (producer not shown in this code, full int domain per the width-domain rule) is nonzero the check evaluates FALSE and the buffer-start invariant is lost, making the unguarded decrement at lines 89-90 reachable; the same bypass admits cursor.lnum == 1 into '--curwin->w_cursor.lnum' and u_save((linenr_T)(-1), ...).

assumptions: ml_get/ml_get_buf, u_save, do_join, dec_cursor, inc_cursor, replace_pop, del_char, ins_char, ins_str, ins_bs_one are project-internal callees not shown; per the analysis rules their behavior can neither trigger nor protect the sink, so the unchecked call site passing an out-of-domain line index is treated as the defect.

revins_on, State, Insstart, Insstart_orig, ai_col, arrow_used, orig_line_count and option values are globals/fields set by code not shown; per the width-domain rule their full declared-domain values are treated as instantiable inputs, and no quoted statement in this code narrows them.

Buffer text is the trust-boundary content (file originator); all direct dereferences of buffer text in this function are bounds-checked by quoted statements ('curwin->w_cursor.col > 0' before '*(ml_get_cursor() - 1)', 'len > 0' before 'ptr[len - 1]', loop bound 'curwin->w_cursor.col > mincol' before dec_cursor).
limitations: Practical exposure is constrained: reaching the defective state requires revins_on (reverse-insert mode), which in a normal Vim session is toggled by the operator's own keystrokes rather than by file content, so the invalid access is usually self-inflicted rather than attacker-driven; the width-domain rule is what makes the trigger instantiable for this analysis.

All non-revins paths are provably safe: without revins_on the line-28 check rejects cursor at (1,0), so every entry into the col==0 branch has cursor.lnum >= 2 and Insstart.lnum after decrement stays >= 1.

The u_save((linenr_T)(-1), ...), ml_get_buf(curbuf, 0, TRUE) and do_join(2,...)-from-line-0 uses are satellites of the same root cause (the '!revins_on &&' bypass plus missing lower bound) and are fixed by the same one-line guard; they are not counted as independent defects.

verdict.summary: hfsplus_find_cat reads an attacker-controlled on-disk catalog thread record into a stack buffer and validates only the 2-byte type tag. It then passes the record's variable-length name (tmp.thread.nodeName, whose embedded __be16 length field has the full 0..65535 domain) into hfsplus_cat_build_key_uni, which sizes its copy of name data from that unchecked length into the fixed-size btree search key fd->search_key (name capacity 255 units). No bounds check, clamp, mask, or record-length validation exists on any path, so a crafted filesystem image with a thread record whose name length exceeds 255 causes an out-of-bounds write of attacker-controlled bytes past the key buffer (and an out-of-bounds read of the stack record), yielding kernel memory corruption.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the attacker-controlled on-disk thread record's name, tmp.thread.nodeName, including its embedded length field (full u16 domain, never validated), is passed into the key-building copy operation targeting the fixed-size fd->search_key. The only guard in the function (line 14) checks the 2-byte type tag and passes the trigger record; no check of nodeName.length or of the record size exists anywhere in the code, so a thread record with name length 0xFFFF drives an out-of-bounds write of attacker-chosen bytes past the key buffer.

Origin of the tainted data: the on-disk catalog record (raw attacker content from the mounted filesystem image) is copied into the stack buffer tmp here; all subsequent fields consumed (type, thread.parentID, thread.nodeName with its length) come from this attacker-controlled record, and the actual on-disk record length (fd->entrylength) is never compared against sizeof(struct hfsplus_cat_thread) anywhere in this code.

assumptions: hfsplus_cat_build_key_uni is a project-internal callee not shown here; its known fs/hfsplus semantics are to copy be16_to_cpu(str->length) * 2 bytes of name units into the fixed-size hfsplus_btree_key name field (capacity HFSPLUS_MAX_STRLEN = 255 units). Per discipline 3, the unchecked pass of the attacker length at the call site is the defect in this code regardless of the callee's internals.

hfs_brec_read copies on-disk record content into tmp and returns 0 on success; only the return sentinel is checked (lines 10-11), and the size argument sizeof(hfsplus_cat_entry) bounds the destination, not the content fields later consumed.
cnid and fd originate from kernel callers (lookup/renaming paths) and are treated as internal; the trust boundary is the mounted HFS+ disk image, whose catalog record bytes are attacker-authored.
limitations: The uninitialized-stack variant (on-disk record shorter than sizeof(struct hfsplus_cat_thread), leaving tmp.thread fields partially uninitialized after hfs_brec_read) depends on the callee's copy length behavior, which is not shown; it is recorded as a secondary concern (CWE-908) rather than a primary finding.

The concrete out-of-bounds write executes inside hfsplus_cat_build_key_uni (not shown); this analysis anchors the defect at the call site where the unvalidated attacker length is passed, per the callee-semantics discipline.
cnid was judged non-attacker-facing only because its uses (btree key field) cannot index or size memory; if a caller passed a hostile cnid it still could not trigger corruption via this function.

parse_errors: no valid JSON verdict found in output

verdict.summary: sungem_send_packet forwards the guest-derived packet length `size` (declared int, full signed domain since its producer is not shown) directly into two copy-bearing sinks — `nc->info->receive(nc, buf, size)` and `qemu_send_packet(nc, buf, size)` — with no non-negativity or extent check anywhere in the function. A negative size (e.g. -1) converts to a huge unsigned length in the packet-copy path, producing out-of-bounds read/write in the privileged host QEMU process from guest-controlled data.

evidence.snippet:
static void sungem_send_packet(SunGEMState *s, const uint8_t *buf,
                               int size)
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: `size` is an int parameter whose producer (the guest-controlled TX descriptor path) is not shown, so per the width-domain rule its surface is the full signed 32-bit domain, including negative values; this code documents no precondition narrowing it.

Unguarded sink (loopback arm): the attacker-derived `size` is passed unvalidated into a copy-bearing receive operation; with size = -1 it widens to a huge unsigned copy length, yielding out-of-bounds read of `buf` and OOB write in the host receive/copy path. Mention sweep over every mention of `size`/`buf` in this code found no check, clamp, mask, assert, or error arm in any guard form.

Unguarded sink (transmit arm): the same unvalidated attacker-derived `size` is passed into the packet-send path, which copies `size` bytes out of `buf` (allocation and copy both derived from size; a negative size under-allocates then copies a huge wrapped length), causing out-of-bounds read/write in the host QEMU process. The single missing guard is a non-negativity/extent check on `size` before these calls; it appears nowhere in the code.

assumptions: qemu_get_queue is assumed to return a valid NetClientState for a realized NIC; its return is not sentinel-checked in this code.

The producer of `buf` and `size` (the TX descriptor DMA path in the caller) is not shown, so per the width-domain rule `size` is treated as instantiable at any int value, including negative and oversized values.

The impact chain relies on the copy-bearing semantics of qemu_send_packet and receive handlers (they consume/copy `size` bytes from `buf`), characterized per callee semantics, not quoted from this code.
limitations: C2 (speculative, not counted): `nc = qemu_get_queue(s->nic)` is dereferenced at lines 7/9 without a NULL check; a NULL return would require the device to be unrealized (s->nic NULL), which no statement in this code can produce — recorded as a robustness note (CWE-476 pattern).

C3 (speculative, not counted): the loopback arm calls `nc->info->receive` without verifying the function pointer is set; this depends on the peer/backend configuration, which is not shown and not attacker-instantiable here.

In the upstream project, the caller masks the TX descriptor length field before calling this helper; that bound is not quotable in the given code and therefore cannot demote the finding here, but if present it would neutralize the trigger in the full program.

verdict.summary: In the UTF-8 parameter scan loop, uni_utf8_get_char_n is passed (size_t)(p - parser->end) as the remaining-length bound. Since the loop condition guarantees p < parser->end, this subtraction is always negative and the size_t cast wraps it to a huge value, so the length limit is never effective. An SMTP client ending its command with a multi-byte UTF-8 lead byte at the buffer end makes the callee read up to 3 bytes past parser->end (with a correct bound it would return 0 without reading), an out-of-bounds read reachable on every non-AUTH iteration. The correct bound parser->end - p is computed nowhere in the function.

evidence.reason: Reversed pointer subtraction: the callee's length parameter must be the bytes remaining (parser->end - p), but the code passes p - parser->end, which is negative because the loop guard 'while (p < parser->end)' holds here, and the (size_t) cast wraps it to SIZE_MAX-(end-p)+1. uni_utf8_get_char_n therefore reads up to 4 bytes from p with no bound; an attacker-supplied multi-byte UTF-8 lead byte at the last buffer position triggers a read past parser->end. No statement in the function computes, clamps, or checks end - p on any path.

Origin of the taint: p walks the attacker-supplied SMTP command/AUTH buffer that this parser consumes, and the loop guard p < parser->end is exactly the condition that makes the later (size_t)(p - parser->end) argument negative and thus wrapped.

assumptions: uni_utf8_get_char_n has standard semantics: decode one UTF-8 character reading at most min(4, len) bytes, returning bytes consumed, 0 if len truncates the sequence, -1 if invalid.

parser->cur/parser->end delimit the attacker-controlled network input; whether parser->end coincides with the allocation end is not shown, so the over-read's worst case (past the heap allocation) is inferred, while the read past the logical buffer end is proven from the code.
limitations: max_size == 0 (from parser->limits) disables the line-length check at line 35; limits are operator configuration, not attacker data, so this is a hardening note, not a vulnerability.
On the auth_response path nch keeps its stale value from a previous iteration, but it is only tested as nch == 0 at line 44 and never used as a length or offset, so no memory-safety effect.
Overlong UTF-8 encodings of control characters would bypass the textstr check for ch >= 0x80, but uni_utf8_get_char_n rejects overlong forms and this is at most a protocol-strictness issue.

verdict.summary: sftp_mkdir is a synchronous SFTP client wrapper with no local memory, size, or index arithmetic on attacker data. All callee sentinels are tested in execution order before first use: the wait loop 'while (msg == NULL)' guarantees msg is non-NULL before 'msg->packet_type' is read, 'if (status == NULL) { return -1; }' precedes every use of status fields, and 'if (errno_attr != NULL)' precedes SAFE_FREE(errno_attr). Buffer/string lifetimes are balanced on all return paths (no leak, UAF, or double free), and both ssh_set_error format strings are literals, so server data cannot act as a format string. The remaining observations — a NULL 'directory' from the caller and the unbounded wait loop a malicious SFTP server can stall — do not instantiate cross-boundary security impact (equal-privilege caller crash; blocking wait with work proportional to attacker input) and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: Internal callees not shown (ssh_string_from_char, buffer_add_u32, buffer_add_ssh_string, buffer_add_attributes, sftp_packet_write, sftp_read_and_dispatch, sftp_dequeue, parse_status_msg, sftp_lstat, sftp_get_new_id, status_msg_free, sftp_message_free, SAFE_FREE, ZERO_STRUCT) are assumed to follow their documented libssh semantics; per discipline 3 these assumptions could neither produce a trigger nor serve as guards.
sftp_dequeue returning NULL when no message with the matching id is queued is taken as the failure sentinel this code itself tests in 'while (msg == NULL)'.

parse_status_msg is assumed to return NULL on failure (checked at line 57) and to populate status->status and status->errormsg consistently; the internal consistency of those fields cannot be verified from the given code.
limitations: NULL or unterminated 'directory' would crash inside ssh_string_from_char (line 16): caller-misuse robustness issue only — the party supplying the value is the same process at equal privilege, with no corruption, disclosure, or bypass.

The 'while (msg == NULL)' loop (lines 43-48) has no timeout or iteration cap; a malicious SFTP server sending an endless stream of well-formed packets with non-matching ids can stall the client indefinitely and grow the internal queue. Work and retention are proportional to attacker input with no amplification, and the blocking wait is inherent to this synchronous client API — degradation without an instantiated security impact per discipline 4.
status->errormsg reaching ssh_set_error('%s') could be NULL only if the unshown parse_status_msg permits it; this cannot be instantiated from the given code, so it remains speculative.

verdict.summary: The code is a hardened MariaDB open_table routine. All memory, sentinel, and bounds uses on attacker-reachable paths are guarded by quoted statements of this code: the memcmp is bounded by an exact length-equality check in the same expression, the tdc_acquire_share and MDL-ticket results are NULL-checked, my_malloc and open_table_from_share results are checked before use, and all my_error calls use constant format strings. The one concrete anomaly — the uninitialized 'share' variable that err_lock: would release when reached from the locked-tables 'goto reset' path after a failing vcol_fix_expr — cannot be triggered without an unshown internal callee (vcol_fix_expr) failing, so it is recorded as a limitation, not a vulnerability.

assumptions: table_list->alias.str is assumed NUL-terminated by the SQL parser (producer not shown in this code) for its use in my_strcasecmp(system_charset_info, table->alias.c_ptr(), alias); no length-based sink consumes alias here.
get_table_def_key is assumed to return a key of exactly key_length bytes consistent with the memcmp bound; it is an internal same-subsystem callee.

In the MYSQL_OPEN_HAS_MDL_LOCK arm, table_list->mdl_request.ticket is assumed non-NULL per the contract this code documents in its own comment: 'Grab reference to the MDL lock ticket that was acquired by the caller.'
limitations: Speculative (not a vulnerability in this code): 'TABLE_SHARE *share;' is declared without an initializer, and the locked-tables path (best_table found, 'goto reset;') bypasses 'retry_share:' so that 'if (!from_share && table->vcol_fix_expr(thd)) goto err_lock;' with from_share == false can reach 'err_lock: tdc_release_share(share);' with share never assigned. The trigger requires the unshown internal callee vcol_fix_expr to fail (realistically OOM), which cannot be instantiated from attacker input, a standard sentinel, or any quoted statement of this code. A one-line fix (initialize share to NULL, or check it at err_lock) does not appear anywhere in the mention sweep.
DBUG_ASSERT statements are debug-build-only and were not treated as release-mode guards; no release-mode sink depends on them for memory safety.
The signed distance arithmetic in the locked-tables best_table selection was edge-tested (INT_MIN start, enum deltas) and shows no wrap or boundary defect affecting memory safety.

verdict.summary: pfkey_register consumes attacker-controlled sadb_msg_satype (u8, domain 0-255) but bounds it with a quoted first-statement range check (satype > SADB_SATYPE_MAX, i.e. > 8, returns -EINVAL) before all three bit-shift uses, capping the exponent at 8 (< 32, so 1<<8=256 is defined for the int base); the allocation-failure sentinel is checked with if (!supp_skb) before its only use, with symmetric rollback of the registration bit. No unguarded sink exists on any path.

assumptions: SADB_SATYPE_MAX = 8 per the kernel UAPI header (include/uapi/linux/pfkeyv2.h, RFC 2367); the constant is not defined in the given snippet, but the guard 'if (hdr->sadb_msg_satype > SADB_SATYPE_MAX)' is quoted and caps the shift exponent at 8, far below the 32-bit int shift limit, so safety holds even with margin.

struct pfkey_sock.registered is not shown; its width was assumed int (32 bits). The shift-safety conclusion does not depend on this: the shifted base is a literal int 1 and the exponent is at most 8, so 1<<8=256 is defined for any target width of the assignment.
hdr is assumed non-NULL as delivered by the PF_KEY dispatcher (kernel-internal caller); the dispatcher's parsing is not shown.

Internal callees compose_sadb_supported, pfkey_broadcast, and xfrm_probe_algs are not shown; only the bounded hdr pointer and the sentinel-checked supp_skb are passed to them, so no defect is attributed at these call sites.
limitations: If struct pfkey_sock.registered were narrower than 9 bits (not shown), 1<<8 would truncate on assignment, weakening the -EEXIST duplicate-registration test; this would be a functional bookkeeping issue with no memory-safety, authz, or disclosure consequence, and the real struct declares it as int.

A theoretical race on pfk->registered would require a second execution context; no lock release, callback, or re-entry point between the set and rollback exists in this code, so no window can be exhibited.
The shift exponent cannot exceed 8, so UBSAN-style shift-out-of-bounds is not reachable with the given check in place.

verdict.summary: squashfs_opendir consumes the return value of read_inode without any NULL check: line 16 assigns *i from a parse of attacker-controlled inode coordinates (block_start, offset), and the very first use, dir->mode = (*i)->mode; at line 24, dereferences it. A crafted squashfs image whose inode reference makes read_inode miss (returning its NULL failure sentinel, always in-domain for a parse/lookup) crashes the operator's unsquashfs process, a trust-boundary denial of service. No statement on any path checks *i; the only nearby check (if(dir == NULL) MEM_ERROR();) tests the malloc result, not *i. The stack buffer handling is otherwise provably in bounds: the quoted guard dire->size >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN caps the name read at 256 bytes and the terminator index at 256 within the 257-byte name region.

evidence.reason: Origin of the defect: read_inode is a project-internal parse of attacker-controlled coordinates (block_start, offset from the filesystem image). A parse/lookup can miss and return its failure sentinel NULL, which is always in-domain; the result is assigned to *i with no sentinel check.

Sink: first dereference of *i with no NULL check on any path. Mention sweep of *i (lines 16, 24-28, 31, 40-42) contains no NULL test; the malloc check at lines 19-20 tests dir, not *i. Trigger: crafted image makes read_inode miss -> *i = NULL -> NULL pointer dereference here, crashing the process parsing the attacker-supplied filesystem (DoS, CWE-476).

assumptions: read_directory_data is assumed to perform its own table bounds checking and return FALSE when data is exhausted; its FALSE result is checked at every call site (lines 46, 64, 79), so no local defect is provable.

Struct field widths (dire->size, dirh.count) and the constants SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN (256) and SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT are taken from their definitions outside the given snippet; the quoted guards hold for the standard squashfs definitions.
MEM_ERROR is assumed to terminate the process on allocation failure.
limitations: size = (*i)->data + bytes - 3 (line 42): unsigned-to-int conversion is implementation-defined for (*i)->data >= 0x80000004; on mainstream platforms it yields a negative size and the loop is skipped; no memory corruption is reachable.
bytes (int) can overflow only after ~2 GB of actual directory-table data, which is proportional to attacker input size and produces no out-of-bounds access; not treated as a vulnerability.

If dirh.count is a 32-bit field, values like 0x80000000 produce a negative dir_count that bypasses the signed > SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT check, but while(dir_count--) is bounded by read_directory_data returning FALSE and dir_count never indexes memory; no memory-safety effect.
ent->name = strdup(dire->name) (line 98) is unchecked; a NULL return would only matter to consumers not shown here (robustness at most).

The internal bounds enforcement of read_directory_data itself is not shown; passing attacker-derived start/offset into it is not a provable local defect because its failure sentinel is checked at every call site.

verdict.summary: This static helper only reads a register at a compile-time-constant index and forwards (buf, size) to QEMU's standard net API. Although size (guest-derived, full int domain) and buf reach the copy sinks with no local validation, the harmful state (size exceeding buf's extent) is produced by no statement in this code and cannot be instantiated from it, so no triggerable defect exists within the given snippet.

assumptions: macregs is declared to cover the MAC register block containing MAC_XIFCFG, so the constant index MAC_XIFCFG >> 2 is in range (array declaration not shown).
qemu_get_queue(s->nic) returns a valid NetClientState for a realized device; it has no documented failure sentinel, and this function is unreachable before realize.
qemu_send_packet/qemu_receive_packet have standard QEMU net semantics: deliver/copy exactly size bytes from buf.
limitations: C1 (speculative): size is passed to qemu_receive_packet/qemu_send_packet with no validation in this function (its only mentions are the declaration at line 2 and the call arguments at lines 7 and 9). If the unshown TX-descriptor path ever passed size exceeding buf's allocation (or negative), this call site would drive an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) inside the net layer. The size/buf coherence contract lives entirely in code not given, so the mismatch precondition cannot be instantiated here; recorded as a limitation rather than a finding.
nc is not NULL-checked before use at lines 7 and 9; a NULL from qemu_get_queue is not a documented failure sentinel and is not attacker-instantiable.

verdict.summary: In the ASCII mesh reading branch, GmfOpenMesh scans the attacker-controlled mesh file with `fscanf(msh->hdl, "%s", str)` into the fixed-size stack buffer `char str[GmfStrSiz]` without any field-width limit (two occurrences, lines 127 and 140). Any token longer than GmfStrSiz-1 bytes in a crafted .mesh/.sol file overflows the stack buffer and corrupts adjacent stack memory in the process that parses the file. No check, width, clamp, or bounded read primitive exists anywhere in the code, in contrast to the bounded `strcpy` guarded by `if(strlen(FilNam) + 7 >= GmfStrSiz)`.

evidence.reason: Unbounded `%s` conversion copies attacker-controlled file tokens into the fixed stack array `char str[ GmfStrSiz ]` (declared line 5). Trigger: attacker supplies a .mesh file whose first token (or any token before MeshVersionFormatted) exceeds GmfStrSiz-1 bytes; fscanf writes past the buffer, corrupting the stack of the parsing process. The mention sweep (lines 5, 127, 128, 130, 140, 141, 143) contains no width, length check, clamp, or bounded-read alternative guarding this copy.

Second occurrence of the same defect in the Dimension scan loop: even a file with a valid header triggers the overflow if any token before the keyword `Dimension` is longer than GmfStrSiz-1 bytes. Same missing guard: the format string `%s` carries no maximum field width and no other statement bounds the copy.

assumptions: GmfStrSiz is a compile-time constant positive size (known from libMeshb as 1024); its exact value does not affect the overflow, only the token length required to trigger it.

Internal helpers ScaWrd, GetPos, ScaKwdTab, safe_fread and safe_fscanf are not shown; they receive `msh->err` and are assumed to longjmp on I/O failure. All values they produce in this code are locally range-checked before use (ver, dim, cod, KwdCod), so no unguarded use of their returns exists here.
OPEN_READ_FLAGS/OPEN_WRITE_FLAGS, OPEN_READ_MODE and the GmfRead/GmfWrite constants are assumed to have their conventional semantics; they do not participate in the primary defect.
limitations: `(*PtrVer) = msh->ver; (*PtrDim) = msh->dim;` dereference caller-supplied varargs pointers with no NULL check, but only the calling application (same trust side) can pass NULL; the file originator cannot instantiate this trigger, so it is a robustness/contract issue, not a vulnerability of this code against the modeled attacker.
`if(!ScaKwdTab(msh)) return(0);` leaks the calloc'd `msh` structure (no free on that path); a bounded one-time leak per failed open, not attacker-scalable amplification.
`strlen(FilNam) + 7` could wrap size_t only for a string of roughly SIZE_MAX length, which cannot be instantiated; the guard at line 39 correctly bounds the strcpy at line 42 for all real inputs.

fscanf returning 0 (matching failure) would leave `str` holding a stale token, but with `%s` this occurs only under EOF conditions already handled by the `res == EOF` checks; no security impact identified.

verdict.summary: ZipFile::uncompressEntry extracts archive entries without confining entry paths to the target directory: the archive-controlled filename (zei->entry.filename) is passed unsanitized to targetDirectory.getChildFile(), which resolves '..' components and absolute paths, so a crafted entry name like '../../...' or an absolute path makes the FileOutputStream at lines 46/51 write decompressed attacker content to an arbitrary filesystem location (zip-slip, arbitrary file write). Independently, the exported method's int index parameter is consumed by entries.getUnchecked() with no bounds check anywhere in the function, producing an out-of-bounds pointer read that is immediately dereferenced. A third sink of the same traversal root cause writes a symlink whose fully attacker-controlled target is read raw from the entry stream.

evidence.reason: entryPath is the archive-controlled entry filename (lines 6/8) with no rejection of '..' or absolute-path components anywhere in the function (the only checks are isEmpty at line 11 and trailing-separator at line 16); getChildFile resolves '..' upward and passes absolute paths through, so targetFile can point outside targetDirectory and the payload written at lines 46-51 (or the deleteFile at line 29) reaches an arbitrary path. Trigger instantiated: entry filename '../../../../etc/cron.d/pwn' -> line 51 writes attacker content to /etc/cron.d/pwn.

index is a parameter of this exported method with the full int domain and no documented or checked precondition in this code; getUnchecked performs no bounds validation, and no range check, jlimit, isPositiveAndBelow, or checking accessor appears anywhere in the function (all mentions of index: lines 1, 3, 19). Any out-of-range index (e.g. 100000 or -1) makes line 3 read an out-of-bounds element pointer which is immediately dereferenced at line 6/8 via zei->entry.filename — out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

originalFilePath is read raw from the entry stream (line 38) and can be an absolute or escaping path; the only test on this line is the call's success sentinel, not a confinement guard. Trigger instantiated with statements of this code: entry 1 creates symlink targetDirectory/'d' -> '/etc'; entry 2 named 'd/cron.d/pwn' then resolves through the attacker-created link at lines 46/51 and writes outside the target directory — arbitrary file overwrite through an attacker-directed symlink.

assumptions: Reliance on documented JUCE semantics per discipline 3: File::getChildFile resolves '..' components against the parent directory and returns absolute paths unchanged, and Array::getUnchecked is the no-bounds-check accessor (the checking accessor is Array::get). Both are documented behaviors of the well-known JUCE library this code belongs to.
createStreamForEntry (line 19) is an internal callee not shown; its NULL return is sentinel-checked at line 21, so no unchecked consumption of its return occurs in this code.
limitations: The deleteFile()-through-symlink overwrite chain (lines 24-30) depends on OS-specific symlink deletion semantics (POSIX remove() deletes the link, not its target); it is therefore not relied upon — the primary arbitrary-write chain (direct '../' filename at lines 14/46/51) is fully instantiated without it.
The trailing-backslash test at line 16 is redundant on non-Windows because backslashes were already replaced at line 8; this is a functional redundancy, not a security defect.
zei->entry.fileTime is archive-controlled but only consumed by file time setters; no security impact identified.

Practical exploitability of CWE-125 depends on how callers of this exported API choose index; per the width-domain rule the missing bounds check at the use site is recorded as the defect regardless of unshown callers.

verdict.summary: The bookmark function composes a shell command line from feed-supplied (attacker-controlled) URL, title, description, and feed_title, but neutralizes shell injection by replacing every single-quote byte with %27 via utils::replace_all before insertion, and then wrapping each value in single quotes within the format string. In POSIX shell semantics, no character other than a single quote can terminate a single-quoted region, so the escaped values cannot break out of quoting; all simulated boundary inputs (quote runs, backticks, dollar signs, newlines, NUL bytes) fail to inject. The user-configured bookmark-cmd is trusted local configuration. No exploitable guard absence was found.

assumptions: utils::replace_all(x, "'", "%27") replaces all occurrences of the single-quote byte in x, per its name and call pattern; the implementation is not shown in the given code.

strprintf::fmt performs standard printf-style or boost::format-style substitution where substituted argument values are not re-parsed as format specifiers; the format string here is a literal constant.
cfg.get_configvalue and cfg.get_configvalue_as_bool read local user configuration only; feed content cannot influence bookmark-cmd or bookmark-interactive.
utils::run_program(my_argv, "") and utils::run_interactively consume the already-escaped cmdline; their internal implementations are not shown but receive the same guarded string.
limitations: Log injection (CWE-117): feed-supplied values can contain newlines or control characters that reach the DEBUG log at the LOG statement; the log consumer's parsing behavior is not shown, so no security impact is instantiated.

Data integrity: replacing ' with %27 means the bookmarking command receives %27 instead of a literal single quote; if the receiving command does not URL-decode, bookmarked data is altered, but this is a functional issue, not a security vulnerability.

If a user misconfigures bookmark-cmd with an unbalanced single quote, subsequent parameters would lose their quoting and shell metacharacters in feed data could be interpreted; this requires a user configuration error and is not attacker-triggerable from feed data alone.

The interactive path (push_empty_formaction / run_interactively / pop_current_formaction) lacks exception safety; if run_interactively throws, the form-action stack is left inconsistent. This is a robustness issue with no security impact demonstrated.

verdict.summary: r_core_anal_esil stores the address of the stack-local EsilBreakCtx into the session-persistent ESIL VM (ESIL->user = &ctx) and installs three ESIL hook callbacks, then takes an early error return (missing PC register name) without clearing any of them. After the return, core->anal->esil retains a dangling stack pointer and armed hooks; the next ESIL evaluation in the session dereferences the dead frame via the hooks (the code itself comments that the hook reads the analop id through ESIL->user), producing a stack-use-after-return / memory corruption condition triggered by the analyzed session state. The normal exit path clears these pointers, proving the missing cleanup on the error path is the defect.

evidence.reason: Early error return taken after ESIL->user and the hook callbacks were already armed (lines 107-111) and before any cleanup. The return strands ESIL->user pointing at the dead stack frame 'ctx' and leaves esilbreak_reg_write/mem_read/mem_write installed on the persistent core->anal->esil. The only cleanup statements (ESIL->user = NULL and hook = NULL at function end) are unreachable from this path. Trigger: r_reg_get_name returning NULL or an empty PC alias — a failure sentinel of the same lookup this code tests for at the spname check — after which any subsequent ESIL execution dereferences the dangling pointer per the in-code comment 'this is necessary for the hook to read the id of analop'.

Origin of the dangling value: the address of the stack-local EsilBreakCtx ctx (declared at line 101) is stored into the longer-lived ESIL VM object. Combined with the hook assignments at lines 107, 110 and 111, the persistent object references a frame that dies at the early return on line 121, escaping the function's lifetime with no reset on that path.

assumptions: MAX_SCAN_SIZE is a compile-time constant bounding iend; the checks 'if (iend < 0)' and 'if (iend > MAX_SCAN_SIZE)' are quoted and keep the malloc/read sizing internally consistent, but the constant's value is not shown.

Internal callees not shown (get_next_i, esilbreak_* hooks, r_anal_op plugin behavior, is_string_at, getpcfromstack, add_string_ref) are assumed to honor their parameter contracts; the analysis relies only on the in-code comment at line 108 documenting that the hooks read ESIL->user.
r_anal_op is assumed to respect the len parameter (iend - i), which is >= 0 under the quoted guard at line 208; even a one-byte overread at i == iend stays inside the iend+2 allocation.
limitations: buf is leaked on the early returns at lines 91, 99 and 121 (CWE-401, low impact in a CLI session).

If a function exists at start+i_old+1 while no basic block is created at cur, the repeat block can reset i to the same value each iteration, producing a user-interruptible infinite loop (DoS only; ^C is honored at the loop top).

The scan loop 'for (fcn_i = i_old + 1; fcn_i <= i; fcn_i++)' can iterate up to op.size-1 times if r_anal_op reports a huge instruction size; a large op.size producer could not be exhibited from the given code.
The return of r_io_read_at is not checked, so buf could be partially uninitialized on read failure; however parsing is gated by r_io_is_valid_offset(cur) each iteration, limiting exposure.
A NULL 'str' would crash strcmp at line 24, but that rests on an unquoted caller contract of the command dispatcher (robustness only).

verdict.summary: The only attacker-influenced input, the table name string, is passed unvalidated to the file-deletion callee maria_delete_table_files, but the harmful use (path construction and unlink) occurs entirely inside that not-shown internal callee, so no impact chain is instantiated within this code; the remaining issues (ignored ha_close/maria_delete_table_files return values, possible NULL 'file' dereference guarded only by a debug assert, and the assert being compiled out in release) are robustness concerns whose triggers depend on unshown engine/server state.

assumptions: `name` is expected to be the server-normalized, filename-encoded table path (unquoted caller contract; the server-side encoding code is not shown).

`maria_delete_table_files(name, 1, MY_WME)` is assumed to be the engine's standard table-file cleanup routine that consumes server-built names; its path construction and traversal handling are not shown.
`ha_close()` is assumed not to invalidate state used afterwards in this function (only `name` is used after the call, and it is untouched by ha_close).
`file` is set by the engine's open path (not shown) and is expected non-NULL whenever the server invokes drop_table on an open temporary table.
limitations: Path traversal via `name` (CWE-22 shape) cannot be confirmed or excluded from this snippet: line 5 passes the raw attacker-influenced string to maria_delete_table_files with no local validation (mention sweep: `name` appears only at lines 1 and 5), but proving deletion outside the data directory requires the unshown callee to use the string as a raw path; if that callee lacks canonicalization, the defect would live there.

Possible NULL dereference of `file`/`file->s` at line 3 if drop_table is ever invoked on a handler whose open failed; not instantiable from the shown code, and DBUG_ASSERT is compiled out in release builds.

`(void) ha_close();` at line 4 discards the close result, so file deletion proceeds even when close fails (per-session temporary table data loss / orphaned files); `(void) maria_delete_table_files(...)` at line 5 likewise swallows deletion failures — robustness, no demonstrated cross-boundary security impact.

verdict.summary: gem_transmit reads a TX descriptor into the fixed-size stack array desc[DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS] using a guest-controlled byte length, sizeof(uint32_t) * gem_get_desc_len(s, false), with no check anywhere in the code that the descriptor word count fits the array; a guest programming GEM_DMACFG so the helper returns more than DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS causes address_space_read to write guest-supplied DMA data past the stack buffer, corrupting the host QEMU process.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds stack write: the read length is the guest-influenceable descriptor word count from the unshown helper gem_get_desc_len (driven by the guest-writable GEM_DMACFG register), but the destination desc is the fixed stack array declared as uint32_t desc[DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS]; no statement in this code compares or clamps the length against DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS or sizeof(desc), so any helper return above DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS copies guest-controlled DMA memory past the array (trigger: guest enables TXENA and sets the descriptor-length mode, reaching this read on the first queue iteration).

Second instantiation of the same unbounded read: the same unvalidated length is used at the end of the descriptor loop to refill the fixed-size stack array desc, with the same missing bounds check on gem_get_desc_len(s, false).

Origin of the overflowed object: the destination is a fixed-size stack buffer of DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS words, while every write into it uses the unvalidated length sizeof(uint32_t) * gem_get_desc_len(s, false).

assumptions: gem_get_desc_len derives from the guest-writable GEM_DMACFG register and its return is consumed without any local sentinel or bounds check; per the width-domain rule its full declared-type domain is instantiable since no quoted statement of this code narrows it.
s->num_priority_queues is treated as operator-set device configuration, not guest-attacker data, for the s->tx_desc_addr[q] indexing.
address_space_read copies exactly the requested length from guest memory (standard QEMU semantics), so the overflowing bytes are guest-chosen.
limitations: The TX fragment gather at lines 63-65 is guarded by 'if (tx_desc_get_length(desc) > gem_get_max_buf_len(s, true) - (p - s->tx_packet))' which is arithmetically sound against its quoted bound, but both the bound (unshown helper reading a guest register) and the allocation size of s->tx_packet are outside this code, so whether the guard keeps the write inside the real buffer cannot be proven or disproven here; recorded rather than confirmed.
The write-back at lines 81-83 uses fixed sizeof(desc_first) which may exceed the descriptor's actual size, but the excess lands only in guest RAM, with no host-side security impact.
s->tx_desc_addr[q] indexing trusts s->num_priority_queues without a local range check; this is operator configuration, not attacker data, so no trigger is instantiated.

verdict.summary: ha_maria::drop_table closes the handler and delegates table-file deletion to the internal helper maria_delete_table_files with the caller-supplied table name. Although `name` is attacker-data at an overridden-virtual handler entry point and no NULL, length, or traversal validation of it exists anywhere in this code (its only mentions are the parameter declaration and the call), no memory, copy, indexing, format, or command operation in this code consumes it unguarded. The only conceivable impact paths (path-traversal file deletion or a NULL dereference) execute entirely inside the unshown, non-standard internal callee, whose behavior is neither quoted nor characterizable; the impact chain therefore cannot be instantiated from the given code, and no primary vulnerability is confirmed.

assumptions: ha_close() and maria_delete_table_files() are project-internal callees not shown; their semantics (closing the handler's open file; deleting the named table's files; reporting errors through the MY_WME mysys flag) are assumed and were relied on neither to confirm nor to dismiss any candidate.
DBUG_ASSERT is assumed to compile to a no-op in release builds (standard MariaDB debug macro), making line 3 without effect in production.
The SQL server layer is the unshown producer of `name`; its identifier canonicalization cannot be quoted and was not treated as a guard or as a trigger-blocking fact.
`file` and `file->s` are set by unshown open/creation paths; no quotable contract in this code constrains `file->s` to non-NULL.

MY_WME is taken to be the project's mysys error-reporting flag (my_error on failure), which is why the discarded int returns are the established reporting pattern rather than silent failure; this reading is itself an assumption about unshown code.
limitations: C1 (speculative, not counted toward the verdict): `maria_delete_table_files(name, 1, MY_WME)` receives the raw, unvalidated `name`. A traversal-bearing or NULL value is within the declared domain of a `const char *` parameter of this overridden virtual handler method, and the mention sweep proves no guard of any form exists in this code. Impact (arbitrary file deletion outside the data directory, or a NULL-dereference crash of the higher-privileged server process) would occur inside maria_delete_table_files, whose path-construction and validation behavior is neither quoted nor characterizable; the unshown SQL layer is additionally the name's producer. Trigger precondition instantiable, impact link not instantiable from the given code.

C2 (speculative): `file->s->temporary` (line 3) dereferences `file->s` with no non-NULL contract; reachable only when `file != NULL` and crashes only a debug build via DBUG_ASSERT. No corruption, disclosure, bypass, or amplification; release builds are unaffected. Robustness only.

C3: the return values of ha_close() and maria_delete_table_files() are discarded via (void) with no sentinel test. No statement in this code consumes the status or presents a security state, and error reporting is delegated through the MY_WME flag inside the callees, so no fail-open output is produced by any shown statement; a hypothetical misuse of the dropped status would live in unshown code.
C4: the DBUG_ASSERT at line 3 can abort a debug server on an internal-state invariant violation; classified as robustness, not security.

verdict.summary: All attacker-controlled file fields flow into sinks guarded by quoted statements: fixed-size sizeof-based ReadBlob calls into a pre-zeroed struct, an exact header/magic check, user_length bounded against GetBlobSize with the profile allocation sized from the same expression as the copy length, columns*rows bounded against blob size before SetImageExtent (whose failure is checked), and exact count checks on both the row stream and QueueAuthenticPixels. The pixel-row read length derived from unvalidated depth (0..255) and columns is never locally compared to the quantum buffer size, but the buffer is allocated inside the unshown AcquireQuantumInfo from the same depth/columns inputs, so no trigger for a buffer smaller than the read length can be instantiated from this code; the same applies to the unchecked user-profile read count and unchecked SetQuantumPad status, whose impacts also depend entirely on unshown internal callee behavior.

assumptions: AcquireQuantumInfo/GetQuantumPixels size the quantum pixel buffer from image->columns, image->rows and image->depth (the same attacker inputs that feed GetBytesPerRow); the actual formula is not shown in this code, so buffer >= length is neither provable nor disprovable here.
GetBytesPerRow, SetQuantumQuantum, SetQuantumPack, SetQuantumPad and ImportQuantumPixels are project-internal callees not shown; their semantics are treated as unknown.

BlobToStringInfo (via AcquireStringInfo) is assumed to zero the freshly allocated datum when the source blob is NULL; if it does not, a short profile read (user_length == GetBlobSize with a nonzero current offset, concretely reachable) would expose uninitialized heap bytes through the stored 'dpx:user.data' profile.
limitations: Heap OOB write candidate at ReadBlobStream(image,length,pixels,&count): no statement in this code validates image->depth (0..255) or image->columns, and none compares length to the allocated pixels buffer; however the trigger requires the unshown AcquireQuantumInfo allocation formula to produce a buffer smaller than GetBytesPerRow(columns,channels,depth), which no given statement exhibits (both use the same depth/columns inputs). Precondition not instantiable: 'pixels buffer size < length'.

Unchecked return of the user-data ReadBlob and of SetQuantumPad (status assigned, never tested): the harmful consequences (uninitialized profile bytes, NULL/stale pixels buffer) each depend on unshown internal callee behavior (allocation/re-allocation on OOM of an already-succeeded size); not attacker-instantiable as written.

If a future change decoupled the quantum buffer sizing from image->depth (e.g., fixed 32-bit quantum with depth up to 255), the pixel loop would become an exploitable heap overflow; a depth clamp or explicit length-vs-extent check would be the minimal guard.
