verdict.summary: On the mlx5_vector2eqn() failure path, mlx5_fpga_conn_create_cq jumps to err_cqwq without freeing the buffer allocated by kvzalloc(); the only kvfree(in) in the function is executed after mlx5_core_create_cq and is bypassed, so each failed attempt permanently leaks the create_cq_in command buffer (CWE-401).

evidence.reason: This error branch jumps to err_cqwq without freeing 'in', which was allocated earlier; the sole kvfree(in) sits after mlx5_core_create_cq and is bypassed by this goto, so the kernel allocation is leaked whenever mlx5_vector2eqn fails. The trigger (a nonzero return of the fallible vector lookup, which this code itself tests for) is fully instantiated, and no release of 'in' exists on this path.
Origin of the leaked allocation: the create_cq_in command buffer whose only release (kvfree at the line following mlx5_core_create_cq) is unreachable from the mlx5_vector2eqn error branch.

assumptions: MLX5_SET/MLX5_SET64 store field values according to the field widths declared in mlx5_ifc.h (macros not shown in the given code).
mlx5_cqwq_create sizes the work queue consistently with the log_cq_size value placed in temp_cqc, so the CQE initialization loop stays in bounds.
fdev->conn_res.uar and conn->cq.wq_ctrl.db are initialized by the driver before this function runs (not shown); a NULL uar would be a NULL dereference only, not memory corruption.
The caller passes a positive, in-range cq_size; this cannot be verified from the given code but does not affect the primary finding.
limitations: cq_size is never validated against 0, negative values, or values above 2^30: roundup_pow_of_two(cq_size) is undefined for cq_size == 0 (shift by 64) and overflows int for cq_size above 2^30, and ilog2(cq_size) can then produce an out-of-range log_cq_size. Within the shown code this causes at most an oversized WQ request that fails inside the unshown mlx5_cqwq_create; no memory corruption is instantiated in the given code, so it is recorded as undefined-behavior robustness rather than a primary vulnerability.

The mlx5_vector2eqn failure that triggers the leak depends on EQ provisioning (e.g., CPU id exceeding the device's EQ table) rather than attacker-supplied input, so the leak's scalability as a denial of service is environment-dependent; the leak itself is concretely present in the given code.
The uninitialized 'out' array is only consumed by mlx5_core_create_cq, which fills it before cqn is printed; no unvalidated read of 'out' is reachable in the shown code.

verdict.summary: All attacker-controlled values (wIndex, wValue, wLength, bRequest, bRequestType from the USB host) reaching memory sinks are provably bounded by quoted guards executed before each sink: wLength is clamped to USB_COMP_EP0_BUFSIZ at entry (and to USB_COMP_EP0_OS_DESC_BUFSIZ on the OS-descriptor path before memset), every copy length is min()'d against w_length or a descriptor sizeof, and every interface index is masked and checked with 'intf >= MAX_CONFIG_INTERFACES' before use. The one unguarded pointer use, 'config->descriptors[0]' in the USB_DT_OTG case guarded only by the provably dead 'if (!config)' after list_first_entry, requires an empty configurations list or a NULL descriptors[0] — a gadget-construction state no statement of this code and no attacker input can instantiate; it is recorded as a limitation, not a vulnerability.

assumptions: cdev->req->buf and cdev->os_desc_req->buf are allocated (at bind time, not shown) with sizes USB_COMP_EP0_BUFSIZ and USB_COMP_EP0_OS_DESC_BUFSIZ respectively; the quoted clamps are sized against those constants.

Unshown same-file helpers (count_configs, device_qual, config_desc, get_string, bos_desc, set_config, count_ext_compat/fill_ext_compat/count_ext_prop/fill_ext_prop/len_ext_prop) write within the ep0/OS-desc buffers when given the bounded arguments this code passes; this code passes only in-domain arguments (clamped w_length, checked interface indices).

Function-driver callbacks (set_alt, get_alt, setup, get_status, func_suspend, req_match) honor USB-spec argument shapes for the raw w_index/w_value passed to them; f itself is always selected through the quoted interface-index guards.
get_gadget_data(gadget) returns a bound composite_dev; composite_setup is only invoked by the UDC after binding.
limitations: USB_DT_OTG case: 'config = list_first_entry(&cdev->configs, struct usb_configuration, list); if (!config) goto done;' — the !config guard is dead (list_first_entry never returns NULL), and 'config->descriptors[0]' is dereferenced with no NULL check in any form on any path. A wild-pointer dereference/memcpy read would occur if cdev->configs were empty or descriptors[0] were NULL when the host sends GET_DESCRIPTOR(OTG). No statement in this code can produce that state, it is not reachable from any attacker input value, and it is not a sentinel of any call made here, so the trigger is speculative in this code (gadget-driver construction would need to bind zero configurations).

OS-descriptor ext-compat path: 'value = fill_ext_compat(os_desc_cfg, buf); value = min_t(u16, w_length, value);' lacks the 'value >= 0' test present in the mirrored ext-prop arm ('if (value >= 0) value = min_t(u16, w_length, value);'); a negative return would select w_length as the response length, but the buffer was zeroed by the quoted 'memset(buf, 0, w_length)' and w_length is clamped to the OS-desc buffer size, so the effect is a zero-filled response, not memory corruption.
OTG GET_STATUS path sets 'value = 1' without regard to w_length (w_length may be 0), queuing a 1-byte response to a 0-length request; write is in-bounds, impact is a USB protocol anomaly only.

'cdev->delayed_status++;' is unbounded, but each increment requires one host control transfer with a function callback returning USB_GADGET_DELAYED_STATUS (unshown callee contract) — amplification is ~1:1, no attacker-scalable retention.
NULL cdev->req / cdev->os_desc_req on first use is possible only through bind-time allocation failure, which no attacker can induce.

verdict.summary: LZWDecodeCompat executes the interrupted-decode restart path without requiring occ0 > 0. The only validation of occ0 is the long-fit round-trip check `if ((tmsize_t) occ != occ0)`, which admits occ0 == 0 and all negative values, and the main loop's `while (occ > 0)` guard runs only after the restart block. When a previous call left dec_restart/dec_codep set (an attacker-crafted LZW string longer than the output buffer), a subsequent call with occ0 <= 0 makes `tp = op + occ` point at or below the buffer start and the do/while copy `*--tp = codep->value; ... while (--occ);` write out of bounds below op0 (occ == 0 writes op0[-1] and continues with negative occ; negative occ0 also drives the chain walk `while (--residue > occ)` past the chain end into a NULL dereference), giving an attacker-controlled heap out-of-bounds write followed by a crash.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write sink. With dec_restart set by a prior call (attacker-crafted overlong LZW string) and occ0 == 0, occ = 0 passes the only check (line 19), residue > occ selects this arm, tp = op, and the first iteration writes *--tp at op0[-1]; `--occ` then yields -1 so the loop keeps writing downward with attacker-chosen codep->value bytes until the chain ends in a NULL dereference. Negative occ0 similarly drives `while (--residue > occ)` past the chain terminus. No statement in the code requires occ > 0 before this sink; the `while (occ > 0)` guard at line 73 executes only after the restart block returns.

Origin of the defect: this is the only validation of the attacker-reachable handler parameter occ0, and it is a long-fit round-trip check only. Edge-tested at the trigger values: occ0 == 0 gives (tmsize_t)0 == 0 (passes), occ0 = -16 is sign-preserved on both 32- and 64-bit long (passes). The missing guard is an `occ0 <= 0` rejection before the dec_restart block; it appears nowhere in the code.

assumptions: NextCode/GetNextCodeCompat (not shown) mask the fetched code to nbitsmask bits and CSIZE == (1 << BITS_MAX); nbits is clamped to BITS_MAX by `if (++nbits > BITS_MAX) nbits = BITS_MAX;`, so `codep = sp->dec_codetab + code;` (line 100) is assumed to stay in-table. This is an unquoted contract, not a guard in this code.

Literal code-table entries (slots below CODE_FIRST) are initialized by not-shown setup code with length 1 and next == NULL; the chain invariant (chain node count == stored length) is maintained by the quoted insertions `free_entp->next = oldcodep;` and `free_entp->length = free_entp->next->length+1;` plus the range checks on lines 105-118. The chain walks at lines 38-40 and 150-152 have no NULL checks and rely on this invariant.
tif_rawcp/tif_rawcc consistency after `tif->tif_rawcc -= (tmsize_t)((uint8*)bp - tif->tif_rawcp);` depends on EOS handling inside the not-shown NextCode macro.
sp->dec_codep and sp->dec_restart are set only in the paired quoted statements at lines 149 and 153, so dec_restart != 0 implies dec_codep points at a table entry with length > dec_restart.
limitations: Chain-walk NULL-dereference candidates (lines 38-40, 150-152) were not confirmed: under the table invariant quoted above the walks terminate inside the chain; a trigger would require breaking the invariant, which the shown range-checked insertions prevent.
`assert(sp != NULL);` compiles out under NDEBUG and sp comes from internal codec state, not directly from attacker data; recorded as robustness, not a vulnerability.
A potential tif_rawcc underflow at line 174 depends on the not-shown NextCode EOS path and could not be instantiated from the given code.

Realistic reachability of occ0 == 0 depends on the not-shown TIFF read machinery computing a zero decode request; per the width-domain rule the handler parameter's full signed domain is instantiable, which is why this candidate stands despite the unshown caller.

verdict.summary: uncompressEntry validates the entry path only lexically (isAChildOf) and checks only PARENT directories for symlinks; it never inspects targetFile's final component before opening it for writing, and it creates symlinks whose targets are unrestricted attacker-controlled strings. An attacker zip containing a symlink entry that points to a not-yet-existing absolute path, followed by a same-named regular-file entry, writes attacker-controlled content to an arbitrary filesystem location even in the safe FollowSymlinks::no mode (arbitrary file write). Additionally, the exported method's int index parameter is passed unchecked to entries.getUnchecked, giving an out-of-bounds read for any out-of-range index.

evidence.reason: Sink: targetFile is opened for writing with no check that its final component is not a symbolic link. A prior zip entry plants a dangling symlink at targetFile via line 47 pointing to an arbitrary absolute path; File::exists() (line 27) follows links so a dangling link returns false and both overwrite branches are skipped; open() follows the link and out << *in (line 57) writes attacker-controlled zip content to the arbitrary location, even when followSymlinks == FollowSymlinks::no. Trigger: symlink entry 'foo' -> '/etc/evil.conf' followed by file entry 'foo'.

The only symlink guard checks the PARENT directory (targetFile.getParentDirectory()), never targetFile itself, so an attacker-created symlink as the final path component is never resolved before the FileOutputStream open at line 52; the check is also bypassed entirely when followSymlinks == FollowSymlinks::yes.

Origin of the taint chain: originalFilePath is the raw attacker-controlled zip entry content (read at line 44) with no validation that it stays inside targetDirectory, so this plants a symlink pointing to any absolute filesystem path, enabling the write-through at line 52 for a later entry with the same name.

Unchecked use of attacker-data: the exported method's int parameter index is never bounds-checked against entries.size() anywhere in this code (mention sweep: index appears only at lines 1, 3, 22); getUnchecked performs no bounds validation, so any out-of-range int (negative or >= entry count) yields an out-of-bounds array read that is immediately dereferenced at zei->entry.filename (lines 6/8).

assumptions: File::exists() and FileOutputStream/open resolve symlinks per POSIX stat(2)/open(2) semantics (existence follows links; creation with O_CREAT through a symlink creates the target); a dangling link therefore reports exists() == false.
JUCE Array::getUnchecked performs no bounds check (name-documented accessor semantics).
hasSymbolicPart internals are not shown; the primary trigger is constructed so it does not depend on them (the final path component is never passed to it on any input).
createStreamForEntry is not shown; the index defect is already established at line 3 before it.
limitations: TOCTOU between the lexical isAChildOf/hasSymbolicPart checks and the writes (a local attacker racing the filesystem) is not instantiated as two ordered in-code operations reachable by another context; treated as speculative.

The overwrite=yes variant against an existing target file depends on deleteFile removing the link itself (POSIX remove()) rather than its target; the dangling-symlink variant sidesteps this, so the primary trigger does not rely on that behavior.
zei->entry.fileTime flows only to setCreationTime/setLastModificationTime/setLastAccessTime; no security effect identified.
followSymlinks == FollowSymlinks::yes disabling the parent-symlink check is caller opt-in; the defect proven here is that the safe mode (no) is still bypassable via the final path component.

verdict.summary: In GmfOpenMesh, every error path longjmps into the setjmp handler that closes msh->hdl / msh->FilDes and frees msh, but the keyword-table parse failure path `if(!ScaKwdTab(msh)) return(0);` returns directly without releasing the calloc'd GmfMshSct or the open FILE handle / file descriptor. An attacker-supplied malformed mesh file that passes the header checks (cod in {1,16777216}, ver 1-4, dim 2-3) but fails keyword-table parsing triggers a permanent leak of a heap structure and a file handle per open attempt; because the caller receives 0 and no handle, the retention is unrecoverable and scales with the number of attacker-supplied files (CWE-772, resource-exhaustion impact per CWE-400). All memory-safety sinks in this function (strcpy into FilNam, fscanf %100s into str, file-derived cod/ver/dim/KwdCod) are guarded by quoted range/length checks.

evidence.reason: On the only error branch that does not longjmp into the setjmp cleanup handler, the function returns 0 while msh (calloc'd at line 13) and the open file resource (msh->hdl from fopen at line 92/122, or msh->FilDes from open at line 82 in the AIO variant) remain allocated. Trigger instantiated: an attacker-supplied mesh file with a valid header but a malformed keyword table makes the parse call report failure; its 0 return is the failure sentinel this code itself tests here. Impact: permanent, caller-unrecoverable resource retention, scalable by repeated attacker submissions — missing release of resource on an error path (CWE-772).

assumptions: GmfStrSiz is the upstream libMeshb value (1000) and the struct field msh->FilNam is declared char[GmfStrSiz]; the strcpy guard at line 39 is correct only under this sizing (the guard itself is quoted and admits strlen <= GmfStrSiz-8).
WrdSiz equals sizeof(int) (4), so ScaWrd/safe_fread writes into msh->ver, msh->dim, msh->cod, KwdCod do not overflow their int fields.

safe_fread/safe_fscanf/ScaWrd/GetPos are project-internal and unshown; per their naming and the passed msh->err jmp_buf they are assumed to longjmp on I/O failure, and any silent failure still leaves ver/dim at calloc'd 0 or garbage rejected by the quoted range checks at lines 105/113/135/149.
OPEN_READ_FLAGS/OPEN_WRITE_FLAGS and GmfKwdFmt indices are assumed appropriate (not shown).
limitations: (*PtrVer)/*PtrDim dereferences at lines 152-153 crash if the caller passes NULL pointers; this is a caller-contract robustness issue (crashes only the caller's own process at equal privilege, no corruption or bypass) — recorded as robustness, not a vulnerability.

KwdCod (line 3) is uninitialized if the unshown ScaWrd fails without longjmp; the comparison at line 113 would then read an uninitialized value, but it is rejected unless the garbage equals GmfDimension exactly — trigger not instantiable from the given code.
In the error handler, close(msh->FilDes) can be called with -1 when open() failed; this is a harmless EBADF no-op.
strstr-based extension detection matches substrings anywhere in the path (e.g. 'x.mesh.txt' classified as Ascii mesh) — functional quirk, no security effect in this function.

The leak's denial-of-service impact scales only if the embedding application opens many attacker-supplied mesh files within one process; a single leak is a few KB plus one descriptor (affects severity, not the existence of the defect).

verdict.summary: The function is MariaDB's open_table() and every memory or indexing sink it contains is covered by a locally present, correctly operatored guard verified in execution order: the locked-tables memcmp is preceded by an exact length equality (table_cache_key.length == key_length), the tdc_acquire_share result is sentinel-tested (if (unlikely(!share))), the my_malloc result is tested before first use, and all seven goto err_lock paths plus both flush paths release the share/table reference exactly once with no use-after-release. The remaining candidates are dismissed as documented interface contracts rather than attacker-instantiable defects: under MYSQL_OPEN_HAS_MDL_LOCK the MDL ticket is taken from the caller under the code's own documented precondition ("the MDL lock ticket that was acquired by the caller"), and table_name.str flows only into internal not-shown callees whose behavior cannot instantiate an impact chain. No unguarded attacker-data sink, injected bounds defect, or sentinel-missed use was found.

assumptions: get_table_def_key(table_list, &key) returns key/key_length describing the same buffer, per its role as the table-definition key producer; key_length is then guarded at the memcmp by an exact == length check.

The MYSQL_OPEN_HAS_MDL_LOCK flag and ot_ctx->get_flags() are set by internal server machinery (open_tables/lock_tables paths), not directly by attacker input; the comment 'Grab reference to the MDL lock ticket that was acquired by the caller' documents the precondition that ticket is non-NULL.

Internal callees (tdc_acquire_share, open_table_from_share, mysql_make_view, set_partitions_as_used, ha_table_exists, tdc_wait_for_old_version) follow their upstream MariaDB contracts; their internals are not shown, so they can neither guard nor break any sink here.
TABLE objects present in thd->open_tables have ->file and ->alias initialized, per the invariants of the locked-tables list.
limitations: mdl_ticket can be NULL on the MYSQL_OPEN_HAS_MDL_LOCK path (else branch assigns from table_list->mdl_request.ticket with no local check) and would be dereferenced at mdl_ticket->get_deadlock_weight() in the flushed-share path; trigger requires the internal caller that sets the flag to violate the documented contract, so it is an interface-contract robustness issue, not an attacker-instantiable vulnerability.

table_list->table_name.str is not NULL-checked (only db.str is); a NULL table_name would first be consumed by internal callees (get_table_def_key/tdc_acquire_share) whose behavior is not shown, so the impact chain is not instantiated in this code.

The retry_share loop can iterate repeatedly while another session repeatedly FLUSHes the table; each iteration waits with timeout and returns on failure, so this is bounded external churn, not attacker-scalable amplification.

my_error(ER_NO_SUCH_TABLE, ...) in the pre-locked branch passes table_list->alias.str where the table name might be expected in the message text; identical in value to the local alias, cosmetic at most.
DBUG_ASSERT statements (e.g., DBUG_ASSERT(table->file->pushed_cond == NULL)) compile out in release builds and were not treated as guards; no release-build memory defect was found behind them.

verdict.summary: bmexec_trans searches an attacker-controlled buffer (text, size) whose every memory access is bounded in execution order by quoted checks: 'if (len > size) return -1;' caps len by size, 'if (size > 12 * len)' makes 'text + size - 11 * len' underflow-free, 'tp <= ep' is re-checked at each iteration top so at most 10 shifts of the delta table keep tp <= text + size - len and every 'd1[U(tp[-1])]' read in bounds, 'while (d <= ep - tp)' admits exactly-at-limit and rejects one-past for the final loop, and the memchr result is NULL-checked ('if (! tp) return -1;') before use. The remaining pointer excursions depend only on the kwset delta/target tables, which are produced by this library's own prep stage from operator patterns and cannot be influenced by the originator of the searched text; per the callee rules the unshown prep stage and bm_delta2_search can neither create nor neutralize a trigger. No candidate with an attacker-instantiated trigger and a fully quoted impact chain survives.

assumptions: kwset fields (delta, mind, target, trans, gc1, gc2) are internal-trusted state produced by this library's prep stage from operator-supplied patterns; the searched file cannot influence their content, so the width-domain rule for attacker data does not apply to them.
The unshown prep stage is designed so delta table entries satisfy 0 <= d1[c] <= len; this invariant is not quotable from the given code and is therefore not used as a guard anywhere in this analysis.

memchr_kwset is a memchr-class bounded scan over exactly the (pointer, length) range passed to it, honoring kwset->trans; bm_delta2_search returns a boolean and, on the false path, leaves *tp within the text buffer and advanced.
The function's return type (not shown) treats -1 as a not-found sentinel, as its callers conventionally do.
limitations: Skip-loop budget: the fixed reserve of 11*len is sufficient only if each delta1 value is <= len. If the unshown prep stage ever emitted a value > len (e.g. len=2 with entries near 255), the ten 'tp += d' shifts could read up to roughly 2500 bytes past text + size. The trigger is not instantiable by the attacker (the searched text selects table entries but cannot set their values) and the prep stage cannot be assumed to misbehave, so this is recorded as a robustness dependency, not a vulnerability in this code.

The termination of the final loop when d == 0 (including the tp == ep edge reached via the break path) depends on the unshown bm_delta2_search advancing *tp on the false path; if it did not, the loop would spin. Not verifiable from the given code.

'12 * len' and '11 * len' are int multiplications that overflow for patterns longer than about 179 megabytes; the overflow makes 'size > 12 * len' false, which takes the safe branch, and such pattern lengths come from the operator, not the attacker.

The len == 1 path delegates to memchr_kwset; whether that helper applies the translation table cannot be verified from the given code (a missed-match would be a functional defect in the unshown callee, not a memory-safety issue here).
The return type and the caller's handling of the -1 sentinel are not shown; the sentinel convention is assumed, not verified.

verdict.summary: In QEMU's Cadence GEM emulated NIC, a malicious guest can corrupt host-process memory through two independent unguarded paths: (1) TX descriptor fragments are bounds-checked only against the remaining space of the current packet's accumulation pointer, while the accumulation pointer and total_bytes persist across multi-descriptor packets, allowing an arbitrarily long sequence of non-last descriptors to push p past the end of the fixed-size s->tx_packet buffer; the guard 'tx_desc_get_length(desc) > gem_get_max_buf_len(s, true) - (p - s->tx_packet)' saturates once p is already past the end and underflows to a huge space value, after which address_space_read writes attacker-controlled length bytes out of bounds; (2) the descriptor word count gem_get_desc_len(s, false), derived from guest-writable register bits with a width domain of 0x0-0xf (needing up to 64 words), is used to size address_space_read copies into the fixed stack array desc[DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS] with no validation that it fits DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS anywhere in the function, causing an out-of-bounds read and stack overflow of the 128-byte buffer.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write primitive (CWE-787). The only guard, 'if (tx_desc_get_length(desc) > gem_get_max_buf_len(s, true) - (p - s->tx_packet))', bounds each fragment against remaining space of the current packet but nothing resets p or total_bytes between packets composed of non-last descriptors, and nothing bounds total_bytes itself. Guest DMA descriptors are attacker data (discipline 4). Trigger simulation: guest sets GEM_MAX_FRAME_LEN high, posts N non-last descriptors each with length near max_buf_len; after p reaches the end, max_buf_len - (p - s->tx_packet) underflows to a huge size_t, the check passes for any uint32_t length, and address_space_read(&s->dma_as, ..., p, tx_desc_get_length(desc)) writes attacker data past s->tx_packet into adjacent CadenceGEMState memory.

Stack buffer overflow / OOB read (CWE-787/CWE-125). desc is declared 'uint32_t desc[DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS]' but the read length 'sizeof(uint32_t) * gem_get_desc_len(s, false)' is never checked against DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS anywhere in the function (mention sweep: DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS appears only in the two array declarations and the sizeof(desc_first) read). gem_get_desc_len derives from the guest-writable descriptor-width register field with a declared width domain up to 0xf, requiring 16-64 words; address_space_read copies exactly that many bytes into the 128-byte stack array, overflowing desc and reading guest memory beyond the descriptor.
Origin of the undersized destination: the fixed-size stack buffer (DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS words) that the guest-controlled read length must fit, with no local validation against its capacity.

assumptions: gem_get_max_buf_len(s, true) and gem_get_desc_len(s, false) are project-internal helpers not shown; their exact masking of guest register bits is assumed only to bound worst cases, and their declared-width domain (guest-writable register fields, per the GEM model) was used for trigger instantiation.

DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS is assumed to be 8 (the classic Cadence GEM value, supporting up to 8-word modes); if it were 64 the desc-overflow candidate would need desc_len up to 0xf, still within the register field's width domain.

gem_get_tx_desc_addr is assumed to return s->tx_desc_addr[q] (per the sibling read of s->tx_desc_addr[q] in this function), making the loop-index OOB candidate dependent on the unshown declaration of tx_desc_addr[]; recorded here because the array bound cannot be quoted from the given code.
limitations: Candidate: the outer loop 'for (q = s->num_priority_queues - 1; q >= 0; q--)' indexes s->tx_desc_addr[q] and helpers with guest-influenced queue index q; no guard on q's range appears in this function, but the capacity of tx_desc_addr[] and the write semantics of gem_get_tx_desc_addr are not shown, so an out-of-bounds verdict on that array alone cannot be fully instantiated here. It is subsumed by the confirmed register/queue corruption reachable via the primary defects.

The divergence between s->tx_desc_addr[q] (updated in the last/wrap branch) and the local packet_desc_addr (recomputed from the queue base on wrap) is a state-consistency functional issue, not a memory-safety defect.

tx_desc_get_buffer returning 0 and zero-length fragments are correctly rejected by the quoted check '((tx_desc_get_buffer(s, desc) == 0) || (tx_desc_get_length(desc) == 0))'; this candidate was considered and dismissed as guarded.

verdict.summary: jp2_decode trusts the CMAP box's numchans to size a channel-to-component LUT but never validates the LUT values (direct-mapped channel numbers, or newcmptno after an unchecked jas_image_depalettize) against the actual component count before passing them as component indices to jas_image_setcmpttype, yielding an out-of-bounds component-array access (CWE-787). Additionally, the CDEF and BPCC entry arrays are iterated with loop bounds (numchans, image numcmpts) unrelated to the arrays' own attacker-controlled entry counts, producing heap out-of-bounds reads (CWE-125), and an unchecked jas_alloc2 result is written through (CWE-476).

evidence.reason: Origin of the out-of-domain component index: for JP2_CMAP_DIRECT entries the channel number itself (0..numchans-1, numchans taken from the attacker's CMAP box at line 233) is stored as a component number; nothing constrains channo < jas_image_numcmpts(dec->image). The CMAP sanity loop (lines 240-250) checks only cmptno and pcol, never this value.

Sink of CWE-787: the attacker-controlled LUT value (up to numchans-1) is passed as a raw component index into the image component-array accessor with no validation on any path. Trigger: a JP2 file whose codestream has 1 component and whose CMAP declares numchans=1000 with all-direct entries (cmptno=0, pcol=0 passes the sanity checks) makes i=1 index a 1-entry component array out of bounds, an out-of-bounds write of the component type.

CWE-125: the CDEF entry array is indexed with i bounded by dec->numchans, but the ents array is sized by the CDEF box's own numents count, which this code never reads or checks anywhere. Trigger: a file with a 1-entry CDEF box and a 4-component codestream (numchans=4 with no CMAP) reads ents[1..3] out of heap bounds; the OOB channo/type/assoc values then feed the channo check and jp2_getct. The quoted check guards only the chantocmptlut index and uses the wrong bound for the ents array.

CWE-125: bpcs[] is indexed with the image's component count while the array is sized by the BPCC box's own numcmpts; the mismatch test at line 172 only emits a warning (no goto error), so a BPCC box declaring fewer components than the codestream (with differing dtypes so samedtype is false) reads bpcs[] past its end.

CWE-476: the jas_alloc2 return is not checked against NULL before lutents[i] is written. numlutents comes from the attacker's PCLR box, so an attacker can force allocation failure (e.g. numlutents = 0x20000000) and the very first loop iteration writes through a NULL base pointer, crashing the process that parses the attacker's file (attacker-scalable DoS at minimum).

assumptions: jas_image_setcmpttype is the library's component-array indexing accessor; per the call-site rule the defect is the out-of-domain index passed here, regardless of any unshown internal validation.

The PCLR lutdata array is laid out as numlutents x numchans entries, so lutdata[cmapent->pcol + i * pclrd->numchans] stays in bounds under the checked pcol < numchans and i < numlutents (max index numlutents*numchans - 1).

The box parser (jp2_box_get, not shown) sizes cdef ents by its numents field and cmap ents by its numchans field; the over-reads arise when this code's loop bounds exceed those counts, independent of parser strictness.
limitations: Line 268 forms &dec->cdef->data.cdef while dec->cdef may be NULL, but cdefd is never dereferenced (used only inside #if 0) - latent UB with no security impact in this code.

jas_image_depalettize's return value (line 279) is ignored; on failure the component it promises is not created, yet chantocmptlut[channo] = newcmptno is still stored, feeding the same out-of-bounds component index sink as the primary defect.

Exact write primitive obtained from the out-of-bounds component index depends on jas_image_setcmpttype internals, which are not shown; the out-of-domain index at the call site is the confirmed defect.

verdict.summary: hfsplus_block_allocate consumes the return value of read_mapping_page without any sentinel check and passes it straight to kmap, so a crafted HFS+ image whose allocation-file pages fail to read (corrupted extents) makes kmap(ERR_PTR(-EIO)) dereference a wild kernel address and panic the kernel. Independently, the allocation write loop advances pages with no `offset >= size` test (the scan loop has one at line 55), so a page-aligned size whose allocation run ends exactly at size causes read_mapping_page/kmap/set_page_dirty to touch a page one past the bitmap file's end. Both are reachable purely from on-disk attacker data at mount time.

evidence.snippet:
page = read_mapping_page(mapping, offset / PAGE_CACHE_BITS, NULL);
	pptr = kmap(page);
evidence.reason: Unchecked failure sentinel: read_mapping_page returns ERR_PTR on read failure (attacker-instantiable by mounting an image with corrupted allocation-file metadata); the result flows directly into kmap with no IS_ERR/NULL test on any path (same unchecked pattern repeats at lines 57-59 and 104-106), so kmap computes an address from an error pointer and line 28 `val = *curr` dereferences it, panicking the kernel.

Missing bounds check on page advance in the write loop: the scan loop guards its advance with `if (offset >= size) break;` (line 55) but this loop has no equivalent, so when the allocation run consumes bits exactly to size and size is a multiple of PAGE_CACHE_BITS (e.g. size = 32768, len = 4096, all-zero run), offset becomes equal to size and read_mapping_page reads one page past the bitmap file's end, which is then kmap'd and marked dirty via set_page_dirty (line 121) — an out-of-bounds read past the file's logical end with no guard anywhere in the loop.

assumptions: PAGE_CACHE_BITS = PAGE_CACHE_SIZE * 8 = 32768 bits per page (1024 u32 words), per standard kernel definitions.
read_mapping_page can return ERR_PTR on read failure, per its documented standard semantics; the code's own behavior with a valid page was traced with that caveat.
size and *max derive from on-disk HFS+ volume structures, so an attacker mounting a crafted image controls them (bitmap size, free-block count, and bitmap content are all image data).
limitations: HFSPLUS_SB(sb).free_blocks -= *max (line 124) can underflow when the on-disk free_blocks is smaller than the allocated count, corrupting allocation bookkeeping; the exploitation chain lies in consumers not shown, so it is recorded rather than confirmed.

The initial read at line 17 performs no offset-vs-size check, but triggering it with an oversized offset additionally requires the unshown caller to pass one; the harmful consequence flows through the same unchecked-kmap defect as candidate A.

Impact is a kernel oops/DoS (plus a dirtied page past EOF); no attacker-controlled out-of-bounds WRITE was instantiated, since the write-loop's post-cross write only rewrites the value it read from the same word.
Reaching the code requires mounting a filesystem image, which on many systems needs privilege; the image content itself is untrusted, so this is judged as crafted-image parser exposure.

verdict.summary: In tgs_build_reply(), the constrained-delegation block overwrites the S4U2Self-allocated impersonation principal (tp, allocated at line 640) and its unparsed name (tpn, allocated at line 648) without freeing them (lines 799-806), leaking one principal object and one attacker-chosen-length string per request on the combined PA-FOR-USER + cname_in_addl_tkt path. The leak happens before the forwardable and check_constrained_delegation authorization checks, so any registered service with a valid TGT can drive unbounded memory retention in the long-lived KDC process.

evidence.reason: Sink: tp and tpn are overwritten here without freeing the values allocated by the S4U2Self block (tp at lines 640-643, tpn at line 648). A mention sweep of every tp/tpn reference (17, 551, 552, 640-648, 686-692, 799-806, and the out: block) shows no free between the two allocations and this overwrite. Trigger: an authenticated service sends a TGS-REQ containing a valid PA-FOR-USER padata (S4U2Self to itself) plus cname_in_addl_tkt with a self-ticket that decrypts under its own key; the leak occurs at these statements, before the forwardable and constrained-delegation authorization checks, so it fires even when the request is subsequently rejected. Memory leak (CWE-401) scalable by request count in the KDC process.

Origin: the S4U2Self block allocates a fresh principal into tp (and krb5_unparse_name at line 648 allocates tpn), replacing the earlier tp = cp / tpn = cpn defaults. These are the allocations that are leaked when the constrained-delegation block at lines 799-806 overwrites tp and tpn without freeing them.

assumptions: ASN.1 decode of KDC-REQ-BODY guarantees non-NULL b->etype.val when b->etype.len > 0 and non-NULL additional_tickets->val when len > 0; the shown code still guards index 0 accesses at lines 75-76 and 756-757.

check_PAC, kdc_check_flags, check_s4u2self, and _kdc_find_etype are internal callees whose NULL-client handling and failure semantics are not shown; their success paths are required only for reachability of the leak, not for the leak statement itself.
limitations: Line 236 and line 255: return value of krb5_make_principal is not checked (unlike line 192); on allocation failure sp stays NULL and is passed to krb5_unparse_name, a NULL dereference. Trigger requires OOM, not attacker-instantiable -> robustness, not counted as a vulnerability.
Line 267: ref_realm = strdup(realms[0]) return not checked; a NULL ref_realm is contained downstream by the 'if (ref_realm)' guard, so no security effect.

Lines 585-587: free_PA_S4U2Self(&self) is missing on the _krb5_s4u2self_to_checksumdata failure path; the failure mode of that unshown internal callee could not be instantiated, so this leak is recorded but not counted as primary.

When _kdc_db_fetch for the client returns HDB_ERR_NOT_FOUND_HERE (tolerated at lines 477-481), client may be NULL when passed to check_PAC and kdc_check_flags; whether those unshown callees tolerate NULL could not be verified.

No attacker-instantiable memory-corruption, off-by-one, or authz-bypass defect was found: val[0] accesses, the etype loop, the kvno ternaries, and the capath pre-decrement are all guarded by quoted checks with correct operators, and the S4U2Self checksum path is fail-closed.

verdict.summary: This is Linux kernel push_pipe() from lib/iov_iter.c. All attacker-influenced values are bounded by quoted guards: size is clamped by 'if (unlikely(size > i->count)) size = i->count;', the partial-page growth 'pipe->bufs[iter_head & p_mask].len += size' is gated by 'if (left <= 0)' whose <= operator is correct at both bounds (size == PAGE_SIZE - off lands len exactly at PAGE_SIZE; one byte more takes the else path), the loop is capped by 'while (!pipe_full(iter_head, p_tail, pipe->max_usage))', the allocation sentinel is checked with 'if (!page) break;' before any buffer write, and every pipe_buffer field including 'buf->flags = 0;' is initialized before 'pipe->head = iter_head;' publishes it, so the Dirty Pipe (CVE-2022-0847) defect is already fixed here. The remaining candidates (ssize_t truncation of size >= 2^63, len growth beyond the page, len = PAGE_SIZE ignoring buf->offset) all require pre-state or caller values that no statement of this code produces and that no attacker-reachable entry point can instantiate. Not vulnerable.

verdict.summary: In composite_setup(), every memory sink reachable by a malicious USB host (control-request fields wValue/wIndex/wLength) is bounded by quoted guards in execution order: the entry clamp 'if (w_length > USB_COMP_EP0_BUFSIZ)' (clamping or rejecting over-limit lengths), 'w_length = min_t(u16, w_length, USB_COMP_EP0_OS_DESC_BUFSIZ);' before the OS-descriptor memset, per-case 'value = min(w_length, ...)' before each memcpy, and 'intf >= MAX_CONFIG_INTERFACES' checks at every interface-array index with correct operators. The only dead guard found ('if (!config)' after list_first_entry(&cdev->configs,...), which can never fire since list_first_entry never returns NULL) leads to an out-of-bounds read only when the gadget driver registered zero configurations, a device-side registration state the USB host attacker cannot instantiate.

assumptions: req->buf and cdev->os_desc_req->buf are allocated with at least USB_COMP_EP0_BUFSIZ and USB_COMP_EP0_OS_DESC_BUFSIZ bytes respectively; the allocation site is not shown in this code.

The width of the f->endpoints bitmap used by 'test_bit(endp, f->endpoints)' is not shown; endp's computed maximum is 31 (((w_index & 0x80) >> 3) | (w_index & 0x0f)), assumed to fit the bitmap per the declared struct.

Unshown internal callees (config_desc, get_string, bos_desc, device_qual, set_config, count/len/fill_ext_compat/prop) bound their writes into req->buf; all arguments passed at the shown call sites are within their declared widths, and the sentinel-negative returns of set_config and fill_ext_prop are consumed under quoted 'if (value >= 0 ...)' / stall paths before first use.
limitations: USB_DT_OTG path: 'config = list_first_entry(&cdev->configs, struct usb_configuration, list); if (!config) goto done;' — the NULL check is dead because list_first_entry never returns NULL. If a gadget driver binds with an empty cdev->configs list, a host GET_DESCRIPTOR(OTG) would make 'config' a container_of garbage pointer, and 'memcpy(req->buf, config->descriptors[0], value)' would perform an out-of-bounds read and copy up to 8 bytes into the ep0 response (crash / disclosure). The trigger precondition (zero registered configurations) is device-driver registration state, not instantiable by the USB host or by any statement in this code, so it is speculative and does not drive the verdict.

In the OS-descriptor USB_RECIP_DEVICE arm, 'value = fill_ext_compat(os_desc_cfg, buf); value = min_t(u16, w_length, value);' lacks the 'if (value >= 0)' sentinel present in the USB_RECIP_INTERFACE arm; a negative callee return would wrap through min_t(u16, ...) to w_length. Harmless here because 'memset(buf, 0, w_length);' zeroed exactly w_length bytes first, so the response exposes no uninitialized or out-of-bounds data; recorded as a robustness/correctness nit, not a vulnerability.

verdict.summary: This is GNU grep's hardened bmexec_trans. Every pointer advance and read is bounded by quoted statements: 'if (len > size) return -1;' bounds len by the buffer, the fast loop is gated by 'if (size > 12 * len)' with top-of-loop recheck 'tp <= ep' inside the documented 11*len reservation, the memchr result is sentinel-checked ('if (! tp) return -1;') before first use, and the tail loop's 'while (d <= ep - tp)' with d in [0,255] (unsigned char table) provably keeps tp within [text, text+size]. The only conceivable out-of-bounds scenarios require either the unshown table builder to emit a delta value exceeding the reservation or ~179MB-scale patterns triggering signed overflow of '12 * len' (which the quoted 'len > size' check forces to be matched by a ~179MB text buffer); neither is instantiable from this code's own statements or standard-callee sentinels.

assumptions: kwset->delta entries are clamped by the not-shown preparer (kwsprep) so that no single skip exceeds the 11*len slack reserved by the fast loop; this is an unshown internal producer contract — per the analysis rules it can neither guard nor manufacture a trigger, and it is the basis for the fast-loop reservation arithmetic documented by the in-code comment 'Significance of 12: 1 (initial offset) + 10 (skip loop) + 1 (md2).'

bm_delta2_search and memchr_kwset (not shown) honor the ep bound and the [start, start+len) scan domain respectively; memchr_kwset's NULL sentinel is the only consumed return and it is checked in this code before first use.

verdict.summary: php_wddx_pop_element dereferences the parent stack entry's zval pointer without a NULL check. The only NULL guard, `ent2->type == ST_FIELD && ent2->data == NULL`, protects ST_FIELD parents only; any other parent entry whose zval has not been created yet (an empty value element containing a nested value, e.g. <string><string>x</string></string> — NULL-data entries are acknowledged by the code's own `if (!ent1->data)` branch) falls through to `Z_TYPE_P(ent2->data)` and dereferences NULL, crashing the process that deserializes attacker-supplied WDDX (remote denial of service).

evidence.reason: Sink: Z_TYPE_P(ent2->data) dereferences the parent entry's data pointer. ent2->data is NULL for any parent value element that received no character data before its child closed; the only NULL guard (line 69) fires solely for ST_FIELD. Simulated trigger: <string><string>x</string></string> — at the inner close, ent2 = the outer ST_STRING entry with data == NULL, so Z_TYPE_P(NULL) reads (*NULL).type and segfaults, remotely crashing the process parsing the attacker's packet.

Root cause: the NULL-data guard is conjjoined with ent2->type == ST_FIELD, so a NULL ent2->data of any other entry type falls through to the unguarded Z_TYPE_P use at line 75. The missing guard — an unconditional `ent2->data == NULL` test before the use — appears nowhere in the function (mention sweep: lines 66, 69, 75, 76 are the only mentions of ent2).

assumptions: The not-shown element-push handler creates value entries with ent->data == NULL and fills the zval lazily on character data; this is corroborated by the given code's own `if (!ent1->data)` early-return branch (line 24), which can only be live for non-ST_FIELD entries closing under the nine element names (well-formedness makes the just-closed element's entry the stack top, and EL_FIELD is not among those names).

wddx_stack_top returns elements[top-1] when top > 0 (standard implementation); it cannot fail here because line 13 (`if (stack->top == 0) { return; }`) and line 64 (`if (stack->top > 1)`) leave top >= 1 after the decrement.
wddx_deserialize feeds network/file-supplied packets into these expat callbacks; element names arrive NUL-terminated per expat's documented contract.
limitations: Lines 24-31: when the closing entry has NULL data and stack->top == 1, the code sets stack->done = 1 and efree(ent1) while the freed entry remains the stack top, unlike the other done path (line 64 else-arm) that deliberately retains the entry as the result. The not-shown deserializer loop that reads the top entry after done=1 would read freed memory (potential UAF); the use site is outside the given code, so the impact chain could not be fully instantiated.

The `Z_DELREF_P(ent1->data); add_property_zval(ent2->data, ent1->varname, ent1->data);` sequence may leave a refcount imbalance depending on whether add_property_zval adds a reference (callee semantics not shown); no memory corruption could be proven from the given code alone.

Reconstruction of objects and the __wakeup() invocation enable classic WDDX object-injection (CWE-502) consequences, but instantiation of dangerous classes is application-dependent and no missing check within this snippet alone was proven.

verdict.summary: In unlzw, the decompression code `code` produced by the unshown input() macro from attacker-supplied compressed data is consumed by the prefix-walk loop without any local mask, clamp, or lower-bound check. All quoted guards (if (256 <= code), if (code >= free_ent), if (code > free_ent)) bound only the upper side; a negative code_int value (code_int is provably signed: oldcode = -1 is assigned and tested, and for (code = 255; code >= 0; --code) terminates) passes all of them, and the unsigned cast at the loop head reinterprets it as a huge value, indexing tab_suffixof/tab_prefixof at a negative offset (out-of-bounds read, value disclosed into the decompressed output) and driving an unbounded *--stackp walk that can write below de_stack.

evidence.reason: Sink: the attacker-derived code is used to index tab_suffixof/tab_prefixof with no lower-bound guard on any path. A negative code (in code_int's signed domain, quotable from oldcode = -1 and the code >= 0 init loop) fails every existing check (256 <= code, code >= free_ent, code > free_ent all compare the upper side only), and the (cmp_code_int) cast reinterprets it as a huge unsigned value, entering the loop and reading out of bounds at a negative index; the loop length is bounded only by out-of-bounds garbage, and *--stackp walks de_stack downward without any bound.

Origin of the tainted value: attacker-controlled compressed-file bits are decoded into code by a macro not shown in this code; no statement in this code applies bitmask, clamps, or range-checks code before its use at lines 141-146, so per the width-domain rule code's surface is the full signed domain of code_int.

assumptions: The input() macro, code_int/cmp_code_int typedefs, MAXCODE, BITS, BIT_MASK, CLEAR, FIRST, INIT_BITS, and the sizes of tab_suffix/tab_prefix, de_stack, inbuf, and outbuf are not shown; per the width-domain rule the unshown macro's masking cannot serve as a guard, and code_int's signedness was inferred only from quoted statements (oldcode = -1 at line 43, if (oldcode == -1) at line 97, for (code = 255; code >= 0; --code) at line 52).
tab_suffixof/tab_prefixof are treated as direct array indexers over 0-based tables, so any negative index is out of bounds regardless of table size.
read_error() and gzip_error() are assumed to terminate; no path in this code continues after them.
limitations: The buffer-underflow WRITE variant (stackp walking below de_stack after the walk exceeds the unshown de_stack size) depends on out-of-bounds garbage keeping the chain alive past that size; its chain is not fully characterizable from the given code, so the fully instantiated impact is the out-of-bounds READ with disclosure into the decompressed output.

If the unshown input() macro provably masks code to bitmask, out-of-range codes could not occur; per the analysis rules that masking is an unquoted contract and may not reject the candidate, but it is the reason confidence is not high.

maxbits < INIT_BITS (maxmaxcode smaller than the initial free_ent), the CLEAR-path free_ent reset, the outbuf flush arithmetic, and the resetbuf shift loop were simulated at boundary values (o == insize, outpos+i == OUTBUFSIZ, rsize == 0/-1) and found to stay in bounds under the quoted guards; the 256 <= code over-rejection concern does not arise because it under-admits negative codes, which is the primary defect.

The single memory-safety-relevant arithmetic, io_size -= ret inside the retry do-while, is guarded in execution order: first entry requires ret > 0 and ret != io_size (with ret bounded above by the iterator count), and each subsequent subtraction is preceded by the loop condition while (ret > 0 && ret < io_size), so io_size can never go negative. Error paths returning negative ret are routed to completion, not arithmetic. iovec lifetime is consistent across all return paths given the error-checked import and the out_free kfree. Remaining concerns rest only on unshown callee contracts (io_setup_async_rw freeing iovec on error, allocating async_data on success; io_import_iovec clamping to MAX_RW_COUNT), which could at worst cause a memory leak, not corruption.

assumptions: io_setup_async_rw(req, iovec, inline_vecs, iter, true) takes ownership of iovec (and frees it internally on its own error path); this contract is not quoted in the given code, so the early `return ret ?: -EAGAIN;` and `if (ret2) return ret2;` paths rely on it to avoid a leak.
A successful io_setup_async_rw allocates req->async_data, so `rw = req->async_data;` followed by `iter = &rw->iter;` is non-NULL; not enforced by a quoted statement here.
io_import_iovec clamps the total iovec length to MAX_RW_COUNT, so io_size = iov_iter_count(iter) fits in ssize_t and cannot be negative; the clamp is not shown in this code.
iov_iter_reexpand/iov_iter_revert maintain the invariant count + truncated <= the pre-read io_size snapshot, so `io_size - iov_iter_count(iter)` cannot wrap; the invariant lives in helpers not shown.
limitations: Candidate `io_size - iov_iter_count(iter)` size_t wrap before iov_iter_revert could not be triggered: no statement in this code can make the current count exceed the io_size snapshot captured before the reads.
Potential iovec leak if io_setup_async_rw fails without freeing it — impact is a memory leak only and depends on unshown callee behavior.
`rw` NULL dereference after io_setup_async_rw success requires the callee to return 0 without allocating; not instantiable from the given code.
This matches the upstream Linux io_uring io_read including the in-loop `io_size -= ret` update that fixed the earlier short-read accounting bug; no variant of that historical defect is present.

verdict.summary: In ReadTIFFImage's generic (RGBA) path, the failure of TIFFReadRGBAImage is tested with the wrong sentinel: the function is documented to return 1 on success and 0 on error (never -1), so the check 'if (tiff_status == -1)' never fires. On any TIFF that passes this coder's own header checks but is rejected by TIFFRGBAImageOK (e.g. 32-bit samples, or the explicitly allowed 64-bit IEEEFP samples), the function proceeds to decode a buffer obtained from AcquireVirtualMemory that is never zeroed anywhere in this code, rendering prior heap contents into the returned image — an information disclosure from uninitialized memory (fail-open error handling).

evidence.reason: Dead failure-sentinel check: TIFFReadRGBAImage returns 1 on success and 0 on error and never -1, so an attacker-supplied TIFF that fails TIFFRGBAImageOK (e.g. bits_per_sample=32 or the explicitly permitted 64-bit IEEEFP) returns 0, which passes this guard. The subsequent pixel loop then decodes the completely uninitialized raster, leaking prior heap memory into the output image.

Origin of the tainted value: the raster buffer is allocated (only its NULL return is checked) and never initialized — no memset/ResetMagickMemory exists for this buffer anywhere in the code (the ResetMagickMemory at line 604 targets the separate pixel_info allocation, which the shadowing 'pixels' declaration hides). When TIFFReadRGBAImage fails without writing, this uninitialized heap memory is what the decode loop consumes.

assumptions: TIFFReadRGBAImage semantics per documented libtiff behavior: returns 1 on success, 0 on error (TIFFRGBAImageOK/TIFFRGBAImageBegin failures), never -1; with stop=0 it still returns 0 when the image cannot be handled at all.

AcquireVirtualMemory is typically malloc-backed (uninitialized) for small allocations; if an anonymous-mmap fallback path were taken the buffer would read as zeros, reducing the impact to a blank image rather than disclosure.
The extra_samples/sample_info loop relies on libtiff returning a count and array that are internally consistent (same tag source), an unshown-internal contract.
SetImageExtent and AcquireMagickResource enforce width/height/memory resource policy before the decode loops; assumed to bound columns/rows below overflow scales on 64-bit builds.
Internal callees not shown (TIFFReadPixels, ImportQuantumPixels, TIFFGetProfiles, DecodeLabImage, TIFFReadPhotoshopLayers) were not evaluated for defects inside themselves.
limitations: On 32-bit builds, columns*rows*4 in the generic method is not covered by HeapOverflowSanityCheck(image->rows,4) (line 918 checks only rows*4); speculative because the code declares 64-bit MagickSizeType arithmetic and typical builds are 64-bit.

The tile-method AcquireMagickResource(WidthResource/HeightResource) acquisitions (lines 579-581) are never relinquished in this function, leaking resource-accounting units per tiled frame in multi-directory TIFFs — a self-process resource-exhaustion vector, not promoted to primary.
The strip/tile read paths use correct -1 sentinels for TIFFReadEncodedStrip/TIFFReadTile (which do return -1), so the sentinel defect is confined to the TIFFReadRGBAImage call.

If the failure-path raster were mmap-backed and zero-filled, the trigger would still produce a mispresented 'successfully decoded' image but without disclosure, weakening only the impact, not the fail-open defect.

verdict.summary: The write phase of hfsplus_block_allocate reloads bitmap pages with no `offset >= size` termination check (unlike the scan loop), so an allocation length (*max, a full-domain u32 from a crafted HFS+ image) that exceeds the remaining bitmap bits causes the full-u32 loop to write 0xffffffff past the logical end of the allocation bitmap and into subsequent pages of the alloc_file, plus a free_blocks underflow.

evidence.reason: The write loop's page reload advances offset and reads the next bitmap page with only an IS_ERR check — unlike the scan loop's explicit `if (offset >= size) break;` — so with len larger than the free space remaining before size, the loop writes 0xffffffff into bitmap pages beyond the logical end (offset >= size), corrupting the allocation file; trigger: *max = large u32, small size, one zero bit near the end of the bitmap.

Full-u32 write loop consumes len (from *max, a u32 whose full domain is instantiable from a crafted filesystem image) with no bound tying it to `size - start` after the first partial word; once len >= 32 persists past size, 0xffffffff words are written past the bitmap end.

assumptions: PAGE_CACHE_BITS assumed 4096 (PAGE_SIZE 4096); the arithmetic conclusions hold for any power-of-two page size since all masks are PAGE_CACHE_BITS-1.

size, offset and *max originate from the mounted HFS+ image (superblock/volume header and alloc_file contents); their producer code is not shown, so per the width-domain rule their surface is the full u32 domain and no narrowing statement exists in this code.

read_mapping_page on an index beyond the allocation file's logical size returns a page whose contents are not the logical bitmap; writing there corrupts the file or fails, but the write to the mapped page memory itself is in-page and the out-of-logical-bounds write is the instantiated impact.
limitations: The end-pointer computation `((size + 31) & (PAGE_CACHE_BITS - 1)) / 32` under-covers the final partial word when size is not a multiple of 32 (e.g. size=4095, offset=0 gives end=pptr+0), causing premature 'bitmap full' — a functional under-allocation/availability issue, not memory corruption, because end never exceeds the page.
A NULL/IS_ERR page is checked on every read_mapping_page call; no unchecked-sentinel defect exists at those sites.
Wrap of offset at `offset += PAGE_CACHE_BITS` requires size near 2^32; the scan loop's `offset >= size` check terminates before wrap for any u32 size, so that path is not triggered as written.

verdict.summary: All consumed external values are guarded by quoted sentinel checks or are internally consistent (loop bound matches the created wq; allocation length matches the consumed pas array). The one unvalidated input, cq_size, can formally reach roundup_pow_of_two/ilog2 with non-positive values causing documented kernel-macro UB, but the simulated impact chain degrades to an undersized CQ or a checked error return at the unshown internal allocator, so no security impact is instantiated in this code.

A one-line 'if (cq_size <= 0) return -EINVAL;' would still be prudent hardening.

verdict.summary: handle_returned_header treats libcurl header callback data (exactly size*nmemb bytes, not NUL-terminated) as NUL-terminated C strings: snprintf %s at line 22 (and strncasecmp/sscanf at lines 11, 13, 16) read past the delivered region because the computed length `bytes` is never used to bound any read, causing a network-peer-triggered heap out-of-bounds read in the server process.

evidence.reason: Root cause: %s reads a C string from the attacker-delivered header buffer, which libcurl does not NUL-terminate and which holds only `bytes` bytes; the write is truncated to sizeof(errormsg) but the READ is unbounded. Trigger: auth backend sends header line 'icecast-auth-message: A' at the end of delivered data; snprintf reads past the 34 delivered bytes into adjacent heap until a NUL, up to sizeof(errormsg) bytes — out-of-bounds read / DoS. No check of `bytes` exists anywhere in the function.

Sibling sink of the same defect: strncasecmp reads up to url->auth_header_len bytes from ptr with no check that bytes >= auth_header_len and no guaranteed NUL inside the delivered region (same at lines 13 and 16), so the comparison itself can read past the attacker-delivered buffer.

Origin of the tainted input: ptr carries the network peer's header content (exactly size*nmemb bytes, not NUL-terminated per libcurl's header-callback contract); `bytes`, the only local length, is computed at line 4 and used only in the return at line 31 — never as a read bound.

assumptions: url->auth_header, url->auth_header_len, url->timelimit_header, url->timelimit_header_len and url->errormsg are configured/allocated in code not shown; their values are treated per the width-domain rule and are not relied on as guards.
stream is the CURLOPT_WRITEDATA userdata this code registered, so auth_user->client is trusted.
errormsg's downstream consumer (whether it is sent to the client) is not shown; disclosure impact beyond the out-of-bounds read itself is therefore unquantified.
limitations: Line 12 sets client->authenticated = 1 after a strncasecmp of only auth_header_len bytes; if the configured auth_header were name-only (e.g. 'icecast-auth: '), any response line beginning with that name would authenticate the client regardless of value. The content of auth_header cannot be quoted from the given code, so this is speculative and does not drive the verdict.
size*nmemb overflow at line 4 would require libcurl to deliver SIZE_MAX-scale dimensions, which the characterizable library contract excludes.
Concrete info disclosure into errormsg depends on the unshown consumer; the instantiated impact is the heap out-of-bounds read itself (crash/DoS potential) in a network-facing server process.

verdict.summary: This is the Linux kernel's add_interrupt_randomness entropy-accumulation path. All memory indices are literal constants (pool[0..3]) or masked with '& 3' against a 4-element array; all copy lengths (sizeof(fast_pool->pool), sizeof(seed)) are compile-time constants; the only direct dereference of the possibly-NULL regs pointer is guarded by 'regs ? instruction_pointer(regs) : _RET_IP_'; and entropy credit is rate-limited to at most 2 bits per HZ per CPU by the quoted time_after gate, precluding interrupt-flood amplification. No attacker-derived length, size, offset, or index reaches any sink.

assumptions: get_reg, fast_mix, crng_fast_load, __mix_pool_bytes, credit_entropy_bits, random_get_entropy, arch_get_random_seed_long are project-internal callees not shown; their behavior is an assumption that cuts both ways and was not used to either confirm or dismiss a candidate.
this_cpu_ptr/this_cpu_add per-CPU access assumes the caller invokes this function with preemption/interrupts disabled, the standard contract for an IRQ-context handler entry point.
limitations: Lines 14 and 22 pass 'regs' (possibly NULL when get_irq_regs() is called outside a hard IRQ) to the unshown callee get_reg with no NULL check on any path in this code; a NULL dereference could not be instantiated because get_reg's handling of NULL is not shown. If get_reg dereferences regs unconditionally, that would be a NULL-deref defect spanning both call sites.

fast_pool->count is never incremented anywhere in the given code (only set to 0 at lines 32 and 61, read at lines 29 and 38); if no unshown callee increments it, the 'count >= 64' fast-load branch is unreachable and crediting falls back solely to the once-per-HZ gate. This under-credits entropy (fail-closed) and has no attacker-facing security effect; recorded as a functional observation, not a vulnerability.
The irq_flags parameter is never used in the function body (dead parameter); no security consequence.

An attacker flooding interrupts can influence the noise mixed into the pool (irq number, timing), but this is the designed behavior of an interrupt entropy source and the quoted rate limit bounds credit to at most 2 bits per HZ per CPU.

verdict.summary: BinaryBroadcastFiveFold drives all loop bounds, copy counts, and pointer strides from params.broadcast_shape (attacker-domain ints, producer not shown in this code) with no validation against the buffer extents. The RuntimeShape bound arguments (unswitched_input1_shape, unswitched_input2_shape, output_shape) are received but never read, so nothing ties the traversal extents (y0*y1*y2*y4, y0*y2*y3*y4, y0*y1*y2*y3*y4) to the actual buffers. Concretely: elementwise_f(y4, ...) and scalar_broadcast_f(y3, ...) write y4/y3 elements per call while output_data_ptr advances unboundedly, yielding heap out-of-bounds writes (and reads on the inputs) of attacker-chosen count. Additionally, the branch 'if (y4 > 1)' under-admits y4 == 0 into the else branch whose comment assumes y4 == 1, so even shape-faithful zero-sized inner dimensions cause scalar_broadcast_f to write y3 elements into a zero-length output.

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted values: broadcast_shape[0..4] are plain ints copied with no clamp, mask, cast, or range check. Their producer is not shown in this code, so per the width-domain rule every 32-bit int value is instantiable, yet these values become loop bounds, copy counts, and pointer strides.

Primary sink: an unvalidated attacker-domain count y4 and unbounded cursors are passed into a bulk elementwise copy/write; output_data_ptr is advanced by y4 (line 57) with no statement anywhere comparing the traversal extent y0*y1*y2*y3*y4 against output_shape or any buffer size (the shape parameters at lines 2/4/6 are never read). Trigger: broadcast_shape = {1,1,1,1,1000} with a smaller output buffer executes elementwise_f(1000, ...) writing 1000 elements out of bounds — heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787).

Second instantiation of the same defect: y3 elements are written per call with an unbounded cursor, and *input1_data_ptr is dereferenced with no extent check. With broadcast_shape = {1,1,1,5,0} the code's own flat-size formulas (lines 38-39) give zero-length buffers, yet this call writes 5 elements out of bounds.

Boundary defect in the only branch consuming y4: the else arm is documented (line 67) as the 'Special case of y4 == 1' but the test only excludes y4 > 1, so y4 == 0 (and negative y4) are under-admitted into a traversal that assumes y4 == 1; with y4 == 0 the implied flat sizes are 0 while the else branch still walks y0*y1*y2*y3 elements, producing out-of-bounds access even for shape-faithful zero-sized inner dimensions.

assumptions: elementwise_f and scalar_broadcast_f (template callbacks) are assumed to write y4/y3 elements at the output cursor per their names and call shape; per the call-site rule the defect is the passage of unvalidated counts and unbounded pointers at lines 54-55 and 82-83 regardless of callee internals.

ArithmeticParams.broadcast_shape is populated by an op-Prepare/decode layer not shown in this code; treated as attacker-data at full int width per the width-domain rule (the model file supplying op parameters is the trust-boundary artifact).
limitations: Negative y0..y4 values make every loop condition (0 < negative) false, so no traversal and no out-of-bounds access occurs on those values; the defect is instantiated with non-negative values.

Exploitation in the full TFLite codebase would additionally require the model to make broadcast_shape inconsistent with the allocated tensor buffers (or use a zero-sized inner dimension); that producer code is not given here, so its strictness can neither be relied on nor used to demote the finding.

verdict.summary: The 32-bit product size*count in `long long allocate = (long long)(size*count + pad+20);` wraps before the cast, so the only size guard `allocate > io.size()` validates a wrapped value. A TIFF RATIONAL entry with count=0x20000000 makes allocate collapse to 20 while the print loop indexes buf up to byte 39, producing heap out-of-bounds reads (printed to output, information disclosure); the same overflow under-protects `buf.pData_[count]=0` (potential OOB write on the XMP path) and the SubIFD loop `byteSwap4(buf,k*size)` with unbound k<count. Independently, the kpsRecursive SubIFD/MakerNote paths recurse with file-controlled IFD offsets and no depth bound, so a self-referential tag 0x8769 entry drives infinite recursion and stack exhaustion (denial of service).

evidence.reason: Integer overflow (CWE-190): size and count are uint32_t attacker values parsed from the TIFF entry (lines 37, 58-63), so the product and the +pad+20 are computed in 32 bits and wrap before the (long long) cast. With type=RATIONAL (size=8) and count=0x20000000, size*count wraps to 0, allocate becomes 20, the guard `allocate > (long long) io.size()` at line 69 passes for any file >= 20 bytes, and DataBuf buf(allocate) is undersized. This wrapped product is the single defective statement; no 64-bit multiply, overflow check, or clamp of count exists anywhere in the code.

The mention sweep over every statement touching count/size/kount (lines 37, 51-63, 68-72, 74, 79, 93-123) found no check of k*size against allocate or buf.size_; the read values are printed at line 107, disclosing heap memory.

Uncontrolled recursion (CWE-400): with option=kpsRecursive and an entry tag 0x8769 (or 0x014a/tiffIfd) whose offset field points back to its own IFD, line 120 reads that offset from buf and line 121 recurses with the identical state; depth is only incremented for indentation (line 3) and never compared against any limit, so the recursion never terminates and exhausts the stack. assumptions: byteSwap2/byteSwap4 read 2/4 bytes at the given byte offset of the DataBuf, and the isXType/typeValid helpers classify the TIFF types whose element sizes the code itself enumerates at lines 58-63; these are Exiv2 internals with evident semantics.
io.read on a short file may leave buffer tails uninitialized; the primary triggers do not depend on short reads.

If isPrintXMP(tag,option) is true for an attacker-chosen tag 0x02bc under the XMP print option, line 159 `buf.pData_[count]=0;` becomes a wild out-of-bounds WRITE (count up to 2^31 with the wrapped allocate) and line 163 `out.write((const char*)buf.pData_,count);` an OOB read, both flowing from the same line-68 overflow; the branch predicates are unshown internal callees, so this is recorded as an additional consequence sink rather than an independent primary.

The MakerNote Nikon path (lines 142-146) can pass a short-read, partially uninitialized heap buffer into MemIo/printTiffStructure, and the IPTC path into IptcData::printStructure; the consumers are not shown, so CWE-908 exposure there is not instantiated here.

Line 127 `byte* bytes=new byte[count]` can request a ~2GB allocation for a tiny file once the line-68 check is defeated by the wrap (memory-amplification DoS); it shares the line-68 root cause and is not counted as an independent defect.
Line 22 `if ( tooBig ) out << ...` is unreachable because line 18 throws first; cosmetic only.

verdict.summary: In block_insert, the multibyte adjustment subtracts the character head offset from both spaces and count (spaces -= off; count -= off;), but the subsequent clamp 'if (spaces < 0) spaces = 0;' protects only spaces. A negative count reaches the allocation size computation 'newp = alloc(STRLEN(oldp) + spaces + s_len + ... + count + 1);' and shrinks the heap buffer below the number of bytes later written by mch_memmove(newp + startcol, s, s_len) and STRMOVE(newp + offset, oldp), producing a heap out-of-bounds write of the line tail and terminating NUL past the allocation when a block insert cuts a TAB and the adjusted position lands at or past the end of a multibyte character (a state the code's own comment 'can happen when the cursor was moved' admits).

verdict.summary: In php_wddx_pop_element, when the top stack entry has NULL data and stack->top == 1, the else arm sets stack->done = 1 but does not remove the entry from the stack before efree(ent1) frees it, leaving a dangling pointer at stack->elements[0] with stack->top still 1. Because this function never reads stack->done and expat invokes the end-element handler for every end tag, the next end tag in the attacker-controlled WDDX packet retrieves the freed entry (wddx_stack_top) and either reads it (use-after-free at 'if (!ent1->data)') or frees it again (double free at efree(ent1) / efree(ent) in the EL_FIELD arm). A malicious packet such as <data><field></string></field>... instantiates a use-after-free/double-free (heap corruption) in the process deserializing untrusted WDDX input.

evidence.reason: Root cause: when stack->top == 1, the else arm marks the stack done but never removes the entry (no stack->top-- or elements clear, unlike the '> 1' arm), then efree(ent1) frees the entry while stack->elements[0] still references it and stack->top remains 1. Trigger: attacker WDDX packet where the first pushed entry is a NULL-data ST_FIELD entry (state evidenced by this code's own checks 'if (!ent1->data)' and 'ent2->type == ST_FIELD && ent2->data == NULL') followed by a mismatched end tag, e.g. <data><field></string></field>.

Second use of the freed entry: on the next mismatched end tag of the EL_STRING..EL_DATETIME group, wddx_stack_top returns the previously freed elements[0] pointer and 'if (!ent1->data)' reads freed memory (use-after-free); a zero read leads back to efree(ent1) (double free), a non-zero read (Zend MM free-list pointer) turns ent1->data into a wild zval pointer dereferenced further below.

Deterministic double free in the EL_FIELD arm: after the top==1 NULL-data free path leaves the freed entry at elements[0] with top==1, a subsequent </field> end tag retrieves that dangling pointer and efree(ent) frees it a second time, corrupting the heap in the process parsing the attacker-supplied WDDX packet.

assumptions: The not-shown push callback (php_wddx_push_element) creates st_entry elements with data == NULL for <field> tags (ST_FIELD); this state is evidenced by this code's own branches 'if (!ent1->data)' and 'if (ent2->type == ST_FIELD && ent2->data == NULL)' and is treated as attacker-document-driven state per the width-domain rule.
wddx_stack_top returns stack->elements[stack->top-1] when stack->top > 0; the early return 'if (stack->top == 0)' bounds this, so retrieval itself is in-bounds.

expat (standard behavior) invokes the end-element handler once per end tag in document order and parsing continues after stack->done is set; this function never reads stack->done, so subsequent end tags are processed.
limitations: php_base64_decode result (line 38) is consumed without a NULL sentinel check, but the non-strict decoder allocates before decoding, so a NULL return is not instantiable from given code (allocation failure only) - speculative.

A stray </field> pops and efrees whatever entry is on top without zval_ptr_dtor (lines 131-135), leaking ent->data/ent->varname; leak size is roughly proportional to attacker input with no meaningful amplification - robustness/DoS-hardening, not counted.

Calling __wakeup (line 51) on attacker-influenced objects and the EG(scope)/add_property_zval magic-property path (lines 112-114) are by-design PHP unserialization semantics; gadget-based impact depends on classes not shown.
The Z_DELREF_P(ent1->data) before add_property_zval (lines 113-114) refcount transfer could not be proven harmful from this snippet alone.

All allocation and lookup results are sentinel-checked before use.
